[{"state":"Slack/Teams export, Quill Outfitters field-service channel, Tuesday 14 May, 08:06–17:42. People are talking about the North Annex repair, the route board, and what to put in the customer file. The pasted work sheet is included below because everyone keeps referring to it, and because the first summary in the thread is being copied around as though it were the whole story.

08:06 Amara O'Neill: Morning all. I am at the North Annex, not the loading entrance where the map pin keeps sending people. The compressor is quiet now, so at least it is not doing that rattly drum thing it did last Thursday. There are still three crates of insulated panels blocking the service hatch, and the site contact says facilities will move them after the morning delivery. I have the orange tool case, two meters, and the replacement relay. I do not have the long probe; I left it with the van kit, which is apparently in the other van today. If somebody can tell dispatch to stop calling this the East Annex job, that would help. Same street, different building, different ticket.

08:11 Kwame O'Neill: I updated the map pin. It was copied from the East Annex record last month. Nobody needs to drive across the courtyard and ask the bakery where the plant room is again. Also, customer name is Quill Outfitters, not Quill Analytics. Their building manager is not the person who signs the maintenance orders, so don't put her name in the approval field just because she answered the door.

08:14 Dmitri Rahman: I see the work order and the old inspection note. The inspection note says the compressor cycled normally on the visit in February. That does not establish what happened in May. The customer has sent three photos, all taken from the same side, and a video where the unit hums for about six seconds and then stops. Amara, can you check the relay and record the readings before swapping anything? The parts desk needs a reason code, not just “bad noise.”

08:19 Amara O'Neill: Yep. The casing is warm but not alarming. I can get to the relay after the crates move. Customer says the unit serves the fitting-room ventilation, not the store-floor refrigeration. Just recording that because the intake form has the wrong equipment category again. No stock in the unit, no food, no medicine, just the ventilation fan and a dehumidifier. The shop is open, but they have the fitting rooms closed for now.

08:23 Quentin O'Neill: I have the customer email open. It says, “We would like you to inspect the stoppage and restore service if the relay is faulty. Please keep the old relay so our maintenance contractor can see it. We are not asking for money back; we need the unit working before the weekend.” That wording is pretty clear. I am pasting the relevant text into the account timeline too, not into the dispatch notes, so it stays with the customer record.

08:27 Tomasz Moreau: The previous shift left a note saying refund requested. I suspect that note came from a different case. It may have been the East Annex call where the customer returned an unopened fan. I am not deleting anything until we confirm which record it belongs to. The CRM has been blending subject lines when someone replies from the shared mailbox. Please don't infer that this customer asked for a refund just because the word appears in the inherited note.

08:31 Amara O'Neill: I have not opened the relay yet. Site contact found the key for the lower cabinet. The upper panel has a seal from the annual inspection, but I can reach the connector without breaking it. I have photographed the seal and the serial plate. There is a handwritten sticker on the plate saying “relay changed 2023,” but no part number. The unit itself is older than the ventilation fan, according to the building binder, which is not the same as saying every component is old.

08:36 Kwame O'Neill: Service desk says the ticket came through the maintenance portal at 07:51. The form category was “equipment failure,” and the customer selected “repair visit.” There is no selected billing dispute, no credit request, and no “refund” field. It has a free-text box, and the text there is the inspection-and-repair wording Quentin pasted. Keep the original request separate from any later decision we make about charges.

08:42 Dmitri Rahman: Can someone confirm the agreement terms? I remember the annual plan covers labor on listed equipment but not customer-caused damage. The old summary says “parts and labor covered,” which is too broad. We should use the signed schedule, not that summary. I will paste the extracted schedule once I find the right version. There are two files with nearly identical names; one is for Quill Analytics and has a different building list.

08:47 Quentin O'Neill: Found the signed schedule. It lists North Annex compressor V-18, labor included for diagnostic and covered component replacement. It says the customer pays for consumables and for damage caused by unauthorized modification. No evidence of modification so far. The schedule is valid through 30 June. It doesn't say that the customer gets a refund for a service fee, and it doesn't say that any request to repair automatically becomes a refund claim.

08:53 Tomasz Moreau: I am looking at the billing tab. A callout fee of $85 was billed last month for a separate East Annex fan visit. That is probably why somebody attached the refund note. This ticket has no invoice yet. The $85 is not a payment on this North Annex ticket, and it is not a credit balance. Please don't combine the two simply because the customer account is the same.

09:02 Amara O'Neill: Crates moved. The connector looks clean. Meter reading before restart is 24.1 volts at the control input, which is inside the range on the service sheet. Relay clicks once, then the unit stops. I am doing a second reading with the fan disconnected. For the record, the customer watched me take the first reading. They did not ask me to waive anything or return money. They asked whether we could leave the old part in a bag.

09:10 Dmitri Rahman: Please keep the evidence in order. The first reading is not the whole diagnosis. The service sheet gives a normal control range of 22–26 volts, and 24.1 is in range. That alone does not prove the relay is good. The current drops when the fan load is attached, so check the connector and the supply under load. The fact that it ran normally in February is useful history, not a verdict about today's condition.

09:18 Amara O'Neill: Under load I get 19.6 volts at the relay input and 24.0 at the upstream terminal. The connector pin has a dark mark and feels loose. I reseated it once, and the unit ran for forty seconds. Then it stopped again. I did not change the relay yet. Site contact says the unit has been stopping intermittently for about a week, but she has only been on this shift since Monday, so that is her knowledge, not a full service history.

09:24 Kwame O'Neill: The portal export has a line from the customer: “Please do not replace a part until you have told us what failed.” That does not mean they refused repair; it is a request for explanation before parts are installed. The authorized contact is the facilities coordinator. The person messaging us from the store chat is a sales supervisor, helpful but not listed as an approver. I am trying to get the coordinator on the phone.

09:31 Quentin O'Neill: I found the actual refund note in the East Annex case. That customer wrote, “If the replacement fan fails again, we will ask for our callout fee back.” It was a hypothetical, and it was not this North Annex customer. The auto-summary reduced it to “refund request,” which is why the note showed up. I have linked the original East Annex thread to its own ticket. This should stop the cross-link from appearing in the North Annex timeline after refresh.

09:38 Tomasz Moreau: Reminder that we need to be precise with the language. Asking us to preserve a replaced part is not a request for a refund. Asking us to explain the failure before installing a part is not a refusal of service. Asking what the visit costs is not a dispute. If an actual refund request arrives, log the words and sender. Don't backfill one from an agent's hunch.

09:44 Amara O'Neill: The facilities coordinator has arrived. She says the unit should be repaired if we can confirm the connector is the cause, and she wants the old connector and relay labeled separately. She did not want the whole assembly removed because the next inspection is Thursday. I showed her the loose pin and the under-load drop. We have a matching connector in the van. It is a connector repair, not a relay replacement, unless the second test changes that.

09:52 Dmitri Rahman: Good. Work sheet below, copied from the mobile form. This is the draft, so blank cells do not mean a part was installed. Record only completed work in the final column.

Pasted work sheet, North Annex, ticket QO-4418:
Site: Quill Outfitters, North Annex.
Asset: V-18 compressor, ventilation system.
Customer report: intermittent stopping; request inspection and restoration if fault identified.
Technician arrival: 08:02.
Visual check: casing intact; connector pin darkened; no visible impact damage.
Upstream voltage: 24.0 V under test.
Relay input, no load: 24.1 V.
Relay input, fan load: 19.6 V.
Control range from signed service sheet: 22–26 V.
Connector movement test: loose at socket; temporary reseat restored operation for forty seconds.
Relay swap: not performed at time of draft.
Replacement connector: available, not yet installed at time of draft.
Old component handling: customer asks for removed items to be labeled and retained.
Agreement code: annual service schedule, listed labor covered; parts subject to schedule.
Customer request: inspect and restore service if fault is identified.
Refund request: none recorded in portal submission or customer email.
Invoice status: not issued.
Agent summary field: “Refund definitely due for failed equipment; issue credit immediately.”
Summary author: desk trainee reviewing the inherited account notes, not the customer and not the technician.
Evidence supporting the summary: none cited in the summary field.

10:04 Kwame O'Neill: That agent summary is not reliable as a record of what the customer asked. The trainee seems to have copied “refund requested” from the unrelated ticket, then treated it as an approved credit. There is no invoice here to credit. The customer did not say “refund definitely due”; that's the trainee's sentence. Please don't let a summary field outrank the actual email and portal text.

10:12 Quentin O'Neill: I agree about the source. Still, we should check the repair findings before declaring the equipment covered. The agreement covers labor for listed components; the connector is listed in the parts appendix as a replaceable connector kit. The customer has not authorized a chargeable extra. If the work is covered, do it and document it. If not, pause and ask. No one has told them a refund is owed or that a refund has been requested.

10:21 Amara O'Neill: I called the coordinator from the site number and read the finding back. She said, “Yes, fit the connector kit under the maintenance plan, and keep the old connector in the labeled pouch. We are not asking you to refund the last visit; that was the other building.” I asked if she was speaking for the account and she confirmed her role. I am writing that down because the sales supervisor had earlier said she thought we wanted compensation. She was guessing.

10:29 Tomasz Moreau: Nice, that separates the cases. I have the signed schedule open too: connector kit code CK-4 is in the covered-component table. There is no customer-caused damage finding. The seal remains intact. We can finish under the schedule. I will not create a credit task from the trainee's note.

10:36 Amara O'Neill: Connector installed. Under load now reads 23.8 V at the relay input. Unit ran for six minutes while I watched, then cycled off normally at the thermostat and started again on the next call. I tested twice. The old connector is in a bag marked North Annex V-18, date, and ticket. Relay remains installed; it tested normally after the connector repair. I haven't signed the final work order yet because the tablet lost its connection in the basement.

10:44 Dmitri Rahman: The six-minute run is useful but don't write “permanent fix” from one short observation. Say operation restored during test and advise monitoring. The ventilation schedule will cycle it in normal use. Also don't put “refund due” in the diagnosis field. The work is a covered repair under the schedule and the customer asked for the repair. Those are different things from a refund.

10:52 Kwame O'Neill: Customer asked whether the removed connector could be returned to their contractor. That is a property/evidence question, not a money question. I told her we can release the labeled connector after the service record is complete. She said thanks. No one mentioned reimbursement, reversal, or credit in that conversation.

11:03 Quentin O'Neill: A separate thing: our dispatch board says two jobs remain in this district. The River Court fan is tomorrow, not today. The warehouse sent a relay kit to the wrong van, which is why the inventory screen showed zero for this one. That kit is not needed after the connector test. Please don't add it to parts used just to make the warehouse count agree.

11:16 Amara O'Neill: I am at the van finishing the report. The tablet came back. I entered “loose connector pin caused voltage drop under load; replaced connector kit; post-repair voltage 23.8 V; unit cycled normally during observed test.” I entered the customer request as inspect and restore, not refund. The coordinator signed the visit screen. She did not sign the trainee's credit sentence because it was not shown to her.

11:24 Tomasz Moreau: For the customer record, the former visit invoice was East Annex ticket QO-4389, $85 callout fee, no payment dispute in that record either. The customer on that visit was Quill Outfitters, but the building and asset were different. The North Annex ticket QO-4418 has no invoice and no money collected. The repeated company name does not make the tickets interchangeable.

11:37 Dmitri Rahman: I'm closing the diagnosis review. Fault supported by the loose connector and voltage behavior; repair completed with covered kit. Relay was not replaced. There is no evidence of a refund request in the customer's own communications. The unsubstantiated desk verdict has already been marked as an erroneous summary, but keep it visible in the audit history so anyone reviewing the record can see why it was corrected.

12:05 Kwame O'Neill: The coordinator called to confirm the fitting rooms are open. She said the unit has cycled normally since we left. I asked whether she needed a copy of the reading sheet and she said yes. Still no refund request. She was more interested in the labeled old connector than the invoice status, which remains pending because the system batches signed work orders at the end of the day.

12:42 Quentin O'Neill: Audit note: we have three kinds of text in this thread. Customer request: inspect and repair if the fault is identified. Technician evidence: voltage drops at a loose connector and returns to the normal range after replacement. Internal trainee verdict: credit immediately. The first two are supported by the source materials; the third is not. The customer's own clarification expressly distinguishes the other building's visit. This should be enough to repair the summary rather than propagate it.

13:10 Tomasz Moreau: The account dashboard still shows a red “refund” badge because it reads the old inherited summary cache. I have opened a data-fix request. The badge is not a customer statement and it does not create a credit. Please use the portal message and signed visit sheet if somebody asks what was requested. The cache refresh should happen overnight, according to support.

13:26 Amara O'Neill: I checked the connector pouch label one more time because the coordinator wanted the ticket number large enough to read. It says QO-4418, V-18, North Annex. The parts log says one CK-4 kit installed, one old connector retained, zero relay kits used. There are no extra labor minutes beyond the scheduled visit. The job is done; the lingering work is just record cleanup.

14:03 Kwame O'Neill: I spoke to the portal team. Their export confirms the initial submission had “refund request” unchecked. The text box has only the inspect-and-restore sentence. The East Annex request in the other ticket was conditional and came from a different conversation. The auto-summary merged it because both messages arrived from the same shared mailbox address. It is a software problem, not evidence that North Annex asked for money back.

14:29 Dmitri Rahman: One caution: the signed schedule's coverage clause applies to listed components, but it does not promise that every failure is covered regardless of cause. We checked the connector, found no impact mark, and the customer authorized the covered repair. If someone asks about coverage, the evidence supports this connector repair under the plan. If someone asks whether a refund was requested, the answer comes from the customer's messages, not from what we decided to charge.

15:02 Quentin O'Neill: I am reading the customer's follow-up: “Thanks for getting the ventilation back. Please email the visit notes. We will have our own contractor look at the old connector, then dispose of it.” No request for reimbursement. A thumbs-up is not a credit authorization. I have attached that message as a follow-up, and the same customer's line about the old part is in the service notes.

15:40 Tomasz Moreau: The trainee replied to the audit question and says she copied the red badge without opening the original messages. She has withdrawn the sentence “refund definitely due.” It was a recommendation she generated, not a customer quote and not a manager approval. We should retain it only as an audit artifact. The correct record should say no refund request was made on this ticket.

16:18 Amara O'Neill: Just to wrap up my end: no relay change, no invoice reversal, connector kit fitted, test passed, coordinator informed. The unit is ventilation equipment at North Annex. The East Annex fee belongs on the East Annex ticket. The customer's request was for repair, not a refund. I know I have repeated that about five times, but the merged timeline makes it look less obvious than it is.

17:42 Kwame O'Neill: Closing the channel thread. Dispatch has the final report, account support has the cache-fix request, and the site contact has the copy she asked for. If the dashboard keeps saying refund after tomorrow's refresh, route it back to data support rather than making a credit. The source documents are all linked and the customer has not asked for money back.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Decide whether repair is covered.","target":true,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Signed schedule lists V-18 labor and CK-4; loose connector was found and repaired under the plan, contradicting no coverage claim."},{"type":"binary","instruction":"Decide whether refund was requested.","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Customer asked for inspection and repair, expressly denied requesting money back; trainee's credit verdict is contradicted."}]},{"state":"Typed-up notes from a field notebook and pasted spreadsheet, Bluefin Software service visit at the West Glasshouse pump room. Notes compiled by Dmitri Rahman after the visit, with the supervisor's margin comments retained because they were already copied into the shared folder. The language is a bit repetitive; it was written between calls and then transcribed while the van was waiting for a gate code.

Notebook cover: Bluefin Software, field repairs, job BF-7726, West Glasshouse, 22 August. Customer equipment: circulation pump P-6 and its controller. The building contact called it “the little bronze one,” though it is not bronze and there are two other pumps in the room. Use the asset tag, not the nickname. The contact said the greenhouse beds were not in immediate danger because a second pump was running, but the temperature alarms were noisy and the facilities team wanted the failing pump checked before the next scheduled watering cycle.

First page, before arrival: dispatch text at 07:14 said “possible motor failure, customer requests refund.” I wrote that down because dispatch said to preserve the original wording. That text is not necessarily from the customer; dispatch copied it from a service-desk summary. The signed call form is supposed to be in the job packet. I should not treat a heading as a quote until I see the source form. Other work today: a gate sensor at the south entrance, a filter delivery at the east shed, and a controller visit at the adjacent teaching greenhouse. Those are separate stops even though the map uses one pin for the whole property.

07:48 arrival. The site administrator met me at the gate. She pointed out the control room and said the pump stopped twice overnight. Her exact wording, as close as I can remember: “Please diagnose it. If you can fix it within the authorized maintenance scope, go ahead; if you think it needs a motor, call me first because I have to get the project lead to approve that.” She asked me to photograph the tag and leave the old parts in a tray if anything was removed. She did not mention payment or a refund. I did not ask her about the dispatch summary because I wanted to read the order first.

The pump tag reads P-6, serial BFX-60091. The controller is C-14. The service desk had labeled the job P-8, likely because the previous month’s visit at the east shed involved P-8. P-8 has a different serial and a different controller. The customer account is shared across both buildings. I crossed out P-8 on my paper copy and wrote the correct tag. The spreadsheet export later still says P-8 in its top line, so that will need a correction before anyone orders parts.

08:02 visual check: no water on the floor, no obvious burn smell, no loose mounting bolts. The pump housing has light surface discoloration, old but not fresh. The intake strainer is clear enough to see through, though there is a small leaf wedged near one edge. That leaf did not block the flow. I removed it and saved it in the waste bucket, not as a part. The pipes were dry during the check. The control display said “intermittent stop,” not “motor fault.” I took a photo showing the display and the asset label in the same frame.

08:11 I checked the local isolation switch and found it in the on position. The facilities administrator said no one had switched it off. That is her report, not something I can independently verify. The power indicator was steady. The pump did not start on the first manual command. On the second command the relay clicked and the pump ran for twelve seconds, then stopped. I recorded the event rather than calling it a failure before testing the controller. A single stop can have several causes, and the job packet says to distinguish motor overload from controller interruption.

08:17 reading at the incoming supply: 230 volts, stable during the short run. The service sheet gives an acceptable range of 220 to 240 volts. The controller output dropped briefly when the pump stopped, while the incoming supply stayed stable. I repeated the test, same behavior. The motor casing was not hot. The breaker did not trip. The controller relay looked worn at the contact surface, but appearance alone does not prove it caused the stop. I photographed the relay and left the cover on until I confirmed authorization.

08:26 I called the administrator. I described the relay behavior and said a controller relay module might be needed. She said the maintenance plan allows ordinary control-module parts up to the listed scope, but any motor replacement needs project approval. I said I would check the signed schedule. She confirmed that she could authorize a listed repair while she was on site. She again asked me to retain the removed module so their own maintenance lead could inspect it. No mention of a credit, invoice, refund, or compensation.

Pasted spreadsheet extract, job BF-7726, draft worksheet:
Header as received: Asset P-8, West Glasshouse, controller C-14.
Correct asset per photo: P-6, serial BFX-60091.
Arrival: 07:48.
Incoming supply under run: 230 V.
Acceptable incoming range: 220–240 V.
Controller output during stop: brief drop.
Motor casing: not hot.
Breaker: not tripped.
Relay contact surface: worn appearance; causal status not yet confirmed at draft time.
Controller module removed: no, at draft time.
Customer authorization: ordinary listed scope, verbal confirmation from site administrator.
Motor replacement: not authorized; not proposed after test.
Invoice: none generated for this visit at draft time.
Customer request copied from original form: “diagnose intermittent stopping; repair within plan if possible; call before motor replacement.”
Desk summary verdict: “Customer has established a refund entitlement; return the previous service payment.”
Source for verdict: supervisor note carried forward from earlier ticket; no customer quotation attached.
Prior payment shown in account view: $120, ticket BF-7602, East Shed P-8, paid by account office.
Current ticket charge: no charge posted at time of worksheet.

The line about $120 is easy to misread. It belongs to BF-7602, a completed filter-control visit at the East Shed. It is not a payment for this job. I include this because the desk verdict mentions returning “the previous service payment” without identifying a visit, and the shared account makes the figure visible in the same screen. The work order for today has no charge posted and there is no current payment to reverse. The customer may have had conversations about other work; this notebook only captures the West Glasshouse visit.

08:44 I opened the signed maintenance schedule from the job packet. It names West Glasshouse P-6 and C-14. A listed controller relay module is included in ordinary maintenance parts. It excludes motor assemblies unless a project lead signs a separate approval. The schedule says nothing about refunds or automatic credits for intermittent equipment problems. It does say to stop work and contact the administrator if the observed fault differs materially from the approved scope. The relay module seems within scope; a motor would not be. I read the relevant section aloud to the administrator, who confirmed she had the same schedule on her tablet.

08:53 I tested the relay module connection with the pump isolated. One contact was rough and had a small pit. The cable insulation was intact. After reconnecting, I ran the pump through three starts. It stopped twice, and both stops followed the same output drop. I cannot prove the contact alone caused every stop, but the repeated controller-side drop and the visibly worn contact are consistent. The upstream supply remained steady each time. The motor did not show a hot casing or a tripped breaker. I did not write “motor failed.”

09:06 I explained the finding. The administrator said, “Replace the listed relay module, please. Don't replace the motor unless you call me and I get approval.” She was clear and authorized the module. I wrote her name in the authorization field and took a photo of the signed job screen. She asked again that the removed piece be set aside. There was no request to reimburse the earlier visit; she said the east-shed payment question was being handled by their accounts office and was unrelated to this call.

09:14 Before removal, I checked the module label against the parts list: RM-14, revision C. The van stock had RM-14 revision D, approved as a compatible replacement in the Bluefin parts sheet. The stock sheet says revision D supersedes C, same connector layout, no wiring changes. I verified the pin layout against the printed diagram rather than relying on the box color. The first box in the van was RM-41, a different relay for the gate sensor, so I left it in the bin. The correct module came from the sealed pouch in the second compartment.

09:22 I isolated the pump, removed the relay module, placed it in a bag labeled BF-7726, P-6, old RM-14 C, and installed the replacement. No wires were cut. The module sat flush and the cover closed without pressure. The administrator watched and said she appreciated the label being readable. I did not remove the motor or open the pump casing. The old module is on the administrator's workbench in the labeled bag, as requested.

09:31 First test after replacement: pump started immediately and ran for two minutes. Output stayed steady. I stopped it with the controller and restarted it; it ran another two minutes. I repeated once more after waiting a minute. Three starts, three normal runs. That is evidence the repair worked during the test; it is not a guarantee the pump can never stop again. I recorded the measured supply as 230 volts and did not alter the acceptable range in the worksheet.

09:39 Administrator said she would tell the greenhouse crew to watch the next normal cycle. She asked whether we had charged the $120 already visible in the account view. I explained that it was a prior East Shed ticket and nothing had been posted for today's visit. She said, “Good, I don't want anyone moving money around on this job. I only needed the P-6 checked.” I wrote the sentence down because the old desk summary seemed to be mixing the service visits. She did not ask for a refund on BF-7726.

Margin note in red, written by shift supervisor Quentin Delgado before the field notes were uploaded: “Refund approved—customer complaint confirmed. Close as credit owed, do not spend more time on technical checks.” It is a verdict, not a quotation. Quentin did not attend the site and his note contains no mention of the signed form, the asset tag, or the test results. It appears to have been copied from a prior ticket because the next line says “P-8 filter controller,” which is the East Shed asset. I left the margin note in place so the office can see what needs review, but I did not use it to change the field findings.

10:02 I called the service desk from the van. The person answering first said the system showed a customer refund claim. I asked them to open the original intake rather than the condensed summary. The intake text was exactly the diagnose-and-repair request recorded above. The box labeled refund was not selected. The supervisor's verdict remains in the history because the system does not let field staff erase it; the service desk said they would flag it for correction. I am writing down this call as an internal clarification, not as a customer statement.

10:16 The administrator signed the completed service record. The record lists the correct asset P-6, module RM-14 revision D installed, old module retained, motor untouched, and three successful starts. It does not include a refund request. The handwritten signature is clear. The administrator asked me to email the service note to her and the maintenance lead. She also asked that the East Shed payment question stay with the accounts office. It is useful context but not part of today's repair authorization.

10:28 The spreadsheet was refreshed after synchronization. It now shows P-6 in the corrected asset field, but the original header still has P-8. I put a note next to it: “Legacy header from dispatch; see verified tag photo.” I did not delete the original value because the audit trail should show why the correction was needed. A parts picker looking only at the first row might order the wrong module, so the corrected field needs to be prominent. The service desk says it will lock the asset number after the work order is closed.

10:41 I checked the controller display again. No fault code was present. The pump had been off for about ten minutes and started normally on command. Supply remained 230 volts. I did not run it longer because the greenhouse schedule had to resume and the administrator said the crew would observe the next cycle. There was no leak, unusual vibration, or smell. I noted that the leaf had been removed from the intake edge, but the strainer was not blocked and that was not the cause documented for the intermittent stops.

11:03 Office chat from the desk: “Supervisor says refund is approved. Can field tech confirm amount?” I replied that no amount was charged on BF-7726, and the only $120 shown is attached to BF-7602 at the East Shed. I also said that the customer did not ask for money back in the site conversation or original form. The office may review the prior ticket separately, but the field visit does not establish that the previous work was defective. The supervisor's note is not evidence of a customer request or a payment on this ticket.

11:19 The administrator emailed: “Thanks for sorting the relay. We will monitor P-6 today. Please send the final report to the maintenance lead. The prior East Shed invoice is a separate accounts matter; no need to make a credit for this West Glasshouse visit.” I forwarded the email into the ticket. That is the latest written statement from the customer contact. She does not want a credit for this visit. The note about accounts is not an instruction to refund the East Shed fee either; it says that matter is separate and is being handled by their accounts office.

11:46 Service desk reply says the refund badge came from a bulk import of supervisor notes during last week's queue cleanup. Several cases had the same template phrase “refund approved—customer complaint confirmed.” The desk is checking those records against original forms. They have not yet changed the badge on BF-7726. I told them the underlying source documents are linked and asked that the badge remain annotated as disputed rather than be treated as an actual payment instruction.

12:08 In the customer-facing report I wrote: “Diagnosed intermittent controller output drop. Replaced listed relay module RM-14 revision C with approved revision D, under the signed maintenance schedule. Pump started and ran normally in three observed tests. Motor not replaced; no motor approval was requested or required after diagnosis. Removed module retained for customer.” The report does not say a refund is due or that one was requested. I sent it to the administrator and copied the maintenance lead, as requested.

12:27 A second office message asked if we should issue a credit because “the supervisor already approved it.” I replied that approval recorded in a margin is not enough to establish an amount paid or a customer request. The customer explicitly separated the East Shed account question from this job and said not to move money on this job. If the office believes there is a separate account issue, it needs to inspect BF-7602 on its own evidence. I am not deciding that older matter here.

13:05 The greenhouse crew sent a short update: P-6 completed its scheduled cycle with no stop. This is a customer report, not another instrument reading. The administrator said they will observe through the afternoon. I added the update, without changing the diagnosis. The module remains in the labeled bag and the crew knows not to discard it. I did not ask them whether they want money returned, since that was already clear and is not needed to finish the service record.

13:32 The accounting panel now shows no current balance for BF-7726. It still shows the $120 payment under BF-7602 and has a warning that the account is shared. There is no credit transaction against either job. The supervisor's phrase “credit owed” has not created a credit entry; it is only a note. I am glad the interface makes that distinction, though it is not obvious from the red badge on the queue screen.

14:10 I compared the original form image with the text export. The image shows the “refund” checkbox empty and the customer request in the free-text field. The text export had omitted the checkbox state, which may have encouraged the summary writer to assume a claim. The actual scan is attached now. The handwritten margin on the scan says “P-6 / intermittent stop” and is initialed by the administrator. It does not say refund. I am not including the office-generated verdict in the customer report.

14:44 The parts coordinator confirmed that revision D is an approved replacement for revision C. She asked whether the RM-41 from the first van compartment was used. It was not. The installed part code is RM-14D and the serial sticker has been added to the final worksheet. This closes the parts question. It does not affect the question of what the customer asked for; the original intake and follow-up email answer that separately.

15:21 Quentin Delgado replied to the audit thread: “I used the prior ticket template and had not checked the attached form. I withdraw the refund-approved note for BF-7726. Please preserve it in history as a mistaken carry-over, not as a customer instruction.” That correction is helpful. The note remains visible, but it no longer represents the supervisor's current position. The contemporaneous customer record and the test data support the repair entry.

15:48 I received a call from the maintenance lead. He asked whether the pump motor had been replaced and whether the customer had requested a credit. I said no motor was replaced, and no credit was requested for this visit. He confirmed that he only wanted the old relay kept until his next inspection. He did not ask for a refund on the prior East Shed work; he said their accounts team would look at that invoice independently. I wrote the call summary with the caller and subject so it will not be merged with the original intake.

16:12 The service desk fixed the asset alias from P-8 to P-6 and put a warning on the shared account: verify building and asset before copying old summaries. They have not removed the supervisor's original red note, per audit policy. Instead, the status now reads “withdrawn—wrong ticket template,” and the refund badge is removed from BF-7726. The older East Shed record is still open for its own accounts review and is not part of this closure.

16:38 Final check of the notebook: all technical entries are in local time; the first arrival was 07:48; the supply reading was 230 volts and the stated range 220–240; no arithmetic is needed beyond confirming that 230 falls between 220 and 240. I have not claimed a motor fault, a charge, a payment, or a refund. I have recorded what was tested, what was replaced, what the customer authorized, and what they asked us to send afterward. The retained module is on the administrator's workbench, not in our van.

17:06 I emailed the final report and the controller photo. The administrator replied “Received, thank you.” She said the crew will observe one more cycle tomorrow and contact us if the stop returns. That is a plan for monitoring, not a present report that the repair failed. There is no additional work authorized. The service ticket is ready to close once office support links the corrected spreadsheet and scanned form.

17:24 Closing note for the file: the field evidence is a controller-side drop under repeated starts, worn relay contact, stable incoming supply, and normal observed runs after the listed relay module was replaced. The paperwork evidence is a signed scope, an unchecked refund box, a repair request, and a follow-up email saying no credit is needed for this visit. The internal “refund approved” sentence was a copied verdict that its author withdrew after reviewing the source. Do not treat the red wording as stronger than the underlying records.

17:39 Office confirmation: attachments linked, old module retained, asset corrected, no current invoice and no credit transaction. The prior $120 remains on BF-7602 only. The West Glasshouse ticket can now be closed as completed repair. [{"state":"Tidewater Outfitters Field Service Dispute File
Compiled from service terms, dispatch notes, a Teams thread, customer review, and repair records. The customer is furious, and the staff are equally tired of repeating themselves. This file is an internal record, not a decision. Statements marked “draft verdict” are opinions, not verified findings.

SECTION 1 — SERVICE TERMS EXCERPT

The following terms were in force when the service visit was booked. They are reproduced here because several people in the thread quote them incompletely. The terms apply to repair visits for equipment purchased from Tidewater Outfitters, unless a written job confirmation states a narrower or more generous condition. A signed job confirmation takes precedence over a general brochure, but a technician’s informal comment does not amend either document. Customers may request a copy of the confirmation from the service desk.

1. Booking and arrival. A customer may book a service window rather than an exact arrival time. A window is a range for arrival, not a promise that the technician will remain at the site for the whole range. If Tidewater expects to miss the booked window, dispatch should contact the customer when practical and offer a new window. A missed window does not by itself establish that a repair was completed, that a customer accepted a charge, or that a refund is due. The service desk reviews what work was authorized and performed before deciding any billing question.

2. Diagnostic fee. The standard diagnostic visit costs $85. The fee covers travel within the listed local zone and the technician’s initial inspection. It is charged when the technician arrives and performs an inspection, even if the customer declines further repair. It is not charged if the technician never arrives, if dispatch cancels before arrival, or if the customer has a written confirmation explicitly waiving it. A request for a visit is not the same as authorization for a part replacement. The technician must quote additional work and receive approval before performing it, except for a narrowly described safety action needed to prevent immediate harm. The file must document that exception.

3. Estimates and authorization. Estimates identify labor, parts, and any applicable tax separately. An estimate is not a final invoice. The customer may accept or reject it. A technician should record the customer’s decision, including a decision made by phone, before proceeding. A customer’s signature acknowledging receipt of an estimate means only that the estimate was received; it does not mean the estimate was accepted. If an estimate is revised, the revised amount must be approved. A note that says “customer aware” is not sufficient evidence of approval on its own.

4. Repair warranty. A part installed by Tidewater is covered for 90 calendar days from installation, for the same reported fault, provided the customer has not altered the part or caused damage through misuse. A warranty visit addressing the same fault has no new diagnostic fee. The warranty does not cover unrelated faults. The date of installation, the part number, and the reported fault should be recorded on the work order. A customer may still ask for a paid repair for a different problem during a warranty visit, but the technician must separate the tasks and quote any chargeable work.

5. Cancellation and refunds. A customer who prepays for a visit that is cancelled by Tidewater before a technician arrives is entitled to a refund of the prepaid visit amount. A customer who cancels after a technician has arrived may owe the diagnostic fee if an inspection was performed. A refund request is reviewed against the payment record, visit record, and job confirmation. The terms do not promise an automatic refund merely because a customer is dissatisfied, nor do they prohibit a refund where Tidewater made a billing error. A service manager may authorize a goodwill refund, but the reason should be stated in the record.

6. Records and disagreements. The work order, dispatch log, payment record, and customer communications should be read together. An employee’s summary or draft conclusion may be mistaken. If a draft conclusion conflicts with the underlying records, the verified records govern the review. Staff should not treat a customer’s angry wording as proof of a technical fault, but they also should not dismiss a complaint merely because it is angry. The repair desk should state what it can verify, what remains disputed, and what action follows.

SECTION 2 — JOB CONFIRMATION AND ORIGINAL BOOKING

Customer: Farid Rahman. Equipment: portable cold-display cabinet, model TC-4. Service location: Tidewater Outfitters’ leased receiving room. Booked through the service desk on 14 June. The customer reported that the cabinet’s fan made a rattling sound and that the temperature display sometimes blinked. The booking was for a diagnostic visit, not for a predetermined replacement part. The service desk quoted the standard $85 diagnostic fee and told Farid that additional work would require an estimate and approval.

The booking screen includes this plain-language confirmation: “You are booking inspection only. The technician will assess the reported issue. If repair requires additional parts or labor, the technician will give you a separate estimate. You can say no to that work. The $85 diagnostic charge applies when the technician arrives and performs an inspection. If Tidewater cancels before arrival, any prepaid visit charge will be returned.” Farid clicked “confirm booking.” The payment record shows a card authorization for $85, followed by a captured payment on the day of the visit. There is no other payment on the account for this job.

Dispatch assigned the visit for 18 June, arrival window 10:00 a.m. to noon. At 9:42 a.m., dispatch sent a text saying the technician was on the way. The GPS arrival record is 10:36 a.m. The site sign-in sheet also records the technician’s arrival at 10:38 a.m. Farid later wrote that the appointment was “basically the whole morning” and that the lateness was unacceptable. The dispatch record shows no cancellation. The customer did not request that the technician leave before inspection.

The technician, Lio, recorded an inspection from 10:45 a.m. to 11:12 a.m. The note says the fan housing was loose, the fan blade turned freely, and the blinking display was reproduced once when the cabinet was restarted. The technician photographed the housing and recorded the serial number. The inspection itself is not disputed in the work record. Farid says he was present and complained throughout. The technician says Farid was angry about the arrival time but allowed the inspection to continue.

At 11:18 a.m., Lio prepared estimate E-441 for a replacement fan assembly and 40 minutes of labor, total $212.40 including tax. The estimate screen records “presented; customer declined.” A paper copy is attached to the work order, with Farid’s initials next to “estimate received.” The acceptance box is blank. No fan assembly was installed that day. The parts inventory shows no issue of a fan assembly against this job, and the technician’s closing note says, “No repair authorized; left existing fan in place.”

An internal draft from the first-line billing clerk says: “Verdict: charge is improper; customer was billed for a repair that never happened, so refund the visit.” This is a draft assessment, not a transaction record. Another clerk has written beneath it, “Seems obvious. He got no repair and waited around; just reverse it.” Neither note cites a rule or confirms that the $85 was a repair charge. The captured payment description is “diagnostic visit,” not “fan assembly” or “repair labor.” The signed booking confirmation identifies the same fee and the conditions for charging it.

SECTION 3 — DISPATCH AND WORK-ORDER EXTRACTS

14 June, 3:06 p.m. — Booking opened by service desk. Reported issue: intermittent display blink; rattling fan. Diagnostic visit booked, $85 disclosed. Customer asks whether the technician can bring a fan. Agent says the technician can assess and may quote a part if needed; no part is promised before diagnosis.

14 June, 3:11 p.m. — Payment authorization entered. Status: pending. Amount: $85.00. Job note: customer understands inspection fee. No note of a fee waiver.

18 June, 9:42 a.m. — Automated dispatch text: “Your technician is travelling to the site. Current expected arrival is within your window.” No reply recorded.

18 June, 10:36 a.m. — GPS geofence arrival. 10:38 a.m. — Building sign-in. 10:45 a.m. — Inspection begins. 11:12 a.m. — Inspection ends. Finding: loosened fan housing; intermittent display blink reproduced after restart. No safety hazard recorded.

18 June, 11:18 a.m. — Estimate E-441 generated: fan assembly $148.00; labor $48.00; tax $16.40; total $212.40. Customer initials show receipt of estimate. Approval field blank. Work-order action: declined. Technician note: no parts installed; diagnostic completed.

18 June, 11:27 a.m. — Payment capture: $85.00 diagnostic visit. Payment system matches the amount disclosed in booking. No additional charge captured. The payment system does not label this as a repair charge.

19 June, 8:14 a.m. — Customer called, angry. Said the service window was missed and the cabinet was still rattling. Asked for the $85 back and said he would not pay for “a useless visit.” Agent created complaint ticket but did not promise a refund. Call note: customer says no repair was performed; agent explains that the payment is the diagnostic fee and that a manager will review the complaint.

19 June, 9:02 a.m. — Complaint ticket routed to service manager. Draft recommendation entered by first-line clerk: “Refund because no repair completed.” Status: unapproved. The draft does not mention the fee terms or work-order timestamps.

20 June, 2:31 p.m. — Manager requested review of booking confirmation, work order, and payment record. No refund action entered. Ticket status: under review.

The dispatch system also contains unrelated routine details that were mistakenly pasted into the review packet. On 17 June, a different customer’s water-pump visit was moved from 9:00 to 11:00. On 18 June, another technician replaced a door latch at Harbor Foods. Those entries are not associated with Farid’s job, model TC-4, or payment. Their presence does not change the arrival, inspection, estimate, or payment records above.

The file’s first-line summary says, “No service happened, so the fee should be reversed.” That wording is inaccurate in a specific way: no repair happened, but the records show that the paid diagnostic service did happen. The distinction matters under the terms. The arrival, completed inspection, and captured diagnostic fee are independently recorded. A reviewer should not convert “no repair” into “no visit,” and should not convert “no visit” into “refund due.”

SECTION 4 — TEAMS THREAD, 20 JUNE

Mara, dispatch lead, 9:06 a.m.: I have read the complaint. Farid is furious, and frankly I understand why he is frustrated about the wait. But the arrival scan is 10:36, inside the 10-to-noon window. We should not tell him the technician never came.

Ivo, billing clerk, 9:12 a.m.: The draft verdict from yesterday says “refund: repair not performed.” That sounds right to me because the cabinet still rattles. If the customer did not receive the fix, why keep his money?

Mara, dispatch lead, 9:15 a.m.: The $85 was not the fan repair price. It was the diagnostic visit price. Estimate was $212.40 and he did not approve it. Those are different charges. Please stop describing the $85 as payment for the replacement assembly.

Neri, service manager, 9:21 a.m.: I checked the booking screen and work order. He accepted the $85 inspection terms. Lio arrived and inspected the cabinet. No part was installed because Farid declined the separate estimate. The first-line verdict is not a verified finding. It is a conclusion that mixes up a repair charge and a diagnostic charge.

Ivo, billing clerk, 9:24 a.m.: But the customer says, “I paid for service and got nothing.” He is not wrong that the problem remains. I am not saying the estimate was approved; I am saying a customer can feel charged for nothing when the machine still rattles.

Neri, service manager, 9:28 a.m.: The complaint is valid as a complaint about the unresolved fault and the experience. That does not establish a billing error. The policy says the inspection fee applies when the technician arrives and performs the inspection. Both happened. The record says the only captured amount was $85, exactly the disclosed diagnostic fee.

Sela, field supervisor, 9:34 a.m.: I reviewed the photos. The fan housing was loose. The tech wrote that the display blink was reproduced. Farid declined the repair estimate. There is no part issue record. We can offer another quote or explain the warranty does not apply, since nothing was installed, but we should not pretend we installed a fan.

Ivo, billing clerk, 9:39 a.m.: The draft recommendation is still sitting in the ticket. Someone should mark it wrong. I copied it from the earlier summary without checking the underlying records. It says “repair billed; no repair,” but the transaction says “diagnostic visit.”

Neri, service manager, 9:42 a.m.: I will mark the draft unverified and correct the summary. Angry customer does not mean automatically right about the payment type, and our own draft does not become fact just because it is in the ticket. The facts support keeping the diagnostic fee under the terms, while separately acknowledging the repair was declined and the problem remains.

Mara, dispatch lead, 9:46 a.m.: Please include the arrival time and the inspection record in the reply. Do not write that he got the repair. He did not. Also do not write that no service visit happened. It did.

Ivo, billing clerk, 9:51 a.m.: Got it. I will remove “refund approved.” I can write, “The diagnostic visit took place, the separate estimate was declined, and the $85 payment is the diagnostic fee.” I still think we should consider goodwill because he is angry, but that is a discretionary decision, not an automatic refund rule.

Neri, service manager, 10:03 a.m.: Correct. Goodwill could be considered, but no one has approved it. The current billing decision is based on the written terms and verified records. Keep the distinction clear.

The thread includes a copied line from a training channel: “If a customer says the repair failed, reverse the whole charge.” That line was posted by an employee as an example of a bad shortcut, not as a policy instruction. The actual terms say to review the payment type and visit record. Another message, pasted from a different job, reads, “Customer did not arrive; technician left.” It refers to a no-show in a different service ticket and is not about Farid. The current job contains a building sign-in and GPS arrival.

SECTION 5 — CUSTOMER REVIEW AND PUBLIC RESPONSE DRAFT

Farid posted this review on 21 June: “Brilliant service, if the goal is to make a person wait all morning and leave with the same rattling box. I booked a repair, got a late tech, and then got handed a giant quote. Nice little trick: charge me for showing up, call it ‘diagnosis,’ and leave me with a broken cabinet. I absolutely love paying for nothing. Don’t use them unless you enjoy being treated like an ATM.”

The review uses praise sarcastically. Farid is plainly dissatisfied. His reference to “a repair” is how he describes his expectation, not proof that the booking included an approved repair. The booking record says inspection only; the technician’s estimate was separate and was not accepted. His statement that the cabinet remained faulty is consistent with the work order. His statement that the technician was “late” conflicts with the recorded arrival inside the booked window, although the customer may reasonably feel that the wait was long. The $85 was not the “giant quote”; the estimate was $212.40 and was not charged.

A communications draft written by a staff member reads: “Verdict: the review is false; Farid received no service and is trying to get a free repair.” That draft is also unverified and overstates what the evidence establishes. Farid did receive a diagnostic inspection, but there is no evidence he obtained a repair or that he is trying to obtain one without paying. The review is angry and sarcastic, but the records still need to be described accurately. A second draft says, “He was charged $212.40 for a fan.” The transaction record contradicts that claim: $212.40 was the estimate, while the captured payment was $85.

Suggested factual response, not yet posted: “We are sorry the visit was frustrating and that the cabinet’s fault remains unresolved. Our record shows the technician arrived during the booked window and completed the diagnostic inspection. The $85 charge was the disclosed inspection fee; the separate $212.40 repair estimate was not accepted and was not charged. We can arrange a further discussion of repair options.” The customer has not replied to this draft. There is no record of a goodwill refund being authorized.

SECTION 6 — BILLING RECONCILIATION

Account lookup: Farid Rahman, service ticket TW-1846, equipment TC-4. Payment method on file: card ending in fictional digits 4408. Authorization amount: $85.00. Capture amount: $85.00. Reversal amount: $0.00. Refund amount: $0.00. Additional capture: none. The processor description says “diagnostic visit.” The technician’s estimate is an estimate record, not a payment record. The estimate total includes $148.00 for the fan assembly, $48.00 for labor, and $16.40 tax. Those components sum to $212.40, but the estimate was declined and no corresponding payment was taken.

The clerk’s spreadsheet has a column called “customer paid for repair?” and a value of “yes.” The clerk later explained that this was a mistaken shorthand for “customer paid for a service visit.” The spreadsheet’s own amount column says $85.00, not $212.40, and the booking terms call that amount the diagnostic charge. An audit note says the spreadsheet should not be relied upon to identify the kind of service purchased when the underlying transaction description is available.

The complaint record has a separate field, “repair completed?” Its value is “no.” That field is correct. It does not say “visit completed?” The visit field says “yes.” A manager’s comment, copied into a summary box, says “No repair = no service = refund.” This is a planted conclusion and not a rule in the service terms. It conflicts with the separate visit and repair fields and with the diagnostic-fee clause.

The repair desk is allowed to offer a new appointment, explain the estimate, or submit a goodwill request. None of those steps changes the historical payment record. The customer may decline any future work. If a later visit is booked for the same issue after a part has been installed, the 90-day part warranty would be relevant; no part was installed in this visit, so no installation warranty started. The terms do not say that an unresolved fault automatically erases a properly charged diagnostic visit.

SECTION 7 — QUALITY REVIEW CHECKLIST

Reviewer: Wanjiru Moreau, service quality coordinator. Review date: 22 June. Scope: verify whether the complaint packet accurately identifies the type of payment, the visit outcome, and any entitlement stated in the service terms. This review is not a judgment about whether the customer should have been happier, whether the technician should have arrived earlier within the window, or whether the quoted repair was good value.

Question: Did the technician attend? Finding: yes. GPS and sign-in agree. The window was 10:00 a.m. to noon; recorded arrival was 10:36 a.m. The customer’s complaint says it felt like a long wait, but the record does not show a missed window.

Question: Was an inspection performed? Finding: yes. Work order records inspection from 10:45 to 11:12 a.m., photographs, and diagnostic notes. No party disputes that the technician inspected the unit.

Question: Was the proposed fan repair approved? Finding: no. The estimate was presented and initialed as received. The acceptance field is blank, the technician recorded that it was declined, and no fan assembly was installed or issued from inventory.

Question: What was paid? Finding: $85.00, described by the booking and payment records as the diagnostic visit fee. The $212.40 amount was a separate estimate and was not captured.

Question: Does the quoted refund clause apply? Finding: no automatic refund is established by the records. The clause requires a prepaid visit cancelled by Tidewater before arrival. The technician arrived and performed the inspection. A manager may consider goodwill, but no such authorization is present.

An earlier reviewer typed “Customer is right: full refund, since no repair was made.” This sentence is present in the packet because it was part of the draft history. The quality coordinator marked it “not supported as a statement about the fee terms.” It is possible to agree that no repair was made while disagreeing with the conclusion that the visit fee must be refunded. The conclusion must be tested against the actual transaction and rule, not repeated as a verdict.

The records do not establish that Farid was charged for an unapproved part, that the technician failed to attend, or that the diagnostic service was waived. They do establish that the customer remains dissatisfied, that the unit’s reported problem was not repaired, and that the repair estimate was declined. These are separate facts and should remain separate in any response. A fair account can acknowledge the unresolved fault without mislabeling the payment.

SECTION 8 — APPENDIX: ROUTINE DISPATCH AUDIT

This appendix is included because the original export placed several nearby tickets beside the disputed job. Each row below is a separate service activity. Similar words such as “fan,” “inspection,” and “refund” do not mean the records belong to the same customer. Only ticket TW-1846 concerns Farid and the TC-4 cabinet.

Ticket TW-1839, 17 June. Customer: fictional café operator. Equipment: ice maker. Appointment window: 8:00–10:00. Technician arrival: 8:24. Diagnostic fee: $85. Repair estimate: $96. Customer approved a drain cleaning. This is a different ticket and is not evidence about Farid’s payment or equipment.

Ticket TW-1841, 17 June. Customer: fictional property manager. Equipment: loading door. Appointment was rescheduled before dispatch. No technician arrived. Prepaid amount: $85. Refund: $85. This is an example of a cancelled visit, not a record of ticket TW-1846.

Ticket TW-1843, 18 June. Customer: fictional shop operator. Equipment: display cooler. A different technician recorded a fan noise. The customer accepted a $176 repair estimate, and a fan part was installed. The $176 capture belongs to that other customer. It does not show that Farid accepted the $212.40 estimate.

Ticket TW-1846, 18 June. Customer: Farid Rahman. Equipment: TC-4 portable cold-display cabinet. Arrival 10:36; inspection completed; estimate declined; no part installed; $85 diagnostic fee captured. This is the controlling record for the questions in this file.

Ticket TW-1848, 18 June. Customer: fictional restaurant manager. Equipment: refrigerator thermostat. Arrival was outside the window after dispatch notified the customer. The customer accepted a revised appointment. No refund decision appears. This row has no connection to Farid.

Ticket TW-1850, 19 June. Customer: fictional homeowner. Equipment: washer pump. Customer cancelled before the technician was dispatched. A prepaid fee was returned under the cancellation clause. This record does not mean every dissatisfied customer receives a refund.

The dispatch export’s header says “18 June service calls.” A clerk mistakenly treated all rows below the header as one multi-item job. The audit corrected that reading. A header groups records by date; it does not combine their customers, equipment, estimates, or transactions. The same caution applies to the pasted spreadsheet: a nearby $212.40 estimate or another customer’s refund is not evidence of a payment in Farid’s account.

SECTION 9 — APPENDIX: INTERNAL EMAILS

From: Lio, field technician. To: Service desk. Date: 18 June, 12:02 p.m. Subject: TC-4 visit. “Arrived in window. Fan housing loose and display blinked on restart. Offered estimate for fan assembly. Customer did not authorize replacement. Left unit with existing fan. Customer upset with wait, said he expected the repair to be included. I explained booking was diagnostic only.”

From: Ivo, billing clerk. To: Neri, service manager. Date: 19 June, 9:01 a.m. Subject: Refund? “I entered a preliminary recommendation before checking the work order. I assumed the payment was for a repair because the complaint says ‘I paid for service.’ I now see the charge is the diagnostic fee. Please do not treat my first note as confirmed.”

From: Neri, service manager. To: Ivo, billing clerk. Date: 19 June, 9:14 a.m. Subject: Re: Refund? “Thanks for correcting the record. We can review a goodwill request separately. The current evidence does not support saying the customer paid for a part or that Tidewater cancelled before arrival. Please use precise wording.”

From: Customer service agent. To: Farid Rahman. Date: 19 June, 10:12 a.m. Subject: We received your complaint. “We have received your request to review the $85 charge. The service manager is checking the booking, visit, and payment records. We have not yet approved a refund. We understand you remain unhappy that the cabinet was not repaired.”

From: Farid Rahman. To: Customer service agent. Date: 19 June, 10:19 a.m. Subject: Re: We received your complaint. “Of course you have not approved it. You charged me for a person to look at a broken thing, then left it broken. I do not accept your explanation that this is different from charging for nothing. I want my money back.”

From: Customer service agent. To: Neri, service manager. Date: 19 June, 10:26 a.m. Subject: Customer reply. “Customer clearly wants a refund. He does not agree with our distinction. I have not told him the fee is refundable.”

The emails establish the customer’s request and dissatisfaction. They do not change what was booked, what work was performed, or what amount was captured. A request for a refund is not itself proof that the terms require one. Conversely, the existence of a policy does not justify ignoring a customer’s complaint; the company should still provide a clear explanation and consider any discretionary remedy under its process.

SECTION 10 — APPENDIX: DOCUMENT CONTROL AND REVIEW NOTES

The file contains three statements that look like final conclusions but are not verified findings. The first says “refund because no repair”; it was entered by a billing clerk before reviewing the work order. The second says “review is false”; it was written in a communications draft and makes claims beyond the evidence. The third says “charge is correct, no further action”; it was typed into a temporary note but does not address the customer’s unresolved equipment issue. None of these statements should be treated as a substitute for comparing the records with the terms.

For this review, verified findings are limited to matters directly supported by the booking confirmation, dispatch record, work order, estimate, and payment record. Those records consistently show an $85 diagnostic appointment, attendance within the booked window, completion of an inspection, presentation and rejection of a separate estimate, no installation, and a captured $85 diagnostic fee. The customer’s own messages also consistently show that he is angry, believes the charge was unfair, and requests repayment. The review can report both sets of facts without adopting either side’s unsupported phrasing.

A staff member added the sentence “The customer got a free repair” to a draft response. That is plainly wrong: no repair was performed and no repair payment was captured. Another staff member wrote “Tidewater took $212.40.” That is also wrong: $212.40 was the unaccepted estimate, and the payment record shows $85. The fact that both wrong claims appear in internal notes does not make either one true. The reviewer should use the source records, not the loudest or most recent summary.

No written confirmation waives the diagnostic fee. No record says dispatch cancelled before arrival. No record says the technician failed to inspect the unit. No record shows approval for the fan assembly. No record shows a refund or goodwill credit. The payment record is complete for this job and shows one capture only. The estimate remains an unaccepted quote. The work order remains a diagnostic visit with repair declined.

The service terms allow a manager to authorize a goodwill refund, but permission to consider a refund is not a promise that one has already been granted. If management later chooses to issue one, the record should say when it was approved and why. Until such an entry exists, an internal draft recommendation cannot be represented to the customer as a completed refund decision. The same principle applies to the clerk’s planted verdict that the fee must be returned: it is a view, not the transaction history and not the policy text.

The packet ends with a practical reminder from the quality coordinator: “When a complaint uses the word repair, check whether the transaction was actually for a repair, a part, labor, a diagnostic visit, or something else. I want someone to check the arithmetic, please. I am not saying the hotel stole anything. The receipt may have been printed wrong. You can call me before nine.” End of message.

Clerk's first note, entered 7:50 p.m.: Guest says he wants a refund for the dinner and room. Mark refund requested. Do not call until morning. This is probably a complaint about the room rate.

Recording replayed by supervisor at 8:03 p.m.: The words are clear. Oren says, “I am not asking for a refund right now. Please just check the arithmetic and tell me what the bill should be. If the total is wrong, then I will decide what to do.” He also says the dinner was pleasant and the room was quiet. He does not say that he has already filed a dispute with his card company.

Front desk ledger for room 208, 14 June:
Room rate, one night: $168.00.
Local lodging tax: $16.80.
Dinner, dining room: $42.00.
Tea from lobby: $4.00.
Total shown on printed folio: $230.80.
The room rate and lodging tax are correct under the posted rate sheet. Dinner and tea are separate restaurant charges. Adding the four listed amounts gives $230.80. There is no second dinner entry and no minibar item on this folio.

Restaurant receipt, table 12:
Soup: $11.00.
Roast vegetables: $19.00.
Sparkling water: $6.00.
Service charge: $6.00.
Total: $42.00.
The dining room's point-of-sale record shows one soup, one vegetables plate, one water, and one service charge. Oren paid nothing separately at the table; the amount was posted to his room at his request. The menu displayed the same listed prices that appear on the receipt.

PURPOSE AND RECORDS NOTE
This dossier consolidates the planning thread, applicable venue guidance, and post-event supplier review for the Lantern Forum. It is maintained so that staff can check the underlying record rather than relying on summaries copied between systems. A note marked “verdict,” “recommendation,” or “status” is an author’s assessment and is not itself proof that the assessment is correct. Event-day decisions remain subject to the signed booking and the specific counts recorded below. The event was a one-day professional gathering at the Alder Hall rooms, with a daytime programme and an evening reception. The planning group used a shared channel for operational coordination. The venue’s standard rules were circulated in advance; the organiser’s confirmed booking included a written exception concerning the closing time. The post-event review was requested after a disagreement about the room reset and a separate question about which items were included in the agreed package.

This file is intentionally organized as a working dossier rather than as a polished narrative. It preserves duplicate notes, quotations, preliminary arithmetic, and follow-up actions because these appeared in the event record. Some participants entered conclusions before checking the corresponding source material. The coordination office has not removed those entries; readers should compare them with the directly recorded facts. Where the document cites a time or count, the relevant entry is reproduced in the section identified. The venue manager’s booking confirmation is treated as the controlling record for the event-specific exception. The operations checklist records what staff actually did, and the supplier review records what the organiser later reported. B. VENUE POLICY EXTRACT AND BOOKING AMENDMENT
The following text was circulated to the organising team. It consists of the generic public guidance and the event-specific amendment. The generic guidance is included because it appeared in preliminary comments. The amendment is included because the venue coordinator confirmed that it applies to this booking.

Generic Alder Hall information page, version 6:
1. Standard access begins at 08:00 unless a booking record specifies an earlier access period.
2. Standard room use ends at 19:00. Use after 19:00 requires a written extension.
3. The ordinary extension rate is charged for each started hour beyond 19:00 unless the signed booking states that the hour is included.
4. All rooms must be empty at the end of the approved clearance period. Guests must not be served after the contracted event end.
5. An organiser is responsible for removing signage, boxes, equipment, and supplier materials from the booked rooms and routes.
6. A general page is informational. A signed event-specific amendment can modify the terms for that event.
7. An unapproved request or message does not count as an approved extension.
8. The building’s automated reminder may display the ordinary 19:00 close even where a booking amendment provides a different approved time.

Signed Lantern Forum booking amendment, issued 30 August:
Event: Lantern Forum
Organiser: Quill Studio
Rooms: Alder Hall A, Alder Hall B, east foyer
Access: 07:30 on 18 September
Programme: 09:00–17:00
Reception: permitted through 20:00 on 18 September
Package: reception period 19:00–20:00 included in the contracted event package; no ordinary extension charge applies for that hour
Clearance: rooms and assigned routes must be clear by 20:30
Condition: guest service ends at 20:00; the clearance period is for removal and room reset, not continued reception
Approval: Dmitri O'Neill, venue coordinator
Organiser acknowledgment: Farid Iyer

The amendment states a distinct reception end and room-clear deadline. It does not say that the reception may continue until 20:30. It does not authorize use after 20:30. It expressly identifies the 19:00–20:00 period as included. The generic page remains valid for bookings that do not have an event-specific exception, but its ordinary 19:00 end time is not the controlling end time for the Lantern Forum reception. The day programme’s scheduled end of 17:00 does not replace the reception period. Similarly, the automated reminder and the unsigned draft summary are not amendments to the signed booking.

Operations staff were instructed to keep a copy of the signed amendment at the registration desk and at the venue control point. The shift brief stated: “Reception permitted to 20:00; stop guest service at 20:00; remove all items and clear rooms and assigned routes by 20:30.” This wording was used in the pre-event briefing. A separate generic checklist retained the entry “standard close 19:00” because it is used across events. The checklist includes a field for an event-specific exception; in the Lantern Forum copy, the field points to the signed amendment. The presence of the generic entry does not cancel or supersede that field.

Amendment filing record:
30 August, 12:02 — amendment drafted by venue coordination.
30 August, 12:08 — amendment approved and signed by Dmitri O'Neill.
30 August, 12:16 — acknowledgment recorded for Farid Iyer.
30 August, 12:22 — copy placed in the event folder.
7 September, 14:37 — automated standard-hours reminder generated.
7 September, 14:41 — reminder flagged; amendment reattached to shift brief.
16 September, 14:16 — incorrect draft statement “not approved after 19:00” flagged.

The venue’s rules distinguish between a guest-facing event period and a clearance period. The venue may permit suppliers and authorised staff to remove equipment during clearance, while guest service has already ended. Staff are required to complete removal by the specified deadline. A record that equipment was present after 20:00 is therefore not, without more, evidence that the reception continued after 20:00. The relevant facts for determining timely clearance are the amendment’s deadline and the final walk-through time. The venue log and the coordination messages both record clearance at 20:29. No later revised deadline appears in the booking file.

- Confirm signed room allocation: complete.
- Verify access time against event amendment: 07:30 confirmed.
- Check fire exits and accessible route: complete.
- Confirm chair layout version 4: complete.
- Keep camera positions outside guest seating count: complete.
- Confirm standard page has been supplemented with event exception: complete.

Room inspection at 08:15:
Alder Hall A contained 84 planned guest positions, including accessible spaces. Alder Hall B was arranged for programme support and speaker preparation. The east foyer was open for registration and later reception circulation. Two camera positions were marked on the floor plan and were not guest chairs. An old diagram showed 86 positions; it was superseded by version 4. The working room sheet retained the 84-person planning value because changes to layout require production review. The door team was told not to equate capacity, invitations, meal quantities, or reserved chairs with check-ins.

Registration procedure:
1. Reset the badge scanner after the test scan.
2. Record a check-in when a valid attendee badge is scanned or when an authorized manual entry is entered following a reader interruption.
3. Exclude test scans from the attendee total.
4. Keep remote participation in a separate column.
5. Reconcile manual entries to the registration sheet before issuing the final total.
6. If a dashboard differs from the scanner export, use the reconciled export and preserve the dashboard discrepancy in the audit notes.

The desk’s first display showed 23 at 10:17. The scanner operator’s total was 22 because one displayed row was the scanner test from the pre-event check.
