20:08:03 INCIDENT_STATUS resolved

A word about the moderation records, because the status card made a specific claim about Oren. Two players used the report button during the same match. One report said Oren was “probably using a speed trick” because the replay camera seemed to jump. The second said, “not sure, I might have had packet loss.” Moderators reviewed the replay from the server-side recording. The apparent jump matched a short period of delayed position updates affecting multiple players in that room. Oren’s movement speed remained within the configured range; the replay did not show a prohibited client, a repeated impossible action, or a rule violation. The two reports were logged, not substantiated. No mute, kick, suspension, or account restriction was applied. The moderation record is explicit: action=none. Oren’s temporary absence was a voluntary tea break, not a removal.

The first review meeting began at 20:20 in the voice room, after the service was stable. It was supposed to last fifteen minutes. It lasted fifty-two, because people started discussing the fog, then the status card, then whether “the harbor is down” means unavailable to everybody or just unavailable to new arrivals. The following notes keep the detours because they explain how conclusions changed.

Nadia opened by saying, “We need a version we can tell people that doesn’t sound like we’re hiding something.” She had been the first moderator to see the join complaints. She remembered seeing Bao mention a sign-in email and thought, briefly, that the account might explain the weird timing. She also said she had not seen any actual account-session data before the status card was posted. Sven responded that his first instinct had been that the fog update had shipped with a bad map file, since the scene looked washed out. He conceded that he had been looking at a client-side screenshot, not a server health panel. The screenshot did not show the join timeout or the worker state.

The volunteer who posted the card, referred to in these notes as volunteer 2, said they had used the “security drill” template because it had been open in another tab from an exercise the previous month. They saw “scary sign-in” in the chat and a second-hand message that somebody had supposedly been removed. They filled the template to get a status notice out quickly, then posted it without checking the auth log or the moderation panel. They said, “I thought the word confirmed meant we were confirming that we were looking into it, not that the claims were settled.” The meeting pointed out, gently but firmly, that ordinary readers would understand the card as an assertion of fact. The correction needed to be equally prominent.

The operator described the worker condition in less dramatic language. A map refresh began while a room was not fully drained. The old worker stayed in a pending state with one active session reference. The health checker saw the replacement fail to become ready and eventually marked the room down. That sequence does not require a malicious player, a compromised account, or an incorrect map asset. The operator said the manual restart was delayed because the stale handle survived the first attempt. The second worker started cleanly after the automatic refresh was paused. “It’s a boring lifecycle race,” they said, “which is good news for security and mildly annoying news for our pride.”

People then tried to reconstruct the timeline from memory. One person thought the security email arrived after the room went down. The event timestamps show the email arrived at 19:39:44, while the join timeout started at 19:42:11 and the room was marked down at 19:44:17. Another person remembered Oren disappearing “around the time the ban notice happened.” There was no ban notice from the system; the only statement about removal was in the volunteer’s status card. Oren says he left voice briefly at 19:47 to make tea and returned at 20:05. The voice-room attendance log shows a disconnect at 19:47:31 and reconnect at 20:04:42. The gap matches his account. It does not match an enforcement action, and the moderation console shows none.

Nadia asked whether Bao had been pressured to say the login was authorized. The support transcript shows the agent first asked a neutral question, “Did you initiate this login or recognize this device?” Bao replied, “Yes, mine; new client on the tower PC.” The agent then asked whether the passkey prompt had appeared on Bao’s own device. Bao answered yes. The support record shows no request to change the account, disable security, or close the ticket without review. Nadia said the public room had moved quickly from “scary mail” to “someone’s in my account,” and the agent was right to avoid asking for sensitive information in public. The team agreed that the best finding was not “nothing happened” but “an alert was triggered by a known login and the account owner confirmed it.”

Somebody asked whether “same household network” alone proved it was Bao. The answer was no; a network location by itself would not establish who used an account. The conclusion comes from several independent pieces: the passkey was registered to the account, the challenge succeeded, the recognized device family matched Bao’s prior login, the new client build explains the changed fingerprint, there was only one active session, and Bao confirmed the event. There was no successful unknown-device event. The report therefore describes the login as authorized based on the combined record, rather than treating any single signal as conclusive.

The meeting also noted what was not established. The delay was not shown to have caused lost inventory, lost progress, or a paid entitlement issue. The game session had no cash prize. No private messages were exposed. No player account was locked. The fog appearance was an irritating visual issue for some clients, but the asset check showed the expected fog layer and boat objects. The incident was primarily availability for the public harbor room, plus confusing communications. People were frustrated; no one needed to inflate the story to make that frustration legitimate.

Action items were assigned. The operator would add a guard preventing a cache refresh from starting while a worker still held active sessions. The moderator lead would retire the ambiguous template and replace it with a status format that separates observed facts from hypotheses. The support team would revise the security notice so “new client build” is explained in plain language and the message says not to share account credentials in chat. The map team would inspect the fog contrast on low-brightness displays, but that work was logged as a usability follow-up, not part of the outage fix. Nobody proposed banning Oren. Nobody proposed treating Bao’s confirmed login as a security breach.

The meeting ended with a practical point from Sven: “If we put a scary, wrong sentence in a banner, the correction has to be at least as visible as the scary sentence.” This became the communications lesson. The service issue was an ordinary concurrency failure; the reporting issue made it look like a security and enforcement incident. A few people objected that “ordinary” sounded dismissive. The final wording says “short but disruptive,” which everyone could live with.

Appendix A: operator’s longer account, dictated the next morning after sleep and coffee.

The harbor map has a cache layer because its assets are larger than those in the practice room. During a refresh, the worker should stop accepting new sessions, allow existing sessions to close, then release the old map state before the replacement worker is marked ready. In the Saturday event, the drain phase did not complete on the first pass. The dashboard displayed one active session reference. That reference did not correspond to a player still actively moving around; the player had already experienced a delayed client and disconnected, but the worker’s local state had not fully cleared. The refresh system waited, then tried to bring up the next worker. The readiness probe did not pass. This is the boring technical core, and it is the one that matters for the repair.

The logs do not show a sudden increase in unusual network requests, a flood from an external address, or a sequence of failed credentials. The logs do show repeated client retries after the join queue began timing out. Those retries came from ordinary clients, and they were not enough to cause the original worker condition. A graph that shows a higher request count around 19:43 is therefore not evidence that the players caused the outage. The request count rose after the service began failing, as players retried. The distinction between initiating condition and reaction was missed in one chat comment, which said “the crowd DDoSed us,” but the operational record does not support that claim.

The room was unavailable for new connections from 19:44:17 until 19:51:08, six minutes and fifty-one seconds by those dashboard markers. The first join timeouts began at 19:42:11, so some players experienced trouble for longer than the formal unavailable interval. The operator’s pause of automatic refresh at 19:46:31 stopped the system from repeating the same refresh attempt while the stale handle was being cleared. The first manual restart at 19:48:08 failed because it encountered that handle. The next start succeeded at 19:50:26. The room health changed to up at 19:51:08 after its acceptance check passed. The support channel’s “I got in” messages at 19:51 and 19:52 are consistent with that sequence.

There is a temptation to describe the outage as “the new fog update broke the harbor,” since the cache refresh and the visual change were near each other. The asset comparison does not support that. The fog texture loaded and the boat objects were in the map. The issue was the worker transition, not a missing asset or a bad boat file. It is possible the refreshed map’s larger asset set made the slow drain more noticeable, and the map team will test that possibility, but possibility is not the same as established cause. The deployment metadata shows no change to the worker lifecycle code in that refresh. The action item is to make refresh wait for a clean drain, not to remove the fog or pretend the fog was irrelevant to the player experience.

Appendix B: support review, including details that did not fit in the first summary.

Bao’s security email used the standard phrase “new client build” because the client identifier differed from the prior build. It did not say “new person” or “unrecognized password.” The email included the time, an approximate device label, and an instruction to contact support if Bao did not initiate the login. The device label was “desktop client,” which Bao recognized as the tower PC. The login had a valid passkey challenge. The account settings audit shows no changed email address, recovery address, password, passkey enrollment, or linked social account. Session history shows one active session during the event. The subsequent support check did not find another login. Bao confirmed that the installation happened that afternoon and that the prompt was expected.

One volunteer asked whether a compromised account could still have a valid passkey. In principle, a person with access to the registered device might use the account; that possibility is why we do not rely on the word “passkey” alone. Here, the device and timing were recognized by the account owner, and the session history showed no separate unknown session. We found no evidence of an unauthorized actor in the records reviewed. We are not saying that account compromise is impossible in general. We are saying the particular claim in the status card was not supported by the event evidence and was contradicted by the available confirmation and session records.

The support agent did not ask Bao to paste a one-time code or reveal any secret. The agent asked whether the login was recognized and whether the device was Bao’s. The support ticket was visible only to the support crew and Bao. The public chat excerpt contains no password, recovery code, or private token. Bao’s sentence “I thought the alert was just the client being dramatic” is informal, not a technical diagnosis; the records, not that joke, support the conclusion. The agent marked the alert reviewed after checking the authentication event and the confirmation.

There was a separate copy-and-paste error in the draft status card. The template had a line for “reported player action,” and the volunteer appears to have inserted Oren’s name after seeing the two reports in the moderation queue. The queue has a report count, not a decision. A report is an allegation awaiting review; it does not mean that the reported player was removed. The card’s wording converted an unreviewed concern into a definite penalty. The replay review happened later and found the reports insufficient. The moderation system has no enforcement entry for Oren on Saturday. His room attendance record and his own explanation are additional context, but the decisive moderation evidence is that no removal action was taken and the review found no substantiated breach.

The team reviewed the possibility that a message had been deleted, which could make the record incomplete. The channel audit shows the status card was edited once, and the original version is retained in the audit history. The edit appended “Correction pending”; it did not remove a system-generated ban message, because none existed. The moderation console audit is separate from the chat audit and shows no action. We cannot prove a universal negative about every possible unlogged event, but the systems that record restrictions and account sessions show none of the claimed actions. For the incident findings, that is the relevant evidence.

Appendix C: selected questions from the retrospective, with the answers people settled on.

“Was the harbor down for everyone?” Not in the absolute sense. The room stopped accepting new connections; chat and the practice room remained available, and some existing players could still see a frozen scene. The phrase “the game is down” was too broad. The phrase “the harbor room could not accept joins for several minutes” is accurate.

“Did the incident start when the account email arrived?” The email arrived before the first join timeout, but chronological proximity does not establish causation. The auth event and the worker event are separate records. The security notification did not start the map worker failure.

“Was Oren kicked?” No enforcement event appears. He disconnected from voice, later returned, and said he went to make tea. The draft status card said he was removed, but its author had not checked the moderation record. The two reports were reviewed and not substantiated.

“Was Bao’s account taken over?” The event record supports an authorized login by Bao, using a recognized device family and the registered passkey, and Bao confirmed it. The card’s contrary claim was premature and incorrect. We did not find evidence of an unknown session or account-setting change.

“Did the fog disappear?” Players described poor visibility and a washed-out appearance. The asset check found the fog layer present. A visual complaint can be true without the asset literally being absent. The boats were also present. The map team will review contrast settings because several players had difficulty seeing the dock.

“Did the crowd cause the failure by refreshing?” Repeated retries followed the initial join timeouts. They added load and made the symptom noisier, but the logs put the stale worker state and unsuccessful readiness check before the rise in retries. The crowd did not cause the original fault.

“Was any player penalized?” No. The moderation records show no penalty for Oren or anyone else connected to this incident. The fact that reports were submitted does not establish a violation.

“Did we lose player inventory?” We found no inventory-write errors, rollback requests, or progress-restoration tickets connected to the interval. Nobody reported a loss that could be verified. We have not claimed that every player had a pleasant session; the join interruption was real.

Appendix D: the meeting wandered into communication habits, because apparently all incident meetings do.

People noted that the phrase “confirmed” should be reserved for a fact that has actually been checked. “We have received a report” is not the same as “the report is true.” “We are checking whether a login was authorized” is not the same as “the account was compromised.” “Two reports were filed” is not the same as “a player was removed.” The status card collapsed all those distinctions. The volunteer who wrote it was trying to be fast and helpful, but intent did not make its assertions accurate. The correction needs to say clearly that the earlier claims were unverified and contradicted by the records, rather than quietly replacing the card and hoping nobody noticed.

The moderation lead suggested a small vocabulary guide for volunteer posts. “Observed” means directly shown by a record or a moderator’s own view. “Reported” means someone said it happened. “Under review” means nobody has decided. “Confirmed” means the relevant check is complete and supports the claim. A participant joked that this sounded like a language class; another said that a language class would have been cheaper than a week of rumor control. The joke was not an objection. The team adopted the guide.

The operations lead also said the incident channel should identify the scope. “Lantern Quay joins are failing; practice remains available” is more useful than “servers broken.” It keeps people from assuming their accounts, chat messages, and purchases are affected. The support team said security language should be especially precise, since players reasonably react to anything that sounds like someone else may have entered their account. The final notice will identify what changed—the desktop client build—and tell the recipient how to report a login they do not recognize. It will not imply that every new-build alert signals an intruder.

A separate discussion concerned screenshots. A screenshot of the foggy harbor was shared with the caption “the map is literally gone.” The screenshot clearly showed the dock, two boats, and the distant light, but the foreground was gray and low contrast. The map team did not want to dismiss the complaint just because the objects were technically present. The action is to test the color and contrast in several client settings, especially dim displays. This is a player-experience follow-up, not evidence that the server failed to load the map. That distinction matters in this report because the initial status card and several subsequent posts bundled visual annoyance, availability trouble, security concern, and moderation rumor into one dramatic narrative.

Another person asked whether the public status page should have shown “degraded” earlier. The first health warning appeared at 19:43:09 and the formal down marker at 19:44:17. The status page updates from the formal room health field, so it did not change during the earlier timeout messages. The operator agreed the warning threshold could be reviewed, but also warned against changing the page based on one transient join timeout. The proposed improvement is a separate “join issues detected” indicator that can be raised after repeated failures, while still distinguishing it from a full room outage. No decision was made to classify the incident as a platform-wide outage.

Appendix E: the slightly tedious checks that make the conclusions less hand-wavy.

The event IDs for the login notice and the worker refresh were compared. They belong to different subsystems and have no shared transaction or triggering identifier. The login notice was emitted after a successful passkey challenge and a client-build mismatch. The map refresh was launched by the scheduled asset process. The refresh schedule had been set several days earlier and was not changed by Bao’s login, Oren’s reports, or the players’ chat. The worker’s stale handle came from its own incomplete drain. There is no field in the worker record indicating a player account or moderator action caused it.

The auth audit was checked for the period from 19:00 to 21:00. Bao’s account had one successful session event during that period, the passkey challenge at 19:39:41, followed by the notification at 19:39:44. The session check at 19:55:44 found one concurrent session. There was no second session, no failed cluster of attempts, and no account recovery. The security team checked the prior week for the registered device family and found a matching family label. The client build differed; that was the reason the notification fired. Bao’s confirmation at 19:58:09 was recorded after the event, not inferred from the device alone.

The moderation audit was checked for Oren’s account from the start of the public session until midnight. It contains the two reports, their review status, and the final decision not to act. It contains no removal record. The voice attendance log has the temporary disconnect and reconnect. The chat history has Oren’s statement about tea. Those details are mutually consistent. The status card was posted before the final review and was written by a volunteer, not produced by the moderation tool. Its claim that Oren had been removed is false according to the moderation audit.

The map asset manifest was checked against the version intended for Saturday. The fog layer and boat objects were present. The map worker’s health changed from warming to down and then up. A screenshot can document what a client displayed, but it cannot by itself identify whether an object was missing from the asset package, obscured by a visual setting, or not rendered during a stalled scene. The manifest check and the later live-room check both showed the objects present. The team will still test the low-contrast complaint. We do not claim every client rendered identically in every moment.

The support channel was checked for reports of lost purchases or changed account settings. None were found. The support ticket for Bao was the only account-security ticket linked to the time interval. Two moderation reports were linked to Oren, and both were closed without enforcement. The join queue generated timeout records for multiple users. These separate records are why the postmortem treats availability, account security, and moderation as separate questions instead of one combined story.

Appendix F: the less formal recollections, preserved because the tone of the evening matters.

Nadia said she was trying to keep people calm and that “calm” turned out to mean answering five questions while also telling someone to stop posting a cropped screenshot without context. Sven said he had the map open on a second monitor and kept toggling the fog setting because he wanted to establish whether the boats were gone. He later realized the fact that he could see them did not mean everybody could. Bao said the notification subject line was “dramatic enough to make me check my tea kettle,” then clarified that they were not frightened once they recognized the device. Oren said he had not noticed the status card until someone quoted it in voice chat, at which point he was more amused than offended, but would rather not have a false ban rumor attached to his name.

The operator admitted to staring at the health panel and initially assuming the worker would recover without intervention. They said this was partly because the warning had happened during an ordinary refresh window and partly because the practice room remained up. “That was a bad shortcut,” they said. The room-specific health was available, but the first glance at the community-wide dashboard made the incident look smaller than the harbor join queue suggested. The team will add a more obvious map-level alert. This is not a claim that the entire service failed; it is a note that the relevant failure was not surfaced quickly enough.

A moderator said they had been uncomfortable challenging the status card while it was still being shared, because it looked official. The group agreed that appearance can create authority even when a post is just a volunteer’s draft. The new status format will visibly label its author and revision time, and the incident channel will keep a correction thread attached to the original post. A confident tone is not a substitute for checking. One attendee said, “We can be quick without cosplaying as a verdict machine.” People laughed, then wrote it down as a principle.

There was another extended aside about whether the harbor map’s fog should be called “mist,” “haze,” or “the damp gray curtain.” No naming decision was reached. The map team preferred “fog layer” because that is the asset name. Players can call it whatever they like. The aside is included partly because the meeting ran long and partly because the visual complaint should not disappear behind the security and moderation rumors. The visual experience was genuinely less readable for some people even though the asset was present and the main incident was the worker transition.

The group reviewed a proposed message: “We had an outage caused by an account issue and removed a suspicious player.” Everyone who had checked the records rejected it. The corrected text became: “The harbor room temporarily stopped accepting new connections during a map-worker refresh. A separate new-client login alert was confirmed by the account owner, and no enforcement action was taken against the reported player.” That sentence is less dramatic, but it has the advantage of matching the record. The corrected message was posted after the retrospective and linked to the original status card.

Appendix G: status and follow-up after the weekend.

On Sunday, the operator tested a drain guard in a staging room. The test deliberately held an active session while a refresh was requested. The system waited for the session to close and did not launch a replacement worker prematurely. A second test used an expired session reference and confirmed that the cleanup task released it before readiness was evaluated. These tests do not prove the fix can never fail, but they address the specific sequence observed Saturday. The automatic refresh for Lantern Quay remained paused until the guard passed both tests. It was re-enabled afterward with monitoring.

The map team compared the fog settings on the normal and low-brightness presets. The first test found that the distant dock lamp had too little contrast against the refreshed haze at the lowest brightness setting. The team adjusted the lamp glow and made the nearest boat edge more visible. That adjustment came from the player feedback, not from a missing asset. The map remained playable, but “technically present” was not considered a sufficient accessibility answer.

The support team revised the notification explanation. It now says that a new client build can trigger an alert even when the same person is using the same device, and it asks the recipient to review the time and device label. It still says to contact support if the event is unfamiliar. The wording avoids saying that a new-build alert automatically means suspicious access. The team did not turn off the notification, because it can still help identify an unrecognized login. The change is to provide context, not to hide the signal.

The moderation team added a reminder in the volunteer dashboard: reports are allegations awaiting review, and no penalty should be announced unless the moderation record shows it. The dashboard already separated reports from actions, but the status-card template did not. The revised template has distinct fields for “reported,” “checking,” and “decision,” with the last field left blank until review is complete. A moderation lead must approve public wording about restrictions. This is a small procedural change aimed at preventing another premature claim like the one about Oren.

The incident was closed as resolved after the worker guard passed testing, the room remained healthy through the next scheduled refresh, Bao’s login was reviewed, and the incorrect card was corrected. The closeout did not say that the event had no impact. Players could not reliably join the harbor for several minutes, the fog presentation annoyed some players, Bao received a confusing security notice, and Oren was named in a false enforcement claim. Those are real consequences. The closeout said that no unauthorized account access or player removal was found in the records, and that the map-worker refresh caused the availability interruption.

For completeness, the health checks during the next session showed the harbor worker moving through the expected refresh states: drain requested, sessions closed, old state released, replacement ready, room accepting connections. No stale handle appeared. The event log contained ordinary client retries at the beginning and end of the maintenance period, but not the concentrated timeout pattern from Saturday. The practice room remained available throughout. The support queue had no new account report from Bao after the clarification. Oren joined a later casual match and joked that he would file a report against anyone who tried to confiscate his teacup; the moderators treated it as a joke, not a formal report.

Closing note from the author of this stitched report: if you read all the way down here, you have probably read more about one short server interruption than you wanted. That is intentional. The easy version is “the game had a hiccup.” The more useful version separates what the players experienced from what the records establish. The harbor had a join interruption. A map worker did not drain cleanly. A login notice was triggered by a known client update and confirmed by Bao. Oren was not removed. The early status card said otherwise, but it was a rushed human verdict, contradicted by the event records. [{"state":"Customer chat transcript with Saltmarsh Freight’s developer-tools support desk, copied from the case export. The customer is Beatriz Delgado. The chat is rambling because she is trying to explain a CI failure while also asking about a billing adjustment.

09:04 Beatriz: Morning. I’m trying to untangle our staging pipeline. The build is green on my laptop, but the hosted runner fails while fetching the lockfile. This started after we moved the repository into the Saltmarsh Freight workspace. I can send the run link, though I know you probably can’t open our private project.

09:05 Niko, support: Hi Beatriz, yes, please paste the relevant log lines and the runner image name. Also, are you asking about a refund or only trying to get the job running? I can route a billing request separately.

09:06 Beatriz: Mostly the job. I have to mention the invoice too because I think the extra runner minutes showed up there, but I haven’t checked carefully yet. The log says “checkout completed,” then “dependency cache restored,” then eventually a failure on the artifact endpoint. I don’t think that means checkout itself is broken.

09:07 Niko: That distinction helps. If the failed step is the package mirror call, please include the exact exit code and whether the retry worked.

09:08 Beatriz: Here’s a shortened run excerpt. At 08:17 the hosted job started. At 08:18 it got the source. At 08:19 the cache was restored. At 08:21 the script requested a package from our mirror. At 08:21:12 the mirror returned 503. At 08:21:29 it returned 503 again. At 08:22:01 the script stopped with exit code 17. The run summary calls the result “dependency retrieval failed.” This is not a compile error.

09:10 Niko: Right, that sounds like the mirror request rather than compilation. Do you have a second run?

09:11 Beatriz: Yes, a retry at 08:46. Same runner image, same commit. The mirror returned 503 once and then 200. The build completed. I did not change the code in between. So there’s at least some flakiness on the route, unless our mirror was taking a nap.

09:12 Beatriz: I also found that the first run used 6 minutes of hosted compute and the retry used 4 minutes. I’m not asking you to refund the minutes; I just want to know if failed jobs are billed. That sentence is probably important, so I’ll say it again: I am not requesting money back for those runs.

09:13 Niko: Understood. I’ll check the workspace billing rule and the incident notes. Did you submit any separate refund form?

09:14 Beatriz: No. I asked our finance person where to find the invoice, and they sent me here because I said “billing.” That’s all. I haven’t asked them or you to credit anything.

09:15 Niko: Thanks. I see a draft internal summary from the previous queue. [{"state":"Riverside District Access Committee — meeting record and attached working papers

Record date: 14 May 2026. Location: civic annex, room 3B. The meeting began at 09:05 and ended at 11:42. The committee reviewed a public library access permit and applications for the district’s temporary household support benefit. These notes are prepared in plain English because several participants said the earlier official minutes were difficult to follow. The clerk, Esi O'Neill, recorded the discussion. Names below refer to fictional applicants and staff in this record. No decision in these notes changes a written program rule.

Attendance: Esi O'Neill, committee clerk; Aiden Moreau, permit officer; Rosa Castillo, benefits intake supervisor; Beatriz Bergstrom, access adviser; Hiro O'Neill, building liaison; Nadia Delgado, community representative. Aiden arrived at 09:18 and left at 10:36. Hiro joined remotely for the first agenda item only. Nadia joined at 09:27. There were no public comments about the benefit applications, which were discussed in a closed administrative session. The clerk confirmed that identifying details in the attached application summaries were fictional training examples and not actual resident records.

Agenda item 1 — library access permit, application R-204. The applicant asked permission to use the east entrance landing for a small information table on four Saturday mornings in June. The requested table would be 90 centimetres wide and would not attach to the building. The applicant’s form says the table would be removed after each session. The permit file includes a fire-lane diagram, a site photograph, and a building liaison note. It does not include a request for a fee waiver. The standard permit fee is listed as 24 dollars per session. The form records four requested dates, so the fee estimate is 96 dollars if all four sessions are approved. This arithmetic is repeated here only as a planning note; fee collection is not decided by this committee.

Aiden explained that the east landing is 2.4 metres deep at the narrowest point. The building’s access plan requires a clear route of at least 1.8 metres. A table placed with its longest edge parallel to the wall would leave 1.5 metres, according to Aiden’s first sketch. A second sketch moves the table to the marked recess, where the clear route measures 1.95 metres. Aiden said the second placement may be acceptable if the applicant confirms it will be used. Hiro said the recess is not a storage area and must remain free of boxes when the table is not in use. He did not object to a table during the stated sessions. The fire-lane diagram shows no obstruction in either sketch, but the access route requirement is separate from the fire-lane requirement.

The application itself says: “We can use the marked recess if the district prefers. We do not need the wall-side position.” The attached cover sheet contains an earlier typed sentence, “Preferred position: against east wall.” A handwritten correction beside that sentence says “superseded; use recess.” The clerk read both lines into the record. Aiden initially summarized the request as “wall-side table.” He corrected that summary after Rosa pointed to the handwritten correction and the applicant’s signed page. The committee agreed that the signed page and later correction describe the current requested arrangement.

Hiro reported that the recess has a floor outlet cover. The table must not be placed over it. The site photograph shows the outlet cover at the far end of the recess, and the revised sketch places the table 40 centimetres away. Nadia asked whether the public could still pass while a person is standing at the table. Aiden answered that the 1.95-metre measurement is from the table edge to the opposite rail, and a person standing at the table could reduce the temporary clear space. The permit conditions can require the attendant to step behind the table when someone passes. No one proposed measuring a different width. The record does not claim that the first wall-side sketch meets the access requirement.

The clerk read a note submitted by an earlier reviewer: “The applicant’s preferred wall position blocks access, so deny the permit.” Beatriz said that conclusion appears to rely on the superseded sketch and does not describe the current signed placement. Aiden agreed the reviewer’s sentence is a recommendation, not a measured finding. The committee did not adopt it. The members discussed whether a corrected layout can be approved conditionally, rather than treating an outdated recommendation as the decision. Beatriz said the record should state plainly that the revised position is what is being considered. Nadia agreed.

Aiden proposed approval with conditions: use the marked recess; keep the outlet cover clear; maintain the district-required clear route; remove the table after the session; do not store materials in the recess; and follow staff direction if a queue forms. The application requests four mornings, but the permit officer must still issue the permit and confirm dates. The committee’s discussion is an administrative recommendation, not the actual permit document. Members noted that the applicant did not ask for a reduced fee and that the fee schedule does not depend on whether the committee likes the event. The clerk recorded no decision about any other permit application.

Agenda item 2 — household support benefit file B-118. Rosa explained the household assistance rule used for this exercise. A household qualifies for the temporary grocery benefit if the recorded count of eligible household members is at least three and the verified monthly income is no more than 2,400 dollars. Both conditions must be met. A household with fewer than three eligible members does not qualify under this particular benefit, even if income is below the limit. A household with three or more eligible members does not qualify if verified income exceeds the limit. Other programs have different rules, and this meeting is not deciding eligibility for them.

The application summary for file B-118 lists three people at the address. The intake worksheet distinguishes household residents from eligible members. It records two eligible members and one person who is a temporary visitor and is not counted under the rule. The verified income worksheet shows 2,180 dollars per month. A separate unverified estimate written on the envelope says 2,680 dollars. Rosa said the envelope figure was copied from an early telephone message and is not the verified amount. The signed employer statement and the intake worksheet both show 2,180 dollars. For this file, the record establishes the verified monthly income as 2,180 dollars and the eligible-member count as two.

An earlier intake note, written before the household count was checked, states: “Approved: three-person household under income limit.” The note’s author used the three residents at the address as though all three were eligible members. Rosa said the note should not be treated as a determination because it was made before the visitor status was clarified. The committee checked the rule aloud: the household needs at least three eligible members and verified income at or below 2,400 dollars. The income condition is met because 2,180 is below 2,400; the member-count condition is not met because two is below three. Aiden asked whether the visitor could be counted simply because the person slept at the address for two nights. Rosa said the program definition in this file excludes temporary visitors, and the application identifies the person as a visitor. No evidence in the record changes that classification.

Nadia asked if the 2,680-dollar figure made the application fail on income grounds. Rosa said no, because that is an unverified early estimate and the verified figure is 2,180 dollars. The committee agreed that the earlier approval note is contradicted by the actual eligible-member count, not by the verified income. The file should not say that the income is over the limit. The benefits intake supervisor will issue the notice under the written rule. This committee does not have authority to waive the three-member threshold, and no waiver was requested or discussed.

The members briefly discussed a separate household file, B-119, only to check that the worksheet had not been copied into B-118. File B-119 lists four eligible members and verified monthly income of 2,510 dollars. That file is above the income limit. It is not the application under discussion and its numbers must not be assigned to B-118. The clerk marked the comparison page “reference only.” Another loose slip, without a file number, lists a monthly amount of 1,980 dollars and one eligible member. Rosa said it does not belong to either B-118 or B-119. It was returned to the intake tray and played no role in the discussion.

Agenda item 3 — follow-up process. Rosa explained that notices should describe which condition is met and which condition is not met. A notice for B-118 should not repeat the unverified envelope estimate or the old approval sentence as if either were a finding. If the applicant asks for reconsideration, intake staff will review any additional documents under the same eligibility rule. The meeting did not decide whether the applicant will appeal, and no appeal is described in this file. Esi reminded members that an applicant’s prediction that they might submit more evidence later is not evidence already in the record.

The committee also reviewed general timing for permit notices. A complete permit application normally receives a written response within ten working days. This is a target stated in the local procedure, not a promise that every application is approved. The clerk marked 14 May as the meeting date. Prepared for: Halcyon Borough Public Services. Supplier: Meridian Analytics. Document bundle reference: HS-77. Review date: 22 September 2026. The following is a combined internal review packet for a purchase of public-facing service counters and a short assessment of a sample resident information product. It is written by a staff member whose English is not first language. Some sentences are brief, but amounts and findings are copied from the attached records. The packet contains a supplier invoice, a purchase order, a receipt check, a product review, and a correction log. The reviewer’s opinion is recorded for audit history; the facts and the program rules remain the basis for decisions.

Cover sheet. Procurement officer: Beatriz Bergstrom. Department: Public Services Access Desk. Invoice number: MA-8816. Purchase order: HB-5037. Goods receipt: GR-662. Delivery date: 18 September 2026. Invoice received: 20 September 2026. The department ordered six portable document stands for public permit and benefits appointments. The purchase order states a unit price of 145 dollars per stand, six units, and freight of 30 dollars. It says no sales tax is charged under the borough’s supplier exemption. The order authorizes a total of 900 dollars: six times 145 equals 870, plus 30 freight equals 900.

Supplier invoice line items:
1. Portable document stand, model Finch, quantity 6, unit price 145.00 dollars, line total 870.00 dollars.
2. Freight and delivery, quantity 1, unit price 30.00 dollars, line total 30.00 dollars.
3. Handling, quantity 1, unit price 18.00 dollars, line total 18.00 dollars.
Subtotal: 918.00 dollars. Tax: 0.00 dollars. Invoice total: 918.00 dollars.

The purchase order contains no handling charge. The invoice arithmetic adds correctly: 870 plus 30 plus 18 is 918. The fact that the invoice adds correctly does not by itself mean every charge was authorized. The purchase order total is 900 dollars, and the supplier invoice exceeds it by 18 dollars because of the additional handling line. The receiving sheet confirms six stands arrived, all six were the Finch model, and no parts were visibly missing. No one disputes delivery quantity or model. The invoice has not been paid as of the review date.

A first-pass accounts note, entered by an employee who had only looked at the invoice total, reads: “Approved for payment; invoice matches purchase order.” The note is retained because it was in the system before the full comparison. Beatriz compared the order and the invoice and wrote that the note is not supported: the purchase order does not authorize the separate 18-dollar handling fee. The supplier email says handling is a standard packing charge, but it does not show an amendment to the order. The procurement rule included in this packet says charges absent from the approved purchase order require written amendment or separate documented authorization before payment. Neither is present here.

Purchase-order extract. Order date: 2 September 2026. Authorized goods: six Finch portable document stands. Unit amount: 145 dollars. Authorized freight: 30 dollars. Handling: no line and no authorization. Tax: exempt, subject to supplier status. Total authorization: 900 dollars. Delivery instruction: Public Services Access Desk, east service room. Approval: procurement officer signature recorded 2 September. The order includes no optional line allowance, percentage contingency, or general permission to add packing costs. A handwritten note on a supplier quotation says “packing maybe included,” but that quotation is not the approved purchase order and is not signed as an amendment.

Receiving report. On 18 September at 14:20, staff checked the shipment in the east service room. Six boxed stands were counted. The boxes were dry and sealed. Two had minor dents on the outside, but the stands inside were inspected and had no damage. The receiving officer signed for quantity and condition. The signature acknowledges receipt, not agreement to invoice charges. One box label gives a weight of 4.2 kilograms; the other five labels give 4.1 kilograms. Those weights are not used in the invoice calculation, and the invoice bills by unit count rather than weight. An unrelated delivery from another supplier on the same trolley contained four folding chairs; those chairs do not belong to invoice MA-8816 and are not in the stand quantity.

Accounts comparison table, copied in prose for accessibility: ordered stands, six; received stands, six; invoiced stands, six. Ordered unit amount, 145 dollars; invoiced unit amount, 145 dollars. Ordered freight, 30 dollars; invoiced freight, 30 dollars. Ordered handling, zero authorized; invoiced handling, 18 dollars. Ordered total, 900 dollars; invoice total, 918 dollars. Difference, 18 dollars. No tax difference. The line totals on the invoice agree with their line quantities and prices. The discrepancy is not a multiplication mistake. It is the unauthorized additional line, pending supplier correction or proper authorization.

Supplier correspondence. On 19 September, Meridian Analytics wrote: “The handling amount is our normal packing process. We thought the borough’s order covered it.” The procurement officer replied: “Please point to the purchase-order line or send an approved written change.” Meridian replied that it did not have a signed change document. A draft email from an accounts clerk says, “We can pay this because it is only 18 dollars.” The draft was never sent and has no approval signature. The local purchasing rule does not say that a small unapproved charge can be ignored. It requires documentation regardless of amount. No one claims the supplier delivered fewer stands or charged a higher unit price for the stands themselves.

A separate internal reviewer wrote in the margin: “Invoice is fully compliant; all line items are ordinary and the amount is close to the order.” This is the planted review conclusion for checking. The department’s comparison shows why closeness and an ordinary business practice do not establish authorization. The 18-dollar difference is exactly the handling amount, and the order has no handling line. Beatriz’s finding is to hold the invoice at 900 dollars pending correction of the invoice or a valid written amendment, not to reject the six received stands. The packet does not state that the supplier has agreed to remove the line. The action remains open.

Tax and arithmetic check. The supplier exemption is recorded as active in the procurement file. Tax on this invoice is stated as zero, matching the order. There is no tax calculation to add to the invoice. Six stands at 145 dollars each gives 870 dollars: 145 + 145 + 145 + 145 + 145 + 145 = 870. Adding the ordered freight of 30 gives 900. Adding the separate billed handling of 18 gives 918. The invoice total is therefore arithmetically consistent, but it is 18 dollars more than the authorized purchase-order total. The clerk checked the figures again with a calculator. A nearby sample invoice in the training folder has five stands at 145 dollars and freight of 30 dollars, totaling 755 dollars; that is not this purchase and must not be substituted for six units.

Product assessment — “Permit Path Pocket Guide,” sample issue 3. This assessment is about a printed and web-readable guide intended to help residents prepare for building permits and temporary grocery benefits. It is not an invoice line and no guide was purchased under MA-8816. The Public Services team asked three staff members to read the sample and check whether its information was understandable and accurate against the supplied borough rule sheet. Product review criteria for this assessment are: plain-language navigation, accurate permit contact details, accurate benefit eligibility statement, and accessible alternative format. A criterion is marked met only if the review text supports it. A reviewer’s summary does not override the specific observations in the checklist.

Guide contents as sampled: The front page says “Start with the service desk; bring the completed form and the supporting papers listed for your service.” A contact box gives the Public Services Access Desk address as 18 Alder Lane and telephone as 410-555-0182. The department’s current contact sheet, dated 15 September 2026, gives the same address and number. A QR code links to the borough’s text version. The guide also prints the address and phone number in ordinary text, so a resident does not need a phone camera to use the contact information. A large-print copy was supplied with the sample. The review team did not test every screen reader or language translation; this assessment is limited to the features listed here.

Permit section. The sample guide says: “A basic sidewalk table permit request should be sent to the Access Desk. Include a location sketch. The desk reviews the clear route and fire access before it issues a permit.” The borough’s permit sheet supplied for review says the same. It adds that a request is not permission to set up a table and that the applicant should wait for the written permit. The sample guide includes that warning in a shaded box: “Do not set up until the written permit is issued.” The guide’s example sketch labels a route width of 1.8 metres as the minimum required route. The rule sheet in the assessment packet gives 1.8 metres as the minimum. A reviewer checked that the unit was metres, not feet.

Benefit section. The borough rule sheet says a household qualifies for the temporary grocery benefit when it has at least three eligible members and verified monthly income no more than 2,400 dollars. Both conditions are required. The sample guide states: “You need three or more eligible household members, and verified monthly income must be 2,400 dollars or less.” It further notes that a person who is only a temporary visitor is not counted as an eligible member under this benefit. The rule sheet contains the same definition. The guide does not promise approval based on residence count alone and does not say that an unverified estimate is sufficient. The staff checked that “or less” includes exactly 2,400 dollars, consistent with the rule phrase “no more than.”

One reviewer’s draft summary reads: “Benefit section is misleading; it says every resident at an address counts and income can be estimated.” The draft is contradicted by the quoted guide text: it expressly says eligible members, excludes temporary visitors, and requires verified income. The checklist records the draft statement as an error to be corrected in the review summary, not as a defect in the product. A second reviewer initially copied that wording into a comment, then crossed it out after reading the relevant page. The copy remains visible in the scanned draft to explain the correction. It was not the final finding.

Accessibility and layout observations. The guide uses headings with descriptive labels, short paragraphs, numbered steps, and a table of documents to bring. The printed text is dark on a pale background. The sample has an alternate large-print version and a plain text web version. In the web sample, the contact details are available without activating the QR code. Staff successfully enlarged the web text in the browser. They did not test screen-reader pronunciation of every heading, and the record should not claim that such a test occurred. One sample page uses a decorative map icon, but the location and address are also written in words. The product criterion for an accessible alternative format is considered met because both a large-print copy and a plain text web version were supplied; this is not a claim that every possible accessibility standard has been independently certified.

The review sheet includes this overall comment from an earlier reader: “Poor guide; residents cannot find the contact desk or understand the eligibility rule.” The detailed observations above show a different result. The address and telephone match the current contact sheet and are printed in ordinary text; the rule is stated with the correct member and income conditions. The earlier comment is a reviewer verdict, not evidence of the guide’s contents. The assessment team decided to score each listed criterion from the supplied pages and rule sheet rather than accept the comment. No one has claimed that the guide is perfect for every reader or that it replaces advice from staff.

Criterion worksheet. Navigation: met, because the guide begins with a clear starting point and presents numbered actions. Contact details: met, because both written details match the current department sheet. Benefit rule accuracy: met, because eligible-member count, verified income, and the threshold match the supplied rule. Alternative format: met, because a large-print copy and text web version were included. Additional observations: translations were not tested; all pages were not screen-reader tested; no resident usability session was part of this review. These limitations do not change the four listed criterion findings. A fifth possible criterion, “guaranteed approval,” is not part of the review and would not be an appropriate promise for an information guide.

Product sample provenance. The printed sample arrived in a plain envelope marked “demonstration copy.” It has issue number 3 and a revision date of 12 September 2026. The web text capture was made on 17 September. The contact sheet was current as of 15 September. A draft from July in the staff archive gives an older telephone number ending in 0118, but that number is not printed in the issue 3 sample. The draft is retained for comparison only. A sticky note on the July copy says “wrong number maybe,” and the current team did not use that older draft as the basis for the assessment.

Review discussion. Beatriz said the invoice and the product assessment are separate matters. A correct guide cannot authorize a handling charge, and an invoice discrepancy does not prove a guide is inaccurate. Another staff member asked whether the close invoice total could be rounded to 900 dollars. Beatriz said there is no rounding question: the exact charge is 918 dollars and the exact authorized amount is 900 dollars. The guide’s displayed benefit threshold also must not be changed to 2,401 dollars simply because a different training example uses that amount. Staff noted that a nearby draft price list shows a 20-dollar handling charge for a different supplier, but that price list does not apply to Meridian Analytics or this order.

Action log. Procurement: request corrected invoice or signed authorized amendment for the 18-dollar handling line; keep payment pending; record that six units and authorized freight are accepted. Supplier follow-up due 28 September 2026. Product assessment: correct the review summary so it does not repeat the contradicted draft verdict; retain the four criterion findings; note testing limitations. Records clerk: keep the original invoice, purchase order, receiving sheet, correspondence, and marked-up reviewer draft in the same bundle. No payment release was made during this review. No claim is made that Meridian has already refunded or credited the handling amount.

Attachment note — unrelated sample records. A training purchase order for a document scanner authorizes 410 dollars, and its invoice is also 410 dollars. A separate benefits brochure uses a 2,200-dollar threshold for a different pilot, not the borough temporary grocery benefit. These materials were present in the shared folder but are not part of the HS-77 evidence. The reviewer flagged them to prevent accidental copying of their numbers into this packet. The correct threshold for the product review described above remains 2,400 dollars, and the correct authorized invoice amount remains 900 dollars.

Final checked summary, 22 September 2026. Invoice MA-8816 bills 918 dollars. Purchase order HB-5037 authorizes 900 dollars for six stands and freight. The 18-dollar handling line lacks an approved authorization, so payment is pending correction or documentation. Receipt of the six stands is confirmed. The Pocket Guide sample matches the supplied current contact sheet and the supplied benefit rule on the four criteria assessed. Earlier reviewer comments stating full invoice compliance and guide inaccuracy are not supported by the compared records. [{"state":"PUBLIC ACCESS PERMIT AGREEMENT — CONSOLIDATED FILE
File reference: PA-4187. Applicant: Oren Tanaka, operating Northwind Freight. Authority: Bellwether Borough Public Realm Office. Site: loading bay and temporary pedestrian diversion at 18 Quill Street. This file contains the executed agreement, amendments, inspection records, and closeout review. All dates and quantities below are the records maintained by the Borough; a staff opinion is not itself a determination of compliance.

Original clause 4, executed 6 February 2026: “The permit holder may occupy the marked loading bay from 07:00 to 10:00 on each authorized weekday. The pedestrian route must remain at least 1.8 metres wide at all times. A marshal shall be present whenever a vehicle is manoeuvring across the public footway. The permit holder shall pay the daily occupation charge shown in Schedule A. No vehicle may remain in the bay outside the authorized period.” Schedule A lists a daily charge of £42.00 and a refundable security deposit of £300. The permit is not transferable. The permit holder must notify the office of any requested change in the route or operating period and obtain written approval before implementing it.

The site plan, revision 2, shows a 2.0-metre clear route along the western edge of the works. A printed note on the plan says “preferred width 2.0 m”; the signed clause’s enforceable minimum remains 1.8 metres. The plan identifies two bollards at the route entrance, each 0.15 metres wide, and a temporary barrier line set 2.2 metres from the building frontage. The clear width is measured between the barrier and the bollard faces, not from the centreline. The measurement method was confirmed by the Borough surveyor in an email dated 8 February.

Initial permit officer’s internal summary, 7 February: “Applicant has a two-metre pedestrian route and paid £42 per day. The opening plan appears compliant. Recommend approval subject to routine monitoring.” The agreement was approved with the signed minimum-width clause, not with a guarantee that the preferred plan width would always be maintained. The summary was an administrative recommendation and does not amend the contract.

Amendment 1, requested by Tanaka on 12 February and approved in writing by the Borough on 14 February: “On 18 and 19 February only, occupation may begin at 06:30. All other conditions, including the 10:00 end time, the 1.8-metre route minimum, and marshal requirement, remain unchanged.” The amendment is limited to those two dates. An email from a neighbouring shop asking for 06:00 access was not an amendment and was not approved.

Amendment 2, requested 20 February: the permit holder asked to move the temporary barrier 0.25 metres toward the building. The office replied on 21 February: “No approval is given. Maintain the approved alignment until a revised plan is issued.” No revised plan was issued. An employee wrote in a chat, “That small shift should be fine; everyone can get through.” The chat did not come from an authorized officer and is not a waiver.

Inspection log, 24 February, 09:12. Inspector measured the narrowest clear gap at the west entrance as 1.72 metres. The tape was placed between the barrier and the nearest bollard face, consistent with the agreed method. The inspector noted that the route was unobstructed and a marshal was standing by the vehicle crossing. A photograph shows one pallet behind the barrier, not projecting into the public route. At 09:30, the applicant’s site lead moved the barrier back to the approved alignment. A second measurement at 09:42 recorded 1.91 metres. The first measure was not corrected or withdrawn; the second establishes that the condition was restored, not that the earlier measurement was mistaken.

Internal case note entered 25 February by reviewer Marta Vale: “The 24 February visit was satisfactory; no permit breach occurred because the route was passable and the pallet stayed behind the line. Mark compliance complete.” The note is a reviewer’s conclusion. It conflicts with the contract’s minimum-width condition and the inspector’s documented measurement. The reviewer did not identify an exception allowing a narrower route when it remained passable.

Charge ledger: 18 February, £42; 19 February, £42; 20 February, £42; 23 February, £42; 24 February, £42. The invoice covers five authorized days at £42 each, total £210. A separate £300 entry is the deposit, not an occupation charge. The applicant’s bank transfer of £210 was received on 26 February and allocated against the five-day invoice. There are no late fees in the ledger. A draft note says “£252 still due, counting the two early starts as extra days”; the amendment explicitly permits early starts on two listed days without adding an extra occupation day, and the invoice does not bill those starts separately.

Closeout measurements: the authority’s form asks whether the route ever fell below the enforceable width during the authorized work. It distinguishes a technical submission failure from the merits of the permit application.

The Directorate’s renewal rule requires a complete application to be received by 17:00 on the final day of the existing permit. A portal receipt showing a completed submission is evidence of receipt. A saved draft, payment authorization, or upload attempt is not a completed submission. When the official portal is unavailable, applicants may use the documented outage email channel; the message must reach the address listed on the service status page before the same deadline. The Directorate does not extend deadlines merely because a user experiences a local device problem. A verified Directorate-wide outage activates a manual grace process only if the applicant sent the complete application to the outage address by the deadline.

Permit terms: Bluefin Labs held access permit BA-204 until 12 May 2026, 17:00. Its renewal application required a signed declaration, current insurance certificate, site plan, and £120 processing payment. The previous permit allowed service access on weekdays, 08:00–16:00. The renewal did not request expanded hours. The supporting plan and insurance certificate were uploaded to the portal. The declaration and processing payment were separate required items.

Timeline from monitoring logs: 11 May, 16:42, user signed into the portal; 16:49, two attachments uploaded; 16:52, payment provider returned authorization code; 16:54, the portal displayed “Draft saved.” At 16:55, the user clicked “Submit.” The application server returned an error before generating a receipt number. At 16:58, the portal status page reported intermittent delays, not a Directorate-wide outage. At 17:06, monitoring confirmed a database connection incident affecting several accounts. The Directorate’s formal incident window began 17:06, after the stated deadline. A successful renewal receipt was not generated on 11 May.

Applicant email to the help desk, 12 May, 08:14: “I completed this yesterday before five and the portal failed on your side. Please renew the permit.” The email included the signed declaration as an attachment and referenced the earlier uploads. It was sent to the ordinary help-desk address, not the outage address listed on the status page. The original application was therefore not completed before the deadline, and the later email did not meet the documented outage-channel procedure. No record shows a complete application reaching the special address before 17:00.

Help-desk first response, 12 May, 09:03: “Your renewal was received at 16:52 yesterday because the payment was authorized. The permit is renewed automatically.” The agent relied on the payment authorization timestamp and misread it as a submission receipt. The portal audit contains no receipt ID, and the status was “Draft saved.” The first response is an erroneous service note, not proof that the system completed the required submission. A supervisor later marked the response “confirmed” without reviewing the log.

Outage report: the database incident affected 14 users from 17:06 to 18:22 on 11 May. The service team investigated whether the error at 16:55 had the same cause. The gateway logs show a rejected session token at 16:55, while the database alerts began at 17:06. Engineers found no evidence that the later database incident caused the earlier rejection. The user’s browser had an expired authentication token, renewed after a fresh login. The postmortem does not blame the applicant; it only assesses the formal renewal conditions. A draft executive summary says, “Directorate outage prevented timely filing; accept as timely.” That verdict is contradicted by the incident timestamps and the required channel record.

The complete application was eventually received through the ordinary portal on 13 May at 10:21. The system generated receipt R-77304. July readings: opening 13,050 litres, closing 13,700 litres, a difference of 650 litres. The volunteer log totals 684 litres because two estimates overlapped for a 17 July session and a 22 July session. The steward removed the duplicate entries in a corrected copy. The recorded meter difference is still controlling under clause 6. All identified July use was irrigation at plots 8–14. A note in the draft closeout says “July use was 684, therefore 16 litres under limit,” but that arithmetic uses the wrong measure; it happens to be below 900, while the meter difference is 650. The draft verdict that July exceeded a limit is not supported by either value.

August readings: opening 13,700 litres, closing 14,645 litres, a difference of 945 litres. The executed August cap is 1,000 litres, so the meter difference is 55 litres below the permitted maximum. The daily log totals 1,032 litres. It includes an estimated 87 litres used on 8 August to wash tools and 36 litres used on 9 August to irrigate plot 15, outside the named plots. The remaining entries total 909 litres of irrigation within the authorized plots. The August meter difference, not the summed daily estimates, determines whether the volume cap was exceeded. The uses at the wrong purpose and location remain separately subject to the permitted-use restrictions.

Inspector’s note, 10 August: “No violation observed. The holder stayed under the 1,000-litre allowance and all water was used on the named plots.” The first part is consistent with the meter difference, but the second part is contradicted by the dated log entries for tool washing and plot 15. A compliance clerk copied the whole inspector note into the closeout decision and selected “fully compliant.” The file contains no evidence that the 87-litre tool-washing entry or the 36-litre plot-15 entry was removed from the log. The holder’s later explanation says the team “did not think a quick rinse counted as water use” and that plot 15 was watered by mistake.

The valve record shows the standpipe valve was left open after the 8 August session. A site steward closed it at 16:18. The meter cannot distinguish water used during the session from water lost while the valve remained open. The 945-litre monthly difference includes all measured water and remains below the August maximum. The permit separately requires the valve to be closed after each use. The record does not quantify any additional amount attributable to the open valve, and the office should not invent a quantity or treat the entire monthly volume as unauthorized. The obligation is about closing the valve, not merely staying under the volume cap.

Email from holder, 11 August: “We stayed under the limit, and we never used water outside the garden.” The first statement is supported by the August meter difference and 1,000-litre cap. The second is contradicted by the log entry for plot 15, which is outside plots 8–14. The plot-15 entry is an irrigation use, not a tool-washing use, and the record describes it as accidental. The contract does not create an intent exception for use outside the named plots. A preliminary manager comment says “holder admits unauthorized commercial extraction,” but no sale is alleged in the underlying records; the holder’s statement concerns watering, not commercial activity.

The file’s evidence index includes a photo dated 9 August showing a hose near the shared path. The image does not establish that water flowed into the path or that the path was blocked. The steward’s inspection says the path was clear. The photo is a distractor for the path-clearance condition and is not evidence of that condition being breached. No complaint from a garden visitor is recorded. The present review is limited to the use restrictions, monthly volume, and valve requirement.

Internal comments, 12 August: Technician: “The 1,032 litres in the log is above the amended cap; mark excess use.” Reviewer: “The clause says monthly meter difference controls. August is 945, not 1,032. That resolves quantity, but it does not erase the separate purpose and location entries or the valve note.” The technician’s draft finding treats the daily estimates as the controlling monthly total. The reviewer’s distinction is consistent with the written terms. A subsequent cover sheet still says “volume breach, 32 litres.” Its author used the draft 1,000-litre cap and daily log total, not the signed amendment and meter reading.

The permit’s definition of “authorized irrigation” includes watering edible and ornamental plants within the named plots. It excludes washing equipment, even if the equipment was used for gardening, and excludes watering any plot outside the listed range. There is no de minimis exception for a brief rinse or a mistaken location. The rule does not say that any unauthorized purpose automatically makes all water use unauthorized; classify each described use on its own facts. It also does not say that an estimated log total overrides verified meter readings for the cap.

Closeout review asks the office to select all applicable findings from the file. A staff member’s pasted verdict says “no findings; the permit holder was below the cap.” That correctly reflects the volume limit alone, but it does not resolve whether every recorded use complied with the purpose and location restrictions or whether the valve was closed as required. Conversely, a finding of excess monthly volume based on 1,032 litres would not be supported by the controlling measurement. The final answer should not convert an accurate conclusion on one clause into a blanket conclusion about all clauses.

Appendix, signature and amendment control: the original permit was signed on 25 May. Amendment A was signed by both parties on 15 June; Amendment B was signed by both parties on 29 July. The unsigned 1,100-litre draft is retained only for audit. The authority has no record of a later amendment, verbal waiver, or correction to the August meter reading. The steward verified the opening and closing values against the meter photographs. The daily log was submitted by the holder and its entries are not disputed. The issue is how those facts map to distinct terms, not whether the records exist.

Appendix, monthly arithmetic: June 13,050 − 12,400 = 650 litres, against 900. July 13,700 − 13,050 = 650 litres, against 900. August 14,645 − 13,700 = 945 litres, against the amended 1,000. The daily log sums should not be substituted for these calculations. The authorized date range and monthly cap are independent of whether a particular use was irrigation at an authorized location. A month may be below its cap while including a prohibited use. The record reports no sale, no blocked path, and no evidence that the entire August meter difference was attributable to any one prohibited act.

Final review instruction: record whether the month-volume limit was exceeded and, separately, which listed conduct is established. The inspector’s and clerk’s global “fully compliant” verdict is contradicted by the logged non-irrigation and out-of-area uses and by the valve record.
