[{"state":"Copperleaf Logistics SaaS Operations Incident Review: Consolidated Case File

Document control
Record: CL-OPS-4817
Review owner: Priya Tanaka, Service Operations
Customer contact: Bao Moreau, Copperleaf Logistics
Service provider: Meridian Stack Services
Opened: 14 June, 08:10 UTC
Compilation purpose: Internal review of the customer report, service events, communications, applicable service terms, and disposition proposed by the incident desk. This file combines the customer chat transcript, the relevant terms-of-service extract, operational entries, and the email thread with quoted replies. All times in the file use UTC unless a line explicitly says otherwise. Statements attributed to a participant are retained as evidence, not automatically endorsed as findings. A proposed disposition is an administrative recommendation and does not supersede the event record.

Executive routing note
At 14 June, 08:10, the service desk received a report concerning the Copperleaf Logistics dispatch workspace. The account uses the Meridian Stack hosted dispatch and reconciliation suite. The initial customer report mentioned access difficulty, repeated notifications, delayed exports, and a question about the monthly service charge. Subsequent messages expanded the report and supplied examples. The incident desk created one parent case and several linked work items. During initial triage, a clerk entered the sentence, “No refund was requested; this is an ordinary support enquiry.” The same sentence was copied into a draft closure recommendation. The source communications below are included so that the record can be reviewed against that recommendation.

This file is arranged as follows: the first section records receipt and routing; the second reproduces the customer chat; the third sets out the applicable service terms; the fourth summarizes the operational record; the fifth contains the email thread and quoted replies; the sixth gives the review log and administrative handling notes. A record may be complete for routing purposes while still containing an unverified statement. “Closed” in the ticketing interface means that a particular work item has been administratively closed; it does not necessarily mean that every reported symptom has ceased. The operational entries preserve that distinction.

1. Receipt and initial routing

At 08:10, the customer portal generated case CL-OPS-4817. The account contact field identified Bao Moreau as the submitting user. The submission was routed to the SaaS operations queue because the affected product was Dispatch Ledger, rather than to the general billing queue. The queue assignment was made automatically from the selected product field. It did not constitute a decision about whether the customer had made a billing request.

The portal form contained the following free-text report, retained without editorial changes: “Since this morning our team cannot reliably open the dispatch board. Some people get in after refreshing and some do not. The export button takes a long time and then the file is missing. We have also received the same status alert more than once. I need someone to check the charge as well, because I may have been billed for the period when we could not use this properly. Please tell me how to request a refund if that is what applies.” The report included two screenshots and one downloaded activity log. The attachments were indexed as evidence items A, B, and C. No attachment was altered during compilation.

A routing clerk added a triage note at 08:14: “Likely usability issue. No refund request is apparent; customer only asks how the process works.” That note was entered before the full chat transcript was reviewed. At 08:19, an operations coordinator added: “Customer says they may have been billed for time unavailable. Billing determination pending.” The two notes are not equivalent. The first is a characterization; the second records a pending review. Neither is a customer statement.

At 08:25, the parent case was assigned to the incident desk. The customer account was marked as a logistics customer with an active enterprise subscription. This classification identifies the account tier, not the cause or severity of the incident. The incident desk opened linked work items for access, notifications, export generation, and billing review. A fifth item was created to maintain customer communications. No linked item was initially created for data loss because the submitted attachments did not establish that a saved dispatch record had been lost. The absence of a data-loss work item is not a finding that data loss was impossible; it reflects only the evidence available at that time.

The initial impact field read “limited to some users; scope under review.” The field was later revised twice as more staff reported access problems. The revision history is retained in section 4. The first automated severity suggestion was “S3, localized inconvenience.” A reviewer did not accept that suggestion as a final severity determination. The incident team applied the service terms and the account impact record instead. A severity label describes the provider’s response classification; it does not itself prove the customer’s particular symptoms.

The portal displayed a standard acknowledgment stating that the submission had been received and that a support agent would respond. The acknowledgment did not promise a refund, a service credit, or a resolution time. Bao replied to the acknowledgment at 08:31: “Thank you. To be clear, I am asking for the refund review now, not only instructions for a possible future request. We have already had a charge for the current service period.” The reply was attached to the parent case and was available to the billing queue at 08:33. The initial triage note was not amended at that time.

2. Customer chat transcript

The following transcript was exported from the customer support interface. Participants are identified by their account names. System-generated routing text is marked as such. The transcript is reproduced in chronological order; a later message does not erase an earlier one unless the speaker expressly retracts it.

08:42 — Bao Moreau, Copperleaf Logistics: We are trying to complete the morning dispatch run. The board sometimes loads, but the lane list stays blank. Refreshing has helped once and failed twice. I also have duplicate status alerts in the shared operations mailbox.

08:44 — Service Desk, Meridian Stack Services: Thank you. Please confirm whether the issue affects one operator or more than one operator, and whether the dispatch board is unavailable continuously or intermittently.

08:46 — Bao Moreau: More than one. I have three people reporting it in this channel, and another colleague is checking. It is intermittent, not a full-time blank screen. The export is a separate problem: the request sits in processing, and one completed request did not leave a file in the download area.

08:48 — Service Desk: We have recorded access and export symptoms. The notification report is also noted. Are you asking for a review of the invoice, or only asking how to file a billing query?

08:50 — Bao Moreau: I am asking for an invoice review and a refund for the service charge covering the period affected, if the charge is not justified under our terms. Please do not treat that as a question about where the form is. I want the request logged, even if the review later decides no money is due.

08:53 — Service Desk: Understood. I will create a billing review item and note that you have requested a refund review. The billing team will assess the subscription charge against the service record and applicable terms. This acknowledgment does not decide the amount or eligibility.

08:55 — Bao Moreau: Yes, that is the request. For the operations issue, the board is still loading inconsistently. We have not confirmed that any dispatch record disappeared. The missing export file is concerning, but it is not the same as a deleted record.

09:02 — Service Desk: The linked operations ticket is open. Please provide the approximate time of the export attempt and the affected workspace name. Avoid sending credentials in chat.

09:04 — Bao Moreau: Workspace is North Yard. First export attempt was shortly before 08:00. Second was after 08:30. We use the same workspace for today’s dispatch plan and yesterday’s reconciliation. No passwords are included in the attachment.

09:09 — Service Desk: We received the activity log. It indicates an export request was accepted and later timed out. We cannot infer from that event alone whether the export file was retained or whether a report was omitted. Engineering is checking the job record.

09:12 — Bao Moreau: The duplicate alerts are from two separate order changes, but each change generated two identical emails. We did not click a resend button. I can provide message headers if needed.

09:15 — Service Desk: Please attach the headers through the secure case upload. The queue will compare them with the event identifiers. We have not yet established whether the duplicate messages were generated by the platform or by mail forwarding rules.

09:18 — Bao Moreau: I will attach them. Also, our second operator, Nia, cannot keep the board open for more than a few minutes. It returns to the loading screen. I am not saying every user is affected; I am saying this is not one person’s browser.

09:21 — Service Desk: Recorded as a multi-user, intermittent access symptom. We will test the service-side session record before asking you to clear browser data. Please keep the affected devices available if a diagnostic session is arranged.

09:28 — Bao Moreau: I have now attached the mail headers and a short screen recording. The recording shows the lane list loading, disappearing, and loading again. The recording does not show a successful export.

09:34 — Service Desk: The attachments are indexed. The incident team is checking the account region and service health. We will not ask you to repeat the dispatch plan in a public channel.

09:41 — Bao Moreau: A teammate has managed to open the board, but then it stopped responding again. Please do not mark this fixed based on one successful load. The export still has no file.

09:46 — Service Desk: Noted. One successful session is evidence of partial availability, not confirmation that the intermittent symptom has ended. The case remains open while the checks continue.

10:03 — Bao Moreau: We can work around the board by using the printed dispatch sheet. That is slower and means we have to reconcile later. It does not resolve the service issue.

10:08 — Service Desk: The workaround has been recorded as a mitigation. The service status remains under investigation. We will provide an update when the job queue and session logs have been compared.

10:19 — Bao Moreau: Please make sure the refund request remains attached to the case. If the service charge is fully justified, tell me why. If some amount is eligible, I want the eligible amount returned or credited, according to the terms.

10:24 — Service Desk: Confirmed. The billing review item states “customer requests refund review for affected service period; amount and eligibility not yet determined.” No refund has been approved or denied at this stage.

10:33 — Bao Moreau: We received two more duplicate status emails, this time for one order change. That makes the notification issue current, not just something from earlier in the morning.

10:38 — Service Desk: We have added the later headers. The notification item remains open pending comparison of message identifiers and account forwarding configuration.

10:51 — Bao Moreau: One person can open the board now, but another still cannot. The export screen says “complete” without a downloadable file. Please keep the access and export items separate; they may have different causes.

10:56 — Service Desk: Agreed. The linked items will remain separately tracked. A displayed completion state is not treated as proof of a successful file delivery when the download area is empty.

11:14 — Bao Moreau: The service desk has asked us to test again. The board showed the lane list for about a minute, then the page returned to the spinner. No dispatch entry was changed during that test.

11:20 — Service Desk: The test result has been added to the case. Engineering has requested a server-side trace for the relevant workspace and time range. That request is being processed; it is not yet a resolution.

11:42 — Bao Moreau: We have a temporary way to export by selecting fewer rows, but the normal daily export still fails for the full dispatch set. We need the full export for reconciliation. Is this being counted as fixed because the smaller one worked?

11:48 — Service Desk: No. The reduced export is a partial workaround. The full-set export symptom remains open. The case’s resolution field has not been changed.

12:06 — Bao Moreau: I have also noticed that two staff members were logged out unexpectedly. They could sign back in, but they had to re-enter their filters. I cannot tell whether that is linked to the board problem.

12:11 — Service Desk: We will record unexpected session termination as an observation and test whether it shares a service event. At present, linkage is unconfirmed. Please do not re-enter any sensitive data merely for testing.

12:36 — Service Desk: Engineering reports a rise in session refresh failures in the account region. A mitigation has been applied to a portion of traffic. The board may load more consistently, but checks are ongoing. The export queue has a separate backlog under examination.

12:41 — Bao Moreau: The board is better for me at this moment, but the other operator is still seeing the spinner. The export has still not appeared. The duplicate emails have also not stopped. That is not a full restoration from our side.

12:49 — Service Desk: Your update is recorded. The mitigation is partial. Access, export, and notification checks remain active. The service desk has not marked the parent case resolved.

13:07 — Bao Moreau: I want to avoid confusion in the final record. We have four reported operational problems: intermittent board access, repeated notifications, a missing full export, and unexpected logouts. There is also the invoice and refund review. The logout issue may be connected, but it happened and should not be omitted.

13:13 — Service Desk: We have recorded the four operational observations separately, with the logout item marked as linkage unconfirmed. The billing review remains a separate work item. The number of work items does not determine the number of confirmed platform defects.

13:28 — Bao Moreau: Another full export request has completed without a file. We can provide its request identifier. The smaller export still works if we split the rows, but that is not an acceptable replacement for the normal report during a busy dispatch period.

13:33 — Service Desk: Please add the request identifier. The full export remains under investigation. A successful smaller export is not being used as closure evidence for the full export workflow.

13:49 — Bao Moreau: The colleague who was logged out has now been able to stay signed in for twenty minutes. The second operator’s board is still intermittent. I am providing this as an update, not withdrawing the report.

13:55 — Service Desk: Understood. We will preserve both the earlier unexpected logout and the later stable session as separate observations. The later session does not retract the earlier event.

14:11 — Service Desk: Current engineering note: session refresh failures have decreased but remain above the account’s normal range. Export jobs for large workspaces are still delayed, and the team has not verified delivery for the failed request identifiers. Notification headers are being compared. No all-clear has been issued.

14:18 — Bao Moreau: Thank you. Please do not close the case while the other operator sees the spinner and the full export is missing. I also repeat my refund request. I understand that asking for a review does not guarantee that the review will find an amount due.

14:23 — Service Desk: The case remains open. The refund request is recorded as an active customer request, with eligibility pending review. The service symptoms are not declared resolved.

14:37 — Bao Moreau: The board has opened twice for me since the mitigation, but the second operator just reported another loading loop. We still have duplicate alerts from one status change. There is no full export file in the workspace.

14:42 — Service Desk: We have added those observations. Please retain the original request identifiers rather than repeatedly submitting the same full export, to avoid creating additional queued jobs.

15:06 — Bao Moreau: Confirming we have not submitted another export. The first two request identifiers are still the ones to investigate. The most recent board test did not stay loaded. This is still active from our perspective.

15:14 — Service Desk: Recorded. The operations team is comparing the trace for those requests. The case status is “investigating,” not “resolved.”

15:32 — Bao Moreau: We can finish today’s dispatch using the paper plan, but someone will need to reconcile it later. That is a business workaround, not a sign-off on the affected service.

15:39 — Service Desk: The workaround and its follow-up burden are recorded. No customer acceptance of a resolution has been recorded.

16:02 — Bao Moreau: The invoice request is still open too. Please ensure finance sees the chat where I said I am asking for a refund review, not merely instructions.

16:07 — Service Desk: The billing item is linked to the parent case and the 08:50 chat message is included. The finance queue has access to the source transcript.

16:26 — Bao Moreau: One of the duplicate alert examples has an identical message identifier in the headers. The other pair has distinct identifiers but the same subject and body. I am not claiming we know the cause; I am saying there were repeated messages.

16:33 — Service Desk: Both examples are retained. The identical identifier may indicate a delivery duplication; the separate identifiers may indicate repeated generation. Engineering has not yet confirmed the mechanism.

16:51 — Bao Moreau: The dispatch board is loading for me again, but the second operator has not confirmed. The full export remains unavailable. We should not treat my access alone as representative of all users.

16:57 — Service Desk: Agreed. The observation is limited to your account and time. The multi-user symptom remains in the review record until checked.

17:18 — Service Desk: Operations update: a queue adjustment has reduced some export delays. Two earlier jobs are still marked complete in the control plane, but the corresponding files have not been found in the customer download area. Notification investigation is incomplete. Session behavior is improved but not verified as normal.

17:26 — Bao Moreau: I checked both file locations and the shared folder. Neither full export is there. The board is open for me at present. The other operator is away from the desk, so I cannot report a new test from them.

3. Applicable terms-of-service extract

Extract identifier: MS-ENT-2025-04, Copperleaf Logistics enterprise schedule. This extract was attached to the review record by the contract administration desk. It is reproduced for the limited purpose of identifying which terms were used in the service and billing review. The original signed schedule controls if an authenticated copy differs from this extract. No discrepancy was identified during this review.

Section 2. Definitions. “Service period” means the subscription interval shown on an invoice. “Service interruption” means a material inability to use a covered function that is attributable to the hosted service, as distinguished from a local device, customer configuration, or third-party network condition. “Customer request” means a communication in which an authorized account contact asks Meridian Stack to take an action or make a determination. A request may be made even where the customer recognizes that the outcome is uncertain. A question asking only for general information, without asking that the customer’s own account or charge be reviewed, is not by itself a refund request. “Service credit” means an account adjustment calculated under section 8; “refund” means a return of money under section 9. The existence of a customer request does not establish eligibility for either remedy.

Section 3. Availability records. Meridian Stack will maintain service health records and may use those records, customer reports, and diagnostic material to assess availability. An isolated successful login does not necessarily establish that an intermittent problem has ended. A customer workaround does not change the recorded availability of the hosted function. Conversely, a failed operation does not by itself establish a service interruption if the failure resulted from an excluded customer-side condition. The service desk may keep distinct symptoms in separate work items pending assessment of whether they share a cause.

Section 4. Reporting. The customer should report a suspected interruption through the support portal or the designated service channel and include the affected workspace, approximate time, and relevant request identifiers where available. A report is not invalid merely because every requested diagnostic detail is not initially supplied. The customer must not include credentials in a public support message. Meridian Stack may request additional evidence through the secure upload facility. The date and time of the first report are determined from the portal receipt and associated messages, not from the time at which an agent completes classification.

Section 5. Exclusions. No service credit is due to the extent that an interruption is caused solely by the customer’s own equipment, customer-managed configuration, an unsupported integration, or a third-party network beyond Meridian Stack’s control. If multiple causes contribute, the review must identify the basis for excluding a portion rather than assuming that any customer-side component defeats the whole claim. A temporary workaround, including manual entry or reduced-volume processing, is relevant to impact but is not automatically a restoration of the covered function. The existence of a workaround does not waive a customer’s right to report an interruption.

Section 6. Maintenance. Scheduled maintenance announced at least forty-eight hours in advance is excluded from the availability calculation for the stated window. Emergency maintenance may be excluded only where the notice and incident record establish that the maintenance caused the relevant effect. A general maintenance notice, without a matching time and function, is not enough to attribute a particular symptom to maintenance. No scheduled maintenance notice matching the reported North Yard event was found in the account record for 14 June. That statement concerns this incident date and does not make a finding about all other dates.

Section 7. Service review. A customer may ask Meridian Stack to review an invoice or the service record. A request for review is not an admission by either party that an amount is owed. Meridian Stack will compare the invoice, subscription schedule, incident record, and relevant exclusions. The customer may request that a possible refund or credit be considered as part of that review. The request must be recorded even if the applicable amount is not yet known. The service desk must not convert an expressly stated request into a mere request for instructions solely because the customer also asks how the terms apply.

Section 8. Service credits. Where the recorded monthly availability for a covered function falls below the threshold stated in the enterprise schedule, the customer may be eligible for a credit calculated under the schedule. Eligibility is assessed by function and service period. A credit is not automatic and is subject to the stated exclusions, the account’s schedule, and the claim procedure. The service operations team provides the evidence; the billing team calculates any eligible adjustment. A preliminary operations status does not constitute approval or denial of a credit.

Section 9. Refund review. A customer may request a refund review for a service charge by identifying the account and the affected service period. The request may be made before a final eligibility determination. Finance will decide whether the agreement permits a refund, whether a credit is the prescribed remedy, or whether no adjustment is due. The customer’s use of the word “refund” is sufficient to record the type of review requested; it does not, by itself, establish that the customer is entitled to money. If a customer asks only for the location of a form and does not ask for review of a charge, the service desk may provide instructions without recording a refund request. If the customer later clearly asks for a review of their own charge, the later message must be recorded as a request from that time.

Section 10. Case status. “Investigating” indicates that one or more material questions remain under review. “Mitigated” indicates that a measure has reduced the observed effect but does not establish that the underlying issue has ceased. “Resolved” is used when the relevant work item has met its closure conditions. Closure of one linked item does not close other items or the parent case unless the remaining items have also met their criteria. The customer’s account of continuing symptoms must be retained and assessed; it need not be accepted without verification, but it must not be omitted merely because a dashboard shows a partial success.

Section 11. Customer communications. An acknowledgment confirms receipt only. An agent may summarize a customer’s report but must preserve material qualifications, including uncertainty about cause, the difference between an observed event and a suspected cause, and the distinction between requesting a review and asserting entitlement. A staff member’s suggested disposition is not a determination unless the authorized reviewing team has completed the required assessment. A previous agent summary does not override the underlying communication where the two conflict.

Section 12. Records and retention. The support transcript, submitted attachments, event identifiers, and case status changes are retained in the case record according to the account retention schedule. A copied note is not a substitute for the source communication. The review owner should identify the source when a disputed summary is relied upon. Entries made by automated systems are evidence of what the system recorded, but their labels may be provisional and must be interpreted in context. A field labelled “complete” may describe a processing stage and is not conclusive proof that a customer received an output file.

Section 13. Review and appeal. The customer may request a second review if they consider a billing or service determination inconsistent with the agreement or with the recorded evidence. Such a request does not alter the original incident chronology. The second reviewer should consider the source records, not merely the first reviewer’s conclusion. The account contact may provide further evidence through the portal. The review team should separately state what the customer requested, what operational facts were verified, what remains uncertain, and what remedy, if any, was authorized.

6. Review log and administrative handling

The review owner examined the portal receipt, chat export, message headers, screen recording, operational entries, terms extract, and email thread. The owner treated the source communications as evidence of what the customer said and the operational records as evidence of what the platform recorded. Where the record did not establish a cause or final outcome, the review preserved that uncertainty rather than converting a provisional statement into a fact.

The review owner noted that the phrase “how to request a refund” appeared in the first portal submission. Read alone, that phrase might describe a process question. The same submission also said that the customer may have been billed for a period when service was not properly usable. More importantly, the 08:31 reply expressly said, “I am asking for the refund review now,” and the 08:50 chat expressly asked for an invoice review and a refund for the affected service charge, subject to the terms. The customer then repeated the request at 10:19, 14:18, 16:02, 18:47, and in the email thread. The record contains no retraction. The customer’s qualification that eligibility is uncertain limits the claim about entitlement; it does not negate the request for review.

The review owner also examined the 14:35 draft statement. Its conclusion that the service was restored was inconsistent with the current “investigating” status, the customer’s continuing reports, and the operational entries describing partial mitigation and unverified export files. Its statement that all reports were customer-side effects was not supported by the session telemetry and had not been reached by engineering. Its statement that no refund was requested was directly inconsistent with the source messages. The draft was therefore retained as a historical planted characterization, not adopted as a finding. The record does not assume that every employee summary is wrong; it checks each summary against the evidence.

The operational record does not make every customer-reported event a fully verified service defect. For access, there is both a customer report and a service-side signal of elevated refresh failures, but scope and cause for each user remain under review. For exports, the customer reported missing full files; the job records show completion markers without verified files in the customer-facing area. The cause of the discrepancy remains unsettled. For notifications, submitted headers support repeated messages, while the mechanism is still under analysis. For unexpected logouts, the customer observed events and linkage to the broader incident is unconfirmed. These distinctions are maintained so that an event report is neither erased nor overstated.

The terms require a separate financial decision. The customer made a request for review; this file does not decide whether any charge was unjustified, whether a credit is the applicable remedy, or whether a refund is due. Finance has acknowledged intake and is comparing the invoice, account schedule, and incident record. The existence of the request must be represented accurately while that work is pending.

The quality reviewer rejected a proposed shortcut under which one successful test would close all operational items. The service terms distinguish mitigation from resolution, and the case has separate work items. The record further distinguishes a reduced-volume export from the full report and a successful session from stable access across the reported users. No account of the customer’s experience is treated as universal beyond the evidence supplied; likewise, a single successful sample is not treated as proof that the intermittent symptoms ceased.

At the time of compilation, the parent case status is investigating. The access, export, and notification items have not all met their closure criteria. The billing review is pending. The customer has supplied a workaround but has not accepted it as resolution. The customer’s request for a refund review remains active. Any subsequent change to these facts must be supported by a later operational record, a completed finance decision, or a clear customer retraction; none is present in this file.

Administrative disposition proposed by review owner: preserve the original triage and draft notes for audit; annotate them as contradicted where appropriate; retain the customer’s express refund-review request as an active request; do not characterize financial eligibility as established; retain the parent incident as investigating; and continue the separate work items until their respective evidence and closure criteria are satisfied. This disposition is a proposal for accurate recordkeeping and routing. It is not a final decision on the customer’s financial entitlement, and it is not an engineering root-cause conclusion.

Appendix B: Status vocabulary used in this file

“Reported” means that a participant communicated an observation. It does not alone establish cause. “Supported” means that another record is consistent with the observation or provides corroborating evidence. “Verified” is reserved for a completed check against an identified source. “Pending” means that the responsible team has not completed its determination. “Mitigated” means that the observed effect has been reduced in some respect, without necessarily meeting closure criteria. “Resolved” requires the relevant work item to satisfy its closure conditions. “Requested” identifies an action the customer asked the provider to take; it does not establish that the requested outcome is owed. “Eligible” identifies a conclusion that must be reached under the applicable agreement and record; it is not inferred from the mere presence of a request.

The case interface has several fields that may be read together but should not be treated as synonyms. The customer’s report field captures the reported experience. The engineering field captures the current technical assessment. The finance field captures the billing review. The parent status summarizes case handling. A draft note can appear in the same interface as a verified event, but visual proximity does not make the draft authoritative. The source, author, timestamp, and subsequent review annotation determine how it should be interpreted.

Appendix C: Handover checklist

The incoming case owner is instructed to verify the current service status before sending any closure language. The owner should check whether the access tests cover the affected operators, whether the reported full export identifiers have customer-facing files, and whether the notification investigation has established a mechanism. The owner should record each completed check with its source and time. If a single user reports a stable session, the report should be preserved as a limited observation. If another user continues to report a loading loop, that report should be preserved as a separate observation. Neither entry should be silently substituted for the other.

The finance reviewer should compare the service period on the invoice with the account schedule and the final operational assessment. The reviewer should record the request as a request for review, not as an admission that money is due. If the outcome is a credit rather than a refund, the response should explain the contractual basis. If no adjustment is due, the response should identify the relevant evidence and term. The customer’s acknowledgment that the outcome is undecided must not be misread as withdrawal of the request.

The communications coordinator should avoid repeating the earlier draft verdict. If a summary is needed, it should state that the customer explicitly requested a refund review, that eligibility remains pending, and that operational checks remain in progress. The coordinator should not claim that all reports were customer-side effects unless engineering establishes that conclusion. The coordinator should not claim full restoration unless the applicable closure criteria are met. An automated field, copied note, or previous agent’s wording should be compared with the source records before being used.

The record should remain available for second review under the terms. If the customer supplies further headers, identifiers, or invoice information, the materials should be attached to the existing case rather than used to erase the earlier chronology. If the customer later expressly withdraws the refund request, that withdrawal should be timestamped and attached; no such withdrawal is currently recorded. If a particular symptom is later resolved, the responsible work item may be updated without assuming that all linked matters have ended.

Appendix D: Compilation note

This consolidated file includes both positive and negative evidence. Positive evidence includes the explicit refund-review language, the session telemetry, the customer-facing absence of the full export files at the time of checking, and the submitted repeated-message headers. Limiting evidence includes the absence of a final root-cause determination, uncertainty about the scope of each user’s access problem, uncertainty about notification mechanism, and the lack of a finance decision. The customer’s own qualification that the remedy is not guaranteed is included, as is the customer’s insistence that the request be logged. The proposed internal verdict is also included, but only as a proposed statement subject to comparison with the facts.

No conclusion in this file should be expanded beyond its stated scope. A confirmed request is not a confirmed entitlement. A mitigation is not necessarily a resolution. A completed processing stage is not necessarily delivery. An unresolved cause does not make a reported event disappear. [{"state":"Saltmarsh Studio support ticket SS-4817. Customer: Nadia Petrov. Product: ceramic pour-over set, order SS-90214. Opened 14 May, last updated 18 May. Ticket owner: Jalen Or. Customer message, 14 May, 09:12: “Hello, the blue ceramic dripper arrived with a hairline crack near the base. The outer carton is not crushed, but the inner paper sleeve was damp. I have attached two photos. I would like a replacement if possible, not money back; I need it for a housewarming this weekend. Please tell me whether I must send the cracked piece back.” Order record: one dripper, one matching server, $48.00 merchandise, $6.00 shipping, total charged $54.00. Payment captured successfully. Dispatch scan 10 May; delivery scan 13 May, 16:42. The product page at purchase described the set as “hand glazed; minor variation in color is normal.” It did not describe cracks as acceptable. Customer added: “I am not saying the color is wrong, the blue is lovely. Crack is the problem.”

Internal comment, Jalen, 14 May, 10:03: Photo reviewed. Crack appears on dripper only. Do not promise refund yet; check replacement stock. Customer did not use phrase refund in initial note. Policy card, version 4.2: For a verified transit defect reported within 21 calendar days after delivery, offer one replacement at no additional charge, subject to stock. If replacement is unavailable, offer refund of the affected item price; shipping is refunded only if the whole order is returned. Customer does not need to return a low-value ceramic part when photos establish breakage, but should be told to dispose of it safely. Color variation is not a defect if the item remains usable. This policy does not say that every complaint receives a refund, and it does not prevent a customer from asking for one.

Stock check, 14 May, 10:26: Dripper, blue, quantity available 17. Server, blue, quantity available 9. Warehouse has confirmed that the pieces are sold separately for replacement purposes. Jalen wrote: “Likely straightforward replacement, but wait for lead review because damp sleeve may mean packing issue.” A second internal note by quality associate Mira, 14 May, 11:40: “Photos show a narrow fracture line and a small chip. This is not glaze variation. We should send replacement dripper; no need return.”

Internal lead review, 14 May, 12:15, by Tomas Venn: “Refund requested. Approve full $54 immediately; no replacement needed.” The note was added as a disposition suggestion, not a customer quotation. In a follow-up clarification, Tomas writes: “I skimmed the queue and assumed refund from the standard complaint wording. I have not read the customer’s full message. Please verify what she actually asks for before selecting the customer-request field.” The case system recorded the lead suggestion in a prominent yellow box, while the customer’s request field remained blank. Jalen’s later note says the yellow box is not evidence of customer preference.

Customer message, 15 May, 08:05: “Thank you. To be clear, replacement is my first choice. I do not need a refund if you can send a sound blue dripper. If it cannot be sent before Friday, please say so and I will decide what to do. I am not asking you to refund the server; it is fine.” This message does not cancel or change the original report. Customer uploaded a clearer image at 08:11. The crack is visible in both images. No image suggests damage to server or shipping carton.

Operations update, 15 May, 10:00: Replacement order created for one blue dripper, with zero charge and standard shipping. Expected dispatch 16 May. The warehouse pick list mistakenly showed a complete set; fulfillment corrected it before shipment, so only one dripper was allocated. Jalen notified Nadia at 10:22: “We will send only the dripper. You do not need to return the broken part. The server stays with you.” Customer replied, “That is exactly what I wanted, thanks.”

Automated customer-intent classifier, 15 May, 10:25, displayed: “Refund requested: YES. Reason: damaged product.” This result was generated from the lead’s yellow note and the word “refund” in the policy, not from customer text. Quality review flagged it as an unreliable summary. Reviewer comment: “Verdict is wrong. Customer explicitly prefers replacement, and her conditional statement about deciding later is not a present refund request.” Jalen later corrected the request field to replacement. The correction was logged without modifying the messages.

Dispatch event, 16 May, 15:32: Replacement dripper left warehouse. Carrier expected delivery 18 May. Customer asked whether tracking number would be emailed; Jalen sent it. A separate inventory alert on 16 May warned that the matching server was temporarily low. It did not affect the replacement dripper shipment. A pricing note says the dripper standalone list price is $31.00, but the policy refund fallback would concern the affected item only, not automatically the full order total. No refund transaction appears in the payment ledger. Ledger: original capture $54.00; later adjustment $0.00; replacement shipment $0.00.

Delivery status, 18 May, 13:07: Carrier marked replacement delivered at front door. Customer at 13:50: “It arrived intact. Thank you for sorting it out. Please close the ticket.” Jalen closed the case at 14:02 as replacement completed. The internal dashboard still showed Tomas’s earlier suggestion for several minutes after closure. Dashboard note from supervisor: “Do not treat an agent’s disposition suggestion as the customer’s request. Use the customer’s own messages for this field.”

Audit appendix: The original ticket included one damaged item, one unaffected item, a request for a replacement, and a question about return logistics. The customer did not ask for compensation for inconvenience, did not report a wrong color, and did not say the entire order was unusable. A draft response, never sent, had mistakenly said “your refund is approved.” Jalen deleted it after reading the full conversation. The customer never accepted that draft, because she never saw it. A system note later stated “refund processed,” but this was a template status error: finance confirmed no refund existed, and the payment ledger contains no credit. Final quality conclusion: replacement delivered; no refund requested or issued; original defect verified; ticket resolved according to the replacement preference.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Refund requested by Nadia in this ticket, according to her own messages and not internal summaries?","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Nadia explicitly says replacement is her first choice; the lead suggestion and classifier verdict are contradicted by her messages."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"What outcome did Nadia actually prefer for the damaged dripper, based on her own statements?","candidates":[{"id":"refund","description":"She asked for money returned; for example, a credit instead of another item."},{"id":"replacement","description":"She wanted the faulty item replaced; for example, a sound dripper sent without charge."},{"id":"none","description":"No preference is stated; for example, she only reports damage."}],"target":"replacement","hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"She twice says replacement is her choice; Tomas’s refund disposition is explicitly based on an assumption."}]},{"state":"Northwind Labs customer support weekly escalation report, prepared by support coordinator Leila Sorensen for manager review. Case NW-66302 concerns customer order NW-771906, a portable thermal printer delivered to Esi Petrov. The report has been assembled from ticket messages, warehouse records, payment records, and internal comments. Dates use local warehouse time. The purpose of the report is to decide which customer-facing remedy is still needed, not to repeat preliminary queue labels.

The evidence relevant to withdrawal is the applicant’s message and portal activity. When reviewing a case with conflicting notes, staff should first identify the exact proposition under review. For example, “the applicant submitted a complete required set” is different from “the applicant satisfies the role’s experience criteria.” Staff then identify the source of the rule, the date and status of each submitted item, and who made each statement. If a comment declares a result without citing a fact, it should be treated as a proposed conclusion. Owner: People Operations, Northwind Freight
Effective date: 1 September
Applies to: external applications for Route Planning Analyst and Fleet Scheduling Associate vacancies
Prepared for: recruitment support and quality review

Section 1 — Purpose and scope
This page sets out the administrative rules used to review submitted applications and records a support inquiry about the Route Planning Analyst vacancy. It is not a scoring rubric for interviews and does not determine whether an applicant is suitable for a role. The purpose is to ensure that staff distinguish mandatory application materials from optional material, distinguish an applicant’s actions from an employee’s interpretation, and use the same recorded facts when answering an inquiry. A hiring manager may assess experience and qualifications under the relevant selection process, but cannot retroactively make an optional file mandatory for the purpose of declaring a previously submitted application incomplete.

Section 2 — Materials required for a valid application
A valid online application for either listed vacancy consists of the submitted application form, the vacancy-specific screening responses, and a résumé file successfully received by the portal. The portal confirmation number is evidence that the form and screening responses were accepted; the file event log establishes whether the résumé was received. The reference-information field is optional at the application stage for these two roles and may be requested later if needed. A cover letter is also optional. Applicants may supply either or both optional items, but a blank optional field is not a defect and must not be described as a missing requirement.

The policy does not require a particular résumé filename, font, or page count. The file must be a readable PDF or DOCX and the portal must report a successful upload. An upload that remains in progress, fails validation, or has no received-file record requires follow-up. A completed event with a stored file identifier is treated as received unless a separate integrity review shows corruption. Staff should not substitute a general portal warning for the item-level record. A banner is a prompt to inspect the relevant fields; it is not, by itself, a decision on completeness.

Section 3 — Status terms
“Draft” means the applicant has not completed the submission action. “Received” means the form submission has been accepted and is available to recruitment staff. “Administrative review” means staff are checking the presence and legibility of required components. “Substantive screening” means the panel is assessing the content against role criteria. “Withdrawn” is used only after the applicant affirmatively requests withdrawal or completes the withdrawal control. “Closed” may describe a support ticket, a vacancy, or an application, and staff must state which record they mean. A ticket being closed does not close an application. A staff member’s proposed “ineligible” or “incomplete” label is not an official status unless the authorized workflow records it with a supported reason.

Section 4 — Evidence hierarchy for administrative inquiries
For a question about what was submitted, review the policy requirements, the application’s item-level portal history, and the uploaded-file receipt. For a question about an applicant’s intention, review the applicant’s own message and any confirmed action. A recruiter’s note, voicemail summary, or quality flag may identify an issue to investigate, but it is not a substitute for the underlying evidence. If a summary conflicts with a timestamped event or a direct statement, staff must document the discrepancy and follow the primary record unless there is a verified reason to doubt it. Repeating an unsupported conclusion in several notes does not make it an established fact.

Section 5 — Withdrawal and conditional language
An applicant withdraws by clearly indicating that they no longer want to be considered, or by completing the portal’s withdrawal confirmation. A statement that an applicant will consider withdrawing later is not a withdrawal. Neither is declining an optional document, asking a question about the process, or saying “I would withdraw if the role required relocation” when no such decision is made. A conditional statement describes a possible future action, not a completed present action. Staff should capture the exact words and speaker rather than shortening a conditional statement into “candidate withdrew.”

Section 6 — What staff must not infer
A quiet period does not establish withdrawal. A missing optional cover letter does not establish incompleteness. A successful submission does not establish that a person meets substantive qualifications. A voicemail left by a recruiter does not prove that the applicant received or agreed with the message. A note that says “candidate confirmed” is meaningful only if the record identifies what the candidate confirmed and when. If a staff member’s conclusion is contradicted by the portal log or the applicant’s words, the conclusion must be marked disputed and must not be used as the sole basis for closing an application.

Category selected by customer: exchange / size preference
Customer's message sentiment: neutral
Requested remedy: exchange for shorter model

INTERNAL COMMENT, 09:21 — R. Vale
Initial read: customer wants an exchange, not a refund. Do not issue a refund merely because the return workflow uses the word “return.” Keep the exchange request linked to the original order. Disposition draft: “Refund requested; customer dissatisfied with product.” This is a convenient dropdown summary, but it does not appear to describe the message above. REFERENCE EXCERPT: RETURNS AND EXCHANGES FAQ, REVISION 8.2
Purpose of this excerpt: clarify the language used in support cases. A return is the physical movement of merchandise back to the fulfillment center. A refund is a payment reversal to the original payment method or another payment method approved by the customer. A refund request requires an explicit request from the customer for money back. A request to exchange an item is not a refund request, even if the customer must return the original item first. A request for store credit is not automatically a refund request; record the remedy the customer actually names. A question about whether money can be returned is not itself necessarily a request to return it. Read the complete sentence and surrounding context.

The FAQ also notes that customers sometimes use “send it back” to describe the physical return step in an exchange, replacement, or repair. That phrase alone does not establish the financial remedy. Agents should not infer a refund from a return label, a warehouse scan, a payment-processing event, or an internal category. Conversely, if a customer clearly asks for money back, do not downgrade that request merely because a menu choice says “exchange.” The customer's own words and the actual requested remedy are the evidence for classification.

For a size or preference exchange, the normal workflow is to confirm stock, reserve the replacement, and issue a return label. The original payment remains associated with the order unless the customer chooses a different remedy or the exchange workflow requires a clearly explained adjustment. Customers should not be charged twice for the same order because two physical parcels exist at different points in transit. If the requested size or model is unavailable, tell the customer what alternatives exist and ask which one they prefer. Do not silently select a refund, credit, or substitute product.

For a defective item, the support agent should record the observed issue and the customer's requested outcome separately. A customer may report a defect while asking for a replacement, a repair, money back, or advice. The mere presence of a defect does not itself establish which remedy the customer requested. Similarly, a customer may be unhappy with an item's appearance but still ask only for information. Do not convert an opinion about product fit into a financial request without explicit words supporting that conclusion.

The following examples are included because similar phrases recur in tickets:
“Please exchange these for the smaller version” means an exchange request.
“Can I send these back and get my money back?” means a refund request.
“I am returning this for store credit” means a store-credit request, not necessarily a refund request.
“Will you refund me if the replacement is also too large?” is a question about a possible future condition, not an immediate request for money back.
“I sent the package back yesterday” reports a physical action and does not specify the remedy.
“The refund is taking too long” reports a concern about an already requested or processed refund, but the case history should still be checked to establish who requested it and when.
The examples are not a substitute for reading the complete message. A customer can correct or clarify an earlier request in a later message. Record the current requested remedy and preserve the relevant sequence of messages.

CASE REVIEW CHECKLIST
1. Read the customer message, not only the selected category or summary.
2. Identify the requested action in the customer's own words.
3. Distinguish the physical handling of an item from the financial result.
4. Check whether a later message changes the requested action.
5. Do not infer a remedy from dissatisfaction, product condition, return eligibility, or the name of a workflow.
6. If a staff note conflicts with the message, record the conflict and follow the message unless the customer later clarifies it.
7. Correct unsupported draft summaries before they are sent or used for reporting.

INTERNAL QUALITY REVIEW, 11:05
The ticket is a useful reminder that a tidy label can be less accurate than an untidy sentence. The proposed “refund requested” summary has been removed. The customer did not say that they wanted a refund; in fact, they said the opposite and requested an exchange. The return label exists because the original lamps must be sent back as part of the exchange process. No money-back request is recorded in the customer messages.

Warehouse scan shows the original lamps accepted at the returns dock. Exchange shipment created for two shorter graphite lamps. Payment status remains unchanged. Customer notified that the exchange shipment will leave after inspection of the returned pair. The customer replied, “That works; the shelves will be relieved.” Ticket remains open pending delivery of the replacement.

SUPPORT OPERATIONS NOTES: HOW TO READ A CASE FILE
A case file may contain customer messages, automated classifications, agent drafts, warehouse events, payment events, and team-lead comments. These materials have different purposes. Customer messages establish what the customer communicated. Automated labels assist routing. Internal drafts are provisional. Warehouse scans establish where goods moved. Payment records establish financial events. No one field should be treated as a universal summary of all the others.

For example, an event named RETURN_RECEIVED establishes receipt of returned merchandise; it does not alone establish that the customer requested a refund. An event named REFUND_QUEUED establishes that a payment action was queued; it does not alone establish who requested it or whether the customer changed their mind. A customer may ask a question about a possible refund without making a request, and an agent may start a refund in error. The support record should distinguish the customer's request from later operational actions.

When staff draft a short summary, the summary should not erase the customer's stated remedy. A summary that says “wants refund” should be supported by an explicit customer request for money back. A summary that says “wants exchange” should be supported by an explicit request to receive another item. If the source message is clear, do not invent ambiguity just because a workflow contains several possible buttons. If it is genuinely unclear, ask the customer rather than resolving uncertainty by guessing.

The phrase “not asking for money back” is a direct denial of a refund request in the present case. The customer also describes the requested alternative: exchange for a shorter model. The two statements agree. The fact that the customer is willing to return the original pair is part of the exchange logistics and does not contradict the stated remedy. The fact that an internal draft says “refund requested” does conflict with the message and is not supported by it.

The customer experience team has asked that employees avoid treating every return as a complaint. Some returns are ordinary fulfillment steps. Some customers request an exchange because a size, color, or configuration did not suit their space. Some ask for a repair. Some request a refund. Some simply want to know what their options are. The correct case note should describe what was asked, not what an agent assumes would be easiest to process.

END OF CASE EXCERPT

ARCHIVE APPENDIX: ROUTING DEFINITIONS
“Exchange”: customer asks to replace an item with another item, typically a different size, color, or model.
“Replacement”: customer asks for another instance of the same item, usually because the first instance is missing or defective.
“Refund”: customer explicitly asks for money back.
“Store credit”: customer explicitly asks for a balance usable for a future purchase.
“Return inquiry”: customer asks how to send merchandise back but has not yet stated a financial or replacement remedy.
“Cancellation”: customer asks to stop an unfulfilled order.
“Complaint”: customer describes dissatisfaction or a problem; this label does not, by itself, identify the desired remedy.

A case can contain more than one of these concepts, but the agent should not merge them. For example, “The lamp is damaged; please replace it” contains a complaint and a replacement request, not necessarily a refund request. “The lamp is fine; please exchange it for a shorter one” contains an exchange request and no stated refund request. “Please refund me for the damaged lamp” contains both a complaint and a refund request. - names you may use (never reuse a name across sources): Leila Kowalski, Oren Castillo, Sven Mensah, Bao Iyer, Amara Petrov, Uma Sorensen; companies: Meridian Health, Bluefin Supply, Larkspur Freight, Granite Foods

    "state": "Meridian Health event support ticket and internal file bundle. Ticket MH-4817, opened 12 May, 09:14. Event: Meridian Health’s two-day staff forum, scheduled for 2–3 June at the Alder Quay Hall. Requester: Leila Kowalski, event coordinator. Assigned: Oren Castillo, support desk. Status shown by portal: closed. Priority shown by portal: normal. Subject: “Room, signage, and final bill follow-up.”

Leila’s opening message, 12 May, 09:14:
“Hi, we held the room booking with Bluefin Supply’s event team for the forum. I need the east room set for 84, not the west room for 84; the west room is only our backup. The first seating map has the lectern on the wrong side, and the arrival signs say ‘staff entrance’ where attendees need the quay entrance. Can you check the supplied bill against the signed order too? Please don’t close this as solved just because the hall booking itself is in the system. We have a single confirmed event booking; I’m asking about the rest of the setup and paperwork.”

Portal extraction, automatically attached:
Account: Meridian Health
Vendor account: Bluefin Supply
Order reference: BS-9034
Event date: 2–3 June
Hall: Alder Quay Hall, east room
Room capacity requested: 84
Backup room: west room, not selected
Ticket requester email: leila.kowalski@example.invalid
Related keywords detected: invoice, refund, booking, access, room, signage.
Automated suggested classification: “Refund / cancellation request.”
Suggested by text model; not reviewed by requester.

East room, 2 days, 1 booking at $1,240 per day: $2,480.

Directional sign set, 6 boards at $28 each: $168.

“Portal says refund/cancel, so likely Leila wants the whole $1,000 deposit returned. I’m marking this a refund request pending review.     "state": "Granite Foods event incident postmortem and reconciliation packet. Prepared 22 September for the Harvest Partners reception held 17 September at the Cedar Lantern Pavilion. Internal distribution: venue operations, catering, finance, and event lead. File owner: Amara Petrov. Event coordinator: Uma Sorensen. Vendor: Larkspur Freight. Guest count planned: 126. Actual check-in count: 119. Event was completed; this report documents delivery, billing, and response issues. Several draft conclusions are preserved in the change log; they are not all verified facts.

Executive summary, version 1, 18 September, 08:00:
“Larkspur Freight failed to deliver the cold-drink crates and charged Granite Foods twice for table service. Granite Foods should receive a refund of $640. The vendor’s actions caused the late start and the missing drinks.”
Prepared by Amara Petrov from a first pass through the incident channel, before matching the signed order, dock log, and invoice. This statement was circulated as a provisional verdict. It was not a payment approval.

Event overview:
Granite Foods hosted a reception for Harvest Partners on 17 September. Dock access opened at 14:00; guest doors opened at 18:30. The signed event order lists 126 guests, 14 banquet tables, 2 service stations, 6 crates of chilled sparkling water, and a rented chilled display. Larkspur Freight delivered equipment and beverage crates. Granite Foods supplied printed menus and name cards. The venue’s own kitchen supplied hot food under a separate internal work order. No other vendor was authorized to provide beverage crates.

Signed purchase order GF-7712, dated 2 September:
Table service: 14 tables at $32 each = $448.
Service stations: 2 at $90 each = $180.
Cold-drink crates: 6 at $44 each = $264.
Chilled display rental: 1 at $210 = $210.
Subtotal: $1,102.
Tax: $88.16.
Authorized total: $1,190.16.
Terms: 40% deposit on confirmation; balance after delivery and reconciliation. Delivery window 14:00–15:30 on 17 September. If the loading dock is unavailable because the venue has not cleared the access lane, the vendor must wait and notify the event coordinator; the delivery time is measured from the moment access is granted. Extra items or quantity changes require written approval from the event lead.

Vendor invoice LF-5591, issued 18 September:
Table service: 14 at $32 = $448.
Service stations: 2 at $90 = $180.
Cold-drink crates: 6 at $44 = $264.
Chilled display rental: 1 at $210 = $210.
Table service handling, duplicate line: 1 at $640 = $640.
Subtotal: $1,742.
Tax: $139.36.
Invoice total: $1,881.36.
Deposit credited: $476.06.
Balance requested: $1,405.30.
Invoice note: “Additional handling due to extended waiting and replacement cold stock.” No written variation attached.

Initial finance note, Bao Iyer, 18 September, 09:10:
“Invoice looks like table service twice: $448 plus separate $640 handling. Difference isn’t a same-rate duplicate; need backup. Deposit matches 40% of $1,190.16 approximately: 0.4 x 1,190.16 = $476.064, rounded to $476.06. Balance on invoice is total $1,881.36 less $476.06 = $1,405.30. Arithmetic is fine, entitlement is not established. Don’t call $640 a refund due until we know what the line is and whether approved.”

Draft conclusion entered by event lead Uma Sorensen, 18 September, 09:42:
“Finding: vendor missed all six drink crates; full $640 refund should be requested for the missing beverages and duplicate service. They also caused a late start.”
This entry combines a claim about delivery with a conclusion about the invoice. It was written before the dock log and signed receiving count were reviewed. It is a person’s preliminary verdict, not a statement from Granite Foods asking for money back.

Incident timeline, compiled from venue door records and radio notes:
13:42 — Pavilion staff report north loading lane partly blocked by a delivery van from the venue kitchen. Larkspur vehicle checks in at the outer gate.
13:49 — Driver calls dispatch: truck is at gate; cannot enter north dock lane.
14:03 — Uma messages venue operations asking them to clear lane. She says the dock is “not actually open yet.”
14:21 — Venue supervisor confirms lane cleared; driver is waved in at 14:24.
14:31 — First equipment cases unloaded.
14:44 — Cold-drink crates scanned to the receiving cart; scan count six.
14:52 — Chilled display positioned in east service area.
15:07 — Larkspur driver reports all ordered items delivered and obtains a receiving signature from Sven Mensah, Granite Foods floor supervisor.
15:18 — Sven notices one crate has warm bottles on the top layer and records it for inspection. The other five crates are placed in the cooler.
16:02 — Kitchen team moves the flagged crate to the venue’s backup cooler. No disposal or replacement request is recorded at that time.
17:46 — A staff member opens the flagged crate; bottles are cool enough for service under the event plan. No guest complaint about drink temperature recorded.
18:30 — Doors open as scheduled.

Gate time is not the start of the contract’s delivery window when the loading lane is blocked. The signed order says the delivery clock is measured from access being granted. Access was granted at 14:24; delivery sign-off was at 15:07, a 43-minute interval, within the 90-minute window ending 15:54. A draft dispatch note says “late 1h25m” by counting from the truck’s 13:49 gate call to sign-off. That computation does not use the order’s stated start point.

Receiving sheet, signed by Sven Mensah, 17 September, 15:07:
“14 table service sets present. Two service stations present. Six sealed cold-drink crates received; crate 4 top layer warm on arrival, isolated for check; five other crates moved to cooler. One chilled display present and working. Packaging intact. No refusal, shortage, or damage recorded. Driver departed after signature.”
Handwritten later at 16:10: “Crate 4 checked; contents usable; placed in backup cooler.”
The receiving sheet contains a checkbox “short / damaged?” marked “no.” A separate note about the warm top layer does not change the recorded quantity received.

Incident channel excerpt:
17 Sep, 14:05, Uma: “Lane still blocked. Vendor is waiting outside. Can someone move the kitchen van?”
17 Sep, 14:16, venue operations: “We are trying to find the kitchen driver. Dock not clear.”
17 Sep, 14:24, Uma: “Gate says Larkspur just got access. Please log our own delay too.”
17 Sep, 15:09, Sven: “All six crates counted. One top layer warm, isolate it, rest in cooler. Signed.”
17 Sep, 16:13, Uma: “Crate checked, contents usable, not short. Keep watch.”
17 Sep, 19:02, Leila Kowalski, guest services: “Some guests asked for water before speeches, but no one reported missing crates. The service station had bottles by then.”
18 Sep, 08:22, Amara: “I saw one note ‘missing drinks’ in the first verbal update. Need verify from receiving sheet before calling it a shortage.”

Table-service reconciliation:
Purchase order line is one line for 14 tables at $32 each, total $448. Invoice repeats that line and adds “table service handling” for $640. Larkspur’s emailed explanation, 19 September, says the $640 refers to a later pickup and sanitizing shift requested during the event by Granite Foods floor staff. The explanation attaches no signed change order. Sven’s radio notes show that at 20:41 he asked the driver whether the used table linens could be collected that evening rather than next morning. The driver said he would check dispatch. At 20:58, dispatch approved an after-hours pickup fee of $640, according to a dispatch screen capture. Sven did not have authority to approve additional charges under the purchase order; written event-lead approval was required. No such written approval was found. The charge may be unsupported by the contract even though a pickup did occur.

Dispatch extract from Larkspur Freight:
Vehicle LF-12 at gate 13:49.
Reason for waiting: customer site access blocked.
Entry permission received 14:24.
Delivery complete 15:07.
After-hours pickup request 20:41.
Dispatch acceptance for pickup 20:58; rate field $640.
Pickup completed 21:32.
The dispatch extract supports that a pickup service occurred and that the vendor recorded the amount, but it does not establish Granite Foods’ written authorization. It also does not show the six drink crates were missing.

Catering and service notes:
The event plan called for chilled water at the east service station before guest doors. Station setup checklist was signed at 17:55. There were bottles at both stations at 18:30. At 18:46 a server moved additional bottles from the cooler. No shortage occurred in the 18:30–19:30 service count. A later draft report describes “no drinks at doors,” but the time-stamped checklist and two server notes say the stations were stocked. The draft phrase came from a guest’s question at 17:58, before the stations were complete. The question was, “Are drinks coming out soon?” and was not a complaint that a paid delivery had been omitted.

Post-event email from Amara Petrov to Larkspur, 18 September, 10:15:
“Your invoice contains a $640 line we did not see on the purchase order. Please send the approval record and describe the work. Also send the signed delivery sheet. We are reconciling, not yet approving or rejecting payment.”
Larkspur response, 19 September, 07:40:
“Six crates and equipment were delivered. One crate’s upper bottles were warm and moved to a cooler. Our crew completed a later pickup requested on site. We billed the pickup at the dispatch rate. We do not have a change form signed by an authorized event lead; the request was verbal from floor staff.”
Amara reply, 19 September, 08:02:
“Thanks. We accept receipt of the six crates per signed sheet. We have not decided the $640 pickup line. Please hold any collection activity until the contract review is done.”

Invoice audit worksheet:
Base authorized subtotal: $1,102.
Base tax at 8%: $88.16.
Authorized total: $1,190.16.
Deposit: $476.06, rounded from $476.064.
Authorized balance if no variation: $1,190.16 − $476.06 = $714.10.
Invoice’s added line: $640 before tax.
Tax on added line at 8%: $51.20.
Added line including tax: $691.20.
Invoice total including extra line: $1,881.36.
Less deposit: $1,405.30 requested balance.
The $640 is not a duplicate $448 line by exact amount or unit calculation. It is a separate after-hours pickup charge. It is nevertheless not shown on the signed order and lacks written approval. The review outcome should distinguish “charge not approved” from “customer is owed $640 refund”: Granite Foods has not paid the invoice balance, and the deposit was applied to authorized items. No $640 payment has been made.

Change log for the executive summary:
18 Sep 08:00, Amara wrote “vendor failed to deliver drinks; refund $640.”
18 Sep 11:35, Bao added comment: “Not supported: signed receipt says six crates; $640 is pickup line, not beverage line.”
19 Sep 08:10, Uma changed draft status to “investigation.”
20 Sep 16:22, Amara revised: “Six crates received; one crate had a warm upper layer but was usable. $640 after-hours pickup line lacks written approval. No refund request has been submitted; finance is withholding approval of that invoice line while reviewing contract authority.”
22 Sep 09:00, review lead approved revised summary and retained earlier versions for audit.

Vendor account ledger through 22 September:
2 Sep: deposit invoice $476.06 issued.
3 Sep: deposit payment $476.06 received from Granite Foods.
18 Sep: final invoice $1,881.36 issued; balance $1,405.30 open.
19 Sep: dispute flag placed on $691.20 tax-inclusive pickup line.
22 Sep: no balance payment, credit memo, refund, or reversal posted.
The vendor account has not sent money to Granite Foods. The dispute flag prevents the invoice from being treated as approved; it does not create a refund transaction.

Postmortem findings, final:
Finding 1, dock delay: The delivery vehicle waited at the outer gate because Granite Foods’ venue lane was blocked. Contract delivery timing began when access was granted at 14:24. Delivery completed 15:07, 43 minutes later, within the delivery window. Initial claim that Larkspur caused a late start is not supported by the access record.
Finding 2, beverage quantity: Six crates were received and signed for. One crate had a warm upper layer but was later checked and used. No shortage or guest-facing service failure was documented. Initial “missing drinks” conclusion was wrong.
Finding 3, pickup line: A later pickup was performed and dispatch records a $640 rate. The signed order requires written approval for extras, and none was found. Granite Foods should not approve that line without resolving authority. This is a disputed unpaid charge, not a refund due for absent drinks.
Finding 4, event timing: Doors opened at the scheduled 18:30 time. A draft “late start” label was based on the blocked dock and a preliminary verbal report, not the event schedule.

Lessons and actions:
Operations will photograph dock clearance before the vendor window begins. Floor staff will not verbally authorize extras; the event lead must submit written changes. Receiving staff will distinguish warm product from missing product and record quantities separately. Finance will compare invoices with signed orders before deciding whether a charge should be paid, credited, or disputed. Draft summaries must say “unverified” until source records are checked. The original verdict is preserved because it was circulated, but should not be copied as the final factual account.

Appendix: event chat fragments not included in the first summary:
16 Sep, Uma: “Confirm six crates, right?”
16 Sep, Larkspur dispatch: “Six on manifest.”
17 Sep, Sven: “Counted six, one top layer warm.”
17 Sep, Uma: “Got it. Not missing. Cool it and we’ll check.”
17 Sep, venue kitchen: “Our van blocked the north lane, sorry; moved it at 14:20.”
17 Sep, Larkspur driver: “Access at 14:24; unloading now.”
These messages were present in the shared event channel but not in Amara’s first verbal briefing.

Appendix: wording review:
The word “refund” appears in the preliminary summary and in the standard invoice footer, which states “Please contact accounts for refund questions.” Neither is a request from Granite Foods. The signed order and correspondence show a reconciliation dispute about an open balance. Amara’s email expressly asks for an approval record and says payment is not yet approved. No sender message asks Larkspur to return money.

Closing note, 22 September, 11:30:
The event was completed with the ordered drinks, table service, stations, and display delivered. The $640 pickup fee remains disputed pending authority review. Granite Foods has neither paid that added amount nor asked for a refund. The first report’s confident verdict was premature and contradicted by the primary records.",
