The chair asked the minute-taker to quote source documents where they differed from staff impressions.

Background. On 2 October, visitor coordinator Jalen Firth arranged rail travel and one night of lodging for a site representative, Mara Edevane. The planned outbound rail journey was on 7 October. The return journey was on 8 October. A single lodging reservation covered the night of 7 October. The original booking confirmation was sent to the traveler and to the accounts mailbox. The itinerary was subsequently changed after the return train was rescheduled by the carrier.

Customer communication. On 6 October, Mara wrote: “The carrier changed my return time and I will take the later train. Please do not refund the ticket; I still need it. I am not requesting cancellation of the room either.” On 8 October, after completing the trip, she wrote: “Please refund the unused seat reservation fee on the outbound rail booking. The train fare itself was used, and the room was occupied. I am asking only about the separate seat fee.” The fee is a separately itemized service on the rail statement, distinct from the fare. The customer’s later message is the request relevant to the refund question.

Draft committee summary by travel clerk Noll Harker: “No refund requested at any point; customer accepted the itinerary change.” The first part of the summary conflicts with the 8 October message, which expressly asks for a refund of the unused seat reservation fee. The second part refers to the later return train and does not resolve the separate outbound seat-fee request. The summary was copied from an early booking-status note and was not checked against the later message. The minutes retain it as an initial assessment for correction.

Documents reviewed. The outbound rail ticket bears a used-travel scan. Its separate seat reservation record is marked “seat not occupied.” The return ticket shows a later departure accepted by the traveler and used. The lodging folio indicates one night occupied. The carrier statement lists the rail fare and seat reservation as separate lines. No supplier credit is present in the accounts ledger. Therefore the records support that the customer requested a refund of one fee, but do not show that the carrier granted or paid it.

Discussion item: distinction among change, cancellation, and refund. Facilities asked whether accepting a later train meant that the traveler had abandoned the entire booking. The records clerk said no: the customer explicitly accepted the changed return time, and the ticket was used. Finance noted that a used rail fare and an unused seat reservation fee may have different service statuses. The current question is the customer’s request, not whether the carrier’s terms require payment. The clerk should not classify the request as a full fare refund or as no request.

Travel charge register. The ledger contains the outbound fare, the outbound seat reservation fee, the return fare, and the lodging charge. The outbound fare is paired with a boarding scan. The seat fee is paired with a reservation record but no occupied-seat record. The return fare is paired with a scan on the later train. The lodging line is paired with the folio. The ledger has no credit entry against any of these charges. A blank credit field indicates no recorded credit, not a finding that no refund was requested.

Actions agreed. Jalen will submit the seat-fee question to the carrier and preserve the customer’s message. Finance will leave the used fares and occupied lodging in their current reconciliation state unless separate supplier documentation is received. The records office will correct the draft committee summary to distinguish the early schedule-change correspondence from the later fee request. No person at the meeting represented that the carrier had approved a refund.

Risk and controls note. Broad labels such as “trip refund” and “no refund” can obscure a request that concerns only one component of a booking. Staff should inspect the item description and the original customer wording. The carrier’s change to the return schedule is not evidence that the customer asked to cancel the return ticket. Similarly, a used outbound fare does not establish that every associated ancillary fee was used. Each service should be recorded separately.

Appendix: source hierarchy. The email archive establishes what Mara asked. The ticket scan establishes travel on the outbound route. The seat reservation record establishes that the reserved seat was not occupied. The hotel folio establishes that the room was occupied. The carrier statement establishes the separate fee line. The early booking-status note and the clerk’s summary are internal characterizations and cannot override the later direct message. The ledger establishes only whether a credit is recorded at the time of review.

Meeting close. The chair directed that the minutes use “refund requested for the unused outbound seat reservation fee; supplier decision pending.” She rejected the draft phrase “no refund requested” after reviewing the source. The decision was procedural and did not guarantee the outcome of the carrier claim. A later supplier response must be attached when received. Report number: FF-IR-519. Issued by the travel service review unit following a booking query concerning a two-night visit by traveler Orla Saye to Morrow Reach. The report includes the customer’s original correspondence, booking-system excerpts, an internal assessment, and the final records-office review. It is written in the standard bureaucratic format and does not constitute a supplier promise or payment authorization.

Section 1: booking summary. The travel desk arranged lodging for 21 and 22 November and a local shuttle from the station on 21 November. The traveler checked into the lodging and used both nights. The shuttle was scheduled for 17:15. The provider’s dispatch record shows that the vehicle arrived at the station at 17:12 and carried the traveler to the lodging. The related invoice lists two room nights, a shuttle service, and a local facility charge. The invoice was paid under the normal monthly account process. No cancellation was recorded.

Section 2: customer correspondence. On 25 November, Orla sent the following message: “I am not asking for a refund. The room and shuttle were provided as booked. I want a copy of the detailed invoice for my records.” The message was received by the shared travel mailbox and attached to the booking. The request is for a document copy, not for repayment or a credit. The customer does not allege that a listed service was missing or defective.

Section 3: preliminary flag. Automated workflow reviewer Darel Wicks entered: “Refund requested—customer disputes travel charges.” This was a preliminary label populated from the generic “billing query” category. The source email says the opposite: Orla explicitly states that she is not asking for a refund and asks only for a detailed invoice copy. The automated flag is retained to show the workflow sequence and must not be treated as the customer’s own request. A subsequent manual review changed the case category to “invoice copy.”

Section 4: evidence inspection. The lodging folio records check-in on 21 November and check-out on 23 November. The shuttle manifest lists Orla as a passenger. The detailed invoice has separate lines for lodging, the shuttle, and the facility charge. The customer’s message does not contest those lines or request a correction. The accounts system shows the invoice as settled and has no refund transaction. That payment status is consistent with the records but is not the decisive evidence of whether a request was made; the decisive evidence is the customer’s direct wording.

Section 5: chronology. The booking confirmation was sent on 10 November. The shuttle service was completed on 21 November. The lodging was completed by check-out on 23 November. The message asking for the detailed invoice copy was received on 25 November. The preliminary workflow flag was generated at 25 November, 09:06, and the email was linked to the case at 09:14. The timing explains how the inaccurate flag arose: the category was selected before the message body was reviewed. It does not change the actual content of the message.

Section 6: staff discussion. The accounts liaison initially stated that every billing query should be treated as a refund request until clarified. The records officer objected that this is not an appropriate substitute for reading the customer’s request. A billing question may seek a copy, an explanation, a correction, or repayment. In this case, the customer specifically requested a copy and specifically denied seeking a refund. The review therefore classifies the customer’s request as an invoice-document request only.

Section 7: service outcome. The lodging provider confirmed two occupied nights. The shuttle provider confirmed the completed pickup. No service failure appears in the evidence supplied. The customer’s message says both were provided as booked. The company is not required by this report to make any payment to the customer, and the report makes no finding about a hypothetical future dispute. It records only the request made on 25 November.

Section 8: records and corrections. The original automated flag remains visible in the audit trail, marked “superseded.” The corrected case category is “invoice copy requested.” The customer’s message is stored without alteration. The internal flag must not be quoted as if it were written by the customer. Any later request, if one is received, will be stored as a separate communication and assessed on its own terms.

Appendix A: invoice review. The accounting clerk verified that the invoice total equals the sum of the listed lines, but the arithmetic is not material to the customer’s present request. The invoice has not been amended. The customer has not asked for a line-item dispute, reimbursement, cancellation, or a credit. The request concerns receiving more detailed documentation of charges already billed. The records unit may provide that document through the normal channel.

Appendix B: classification controls. The system offers “refund requested,” “invoice query,” “cancellation,” and “other.” A preliminary selection is not a verified customer statement. Staff are required to read the source message before closing a case. When an internal verdict conflicts with the customer’s direct wording, the customer’s wording is the evidence for the requested remedy. A system flag may indicate a processing error, but it does not establish that the customer asked for money back.

Final review. The manual reviewer confirms that no refund request appears in the customer’s message. The phrase “I am not asking for a refund” is explicit, and the stated purpose is obtaining a detailed invoice copy. The initial automated verdict that a refund was requested is incorrect. I know we have already talked about the spring forum about six times, and I am sorry this is another long email. The packet came from Foxglove Studio in pieces, with a revised invoice, the signed order, the venue receipt, and a couple of old planning exports mixed together. I have put the source documents into the attached structured record rather than pretending the email chain itself is the accounting system. Please use the documents and their stated precedence notes. The preliminary status field is copied from Foxglove’s cover sheet, not checked by me.

The forum is booked for May 18 at the Alder Quay Hall. The event team has been fiddling with room layouts and coffee arrangements, but this reconciliation is only about the records in the packet. A few older estimates remain attached because people asked whether they were duplicates. They are labeled as estimates or superseded records; they are not additional orders. I left them in place so nobody has to hunt for the provenance later.

I’m also including the boring document-control notes, because last time somebody mistook a draft for a signed commitment. The signed order is the controlling order. A later written change is controlling only when it has an approval reference and is marked executed. A quote, an internal spreadsheet, a delivery receipt, or a vendor’s description of what it thinks was agreed does not amend the signed order by itself. - genres to spread across the sources: customer chat transcript, email thread with quoted replies, meeting notes
- tone: angry
- instruction style for this batch: imperative decisions ('Decide whether the customer asked for a refund.')
- candidate-description style for this batch: a definition plus a short example
- names you may use (never reuse a name across sources): Xiu Bergstrom, Yara Castillo, Jonas Haddad, Aiden Alvarez, Xiu Haddad, Esi Lindqvist; companies: Saltmarsh Software, Larkspur Health, Saltmarsh Dental, Granite Supply
- focus traps: planted_verdict. Every question in this batch uses this trap (others may occur naturally).

[{"state":"Customer chat transcript, Saltmarsh Software small manufacturing shop, case CS-4817. The shop makes custom brackets and short-run stainless assemblies. The transcript was exported with internal notes and customer messages interleaved; speaker labels identify who wrote each line. The customer is angry about the order, but the shop must record what was actually requested rather than what a hurried staff member concluded.

09:02, Xiu Bergstrom, customer: I have been waiting since Monday for someone to tell me what is happening with order 7741. The carton arrived yesterday, the outside looked fine, and the packing slip says twelve BX-4 mounting brackets. I ordered twelve. I have already sent photographs, and I do not want another generic apology that says the team is looking into it. Please read the dimensions in the photos before answering.

09:05, Yara Castillo, support: I can see the order and the photos. The order record says twelve brackets, brushed finish, 80 millimeters long. I am checking the inspection sheet now. Before I offer a remedy, could you tell me whether you want replacement pieces, a repair, or money returned? We can document more than one requested remedy if that is what you want.

09:07, Xiu: The label on the bag says BX-4, so that part is right. I measured three of them. They are 78 millimeters, not 80. I need the pieces for a frame that is being assembled tomorrow. If you can get the right parts here in time, send them. I am not asking you to refund anything at this point. Do not turn “I need this fixed” into “refund” just because that is easier to enter in your system.

09:09, Yara: Understood. The shop’s remake queue normally takes four working days, so I cannot promise arrival tomorrow. I can ask the floor lead whether there is a suitable stock item, but I should not promise a delivery date until the carrier pickup is confirmed. Are all twelve short, or only the three you measured?

09:11, Xiu: I checked all twelve. Ten are 78 millimeters. Two are 80. The surface on the ten is also rougher than the sample we approved. I have not checked every hole with a gauge yet. The photo shows one hole, but please do not write that all twelve holes are wrong; I do not know that.

09:13, Yara: Thank you for being specific. I will record ten pieces measured short and two measured to length, with a finish concern on the ten. The inspection sheet says the batch was recorded as 80 millimeters, but I need to compare its entries with the machine traveler. I am not going to assume the sheet is right merely because it is in the system.

09:16, Xiu: Also, your colleague told me yesterday that the order was “perfectly within tolerance.” That is absurd. I am not praising you. I am telling you that the answer was useless. The drawing calls for 80 millimeters plus or minus 0.5. A 78 millimeter piece is not a near miss. I have attached the drawing again because apparently the first attachment vanished into the same hole as the promised callback.

09:18, Yara: I see the drawing. You are right about the stated tolerance: 78 is outside the drawing range of 79.5 to 80.5. I am sorry the earlier response treated the inspection entry as conclusive. I will add the drawing range and your measurements to the case, and I will ask the floor lead to verify the ten measured pieces against the drawing.

09:21, Xiu: I am furious, but I still want the order completed correctly. Please send ten replacements if those ten are confirmed wrong. The other two seem usable, and I do not want them remade just for the sake of making the quantity look tidy. If the shop can provide a confirmed ship date, I will decide whether that works for the frame. I have not asked you to return my money.

09:23, Yara: I have entered a request for ten replacement brackets, contingent on floor verification. I have not entered a refund request. The case menu has a field called “customer remedy,” and the options include replace, repair, refund, and no remedy requested. I will keep the record aligned with what you said rather than selecting refund because the order is disputed.

09:26, Xiu: Good. I want the ten correct parts. I also want a straight answer about the price. The invoice shows $468 for twelve, which is $39 each. I am not saying that amount is wrong; it matches the quote I approved. Do not let the fact that I mention the invoice turn this into a billing complaint. The problem is the ten short brackets and the delay in getting a useful answer.

09:29, Yara: I checked the quote and invoice. Both show $39 per bracket and $468 total for twelve, before the separately listed freight charge. There is no price discrepancy shown. I am noting that you accept the quoted item price, while raising a dimensional and finish issue. That distinction should help the next person avoid treating every mentioned invoice as a disputed charge.

09:32, Xiu: The freight is $28, and I know it is on the quote. I am not asking for that back either. I would expect the replacement shipment to be handled fairly, but I did not ask you to credit the original freight. I want the shop to stop adding things to my request that I did not say.

09:35, Yara: I understand. I have not recorded a freight-credit request. I have asked the floor lead to determine whether the ten pieces can be confirmed against the drawing this morning. I will send you the result, including what happens to the two pieces that measured 80, rather than making you repeat the same details.

09:41, internal note by Jonas Haddad, support supervisor: Customer is heated and says the service has been terrible. Likely refund request. Mark refund requested so the queue can route this to billing. This is my recommendation based on the overall tone, not a quotation from Xiu. If the actual messages say otherwise, correct the field before closing the case.

09:44, Yara: I saw Jonas’s note. I am leaving the remedy field as replacement requested, not refund requested. The note is a staff opinion and conflicts with the customer’s explicit statements at 09:07 and 09:21. I have asked Jonas to review the record before anyone changes it.

09:48, Xiu: I can see the case portal now. It says “refund request under review.” That is not what I asked for. Please fix it. I am asking for ten replacements if your check confirms the dimensions, and I want you to tell me when they can ship. If the answer is that you cannot do that, tell me plainly; I will then decide what to do. A possible later decision is not a request I have made today.

09:51, Yara: I have corrected the portal to show a replacement request pending verification. The system will retain the earlier change in its audit history, but the current remedy field is corrected. I will not treat your statement about what you might decide later as a present request for a refund or cancellation.

10:03, Xiu: Someone just called and said the floor team measured one bracket at 80. I know two measured 80. That does not answer the question about the ten that measured 78. Please do not close the case because one item passed. I need a written result for the ten, plus the finish question.

10:07, Yara: I have reopened the verification task. The first floor message referred to the two pieces already measured at 80, not to the ten short pieces. I will ask for ten individual readings or a documented sampling method and a finish comparison against the approved sample. We should not report “all parts pass” based on the two measurements that were already acceptable.

10:14, Xiu: Thanks for correcting that. I am still angry that I had to catch it. I will accept a written measurement table. I will not accept “within tolerance” without the actual readings, because the drawing tolerance is written in plain numbers and the first answer ignored it.

10:20, Yara: I have added that requirement to the case. For clarity, a result between 79.5 and 80.5 millimeters satisfies the drawing length requirement. The stated measurement of 78 does not. The surface finish is a separate inspection point and should not be marked failed merely because it looks different in a compressed chat image; the floor team needs to compare the physical pieces with the approved sample.

10:31, internal note by Jonas Haddad: The customer used the word “money” in the transcript and is angry about the invoice, so my first summary remains “refund requested.” I would rather avoid another edit. The customer may be using replacement language as leverage. Do not make a billing task unless a lead insists.

10:36, Yara: I am correcting the summary again because the word “money” appears in a sentence explicitly saying Xiu is not asking for a refund. The invoice amount was described as matching the approved quote. The customer’s stated current remedy remains ten replacement parts if inspection confirms the fault. Jonas’s interpretation is not evidence of a customer request.

10:42, Xiu: I am not trying to trick anyone. The replacement request is simple. If you find that the ten are in fact 78, send ten that meet the drawing. If you find something different, explain it. I have not asked for a refund, and I have not said that I am cancelling the whole order. I have asked you not to close the complaint before checking the parts.

[{"state":"CLINIC ADMINISTRATION CASE REVIEW — CONSOLIDATED FILE
Prepared for internal scheduling quality review. This packet combines a customer chat transcript, extracts from the clinic’s appointment policy page, an FAQ excerpt, scheduling notes, and a staff audit log. The review concerns appointment records, not clinical advice. Names and organizations in this file are fictional. Some entries contain preliminary staff conclusions; those conclusions are not automatically authoritative. The source documents themselves are reproduced below, including typos and duplicated material. Times are local clinic time unless an entry says otherwise.

SECTION A — CUSTOMER CHAT TRANSCRIPT (reproduced in export order)

09:02, queue greeting: Thanks for contacting the clinic desk. Please do not send urgent medical questions through scheduling chat. We can help with appointment times, reminders, check-in questions, and changes to contact details. If you need to reschedule, tell us the appointment date and the name on the booking. A coordinator will review the record before making changes. Chat messages may arrive out of sequence in the export when an agent opens multiple case tabs.

09:04, Dalia Bergstrom: Hi. I’m checking on my appointment for Tuesday, 14 May. I got a reminder saying I had not confirmed it, but I did confirm yesterday. I am still coming. Can you see it?

09:05, automated case banner: CASE TYPE: confirmation question. Suggested disposition: unconfirmed booking. This banner is generated from the customer’s initial message and may not include later messages or account activity. Do not use the suggestion without checking the event history.

09:07, scheduling agent: I can look. Is this the 10:30 visit at North Desk, not the 11:00 call-back?

09:08, Dalia Bergstrom: Yes 10:30. I pressed confirm in the link on Monday at 16:18. The page said “you’re all set.” I didn’t cancel anything.

09:09, scheduling agent: Thanks, I see a confirmation event on Monday. The banner may be stale. I’ll check what the appointment card currently says before I close this.

09:10, staff-only note, entered by agent: “Patient did not confirm; probably should mark as unconfirmed and release slot.” Note was typed before the event history was opened. This is a preliminary opinion, not a completed status change.

09:11, Dalia Bergstrom: Please don’t release it. I need that time. My old reminder from Friday says confirm, but the Monday page said confirmed. I can forward the screenshot if that helps.

09:12, scheduling agent: I see the Monday event now. It records confirmation from the account link at 16:18. Your appointment is still on the schedule. I am not changing it to unconfirmed.

09:14, system event copied into chat: Appointment AP-4831, 14 May, 10:30, status CONFIRMED. Confirmation received 13 May, 16:18. Reminder job had been queued before confirmation and was not withdrawn from the outbound queue. The reminder wording did not update after the confirmation event.

09:15, Dalia Bergstrom: That explains it. The reminder made it look like nobody saw my reply. Thanks.

09:17, scheduling agent: You’re welcome. The appointment remains confirmed. Please arrive a few minutes early for check-in.

09:21, internal supervisor comment: “No confirmation was received; the patient is unconfirmed.” This comment was copied from the automated banner and the early staff note. It conflicts with the event record displayed above. Supervisor did not inspect the time-stamped confirmation event before writing the comment.

09:26, quality reviewer: Keep the account event as the primary record for whether confirmation was received. Reminder delivery is a separate process and does not undo a confirmation. No slot release is authorized from this chat.

CHAT EXPORT FOOTNOTE: The patient’s reference to an older Friday reminder is not evidence that the appointment itself was unconfirmed on Monday. The appointment was not moved to another day. The call-back mentioned by the agent is a separate appointment type and is not the booking under review.

SECTION B — APPOINTMENT POLICY PAGE EXTRACT
Page title: Confirmations, cancellations, arrival, and no-show coding
Last revised: 2 May. A “confirmed” appointment is one for which the booking system has stored a confirmation event from the patient or an authorized representative. A reminder sent by the clinic is not itself a confirmation. A reminder that remains queued after a patient confirms does not reverse that confirmation. Staff should inspect the event history if the reminder text and appointment card appear inconsistent.

A cancellation is a request from the patient or authorized representative to remove the booking. A conditional statement about canceling later is not a cancellation. A question about how cancellation works is not a cancellation. If an agent receives a cancellation request, the agent should record who made the request, the appointment affected, and the time received. Do not infer that a forwarded message is the current sender’s request; read the quoted text and identify its author.

A no-show is an appointment where the patient neither attended nor checked in, and where no timely cancellation or approved change was recorded. A patient who arrives and checks in is not a no-show merely because the appointment later appears on an incomplete rooming list. A staff member’s preliminary note does not replace the check-in log. If the check-in log and a draft disposition disagree, verify the underlying event before finalizing.

The desk may label an appointment “late arrival” only when arrival is after the scheduled time and the patient has not already been checked in at the scheduled time. An appointment at 10:30 checked in at 10:24 is not late. A clock display in a workstation screenshot may use a different time zone; use the clinic-local event time unless an explicit conversion is provided. Do not calculate a different time zone when the record already gives clinic-local time.

An appointment marked CONFIRMED can still later be canceled, moved, or completed. The current status is determined by the latest valid status-changing event, not by whichever line appears last in a copied email. A confirmation event changes the confirmation field but does not establish that the patient attended. A check-in event establishes arrival but does not by itself establish that the visit was completed. Keep these states distinct.

If a staff member enters a conclusion before reviewing all records, that conclusion is a note, not a status event. A manager’s text such as “no confirmation,” “late,” or “no-show” is not proof merely because it sounds definitive. The events, their timestamps, and the identity of the person taking the action are the evidence. When records are incomplete, do not claim a fact not supported by the available record.

Reminder workflow: the system builds reminder batches at 15:00 on the preceding business day. If a confirmation comes in after the batch is prepared, the queued message may still be sent. The message can therefore say “please confirm” even though the appointment card shows CONFIRMED. The reminder queue records message delivery, not the patient’s response. A delivery receipt from the messaging vendor means only that the message reached a device or mailbox; it does not establish that the patient read it.

Check-in workflow: a front-desk user selects the appointment, verifies the patient, and presses CHECKED IN. A successful action creates an event with a clinic-local time and the staff terminal identifier. A paper sign-in sheet is useful for investigating a missing digital event but does not automatically change the system status. If an event is duplicated, use the valid event tied to the correct appointment identifier. A test appointment has a separate TEST prefix and must not be treated as a real visit.

Staff may not erase a confirmed event simply because an old reminder was delivered. To correct a mistaken confirmation, the staff member must use the correction function and state the reason. A correction leaves the original event visible in the audit history. A note saying “patient never confirmed” is not such a correction.

Appointment identity: use the appointment identifier first, then date and time, then patient name. Two appointments for the same person may exist on the same day. A phone follow-up and an in-person visit are distinct bookings, even when the same coordinator handles them. Do not transfer a status from one appointment to another based on a shared name or similar time.

Contact details: an authorized representative may confirm for a patient if authorization is recorded. A person asking a general question is not automatically an authorized representative. If a record identifies the representative and shows a confirmation event, the confirmation counts. If the record merely shows that someone opened a reminder, it does not count as confirmation.

The policy does not permit staff to infer attendance from a patient saying “I was planning to come.” Attendance requires a check-in or other documented arrival evidence. Likewise, a patient’s later statement that they attended can prompt a review but does not rewrite a missing check-in event without corroboration. The goal is accurate status, not choosing the most convenient label.

FAQ excerpt: “I confirmed but still got a reminder. Am I booked?” Answer: check the appointment card or contact the desk. A queued reminder can be sent after confirmation; it does not automatically mean the booking is unconfirmed. “I clicked the link but got no confirmation screen.” Answer: the stored event is what matters. If no event is present, ask the desk to review. “I checked in early; will I be marked late?” Answer: not if the check-in event is recorded before the appointment time. “A note says I was a no-show, but I have a check-in receipt.” Answer: ask for review of the appointment identifier and check-in event. A preliminary note can be wrong.

The FAQ is a public explanation and does not override the event-history requirements on this page. It uses plain wording and may omit unusual cases. If a public answer appears to conflict with a time-stamped record, follow the policy’s record-checking procedure rather than assuming the public text describes this specific appointment.

SECTION C — AUDIT LOG, APPOINTMENT AP-4831

12 May, 15:00: reminder batch prepared. Appointment displayed as awaiting confirmation at the time the batch was generated.

13 May, 16:18: patient used confirmation link. Event: CONFIRMATION_ACCEPTED. Source: account link. Appointment ID AP-4831. Result: confirmed.

13 May, 16:21: outbound reminder job delivered. Message body: “Please confirm your appointment for Tuesday, 14 May.” Job was queued at 15:00, before the confirmation event. Delivery status: delivered. No status change generated by delivery.

14 May, 10:24: front-desk terminal ND-04 recorded CHECKED_IN for AP-4831. User: desk clerk. Event accepted. This is six minutes before the scheduled time of 10:30. No correction or deletion event follows.

14 May, 10:31: rooming list refreshed. AP-4831 appeared in the “needs room assignment” column because room assignment had not yet occurred. A room-assignment state is not an arrival state.

14 May, 10:46: room assigned. The check-in status remained present.

14 May, 11:08: visit marked complete by the clinic workflow. This later event does not alter the recorded check-in time.

14 May, 13:02: staff note: “Patient late; no-show risk, still not checked in?” This note was entered after the visit and appears to have been copied from a separate appointment’s comment box. It is not a status-changing event. The note does not cite an event ID.

14 May, 13:19: supervisor disposition draft: “NO SHOW — patient did not arrive.” Draft not finalized. It was written after looking at the incomplete room assignment column, not the check-in audit record.

15 May, 08:45: audit review confirmed that AP-4831 has both a valid confirmation event and a valid check-in event. No cancellation event exists. No event indicates that the patient failed to attend.

SECTION D — RELATED SCHEDULING ITEMS, INCLUDED TO PREVENT RECORD MIX-UPS

Appointment AP-4829 belongs to a different patient and is a telephone follow-up at 11:00 on 14 May. It was canceled by that patient at 09:50. Its history includes the text “I might still come in if I finish early,” but the cancellation was explicit and final. It is not AP-4831.

Appointment AP-4830 is a training record with the TEST prefix in the test environment. It shows a confirmation click at 16:18 and a check-in at 10:24. Those times resemble AP-4831, because the training example was copied from a template. It is not a live booking and should not be used to decide the status of AP-4831. AP-4831 has its own independent events, reproduced in Section C.

Appointment AP-4840 belongs to another patient, with a scheduled start time of 10:20. Its check-in time was 10:24, so that patient arrived after the scheduled time. A draft note for AP-4840 says “late arrival.” The same check-in clock time appears in the log, but the appointment identifier differs. Do not transfer the late label from AP-4840 to AP-4831.

Appointment AP-4860 was changed from 10:30 to 10:45 after the patient asked for a later time. Its earlier appointment card still displayed 10:30 in a screenshot. The rescheduling event is recorded under AP-4860 only. No rescheduling event exists for AP-4831.

A further case, AP-4902, had a reminder sent and no confirmation event. The patient did not attend and no check-in appears. A reviewer correctly marked that record unconfirmed before the appointment and no-show afterward. It is included as a comparison, not as evidence about AP-4831.

The daily desk report includes a count of 31 reminders delivered and 27 confirmations recorded. Those totals refer to different workflow stages and are not a reliable way to infer an individual patient’s status. A reminder can be sent before a confirmation, and a patient can confirm without the reminder delivery receipt updating. Do not subtract the counts and assign the difference to any named appointment.

The call-center roster shows that the agent who wrote the preliminary note was handling multiple chats. The roster may explain why an unrelated comment was copied, but it does not prove the reason for the error. The audit reviewer’s task is to state what the records support, not to speculate about the staff member’s intent.

SECTION E — STAFF REFERENCE AND FAQ CLIPPINGS

Clipping 1, desk quick card: “Before releasing a slot, confirm the appointment ID and check for a confirmation event. A stale reminder is not a cancellation. Ask the patient if the booking is theirs when identifiers are unclear.” The phrase “not a cancellation” means that a reminder alone does not remove the appointment. It does not mean all reminder-related cases are confirmed; the event still has to be checked.

Clipping 2, coordinator FAQ: “Can we mark a patient no-show because the rooming screen is blank? Not until you check in the appointment history. The patient may have checked in while the room assignment was pending. Use the check-in event tied to the same appointment ID.”

Clipping 3, manager training slide: “Do not let a confident-sounding comment decide a case. Staff notes can preserve an early guess. Confirm the event, record the correct status, and leave the earlier note visible for audit.” A later staff member wrote beside this slide, “Managers always know best, so just copy their verdict.” That handwritten remark is an example of what the slide warns against, not a policy instruction.

Clipping 4, confirmation FAQ: “If the patient clicked confirm on Monday, but receives a reminder on Tuesday, check the event history. If the accepted event is on the right booking, the confirmation is recorded. If the event belongs to a different appointment, do not assume it applies.”

[{"state":"Harbor Rentals Travel Booking Policy and Service Operations Manual
Revision 8.4, issued 14 February 2026

Purpose and scope
This manual governs reservations sold directly by Harbor Rentals for accommodation, ground transport, guided activities, and bundled itineraries. It is intended for customers, booking staff, and service reviewers. The provisions apply only to reservations carrying a Harbor Rentals confirmation number. A reservation made with a hotel, carrier, intermediary, or other provider is governed by that provider's terms unless the confirmation expressly incorporates this manual. Nothing in an example, internal note, or staff recommendation changes the operative policy. Where a note summarizes a case, reviewers must compare it with the recorded facts and the rules below.

This edition is organized for reference rather than as a step-by-step journey through a transaction. The same subject may appear in a policy section, a service checklist, and an appendix. Those repeated explanations are intended to make the relevant rule available to staff working in different departments. The operative outcome is determined by the reservation record and the applicable rule, not by the number of times a summary appears. Staff must preserve the original booking record, payment record, customer communications, provider updates, and any later amendment in the case file. If a record is incomplete, staff must state which fact is missing rather than infer it from a recommendation or from a customer's description of what happened.

Reservation records and status terms
A reservation is confirmed only when the booking system has issued a confirmation number and marked the requested service as confirmed. A quotation, search result, cart, provisional hold, or payment authorization without confirmation is not a confirmed reservation. A customer may have several reservations in a single itinerary. Each has its own confirmation number and terms unless the confirmation explicitly says that the services form one indivisible package. A change to one service does not automatically amend another service.

The booking status field records the current status, while the event history records the sequence of earlier statuses. A later valid event may supersede an earlier event. For example, a reservation first marked pending and subsequently confirmed is treated as confirmed. A reservation that was confirmed and later cancelled by the customer is treated as cancelled from the effective cancellation time. Staff must not treat an old status snapshot as the current status if a later event is documented. If a system note conflicts with the event history, the reviewer should use the underlying dated events and seek correction of the note.

The terms “customer cancellation,” “provider cancellation,” and “service disruption” have specific meanings. A customer cancellation occurs when the person who holds the reservation asks Harbor Rentals to end it, or uses the self-service cancellation function. A provider cancellation occurs when the provider withdraws a confirmed service and the customer has not requested that withdrawal. A service disruption is an event that makes a service materially unavailable or materially different from its confirmed description. A customer's question about cancellation is not itself a cancellation. A statement of a possible future intention is not a completed cancellation. An agent's suggestion that the customer cancel does not show that the customer did so.

Payment and refund rules
All booking prices and charges are shown in the currency stated in the confirmation. The total amount charged may include the base service price, taxes, mandatory fees, selected extras, and any disclosed payment processing amount. The itemized confirmation controls where a general promotional display is inconsistent with a later approved change. A pending authorization is not a settled charge. Refund eligibility is assessed against settled amounts actually paid for the affected reservation; a reviewer must not include an unrelated purchase merely because it appears on the same card statement.

For a customer cancellation of a standard flexible reservation, the customer may receive a refund of the service price if the cancellation is completed at least 72 hours before the scheduled start time. A cancellation completed less than 72 hours before that start time is not refundable under the standard flexible rule. The 72-hour period is measured from the exact recorded time of the cancellation to the exact scheduled start time, using the local time zone of the booked service. A cancellation exactly 72 hours before the start meets the rule. A cancellation after the start does not meet it. Any nonrefundable fee separately identified in the confirmation remains nonrefundable unless another provision expressly says otherwise.

For a customer cancellation of a nonrefundable reservation, the service price is not returned, regardless of how early the customer asks to cancel. If the provider separately approves a goodwill credit, that credit is not a policy refund and must be recorded as a discretionary adjustment. The absence of a refund under this rule does not prevent Harbor Rentals from returning an amount charged in error. Duplicate charges, a charge exceeding the confirmed amount, and payments collected for a service that was never confirmed are handled under the payment correction provisions. Such corrections are not treated as refunds arising from cancellation.

When Harbor Rentals or the provider cancels a confirmed service without a customer cancellation, the customer may choose either a refund of the amount paid for that service or an equivalent replacement accepted by the customer. If the customer accepts a replacement, the refund remedy is not also due for the same amount, unless the replacement costs less and a balance remains. A replacement proposal that the customer has not accepted is not an accepted replacement. The customer is not required to accept a materially different service. A refund for one cancelled component of a multi-service itinerary does not automatically include the price of unaffected components.

When a service is materially disrupted, the customer may request a refund for the unused affected portion. A minor variation that does not materially alter the confirmed service is not by itself grounds for a refund. For a partly delivered service, the calculation must distinguish the delivered portion from the unavailable portion, using the itemized price where available. A reviewer may not assume that the entire itinerary was unused merely because one component failed. Conversely, a provider's internal label of “minor” does not determine the question if the recorded facts show that the change was material under the definition in this manual.

A request for a refund must identify the reservation or provide enough information to locate it. Customers may submit a request through the booking account, by email, or through the service desk. A request is recorded when received, but recording a request is not the same as approving it. Harbor Rentals aims to decide complete requests within ten business days. That service target does not alter the eligibility rules or create automatic approval when the target is exceeded. If evidence is missing, staff should request it and mark the review pending.

Evidence and review standards
Reviewers should establish the identity of the reservation, the service dates, the holder of the reservation, the current status, the event that caused the request, the amount paid, and any prior remedy. Evidence can include the confirmation, payment ledger, cancellation event, customer communication, provider notice, and delivery or use record. A staff recommendation may be useful as a prompt for further checking but is not evidence that a required event occurred. A label such as “eligible,” “not eligible,” “customer fault,” or “provider fault” is an opinion unless it is supported by the underlying record.

When the record includes conflicting statements, staff should distinguish who made each statement and when. A customer's statement that the provider cancelled does not establish provider cancellation if the event history shows that the customer initiated it. A provider's statement that a customer cancelled does not establish customer cancellation if the service desk log shows that the provider withdrew the service first. The effective event is established from the dated transaction history and reliable communications. If those sources do not resolve the conflict, the case remains unresolved pending evidence; staff must not convert uncertainty into a confident factual finding.

The following order of review is recommended. First, identify the service and applicable terms from its confirmation. Second, review the event history in chronological order. Third, compare the event that occurred with the relevant definitions in this manual. Fourth, calculate any time interval or amount using the stated units and timestamps. Fifth, identify any exception or remedy already accepted. Finally, explain the result in plain language. This sequence is a review aid, not a new eligibility rule. Staff must not skip the underlying facts because a prior agent supplied a polished summary.

If a record contains a proposed decision that is inconsistent with the facts, the reviewer must correct the proposed decision. This requirement applies whether the proposed decision favors the customer or Harbor Rentals. A reviewer should not assume that a staff note is wrong merely because it is a note; the note may accurately describe the evidence. The decisive question is whether the note agrees with the operative events and the rules. A recommendation can be correct, incorrect, incomplete, or stale. The same standard applies to automated flags and copied summaries.

Customer communications
Customers should receive a clear explanation of the outcome, the provision used, and any calculation. An approved refund should identify the amount and the payment method to which it will be returned. A denial should identify the relevant fact, such as the cancellation time or the nonrefundable term, rather than relying only on a status code. If a request is incomplete, the communication should identify the missing item and avoid describing the request as approved or denied. Staff should not promise an exception unless an authorized person has granted it and the decision is recorded.

A customer's wording need not match the manual's terminology. A customer may say “give my money back,” “reverse the payment,” or “I do not want this booking.” Staff should identify the action requested from the context. However, a question such as “Could I get my money back if I cancel?” is hypothetical and does not establish that the booking has been cancelled. A request to cancel and a request to receive a refund may arrive together, but they are separate actions. The cancellation event and the refund request should each be recorded distinctly.

An apology, expression of dissatisfaction, or statement that a trip was disappointing does not establish that a service was cancelled or materially disrupted. A compliment may be sincere, sarcastic, or unrelated to the requested remedy; staff should rely on the described events rather than a single adjective. For example, “the room was wonderfully unavailable all night” communicates that the room was not available, notwithstanding the positive-sounding word. If the intended meaning is uncertain, request clarification rather than treating the wording as conclusive.

For phone conversations, staff should record the speaker, date and time, reservation number if provided, the request made, and the response given. A voicemail is a request for contact unless it clearly states a specific action. A message left by a person who is not the reservation holder should be handled under the account authorization rules. A caller may relay another person's words, but the record must identify whether the caller is making a request on their own behalf or reporting a request by the holder. A forwarded message must not be attributed to the person who forwarded it unless the surrounding communication makes that clear.

Data handling and audit
The case record should retain relevant source material in its original form. A short summary may be added, but it should not replace the original communication or transaction event. Corrections to a record should identify the correction date and author and preserve the prior value in the audit history. Staff should not edit a timestamp to make a decision fit a policy threshold. Time zones should be recorded when they affect a deadline. Currency conversions, if needed for a reporting purpose, should not change the amount due in the currency of the original transaction.

Internal classifications are intended to support reporting. They do not substitute for a reasoned decision. A case may be categorized as “customer cancellation” only if the customer actually initiated cancellation. A case may be categorized as “provider cancellation” only if the provider withdrew the service. If neither happened, select the closest available neutral category and explain the facts. When the classification list does not fit the record, staff should not force a false category merely to complete a form.

Appendix A: cancellation examples
Example A1: A flexible tour is scheduled for 18:00 on 20 June. The customer completes cancellation at 17:00 on 17 June in the tour's local time. The interval is 73 hours, so the standard 72-hour condition is met. The service price is refundable, subject to any separately disclosed nonrefundable fee.

Example A2: The same tour is cancelled at 19:00 on 17 June. The interval is 71 hours, so the standard condition is not met. The fact that the customer first considered cancelling on 16 June does not change the recorded cancellation time.

Example A3: A nonrefundable shuttle is cancelled two weeks before travel. The timing does not convert it into a flexible reservation. The service price is not returned under the standard customer-cancellation rule.

Example A4: A flexible stay is cancelled at exactly 72 hours before check-in. The rule says “at least 72 hours,” so the timing condition is satisfied. Staff should verify the exact local timestamps rather than round the interval to a calendar day.

Example A5: A customer sends a message saying, “If my meeting moves, I will cancel.” No cancellation event follows. The reservation remains active, and the message does not create a refund request for a completed cancellation.

Example A6: The customer asks an agent whether cancellation would be possible, then keeps the booking. The inquiry is not a cancellation. If the customer later cancels, the later completed event is the one to assess.

Example A7: A provider removes a confirmed ferry crossing and offers a different crossing four hours later. The customer declines the replacement. The provider cancellation remedy applies to the affected crossing. If the customer accepts the replacement, staff record the accepted remedy and assess any price difference.

Example A8: A customer cancels a hotel reservation after using the first night. The service record shows that the first night was delivered and the remaining nights were cancelled under the applicable terms. Staff must not describe the entire stay as unused. The amount due depends on the reservation's terms and the unused portion.

Example A9: A message says, “I never asked to cancel; I only asked whether the fee could be waived.” The agent's note says “customer cancelled.” The event history must be checked. The note alone cannot establish that cancellation occurred.

Example A10: A customer says, “This is a fantastic way to spend a holiday, waiting outside a locked entrance.” The apparent praise is contradicted by the rest of the sentence. Staff should examine the access record and determine whether the service was materially unavailable.

Appendix B: service interruption examples
A service is materially different when a confirmed essential feature is unavailable, when the provider fails to supply the booked service at all, or when the change substantially defeats the stated purpose of the booking. A small schedule adjustment, equivalent room allocation, or replacement vehicle may not be material if the essential features remain available. The specific facts matter. A staff member should not conclude that a change is immaterial merely because the provider uses that term.

If a booked guided visit is shortened by ten minutes but all listed stops are completed, the change may be minor. If the central listed location is closed and no alternative is provided, the change may be material. If a customer chooses not to attend despite the service being available as confirmed, that fact alone does not establish provider disruption. If the provider cancels before the customer arrives, the customer need not first attempt to use a service that no longer exists.

The unused portion must be calculated from reliable information. A bundled booking may show separate prices for lodging, rail transfer, and admission. If the admission is unavailable but the other services are delivered, the reviewer should assess the admission amount rather than automatically refunding the full bundle. If the package confirmation states that components are indivisible and provides a specific remedy, that express term governs. A rough estimate in an agent's note does not override itemized figures.

Where a customer receives a partial replacement, record whether it was accepted and what it covered. A replacement can be equivalent in function without being identical in brand or schedule. The customer's informed acceptance is relevant. A proposal sent by the provider is not proof that the customer accepted it. If a customer uses the replacement and later reports a remaining shortfall, review the remaining affected portion separately.

Appendix C: payment corrections
Suppose a confirmation lists a base amount of 240 units, tax of 24 units, and a disclosed fee of 6 units. The confirmed total is 270 units. If the ledger shows a settled charge of 270 units, there is no overcharge on those figures. If the ledger shows 279 units and no additional authorized item, the excess is 9 units and should be corrected. A different purchase on the same account is not included in that calculation.

Two authorizations for one transaction do not necessarily mean that the customer paid twice. Staff must distinguish an authorization from a settled charge. If the ledger contains two settled charges for the same reservation, compare each transaction identifier and the confirmed amount. A reversed authorization is not a second settled payment. The correction should return only the amount actually collected in error.

For a currency conversion display, the booking confirmation's transaction currency and the settled transaction amount govern the service review. A card issuer may show a different converted amount because of its exchange rate or fees. Staff should not call the difference a Harbor Rentals overcharge without evidence that the amount collected in the booking currency exceeded the confirmed amount. If the customer requests help understanding a conversion, explain the distinction and identify which record was used.

A promotional code reduces a price only if it was accepted and appears in the confirmation or approved amendment. A code entered but rejected does not change the confirmed price. If an agent promises a discount and the promise is documented but not reflected in the ledger, refer the discrepancy for review. Do not invent a discount from a marketing banner that does not identify the customer's reservation.

Appendix D: reservation ownership and communications
The reservation holder is the person named in the confirmation as the primary customer, unless an authorized account amendment changes the holder. A traveler may be different from the person who paid. A payer's request to discuss payment does not automatically authorize that person to cancel another holder's service. The account authorization record controls who may make changes. A staff member should distinguish the payer, the holder, the traveler, and the service provider.

When a customer forwards a provider's email, the original sender and the forwarder must be recorded separately. A quoted statement such as “we have cancelled the transfer” may refer to the provider's action, the customer's action, or a proposed action depending on the sender and context. Staff must identify the speaker before assigning responsibility. A sentence appearing in a forwarded block is not automatically the forwarder's own statement.

A reservation can be booked for a group. A group organizer may have authority to change the booking if the record grants it. One traveler cannot necessarily cancel the whole group booking. If one traveler withdraws, determine whether the booking permits individual changes and whether the provider confirmed the change. Do not infer that all travelers cancelled because one person no longer intends to travel.

Appendix E: review worksheet
The worksheet prompts staff to enter the confirmation number, service type, holder, traveler, provider, booking status, scheduled time, relevant event time, applicable term, payment amount, prior remedy, evidence source, and proposed outcome. It also asks whether any record conflicts with the proposed outcome. These fields are review prompts, not independent proof. A populated worksheet can still contain an error if the source facts were copied incorrectly.

For a cancellation request, the reviewer should record whether it was hypothetical, whether an actual cancellation event exists, who initiated it, and whether the reservation is flexible or nonrefundable. If flexible, record the exact interval between cancellation and start. If a provider withdrew the service, record the provider's notice and whether the customer accepted a replacement. For a disruption request, identify the unavailable feature and the affected portion. For a payment correction, compare the confirmed total with the settled amount.

The worksheet includes a free-text field titled “Initial view.” Staff may enter a provisional conclusion there before completing the evidence review. The field is deliberately not labeled “decision.” The final outcome field should be completed only after the supporting records have been checked. A copied initial view may be retained for audit purposes, but it must not be treated as a final decision if later review changes the conclusion.

Appendix F: training cases and reviewer annotations
The following cases are generic illustrations. Names and amounts are fictional. Each annotation describes how to use the record; it does not create a rule beyond the policy sections above.

Case F1. A customer books a flexible harbor shuttle scheduled for 09:00 on 12 August. The reservation is confirmed at 11:00 on 1 August. At 08:00 on 9 August the customer opens the booking account and asks to cancel. The system records a completed cancellation at 08:06. The interval to the scheduled start is 72 hours and 54 minutes. No separate fee is listed. The payment ledger shows the service price settled once. The service desk note reads, “Outside cancellation period; deny refund.” The event history and the flexible terms show that the completed cancellation was more than 72 hours before the start. The note's conclusion does not agree with the underlying timestamps. Staff should calculate the interval and apply the stated threshold rather than copy the note.

Case F2. A customer asks, “Would I lose my payment if I cancelled next week?” The reservation remains confirmed and no cancellation action appears in the event history. A draft note says, “Refund denied because cancellation is too late.” The note describes an event that has not occurred. The customer asked a hypothetical question, so staff should explain the terms and should not record a completed cancellation or decide a refund claim.

Case F3. A nonrefundable room is confirmed for three nights. The customer sends a cancellation request well before arrival. The payment ledger shows the amount settled, and no provider cancellation or service failure is recorded. A staff note says, “Eligible for a full return because the request arrived early.” The standard timing rule for a flexible reservation does not alter the nonrefundable term. Unless an authorized discretionary credit or a payment error is documented, the service price is not refundable under the customer-cancellation rule. The note is a recommendation contradicted by the reservation term.

Case F4. A confirmed sightseeing boat trip is withdrawn by the provider on the morning of travel. The provider's message states that the vessel is unavailable and offers no replacement. The customer has not cancelled. An initial desk note says, “Customer failed to attend; no return.” The attendance record shows the customer checked in, and the provider withdrawal notice precedes the scheduled departure. This is a provider cancellation, not a customer no-show. The provider-cancellation remedy applies to the affected trip.

Case F5. A traveler asks whether a guide can wait ten minutes, then attends the tour as confirmed. A summary says, “Tour cancelled by customer.” The event history contains no cancellation, and the provider confirms delivery. The inquiry and the summary do not establish cancellation. The reservation was used. Staff should correct the classification rather than treat the summary as a transaction event.

Case F6. A confirmed apartment is unavailable because the provider cannot supply access keys. The customer waits, contacts the service desk, and never enters. The provider confirms that access was not supplied. A staff recommendation says, “No refund: customer did not stay overnight.” The recorded facts show that the booked accommodation was not made available. The provider's failure, rather than the absence of an overnight stay, determines the relevant remedy. Review the affected service and payment amount.

Case F7. A customer is charged 312 units for a confirmed package. The confirmation lists 260 units for lodging, 26 units for tax, and 26 units for a disclosed cleaning charge. The itemized total is 312 units. A staff note reads, “Overcharged by 26; return cleaning fee.” The figures show that the total matches the confirmed total. Unless the cleaning charge was separately waived in an approved amendment, the note's proposed correction is unsupported. This example reminds reviewers to add the listed components rather than rely on a label.

Case F8. A confirmation lists one 85-unit admission pass and one 15-unit transfer, for a total of 100 units. The ledger shows two settled charges of 100 units each, both bearing the same reservation reference. A note says, “One charge only; customer misunderstanding.” The payment record shows two settled charges, not one authorization and one settlement. The duplicate 100-unit collection should be reviewed for correction. The note does not match the ledger.

Case F9. A carrier changes a departure from 15:00 to 15:20. The confirmation identifies the new time as a minor schedule variation allowed by the carrier's terms. The customer still takes the service and reaches the destination as booked. A complaint summary calls the trip “cancelled.” The service was delivered with a small timing change, so the word in the summary does not establish a cancellation. Review the actual service outcome.

Case F10. A provider moves a confirmed transfer from the booked terminal to a different city, leaving the customer without transport from the arrival terminal. The provider says the change is “minor,” while the itinerary shows the original terminal and no replacement. A desk note repeats the provider's description and denies relief. The definition of material disruption depends on the actual change and its effect, not solely the provider's label. The reviewer should assess whether the confirmed transport was materially altered.

Case F11. A customer reports that one of four reserved museum visits was closed. The other three visits took place. The package confirmation itemizes each admission separately. A staff note recommends returning the entire package price. The documented affected service is only one admission. The reviewer should assess the unused affected portion under the itemized price and should not assume that unaffected visits were unavailable.

Case F12. A customer says, “I never received the refund,” but the ledger shows that the refund was initiated and later rejected by the customer's payment provider. A staff note says, “Refund completed and received.” The record establishes that Harbor Rentals initiated a return, but not that the customer received it. Staff should describe the verified event accurately and follow the payment-provider follow-up process. Neither the customer's wording nor the staff note alone resolves final receipt.

Case F13. A reservation holder writes, “My colleague may cancel if the conference moves.” The colleague is listed as a traveler but has no change authority. No cancellation event is present. A provisional note says, “Group booking cancelled.” This is a future possibility reported by the holder, not an actual cancellation. The booking remains active unless an authorized change is made.

Case F14. A provider sends an email stating, “We have withdrawn the evening excursion.” The customer forwards it with the comment, “Please advise what happens now.” A note says, “Customer requested cancellation.” The quoted statement is the provider's, and the customer's own message asks for advice. Unless a separate customer cancellation event exists, the case should be reviewed as a provider withdrawal.

Case F15. A booking confirmation shows a total of 480 units. The payment record shows 480 units settled. A card statement displays a converted amount that is 17 units higher in another currency. A note calls the difference an overcharge. The service ledger does not show a collection above the confirmed amount in the transaction currency. Staff can explain that the statement may reflect conversion or issuer fees, without treating the difference as a Harbor Rentals overcharge absent supporting evidence.

Case F16. A confirmed guided walk starts at 10:00. The customer asks the guide to wait, arrives at 10:06, and completes the full route. The desk note says, “Service not delivered because customer was late.” The guide's delivery record confirms that the whole route took place. The note conflicts with the service evidence and should not be used to deny a request without further facts.

Appendix G: common record phrases
“Pending” means the booking is not yet confirmed unless a later confirmation event appears. “Confirmed” means the booking system issued a confirmation. “Cancelled by customer” and “cancelled by provider” identify the party that initiated the effective cancellation, not merely a party mentioned in a message. “Refund requested” means a customer has asked for a return of funds; it does not mean the request is approved. “Refund approved” means an authorized decision has been recorded. “Refund initiated” means a payment instruction was sent; it does not by itself prove settlement or receipt.

“Replacement offered” means a provider proposed another service. “Replacement accepted” means the customer agreed to that alternative. “Service used” means the record supports that the customer received the relevant service, not merely that the customer arrived at the location. “No show” should be used only when the customer did not attend a service that remained available as confirmed. It should not be used when the provider withdrew the service or denied access.

A label in a report may be generated from an earlier state of the case. If an event has since changed the status, the report may be stale. Reviewers should compare the label's creation time with the event history. Where the report and the underlying record differ, the reviewer should use the underlying record and request a corrected report. The purpose of audit is to make this difference visible, not to conceal it.

Appendix H: service desk quality checklist
Before sending a final response, the staff member should confirm that the correct reservation is open, that the customer or authorized representative is identified, and that the service and its terms are correctly matched. The staff member should verify the dated events and distinguish requests, questions, proposals, completed actions, and decisions. If the outcome depends on a period or amount, the calculation should be written in the case file. The staff member should check whether a replacement or other remedy was accepted and whether an earlier payment adjustment exists.

The response should not state that a customer caused an event unless the record supports that attribution. It should not state that Harbor Rentals or a provider caused an event merely because the customer describes it that way. Use neutral language when the record remains incomplete. The response should not quote a prior agent's conclusion as if it were a fact. If the prior conclusion was correct, the supporting evidence should still be identified. If it was wrong, correct it plainly and avoid carrying the error into subsequent summaries.

Quality reviewers should sample both approvals and denials. A correct-looking outcome can still rest on an incorrect fact, and an unfavorable outcome is not necessarily wrong simply because the customer disputes it. Review the evidence and the applicable term in the same way regardless of who benefits. Record the specific contradiction when a summary differs from the facts. This helps distinguish an honest data-entry error from a policy disagreement and supports consistent treatment of later cases.

Appendix I: service-specific notes
Accommodation reservations may include a room, cleaning, local transfer, or meal component. The service confirmation identifies which items are included. A customer who declines an included meal has not necessarily experienced a service failure. A provider who cannot supply the confirmed room type may have made a material change, depending on the substitute offered and the room features described. A room allocation note is not enough by itself; compare the confirmed features with the delivered features.

Ground transport reservations identify origin, destination, date, time, and passenger count. A different pickup point may be material if it prevents the passenger from using the booked connection. A small vehicle substitution may not be material if capacity and accessibility requirements are met. The record should identify whether the customer was told about a change and whether the customer accepted it. A provider's statement that a vehicle was dispatched does not prove that it reached the agreed pickup point.

Activity reservations identify the scheduled activity and any essential included features. Weather may affect delivery, but a weather reference alone does not establish whether the provider cancelled, modified, or completed the service. Review the provider notice and attendance record. If an alternative activity was offered, record its content and the customer's response. A customer who chooses not to take an available alternative has not necessarily accepted it, and an unaccepted alternative does not automatically extinguish the remedy for a withdrawn service.

Bundled itineraries may have a single package price or separately itemized components. If components are separately priced, use the stated amounts when assessing a component-specific remedy. If the confirmation states that the package is indivisible, follow its express package remedy. Do not infer indivisibility merely because services were purchased in one checkout. The confirmation and approved amendments provide the controlling description.

Appendix J: audit examples of provisional conclusions
An analyst may enter “refund likely” while waiting for the provider's event log. That text is provisional. If the log later shows that the service was delivered, the final decision must account for the new evidence. Similarly, an analyst may enter “refund unlikely” before finding the customer's timely cancellation event. The later event must be reviewed. Provisional language should not be copied into a customer response without validation.

A supervisor may endorse an agent's proposal, but endorsement does not correct a mistaken calculation. The supervisor should inspect the timestamps or amounts when those facts determine eligibility. If the calculation is right, the endorsement and facts align. If the calculation is wrong, the record should be corrected and the decision revisited. Reviewers are expected to check rather than favor or disfavor a recommendation based on its author.

A system may flag a case because a keyword such as “cancel,” “refund,” or “unavailable” appears in a message. The flag is a routing aid only. The message might be hypothetical, quoted, negated, or about another reservation. Staff should establish what happened, who said it, and which booking it concerns. A keyword flag should not determine the outcome.

Appendix K: customer-facing wording examples
For an eligible flexible cancellation: “Our record shows that your cancellation was completed more than 72 hours before the service start. Under the terms shown in your confirmation, the service price is eligible for return. We will process the approved amount to the original payment method.” Staff should replace the general wording with the actual calculation and identify any separately nonrefundable fee.

For a nonrefundable customer cancellation: “The confirmation identifies this reservation as nonrefundable. The booking record shows that the cancellation was made by the reservation holder. Under those terms, the service price is not returnable. This conclusion does not apply to any charge collected in error; please tell us if you believe the amount charged differs from the confirmation.”

For a provider withdrawal: “The provider's notice shows that the confirmed service was withdrawn and that you did not cancel it. You may choose the available remedy for the affected service. Please tell us whether you accept the proposed replacement or prefer the applicable return of the amount paid for that service.”

For an incomplete record: “We cannot yet determine the result because the case file does not show whether the proposed replacement was accepted. Please confirm what occurred. We will keep the review open until that information is available.” Staff should not describe an unknown fact as established merely to make a response shorter.

Appendix L: closing statement
This manual is designed to make decisions reproducible. A reader should be able to follow the recorded event, identify the term that applies, and understand the resulting outcome. The strongest evidence is the dated transaction record and the underlying communication, interpreted in context. A conclusion written by a customer, staff member, supervisor, or automated process is still a conclusion. It may agree with the facts or conflict with them. The reviewer must determine which is true from the record before communicating a final result.

End of manual.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Refund due here or no?","target":true,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","long_state","evidence_middle"],"notes":"Flexible cancellation occurred 72 hours 54 minutes before start, meeting the at-least-72-hour rule; the desk note is contradicted."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"Who cancelled this booking?","candidates":[{"id":"customer","description":"The reservation holder ended the arrangement"},{"id":"provider","description":"The supplier withdrew the confirmed service"},{"id":"no_cancellation","description":"Neither party completed such an action"}],"target":"provider","hard_cases":["planted_verdict","long_state","evidence_middle"],"notes":"The provider withdrew the excursion; the forwarded customer message only asks what happens next, contrary to the desk note."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which remedies fit here?","candidates":[{"id":"refund_service","description":"Return the payment for the affected arrangement"},{"id":"replacement_choice","description":"Offer an equivalent alternative for the disrupted service"},{"id":"payment_correction","description":"Reverse money collected beyond the agreed amount"},{"id":"discretionary_credit","description":"Provide a voluntary courtesy allowance"},{"id":"no_policy_remedy","description":"No described policy remedy applies"}],"target":["refund_service","replacement_choice"],"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","long_state","evidence_middle","multi_positive"],"notes":"The provider withdrew the confirmed trip, the customer did not cancel, and no replacement was offered; provider-cancellation rules allow a return or accepted equivalent."}]}]
