It explains why prior experience is helpful but not required.

The job posting was checked against the archived copy by the coordinator. The wording is the same in both places. The relevant line reads: “Minimum: secondary school completion or equivalent. Basic spreadsheet comfort. Availability for the scheduled weekday shift. College study and previous inventory work are assets, not conditions of eligibility.” The coordinator wrote below it: “This is not a case where the wording says degree required and someone is trying to waive it. It says the opposite.” The note is a clarification, not a new policy.

Voicemail transcript, made by the office assistant after listening twice:

“Hi, this is the applicant calling about the inventory analyst role. I sent the form yesterday. I saw that the system says received, so I am not calling because I think the form disappeared. I wanted to check whether the spreadsheet file opened. It should have three tabs. On the first tab I totalled the quantities. On the second I sorted the entries by item name. On the last I marked the row where the packing slip and the shelf count do not match. I did not study inventory management at college; I did not go to college. I finished secondary school, and in the stockroom job I used a spreadsheet most weeks. If the role needs a degree, I understand, but I read the advert as saying it was not required. I can work the weekday hours written there. Please call if the attachment is damaged. Thanks.”

The assistant's transcript is not an evaluation of the exercise. It is only a record of the message. At the end, the assistant wrote, “Sounds confident, probably has advanced spreadsheet background.” That is an impression, not a factual credential. The applicant said they used spreadsheets for totals and sorting; the file does not say they have advanced expertise. Another line in the margin says, “No degree, so not eligible,” which repeats the earlier mistaken verdict. These comments should not be substituted for the posted criteria or the application answers.

The application form's education response is not ambiguous: the applicant selected “secondary school completed” and entered the completion year. The form's optional college field was left blank. The system's help text says that field may be left blank by applicants who have not attended college. It does not say a blank college field means the minimum education requirement is unmet. The applicant's résumé gives the same secondary school information, and the application screen marks the required education question complete.

The spreadsheet exercise was printed from the attachment. It has a small table of six item codes, expected counts, and observed counts. The instructions ask the applicant to calculate the difference for each row and flag any mismatch. The applicant used a simple subtraction formula, sorted the table by item code, and marked the row where the observed count was two fewer than the expected count. The row is flagged correctly. The exercise is not a complicated forecasting model. It is an entry-level check of whether the applicant can use a spreadsheet for basic organization and arithmetic. A reviewer wrote, “This seems too simple to show competence,” but the posting asks for basic comfort, not advanced modeling, and the application demonstrates the requested basic operations.

Handwritten-style note, typed up by Dalia because the original was difficult to read:

“Tuesday, after opening the folder. I thought at first the degree line meant no degree, no interview. Then I looked again at the ad. It says college study is useful but not required. I should not let the red rejection label do the reading for me. The applicant says secondary school finished, which matches the minimum. Also says yes to schedule and has a spreadsheet file. Need to check the file, not guess from the résumé. Someone wrote ‘friend referral’ on the cover, but the system shows no referral. Do not turn that into evidence either way about the minimums. This job is junior, and the first-week orientation is part of the plan.”

The typed note continues in the same chatty style:

“I keep finding little statements that sound definite because they are short. ‘Not qualified.’ ‘Must have degree.’ ‘No spreadsheet skill.’ Those are verdicts, not the underlying information. The actual listing has its own sentence, the form has its own answers, and the work sample is attached. We ought to read them in that order. I am not saying the applicant automatically gets the job. I am saying the current file does not support the specific claim that a college degree is mandatory or that the basic application is missing. Selection may depend on the interview and comparison with other candidates, but that is a different question.”

There is a second typed note, likely added later by a reviewer who was still unsure:

“Recommendation: do not advance. Candidate does not meet education criterion because no bachelor’s degree. The listing appears to require a bachelor’s degree for accuracy-sensitive work.”

This recommendation is inconsistent with the listing in two ways. The listing says secondary school or equivalent is the minimum, and it says a college credential is not required. It also does not specify a bachelor's degree at all. The recommendation may reflect an assumption about what an inventory analyst ought to have, but the packet does not establish that assumption as a company rule. The candidate's education record shows the stated minimum credential. The verdict in the recommendation cannot make the requirement different from the wording in the posting.

A third note, written on the back of the screening worksheet, says: “Could be a strong candidate, degree not needed, spreadsheet basics demonstrated.” This is closer to the documents but still should not be treated as a final hiring decision. It does not prove that the applicant is the strongest candidate, and it does not promise an interview. It merely agrees with the minimum-qualification facts. The review questions in this packet concern what the file supports, not whether a particular person should be hired.

The panel's draft rubric is included because a panel member asked whether reviewers could mark education as “pass” when the applicant had secondary school but no college. The rubric says:

Education, required: secondary school completion or equivalent, demonstrated by application or résumé. Pass if present; hold for clarification only if the record is genuinely unclear.

Spreadsheet, required: basic comfort using a spreadsheet to organize or check information. Pass if the applicant provides a relevant example or completes the short exercise at the basic level. Do not require advanced formulas or prior use of Larkspur's internal stock system.

Schedule, required: availability for the weekday shift specified in the listing. Pass if the applicant confirms availability.

Prior inventory work, preferred: useful context for interview questions, but not a screening gate.

College study, preferred: useful context for interview questions, but not a screening gate.

The rubric draft is not signed off as a final scoring instrument, but its requirements match the advertisement. It was circulated to prevent reviewers from making preferences into requirements. A reviewer added a comment, “Maybe make college a must for the next opening.” That is a suggestion about a future posting, not a change to this one. The current file must be read under the current listing.

The coordinator's file history shows that the first rejection was entered at 10:02 a.m., before the reviewer opened the spreadsheet exercise at 10:16 a.m. The status then remained unchanged while the packet was being assembled. The coordinator has not erased the original entry because the audit trail should show what happened. A status label can be factually inaccurate without being evidence that the underlying applicant lacks a qualification. The audit record tells us when the label was entered; the attached materials tell us what the applicant submitted.

A chat exchange between two panel members was pasted into the shared notes:

Panel member one: “I saw the red fail mark. Are we sure the degree is required?”

Panel member two: “I thought so, because accuracy matters.”

Panel member one: “The posting says secondary school minimum and degree preferred. I checked the archived copy.”

Panel member two: “Then the mark is wrong. Accuracy matters, but that does not add a degree requirement.”

Panel member one: “Right. We can still ask about careful checking in the interview. The exercise flags the mismatch.”

This exchange is included as a discussion, not as a final interview result. It does show that the red mark was challenged after someone checked the text. The applicant has not yet been told that the review is complete.

The assistant who transcribed the voicemail later added a correction to the log. The first transcript had said “I have college spreadsheet experience,” but on replay the assistant heard, “I used a spreadsheet in the stockroom; I did not study inventory management at college.” The corrected transcript above uses the replayed wording. The original rough line remains in the margin to preserve the transcription history. It must not be read as proof of college attendance. The application, résumé, and corrected recording all state or indicate no college degree. That is not a problem under the stated minimum.

The distinction between a credential and a skill is worth spelling out because the file has blurred them. The candidate's lack of a college degree is stated plainly. The candidate's basic spreadsheet use is also stated plainly and is supported by the exercise. A person can lack a degree and still meet a basic spreadsheet criterion. Conversely, a degree alone would not automatically establish that a person can do the particular spreadsheet task. The listing asks for both the minimum education and basic comfort, and the packet contains evidence for each of those minimums.

There is a small list in the coordinator's notebook titled “Things not to infer.” It reads:

Do not infer that the applicant has a degree from the phrase “spreadsheet experience.” The applicant says no degree.

Do not infer that the applicant lacks the required school credential from the blank optional college field. The form records secondary school completion.

Do not infer that the applicant was referred by a friend from the handwritten “friend referral” note. The system records no referral, and referral status is not a stated qualification.

Do not infer that the applicant has advanced spreadsheet expertise from the assistant's impression. The exercise supports basic operations only.

Do not infer that the applicant has failed because a reviewer typed “fail.” That label conflicts with the criterion as written.

Do not infer that passing the minimums guarantees selection. Other applicants, interviews, and later assessments are outside the question of whether these specific minimums are evidenced.

A loose page from the operations team gives examples of the first-month tasks. The new analyst checks that quantities on a receiving document match quantities entered into a stock sheet. If the total differs, the analyst records the difference and asks a lead to verify the source documents. New hires are shown the internal stock interface; the company does not expect them to arrive knowing it. The examples are deliberately small: comparing a carton count, sorting a replenishment list, and noting a duplicate item code. The operations lead wrote, “Carefulness is more important than fancy spreadsheet tricks for the junior opening.” This is an explanatory preference, not a new qualification.

Another reviewer wrote on that page: “No degree means the person cannot understand discrepancy work.” The page does not support that conclusion. The candidate's exercise identifies a discrepancy, and the résumé describes comparing packing slips with shelf labels. The reviewer may be expressing a concern worth discussing, but the claim that the applicant cannot do the work is contradicted by the included examples. The file does not claim the candidate has been tested on every possible inventory problem. It does show the basic activity requested in the posting.

The company has a general hiring guide in the folder. It says that a posting's required qualifications are screening requirements and preferred qualifications may help rank applicants who meet the requirements. It cautions: “Do not convert a preferred item into a mandatory item during review. If a posting is unclear, ask the recruiter before rejecting an applicant.” The guide is not an exception to the specific advertisement; it reinforces the distinction already stated there. A reviewer has underlined “accuracy-sensitive work” in the guide's example section and written, “This must mean degree.” The example section says no such thing. Accuracy-sensitive work is a reason to check evidence carefully, not a license to invent a credential rule.

The application was received before the posting closed. The date is not in dispute, and no one has alleged a late submission. The file has no information suggesting the applicant withdrew, changed availability, or asked to be considered for a different opening. A coordinator's quick summary says, “Application complete; requirements appear met; review exercise.” A manager's subsequent summary says, “Ineligible, degree missing.” Those summaries cannot both accurately describe the stated education requirement. The original listing and application fields resolve the disagreement.

There are several small chatty comments about the applicant's communication style. One person says the voicemail was “a bit long but perfectly understandable.” Another says the cover note has “a few awkward phrases but gets to the point.” A third says, “I like that they said if the attachment is broken, call; that is sensible.” None of these remarks changes the requirements or establishes a communication failure. The job asks for clear notes, but the packet contains no formal writing test or score. It would be unfair to turn casual impressions into a categorical claim that the candidate has failed a criterion that was not scored.

The copy of the résumé includes a line that reads: “Used spreadsheet for weekly stock list; checked totals before sending.” A reviewer highlighted “checked totals” and wrote, “This is not advanced.” The job criterion does not say advanced. The spreadsheet exercise shows the applicant can enter a formula, sort data, and identify a mismatch. The evidence supports the stated basic level. It does not establish proficiency in macros, complex forecasting, or database design, and the posting does not request those skills. One note says, “Maybe ask about formulas in an interview,” which would be reasonable as a follow-up, but it does not undo the evidence already present.

The coordinator made a short audit table:

Item: minimum education. Stated rule: secondary school or equivalent. Application evidence: completed secondary school. Reviewer verdict: fails because no degree. Check: verdict uses a preferred credential as if required.

Item: basic spreadsheet comfort. Stated rule: basic use. Application evidence: self-report plus short exercise with totals, sorting, and mismatch flag. Reviewer verdict: no evidence. Check: exercise is attached and shows the requested basic operations.

Item: weekday availability. Stated rule: confirm the posted schedule. Application evidence: yes on the form and in voicemail. Reviewer verdict: not reviewed. Check: evidence is present; final scheduling confirmation can still be obtained later.

Item: prior inventory work. Stated rule: preferred only. Application evidence: temporary stockroom tasks. Reviewer verdict: unclear. Check: helpful background, not a minimum.

Item: college credential. Stated rule: preferred, not required. Application evidence: none; applicant says no college degree. Reviewer verdict: mandatory and absent. Check: the verdict conflicts with the rule.

At the bottom of the table, the coordinator wrote: “The point is not to rubber-stamp someone because one note says they pass. Check the documents. Here the documents show the minimum school credential and the requested basic spreadsheet example. The strong red fail note is not supported.”

A separate manager memo states: “After review, applicant is ineligible. Degree required for this role. No evidence of spreadsheet skill. Do not schedule.” It is signed and dated. Because the memo is formal, it has been copied several times and is sometimes treated as authoritative. The memo's formality does not make its factual claims correct. It says “degree required,” while the posting says degree not required. It says “no evidence of spreadsheet skill,” while the application includes both a self-reported example and a completed exercise. The memo is a planted verdict in the file: it states a conclusion that the underlying records contradict. It is relevant as evidence of what one manager decided, but not as a reliable statement of the candidate's actual qualifications under the listing.

A note from the recruiting lead, added after the manager memo, says: “Please retain the memo, do not erase it. Record that the decision was based on an incorrect reading of the minimums. The applicant may be reviewed under the same stated criteria as the others. That does not guarantee an interview, and the panel should still compare the work sample consistently.” The lead does not say the applicant should be hired. The lead asks that the evidence be evaluated correctly.

The work sample itself has a cover page. The applicant wrote: “I used the directions in the email. I kept the original numbers visible and added a difference column so the mismatch would be easy to see. I did not use any special inventory program. If you wanted a different format, I can change it.” The file contains no instruction requiring a particular layout. The total on the first tab matches the numbers shown. The sorting on the second tab is in item-code order. On the third tab, one row is marked. The coordinator's answer key says that row is the only row with a discrepancy. A reviewer says, “The colors are plain,” which is true but irrelevant to the stated basic spreadsheet criterion.

A fragment from a call with the operations lead was typed into the folder:

Coordinator: “Would someone need prior stockroom work to start?”

Operations lead: “No, it helps. We teach our own stock screen.”

Coordinator: “Would they need a degree?”

Operations lead: “Not for this junior opening. The minimum is the school credential in the ad.”

Coordinator: “What does basic spreadsheet comfort mean here?”

Operations lead: “Being able to enter figures, total a few rows, sort a list, and notice when two documents do not agree. The sample is about that level.”

Operations lead: “I do not want us to pretend we can judge every work habit from a worksheet. The interview will give us more information.”

This is a conversation about the requirements, not an interview with the applicant. It agrees with the wording of the listing and explains the work sample. It does not supply new evidence about the candidate beyond what is already in the application.

The applicant's cover note is brief and slightly rambling. It says they are interested in practical work where careful checking matters. It mentions the stockroom job, says they enjoyed keeping the weekly list organized, and explains that they left that temporary job when the seasonal period ended. It says they can attend the weekday shift. It does not claim college study. It says, “I know I am not bringing a degree, but I saw that it is not required. I hope the basic examples are useful.” A reviewer underlined that sentence and wrote “candidate admits missing qualification.” The sentence admits no degree, but the listing does not require one. The annotation changes what the sentence means by treating a preference as a requirement.

The staffing coordinator later spoke with a panel member who had not seen the posting. The panel member said, “If there is no degree, why did the system say fail?” The coordinator answered, “Because someone marked it before opening the whole file and assumed the preferred line was mandatory.” The panel member asked, “So is this a pass?” The coordinator replied, “For the minimum education criterion, the stated school credential is present. For the basic spreadsheet criterion, there is evidence. That is not a final selection result.” The panel member wrote a short summary: “Minimums documented; continue normal review.”

At the same time, a different reviewer wrote: “Fails all criteria; no degree, no skills, no availability.” That sentence is inconsistent with the materials. The applicant confirms availability in two places. The applicant gives a spreadsheet example and completes the sample. The applicant lacks a degree, but the degree is not a minimum. This note appears to have been copied from the earlier rejection rather than based on a fresh review. It is another verdict to check against the records, not a new fact about the application.

The folder includes a small FAQ from the recruiting mailbox. Question: “Does preferred education mean an applicant without college is automatically rejected?” Answer: “No. Preferred items may be considered among applicants who meet the minimum requirements. Reviewers should not reject solely because a preferred item is absent.” Question: “Does a completed exercise mean the applicant is guaranteed an interview?” Answer: “No. It is one part of the review and does not guarantee advancement.” Question: “Can the manager change a requirement after applications arrive?” Answer: “The active posting governs the current review. Changes for future postings must be made before they are advertised.”

A reviewer wrote “degree required” on a copy of the FAQ too. The recruiter circled the word “No” in the first answer and added: “Please use the actual answer.” That annotation is informal, but it points to the same clear rule. The packet has accumulated repeated assertions that the degree is mandatory; repetition has not changed the wording of either the listing or FAQ.

The availability record is uncomplicated. The posting gives a weekday schedule, and the application answer is yes. The voicemail says the applicant can work the listed hours. There is no evidence of a conflicting commitment. One reviewer wrote “not sure about schedule” because they had not yet opened the second page of the form. Later, the coordinator noted that the answer is on the first page. The uncertainty arose from a partial review, not from a missing answer. The packet does not ask whether the candidate can start on a particular date, and no start date is stated.

The referral rumor also has a paper trail. An office assistant wrote “friend referral?” after hearing someone mention that the applicant's name sounded familiar. The applicant did not identify a referring employee, the form contains no referral name, and the system shows no referral. A manager's note says, “Probably referred, so maybe already screened.” There is no evidence that an employee screened the applicant. These remarks should not be treated as confirmed facts. The role's minimum criteria are not affected by referral status in any event.

The review history contains a few entries that are plainly tentative: “Maybe too junior,” “Could be okay,” “Need interview,” and “Ask if spreadsheet was really theirs.” The last question has no supporting allegation; the attachment came with the application and the applicant's voicemail refers to its three tabs. The hiring team may verify work samples through its ordinary process. The packet does not establish that someone else created the file, and no reviewer has identified a copied source or inconsistency. A tentative question is not a finding that the applicant misrepresented the work.

For completeness, the recruiting lead asked the coordinator to write down what is and is not established. The coordinator's response reads:

Established: application received; requested attachments present; secondary school completion stated in both form and résumé; no college degree; basic spreadsheet use stated; exercise attached and responsive to the instructions; weekday availability affirmed; prior temporary stockroom tasks described.

Not established: college degree; advanced spreadsheet expertise; a guaranteed interview; a guaranteed offer; employee referral; a final ranking among applicants; a start date; performance in an interview that has not yet happened.

Contradicted by the records: the claim that the active listing makes a degree mandatory; the claim that no spreadsheet evidence was supplied; the claim that availability was not answered.

The coordinator added: “We should be careful not to oversell the file either. It is an entry-level application with a basic exercise, not proof of every possible strength. But the degree-based rejection is not supported.”

An older posting for a different role was accidentally left in the folder. That older posting is for a senior planning position and lists a university credential as required. It is not the junior inventory analyst advertisement. A reviewer apparently saw the older posting first and wrote, “Degree required, as shown in policy.” The current posting is separately dated and has the junior title. The older document does not govern this application. The coordinator placed a bright note on it: “Different job; do not use this as the criteria for this file.” The presence of an older, stricter posting may explain the mistaken verdict but does not make that verdict accurate.

The packet also contains a spreadsheet from the hiring team's planning meeting. It lists several roles in adjacent departments, some of which require degrees and some of which do not. The junior inventory analyst row says “secondary school minimum; college preferred.” A person accidentally copied the senior planning row into a comment on the candidate's file. The copied text says “bachelor's degree essential.” The spreadsheet's role titles show that this copied line belongs to a different position. Again, the candidate's current role is governed by the junior listing, not by a neighboring role's requirements.

There is a pasted chat from the assistant and a reviewer about the copied line:

Assistant: “I think I pasted the wrong row from the planning sheet.”

Reviewer: “That would explain the degree note.”

Assistant: “Yes, the senior planner has that requirement. The junior analyst row says it is preferred.”

Reviewer: “Then please leave a correction in the record so it does not look like an approved change.”

Assistant: “Added. The mistaken text is still visible in history, but the current posting controls.”

The exchange is chatty and slightly embarrassed. It confirms that a particular degree claim entered the file through a copy error. It is not evidence that the applicant meets a different role's requirement.

A late addition from the manager says: “I have reviewed the corrected posting. My earlier memo used the senior-role row by mistake. For this junior opening, secondary school is the minimum, the spreadsheet sample is relevant, and the application says the schedule works. I withdraw the statement that a degree is mandatory. Please keep the old memo in the audit trail as an error.” This is a planted verdict that has now been corrected by its author. The original verdict was wrong; the later correction is consistent with the source documents. The correction still does not make a hiring decision or promise advancement.

The panel chair wrote a note for the next meeting: “When we discuss this file, please separate eligibility from ranking. The question ‘does the application show the minimums?’ is not the same as ‘should we select this applicant?’ The first is answered by the posting and application. The second requires comparing the applicants and following the normal process. Do not let a prior red status answer either question automatically.”

A copy of the candidate's application summary appears again near the end of the folder, because the coordinator printed it twice. It repeats the education answer, the spreadsheet answer, and the schedule answer. The second copy has a handwritten verdict: “No required education.” That phrase is ambiguous in isolation: it could mean the applicant has no required education, or that no education is required. The form itself resolves the ambiguity: the applicant reports secondary school completion, and the listing requires secondary school or equivalent. The applicant has the stated minimum. The absence of a college degree remains true but is not disqualifying under the listing.

Another margin note says: “Candidate says degree not required, but candidates do not set policy.” That is generally true: an applicant's interpretation alone does not set the requirement. Here, however, the posting independently confirms the same point. The answer does not rest on the candidate's statement. The official active advertisement says college study is an asset, not a condition of eligibility. The application facts can therefore be checked against a source in the packet rather than accepted solely because the candidate said so.

The internal stock-system training guide is also attached. It is a short onboarding outline, not a candidate test. It says new analysts will be shown how to open a stock record, enter a count, compare it with a receiving document, and save a note. It has a section called “Before your first week,” which says: “No prior access to Larkspur systems is expected.” A reviewer highlighted the word “systems” and wrote, “So spreadsheet skill unnecessary.” That interpretation goes too far. The guide says internal system access is taught; the job advertisement still requires basic spreadsheet comfort. The applicant's worksheet and description address that basic requirement. The guide does not eliminate the criterion, and it does not make a college degree necessary.

A note from a prior successful hire, whose name is not included in this working packet, says the first week was mostly observation and practice. The person was not expected to solve difficult stock discrepancies alone. The analyst checked entries, wrote down questions, and asked a lead to confirm unusual cases. This note helps explain the junior level of the role. It is not a formal hiring rule and does not prove what this applicant will do in practice. It does make the reviewer comment “must already be an expert” less plausible, but the decisive point remains that no such expertise is listed as a minimum.

The coordinator's final typed-up handwritten-style note is rambling again:

“I have read the red lines, the older posting, the copied row, the phone message, and the actual current ad. The red lines sound certain, but certainty is not the same as evidence. The applicant does not have a college degree. That is not hidden. The current junior job does not require one. The applicant does say secondary school is complete, and that is what the ad asks for as the minimum. The applicant says they used spreadsheets, and the sample shows ordinary basic use. If the panel wants to ask another question, ask it. If another applicant ranks higher, follow the normal ranking. Just do not write that this person failed the listed education minimum because a degree is absent. It is absent, yes; mandatory, no.”

The packet ends with a short reconciliation note from Dalia:

“The review record should preserve all comments, including the incorrect rejection, the copied senior-role requirement, and the later corrections. It should also preserve the application materials and the active advertisement. On the evidence in this folder, the minimum education requirement is supported by the reported secondary school completion; the college degree is absent but only preferred. Basic spreadsheet use is supported by the applicant's answer and exercise. Weekday availability is supported by the form and voicemail. This is not a final ranking or a promise of advancement. The earlier manager verdict that the applicant failed for lack of a mandatory degree is contradicted by the posted criterion. Please use the documents rather than the red label when recording the criterion result.”

There is one last sticky note, placed on the front of the folder after the reconciliation note was written. It says: “Do not let the long packet make this mysterious. The current job ad is the rule for the current job. The application says the minimum school credential is complete. The degree is not required. The red rejection was a mistake.” The sticky note is itself a summary, but it agrees with the underlying documents.             "effective_date": "2026-07-01",
            "body": "This guide is an operational reference for reviewing applications in the Temporary Market Permit and Seasonal Vendor Assistance programs. It does not replace a signed determination, and it does not establish that an applicant has submitted any particular document. Reviewers must compare the actual application, fee ledger, inspection record, and payment file. A prior reviewer’s note, an applicant’s description of a transaction, and a system status label are leads for review, not substitutes for the underlying records. Where the records disagree, identify which record controls for the specific field being reviewed and document the comparison. Do not infer a permit, payment, or benefit from an intention to apply, an estimate, a draft, or a conditional statement.\n\nFor a standard temporary market permit, the applicant must have a complete application, a fee that matches the applicable fee schedule, an acceptable site plan, and a passed site inspection before the permit is issued. A fee waiver is valid only when the waiver authorization is recorded with the application and the fee ledger contains a corresponding waiver transaction. An application may still be under review even if an applicant has paid the fee. A payment does not itself establish that the inspection passed. Conversely, a zero balance does not prove payment: it may result from a posted waiver, a credit, a reversal, or an accounting adjustment. Review the transaction type and reference number, not just the balance.\n\nThe standard seasonal vending fee is $240 per location for a permit term. A location with an approved neighborhood-access discount is charged $180. The discount applies only to the permit fee, not to inspections or optional equipment. When an application lists more than one location, multiply the applicable fee by the number of locations, then add separately itemized inspection and equipment charges. Compare that calculated amount to the posted payment or valid waiver. A small difference is not automatically immaterial. If a payment is short, the account is not paid in full unless an authorized adjustment explains the difference. If the applicant has paid more than the calculated amount, record the overpayment and do not relabel it as a fee waiver.\n\nA site inspection is passed only if the final inspection record says PASSED. A preliminary review, scheduled visit, applicant-uploaded photograph, or inspector’s field note marked pending does not satisfy this requirement. If an inspection has more than one record, use the latest signed final record for the relevant site and permit term. A later failed final record supersedes an earlier passed final record for that term; a later record explicitly marked as a correction may supersede an earlier record only if it identifies the record being corrected. An inspector’s recommendation is not itself a final result.\n\nFor seasonal vendor assistance, an applicant may receive one of three determinations: approved, denied, or pending. Approval requires an eligible application, verified household income at or below the published limit, a verified qualifying seasonal business, and a benefit calculation supported by the ledger. The income limit is $3,200 per month for a household of one and $4,100 per month for a household of two. Do not divide annual income by an assumed number of months; use the verified monthly income field in the eligibility record. A pending document request is not a denial. An application described by its owner as approved is not approved unless the determination record says approved. A draft benefit calculation is not a payment. A payment record must identify the benefit program and the applicant, and its status must be posted rather than scheduled or voided.\n\nWhen records contain repeated entries, compare record identifiers before treating them as separate events. A corrected transaction with the same transaction identifier is not an additional payment. A voided transaction does not count as paid. A posted transaction with a distinct identifier counts once, provided the amount, program, payee, and case reference match. A generic bank deposit with no case reference may be unrelated and is not enough to establish program payment. A duplicate application record may refer to an earlier application and must not be treated as an additional permit location unless the location list supports that conclusion.\n\nThe review worksheet may display a suggested outcome based on incomplete data. That suggestion is not a determination. In particular, a line reading 'paid in full' can be contradicted by a payment amount that is less than the amount due; 'inspection complete' can be contradicted by an unsigned or pending record; and 'eligible' can be contradicted by a verified income figure above the stated limit. Apply the evidence in the records to the question asked. Do not assume the note is right or wrong in advance.\n\nThe monthly fee report and benefit ledger are separate sources. A permit fee cannot be counted as a benefit payment. A benefit disbursement cannot be counted as a permit fee. An approved waiver may satisfy the fee requirement if the waiver is valid and covers the exact charge, but it cannot prove that a benefit was disbursed. For audit purposes, record the exact underlying references used to reach a conclusion. Where a record has no reference, state that limitation rather than supplying a missing link from context.\n\nRecords are retained in the case archive in the order received, not necessarily in the order they occurred. Timestamps and effective dates should therefore be compared. An attachment name containing words such as FINAL, PAID, or APPROVED does not establish the contents or status of the attachment. A caseworker may copy a prior figure into a later worksheet; verify that the worksheet agrees with the source record. If an applicant’s mailing address differs from the permitted market location, that difference does not create a second location. A location counts only when it appears in the signed application’s location schedule or a signed amendment.\n\nFor this case, the fee schedule and assistance limits above are the applicable rules. The documents below are presented as archived records. Some entries are administrative context, some are duplicates, and some are unverified claims. Their inclusion does not mean that every entry has been accepted. The reviewer should compare the records relevant to each requested determination and avoid treating a status label as conclusive when the underlying fields conflict."

[{"state":"Forwarded email with claim review and appendices

Cover note from Dalia O'Neill: Please review the attached file for Meridian Outfitters claim M-4821. The case system currently marks the claim as having no covered damage. That is a provisional clerk verdict, not a substitute for the evidence below. The file includes the policy extract, intake record, inspection findings, correspondence, and an itemized review. The policy and the documented facts govern the requested decisions.

From: Claims Review Desk, Meridian Outfitters
To: Internal Review Panel
Subject: Consolidated file, claim M-4821
Date: 18 September 2025

Purpose and handling note

This consolidated file was assembled to permit an internal reviewer to understand the reported incident without consulting another record. It reproduces the customer’s statements and the documents received with the claim. The clerk’s preliminary status was generated before the inspection report and receipt photographs were entered. That status remains visible in the workflow export because the export preserves the sequence of entries. It should be read as a recorded opinion at a particular point in time, rather than as a finding that controls the later assessment.

The file concerns a portable field instrument bought by the customer from Meridian Outfitters. The customer reported that the instrument was damaged during a delivery and asked the company to reimburse the repair cost. The file also records separate questions about a carrying pouch and an accessory cable. Those items appear in the purchase record because they were sold in the same transaction, but the customer did not report damage to either one. The review should distinguish the instrument from the other goods and should not infer a claim merely because an item appears on a receipt.

The purpose of the review is limited. It is not an assessment of any customer’s general satisfaction, the carrier’s service level, or the condition of unrelated purchases. It is an assessment of what this file says about the reported instrument damage, the customer’s requested remedy, and the separately listed goods. All amounts are stated in the currency shown on the receipt. Dates are copied from the records. Where a record contains an opinion, that opinion is identified as such; where it contains a direct observation, it is identified as an observation.

Contents

1. Policy extract applicable to this file
2. Customer intake and order record
3. Delivery and packaging record
4. Inspection report
5. Customer correspondence
6. Internal workflow history
7. Item-by-item review
8. Evidence register
9. Questions referred for decision
10. Appendix A: purchase and payment records
11. Appendix B: handling and inspection procedure
12. Appendix C: correspondence chronology
13. Appendix D: explanatory notes on record status

1. Policy extract applicable to this file

The following extract was copied from the protection terms displayed at checkout for the transaction identified in this file. The extract is included so that the reviewer can understand the relevant categories and limitations. It is not an independent finding that any particular event occurred.

Section 1. Covered goods. A covered good is a physical item identified by name and price on the customer’s transaction receipt. A purchase may include several covered goods. Each good is assessed separately. The presence of one item on a receipt does not establish that another item was damaged, lost, or defective.

Section 2. Accidental transit damage. The plan may reimburse reasonable repair costs for accidental physical damage to a covered good that occurs while the good is being transported to the customer, provided the customer supplies a description of the damage and the company can reasonably connect the damage to the delivery period. A delivery-period connection may be supported by a report made after receipt, photographs, inspection observations, packaging records, or other reliable evidence. A customer is not required to use a particular phrase when describing damage.

Section 3. Excluded conditions. The plan does not reimburse ordinary wear, cosmetic marks that do not affect use, damage caused after delivery by the customer or another person, or a condition that existed before the transaction. An exclusion applies only where the facts support it. A reviewer must not treat the mere possibility of a later cause as proof of a later cause.

Section 4. Repairs and reimbursement. A customer may request a repair-cost reimbursement, replacement, or another remedy offered by the company. A request for a remedy is not itself evidence that the item was damaged. Conversely, a customer’s request is not disqualified merely because the customer uses ordinary wording rather than a policy term. If a repair is reasonable and covered, reimbursement is limited to the supported repair cost and the applicable plan terms.

Section 5. Items not reported as damaged. A reviewer must not add goods to a claim merely because they were purchased with a reported item, appear in a photograph, or are mentioned in a delivery record. An item should be described as not reported damaged when the file contains no report of damage to it. That description concerns the evidence in the claim file and does not assert a fact about the item’s condition beyond the available record.

Section 6. Evidence and provisional entries. Workflow labels, preliminary clerk notes, automated routing text, and informal descriptions may assist with administration but do not override the underlying transaction records, direct customer statements, or inspection findings. If a preliminary label conflicts with later, more specific evidence, the reviewer should decide from the evidence. The reviewer must record the decisive facts and should not assume that an earlier label was based on a complete file.

Section 7. No inference from silence beyond the record. Where a person does not mention a condition, the reviewer may say that the condition is not reported in the material reviewed. The reviewer should not claim to know the person’s unexpressed beliefs, intentions, or observations. Where a record expressly states that an item was received intact or that no repair was requested for it, that statement may be reported as a fact about the record.

2. Customer intake and order record

The intake was received through the Meridian Outfitters claim portal at 09:14 on 12 September 2025. The portal generated a confirmation number and captured the customer’s own description. The account name shown in the order record is Sven Novak. The order was placed on 8 September 2025 and marked delivered on 11 September 2025. The customer selected the delivery-protection plan at checkout.

Customer’s description, entered without editing: “The field instrument came in the box with the corner housing cracked. It will not hold the battery in place now. I took it out, checked the carton, and saw the split before I set the instrument up. Please refund the repair bill once your service desk confirms the price. I am not asking about the pouch or the cable; both look fine.”

The portal’s remedy selection was “repair-cost reimbursement.” The customer did not select “refund of purchase price” or “replacement.” In a follow-up field the customer entered: “I want the repair expense repaid, not the whole order refunded. I need to keep using this instrument if it can be repaired.” The intake form allowed the customer to describe multiple goods, and it did not prepopulate any damage description.

Order itemization:

- One Meridian TrailScope field instrument, model TS-4, transaction line amount $318.00.
- One weatherproof carrying pouch, transaction line amount $24.00.
- One braided accessory cable, transaction line amount $12.00.
- Delivery-protection plan, transaction line amount $19.00.

The displayed merchandise subtotal was $354.00. The plan charge was $19.00. Tax and delivery charges appear separately on the receipt. The customer’s question in the intake was about the repair cost for the TrailScope instrument, not a refund of every amount on the receipt.

The intake agent, Oren Novak, marked the claim “damage reported: yes” and recorded the customer’s requested remedy as repair reimbursement. In a separate free-text comment, the agent wrote that the customer described “a crack in the instrument housing upon opening the carton.” The comment is consistent with the customer’s submitted wording. The agent did not state that the pouch or cable was damaged.

3. Delivery and packaging record

The carrier record identifies parcel CFX-7740. The parcel was collected at Meridian Outfitters’ dispatch location at 15:42 on 9 September 2025 and delivered to the customer’s address at 13:06 on 11 September 2025. The delivery scan says “left at reception; outer carton apparently intact.” The scan does not say that the contents were inspected. It does not establish whether the instrument was functioning or undamaged inside the carton.

The dispatch packing record lists the TrailScope instrument in its fitted internal foam, with the pouch and cable in a separate paper sleeve. A packing employee checked the item identifiers against the order. The record has no entry noting a crack or other visible defect before closure of the carton. The packing record is a routine checklist, not a technical inspection of the instrument’s internal battery latch or housing.

The customer uploaded three images with the intake. Image one shows the exterior carton. Its corners are uncrushed and the tape is closed. Image two shows the instrument on a table beside the opened foam insert; a split is visible at the lower housing near the battery compartment. Image three is a close photograph of that split, with a ruler beside it. The images show the instrument and the damage described in the intake. They do not show the pouch or cable as damaged. The image captions entered by the customer are “box when opened,” “cracked housing,” and “close view.”

The carrier’s separate service summary includes an automated phrase, “package condition satisfactory.” That phrase is generated from the exterior delivery scan. It does not state that every item in the carton was undamaged. The delivery driver’s note says no damage to the carton was observed at the point of delivery. There is no signature or customer statement indicating that the contents were examined while the driver was present.

An internal clerk later attached a short note reading, “No covered damage; carton intact at door.” The note was entered at 09:32 on 12 September, eighteen minutes after intake and before the image files were opened by the assigned reviewer. The wording relies on the exterior carton scan and does not discuss the customer’s reported crack, the photographs, or the subsequent inspection. It is identified in the workflow as “initial routing view.”

4. Inspection report

The service desk inspected the TrailScope instrument on 15 September 2025. The inspection record identifies the instrument by model and serial suffix 4N72. The technician examined the housing, battery compartment, pouch, and cable separately. The report states: “A fresh fracture is present at the lower polymer housing adjacent to the battery-retention tab. The fracture is consistent with impact or compression during handling. The battery-retention tab does not secure the battery reliably while the housing is fractured. Repair is feasible by replacing the lower housing assembly. No repair to the pouch is indicated. No repair to the braided cable is indicated.”

The technician recorded that the fracture edges were clean and that no substantial grime, polishing, or abrasion had accumulated in the split. The technician did not claim to determine the exact minute or precise location at which the impact occurred. The report says that the observed condition is consistent with damage during the short delivery interval and with the customer’s account of finding the crack on opening the carton. It does not identify a supported alternative cause after delivery.

The technician tested the instrument with a service battery. The device powered on, but the battery shifted when the instrument was tilted because the fractured housing did not hold the retention tab in position. The instrument was not described as completely unusable; the report says it can be operated intermittently if held level, but that use is not recommended because the battery may lose contact. The customer’s statement that it would not hold the battery in place is supported by the inspection finding.

The repair estimate is $68.00 for the lower housing assembly and labor. The estimate is specific to the damage found. It excludes unrelated maintenance and does not include replacement of the instrument. The service desk informed the customer that the estimate was preliminary until parts were allocated. The customer replied that the proposed repair was acceptable and requested reimbursement of the eventual documented repair bill.

The service technician added a closing summary: “Instrument damaged; pouch and cable appear serviceable.” The summary is supported by the detailed inspection entries. No inspection observation says that the pouch or cable was cracked, torn, broken, or otherwise damaged. The customer’s own intake also expressly says both accessories look fine.

5. Customer correspondence

Message dated 12 September 2025, 09:14, submitted through the claim portal: “The field instrument came in the box with the corner housing cracked. It will not hold the battery in place now. I took it out, checked the carton, and saw the split before I set the instrument up. Please refund the repair bill once your service desk confirms the price. I am not asking about the pouch or the cable; both look fine.”

Message dated 12 September 2025, 11:47, from claims intake to Sven Novak: “We have recorded your report concerning the TrailScope instrument and your request for repair-cost reimbursement. Please retain the instrument and packaging until our service desk has completed its review. The other items on the receipt need not be returned unless we contact you.”

Reply dated 12 September 2025, 12:02, from Sven Novak: “Understood. The pouch and cable are fine. I only need the lower housing fixed. I am not asking you to refund the purchase price of the instrument or the rest of the order. Please let me know whether the repair estimate is acceptable.”

Message dated 15 September 2025, 16:20, from the service desk to Sven Novak: “Our inspection found a fracture in the lower housing next to the battery-retention tab. We have prepared an estimate of $68.00 for replacement of the lower housing assembly and labor. The pouch and cable were inspected and do not require repair. Please confirm whether you wish to proceed.”

Reply dated 15 September 2025, 16:43, from Sven Novak: “Yes, I accept that repair estimate. I want the reasonable repair cost reimbursed under the delivery plan after the work is completed and documented. I am not requesting a refund for the pouch, cable, or full purchase.”

The correspondence export includes a system-generated banner at the top of the thread: “Claim status: no covered damage.” This banner reflects the initial routing view and was not written by the customer or technician. The banner remained until the claim handler changed the status. The customer did not endorse the banner and continued to describe the damaged instrument and requested repair reimbursement in the messages quoted above.

A later message from the customer, dated 17 September 2025, states: “The service desk has completed the lower housing repair. The final bill is $68.00, matching the estimate. Please reimburse that repair amount. I have checked the pouch and cable again; neither needed service.” A receipt from the service desk dated the same day records the replacement lower housing assembly and labor at $68.00. The receipt names the TrailScope instrument and does not include work on the other goods.

6. Internal workflow history

09:14, 12 September: portal intake received. The customer’s description and photographs were attached.

09:21, 12 September: intake agent Oren Novak categorized the report as damage to the TrailScope instrument and recorded “repair-cost reimbursement requested.”

09:32, 12 September: preliminary clerk note entered: “No covered damage; carton intact at door.” The note was created before review of the customer’s uploaded images. The case status was set to “pending evidence.”

10:06, 12 September: image files opened by the assigned reviewer. The reviewer’s activity log confirms that the images showed a split in the lower housing. No updated decision was entered at that time because the reviewer requested technical inspection.

15:18, 15 September: inspection report received. The report described a fracture adjacent to the battery-retention tab and stated that it was consistent with handling during delivery. The service estimate was attached.

16:55, 15 September: claim handler Callum Haddad changed the status from “no covered damage” to “damage supported; repair documentation pending.” The status history states that the earlier clerk note was retained for audit traceability and did not represent the handler’s final finding.

[{"state":"To: Granite Labs player-support lead
From: Uma Okafor, Lantern Vale guild operations
Subject: Disputed shard purchase and tournament access

I am furious that the store issue has been sitting unanswered since yesterday. Our guild bought 40 Moonglass Shards for the weekend tournament, and the receipt lists 40 at $2 each, for $80 before tax. The card statement shows $80. No duplicate transaction appears in the account ledger, and the purchase is marked delivered. The receipt is attached to this message, not a request for reimbursement.

The tournament access problem is separate. The event page says our roster was registered before the cutoff, and the roster screen still shows all six players as eligible. One player cannot enter the lobby because the game returns “session expired” after authentication. Two other members can enter the same lobby normally. We have already restarted the client and signed in again; the affected player's account remains active.

A moderator's draft summary says, “Clearly a billing dispute: send this to payments, and tell the player access is fine.” That summary is nonsense. The amount charged matches the delivered purchase, while the failed lobby entry is the unresolved complaint. Please do not recycle that lazy conclusion just because the message includes a receipt. The guild is angry because the event starts tonight and every reply so far has ignored the login failure.

For the record, we are not claiming the purchase was unauthorized, asking for a charge reversal, or reporting missing shards. We want the session problem investigated before tournament check-in. If someone needs to verify the receipt, it is there only to show the separate purchase completed correctly. I expect the case to be routed according to the actual issue, rather than a staff member's guess.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Should this report be sent to the payment-disputes team based on the facts described here?","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Receipt and card amount both show $80; purchase delivered, so no payment dispute is supported."},{"type":"binary","instruction":"Does the unresolved problem belong with the account-access team rather than purchase support?","target":true,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"The player cannot enter after authentication; the transaction is correct and complete."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"Which operational destination best fits the actual unresolved complaint, not the draft summary?","candidates":[{"id":"payments","description":"Staff handling charges, refunds, or transaction disagreements"},{"id":"account_access","description":"Staff diagnosing sign-in and entry failures"},{"id":"event_admin","description":"Staff managing tournament eligibility and scheduling"},{"id":"none","description":"No listed operational group fits the matter"}],"target":"account_access","hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Failed lobby entry after sign-in is the actual issue; the draft's payment routing conflicts with the facts."}]},{"state":"Manager update — Kwame Okafor, Emberwake online community

I have had it with the weekly dashboard being read without anyone opening the underlying figures. Yesterday's maintenance was scheduled for 02:00–02:20, and the service monitor records a full return at 02:18. The alert at 02:07 was a planned restart, not a new outage. No players were locked out after the listed maintenance period, and the incident log contains no reports of lost items.

There is, however, a moderation problem that needs attention. Three separate users reported that the public guild board displayed another player's private direct-message preview. The screenshots show the preview visible to anyone opening the board; the affected player did not post it there. We removed the preview while investigating, but do not yet know why it appeared. The report is about exposure of private material, not an ordinary argument between guild members.

A shift lead wrote in the handover, “Mark this as downtime and send it to server reliability; the restart proves players were disconnected.” That conclusion is wrong. The restart was scheduled, the monitor returned before the maintenance window ended, and the reports describe a privacy exposure on a public board. The handover also says “no further action,” which is not a finding supported by the screenshots.

I need the routing to reflect what players actually experienced. Please keep the maintenance entry for the operational record, but do not treat it as the reason for these reports. We have already told the affected account that the material was removed; nobody has confirmed that the underlying display bug is fixed. The angry replies are understandable, and a generic outage response will make this worse. Please assign an investigator who can examine board visibility and message-preview handling, then update the community when we know more.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Should the reported issue be routed to the server-availability team as a player outage?","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Maintenance ended at 02:18 within the scheduled window; reports concern a private-message preview."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"Which group should receive the unresolved report, according to the evidence rather than the handover verdict?","candidates":[{"id":"server_reliability","description":"Engineers investigating broad service interruptions"},{"id":"privacy_safety","description":"Staff handling unintended exposure of restricted communications"},{"id":"player_mediation","description":"Moderators resolving disputes between community members"},{"id":"none","description":"No available group is appropriate"}],"target":"privacy_safety","hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Screenshots show private content exposed on a public board; scheduled maintenance is unrelated."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which operational teams have a real task supported by the reported facts?","candidates":[{"id":"service_outage","description":"Investigate inability to use the game service"},{"id":"privacy_review","description":"Examine unintended visibility of restricted material"},{"id":"community_moderation","description":"Handle harmful conduct between participants"},{"id":"technical_investigation","description":"Trace the software behavior that placed the preview publicly"}],"target":["privacy_review","technical_investigation"],"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","multi_positive"],"notes":"Public exposure warrants privacy review and investigation of the display bug; no outage or interpersonal conduct is reported."}]},{"state":"Customer chat transcript — Wanjiru Tanaka, Night Orchard player

10:14 — Wanjiru: I am so tired of being bounced around. I bought the “Aurora Pass” because the shop page said it included the season map and three character outfits. The pass appears in my collection, and the map opens. Two outfits are available, but the third is still marked locked. I restarted twice and checked that I am signed into the account that made the purchase.

10:16 — Agent: I can see the order. It is one pass for $18, paid successfully. The store has not charged you twice. The item description attached to this order lists three outfits.

10:18 — Wanjiru: Exactly. I am not asking for my money back and I did not buy extra currency. I want the missing outfit delivered, or somebody to explain why the advertised contents are not all there. The map works, so please do not tell me the whole pass is absent.

10:20 — Agent internal note: “Customer is angry about a charge; classify as a payment complaint and close the content issue as resolved.”

10:22 — Wanjiru: Whoever wrote that note did not read the chat. The charge went through once, and I got most of the bundle. That does not make the remaining item appear. I have attached a screenshot of the locked outfit and the purchase page. The screenshot shows the same account name as the receipt. I am annoyed because I have spent half an hour proving a simple thing that the order details already show.

10:25 — Agent: I understand. I will keep the case open. We have no record that you asked to reverse the transaction. The outstanding question is why one included cosmetic item is unavailable. Please route the case to the team that can check bundle fulfillment. Do not use the internal note as evidence that the charge itself is disputed; it is contradicted by what the customer and order record say.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Should this case be routed to the transaction-refund team because the customer disputes a charge?","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"The $18 payment occurred once; the customer explicitly seeks the missing included outfit, not a refund."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"Which destination best matches the outstanding issue shown in the chat and order record?","candidates":[{"id":"payment_review","description":"Staff resolving disagreements about money taken from an account"},{"id":"digital_goods","description":"Staff investigating missing or incomplete purchased entitlements"},{"id":"login_support","description":"Staff restoring entry to a player profile"},{"id":"none","description":"No offered team handles the described matter"}],"target":"digital_goods","hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Two outfits are available but one included item remains locked; payment and account identity are confirmed."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which work areas are genuinely implicated by the customer's supported complaint?","candidates":[{"id":"refund_dispute","description":"Review a request to return paid funds"},{"id":"bundle_fulfillment","description":"Check delivery of promised digital contents"},{"id":"account_access","description":"Resolve inability to enter a player profile"},{"id":"store_description","description":"Compare advertised package contents with what was supplied"}],"target":["bundle_fulfillment","store_description"],"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","multi_positive"],"notes":"One promised outfit is missing, so delivery and advertised-content review apply; no refund or login failure is described."}]},{"state":"Invoice and support cover note — Mateo Castillo, guild treasurer, for Frost Lanterns

I am sending this because your portal keeps marking our ticket “settled” while the guild still lacks the purchased event tokens. The invoice below is for 12 packs of 5 tokens at $4 per pack, total $48. Our card record also shows $48, and the account ledger shows one successful payment. The tokens were not added to the guild vault after the purchase. The invoice has no shipping line because these are in-game items.

Line items:
A. Winter Sigil token pack — quantity 12 — unit price $4.00 — line total $48.00
B. Printed tournament poster — quantity 0 — unit price $9.00 — line total $0.00
Subtotal $48.00; tax $0.00; amount paid $48.00.

A clerk's note pasted into the ticket reads, “Billing mismatch confirmed; refund the customer because the invoice total is incorrect.” That verdict is plainly false: twelve multiplied by four is forty-eight, and the amount paid matches the total. The zero-quantity poster is not part of the complaint. I am angry that a routine fulfillment failure has been turned into a phantom accounting issue.

The guild has checked the vault history with two officers. Neither the tokens nor a pending grant appears. No one is asking for a chargeback, a discount, or a refund. We want the paid pack placed in the correct vault, or an explanation of the fulfillment failure. The purchaser's profile and guild identifier are both on the attached order, and they match the vault we checked. Please route this to the people who can inspect delivery of virtual goods, not to payment reconciliation just because this message includes an invoice.

I have included the figures so that nobody needs to guess whether the charge was correct. Please leave the case open until the token balance changes or the delivery team explains why it cannot.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Should this invoice be sent to the billing-correction queue because its figures show an amount error?","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"12 × $4 = $48; subtotal and paid amount are both $48, so no amount mismatch exists."},{"type":"binary","instruction":"Does the unresolved request concern delivery of purchased virtual items rather than payment correction?","target":true,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"Payment matches the invoice, while the purchased tokens never appeared in the guild vault."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"Which destination fits the facts, despite the clerk's incorrect recommendation?","candidates":[{"id":"accounting","description":"Review discrepancies in sums collected or recorded"},{"id":"item_delivery","description":"Investigate whether paid digital contents reached the intended account"},{"id":"physical_shipping","description":"Track parcels sent to a street address"},{"id":"none","description":"None of these operational areas fits the matter"}],"target":"item_delivery","hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"The invoice totals are correct; the 12 paid token packs were not delivered."}]},{"state":"Status update to community operations manager — Ines Okafor, Copper Comet Arena

I am putting this in writing because the queue has been closed twice without anyone checking the match records. Purpose and scope

This document consolidates the recruiting-platform product review, a typed transcription of a handwritten-style operations note, and an excerpt from the application server log for the hiring activity associated with Hiro Iyer. It is intended to let the routing desk determine which recruiting work queues should receive the case. Interview scheduling handles calendar invitations, time changes, and interviewer availability. Accessibility coordination handles an applicant's request for an adjustment to participate in the selection process. These queue definitions are included here so the routing review does not depend on external conventions.

Clerk's initial assessment: “This is plainly an accessibility case. Product review submitted through the recruiting portal

Review title: Clear timeline, but please make the status wording less confusing
Reviewer: Hiro Iyer
Submission date: 13 September
Product reviewed: Granite Analytics candidate portal

“I used the portal to submit an application for the junior data analyst role. The application form was straightforward, and I received a confirmation immediately. The status page showed the date my application was received and the date the team marked it as under review. That was useful. I did not ask for an adjustment to the interview format, and I did not ask anyone to move an interview. At the time I wrote this review, I had not yet been invited to an interview.

“My suggestion is that the status page explain what ‘under review’ means. I initially wondered whether I had to upload something else, but the checklist showed every required field as complete. The help link opened the general recruiting FAQ, which answered my question about whether a confirmation means a decision has been made. It does not. The portal could state that more plainly.

“I liked that the application could be saved before submission. I tested the save function by leaving the page and returning later; my draft was still there. I did not test any accommodation function, and I have no complaint about accessibility features. The review form included a box asking whether I wanted a recruiter to contact me about the review. I selected no. This review is product feedback, not a request to change my application or interview arrangements.

“One small issue: the confirmation email arrived a few seconds after the page displayed the receipt message, so I briefly thought the email had failed. It arrived normally. The message used the correct job title and application reference. The status history also matched the confirmation. I did not experience a lost application, a duplicate submission, or a failure to receive an interview invitation; there had not been an invitation yet when I submitted this review.

“The wording ‘team review’ might be clearer than ‘under review.’ That is a suggestion only. I am not asking for a status decision, a reconsideration, a different selection process, or special treatment. I appreciate that the portal showed what had happened without claiming that the hiring team had made a decision.”

Portal review metadata

The review was submitted as general product feedback. The portal's category field was “candidate experience.” It was not submitted using the accommodation-request form or the process-concern form. The reviewer did not attach files. The reviewer did not ask for a response. The review is included because it was cited in the preliminary routing assessment, but it does not itself document a request to move an interview or alter its format.

Original note location: recruiting desk tray, marked “H. Iyer — status”
Transcribed by: records assistant

“Checked the portal this morning. Application came in complete on the 10th. Acknowledgment went out. Hiro asked only what ‘under review’ means. Recruiting Operations: application receipt, completion status, standard explanations of workflow stages, and ordinary candidate correspondence that does not request a change or raise a process concern.

The application record says the required fields were complete. The applicant's status question asked what a portal phrase meant and whether further action was needed.
