[{"state":"Granite Works Small Manufacturing Shop
Managerial Status Update and Supporting Record
Reporting period: 1–30 September
Prepared for: Greta Delgado, Operations Manager
Prepared by: Nadia Kaur, Production Clerk
Document control: Internal administrative copy; all entries below are included for review of the September operating position.

1. Purpose and scope

This update records the production, inspection, dispatch, equipment, and customer-service activity entered in the shop’s ordinary September registers. It is intended to give the operations manager a consistent summary and to preserve the supporting facts behind the summary statements. The document covers work performed at the small manufacturing shop, including cutting, drilling, finishing, assembly, packing, and the transfer of finished goods to the dispatch area. It also records the checks performed by the clerk when reconciling the daily job sheets with the inspection register and the dispatch book.

The status statements in section 2 were drafted before the attached register extracts were reconciled. A statement marked “preliminary” is an administrative assessment, not a substitute for the underlying dated entry. The shop’s normal process is to retain the original job sheet, the inspection entry, and the dispatch record as evidence. Where an assessment and a dated record differ, the dated record is retained without alteration and the discrepancy is noted for manager review. No entry is to be removed merely because it does not support an earlier summary.

The reporting period is the calendar month of September. The figures and dates in this update are drawn from the shop’s local records. No external production system or supplier portal was consulted. Times are local shop times. Quantities are in finished units unless a line expressly says otherwise. The report does not treat a forecast, an unapproved draft, or a conditional instruction as a completed event.

2. Preliminary status statements

The following statements were copied from the first draft of the manager’s summary. They were entered by the reporting clerk as provisional items to verify. The statements are reproduced for audit purposes and are not certified conclusions.

2.1 Equipment statement: “The bench micrometer calibration is overdue.” The draft writer relied on a handwritten reminder on the August planning board. The reminder was not checked against the equipment register before the sentence was entered.

2.2 Order statement: “The September 18 delivery to Larkspur Logistics was short by six housings.” This draft statement was based on a preliminary packing estimate and a message received before the signed receiving slip had been filed. The draft writer did not compare the estimate with the final dispatch and receipt records.

2.3 Customer-quality statement: “The Larkspur Logistics order had no reportable defects; the customer’s list is administrative noise.” This sentence was copied from an internal disposition note. The note was written before the customer’s detailed inspection list and the shop’s own corrective-action entries were reconciled. It is included here as a planted preliminary verdict, not as a final finding.

No one should interpret the presence of a statement in this section as proof that the statement is correct. The verification duty for this update is to compare the preliminary wording with the original records set out later in the document. The clerk has retained the draft language verbatim so that the point of disagreement is visible. The report does not revise the preliminary statements silently, and it does not assume that a confident-sounding summary is supported merely because it was entered in a management document.

3. Shop operating context

The shop operates one day shift, Monday through Friday, with occasional authorised Saturday work. The regular production area contains two cutting benches, one drill press, a small deburring station, a finishing bench, and a packing table. The shop does not maintain a separate warehouse. Completed work is placed in a marked dispatch zone after inspection, and the dispatch clerk records the count when the carrier collects it. For customer collections, the receiving party signs the same dispatch record or a separate collection slip.

The shop’s work instructions require operators to use the current revision of a drawing and to enter any substituted material or changed dimension on the job sheet. The inspection clerk checks the finished item against the order-specific drawing and records pass, hold, or rework. A pass entry is not inferred from an item’s presence in the dispatch zone. Similarly, a preliminary packing count is not treated as a final dispatch count if a later signed count is present.

The equipment register is maintained in the tool cabinet. Each controlled measuring instrument has an identification number, a calibration date, and a next-due date. A board reminder can prompt staff to check the register, but the board is not the controlling record. Calibration is considered current through the date printed as the next-due date, inclusive. If the next-due date has passed, the instrument is marked out of service until the required action is completed. The report uses this procedure as written and does not infer an overdue status from an undated note.

The customer-service register records complaints and requests separately. A customer’s initial message may be followed by a clarification, correction, or withdrawal. The record of what the customer actually reported is kept distinct from the shop’s internal disposition. A note stating that a matter is not reportable does not erase an underlying observation. The shop’s quality procedure requires each distinct customer-reported issue to be assessed, whether or not the issue ultimately proves to be a manufacturing defect.

4. Production and scheduling summary

During September, the shop processed small batches of metal housings, mounting plates, and fastener kits. The job board was reviewed at the start of each shift. Each job packet included a work order, a drawing revision, a material issue slip, and, where applicable, a customer-specific packing instruction. Staff were instructed to record completion on the job sheet after the operation was done, rather than at the time it was planned. Planned dates and actual dates were kept in separate columns.

The planning board included several reminders carried forward from August. Such reminders were used to prompt an administrative check and were not treated as evidence that a task remained incomplete. The August board had a note concerning the bench micrometer, and that note remained visible during the first week of September. The equipment register, rather than the continued visibility of the board note, determines the instrument’s calibration status. The clerk’s first draft relied on the note without completing that comparison.

The September production schedule included the Larkspur Logistics housing order, recorded under job number LL-418. The order called for 48 finished housings in accordance with drawing revision C. The production sheet recorded the quantities at each operation. Cutting was completed before drilling, deburring, inspection, and packing. The number entered at an intermediate operation was not necessarily the final quantity, because pieces could be held for rework or rejected. For that reason, the signed final dispatch count and the customer’s signed receiving slip are the appropriate records for determining how many units were sent and received.

The shop’s standard closeout procedure is to reconcile the job sheet, inspection record, packing list, and carrier or customer receipt. If the initial packing estimate differs from the final record, the discrepancy is retained and explained rather than resolved by choosing whichever number appeared first. A packing estimate made before final inspection is provisional. A signed dispatch count made after inspection is the final outgoing quantity unless a later correction is documented. A signed receipt records what the receiving party accepted at the delivery point; it is not replaced by an unsigned draft note.

Controlled instrument: bench micrometer
Identification: BM-04
Location: inspection bench, east wall
Calibration completed: 12 September
Next calibration due: 12 December
Status entered in register: current
Register checked by: Nadia Kaur
Check date: 16 September

The equipment file contains the calibration certificate dated 12 September. The certificate records the instrument identification as BM-04 and confirms completion of the scheduled calibration. The register’s next-due field reads 12 December. Under the shop procedure stated above, the due date is inclusive; an instrument is not overdue before that date. The 16 September register check therefore found the instrument current. The certificate and the register entry are both retained in the controlled equipment folder.

The August planning board contained the handwritten words “micrometer—check calibration” beside a task list. The board entry did not give a due date, did not say that the instrument had failed calibration, and did not record that calibration was outstanding. It was a reminder to check the equipment file. The check was completed and the result is recorded in the register. The wording of the reminder was copied into the preliminary manager summary as though it established an overdue condition. The underlying dated records do not support that interpretation.

The equipment custodian’s September checklist shows that BM-04 was stored in its assigned location when not in use. The checklist records a visual inspection of the instrument body and case, confirmation that the identification label was legible, and confirmation that the calibration certificate was filed. No entry in the checklist indicates a failed calibration or a restriction on use. The checklist is not itself the source of the due date; it corroborates that the instrument was reviewed and that its controlled documentation was present.

Other measuring devices are listed in the same register. Their status does not determine the status of BM-04. A separate digital caliper has a November due date, and a depth gauge has a January due date. These entries were not used to reach the micrometer conclusion. The BM-04 entry and its certificate are the directly applicable records for the preliminary statement about the bench micrometer.

The clerk’s reconciliation note reads: “Draft says overdue; register says calibration completed 12 September, due 12 December, current at 16 September check. Correct the summary after manager review.” The note does not change the instrument’s status; it records the comparison. No evidence in the equipment folder indicates that the 12 September calibration was cancelled, rejected, or superseded. No later entry in September changes the next-due date.

6. Larkspur Logistics order file: LL-418

Customer: Larkspur Logistics
Order reference: LL-418
Item: machined metal housing
Drawing: revision C
Quantity ordered: 48
Required delivery date: 18 September
Packing instruction: count completed, inspected units and obtain receiving signature

The work order was released to production on 9 September. The material issue slip records the quantity of stock issued for the batch, and the job sheet records the completion of cutting, drilling, and deburring. The inspection register lists 48 housings against the final inspection entry. Each unit was assigned a pass mark for the dimensional checks specified on drawing revision C. The inspection entry was completed before packing. No line on the final inspection record shows a rejected or held housing for this order.

The preliminary packing worksheet, completed during the earlier packing stage, contains the estimate “42 packed; verify remaining six.” That worksheet was not the final count. The phrase “verify remaining six” was a work prompt indicating that the packer was to finish the count after the remaining inspected units were moved to the packing table. It was not a declaration that six units were missing from the order. The worksheet was left in the file as a preliminary record and was not signed as the final dispatch document.

The final packing list is dated 18 September and records 48 units. It bears the initials of the packing clerk and the dispatch clerk. The dispatch book entry for LL-418 also records 48 units collected on 18 September. The carrier’s handover line lists one sealed container and the order reference. The signed receiving slip returned by Larkspur Logistics records 48 units received on 18 September. A short message sent to the shop before the receiving slip arrived stated: “Initial count looks like 42; checking the other carton.” The message was entered in the communications log as preliminary information. A later message in the same thread states: “Confirmed all 48 received; signed slip attached.” The two messages concern the same order and must be read in sequence. The first message did not constitute a final shortage report. The signed receiving slip and the later confirmation support the completed quantity.

The first draft of the manager’s summary used the preliminary estimate and stated that the delivery was short by six housings. The draft was made before the final packing list and signed receipt were reconciled. The final records all show 48 units: the order requested 48, the inspection register records 48 passed units, the final packing list records 48, the dispatch book records 48, and the customer’s receipt records 48 received. The preliminary estimate of 42 was superseded by completion of the count and is not evidence of a final shortage.

The order file contains no credit request for a quantity shortage and no replacement shipment against LL-418. This absence is consistent with the signed receipt but is not needed to establish the quantity received. The determination is based on the direct quantity entries. No calculation beyond comparing the ordered quantity with the received quantity is required: 48 ordered and 48 received. The preliminary statement that six housings were missing is contradicted by the final records.

The customer-service record for LL-418 contains a message from Larkspur Logistics dated 19 September. It reads: “Inspection on receipt found one housing with a burr along the lower edge, one housing with a dent at the rear corner, two housings with the blue finish applied to the wrong face, and one fastener kit absent from the carton. They were reported as observations made during receipt inspection.

The shop’s internal disposition note, written earlier on 19 September, says: “No reportable defects; customer list is administrative noise.” The note was drafted from the preliminary closeout screen, before the detailed customer message was attached to the order record. The internal response sent on 21 September acknowledged receipt of the list and advised the customer that the shop would review the records. It did not state that the customer had made no report. A later draft email proposed wording that the matter was “administrative only”; that draft was not sent and is retained only in the correspondence folder. The quality review subsequently recorded that the burr was present on the reported housing, the dent was present on another reported housing, the finish orientation differed from the specified face on the two units identified by the customer, and the kit was not listed on the packing check. The clerk reconciled the preliminary manager statements against the controlled records on 24 September. The claim that there were no reportable observations was unsupported because the customer listed four distinct issues.

A discrepancy is not resolved by deleting the first draft. The draft remains attached to this update so a reviewer can see why the preliminary wording changed. The reconciliation note records the evidence considered, the date of review, and the conclusion for each statement. The records are not altered to make them agree with the draft. A. BM-04 calibration certificate, completed 12 September; filed under equipment records.
B. BM-04 equipment register extract, checked 16 September; next calibration due 12 December.
C. August planning-board reminder, “micrometer—check calibration”; retained as a non-controlling prompt.

H. LL-418 dispatch book entry, 48 units collected 18 September.
I. Larkspur Logistics signed receiving slip, 48 units received 18 September.
J. Preliminary message reporting an initial count of 42 while another carton was being checked.
K. Follow-up message confirming all 48 were received and attaching the signed slip.
L. Larkspur Logistics quality message dated 19 September listing a burr, a dent, incorrect finish placement, and an absent fastener kit.

The index identifies the records used and their function. It does not declare every document equally authoritative. The planning-board reminder and preliminary packing worksheet are included because they explain the source of the draft statements. The signed register and final transaction records establish the applicable dates and quantities. The customer’s message establishes what was reported. The internal disposition note is preserved as an example of a preliminary conclusion contradicted by the factual record.

11. Closeout note

The reconciliation is complete for the three preliminary statements reproduced in section 2. The bench micrometer is recorded as current, not overdue. The LL-418 order was delivered in the ordered quantity, not short by six housings. The customer did report quality and packing concerns, notwithstanding the internal note saying there were none. The closeout note is based on the underlying records described above and not on the draft verdicts.

No inference should be made that an issue is absent merely because a preliminary internal note says so. Conversely, the fact that a preliminary note is contradicted in this report does not mean every internal note is necessarily wrong. Each statement has been checked against its own direct record. The statements below are phrased for a simple evidence check. A “yes” means that the statement is supported by the records in this update. A “no” means that it is not supported. The preliminary verdicts remain visible in the body of the report because the reviewer is expected to verify them against the facts, not to accept them automatically.

[{"state":"GRANITE LABS COMMUNITY OPERATIONS — ANGRY STATUS UPDATE, THREAD EXTRACT, AND REVIEW NOTES
Prepared for the community operations manager by Bao Moreau. Reporting period: 4–18 September. This is not a defense of the moderation team. Players have been waiting for answers while we argue about labels, and the number of contradictory internal summaries has made an already bad situation worse. The material below combines the live status update, the relevant email thread, and the notes from the review meeting. Names, times, and event records are included so that conclusions can be checked rather than repeated because somebody wrote them in a prominent field.

STATUS UPDATE TO MANAGER
Subject: Rift Harbor outage, disputed account action, and player compensation queue

I am angry that the public status page said “resolved” while players were still losing match results, and I am angrier that a later internal report called every complaint a refund request. Those are different matters. We need to separate what players actually asked for from what we think would be a fair remedy. The queue has been delayed partly because staff treated the phrase “I want this fixed” as if it meant “send money back.” That is not a reliable reading, and it has wasted everyone’s time.

The Rift Harbor season launch began at 18:00 UTC on 4 September. The first widespread disconnects started at 18:17. Between 18:17 and 19:02, the matchmaking gateway intermittently assigned players to an old region shard. The game client displayed the ordinary reconnect banner but did not always preserve a round result after a reconnect. Some players lost ranking points; others reported that a match was abandoned even though they had returned before the final round. We cannot responsibly treat those reports as identical. The telemetry supports a real routing fault, but it does not establish that every account in the queue experienced the same effect.

At 19:26, the incident lead disabled ranked matchmaking for the affected shard. At 20:11, the client patch began rolling out. At 21:04, the status page was changed to “monitoring,” not “resolved.” The page’s public wording was too reassuring earlier in the evening, but the preserved version history shows no claim that all individual account issues had been corrected. At 23:40, the team restored ranked access after a controlled test. The following day, players continued to report missing points and repeated queue failures. Those follow-up complaints are being investigated separately from the launch outage.

There are three customer-facing work queues. The first covers restoration of a lost match result or rank points. The second covers account penalties that may have been triggered by a disconnect. The third covers requests for money or currency to be returned. Agents must not merge them just because a player is upset, uses the word “compensation,” or says that the service was unacceptable. Our written policy calls a refund request a request to return money or paid currency from a transaction. A request to restore rank, correct a record, remove a penalty, or provide an explanation is not by itself a refund request. A player can ask for more than one remedy, but the record must show the request actually made.

The immediate operational failure is not simply that the launch had a defect. It is that our case notes allowed interpretations to overwrite quotations. In several records, the “agent conclusion” field was copied into the customer-request field. Once that happened, a manager reading the table could mistake an internal recommendation for the player’s own words. I have asked the queue owner to preserve the original messages in the case file, list requested remedies separately, and mark any proposed remedy as staff-authored. We should be able to disagree about eligibility without inventing a request.

The case most often used to justify the blanket refund count is ticket RH-4418, filed by player Xiu Mensah. The ticket concerns one ranked match during the 18:17–19:02 routing fault. The game history shows Xiu reconnected before the final round. The account record then applied an abandonment penalty anyway. The event log indicates that the client sent a reconnect acknowledgement at 18:43:12, while the penalty service recorded a disconnect at 18:43:19. The seven-second disagreement is under technical review. That disagreement is not proof that Xiu asked for money back. The submitted ticket text and the subsequent replies are reproduced in the thread extract below.

An earlier internal spreadsheet summarized RH-4418 as “refund requested; approve apology credit.” That wording was entered by a supervisor who had not opened the ticket. The same supervisor’s note was then copied into the daily dashboard. I am not accepting the dashboard label as evidence of what the player said. It is a planted conclusion that needs to be checked against the actual exchange. If the exchange contains a refund request, the request should be visible there. If it does not, the spreadsheet does not create one.

The player’s reported loss is also not the same thing as a cash loss. Xiu’s profile had 1,240 ranking points before the match and 1,212 after it, a decrease of 28. The season rules award or subtract points according to the match result and party rating; they do not convert each ranking point into a fixed cash value. Xiu had bought a 900-shard cosmetic bundle two months earlier, but the purchase receipt shows no purchase on 4 September and no unused paid shard balance was removed during the outage. The bundle is mentioned in the ticket because the player says that paid cosmetics do not excuse a broken ranked mode. That criticism should not be edited into a demand to return the bundle price.

We also need to stop treating “credit” as a magic word. In different parts of the community, it can mean acknowledgment, reputation, account recognition, a public correction, or an in-game balance adjustment. The agent must read the full sentence. Xiu writes that the team should “credit the affected players with a straight answer.” In context, that is a demand for acknowledgment and an explanation, not a request to add paid currency. The policy distinction is not difficult; the careless summaries are making it look difficult.

The status panel for this incident currently shows 63 reports received, 41 with confirmed match-history discrepancies, 12 pending client-log review, and 10 that appear to concern unrelated network interruptions. These figures are reports, not unique customers: some people submitted more than one ticket. Of the 41 confirmed discrepancies, 29 show a lost or misrecorded result, 8 show a reconnect penalty with a preserved result, and 4 are still being reconciled against party logs. These numbers do not tell us how many people asked for refunds. The request category must come from the communications, not from the match outcome.

I have also rejected a proposed public response that said “we have refunded all affected players.” No mass refund was issued. The finance export shows a small number of manual currency adjustments for unrelated purchases, and two courtesy grants of non-purchasable event tokens. Neither item establishes that the Rift Harbor reporters asked for refunds. The export also includes a reversal of a duplicate token grant; counting both the original grant and reversal as separate customer benefits would be absurd. We need to report actual actions precisely and keep them separate from requests.

The incident has harmed trust beyond the measurable match records. People who bought cosmetics are entitled to complain about service quality even if those purchases were not involved in the fault. People who did not pay are entitled to report lost points. People who ask for a refund are entitled to have that request assessed under the terms. People who do not ask for one should not be forced into a refund workflow because an internal column says so. I am not pleased that this has to be spelled out, but the queue cannot be repaired by pretending all angry players said the same thing.

EMAIL THREAD EXTRACT — TICKET RH-4418
Original message from Xiu Mensah, 4 September, 21:16 UTC

“I’m writing about the Rift Harbor ranked match that dropped me into the wrong shard. I got back in before the last round, but the match history now says I abandoned it and my rating is down 28 points. Please correct the match record, remove the abandonment penalty, and tell me why the client let me rejoin while the penalty service marked me gone. I want this fixed before the next placement set. I am not asking you to return the price of my cosmetic bundle; that purchase is not the issue. I am asking for my record to be corrected and for a real explanation instead of another cheerful banner saying everything is fine. Also, credit the affected players with an honest acknowledgment rather than acting as if we made this up.”

Automated receipt, 4 September, 21:17 UTC

“Your report has been received. This message does not confirm eligibility for a rank adjustment, account penalty removal, currency adjustment, or refund. Please do not submit repeated copies; they can delay review.”

First agent response from Oren Haddad, 5 September, 09:03 UTC

“Thanks for the detailed report. I can see the reconnect event and the penalty entry, and I have sent the mismatch to the match-history team. I cannot promise a point correction until they finish comparing the event record with your party’s logs. We do not have evidence here of a paid purchase taken during the match. If you mean a money or paid-currency refund, please say so explicitly, because your message currently asks for a record correction and explanation.”

Reply from Xiu Mensah, 5 September, 09:19 UTC

“I do not mean a money refund. Please stop turning this into one. I want the incorrect abandonment removed and the match record fixed. If the review proves the score itself should stand, explain that and show me the relevant rule. I am furious that I have had to write this twice.”

Internal agent note, 5 September, 09:25 UTC

“Customer explicitly denies wanting money back. Continue rank-record investigation. Do not tag as refund unless customer later changes request.”

Supervisor note added 6 September, 13:40 UTC, after the case was escalated

“Refund request—player lost value during launch and asks for credit. Approve apology credit if policy permits; close as compensated.”

The supervisor did not quote any customer language in that note. The phrase “lost value” is the supervisor’s characterization of the 28-point rating change. “Approve apology credit” is a proposed staff action. Neither phrase appears in Xiu’s original request as a demand for money or paid currency. The case remained open after the note. It was not closed as compensated.

Second agent response from Oren Haddad, 7 September, 16:42 UTC

“The match-history team confirms your client reconnected before the final round. The penalty service nevertheless received a stale disconnect event. We have removed the abandonment penalty. We have not changed the match result because the match reached its recorded conclusion and the rules do not award a win solely for reconnecting. The 28-point change is being recalculated against the recorded loss; we will update you if the rating computation changes. To be clear, our correction is an account-record action, not a refund.”

Reply from Xiu Mensah, 7 September, 17:10 UTC

“Thank you for removing the penalty. I still disagree with leaving the match result as a loss, but at least that is an answer. I have not asked for a refund, and I am not accepting a token in place of correcting the history. Please keep the report open until you explain the rating calculation.”

Internal case update from the match-history team, 8 September, 11:05 UTC

“Penalty flag removed. Match result remains loss under rule 7.4: a disconnected player who returns before match end is not automatically awarded a win; the result follows the round outcome. Rating change reviewed: 28-point decrease is consistent with the recorded result and party rating. No paid currency transaction or balance deduction associated with ticket event.”

Third agent response from Oren Haddad, 8 September, 12:21 UTC

“I have attached the relevant rule and the event times. Your abandonment penalty has been removed; the match result and 28-point calculation remain unchanged. I understand that this is not the correction you wanted. You can request a second review of the rule application, but there is no additional account action available from this ticket at this time.”

Final reply from Xiu Mensah, 8 September, 12:53 UTC

“That is still a terrible outcome, but I understand what you decided. Do not send me an apology token. I want the public incident page to acknowledge the bad penalty handling and the misleading status wording. The ticket can close after you confirm the public note will include that.”

Public note posted 9 September, 10:00 UTC

“During the Rift Harbor launch, a stale disconnect event caused some returning players to receive an incorrect abandonment penalty. We have removed confirmed incorrect penalties. Match results and rating changes were reviewed separately under the published rules. The incident status wording was updated to distinguish monitoring from resolution.”

Follow-up note from Xiu Mensah, 9 September, 10:14 UTC

“I saw the note. It is better than the first banner, though it does not say how long the wording was wrong. I am not requesting money or paid currency. Please record that this report is about the account penalty, match history, and public acknowledgment.”

The thread has been reproduced from the case archive in chronological order. The archived copy contains the original customer messages, agent messages, automated receipt, and staff-only notes. The quoted supervisor note is included because it has been used as evidence in later summaries; its presence in the archive does not make it customer-authored. The request was first made at 21:16 on 4 September. The customer then explicitly clarified the meaning at 09:19 on 5 September and repeated the clarification on 7 and 9 September. There is no later customer message changing the request to a money or paid-currency refund.

MEETING NOTES — REVIEW SESSION, 10 SEPTEMBER
Attendees: Bao Moreau, Priya Nakamura, Viktor Castillo, and Xiu Mensah joined for the first fifteen minutes as the reporting player whose case had been repeatedly cited. Notes recorded by Bao Moreau. The room was already tense when the meeting began. The group had been sent three different dashboards, each with a different total for “refund cases.”

Opening issue: Priya Nakamura said the escalation count had climbed from 9 to 26 after the support dashboard imported the supervisor-note column. She objected that the count had been described in the manager channel as “players demanding their money back.” The import rule treated any record containing “refund,” “credit,” or “lost value” as a refund request, without checking who wrote the text or whether it was a negation. Viktor Castillo replied that the import was intended as a temporary triage aid. Xiu said that a temporary shortcut had become a public assertion about what players wanted, and that nobody had asked the people in the tickets before repeating it. No one disputed the chronology.

The team reviewed the relevant fields. “Customer statement” is meant to hold the customer’s own words. “Agent interpretation” holds a staff member’s categorization. “Proposed remedy” describes an action the company might take. “Completed action” records what actually happened. The imported dashboard had treated all four as equivalent. The group agreed that this was a data-handling error, not proof that players had changed their requests. A staff member may recommend a courtesy credit even when the player has not requested one; a player may reject a courtesy token while still requesting a rank correction; a word appearing in a note is not enough to identify the speaker’s intent.

Viktor asked whether “credit the affected players with an honest acknowledgment” could be read as a request for in-game currency. Xiu answered that the sentence immediately contrasts credit with “acting as if we made this up,” and the later messages expressly reject money and paid currency. The group agreed that in this exchange “credit” means acknowledgment. Bao noted that a reader should interpret the whole sentence and the subsequent clarification, not select one word and ignore the rest. The angry tone does not make the requested remedy unclear.

The match-history decision was reviewed separately. The client reconnect time is 18:43:12 and the penalty-service disconnect time is 18:43:19. The service discrepancy was real, and the penalty was removed. The match outcome itself remained a loss under rule 7.4. The rating decrease of 28 points was consistent with the recorded result and party rating, according to the team’s calculation. Xiu disagreed with the rule and disliked the result, but disagreement is not evidence that the stated calculation was changed. No money was charged as a result of the match, and no paid balance was debited. The prior cosmetic purchase was not part of this incident.

Priya asked the room not to use the phrase “fully compensated.” The player received an account correction, namely removal of the incorrect abandonment penalty, but did not receive money, paid currency, or the desired match-history change. Calling the player compensated without qualification could suggest a financial remedy that did not occur. The team settled on separate reporting categories: penalty corrected; result unchanged; rating calculation confirmed; monetary refund not requested; public acknowledgment requested and posted. This was not a concession about the quality of the original outcome. It was a commitment to describe the outcome accurately.

A second dispute concerned whether the case should be marked as a “refund request declined.” The supervisor’s note had recommended an apology credit. A staff recommendation is not a player request, and the player expressly said not to send a token. The team agreed that the case should not be placed in a refund-declined category either: there was no refund request to deny. The accurate customer-request description is correction of the account record and penalty, an explanation of the rule and rating calculation, and acknowledgment of the incident. The staff action was to remove the penalty, preserve the match result and rating change, and publish the public note.

Xiu said the case still felt like a refusal to fix the central problem. The team acknowledged that the match result remained unchanged and that the customer was dissatisfied. The support record must not convert dissatisfaction into a remedy request. An angry customer can want a different result without asking for money. The customer can also criticize a purchase or mention paid cosmetics without requesting the purchase price back. These distinctions are not technicalities invented to deny help; they are necessary if the queue is meant to reflect what the customer actually asked us to do.

Action item: Priya will remove the supervisor-note import from the customer-request dashboard. Existing classifications will be rechecked against the original messages. The revised dashboard will retain a link to the source text and label staff-authored notes. Viktor will compare the status-page timeline with the incident logs before approving another “resolved” banner. Bao will send the manager a corrected count that distinguishes requests for money or paid currency from requests for account changes, explanations, and public acknowledgment. Xiu asked to be notified when the correction is live; Bao agreed.

APPENDIX A — QUEUE AUDIT METHOD AND INTERPRETATION RULES
The review team sampled 63 reports from the launch period. The sample was selected from the incident queue, not from the account-purchase database. Each report was read as a whole, including the first customer message, later customer clarifications, the agent response, and any quoted text. Staff-only notes were not treated as customer statements. Where a later customer message explicitly changed or clarified a request, the later statement was considered alongside the original. A staff member’s description of what a customer supposedly wanted was not substituted for the customer’s own words.

The audit used four request categories. “Money or paid-currency return” required a customer request to return money or paid currency. “Account or match correction” included removal of a penalty, adjustment to a match record, restoration of rank points, or correction of an account status. “Explanation or review” included a request for the rule, event record, calculation, or second review. “Acknowledgment or communication” included a request for a public statement, correction of misleading wording, or recognition of an outage. One report could contain multiple requests. The categories were not mutually exclusive; however, a report was not assigned to the money-return category merely because it contained the word “credit,” “value,” “purchase,” “compensation,” or “refund” in a staff note or a negated customer sentence.

For each report, auditors recorded the exact sentence supporting each category. If no customer sentence supported a money-return request, the auditor marked that category absent even when an agent had offered a courtesy grant or a supervisor had recommended a credit. If the customer said “I am not asking for a refund,” that was evidence against classifying the message as a refund request, unless a later customer message clearly reversed the position. If the customer said “if this happens again, refund me,” the conditional was recorded as a possible future request, not a current request for an immediate refund. The audit deliberately separated a threat, a hypothetical, and a request made now.

The initial automated count was 26. It was not produced by reading 26 customer demands for money. It was produced by searching staff notes and customer text for a set of terms, then assigning the whole ticket to a single label. The search captured a player saying “not a refund,” a supervisor proposing an apology credit, a player criticizing the price of a cosmetic, an agent asking whether a refund was intended, and an unrelated transaction reversal. It also missed requests phrased without the word “refund.” A word search can help find records for review; it cannot decide what remedy a customer requested.

The audit found 9 reports with an explicit request to return money or paid currency. There were 14 reports asking for an account or match correction, 21 asking for an explanation or review, and 11 asking for public acknowledgment or a correction to communications. Some reports fell into more than one category. These figures should not be summed as if each category described a separate person. The audit also found 8 reports in which the customer’s requested remedy was not clear from the preserved record. Those remained unclassified pending follow-up. “Unclear” was not silently converted to “refund.”

The audit did not decide whether every requested remedy was available under the game rules. It did not award points, reverse purchases, or promise compensation. It answered a narrower operational question: what did the customer ask for? Eligibility and action were evaluated afterward under the relevant policy. A customer may request something the policy does not allow, and a staff member may take an action the customer did not request. Neither fact changes what the customer said.

APPENDIX B — EVENT TIMELINE AND DATA LIMITATIONS
The incident timeline was reconstructed from the gateway logs, client acknowledgments, match-history service, penalty service, status-page revisions, and support case archive. The clocks are synchronized to UTC to the nearest second for gateway and service events; the public status page stores timestamps to the nearest minute. A discrepancy between these systems is possible, particularly during the initial shard-routing fault. The audit does not claim that every player’s local device clock matched the server clock.

At 18:00, the season launch opened. At 18:17, the first recorded burst of routing errors began. At 18:22, the incident channel received reports from players in two regions. At 18:31, the on-call operator reproduced the wrong-shard assignment. At 18:36, the first internal warning was posted. At 18:43:12, the RH-4418 client sent its reconnect acknowledgement. At 18:43:19, the penalty service received the stale disconnect event. At 18:49, a second test showed the same ordering in a different match. At 19:02, routing errors fell below the alert threshold, though the team had not yet confirmed that all match-history records were safe. At 19:26, ranked matchmaking was disabled for the affected shard. At 20:11, a patch began rolling out. At 21:04, the public status text was changed to “monitoring.” At 23:40, the controlled test passed and ranked access resumed.

The time sequence supports the conclusion that the penalty service retained a stale event after the player had reconnected. It does not, by itself, establish that the player won the match. The match result is derived from the round record. The review found that the result remained a loss under the published rule. The rating service applied a 28-point decrease to the account. A separate recalculation found that the decrease was consistent with the recorded loss and party rating. The fact that the player returned before the final round explains why the abandonment penalty was incorrect; it does not automatically change the result under rule 7.4.

The support archive records the customer’s original message and subsequent replies. The account has an earlier 900-shard purchase, but the purchase date is two months before the incident. The transaction export shows no purchase on 4 September associated with this ticket. No paid shard balance was removed during the match. These details matter because staff repeatedly described the rating decrease as “lost value.” In this game, rating points are a ranking measure, not purchased currency. The available records show no basis for treating the 28-point change as a charge or a debit of paid currency.

The finance export includes unrelated transactions from the same period. Two courtesy grants of event tokens were applied to accounts reporting a different event challenge problem. One duplicate token grant was reversed the following day. Those entries are not evidence of a refund for RH-4418. The records identify the accounts and transaction reasons separately. The fact that a transaction appears in the launch-period export does not make it connected to every launch ticket.

The public status page initially used a broad “resolved” heading while the team was still monitoring individual records. The version history confirms the heading was later replaced. The status page does not show that all players’ account cases were resolved at that time. The complaint about misleading wording is supported by the page history and by the timing of the correction. It remains a communication issue distinct from whether the player requested money back.

APPENDIX C — NOTES ON THE MISLEADING SUPERVISOR SUMMARY
The supervisor summary was entered on 6 September at 13:40, after the first agent had already recorded that the customer denied wanting money back. The supervisor’s entry reads: “Refund request—player lost value during launch and asks for credit. Approve apology credit if policy permits; close as compensated.” The entry does not quote a customer sentence, cite a transaction, or identify whether “credit” means an acknowledgment or a balance adjustment. It also proposes an action in the imperative “Approve,” which is plainly staff-directed. The phrase “close as compensated” describes a suggested administrative disposition, not a customer statement.

The summary contains three claims that need independent checking. First, it calls the case a refund request. The customer’s original message asks for a record correction, penalty removal, and explanation, and says the bundle price is not the issue. The customer then explicitly says, “I do not mean a money refund.” Later messages repeat that no money or paid currency is requested. Second, the summary says the customer asks for credit. The original language asks the company to “credit the affected players with an honest acknowledgment,” in a sentence about acknowledging the incident. The customer later rejects a token. Third, the summary calls the case compensated. The case history shows a penalty removal and public communication, but no money or paid-currency return, and the customer continued to disagree with the match result.

The group’s review of this note is not a general rule that staff summaries are always wrong. A staff note can accurately summarize a customer request if it quotes or faithfully paraphrases the message. The problem here is that the summary’s central claim conflicts with the source text. The team must follow the source text. An internal label does not become true by being copied to a dashboard, and repetition across several dashboards does not create independent evidence.

The review also checked whether any later message changed the request. The 7 September reply says, “I have not asked for a refund,” and rejects a token in place of correcting history. The 9 September follow-up says, “I am not requesting money or paid currency,” and asks that the report be recorded as concerning the penalty, match history, and public acknowledgment. No later customer statement asks for a refund. The supervisor note therefore cannot be treated as an intermediate request that the customer later withdrew; it was never the customer’s request in the first place.

APPENDIX D — CUSTOMER-FACING OUTCOME AND OPEN QUESTIONS
The confirmed account action was removal of the incorrect abandonment penalty. The match result remained a loss. The rating calculation was reviewed and remained a 28-point decrease. The player received an explanation referencing rule 7.4 and the event timestamps. The public incident note acknowledged that a stale disconnect event caused incorrect penalties and that status wording had been updated. The customer said the public note was better but still criticized how long the wording had been wrong. The ticket was not closed as a refund case, and no refund was issued.

There are open questions about the service itself. The team is testing why a stale event could arrive after the reconnect acknowledgement and whether the same race condition occurred outside the confirmed sample. The team is also reviewing whether rule 7.4 is clearly presented to players who reconnect before the final round. Those engineering and policy questions should not be hidden behind the refund classification dispute. Correctly identifying the request does not prove that the service was acceptable, and it does not prevent the company from offering a remedy voluntarily. It only preserves an accurate record of what was asked.

The customer’s request for a public acknowledgment was fulfilled in part by the 9 September note. The note acknowledged the incorrect penalty and clarified that match results were reviewed separately. It did not provide a minute-by-minute account of the misleading status heading. The customer expressed dissatisfaction with that omission. The case file should preserve this distinction: a communication was posted, but the customer did not say the entire concern was resolved. The customer also did not turn that remaining dissatisfaction into a request for money.

The same standard should apply to the rest of the launch queue. A customer’s request for a refund should be counted when the customer asks for money or paid currency to be returned. A customer’s request to correct rank, remove a penalty, explain an event, or acknowledge a communication failure should be recorded under those remedies. A staff member may offer a courtesy item, but an offer is not a request. A staff member may recommend a refund, but a recommendation is not a request. A customer may reject an offered token, and that rejection does not establish a refund request. The wording and sequence of the actual exchange decide the classification.

The incident report remains angry because the process gave players a cheerful status banner, then gave managers a false count. The anger is justified by the documented failures, but anger alone is not a substitute for evidence. The record shows a real routing problem, an incorrect penalty, an unchanged match result, a calculated rating decrease, a public correction, and a player who repeatedly asked for account correction and explanation while explicitly declining a monetary refund. We should not flatten those facts into the supervisor’s convenient label.

APPENDIX E — FINAL MANAGER CHECKLIST
Before circulating another total, verify that every item marked as a customer request is supported by customer-authored text. Preserve the original message and any later clarification. Keep staff interpretations in a separate field. If a customer says “not a refund,” do not count the ticket as a refund unless a later customer message clearly reverses that statement. If a customer uses an ambiguous term such as “credit,” read the surrounding sentence and subsequent replies. Do not infer a purchase-price request from the existence of a prior purchase. Do not infer a refund from a ranking loss, a bad match outcome, or a recommendation written by a supervisor.

For this incident, the correct case description is: the player asked for an incorrect abandonment penalty and match record to be corrected, requested an explanation of the match and rating decision, and requested acknowledgment of the misleading incident communication. The team removed the penalty, left the match result and rating calculation unchanged, supplied an explanation, and posted a public note. The player did not ask for money or paid currency to be returned. The supervisor’s contrary label is not supported by the customer-authored thread.

This report is intended to prevent another round of dashboard arguments, not to excuse the outage. The launch was mishandled, the initial status wording was too broad, the stale event caused a bad penalty, and the queue classification amplified the damage. We can own all of those failures without claiming that a customer requested a remedy they expressly rejected. [{"state":"Granite Labs Autumn Forum planning packet

Respectfully prepared for the event team, with apologies for the length and with sincere thanks to everyone who kept the arrangements orderly. This packet combines a typed transcription of a handwritten-style note, the venue invoice, meeting notes, and a courteous administrative appendix. The packet concerns one event only: Granite Labs’ Autumn Forum, scheduled for 18 October at the Bracken Hall Conference Centre. It is intended to preserve the information in the documents, not to replace the signed agreements or the original invoice. Where a summary or personal comment differs from a dated source document, the dated source document and the recorded exchange are reproduced so that readers may check the facts for themselves.

Document register

1. Typed transcription of the planning desk note, entered 2 September.
2. Venue invoice GH-418, issued 28 August, with its line items and payment annotation.
3. Meeting notes from the planning meeting of 3 September.
4. Follow-up correspondence and operations register, through 12 September.
5. Appendices containing room arrangements, supplier contacts, attendee-service notes, and routine reminders.

The materials below are presented in the order in which the planning assistant found them in the shared event folder. The assistant has retained the original wording where practical and has respectfully expanded abbreviations only where a short form might otherwise be unclear. Repeated details are left in place because different team members requested that the record be easy to use without consulting another page. We hope this arrangement is convenient.

Typed transcription of handwritten-style planning note

Found folded beneath the blue event folder, dated Monday, 2 September. The original was written in pencil on a sheet headed “Autumn Forum—please keep together.” The typed transcription reads:

“Dear team, many thanks for helping with the Forum. I have checked the papers in the envelope and would be grateful if we could keep the signed booking pages with the payment slips. The catering team have kindly confirmed that their tasting appointment is only a tasting appointment; it is not a service booking for the day. Please do not count a sample menu as a booked meal service. The hall, projection package, and evening cleaning are the venue items shown on the invoice. I have not yet found the supplier confirmations for the other arrangements, but perhaps those are in the green folder. Very sorry to trouble everyone with this.”

In a different hand, in the lower margin, is the following comment: “No refund was requested. This is settled; there is nothing to reimburse.” The note is unsigned. The comment appears to be a personal summary rather than a quotation from a customer or a supplier. The transcription clerk has not altered it. Since the comment is short, it is reproduced here in full rather than paraphrased.

A small note on the reverse says: “Please call the venue before moving the lectern. The hall team have been kind about access. The display stands are not to be placed in front of the west doors. Kindly leave the aisle clear even if the poster boards arrive early.” There is no date or signature on the reverse. These details are included for completeness; they do not amend the invoice or the meeting record.

Venue invoice GH-418

Granite Hall Events, billing address as shown on the original invoice: 14 Wren Court, Alder Quay. Invoice number GH-418. Issued 28 August. Event date 18 October. Customer: Granite Labs. Attention: Events desk. Payment due: 12 September. The invoice is marked “Pro forma; balance due by stated date.” At the top right, someone has written “Thank you, paid in part,” though no amount accompanies that phrase.

Line items, copied from the invoice:

Main hall hire, 18 October, 08:00–18:00 — 1 unit — $1,480.00.
Projection and screen package — 1 unit — $320.00.
Evening cleaning after event — 1 unit — $180.00.
Additional lectern microphone — 1 unit — $65.00.
Subtotal — $2,045.00.
Local service tax — $163.60.
Invoice total — $2,208.60.
Deposit received, 28 August — $600.00.
Balance due — $1,608.60.

The invoice’s payment box includes a handwritten entry dated 30 August: “Deposit transferred, thank you.” A second handwritten entry, dated 4 September, reads: “Please return the deposit if the hall cannot provide the agreed step-free access. We cannot accept a venue without that access.” Below it, the venue coordinator wrote: “Access confirmed in writing on 5 September. No cancellation made; deposit remains credited to the booking.” The original invoice does not show a refund transaction. The customer’s request concerned reimbursement of the deposit in the stated contingency; the venue’s reply says that the contingency did not occur and that the booking remained active. The invoice total and balance have not been recalculated or amended.

Invoice notes, faithfully copied:

“Please quote GH-418 on correspondence. This invoice covers venue hire and the listed venue services only. It does not include food, floral arrangements, photography, interpretation, or transport. Separate suppliers should invoice Granite Labs directly unless otherwise agreed in writing. Thank you for your courteous attention.”

A sticky note attached to the invoice says: “Events desk summary: refund request absent; the customer accepted the venue without conditions.” The sticky note is unsigned and does not quote the 4 September annotation. The annotation is legible on the invoice copy and is reproduced above. A separate line in the venue’s access email, filed behind the invoice, states: “We are pleased to confirm step-free access, including the east entrance and the lower platform, for 18 October.” That email is dated 5 September.

Meeting notes, 3 September

Present, according to the attendance line: Mateo Fischer, Esi Iyer, Callum O’Neill, and the Granite Hall coordinator by telephone for the first twelve minutes. Apologies were offered for beginning two minutes late. The chair thanked everyone for making time and asked that decisions be recorded carefully. The event is a one-day internal-and-partner forum for approximately 85 guests, with a morning programme, lunch, afternoon sessions, and a short evening reception. The team agreed to avoid promising any supplier service until a written confirmation or signed booking had been received.

Opening review. Mateo Fischer read the draft schedule. Esi Iyer confirmed that the registration table could be staffed from 08:00. Callum O’Neill noted that the guest list was still being checked and that the number 85 was an estimate rather than a guaranteed attendance count. The chair requested that this distinction be kept in the public invitation. The venue coordinator confirmed the hall booking and the projection package on the call, then undertook to send written access confirmation. The meeting did not treat the spoken confirmation as a substitute for the written access note. The group expressed thanks for the coordinator’s patience.

Room use. The main hall is to be arranged in classroom rows for the morning and in small discussion groups after lunch. The east entrance is the step-free route. The west doors are to remain clear. The lectern stays on the low platform, with the additional microphone supplied under invoice GH-418. The projection screen is on the north wall. A technician is expected to be available during setup; the team is to verify that detail one week before the event. The coordinator asked that the team not tape signs to the painted doors. The group agreed, very politely, and recorded that freestanding signs would be used instead.

Supplier register reviewed at the meeting. The notes distinguish between “confirmed booking,” “written acceptance,” “quotation only,” and “still being explored.” The chair emphasized that a quotation, sample, tentative conversation, or proposed option is not a booking. This distinction is repeated because a draft agenda had used the heading “confirmed partners” for a list that included several proposals. The team agreed to correct that heading before circulating the agenda.

The signed booking page for Juniper Table Catering was in the blue folder. The service covers lunch and afternoon refreshments for the event date, with final guest numbers due 10 October. The signed page shows acceptance by both parties on 29 August. The catering manager’s email says, “We are delighted to provide the agreed service; thank you for choosing us.” The note about the 2 September tasting is separate and does not change the event-day booking.

The signed agreement for Lantern & Loom Florals was in the green folder. It covers six table arrangements and two entrance pieces for delivery on 18 October. Both signatures are dated 30 August. The planner’s email says the agreed arrangements can be adjusted in color but not increased in number without a revised quotation. The team agreed to keep the requested palette to deep blue, pale gold, and white. A sample photograph, attached to a later email, is marked “inspiration only”; it is not an additional order.

The signed agreement for Blue Finch Audio was attached to its confirmation email. It covers two wireless microphones, one lectern microphone, and a sound check before doors open. The agreement is dated 31 August and accepted by Granite Labs that afternoon. The vendor’s message thanks the team for the clear room plan. The team noted that the lectern microphone also appears on the venue invoice; Mateo was asked to clarify whether the venue’s microphone is a backup and whether it should be removed from the final equipment list. The vendor booking remains recorded as accepted, irrespective of that equipment check.

The signed booking for Northstar Interpreting was filed in the correspondence folder. It covers interpretation between English and French for the morning plenary only, using the vendor’s portable receiver set. The booking form is dated 1 September and bears both signatures. The supplier confirmed receipt of the deposit and asked for the final speaker list by 11 October. The team agreed not to describe the service as covering the afternoon breakouts. The four supplier agreements listed above are the only signed event-day supplier bookings identified in the review.

Items not booked as of the meeting. The catering tasting was completed for menu selection, but it is not an extra service booking. A draft from Orchard Street Bakery requests approval for a dessert proposal; no acceptance or signature appears. A quotation from Bright Arc Photography is under review and has not been accepted. A message from Quiet Current Transport offers two shuttle options but asks the organizer to choose a schedule; no booking is shown. The team thanked each supplier for the information and agreed to respond once requirements were clearer.

A tentative discussion with Morrow Lane Rentals concerned extra chairs. The rental company asked for a count and a delivery window. The meeting notes say, “Please do not list as booked until a signed order is returned.” There is no signed order in the folder. The possibility of renting a second registration table was also discussed internally, but no external vendor was contacted. These points were noted to prevent a tentative conversation or an internal idea from being mistaken for a confirmed service.

Budget review. The venue invoice total is $2,208.60 and the deposit is $600.00, leaving $1,608.60 due. The chair asked whether the deposit could be recovered if accessibility failed. The coordinator said that the venue would review a refund if the promised access was unavailable, according to the booking terms. Mateo wrote, “Please request return of deposit if the step-free route is not provided.” The group agreed this was a conditional request, not a cancellation. On 5 September the venue confirmed the route in writing; the booking remained in place. The 4 September invoice annotation is therefore retained as a request made under the stated condition, rather than evidence that a refund was paid or that the event was cancelled.

The team reviewed a budget worksheet that included the venue amount, four supplier estimates, and a small contingency. Several figures were preliminary. The catering proposal was priced per person, while the invoice was a fixed venue charge. The florist quote included delivery; the interpreting quote included receiver hire. No one treated the estimates as accepted liabilities. The chair asked that the next budget version show “contracted,” “quoted,” and “unpriced” in separate columns. Everyone agreed, and the minute taker recorded the request with thanks.

Communications. The invitation should say that lunch and afternoon refreshments are arranged, and that interpretation is available for the morning plenary. It should not claim that transport, photography, or an additional dessert service has been arranged. The agenda should identify Blue Finch Audio as the sound supplier and Lantern & Loom Florals as the floral supplier. Juniper Table Catering should be listed for lunch and refreshments. Northstar Interpreting should be identified only for the morning plenary. The wording should be appreciative without implying that unbooked suppliers have accepted work.

Accessibility and guest care. The venue’s written confirmation is required before the event page is finalized. The team confirmed that no guest should be asked to use the west doors as the step-free route. The east entrance will be signposted. Any individual access requests are to be handled discreetly, with thanks to the guest for letting the team know. The venue has promised a low platform route, but the team will verify the arrangement during setup. No dietary requirements were finalized at the meeting; the form remains open. The catering manager will receive the confirmed count and dietary summary by 10 October.

Equipment and setup. Registration begins at 08:30 for guests. The setup team arrives at 07:15. The projection package is included on GH-418. The team will use existing Granite Labs banners and freestanding signs. The west doors must remain unobstructed. Programme. The morning plenary begins at 09:15. The first presentation is scheduled for 09:30, with a short break at 10:45. The lunch period begins at 12:15. Afternoon sessions begin at 13:15 and conclude at 16:30. The reception is expected to finish by 18:00, in accordance with the hall hire. The programme should not describe the afternoon breakouts as interpreted, since Northstar’s agreement covers the morning plenary only. Action list. Mateo Fischer: confirm microphone overlap with Blue Finch Audio and Granite Hall. Esi Iyer: send the updated room plan to the florist and venue. Callum O’Neill: reconcile the guest list and provide the number to Juniper Table Catering by 10 October. Chair: revise the invitation so that only confirmed arrangements are stated. The invoice is a venue document and includes room hire, projection, cleaning, and a microphone. Its total is $2,208.60; the recorded deposit is $600.00; the remaining balance is $1,608.60. The four supplier bookings identified in the signed documents are catering, florals, audio, and morning-plenary interpretation. They are distinct from the venue invoice. The tasting, bakery proposal, photography quotation, transport options, and chair inquiry do not meet the team’s stated standard for a confirmed event-day booking. The distinction is documented more than once so that the event page, budget worksheet, and run sheet can be reconciled without inconvenience.

Appendix D: courtesy correspondence excerpts

From Mateo Fischer to Juniper Table Catering: “Dear team, many thanks for sending the signed page. We are pleased to confirm the agreed lunch and afternoon refreshments. We will send the final count and dietary information by 10 October. Please accept our thanks for your assistance.” Juniper Table Catering replied: “Thank you; we have countersigned and attached the booking confirmation.”

From Esi Iyer to Lantern & Loom Florals: “Dear colleagues, thank you for the revised palette. We accept the order as written for six table pieces and two entrance pieces. From Callum O’Neill to Blue Finch Audio: “Thank you for the agreement. Granite Labs accepts the listed sound service for 18 October. We will send the final stage plan shortly.” Blue Finch replied: “With thanks, we confirm the booking and will schedule the sound check.” The email thread is dated 31 August.

From the Granite Labs events desk to Northstar Interpreting: “Please find the signed booking for the morning plenary attached. We appreciate your help and will send the speaker list by 11 October.” Northstar replied: “Thank you; the signed booking is received and confirmed for the morning plenary.” The thread is dated 1 September.

From the Granite Labs events desk to Orchard Street Bakery: “Thank you for the menu proposal. We are reviewing costs and have not yet accepted the proposal. We will come back to you if we wish to proceed.” No later acceptance is filed.

From Bright Arc Photography to Granite Labs: “We would be delighted to reserve the date once you approve the quotation.” The event desk replied: “Many thanks. We have not approved this quotation, so please do not reserve the date yet.”

From Quiet Current Transport to Granite Labs: “We can provide either of the proposed shuttle schedules if you select one and authorize the booking.” The events desk wrote in the margin: “Options only; no selection made.” No confirmation followed.

The quoted exchanges above are included to preserve clear evidence of acceptance or non-acceptance. Each message is politely phrased, as requested by the planning team. A friendly expression of interest does not itself change the status recorded on the signed booking forms.

Appendix E: final folder review notes

The folder reviewer checked the invoice number, customer name, date, and balance. The amounts on the invoice add as printed: $1,480.00 plus $320.00 plus $180.00 plus $65.00 equals $2,045.00; tax is $163.60; total is $2,208.60. The reviewer recommends that future summaries quote the relevant contract status rather than rely on a short handwritten verdict. The event desk has been asked to revise the summary after checking the signed documents. No changes to the event plan were authorized by this administrative review.
