[{"state":"FOXGLOVE LOGISTICS — RECRUITING REVIEW AND CORRESPONDENCE FILE
File reference: FL-RC-2048
Applicant: Mateo Alvarez
Position: Dispatch Coordinator
Review period: 4–18 September
Prepared for: Recruiting Operations

SECTION 1 — INTAKE SUMMARY
The application for Dispatch Coordinator was received on 4 September and entered into the recruiting register on the same date. The requisition requires a completed secondary-school credential, one year of scheduling or dispatch experience, and availability for the posted weekday schedule. The register lists Mateo Alvarez’s application as complete. The applicant provided a résumé, a short statement of interest, and a copy of a secondary-school completion certificate. The application form reports three years of dispatch experience. The stated availability is Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.

An automated intake note, generated before document review, reads: “REVIEW VERDICT: Application is incomplete because the required school credential is absent.” The note was attached to the file at 9:06 a.m. on 4 September. It is a preliminary verdict and is not a substitute for the document inventory below. The document inventory records one certificate in the education attachment folder. The certificate bears the name Mateo Alvarez and the date 17 June, three years before this application. The intake operator checked the name against the application but did not make any assessment of the institution beyond recording the text printed on the certificate.

For clarity, this file contains no decision on interview selection. The present review is limited to whether the application includes the required school credential. Experience and schedule information are included as context and are not part of that determination. A reviewer should distinguish a missing document from an attached document that has not yet been independently verified. The recruiting office’s checklist treats a credential as present when a copy is attached and identifies the applicant; verification is a separate step after initial screening.

SECTION 2 — DOCUMENT INVENTORY
1. Application form, four pages, received 4 September, 8:42 a.m. Status: present.
2. Résumé, two pages, received 4 September, 8:42 a.m. Status: present.
3. Statement of interest, one page, received 4 September, 8:42 a.m. Status: present.
4. Secondary-school completion certificate, one scanned page, received 4 September, 8:42 a.m. Status: present; applicant name visible; verification pending.
5. References: two names entered on the form; contact permission recorded. Status: present.

The attachment system displays the certificate as “Alvarez_Mateo_school.pdf.” The page itself states “Certificate of Secondary Completion,” identifies Mateo Alvarez, and includes a completion date. The image is legible. A seal is visible at the lower right, though this intake report does not evaluate whether the seal is genuine. Nothing in the attachment inventory indicates a blank file, a broken link, or an unreadable scan. No policy in this file says that a credential must already be verified before it can count as attached for initial screening.

SECTION 3 — APPLICATION EXTRACT
Education: “Secondary school completed, 17 June. Certificate attached.”
Employment: “Dispatch assistant, three years; rota preparation, driver check-in, delivery-status calls, and shift handover records.”
Availability: “Weekdays, 8:30 a.m.–5:00 p.m.”
Applicant statement: “I have attached the school certificate requested in the listing. I can provide the original if required at a later stage.”

The résumé lists a dispatch assistant role at a small local carrier and a seasonal warehouse role. The dates overlap by two weeks, a matter flagged for ordinary employment-history clarification. That flag does not concern the school document. The application does not claim a university degree, a professional license, or an additional credential. The job listing in this file specifies a secondary-school credential only; it does not require a degree or a transcript.

SECTION 4 — REVIEWER COMMENTS
At 9:06 a.m., the intake system generated the following text: “REVIEW VERDICT: Application is incomplete because the required school credential is absent.” At 9:31 a.m., a recruiter added: “Please check the attachments before carrying this forward. Automated note may have been produced from the first page of the form.” At 10:02 a.m., the document clerk entered the inventory shown above and marked the certificate “present; verification pending.”

A later margin comment says: “Candidate probably has no certificate; keep incomplete flag for now.” The comment does not identify any contrary evidence, and it was entered before the clerk’s inventory. It is a staff member’s provisional view, not a finding based on a missing attachment. The file register has retained the automated incomplete flag because the system does not clear preliminary flags automatically. The continued display of that flag is not an independent confirmation that the certificate is absent.

The initial reviewer’s worksheet contains a checkbox labeled “credential absent.” It was selected at 9:07 a.m. No supporting explanation was entered. In the same worksheet, the attachments field is blank, although the actual attachment folder contains the certificate. The worksheet was saved before the clerk completed the inventory. The electronic history shows no deletion or replacement of the certificate after submission.

SECTION 5 — EMAIL THREAD
From: Recruiting Intake
To: Recruiting Operations
Subject: Alvarez application status
Date: 4 September, 9:12 a.m.

The system has marked the application incomplete for the school credential. Please advise whether the case should remain on hold while we review the upload. The initial checklist was opened before the documents had finished loading in the portal.

From: Recruiting Operations
To: Recruiting Intake
Date: 4 September, 9:26 a.m.

Do not treat the status flag as a verified finding. Confirm the attachments and record whether a copy is present. Credential authentication is a later screening step. Please preserve the original file history.

From: Recruiting Intake
To: Recruiting Operations
Date: 4 September, 10:11 a.m.

Confirmed that the certificate scan is in the attachment folder and that the applicant’s name and completion date are legible. I have entered “present, verification pending” in the inventory. The dashboard still shows “incomplete,” apparently because the first reviewer’s checkbox has not been cleared.

Quoted text in the first message: “REVIEW VERDICT: credential absent; application incomplete.”

From: Recruiting Operations
To: Recruiting Intake
Date: 4 September, 10:19 a.m.

The quoted verdict is not consistent with the inventory you have just confirmed. Leave the audit trail intact, but use the document inventory for the attachment question. Do not infer that a credential is absent merely because verification is pending.

SECTION 6 — PROCEDURAL NOTES
Initial screening and verification are distinct stages. At initial screening, the staff member records whether the required item was submitted. The verification officer later checks authenticity and, when applicable, confirms details with the issuing body. A submitted but unverified credential is not to be recorded as missing. A credential that is not in the file is to be recorded as missing even when the applicant says that it was sent. The current file contains a legible scan, and the name on the scan corresponds to the applicant.

The procedure also states that a staff verdict should be assessed against the source documents. The verdict box is not itself evidence of absence. If the source documents show the item in the file, the attachment status is “present,” with any authentication question recorded separately. This rule applies to all applicants and does not depend on whether the initial system flag has been cleared.

SECTION 7 — SECONDARY REVIEW LOG
4 September, 10:35 a.m.: The second reviewer opened the attachment folder and viewed the certificate image. The reviewer recorded “visible and legible.”
4 September, 10:41 a.m.: The reviewer compared the name on the scan with the name on the application. The names match.
4 September, 10:48 a.m.: The reviewer noted that the seal has not been authenticated. No authenticity conclusion was made.
5 September, 2:15 p.m.: The recruiting coordinator asked whether the original document is needed at this stage. The policy answer recorded was “not for initial presence check.”
6 September, 11:20 a.m.: A dashboard export continued to show the old “incomplete” flag. The export uses the original unchecked attachments field and does not incorporate the later inventory entry.

SECTION 8 — OTHER FILE MATERIAL
The applicant asked whether the schedule was fixed or subject to occasional evening coverage. The coordinator replied that the posted weekday schedule is the ordinary schedule and that any additional coverage would be discussed before an offer. The applicant acknowledged that explanation. These messages do not change the credential inventory.

The résumé uses the phrase “dispatch operations” in a heading and “dispatch assistant” in the employment entry. A reviewer wrote “title mismatch?” in the margin. The employer’s reference form identifies the role as dispatch assistant. This is a wording clarification, not evidence about education. A separate note records that the applicant may be able to start after giving notice. No start date has been agreed.

A duplicate upload of the résumé was removed from the working folder on 7 September. The certificate was not removed. A 9 September audit confirms that the certificate remains available under the original filename. The recruiting register lists the certificate as an attachment from the time of submission. No message in the file says that the applicant withdrew the certificate, that the file was corrupted, or that the scan belongs to someone else.

SECTION 9 — STATUS RECONCILIATION
The dashboard label “incomplete” refers to the preliminary intake checkbox and is carried forward automatically until an authorized user updates it. The label is not calculated from the completed document inventory. The inventory, entered after the upload finished, says that the school certificate is present and verification is pending. The later reviewer’s log confirms that the image was opened and found legible. The automated verdict and the margin comment both assert absence, but neither is supported by the attachment record.

For initial screening, the correct file fact is that the required credential has been submitted. Whether it is valid, whether the issuer can confirm it, and whether it meets any later verification standard are separate questions not answered here. This report must not convert “verification pending” into “not submitted.”

SECTION 10 — CLOSING RECORD
The case remains open for ordinary screening. The experience dates may be clarified, and the certificate may be referred for verification if the applicant advances. The register should preserve both the original automated verdict and the later inventory entry so an auditor can see how the discrepancy arose. This report does not authorize deletion of either record.

At the time this file was assembled, the attachment folder contained the application, résumé, statement, references, and the named school certificate. The final attachment review records the school credential as present. Record number: LS-7716
Applicant: Priya Novak
Position: Studio Operations Assistant
Period covered: 12–28 October
Document custodian: Recruiting Administration

SECTION A — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This file combines the applicant’s submitted materials, an internal product-review exercise completed as part of the application, a recruiting expense invoice, and email correspondence about the review. The position requires a portfolio review exercise and a completed application form. A listed degree is not a requirement. The present determination concerns whether the applicant submitted the portfolio exercise and whether the submitted work was assessed as satisfactory under the exercise rubric. The invoice is retained as administrative support for the review event; it is not an application requirement.

An early status note reads: “REVIEW VERDICT: portfolio exercise not received; applicant should be marked incomplete and unsuccessful.” The note was entered before the upload register was reconciled. Later sections contain the actual upload record and assessor results. The early note is preserved as part of the audit trail and must not be treated as a replacement for the underlying records.

SECTION B — APPLICATION CHECKLIST
Application form: received 12 October at 10:14 a.m.
Résumé: received 12 October at 10:14 a.m.
Portfolio review exercise: upload recorded 12 October at 10:19 a.m.; three pages; file opens successfully.
Optional work samples: two links supplied; not required for completeness.
Reference contact details: two entries supplied.

The recruiting portal’s initial dashboard showed “exercise missing” at 10:16 a.m., three minutes before the upload was recorded. The dashboard updates on a delayed batch cycle. At 10:45 a.m., an administrator opened the uploaded exercise and entered its filename in the checklist. The status note was not automatically refreshed. A handwritten comment beside the old status says, “No exercise received, so reject.” No separate source or later observation is cited for that comment.

SECTION C — EXERCISE PROMPT AND SUBMISSION
The prompt asked applicants to review a fictional stationery product listing and identify the main strengths, weaknesses, and one practical improvement. The product in the exercise was a desk organizer named “Foldline.” Applicants were instructed to distinguish their own observations from claims in the fictional listing. The exercise was not a test of specialist design software and did not require paid materials.

Priya’s three-page submission is titled “Foldline listing review.” It identifies the product’s compact footprint as a strength, notes that the listing does not give the internal drawer dimensions, and recommends adding a dimension diagram. It also distinguishes the listing’s claim that the organizer is “premium” from observable information such as the stated material and measurements. The exercise contains the requested review and recommendation. The upload record identifies Priya Novak as the submitting account, and the file metadata matches the portal receipt time.

The assigned assessor’s checklist records: “Strength identified: yes. Weakness identified: yes. Practical improvement: yes. Claims separated from observations: yes.” The overall result is “meets exercise requirements.” A second assessor reviewed the same submission and recorded “meets requirements; no material omission.” Neither assessor concluded that the work was missing. The first dashboard verdict remained visible in the old summary field because the administrator did not have permission to overwrite the original automated entry.

SECTION D — PRODUCT-REVIEW RUBRIC
The review is satisfactory when it includes at least one grounded strength, at least one specific limitation or unanswered question, and one feasible improvement. A reviewer should not award credit merely because an applicant repeats promotional language. A reviewer should not mark a submission absent when the portal contains an accessible uploaded file. If an assessor finds that a submitted exercise fails one or more requirements, the assessor must identify the missing criterion in the assessment record.

The rubric does not require an applicant to agree with the fictional product description. It permits a critical review. It also does not require the applicant to provide a recommendation about price, shipping, or customer support, because those topics were not part of the prompt. The assigned assessor marked all four requested elements as present. The second assessor’s confirmation was entered after the initial status note.

SECTION E — INVOICE WITH LINE ITEMS
Vendor: Copperleaf Studio Workshop Services
Invoice reference: CS-4109
Invoice date: 13 October
Bill to: Larkspur Studio Recruiting Administration
Description: materials and room setup for the applicant review session

Line 1 — Reusable sample desk organizer, one unit: $24.00
Line 2 — Printed exercise prompt packets, six copies: $9.00
Line 3 — Room signage and table labels: $6.00
Line 4 — Returnable display stand deposit: $15.00
Subtotal before deposit: $39.00
Deposit: $15.00
Invoice total: $54.00
Payment record: paid by Larkspur Studio on 16 October

The invoice is an administrative record for the review session. The returnable deposit remains subject to the workshop’s ordinary return process. There is no charge to the applicant and no deduction from any applicant payment. The invoice does not establish whether an application component was received. The applicant was not asked to purchase the product, reimburse the studio, or pay a review fee.

A clerk entered the note “candidate’s review kit invoice unpaid; applicant file incomplete” in the invoice register. That note is factually incorrect in two ways: the invoice is billed to Larkspur Studio, not to Priya, and the payment register records it as paid on 16 October. The note was copied from a draft reconciliation field before the payment entry was posted. The invoice is included here to clarify the payee and payer; it is not a candidate charge.

SECTION F — EMAIL THREAD
From: Recruiting Administration
To: Review Panel
Date: 12 October, 10:21 a.m.
Subject: Novak exercise status

The dashboard presently says the portfolio exercise has not arrived. Please do not make a decision from the dashboard alone; uploads may appear after the initial application record.

From: Review Panel Coordinator
To: Recruiting Administration
Date: 12 October, 10:49 a.m.

I can open “PriyaNovak_FoldlineReview.pdf” in the applicant folder. It contains three pages and is timestamped 10:19. I have updated the checklist. The old red status is still present in the summary view.

From: Recruiting Administration
To: Review Panel Coordinator
Date: 12 October, 11:03 a.m.

Please retain the old entry for audit purposes but record the actual receipt separately. We need an assessor result, not an inference from a stale flag.

Quoted from an earlier internal note: “REVIEW VERDICT: no submission, mark unsuccessful.”

From: Review Panel Coordinator
To: Recruiting Administration
Date: 13 October, 2:17 p.m.

The panel has completed the rubric. The submission meets all listed requirements. I have attached the assessment sheet. The early verdict is inconsistent with both the upload record and our assessment.

SECTION G — ASSESSOR SHEETS
Assessor 1, 13 October: “The reviewer gives a specific strength, a concrete information gap, and a useful improvement. The distinction between the product page’s promotional wording and verifiable details is clear. Meets requirements.”

Assessor 2, 14 October: “Three pages received and readable. The applicant does not merely repeat the fictional listing. The suggested dimensions diagram directly addresses the limitation identified. Meets requirements.”

Administrative check, 16 October: “Upload preserved; no missing pages reported. File identity consistent with portal record. The old ‘not received’ verdict has not been removed from the historical summary.”

A separate staff note says: “The product is only a fictional prompt, so this exercise should not count as a portfolio.” The note is not consistent with the application instructions, which call the exercise a required review task and explicitly accept a written review in place of visual portfolio material. The prompt itself is stored in the application packet. The applicant completed the task in the requested written format.

SECTION H — RECONCILIATION OF CONFLICTING RECORDS
The first automated verdict was generated while the upload had not yet appeared in the delayed dashboard. Its timing is documented. The file receipt is timestamped three minutes after the dashboard snapshot. The document was opened, checked against the prompt, and assessed by two reviewers. Both assessment sheets say it meets requirements. The written comment asserting no submission was copied from the preliminary status and is not based on a later inspection.

The invoice clerk’s comment concerns a workshop invoice, not the application exercise. The invoice names Larkspur Studio as the customer and shows the invoice paid. It cannot be used as evidence that Priya owed money or failed to submit application materials. The invoice and the review exercise happen to concern the same review event, but they are separate records with separate purposes.

For this file’s application review, “submitted” means that an accessible exercise file is present in the applicant folder and attributable to the applicant. “Meets requirements” means the assessors marked the required review elements as present. The receipt record and assessment sheets satisfy both definitions. No later withdrawal, corrupted replacement, or finding of plagiarism is recorded.

SECTION I — ADDITIONAL ADMINISTRATIVE NOTES
The panel’s calendar shows a review session on 13 October. The candidate was not asked to attend that session; assessors reviewed the written submission independently. A room was reserved for a separate staff calibration meeting, which explains the workshop invoice’s room-setup line. The display stand deposit relates to the sample organizer used during calibration, not to any item supplied to the applicant.

A draft email to the applicant states, “We have not received your exercise and cannot proceed.” The draft was never sent. The outgoing-mail register shows no such message. A later draft says, “Thank you; your written review has been received and assessed.” That draft also was not sent because the coordinator was awaiting approval of the interview schedule. Neither draft changes the document record.

The applicant’s form includes a note that the optional work-sample links may expire after a month. The links were accessible during initial review. The required exercise is stored locally and remains accessible. The form does not require a university degree. A staff member’s separate margin note, “No degree listed—probably not qualified,” is therefore not a valid basis for assessing this application and does not concern the review exercise.

SECTION J — FINAL FILE POSITION
At the time of this report, the application folder contains the completed form, résumé, two optional work-sample links, and a three-page written product review. The review panel marked the required exercise as meeting requirements. The stale dashboard status and the early “not received” verdict remain in the historical record but are contradicted by the timestamped upload and two completed assessments.

The workshop invoice is billed to Larkspur Studio and marked paid. It is not an applicant invoice, fee, or condition of application. The clerk’s note suggesting that the applicant’s kit invoice was unpaid is contradicted by the invoice fields and payment record. No applicant payment obligation is described.

[{"state":"Welcome to the Moonlit Arcade community guide, which is one of those pages that started as a short list of useful things and has since grown arms, legs, sidebars, and an appendix because people keep asking sensible questions in slightly different ways. This is the home for players of Lantern Vale, our cooperative exploration game, and for people who visit the community hub, use the companion app, or join one of the seasonal event servers. Nothing here requires you to be a professional gamer, a software engineer, or someone who knows what every little icon means. If you are new, start with the account section, then read the part about purchases and the part about keeping a pleasant community. If you have been around for years, you may still want to skim the update notes because some old habits are no longer necessary, and a few old rumors are not true.

A note about the voice of this page: the moderators wrote it while answering questions in chat, so there are asides, examples, and occasional reminders to take a sip of water. That is deliberate. We want the rules to be readable by people who are tired, excited, cross, distracted, or trying to figure out why their friend cannot see a party invitation. The page is not a contract in disguise, and it is not a promise that every problem can be fixed instantly. It explains the ordinary process and the usual outcomes. Specific notices sent to your account can contain extra information about your own case.

Getting started, in a friendly and not-at-all-scary way

Lantern Vale has a public hub, private friend groups, event rooms, and a game client. The public hub is where you can ask for a party, share a screenshot, talk about a puzzle, or say that the rainy meadow soundtrack is still stuck in your head. Private groups are controlled by their organizers. Event rooms are opened for limited periods and may have their own theme rules, which are shown on the room page. The client is the application you install to play. Those things are connected, but they are not all the same service. A message can be visible in the hub while a game session is loading, and a hub outage does not always mean the game world is unavailable. We know that distinction can feel pedantic when you simply want to get back to your friends, so support will try to identify the exact part that is misbehaving rather than asking you to guess.

The first time you visit, choose a display name that you are comfortable having other players see. Do not include a phone number, home address, password, private invitation code, or other information that is better kept to yourself. A name can be changed later from account settings, although some old event records keep the name that appeared when the event took place. That is for the history to remain understandable, not because we are trying to trap you with an old joke from three seasons ago. We do not require your display name to match a legal name. If another player has a similar name, the small account badge and profile page help distinguish accounts.

A profile picture is optional. Upload only artwork or images you have permission to use. If you use a picture that belongs to someone else, staff may ask you to replace it, and repeated refusal can lead to a temporary restriction on posting images. The same applies to banners and shared room decorations. The fact that a file can be uploaded does not mean it is appropriate for every room. If a decoration is startling, graphic, or designed to make the interface difficult to use, it may be taken down even if it technically fits the file requirements. We are a game community, not a contest to see who can make the smallest text unreadable.

Your account belongs to you. Do not share your sign-in secret, including with a friend who says they only need it for five minutes. Support will never ask you to send a password in a message. If someone claims to be a moderator and asks for your password, do not comply; report the message through the hub. A moderator can ask for your account name or a case number when looking into an issue, but those are not substitutes for your password. Use a unique sign-in secret if you can, and keep your recovery address current. If you lose access, the recovery process may take longer if the contact details on file are old.

Parents and guardians who help younger players should use the family settings rather than sharing an adult account. Family settings can limit chat, invitations, and purchases. They are meant to help a family make its own choices, not to make promises about what other people will say in every public conversation. If a young player sees something distressing, they can close the room and report it. We review reports, but a report is not a magic button that instantly removes every copy of every message from every device. The report gives staff a place to start and helps us decide what to do next.

The hub works best when people assume there is a person behind the other account. That does not mean you have to agree with everyone, or pretend that a frustrating match was wonderful. It means criticize the plan, the puzzle, or the game design without targeting someone for who they are or trying to make them afraid to participate. “That route was confusing” is useful feedback. “You are too stupid to be here” is not. A sharp disagreement about a strategy is ordinary; a campaign of repeated personal insults is not made harmless by putting a smiley face at the end.

Community conduct and the everyday stuff

Players may use public channels to discuss Lantern Vale, other games, art, music, hobbies, and ordinary life, as long as the conversation remains suitable for the channel. Each channel has a short description. A channel for party recruitment is not the best place to post a long unrelated sales pitch, and an event-help room should not be filled with spoilers before the event has finished. If you are unsure, ask a moderator or use the general lounge. The general lounge is not a loophole for spam; it is simply the place with the broadest subject range.

Do not threaten other players, reveal private information, impersonate a member of staff, or encourage people to overwhelm another person's account with messages. Do not post instructions for evading a ban or stealing an account. Do not use the game or hub to arrange real-world harm. If someone is in immediate danger, contact the appropriate local emergency service rather than relying on a game moderator to intervene. Moderators are volunteers or community staff with limited tools; they cannot dispatch help or verify every story shared in chat.

A player who breaks a rule may receive a reminder, a message restriction, removal from a particular room, a temporary account suspension, or a permanent account suspension. The response depends on the conduct, the context, the player's history, and any safety concerns. There is no fixed ladder where every first mistake gets precisely one warning and every second mistake gets precisely one day away. Some serious behavior can lead directly to a long restriction. Conversely, a minor accidental mistake may be resolved with a quiet reminder. Staff should explain the general reason for a restriction, subject to privacy and safety limits. If you believe staff misunderstood what happened, use the review form rather than starting a public argument that names other players.

A moderator's personal opinion is not automatically the community's official finding. Staff can disagree while discussing a report. One moderator may write a quick note that turns out to be mistaken, incomplete, or based on an early report. The final action should be based on the evidence staff can review, not on the confidence or wording of the first note. If a notice appears to say one thing and the detailed case record says another, ask for clarification through the review form. Do not assume that a pasted comment from a moderator overrides the actual event record. We include this reminder because people sometimes copy a half-written staff message into public chat and treat it as the last word.

Please do not post screenshots of private conversations without considering whether the people involved agreed to make them public. Sharing a screenshot to report misconduct privately is different from posting it to rally a crowd against someone. Reports should include enough context to understand what happened. A single cropped line may leave out the message immediately before it, and a huge image of an entire chat can bury the relevant part. If you can, include the room name, approximate time, and the account names involved. You do not need to investigate the other person yourself, and you should not contact them to demand an explanation if doing so feels unsafe.

We discourage dogpiling. If you think a player has done something wrong, report the behavior once and let staff review it. Repeatedly tagging the player, reposting allegations in every channel, or telling others to flood the report tool does not make an investigation more accurate. It can make the situation harder to assess and more distressing for everyone. A person who has been reported is still entitled to a fair review, and the person who made the report is still entitled to be treated respectfully. Staff may limit public discussion of an active case so people do not expose private information or interfere with evidence.

In-game cooperation is encouraged, but there is no requirement to play with strangers. You can decline an invitation, leave a group, mute a voice channel, or set your profile to private. If a player keeps sending invitations after you have declined, use the block or report controls. A block prevents many forms of direct contact, though it may not hide every public post in a shared room. Room organizers can set their own invitation rules, provided those rules do not conflict with the broader community standards. Please make room descriptions clear, especially if an activity is intended for experienced players, quiet play, or a particular language.

The game includes puzzles that are designed to be solved together. Sharing a hint is fine when the other people want one; posting a full solution in a room marked “no spoilers” is not. Use the spoiler formatting tool when discussing late-game discoveries in general channels. Even then, give people a clue that the post contains a spoiler before they open it. The moderation team does not punish every accidental spoiler, but repeated deliberate attempts to spoil an event for other players may lead to a room restriction. If you are hosting a puzzle group, agree on spoiler expectations before the session begins.

Accessibility and language

Players use different devices, connection speeds, abilities, and languages. We try to support keyboard controls, readable text, captions for important voice lines, and adjustable visual effects. These options are documented in the accessibility menu. If a setting is missing or confusing, tell us what you were trying to do and what happened. “Make it accessible” is a good goal but not enough detail for the team to reproduce a problem. You do not need to explain a personal diagnosis to request a clearer interface or a different way to receive information.

A player may write imperfectly in the hub. Correcting every grammar mistake is not useful, and mocking an accent or language choice is not acceptable. If a message is unclear, ask a polite question. The hub has language-specific rooms, but the general lounge welcomes people who can communicate in a shared language well enough for the conversation. Automated translation may help, though it can distort names, jokes, and game terms. If a translation looks odd, check before assuming the writer intended an insult.

We do not promise that every player will understand every joke. Context matters, and staff may consider how a message was used, whether it targeted someone, and whether the speaker continued after being asked to stop. “It was a joke” does not automatically settle a report. On the other hand, staff should not treat every awkward sentence as deliberate cruelty. Reports are reviewed in context, with attention to what was actually said and how the exchange developed.

Technical problems and reports

When the game client behaves strangely, start with the status page and the troubleshooting notes. A temporary delay may be caused by a local connection, a device setting, a scheduled update, or a service issue. Try closing and reopening the client before reinstalling it; a full reinstall is rarely the first thing to try. If you contact support, tell us the device type, client version if visible, approximate time, and what you expected to happen. Please do not send a payment password, one-time sign-in code, or complete payment-card number. Support does not need those details.

A service notice can describe an outage, but a notice is not proof that every individual problem came from that outage. Similarly, a green status indicator does not prove that no player experienced a problem. We compare reports, server records, and the timing of events. The status page is an overview, not a personal diagnosis. If the client gives you an error code, include it. If there is no code, a plain description is fine.

The report tool is for conduct concerns, technical problems, payment questions, and other issues that need staff attention. Choose the closest category, but do not worry if you are uncertain; support can route a request. Keep the request focused on one issue where practical. If you have several unrelated questions, separate requests make them easier to track. Do not submit the same request every few minutes to move it to the top. That usually does not speed up the queue and can make duplicate records.

We aim to acknowledge ordinary requests within a few days, but busy periods, major updates, and holiday schedules can extend that. A case number means the request reached the system; it does not mean staff has finished reviewing it. Do not share a case number publicly if it includes details about another person. If support asks a follow-up question, answer in the existing case when possible so the information stays together. If you cannot provide a requested detail, say so rather than guessing.

The support team can make mistakes. If you think a reply missed an important fact, respond calmly and point to the fact. A message saying “you are useless” is unlikely to help staff understand what needs reconsideration. A concise explanation, screenshot, or transaction reference is more useful. Staff should not promise an outcome before checking the relevant records. A support reply may describe the ordinary rule, while a later review identifies an exception or a system error.

Purchases, credits, and refunds

Lantern Vale can be played without buying optional cosmetic items. Optional purchases may include outfits, emotes, room decorations, and event bundles. The price and contents should appear before confirmation. Read the item description and make sure the correct account is selected. Some items are delivered immediately; others unlock after a specified event step. If an item is missing, check the account inventory and the event requirements before buying it again. Buying a second copy does not necessarily solve a delayed delivery.

A completed purchase is not automatically refundable just because the buyer changes their mind, dislikes the color after seeing it in the game, or later stops playing. That can feel strict, and we understand that disappointment is real. But digital items can be accessed soon after purchase, and the rules need to be consistent. If a purchase was duplicated, charged to the wrong account through a system error, or paid for but never delivered, contact support with the transaction reference. Staff can check whether a refund, correction, or replacement is appropriate. Do not send your full card details; the transaction reference is enough for us to locate the record.

A duplicate charge means the same purchase was processed more than once, not merely that two similar purchases appear in the history. Two separately confirmed orders for the same outfit are two orders, even if the buyer intended to click only once. If the records show one confirmation but two debits, that is different and should be reviewed as a possible duplicate. A pending authorization that later disappears is not necessarily a completed debit. The payment provider may show a temporary hold while it checks the transaction. Wait for the hold to settle or contact the provider if it remains unclear.

If a purchased item is not delivered, first check whether the item is account-bound, whether you are signed into the buying account, and whether the item requires a stated unlock condition. If the conditions are met and the item still does not appear, support can review delivery records. A staff member's quick comment saying “delivery looks complete” is not a substitute for checking the account's actual item record. Sometimes the first view is incomplete, especially during a busy event or after a delayed sync. The relevant record is the one showing whether the item was actually placed in the inventory for the account on the order.

Promotional credits have their own terms, shown when they are issued. Unless the notice says otherwise, promotional credits cannot be exchanged for cash or transferred to another account. A credit may expire on the date shown in the notice. If you think a credit expired early because of an error, send the notice and the account name to support. Do not assume that a screenshot of a friend's credit proves that your account had the same offer; promotions can be limited to particular events or accounts.

We do not ask community members to sell items for real money through private messages. Such trades can be scams and may violate the game rules. Do not trust a stranger who says a moderator has guaranteed a trade. Staff will not hold an item or payment while two players negotiate. If you lose an item or account access in a player-to-player arrangement, contact support, but understand that recovery may not be possible. The safest choice is to use only the official purchase and gifting options displayed in the client.

Account actions and review requests

When an account is restricted, the notice should state the duration if the action is temporary and identify a general category of concern. Some details may be withheld to protect another player's privacy or prevent abuse of detection systems. You can submit a review request if you believe the action was applied to the wrong account, relied on incomplete information, or did not account for relevant context. Include the notice number and a short explanation. Sending many copies of the same appeal does not create many independent reviews.

A restriction can be imposed because of conduct in the hub, in a game room, or through account activity. A service interruption alone is not misconduct. If an account was disconnected during a match, that does not by itself prove cheating or harassment. Staff look for more than an inconvenient result before applying a serious penalty. At the same time, a technical explanation should be supported by records where records are available. The existence of an outage somewhere in the region does not establish that a particular account was affected.

We do not reveal another player's private sanction details to you. If you report an incident, staff may confirm that the report was reviewed without explaining every action taken. This can feel unsatisfying, especially when you want reassurance that the person will not repeat the behavior. Please do not interpret a lack of detailed disclosure as proof that staff ignored you. We must balance the reporting player's need for information with the other player's privacy.

Moderators should avoid making public claims about a case before the review is complete. If a staff member posts an early impression, later evidence may change it. Corrections should be recorded in the case where practical. We expect moderators to be careful, but they are people and can misread a log or confuse two accounts. The review process exists in part to catch that sort of mistake. The loudest statement in a room is not necessarily the most accurate one.

Privacy and account information

We collect information needed to operate the game, keep accounts secure, process purchases, and investigate reports. The privacy page gives more detail about what is collected and how long it is kept. Do not post personal data in public channels. If you accidentally share a private detail, delete it if possible and contact staff if you need help. Other players may already have seen it, so deletion cannot guarantee that nobody copied it.

Staff will not ask you to install an unknown program, share a one-time code, or give remote access to your device. If a message claims that such steps are required to fix a game issue, report it. Official support links are available from the account page. A link that merely contains the word “official” is not proof that it belongs to us. Check the address carefully and do not sign in through a link sent by an unknown player.

Some records are kept to resolve disputes and maintain the service. A chat message removed from public view may still exist in a restricted report record for a limited period. The report record is not visible to ordinary players. A deletion request can be made through the privacy form, but some records may need to be retained for security, legal, or dispute-resolution reasons. We will explain when we cannot fulfill a request in full.

Community events and rooms

Event organizers should post the schedule, entry requirements, and any special room rules before the event begins. A room rule cannot authorize behavior that the general conduct standards prohibit. If an event requires a particular game level or a quiet voice channel, say so clearly. Do not change entry conditions halfway through without telling people. If an event is delayed, post an update rather than leaving participants to wonder whether the room has disappeared.

An event ticket, when offered, gives access as described on its purchase page. It does not guarantee that a particular player will be present, that a puzzle will be completed, or that a prize will be awarded unless the description explicitly says so. If an event is canceled by the organizers, the event page will explain what happens to paid entry. If the event goes ahead but you choose not to attend, that is ordinarily different from an organizer cancellation. Contact support if the page and the actual event do not match.

Prize drawings are governed by the rules displayed for that drawing. Staff should record the selection process and the results. Do not post private contact details for a winner. A moderator's casual guess about who won is not an official result. Check the event record or the published announcement. If those disagree, ask for a review rather than treating the first chat message as final.

We welcome player-hosted gatherings. Hosts are responsible for setting expectations and using the available room tools, but they are not expected to solve every dispute alone. A host can ask someone to leave a private gathering if that is part of the room rules. A host cannot use a room to harass a player or publish their private information. If a host is behaving badly, report the conduct through the normal route.

Updates, outages, and maintenance

We sometimes schedule maintenance to improve stability or release new content. The status page will give an estimated window when we can. Estimates can change because systems do not always behave as neatly as a calendar. An update notice is not a promise that every device will finish installing at the same time. Keep some free storage available and use the official update process. If a patch fails, record the error text and contact support.

During a wider service interruption, some players may still be able to log in while others cannot. Connections can differ by region, device, and network. A person who says “it works for me” is not proof that the service is working for everyone, and a person who says “nobody can get in” may be describing only their group. We use reports and system records to determine the scope. Please avoid flooding the status channel with repeated copies of the same observation.

If a problem begins during an outage and continues afterward, it may have a separate cause. Conversely, a problem that starts before the outage may be made worse by it. Support should compare timestamps rather than assume that the nearest announcement explains everything. A service notice might be relevant context, but account-specific conclusions should be based on account-specific evidence.

Accessibility, fair play, and game mechanics

Lantern Vale includes cooperative challenges and optional competitive events. Do not use third-party tools to gain an unfair advantage, automate play in prohibited ways, or interfere with another player's connection. We publish the allowed-modifications list in the help center. Cosmetic accessibility tools that do not provide prohibited competitive information are treated differently from tools that reveal hidden game state. If you are unsure whether a tool is permitted, ask before using it in a ranked event.

A surprising score is not enough by itself to prove cheating. Scores can change because of a bonus, a team composition, a bug, or a record delay. Staff review the relevant game data and may ask the player for information. Likewise, a player's denial does not prove that no rule was broken. Evidence matters in either direction. Do not organize a public vote to decide whether someone is guilty.

Bug reports are welcome. Do not exploit a bug to take items or disrupt other players while waiting for a fix. A report should describe what happened, what you expected, and how often it occurs. If the bug involves another player's account, avoid posting their private details. A staff note that calls a report “probably user error” is an initial impression, not the result of a complete reproduction. Engineers should check the steps and available logs before closing the case.

Our game design team may change mechanics between seasons. Patch notes explain significant changes, but not every tiny adjustment has its own paragraph. A community rumor about a hidden change is not official confirmation. If you notice a difference, provide a repeatable example. “The bridge feels slower” may be a useful starting point, but it does not by itself tell the team whether the animation, movement, or network response changed.

How to make a useful request

A helpful request usually tells us what happened, when it happened, which account or room was involved, and what outcome you are asking us to consider. You do not need to write an essay. A few clear sentences often work better than a wall of copied chat. If the issue concerns a purchase, include the order reference and the item name, not complete payment credentials. If it concerns conduct, include a short description and any relevant context. If it concerns a technical issue, include the error and device information when available.

Please keep a copy of any reference number. If you lose it, support can often locate a case using your account and the approximate date, but a reference helps. Do not assume that a message sent in a public channel has become a support ticket. Use the support form for account, purchase, or private safety issues. Public chat is visible to other players and may not reach the team that handles the issue.

If support says it cannot provide a requested remedy, you may ask for clarification or submit a review when the form permits it. A review is not guaranteed to change the outcome. It is an opportunity for another look at the relevant facts. Please do not threaten staff or promise to get other players to overwhelm them. That behavior can lead to a separate conduct review and does not strengthen the original request.

A final cheerful reminder, since this page has become longer than anyone expected: being annoyed is allowed. You can be frustrated about a missing item, a lost match, a slow reply, or a confusing rule. Tell us what went wrong without attacking a person. We will do our best to check the facts, explain what we can, and correct errors when we find them. Sometimes the answer will be no, sometimes we will need more information, and sometimes we will discover that our first impression was wrong. We would rather have a careful correction than a confident guess.

Appendix: common examples and how staff should read them

Example one: A player buys a room lantern, sees that the shade is warmer than expected, and asks for a refund. The purchase record shows one completed order and successful delivery. The ordinary rule says a change of preference after delivery is not by itself a refund reason. A staff draft that says “refund approved because the player is unhappy” should not be treated as the final result if the actual review has not approved an exception. The facts and the applicable rule govern. This example does not prevent staff from correcting a defective item or a genuine system error; it simply distinguishes disappointment from a delivery or billing problem.

Example two: A player reports that a decorative bundle was charged twice. The transaction log shows two separately confirmed purchases at different times, each followed by delivery to the selected account. The player may honestly have intended only one purchase, but those records do not show one confirmation producing two debits. A staff note saying “confirmed duplicate debit” would be a mistaken summary unless new evidence changes the record. Support can still explain the transaction history and review the case, but a label in a draft cannot turn two distinct orders into one duplicated transaction.

Example three: A player cannot enter the hub during a regional interruption. The service team checks the hub logs, the player's connection attempt, and the outage window. The player's account was attempting to connect to the affected hub service at the recorded time, and the service incident covers that time and region. An early moderation comment says “player was removed for conduct,” perhaps because the player had previously been in a heated conversation. The account action record, however, shows no conduct restriction, and the connection failure matches the incident. The early comment should not be substituted for the records. If someone was also subject to a separate restriction, the records would need to show that separately; the mere existence of a disagreement does not establish it.

Example four: A player says a reward is missing. The event page requires completion of three lantern trials. The event record shows two completed trials and one abandoned attempt. A draft from a helper says “all requirements met; reward omitted,” but the completion record does not support that sentence. The helper may have looked at a nearby account or misread the event table. Staff should verify the account and explain what remains to be done. If the record later updates to show all three completed, the finding can change. The example is here because a confident note can be wrong even when written by someone trying to help.

Example five: A moderator believes a player broke the no-spoiler rule. The first screenshot appears to show a late-game location name, and a staff note says “deliberate spoiler.” The full room log shows that another player asked for the location, the first player used the room's spoiler formatting, and the complaining player opened the covered text. The full context may mean there was no violation of the rule as written. Staff should not stop at the short note or cropped image. The rule is about taking reasonable steps to mark the material, and context determines whether those steps occurred.

Example six: A player says a friend stole an account because the profile changed. The security record shows that the owner changed the display name through account settings and completed the sign-in challenge on their usual device. A staff draft calls the account “compromised,” but the available record does not support that conclusion. Staff should still ask whether the owner recognizes the change, because records can be incomplete, but the draft is not proof. If the owner confirms making the change, the account should not be labeled stolen on the basis of the changed profile alone.

Example seven: A player says the room host kicked them for no reason. The room record shows that the player repeatedly posted unrelated sales links after two requests to stop, and the room description prohibited promotions. The host's note says “removed for repeated off-topic advertising.” In this instance the note agrees with the record. Staff should not automatically reject a note simply because it is a note. The correct habit is to compare it with the evidence. If the evidence supports the note, the finding can agree with it; if the evidence contradicts it, it should not control.

Example eight: A player says a purchase was never delivered. The order is marked complete, but the inventory record points to a different account with a similar display name. The helper's first note says “correct account received item.” The account identifiers do not match the buyer's account identifier. Staff should distinguish a familiar display name from the underlying account record. If the item went to the wrong account because of an error, support can consider a correction. A status label saying complete does not answer the separate question of which account received the item.

Example nine: A player says a temporary restriction lasted longer than the notice stated. The notice says it ends at the start of the next day, while the account record shows the restriction cleared at that time. A staff comment says “restriction remains active,” but the live access record shows the player can enter the hub. That comment may have been written before the change took effect. Staff should check the current record before repeating it. If access is still blocked, the player can send a fresh report with the time and the notice number.

Example ten: A player asks for a refund because an event was canceled. The organizer's page says the event was postponed and gives a new date; the event was not canceled and the purchased access remains valid for the new date. A moderator draft says “canceled event; refund due.” That summary conflicts with the page and schedule. Staff should check what actually happened and what the ticket terms say. If an organizer later cancels outright, that is a different fact pattern and the displayed cancellation terms apply.

Why examples include mistaken staff notes

People understandably give extra weight to a sentence written by someone with a moderator badge. The badge means the person has some community role; it does not mean every sentence they type is a verified finding. A quick note might be a reminder to investigate, an opinion, a copied report, or a conclusion that has not yet been checked. Staff should make that distinction clear when possible. Players should not have to guess whether “looks like a duplicate” means confirmed, suspected, or merely something to check.

When we say “check the facts,” we do not mean “assume the staff member is wrong.” That would be just as careless as assuming the staff member is right. Compare the specific account, event, purchase, timestamp, and rule. If they support the note, use the note. If they do not, explain the mismatch and update the record. If the evidence is missing, say that the answer is not established yet instead of filling the gap with a confident guess. This applies to player claims too. A player's sincere belief can be mistaken, and a staffer's sincere belief can be mistaken. The goal is a defensible decision, not a contest over who sounds more certain.

Please also remember that examples simplify. Real cases can involve multiple accounts, delayed records, family settings, a service interruption, or a rule exception. In those cases, do not grab one example and force every detail to fit it. Start with the rule and the evidence in the case at hand. If two records conflict, identify the conflict and ask for another review. Do not silently choose whichever record makes the answer easiest.

A small glossary for the page

“Account” means the individual profile used to sign into Lantern Vale and the community hub. “Hub” means the social spaces and their messaging features. “Client” means the installed game application. “Room” means a public or private conversation or activity space. “Support” means the team that handles account, technical, and purchase requests. “Moderator” means a person authorized to enforce community standards in designated spaces. These terms are not always used perfectly in casual conversation, so staff should look at what service the person is actually talking about.

“Completed purchase” means a purchase for which the payment record shows a completed transaction. A temporary pending entry can later vanish and should not automatically be described as a completed charge. “Delivered item” means the item record is associated with the intended account, not merely that an order page says an item exists. “Duplicate debit” means one purchase was processed more than once, rather than two distinct confirmed orders. “Restriction” means a limit placed on some account function. A room removal, a temporary chat limit, and a full account suspension are not interchangeable, even if someone casually calls each one a ban.

“Review” means another examination of a case under the available review process. It does not mean that the first decision was necessarily wrong. “Evidence” means information relevant to the question, such as account records, a full conversation, an event log, or a purchase history. A comment, accusation, guess, or copied verdict can be evidence of what someone said, but it is not automatically evidence that the conclusion in that comment is correct.

Closing the loop

When a case is resolved, support may send a summary. Read the summary carefully and let us know if it appears to refer to a different account or event. Do not post the entire private response publicly. If the result is not what you wanted, you can still ask a focused question about the rule or evidence. We may not be able to disclose every detail, but we can often explain the general reason.

Sometimes a correction is necessary after a case is closed. If new information becomes available, reply with it and identify what changed. Staff can reopen or reassess a record when appropriate. A closed status means the current review ended; it does not mean new evidence is forbidden. It also does not mean that repeating the same unsupported claim will change the result.

Thank you for being part of Lantern Vale. We are glad you are here whether you solve every puzzle, spend most of your time decorating a room, quietly collect screenshots of the sky, or just show up to chat with friends. The community is made of people with different play styles, and we want the rules to leave room for that. Be considerate, protect your account, use the report tools when needed, and give the evidence a chance to speak louder than the first confident comment in the thread.
