[{"state":"Bluefin Outfitters field service review packet — prepared for the repair coordination desk. The packet combines a customer chat transcript, internal meeting notes, and the applicable service policy page. Staff who read it should rely on the recorded exchanges and work entries, not on an earlier person’s conclusion. The writing is from several staff members; English is not the first language of all contributors.

SECTION A — CUSTOMER CHAT TRANSCRIPT

09:02, Customer Uma Kaur: Hello. I am writing about the portable chiller we bought for the pop-up stall. The serial label says BF-CH-4418. It was installed at our east counter on 12 May. I need someone to inspect the rattling and the temperature display. We can make the unit available after 16:00 today.

09:04, Service desk, Neri: Thank you. I can make a case. Please tell me if you are asking to return it or asking for repair.

09:05, Customer Uma Kaur: Repair, please. I am not asking to return it and I am not asking for money back. We need the chiller working because our chilled drinks are stored there.

09:07, Neri: Understood. I will record a repair visit. Is the unit still cooling?

09:08, Customer Uma Kaur: It cools, but the display sometimes goes blank for maybe two seconds. The rattle is louder when the compressor starts. I have moved nothing inside and the unit has not been dropped.

09:10, Neri: I see a previous note on the account saying “customer requests full refund; close as refund pending.” Is that what you want today?

09:11, Customer Uma Kaur: No. That note is not from me. I did not ask for a refund. I think a different account was mixed in, or somebody selected the wrong box. Please leave my case as repair.

09:13, Neri: I will correct the case details. Can you confirm the phone number ending 6081?

09:14, Customer Uma Kaur: Yes, that is the shop phone. The number ending 6081 is correct.

09:17, Neri: Thank you. The first available field engineer is Quentin Delgado, tomorrow between 10:00 and 12:00. Does that work?

09:18, Customer Uma Kaur: Yes. Please send Quentin. He can call the shop when he is outside, because the loading entrance is not obvious.

09:20, Neri: Visit booked. The job is inspection and repair, not collection. The old refund note will stay in the audit history but I have marked it disputed.

09:22, Customer Uma Kaur: Good. Please do not cancel the repair visit because of that old note.

09:24, Neri: Confirmed. We will keep the visit.

09:41, Automated case banner: Prior classification: REFUND REQUEST. Suggested action: issue refund and close repair case. This banner is generated from the old note and has not been checked against the customer’s current messages.

10:03, Customer Uma Kaur: One more detail: I can hear a light rattle, and the display flashed off once while I was watching it. It came back without touching anything. I still want repair, not refund.

10:05, Neri: Added to job description: intermittent display and rattle at compressor start. Repair visit remains active.

Next day, 09:48, Quentin Delgado, field engineer: I am on the way. Arrival expected in about twenty minutes.

10:12, Customer Uma Kaur: I am at the east counter. Use the service entrance on the side near the blue delivery sign.

10:31, Quentin Delgado: I have arrived and checked the model and serial. The unit is operating now. I will take readings before opening the panel.

10:36, Quentin Delgado: Supply voltage is within the range printed in the service sheet. There is a small vibration at start-up. I have not found damage to the casing.

10:42, Customer Uma Kaur: It is doing the noise now. It is not very loud but it is noticeable from the counter.

10:45, Quentin Delgado: I have reproduced a short rattle during start. The temperature display is on at this time. I will inspect its connector and sensor.

11:06, Quentin Delgado: Connector is seated. Sensor reading is stable in my test. I found a loose retaining clip on the fan guard, and I have secured it. I will run the unit again and check if the rattle comes back.

11:23, Quentin Delgado: The rattle is not present during three start cycles after securing the clip. Display has stayed on. I am recording this as a repair completed on site, with monitoring advised.

11:25, Customer Uma Kaur: Thank you. I will watch it. I did not ask you to take it away, and I am not asking for a refund.

11:29, Quentin Delgado: No collection was done. Unit remains at the east counter. Customer accepted the repair and monitoring advice.

12:02, Service desk, Neri: Case note updated to “repair visit completed; customer did not request refund.” The historical banner is still visible in the audit section, because it cannot be deleted.

12:06, Customer Uma Kaur: That is correct. Please make sure no refund is put through by mistake.

12:08, Neri: Confirmed. No refund transaction has been entered.

SECTION B — FIELD ENGINEER’S VISIT RECORD

Job reference FS-88214. Customer account: Bluefin Outfitters. Contact on site: Uma Kaur. Asset: portable chiller, model BF-CH-4418. Location described by customer: east counter, service entrance beside blue delivery sign. The job was raised as a repair appointment. There is a previous account annotation saying “full refund requested,” but the live chat records the customer denying that request and asking for repair. The annotation is retained solely for audit.

Engineer arrival and departure were logged on the service tablet. Arrival 10:31; departure 11:34. These times describe the visit duration and do not themselves establish the original request type. The engineer checked the asset identity before testing. The serial plate was legible. The unit had power and was cooling when the engineer began. The customer described an intermittent blank display and a brief rattle at compressor start. The engineer personally heard a brief rattle on a start cycle. He did not observe a persistent display failure during the visit.

The inspection checklist includes the following entries:

- Casing: no visible impact damage.
- Feet: level on counter.
- Air path: clear at inspection.
- Power connection: secure.
- Supply reading: within the service-sheet range.
- Compressor start: short vibration heard on first cycle.
- Fan-guard retaining clip: loose before adjustment.
- Display connector: seated on inspection.
- Display: illuminated during checks.
- Sensor reading: stable during the measured test.
- Repair action: retaining clip secured.
- Post-action test: three start cycles; no rattle reproduced.
- Customer response: accepted repair and monitoring advice.
- Removal from site: none.
- Refund payment: none entered by service engineer.

A supervisor’s draft summary was copied into the tablet at 10:20, before the engineer had completed the physical inspection. It reads: “Likely customer wants refund rather than repair; no technical issue confirmed. Recommend refund closure.” The engineer did not author this sentence. The tablet kept it because the supervisor had used the “draft assessment” field. Later, the same record has a second supervisor comment, added at 12:15: “I reviewed the full chat. The customer requested repair and explicitly rejected refund. The earlier draft was based on an old classification and should not be treated as the customer’s request.”

A separate automated text extraction identifies the phrase “full refund requested” in the account history and labels the case “refund intent likely.” That extraction does not distinguish the historical annotation from Uma Kaur’s current words. It also contains the following disclaimer: “This label is a search aid only; it is not verified customer intent.” The case-management interface displays the label in orange. Orange means “unreviewed system suggestion,” not “confirmed.”

The engineer’s test notes continue: After securing the fan-guard clip, he listened at the counter with the customer standing approximately one metre away. The unit completed three restarts. No rattle was heard in those cycles. The display remained illuminated for the period of observation. These observations do not prove the symptom can never recur, and the engineer did not state that it could never recur. He advised the customer to contact the desk if the rattle or blank display returned. The customer confirmed the advice was understood. There was no discussion of a price adjustment, exchange, credit, or return. The customer said the unit was needed for chilled drinks and should remain on site.

The service desk entered the completion code “repair completed.” This code does not mean that every possible defect has been ruled out; it means the engineer completed the recorded intervention and performed the specified immediate retest. A monitoring recommendation was added because the customer described intermittent behavior that was not continuously present during the test. The completion entry does not change the nature of Uma Kaur’s request.

A later audit user checked the case on the same day. The audit note says: “Do not merge with the unrelated refund case from the west counter. Different contact and asset. The east-counter customer asked for a repair. Keep original history for traceability, but current disposition is repair.” No payment record is attached to this audit note. The customer account contains no refund authorization, refund amount, or refund date for this asset.

SECTION C — COORDINATION MEETING NOTES

Meeting title: Bluefin Outfitters service follow-up and record-quality review. Date: 18 June. Attendees: service coordinator, field lead, desk supervisor, parts coordinator, and account liaison. Notes were typed by the coordinator, whose English is developing; short phrases below are preserved from the working record. The meeting covered several cases, not only FS-88214. Participants were reminded to keep different asset records separate.

Opening: The service coordinator said the purpose is to review completed jobs and see if the data in the service system is giving correct picture. They are not deciding a refund for any customer in this meeting. Any refund decision needs its own authorization and customer request. Old automated flags cannot replace the actual conversation.

Case FS-88214 was discussed after the coordinator read the customer chat, not before. The desk supervisor said the earlier draft on the tablet was wrong because it relied on an inherited note. The customer’s words at 09:05 and 09:11 were clear: repair requested; refund denied. The field lead agreed that the physical work was appropriate for the symptom that was reported. The notes show a loose retaining clip found and secured, then three cycles with no reproduced rattle. The coordinator wrote, “Do not write ‘refund asked’ in current intent field. It is old history only.” The account liaison added that the customer did not ask to remove the chiller and wanted it left at the counter.

The group checked whether the customer had been promised a replacement. The desk supervisor searched the chat and found no promise. The engineer’s note says no collection occurred. The meeting agreed that the correct present status is “repair completed; monitor.” This status is not a statement that the equipment can never fail again. It is a concise description of what happened during the visit. The group also agreed not to erase the old classification, because retaining a mistaken entry with a correction helps the audit. The correction must remain visible beside the old text.

One participant read the orange banner and said, “It recommends refund closure.” Another participant replied that it is only a system suggestion derived from an unverified old phrase, not evidence of a current request. The meeting chair instructed staff not to use the banner as a substitute for the conversation. The action item was to add an explanation to the record and make sure the next analyst sees both the customer’s denial and the correction. No one voted to issue a refund. There was no refund amount discussed. No refund transaction was authorized.

The account liaison noted a general service issue: customers sometimes use the word “return” when describing a previous delivery, not when asking to return the item now. Staff need to read the whole sentence and identify the speaker and date. In this case Uma Kaur did not say she wanted to return the chiller. She said, “I am not asking to return it and I am not asking for money back.” The liaison asked that this sentence be copied into the verified-intent field so it is not missed by a search system that only looks for the words “return” or “refund.”

The field lead described the physical work. He said the retaining clip was loose, which matched the short vibration heard at start-up. He did not call it a major mechanical breakdown. He said the display issue was reported by the customer but not reproduced during the visit; the connector was seated and the display remained on during the test. The meeting kept both facts: customer-reported intermittent blanking, and no failure observed during the engineer’s test. The team did not say the customer invented the symptom. The monitoring advice is appropriate because intermittent faults may not show during a short visit.

The coordinator asked whether the customer accepted the repair. The transcript has the customer thanking the engineer and agreeing to watch the unit. The field lead said this is acceptance of the repair and monitoring advice, not acceptance of a refund. Meeting notes were updated accordingly.

Other agenda items followed. These items are included to preserve the meeting record and must not be mixed into Uma Kaur’s case. A separate Harbor Supply account reported a delayed delivery of replacement seals. A Saltmarsh Foods site asked about cleaning a condenser. Neither account is part of FS-88214. The parts coordinator reported that the retaining clip used in Uma Kaur’s job was an existing service part from the van stock, and there was no parts charge to the customer. This does not create a credit or refund. The account liaison said no invoice adjustment is needed from the information currently in the file.

The group reviewed data quality. A batch import last month mapped some old service notes into the current “customer intent” display, although those notes had been entered as free text and were not verified requests. The system team is investigating. Until then, staff should inspect the message chronology and record whether the customer has affirmed or denied the old phrase. A previous classification is not reliable only because it appears in a colored banner. The supervisor must verify it against the source conversation.

The chair gave an example from another file: a clerk wrote “customer accepted replacement” when the customer had only accepted a replacement appointment time. That example is not about Uma Kaur, and it does not mean she asked for a replacement. The chair emphasized that a convenient summary should not overwrite precise words from the source. Each action must be attributed to the correct speaker. The engineer’s conclusion about the secured clip is not a statement about what the customer requested. The customer’s words about repair are not a technical diagnosis. Both kinds of evidence have their own place.

A draft line in the meeting agenda, written before the chat was checked, said: “Outcome: refund case completed, customer dissatisfied.” The coordinator marked that line “incorrect draft; remove from current summary, retain in edit history.” The facts reviewed in the meeting contradict the draft: the customer requested repair, the engineer performed a repair action, the customer accepted the advice, and no refund was issued. The meeting did not infer that the customer was fully satisfied in every respect; it recorded only that she thanked the engineer and agreed to monitor the unit. The customer did not make a complaint about the engineer’s conduct.

The meeting’s final action list:
1. Keep the repair visit record linked to asset BF-CH-4418.
2. Set current intent to repair, not refund.
3. Preserve the superseded draft and its correction for audit.
4. Add a note explaining that the orange banner is unverified.
5. Do not open a refund workflow without a customer request and required authorization.
6. Retain the customer’s reported intermittent display behavior in the symptom field.
7. Retain the engineer’s successful immediate retest in the work field.
8. Leave the monitoring recommendation active for the customer.
9. Do not combine this case with other Bluefin Outfitters assets or other customers’ records.
10. If the symptom returns, open a follow-up repair job using the existing case history.

At the close, the chair asked if any participant had evidence that Uma Kaur requested a refund. No participant identified such evidence. The supervisor said the old annotation was the source of the mistaken draft. The account liaison read the customer’s denial once more. The meeting ended with the current disposition recorded as repair completed, monitoring advised.

SECTION D — SERVICE POLICY PAGE, INTERNAL EXTRACT

Policy title: Field repair request and case classification. Applies to service-desk staff, field engineers, and account coordinators. The policy is written for operational recording and does not independently authorize money payments. Staff must distinguish the customer’s present request from historical notes, system suggestions, staff interpretations, and technical findings.

1. Request classification. The current request is the action the customer is asking the company to take in the conversation relevant to the case. A request for a visit to inspect or fix equipment is a repair request. A request to return equipment or receive money back is a return or refund request. If the customer clearly denies a request, staff must not classify that denied request as current intent merely because an earlier note or automated search result contains the same keywords. A customer can report a prior refund discussion without requesting a refund now. A staff member’s belief about what the customer “probably wants” is not a customer request.

2. Source order. When the source materials appear inconsistent, staff should inspect the actual dated customer communication and identify who wrote each statement. A customer’s direct current statement is primary evidence of the customer’s present intent. A service engineer’s work note is evidence of work performed and observed technical conditions. An internal draft is evidence that someone made a draft, not proof the customer said it. An automated tag is a navigation aid and may be based on incomplete matching. A later correction should be recorded without deleting the audit trail, but the correction does not make the earlier draft true.

3. Role identification. Quotes, forwarded messages, copied summaries, and account-history snippets may be written by someone other than the current customer. The phrase “refund requested” must not be attributed to a customer unless the source identifies that customer as its speaker and the chronology supports it. If the customer says “I did not ask for a refund,” the denial should be entered clearly. Staff must not turn a quotation of an incorrect prior note into a verified request.

4. Repair outcomes. A repair can be completed even when an intermittent symptom cannot be reproduced at every attempt, provided the recorded intervention and required retest are completed. Staff should describe what was observed, what action was taken, and what remains uncertain. “No fault can ever recur” is not an approved conclusion from a short test. An immediate successful retest does not imply a refund request or a replacement request. Customer acceptance of a visit time is not acceptance of a refund or exchange.

5. Money workflows. A refund is not to be issued merely because a banner recommends it or a draft summary says it. The company must have a valid request or other approved authorization, with the relevant amount and transaction details checked under the separate finance procedure. A note that no refund was entered means only that no payment transaction is recorded. It does not itself prove what the customer requested; that question must be answered from the conversation.

6. Audit corrections. If a wrong classification has already been entered, retain the historical entry where required, mark it as superseded or disputed, and state the reason. Do not leave a wrong draft as the only visible summary. SECTION C — APPLICABLE CUSTOMER FAQ EXTRACT
FAQ edition 6.2, effective 1 August 2026. The following excerpt was provided to staff and customers through the help center. It is reproduced here with its original operational labels.

Q: When should a traveler contact the Billing Queue?
A: Billing handles a request to collect or return money, a reported incorrect or duplicate transaction, a payment authorization or settlement failure, a fare or tax amount that the traveler disputes, or a request to correct an amount on an issued financial document. A receipt supplied only to identify a reservation does not, by itself, make a contact a billing matter. Staff should classify the request by the action the traveler is seeking and the facts recorded, not by attachment type or isolated words in a message.

Q: What should be routed to Travel Operations?
A: Send questions about departure locations, station entrances, boarding points, transfer arrangements, itinerary display, supplier operating instructions, and changes to non-financial travel details to Travel Operations. A traveler may attach a receipt or invoice while asking such a question. The presence of a payment document does not change the route unless the traveler also reports or requests a financial action.

Q: Does a mention of “refund” establish that a refund is requested?
A: No. Staff must read the sentence in context. A traveler may deny seeking a refund, ask what a policy would say in a hypothetical situation, quote a general help article, or refer to a refund previously discussed by somebody else. Route an actual request for money back to Billing. Do not treat a negated or merely quoted reference as a request.

Q: Does the system’s preliminary bucket decide the destination?
A: No. The bucket is a search aid. Where an intake label conflicts with the traveler’s recorded request and the operative account data, the responsible desk must use the request and data. An unverified staff annotation does not supersede a signed form, recorded customer statement, payment ledger, or supplier event log.

Q: Who may request a financial adjustment for an organization booking?
A: The traveler may ask a question, but only an authorized account contact can approve a change to the organization’s payment instruction. This authority rule concerns approval of a financial action. It does not turn a location or itinerary-display question into a billing request.

Q: Is a payment receipt sufficient evidence that a payment is disputed?
A: No. A receipt can demonstrate that a transaction occurred. To route a matter as a payment dispute, the contact must report an error or request a financial action, or the transaction records must show an unresolved payment issue. A settled transaction with no requested change is not a dispute merely because the receipt is present.

Q: What if staff disagree about the right queue?
A: Review the originating message, any correction by the traveler, the account record, and the event log. A routing annotation is a working opinion. It is not an adjudication. If the evidence shows only a travel-information task, Travel Operations owns the task even if a staff member selected a payment-related tag.

The FAQ excerpt was current on the dates of the contacts recorded in this file. No later amendment to the FAQ is recorded in the case.

SECTION D — EXECUTED BOOKING TERMS

Clause 3.1 — Booking price and settlement. The package total is recorded in the customer account at purchase. A question about an itinerary field, place name, boarding location, or display format is not a request to alter the package price. A payment adjustment requires an express request or an identified transaction error.

Clause 3.2 — Customer requests. A request is classified by its requested outcome. A request for directions, travel instructions, a supplier confirmation, or a correction to non-financial itinerary text is an operations request. A request to return funds, collect additional funds, reverse a charge, change the charged amount, or investigate a stated transaction error is a billing request.

Clause 3.3 — Documents supplied with a request. The customer may attach an invoice, receipt, confirmation, or payment notice to identify a booking or provide context. The attachment is evidence, not an independent instruction to change the account. Where the text of a request and an internal tag conflict, the text of the request and the recorded account events govern classification.

Clause 3.4 — Staff annotations. Notes, proposed classifications, draft conclusions, and automated labels are not binding amendments to this agreement. Such entries must be checked against the customer’s request and the underlying records before a task is assigned. A note may be accurate or inaccurate; its status as a note does not determine its accuracy.

Clause 3.5 — Supplier information. Departure locations and boarding arrangements may change for operational reasons. Travel Operations communicates those details. A supplier’s location notice does not change the amount paid unless a separate financial adjustment is recorded.

Clause 3.6 — No implied cancellation. Asking about a location, receipt wording, or a possible travel arrangement does not cancel a booking. Cancellation takes effect only through a recorded cancellation instruction accepted under the applicable booking process.

The profile also lists her as an authorized account contact for financial changes, so there is no need to resolve authority before classifying an actual payment request. That authority does not establish that she made one.

The account’s communication preferences are secure message and email. The customer selected “please answer in writing” on the original form. The profile includes a standing preference to receive receipts for every booking amendment. That preference explains why the receipt appears with the location amendment package. It is not a standing request for a refund or a financial review.

The customer’s earlier bookings show that she sometimes asks operations to verify station names before travel. Prior conduct is not required to interpret the current request, but it is consistent with the text. No prior payment dispute is attached to this booking. The account does not contain a general instruction that every receipt must be reviewed by Billing.

SECTION K — DOCUMENT CONTROL AND AUDIT TRAIL
The original web form is stored with its selected answers, timestamp, and unedited customer text. A PDF rendering was generated at 08:49. The rendering places the receipt thumbnail above the customer’s question, which may make the attachment appear prominent when read quickly. The underlying fields remain available and show “No” for payment change, refund, and cancellation.

The 09:13 billing tag was entered after the form was received. It is not part of the customer’s text. The audit trail records the tag author and the comment. The tag was not approved by a supervisor and did not create an account action.

The telephone note was entered at 10:17. A quality reviewer checked the recording on 20 September and confirmed that the note accurately represents the traveler’s statement. The reviewer did not alter the recording or add a financial request.

The 19 September tag was entered after the customer’s written clarification had arrived. Its comment references words in the file but does not quote an affirmative request for money. The audit trail shows no linked Billing case number. The absence of a linked case does not alone determine classification; it is consistent with the ledger and the recorded request.

Agent call summary, 18 September, 10:17: “We asked whether the charge was incorrect. Customer said no; she referred to the receipt because its location line identifies the package. She asked which entrance leads to the east coach bay.”

Customer secure reply, 19 September, 07:51: “The payment FAQ may be useful to someone who needs a refund, but that is not my situation. I have not asked for one. Please tell me where to board and make the itinerary show the current location.”

Customer follow-up, 20 September, 14:31: “Thank you for confirming the east bay. The online itinerary still shows the old label. Please update that location note. I do not need a new invoice, and the existing payment is correct.”

Operations response, 20 September, 16:02: “Your existing reservation remains valid. The current boarding point is Quay Interchange east coach bay. We have queued a refresh of the itinerary display.”

There is no message from the customer withdrawing a payment dispute, because no payment dispute was submitted. There is also no affirmative request by the customer to issue funds, alter a charge, investigate a transaction, or change the total.

SECTION M — PRELIMINARY AUTOMATION EXPLANATION
The form classifier was configured to flag a record when any of three terms—“refund,” “charge,” or “receipt”—appeared in the free-text area. The configuration did not distinguish between affirmative and denied requests. The flag was designed to prompt human review and was not designed to route a completed payment task automatically.

The classifier’s saved explanation says “possible billing-related language detected.” It does not say a transaction was found. The first clerk’s comment converted that possibility into “likely refund” without citing a request. The second clerk’s comment likewise relies on terms, not on the meaning of the complete message. The customer’s repeated clarification and the account records are available to reviewers.

The automation owner states that the detector was not trained to decide whether a customer actually wants money back. A positive keyword result should therefore be treated as a retrieval hint. The detector has no access to the payment processor’s authorization state, and it cannot create a refund. In this record, the actual ledger supplies that additional information and shows a completed, unchanged settlement.

SECTION N — INTERNAL REVIEW CHECKLIST
1. Identify the action requested by the customer, rather than the document attached. The first request asks for an entrance and confirmation of a location label.
2. Check whether the customer requests a financial action or reports a payment error. The form fields and later messages say no; no amount is disputed.
3. Review the operative financial record. It shows one completed payment and no open payment task.
4. Review the applicable route definition. Location instructions and itinerary display are assigned to Travel Operations; a receipt used for identification does not alter that rule.
5. Treat preliminary labels and opinions as claims to verify. The two staff tags are not substantiated by a customer request or transaction event.
6. Assign the unresolved task according to its substance. The open task concerns a location note refresh.

The checklist is procedural. It does not create additional facts or a separate customer request.

SECTION O — BOOKING DISPLAY DATA
Customer-facing itinerary version 1, generated 12 August: “Central Hall, Old Quay Terminal.” The fare and taxes are displayed in separate fields and sum to the booked total of 684.00 BU. The system marks the payment status as “paid.”

Customer-facing itinerary version 3, generated 8 September: the station label changed to “Quay Interchange,” but an older map thumbnail remained cached. The fare fields and payment status were unchanged. The supplier bulletin explains the difference between the new location label and the old entrance sign.

At the time of the customer’s first contact, the itinerary’s text and cached map could reasonably prompt a location question. Neither field indicates an incorrect price. The requested resolution is a correct display and clear boarding direction.

SECTION P — SUPERVISORY OBSERVATION
A supervisor reviewed the disagreement on 21 September. The supervisor recorded: “Given the two tags, send to Billing; receipt plus refund language is enough to establish a billing matter.” The observation is labeled “proposed decision,” not “verified finding.” No source is cited for the assertion that the traveler requested money or alleged an incorrect amount. The supervisor did not review the ledger before entering the observation.

A later quality check compared the observation with the form, call recording, subsequent messages, and ledger. The quality check did not erase the proposed decision. It added this note: “Confirm the route against the customer’s actual requested outcome and account events; the preliminary conclusion may not be supported.” The audit file retains both comments to show how the case was handled.

The two comments conflict in their level of certainty. Neither changes the actual request or payment record. The routing decision should be based on those underlying facts and the written service definitions.

SECTION Q — HANDOFF STATUS
Current case owner: Intake Review Unit.
Unresolved work item: refresh itinerary location note and retain the east-bay directions in the customer-facing itinerary.
Completed work: traveler advised of the east coach bay; current reservation status confirmed.
Financial work item: none recorded.
Payment account status: settled, balance due 0.00 BU.
Refund status: none requested, none authorized, none processed.
Cancellation status: active reservation; no cancellation instruction.
Supplier status: travel manifest active.

The handoff system requires the receiving queue to accept ownership of the actual open work item. It does not require the receiving queue to adopt prior annotations. The desk may preserve the annotations for audit purposes while assigning the location-display task to the responsible operational team.

SECTION R — POLICY CROSS-REFERENCE
The FAQ describes routing by requested action. Clause 3.2 of the accepted terms uses the same distinction. The supplier bulletins identify entrance and boarding-point questions as operational. The ledger identifies no financial anomaly. These sources are consistent with one another on the classification criteria.

The preliminary billing tags are also part of the file, but they describe staff interpretation rather than an independent event. One tag is based on receipt and refund words; the other repeats those terms. Neither identifies a disputed amount or an affirmative request. The customer’s repeated statements are explicit and concern the location and display.

If a future message were to report that the 684.00 BU settlement was duplicated or incorrect, that later message could create a separate billing task. No such message is included in this file. A possible future financial contact is not the present task.

SECTION S — RESOLUTION RECORD
At 16:20 on 21 September, Travel Operations accepted the display-refresh item. The acceptance event reads: “Route accepted — location information and itinerary presentation.” The event does not contain a payment instruction. The system retained the two billing tags as historical metadata and marked them “not validated.”

At 16:24, an automated reconciliation again confirmed one settlement of 684.00 BU and zero outstanding balance. The reconciliation did not determine the route by itself; it confirmed that no open payment issue was present in the account data at that time.

At 16:31, the customer was sent a written confirmation that the current boarding location is Quay Interchange east coach bay and that the itinerary display refresh is pending. The message did not mention a refund because the traveler had not requested one. The customer’s latest recorded preference is written confirmation.

SECTION T — CLOSING ADMINISTRATIVE NOTE
This file is intentionally preserved with contradictory staff annotations so that reviewers can distinguish a proposed routing verdict from the underlying evidence. The existence of a confident note, a repeated tag, or an automated suggestion does not make it correct. Conversely, an annotation should not be rejected merely because it is an annotation; it should be checked against the recorded request, applicable definitions, and account events.

For this booking, the records specify a settled payment, no reported amount error, no request for money, an active reservation, and an outstanding location-display task. The traveler’s text consistently seeks travel information and itinerary correction. The financial-looking words occur in a denied request, an attached receipt, and staff commentary. The supplier’s location change explains why the traveler asked for help, while the accepted terms and FAQ explain which operational team handles that help.

- tier: hard
- write 5 sources, 2-4 questions each
- state length: about 1946 words each (a long thread, a multi-section document, a log dump or a report with appendices); every state within ±30% of that
- instruction length: medium (10-25 words)
- domain: contracts and legal notices
- genres to spread across the sources: support ticket with internal comments, meeting notes, SMS exchange
- tone: angry
- instruction style for this batch: questions that first define the term ('A refund request means the sender explicitly asks for money back. Is there one here?')
- candidate-description style for this batch: descriptions phrased from the sender's point of view ('I want my money back')
- names you may use (never reuse a name across sources): Farid Lindqvist, Chiara Fischer, Callum Haddad, Wanjiru Tanaka, Beatriz Haddad, Amara Castillo; companies: Meridian Outfitters, Bluefin Analytics, Kestrel Logistics, Foxglove Labs
- focus traps: planted_verdict. Every question in this batch uses this trap (others may occur naturally).
- multiclass: when a question offers a 'none of the above' candidate, make it the correct answer in about 1 of 10 such questions across the batch; otherwise a substantive option applies even if the text phrases it loosely
- multilabel: at least one question in the batch has 3-5 correct candidates

The operative question is what the parties agreed about termination and renewal, not what any participant wished the agreement had said.

The master services agreement was signed 11 February by Bluefin Analytics and Juniper Array. Section 8.2 provides for automatic renewal for successive twelve-month periods unless either party gives written notice of non-renewal at least 60 calendar days before the current term ends. The current term ends 31 October. Section 8.4 separately allows termination for material breach after written notice and a 30-day opportunity to cure. No breach notice or cure period is at issue in this meeting. The notice section specifies email to the named contract contacts, with receipt acknowledged by an automated delivery record; a sales chat message is not listed as a valid notice method.

Eleni displayed the contract portal export. Juniper’s named contract contact, Niko Vale, emailed the non-renewal notice on 3 September at 10:06. The message says, “We will not renew after the current term. Please confirm the wind-down steps.” The portal’s automated record shows delivery to Bluefin’s named legal contact at 10:06 the same day. Counting backward from the stated 31 October end date, 60 calendar days before that date is 1 September. The email arrived two days after that deadline. For clarity, no business-day adjustment appears in Section 8.2; the clause says calendar days. The notice was unambiguous as to intent and sent by the prescribed method, but timing is a separate requirement.

Tomas interrupted: “The customer gave notice on time. I remember them saying it in July.” Eleni searched the meeting archive and found a 19 July sales-chat message from Niko: “We may decide not to renew; I need approval from our board.” The same chat includes Niko’s next line: “This is not formal notice, just a heads-up while we review budgets.” The chat did not go to the named legal contact, and Section 8.2 requires written notice through the specified channel. Tomas conceded that the chat was not the email notice but argued that it should count because the team had seen it.

Wanjiru asked whether the July note or later communications changed the signed clause. Eleni found no signed amendment and no written waiver. A 25 July sales email from Tomas says, “Thanks for the heads-up; no action needed until you know.” It does not say Bluefin waives the 60-day period. The contract’s entire-agreement clause says amendments and waivers must be in a writing signed by both parties. The group noted that a casual reply might be relevant to a separate dispute, but the meeting had no basis to treat it as a signed amendment.

Export prepared 6 November for a contract dispute between Kestrel Logistics and Cedar Quay Imports. The thread participants are Callum Haddad, Cedar Quay’s operations manager, and Beatriz Haddad, Kestrel’s contract-notice coordinator. Messages are reproduced in chronological order from the business phones. The participants are not related; their shared surname appears in the account directory exactly as typed. The contract file is appended in plain language because both sides have been accusing each other of changing the rules after the shipment failed.

Contract cover sheet: Cedar Quay and Kestrel signed a two-month storage and handling agreement on 1 September. Clause 6 says Cedar Quay may terminate for a missed temperature-control obligation only if it sends a written breach notice to Kestrel’s designated notice address and allows five calendar days to cure. If the breach remains uncured at the end of that period, Cedar Quay may terminate immediately by a second written notice. Clause 11 says operational SMS messages are not formal notices, even if a manager reads them. The designated notice address is notices@kestrel.example. The agreement does not require Cedar Quay to request a refund as a condition of termination; payment consequences are governed by the final invoice clause.

The temperature clause requires the storage room to remain between 2 and 8 degrees Celsius. If a logged excursion lasts more than 45 continuous minutes, Kestrel must notify Cedar Quay and move the affected goods to the backup bay. The device records one-minute samples. A brief excursion lasting 45 minutes or less does not trigger the contractual breach procedure, though it must still be recorded. The parties inserted this threshold after earlier disagreement about sensor noise. The signed schedule lists the threshold and backup-bay process; no later amendment is in the file.

SMS, 12 October:

Callum, 07:16: “The dashboard says bay 4 hit 9.2 overnight. This is unacceptable. Are you moving the crates?”

Beatriz, 07:22: “I’m checking the sensor export. Don’t call it a breach before we see the duration. The alert is an initial flag, not a finding.”

Callum, 07:39: “You always have an excuse. We have expensive samples in there.”

Beatriz, 08:04: “Export says 9.2 from 02:14 through 02:48, then back under 8. That is 34 minutes. No continuous excursion over 45. I asked the floor lead to inspect the bay anyway.”

Callum, 08:10: “So you admit the temperature was out of range.”

Beatriz, 08:13: “Yes, it was out of range for 34 minutes; I am not saying the threshold was exceeded.”

Sensor file cross-check: samples from 02:14 to 02:48 inclusive show values above 8; the first normal reading is timestamped 02:49. The device’s continuous-interval report defines duration as elapsed time from the first high sample to the first normal sample: 35 minutes. Even using the more generous count of 35, the episode remains below 45. A separate sensor in bay 2 recorded 52 minutes at 8.4 degrees on 4 October, but the affected inventory belonged to another Kestrel customer. The bay-2 line is included in the export because the dashboard groups the whole facility by date. Cedar Quay’s pallets were in bay 4, not bay 2.

SMS, 13 October:

Callum, 09:01: “I’m sending formal notice right now. You failed the temperature term. Fix it within five days or we terminate.”

Beatriz, 09:09: “This text is not the notice address in clause 6. Please email notices@kestrel.example if you mean to invoke the cure process.”

Callum, 09:14: “You have read it. Stop pretending the contract lets you ignore it.”

Beatriz, 09:19: “I have read your text. Clause 11 says SMS is not formal notice. I have not received an email notice.”

The mail gateway log shows no message from Cedar Quay to the designated address between 1 and 20 October. Callum sent an email on 14 October to his own team, copying Beatriz by mistake, with the subject “Possible exit if they don’t fix this.” The body says, “I may send formal notice after legal looks at the sensor data.” It is not addressed to Kestrel’s notice address and expressly describes a possible future action. Beatriz replied only to correct the recipient mistake and did not treat the message as a formal notice.

The full refund number also ignores the clause limiting any refund to unused prepaid fees after an effective termination. The calendar and payment ledger show that services were provided for nine months before the disputed visit. No one in the meeting adopted Neris’s conclusion as a decision.

Mail gateway search: no message from Foxglove to legalnotices@ashdown.example describing a failure or invoking a cure period appears between 1 April and 10 January. The legal question is whether the signed conditions for the contractual refund were met, not whether the parties might negotiate a different outcome.

Pavel displayed the exception in Section 4.2. Neris argued that a visit five days after 27 December was automatically a breach. Sela noted that the clause allows up to five calendar days of delay where customer unavailability caused it. The calendar records Foxglove’s lab closure on 23 December and its rejection of the 24 December slot. The report does not prove the closure caused every day of the delay, but it does show a customer-side availability issue relevant to the exception. In any event, the later contractual refund condition still requires formal notice, a cure period, and effective termination. The participants agreed not to call the visit “automatically excused” or “automatically a breach” without evidence about causation.

Ledger appendix: $18,000 paid 1 April; monthly value under the finance allocation is $1,500; the service year contains 12 months. The ledger marks nine monthly allocations as consumed by 31 December. The remaining three allocations total $4,500. This arithmetic is included because Neris’s tracker requests the entire $18,000. It does not establish that $4,500 is payable: Section 9.3 makes any proportional refund conditional on an effective termination under Section 9.1. No amount is currently authorized for return. No one disputes that she wants to exit; the dispute is whether that intent became an effective contractual termination.

Neris’s tracker entry is retained to document how the dispute arose, not to establish its conclusion. [{"state":"Larkspur Labs / Harbor Logistics — claim file working packet

Compiled from the claims workbook, the current policy wording and amendment log, and the email chain. This packet is chatty because everyone kept adding context, and it is intentionally not a polished coverage opinion. The facts, not the comments column or anyone’s confident summary, are what the reviewer is meant to use. Dates in the workbook are local dates as entered by the claim team. Dollar amounts are USD unless a row says otherwise. “Customer” in this packet means the insured making the claim, Larkspur Labs; Harbor Logistics is the carrier whose warehouse accident is alleged to have caused the loss.

Workbook paste, tab “Claim intake and timeline”:

Row 1 | File ref | Insured | Alleged responsible party | Incident | Claim opened | Intake note
Row 2 | LL-4817 | Larkspur Labs | Harbor Logistics | pallet rack collapse at Harbor’s storage site | 14 May | Bao Petrov says some diagnostic kits were crushed and a temperature-controlled cabinet stopped working after the impact.
Row 3 | Related policy | Policy period | Limit | Deductible | Endorsement note
Row 4 | PL-9926 | 1 Jan–31 Dec | $80,000 per occurrence | $2,000 | Amendment 2 governs notice and repair authorization; see clause excerpt below.
Row 5 | Initial reserve | Proposed amount | Source | Status
Row 6 | reserve only | $12,400 | intake estimate from Bao | not an admission or approved payment
Row 7 | Customer contact | Channel | Date | Exact gist | Logged by
Row 8 | Bao Petrov | phone | 14 May | “I’m reporting the damage and asking what forms you need. We haven’t decided what to replace yet.” | Nadia Sorensen
Row 9 | Bao Petrov | portal | 16 May | “Please send a technician to inspect the cabinet. We’re not asking for reimbursement at this stage.” | auto-import
Row 10 | Bao Petrov | email | 22 May | “Could you tell us whether our business-interruption cover applies? This is a coverage question, not a request for a check.” | Quentin Iyer
Row 11 | Bao Petrov | portal | 2 June | “We now want $6,800 back for the cabinet repair already completed, and we’ll submit the kit inventory separately.” | auto-import
Row 12 | Bao Petrov | email | 3 June | “For clarity, the $6,800 is the amount we are seeking as reimbursement for the cabinet repair. The kits are a separate part of the claim.” | Nadia Sorensen
Row 13 | Harbor Logistics | email | 4 June | “We accept that our forklift struck the rack, but we dispute the claimed value of the kits.” | Quentin Iyer
Row 14 | Reviewer annotation | entered 4 June | text | “No refund requested: customer only asked about cover and an inspection.” | unknown clerk; verify against dated customer messages

Row 14 is an annotation, not a customer communication. It appears to summarize only the early contacts; it was not updated after the 2 June and 3 June messages. A note in the workbook says the first intake reviewer was working from a printout made on 23 May, before the later requests arrived. Another clerk copied the “No refund requested” line into a reserve comment, and the line was then repeated in a handover email. The repeated wording does not make it a new customer statement. The intake team uses “refund” loosely to mean a return of money, including an insurance reimbursement, although the policy’s payment section uses “indemnity.” The customer’s wording is therefore relevant even though the customer did not use the word refund in the 2 June portal entry.

Workbook paste, tab “Items and valuation”:

Line A | cabinet repair | invoice amount $6,800 | invoice date 29 May | paid by insured 30 May | repair shop Copperleaf Dental Service Unit | supporting receipt uploaded 2 June | claimed by insured 2 June
Line B | diagnostic kits, 14 sealed cartons | invoiced value $4,200 | inventory count dated 17 May | estimated salvage $300 | claim amount requested 3 June: $3,900 net of salvage
Line C | sample labels and outer cartons | $460 | included in original $4,200 invoice | not separately claimed
Line D | business interruption | preliminary estimate $1,700 | no final calculation submitted | coverage inquiry only on 22 May

A reconciliation note says Line B’s net amount is $3,900 because $4,200 minus $300 salvage equals $3,900. One earlier worksheet mistakenly recorded $4,000, apparently subtracting only $200. A supervisor crossed out the mistaken amount and wrote “use claimant’s supported net figure pending review.” The $460 labels are already part of the $4,200 kit invoice and should not be added a second time. A separate reserve worksheet adds $6,800 and $3,900 to reach $10,700 in requested property payments, before deductible and coverage review. That is not the same as an approved payment, and the $1,700 business-interruption figure is not included in the request total because it was described as preliminary and no final amount was submitted.

Workbook paste, tab “Tasks and calls”:

14 May, 10:10 — create file, request photographs, do not promise coverage.
14 May, 12:40 — customer asks which form to use; staff sends loss schedule.
16 May, 09:05 — arrange inspection; no payment request recorded then.
18 May, 15:22 — Harbor admits forklift contact with rack; no admission about amount or policy response.
22 May, 11:36 — answer coverage question; ask for invoices and downtime records if customer later claims interruption.
29 May, 16:00 — cabinet repair invoice received by insured.
30 May, 08:45 — insured pays repair shop; receipt later uploaded.
2 June, 14:18 — portal entry asks for $6,800 reimbursement for completed cabinet repair.
3 June, 09:15 — email confirms cabinet request and adds a separate kit inventory request.
4 June, 13:50 — reviewer writes “No refund requested”; note flagged for date check.
5 June, 10:04 — claims lead says to assess evidence, not rely on copied reviewer text.

The workbook has a few operational comments that are easy to overread. “No payment set up” is a workflow status, not a statement that the customer never requested money. “No cheque issued” is also a payment status. “Not a refund” appears in one internal note where the author meant that this is an insurance indemnity rather than a retail-store refund. Nothing in those internal labels withdraws the customer’s request. In the portal export, the 2 June entry remains active and was not marked as a draft or deleted. The 3 June email was sent from Bao Petrov’s verified Larkspur Labs address and the adjuster replied to it the same day.

Policy wording, excerpted for file review:

Section 1 — Insuring agreement. Subject to the limits, exclusions, conditions and endorsements, the insurer will indemnify the insured for covered direct physical loss to scheduled business property caused by an accidental event during the policy period. Indemnity is subject to proof of ownership or financial interest, reasonable valuation, salvage credit, and the deductible. A reserve, acknowledgment of receipt, inspection arrangement, or request for more documents does not establish that a loss is covered and does not constitute acceptance of liability.

Section 2 — Occurrence and deductible. One deductible applies to direct physical loss arising from one event or a series of related events attributable to one cause. The deductible is $2,000. Where separate categories of property are damaged by the same rack collapse, the categories are assessed together for purposes of the occurrence deductible unless an applicable endorsement expressly says otherwise. The policy limit is $80,000 per occurrence. The amount of the limit does not mean that every claim below that amount is payable; coverage and substantiation still have to be established.

Section 3 — Notice. The insured must notify the claims administrator as soon as reasonably practicable after discovering physical damage. Notice of an incident may be given before the insured knows the final amount. A preliminary notice or a request for instructions is not, by itself, a demand for indemnity. Conversely, a later communication that identifies an amount sought for a covered loss may constitute a demand even if the first notice did not request payment.

Section 4 — Mitigation. The insured must take reasonable steps to prevent further covered damage, so long as those steps are safe and proportionate. This condition does not require the insured to leave property unrepaired while waiting for the insurer where delay would cause avoidable damage or materially disrupt essential operations. The insurer may ask for inspection before non-emergency work where practicable. An insured’s decision to obtain an inspection is not a waiver of any later claim for reasonable repair cost.

Section 5 — Proof and payment. The insured must provide records reasonably requested to evaluate the loss. Payment is not due merely because a claim has been opened, a reserve entered, or a third party has admitted a physical act. Any payment is calculated after applying the deductible and any applicable coverage restrictions. The insurer may dispute an amount while still acknowledging receipt of a demand. A communication seeking reimbursement for a completed repair is a request for indemnity even if it uses “reimbursement,” “repayment,” or another ordinary-language term instead of “claim payment.”

Section 6 — Exclusions. This policy does not cover ordinary wear, unexplained deterioration, or loss of use without covered direct physical damage, except to the limited extent an endorsement specifically provides. Contamination is excluded only when the claimed damage is solely due to contamination and not when it results from a covered physical impact. The insured must establish the factual cause of the claimed damage. A supplier’s invoice is evidence of value but is not by itself proof that each invoiced item was physically damaged.

Section 7 — Records and communications. Claim communications may be oral, written, or submitted through the portal. A specific request for an amount as reimbursement or indemnity is to be recorded as a demand whether or not an internal reviewer uses the same label. Internal summaries are aids to handling and do not replace the underlying customer communication. If a summary conflicts with a dated source record, staff should check the source record and correct the summary. No employee may alter the policy wording by entering an informal comment in a spreadsheet.

Amendment log:

Amendment 1, effective 1 January — no change to the per-occurrence limit or deductible; revised contact address only.

Amendment 2, effective 1 April — adds the following condition: “For emergency repair work undertaken to prevent further damage, the insured should notify the administrator before work begins where reasonably practicable. If advance notice is not reasonably practicable, the insured must notify the administrator promptly afterward and preserve invoices, photographs, and replaced components when feasible. Failure to obtain prior written approval does not automatically defeat an otherwise covered emergency repair, but the insurer may review whether the work and cost were reasonable.” The amendment does not say that notice of an incident must include a final amount. It does not change the meaning of a demand under Section 5.

Amendment 3, proposed 10 May but never signed — draft language about a separate $1,000 deductible for temperature-control equipment. The policy system marks the draft “not bound.” It is included in the file because someone printed it during the initial coverage review, but it has no effect. A claim note says “cabinet deductible possibly $1,000”; the author later wrote “draft amendment only; disregard unless executed.”

Contract administration comments, attached to the excerpt:

The scheduled property list includes the temperature-controlled cabinet and the diagnostic kits. It does not list the removable labels as a separate category. The cabinet was purchased by Larkspur Labs and remains its property. The kits were purchased by Larkspur Labs for resale and were stored at Harbor Logistics under a warehouse agreement. Harbor’s acknowledgment of the forklift strike supports the occurrence narrative but does not prove that every kit carton was crushed or establish the exact payable amount. The photographs show fourteen cartons with visible compression on several corners; the inventory does not state that every inner kit was unusable. The claims examiner asked for a salvage estimate and received the $300 figure. No final decision on kit valuation is recorded.

Email thread, with quoted replies retained:

From: Bao Petrov, Larkspur Labs
To: Nadia Sorensen, claims administrator
Date: 14 May, 10:10
Subject: Harbor rack incident — what should we send?

Hi Nadia, we had a messy morning at the Harbor site. A forklift clipped the rack and several boxes came down onto the cabinet. The cabinet alarm went off afterward. We are opening a claim and need to know which photos and forms you want. I don’t have a reliable total yet, and I’m not asking you to pay anything today. We’re trying to keep the samples safe and work out what is damaged. Harbor’s supervisor says they’ll cooperate, though their first written note just says “contact with rack” and doesn’t mention the boxes.

From: Nadia Sorensen
To: Bao Petrov
Date: 14 May, 12:40
Subject: Re: Harbor rack incident — what should we send?

Thanks, Bao. Please upload photographs, an inventory, and any repair estimate. This is an acknowledgment that the file is open, not an agreement that the policy covers the loss. If a repair is urgent, tell us what you plan to do and why; the current wording asks for advance notice where reasonably practicable. We can arrange an inspection. I have not set up a payment and cannot tell you a final amount until the evidence is reviewed.

From: Bao Petrov
To: Nadia Sorensen
Date: 16 May, 09:05
Subject: Re: Harbor rack incident — inspection

An inspection would be useful, thanks. To avoid misunderstanding, we are not asking for reimbursement right now. The cabinet technician can come next week.
