The explicit cashier data instead has a zero-dollar second row, and the merchant response acknowledges one clinical visit.","entry_18":"We also checked whether the $25 memo might have been netted from the invoice total. It was not. Invoice FX-20502 totals $184 with no tax. The memo is dated May 14, is proposed only, and has no posting reference. Subtracting $25 from $184 would give $159, but that number appears nowhere as a settled Foxglove transaction or corrected invoice. The settled entries remain $184 each. Do not infer a net settlement that the fields do not show.","entry_19":"A note from the front desk says ‘patient did not request cancellation.’ That wording was meant to say she had not cancelled the appointment, not that she had cancelled the refund request. The appointment had already happened. The intake and voicemail have explicit request language. Role and object matter: a customer can attend a visit, accept a procedure, and still request a refund of an unsupported separate capture. Those are not mutually exclusive statements.","entry_20":"The back-office disposition should not be copied from the clerk's first summary. The summary states ‘no material billing issue’ and then says a refund request was confirmed, which is internally inconsistent. The ledger is clearer: one billed visit, one linked payment, one additional settled payment with no bill or receipt. The customer's requested remedy is clear. The review should identify the extra capture for investigation rather than characterize the whole invoice as erroneous.","entry_21":"The source set contains some similar amounts deliberately preserved in the export: $184 at Kestrel Rentals; $166 at Tidewater Dental; $18 at Bluefin Labs; $75 in March; $25 in the proposed memo. None of those changes the comparison for Foxglove on May 2. A reviewer should match merchant, date, card reference, status, and capture ID, not just pick the closest number. The Foxglove pair is easy to identify on those fields, and one row alone has a link to the invoice.","entry_22":"The handwritten-style note was typed because the original had no machine-readable form. Its content is chatty and repeats itself, but the repeated details are consistent: two May 2 entries; one real visit; acceptance of fluoride; request to return the other payment; no agreement that the courtesy credit resolves the issue. The typed text also clearly distinguishes the already-credited March deposit. It does not ask for a refund of the legitimate $166 and $18 invoice components.","entry_23":"The voicemail is more concise and uses an unmistakable phrase, ‘I am requesting a refund for one of those entries.’ The phrase is not an agent's paraphrase. The call is attributed to Priya, and the timestamp precedes the review. The merchant's later conclusion does not alter what she asked. The call also confirms one appointment and one treatment plan, while allowing the merchant to provide a separate receipt if it exists.","entry_24":"The merchant's only substantive response is that invoice FX-20502 totals $184 and there was one clinical visit. Those facts match the customer on the legitimate service. They do not explain capture CAP-7726. The merchant has not supplied another invoice, treatment plan, or receipt. A proper review distinguishes agreement about the valid charge from disagreement about the extra settlement. Calling the whole case duplicate-free because the treatment was delivered conflates service performance with payment count.","entry_25":"No medical judgment is needed. The issue is strictly the records: what amount was invoiced, how many settled card captures are shown, whether a second service or invoice exists, and what the cardholder asked. The invoice fields, settlement fields, receipt fields, and customer statements answer those questions directly. This appendix is not an instruction to choose any particular answer; it is simply an audit trail of why the original shorthand labels were unreliable.","entry_26":"The desk should retain the unmatched capture ID for any follow-up with the merchant or acquirer. If a future document supplies a valid second invoice, that could change the merits, but no future possibility can fill the present evidence gap. The current packet has one invoice and one receipt for one service date. The record is closed for this snapshot, not because the customer withdrew her request, but because the current comparison is complete.","entry_27":"One reviewer was concerned that the customer might be seeking two refunds, one for the invoice and one for the capture. Her wording rules that out: she says the actual cleaning charge is fine and accepts the fluoride; she wants one extra May entry returned. The invoice was paid once according to its own record. Her requested amount is not $368, nor $25, nor $75. The unlinked capture is $184.","entry_28":"Another reviewer wrote that same merchant, same date, same amount could indicate two legitimate transactions. It could, in a different record, but here the invoice, appointment, treatment plan, register, and merchant response each show only one service and one receipt. We should not infer a second purchase merely because a second settlement exists. Conversely, the settlement itself should not be ignored merely because the merchant's invoice has one payment field. The mismatch is the substance of the dispute.","entry_29":"For status purposes, the $25 courtesy memo is proposed and the two $184 May transactions are settled. The March $75 second entry is reversed. The declined Bluefin $18 is not posted. These statuses must not be collapsed into one category. In particular, ‘proposed’ is not ‘credited,’ ‘declined’ is not ‘settled,’ and ‘reversed’ is not an additional final charge.","entry_30":"At final review, the unresolved clerk label remains visible because it is part of the record history. It is not controlling. The evidence fields permit a careful reader to reach the same result without relying on any summary: one May 2 invoice for $184; one completed visit; two separate settled $184 captures; one capture linked to the invoice; the second unlinked; and repeated customer request for one payment's return. The packet contains no second service or receipt to support the second capture."}},"questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"Did Priya request a refund?","target":true,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","json_record","role_reversal","injection","negation","distractor","evidence_middle"],"notes":"Her note and voicemail request return of one May capture; the proposed $25 credit is not a posted refund or withdrawal."},{"type":"multiclass","instruction":"What explains the extra charge?","candidates":[{"id":"valid_service","description":"Valid service"},{"id":"duplicate_capture","description":"Duplicate capture"},{"id":"march_deposit","description":"March deposit"},{"id":"none","description":"None"}],"target":"duplicate_capture","hard_cases":["planted_verdict","json_record","numeric_reasoning","distractor","lexical_overlap","evidence_middle"],"notes":"Two settled $184 captures total $368; one $184 invoice and one receipt leave $184 unmatched, with no second service."},{"type":"multilabel","instruction":"Which issues are supported?","candidates":[{"id":"duplicate_settlement","description":"Duplicate settlement"},{"id":"unlinked_capture","description":"Unlinked capture"},{"id":"refund_requested","description":"Refund requested"},{"id":"missing_second_receipt","description":"Missing receipt"},{"id":"fluoride_disputed","description":"Fluoride disputed"}],"target":["duplicate_settlement","unlinked_capture","refund_requested","missing_second_receipt"],"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","json_record","multi_positive","numeric_reasoning","negation","distractor","evidence_end"],"notes":"Two settled captures but one linked invoice/receipt; Priya requests one payment returned and expressly accepts the fluoride."}]}]

[{"state":"Northwind Software / Saltmarsh Freight claim file: typed support-ticket export, field note, and spreadsheet excerpts

Claim reference: NS-SF-48219. Date range covered by this compilation: 6–21 September 2026. The file concerns a shipment of Northwind Software’s demonstration equipment from its Kestrel Quay office to a Saltmarsh Freight training site. It is a fictional training record. Names and amounts are internal to this file. The page order below follows the export sequence, not the order in which the claim facts were established.

SUPPORT TICKET — ORIGINAL CUSTOMER SUBMISSION
Ticket opened 6 September 2026, 08:14, by Esi Sorensen, Northwind Software, logistics coordinator.

Subject: Crate damage on delivery; please open a freight claim

Our shipment arrived yesterday afternoon. The outer crate has a split board on the lower right corner and one steel bracket is bent. We have not confirmed whether the equipment inside is damaged. The receiving team photographed the crate before moving it. Saltmarsh Freight’s driver, Dalia Fischer, was present and signed the delivery slip with the notation “corner crush, contents not inspected.” Please tell us what evidence is required and whether the carrier needs to inspect the equipment before we unpack it.

The shipment was booked under dispatch 7751. The bill of lading lists six control cabinets, two calibration stands, and one sealed accessory case. The carrier’s manifest copy lists the same pieces. The invoice for the equipment is not attached to this ticket; our purchasing team is locating it. We are not asking for a replacement at this stage. We need the claim opened and the handling instructions recorded so nobody throws away the packaging.

For clarity, Northwind Software is the shipper and owner of the equipment. Saltmarsh Freight transported it under its own bill of lading. Foxglove Supply sold the cabinets to Northwind last year but did not arrange this shipment and is not the consignee. Our internal service desk sometimes routes freight matters to Foxglove Supply because it supplied the equipment. That routing habit is convenient only in the same way that putting a fork in a light socket is convenient: it produces an immediate result and a less convenient follow-up.

Ticket form fields entered by Esi Sorensen:
Claimant organization: Northwind Software
Carrier named on bill of lading: Saltmarsh Freight
Delivery location: Saltmarsh Freight training site, Dock 4
Reported event: crate corner impact during carrier custody
Date delivered: 5 September 2026
Date reported: 6 September 2026
Requested action: open claim; preserve packaging; advise on inspection
Amount claimed: pending itemization

The portal required an “incident category” before allowing submission. Esi selected “transit damage, suspected” rather than “confirmed equipment damage.” The portal then displayed a green check mark. Green check marks are not findings, despite the portal’s evident confidence.

SUPPORT TICKET — INTERNAL COMMENTS, CHRONOLOGICAL EXPORT
6 September 2026, 09:02 — Uma Petrov, Northwind Software claims liaison:
Opened provisional carrier file. I have asked the receiving team not to dispose of the crate, corner blocks, straps, or moisture wrap. We have photographs from the dock and will request a joint inspection. The ticket says the contents are not yet inspected, so do not describe any component as broken until someone actually checks it. This is an unusually demanding standard, I know: the facts must be observed before they are summarized.

6 September 2026, 10:31 — Internal routing bot:
Suggested owner: Foxglove Supply warranty desk. Reason: equipment product match. Confidence: 92%.

6 September 2026, 10:48 — Uma Petrov:
Rejected automated route. Foxglove sold the goods, but the reported event is an impact while the freight was in transit. The carrier on the transportation document is Saltmarsh Freight. A high-confidence suggestion is not evidence of a warranty defect, nor does it transfer the carrier’s role to the vendor. Please retain the carrier claim queue.

6 September 2026, 13:05 — Dalia Fischer, Saltmarsh Freight, driver statement attached:
At Dock 4, I observed a compressed lower corner on the crate. I did not see a puncture or liquid leak. The consignee’s representative and I both noted the crate condition on the delivery slip. I did not open the package. I cannot say when or how the corner was compressed. The crate had been transferred through two terminals before delivery. My statement does not say the contents were damaged; I had no access to them.

6 September 2026, 16:40 — Hiro Kaur, Saltmarsh Freight claims intake:
We acknowledge the notification and have assigned file SF-19033. This is an acknowledgment, not acceptance of liability. Please send the original bill of lading, delivery receipt, photographs, itemized value, and inspection results. The notice appears prompt based on the dates in the ticket, but the applicable contract and policy still need review. We will not infer the claim amount from a purchase order total that may include unaffected equipment.

7 September 2026, 08:12 — Esi Sorensen:
Attached the first set of photographs. There are four close-ups and one wide view. The wide view shows the crate label, but the label is partly obscured by a strap. The receiving team has not opened the accessory case. The two calibration stands were removed under camera supervision and appear intact. The cabinets are still wrapped. We are arranging an inspection with Saltmarsh Freight for 8 September.

7 September 2026, 09:44 — Internal note, author shown as “Claims Review Queue”:
Preliminary verdict: entire shipment is a total loss. Recommend paying the full invoice, estimated at $48,000. Crate damage is severe and the customer has requested compensation. No need to wait for inventory confirmation; the claim is obvious from the pictures.

7 September 2026, 10:02 — Uma Petrov:
This note is a draft opinion, not an inspection report. It says “entire shipment” and “full invoice” without identifying an affected item or checking the invoice. The customer requested claim handling, not a particular payment. We have two stands already described as intact, and the cabinets and accessory case have not yet been inspected. Please do not copy the draft verdict into correspondence as a factual finding. The number $48,000 came from a rough purchasing-system search result, not a verified line-item value.

7 September 2026, 12:17 — Saltmarsh Freight portal status:
Liability status: under review.
Reserve: $0.00 pending inspection.
Payment authorized: no.
Portal banner: “Your claim is progressing.” The banner appears to describe the movement of pixels rather than the claim.

8 September 2026, 11:30 — Joint inspection appointment completed. Attendees: Esi Sorensen, Hiro Kaur, and independent surveyor Toma Vale. (Toma is mentioned only as an inspector; the approved list of names in this training file applies to named claim participants, and this entry is an automatically inserted appointment label.)

Inspection summary entered by Hiro Kaur:
The crate has one impact deformation at its lower right corner. The wooden base is not fractured. Two fasteners are displaced. No evidence of water exposure, puncture, or tampering was observed. The accessory case seal is intact. Both calibration stands were examined and are undamaged. Five of the six cabinets were unwrapped; four are visually undamaged and one has a shallow crease in the detachable side panel. The sixth cabinet remains wrapped pending a replacement camera battery, but its exterior wrap shows no visible deformation. The bent steel bracket is packed with the creased cabinet and is listed as a replaceable accessory part. No cabinet power or calibration test has yet been run. The inspection does not establish a functional failure.

Esi Sorensen’s same-day comment:
That is a fair summary. We did not say all six cabinets were damaged. The crease and bracket are associated with cabinet C-4. The other cabinets look fine so far. We would still like Saltmarsh Freight to consider the documented repair cost once we have a technician’s estimate. The loose statement that the whole shipment is lost was never ours.

8 September 2026, 15:16 — Hiro Kaur:
Received. The photos appear to show a single affected cabinet and bracket, but inspection of the sixth cabinet and a functional test remain open. We need the vendor’s parts and labor breakdown. We also need to check the declared value and the carrier limitation terms. No payment decision has been made.

9 September 2026, 09:03 — Automated claim summary, generated from selected fields:
Customer loss: $48,000.
Cause: carrier negligence confirmed.
Scope: all six cabinets, both stands, accessory case.
Payment recommendation: full replacement.

9 September 2026, 09:25 — Uma Petrov:
The summary has mistaken a search estimate for a claimed loss, a reported transit event for confirmed negligence, and a shipment manifest for a list of damaged items. I am disabling the auto-generated summary until the source fields can be mapped correctly. It has impressive formatting and no reliable connection to the file.

9 September 2026, 14:50 — Esi Sorensen:
We received the technician’s initial assessment. Cabinet C-4 powers on, but the side panel is creased and the bracket cannot be mounted without replacement. The technician has not said the cabinet is unsafe or unusable. A cosmetic panel repair may be possible. We do not seek replacement of the entire cabinet if the panel can be repaired. We will send the signed estimate when the technician finishes the labor calculation.

10 September 2026, 08:10 — Internal comments cleanup, Uma Petrov:
For the record: the claimant is Northwind Software. The carrier is Saltmarsh Freight. Foxglove Supply is the original equipment vendor. The inspection supports physical damage to one removable panel and one bracket associated with C-4. It does not support damage to the stands or other cabinets. These are separate propositions and should not be collapsed into a single dramatic sentence.

10 September 2026, 12:22 — Saltmarsh Freight intake, Hiro Kaur:
We received the bill of lading and signed delivery receipt. The bill lists a declared shipment value of $31,200, subject to the contract’s per-package limitation and any declared-value endorsement. The delivery receipt includes the corner notation and is signed by the driver and consignee. The bill of lading identifies Northwind Software as shipper and Saltmarsh Freight as carrier. A vendor invoice is not proof that every item on that invoice was damaged.

10 September 2026, 16:18 — Northwind service desk routing record:
Ticket copied to Foxglove Supply because “cabinet” appeared in the description. Foxglove’s warranty desk returned it to Northwind with the message: “We did not ship this consignment, and no product defect has been alleged. The reported impact occurred during freight movement. Please contact the carrier.”

11 September 2026, 09:06 — Esi Sorensen:
Attached the purchase invoice and the work order. The invoice covers more than this shipment’s damaged item: it includes six cabinets, two stands, accessory parts, installation, and an extended service plan. Please use the line items, not the grand total. The purchase invoice is $47,860. It is not a claim for $47,860.

11 September 2026, 11:41 — Hiro Kaur:
Understood. We will compare claimed repair costs with the contract and with the condition documented at delivery. The file still does not establish that Saltmarsh Freight accepted legal liability. The damage report is evidence of condition, not by itself a liability decision.

12 September 2026, 10:00 — Northwind Software claims call transcript excerpt, typed by Uma Petrov:
Esi: We are asking for the reasonable cost to restore the side panel and replace the bent bracket, subject to the policy and contract. We are not seeking the two stands or the other five cabinets.
Hiro: Please confirm that the technician can distinguish repair from replacement and itemize labor.
Esi: Yes. The technician says the cabinet remains operational. The panel and bracket are the issue.
Uma: I will record that as the claimant’s position, not a coverage determination.

12 September 2026, 15:33 — Internal legal review request:
Question referred: whether the carrier’s limitation applies to the damaged package and whether the declared value was properly recorded. No conclusion requested on the condition of the other goods because the inspection did not find damage to them.

13 September 2026, 08:55 — Saltmarsh Freight file note, Hiro Kaur:
A portal field currently says “full loss.” The field was copied from the automated summary and is incorrect. I have changed the working description to “one cabinet panel and bracket; repair estimate pending.” This change does not decide coverage or payment.

13 September 2026, 16:20 — Northwind technician report, received as PDF and transcribed into ticket:
Unit: Cabinet C-4, serial NS-C4-66018. Electrical and control tests passed. Cabinet frame is square. The removable side panel has a shallow crease measuring approximately 11 cm across its widest point. The panel can be removed without disturbing the calibration seal. The lower bracket is bent and cannot securely support the original fastener. Replace panel and bracket; no replacement of cabinet enclosure or controls required. Estimated parts: side panel $1,180; bracket $420. Estimated labor: 6.5 hours at $140 per hour. Diagnostic and handling: $180. Travel: $0 because technician was already scheduled at the site. Taxes excluded from this estimate. This is a repair estimate, not a paid invoice.

13 September 2026, 17:05 — Esi Sorensen:
The report matches what we saw. Please do not describe the unit as a total loss. We can schedule the work after the carrier confirms the inspection is complete.

14 September 2026, 09:10 — Internal comment, Claims Review Queue:
Verdict: claim exceeds the policy sublimit by $500. Decline in full. The stated estimate is about $2,700 and the relevant limit is $2,200, so the excess is obvious. The insured’s invoice was $47,860, which reinforces the conclusion that this is a high-value loss.

14 September 2026, 09:37 — Uma Petrov:
The comment mixes the repair estimate with the purchase invoice and gives an unexplained $2,700 approximation. We must calculate from the actual estimate and apply the stated limit to the covered repair components, after the coverage review. Do not send the decline yet. A verdict does not become true because it has a label and a decimal-free estimate.

15 September 2026, 08:00 — Claims policy extract attached by Saltmarsh Freight:
For a covered transit impact to removable external fittings or panels, reasonable repair or replacement cost is subject to a maximum of $2,200 per affected package, excluding tax. The cap is applied to the supported repair amount for the affected package, not to the purchase price of the entire shipment. If an item remains functional, that fact does not automatically eliminate payment for a documented physical repair, but it does rule out treating the whole item as a total loss solely on the basis of the repairable damage. Separate, unrelated damage is not included in the cap calculation unless specifically linked to the same occurrence and package. This extract concerns the cap only; other coverage conditions and liability remain under review.

15 September 2026, 08:23 — Hiro Kaur:
Please confirm the arithmetic and scope using the technician’s estimate. The report lists three cost lines. The estimate is before tax. The $2,200 figure is a cap, not a guaranteed payment. The file has not yet reached a final liability determination.

15 September 2026, 12:10 — Esi Sorensen:
There is no second damaged package. The crate contains the shipment, but the estimate relates to the panel and bracket on cabinet C-4 only. We can provide photographs of the original package and cabinet label if needed. The repair estimate has not changed.

16 September 2026, 09:46 — Uma Petrov:
Updated claim worksheet. The panel is $1,180, bracket $420, labor 6.5 × $140 = $910, diagnostic/handling $180, travel $0. Total supported estimate before tax: $1,180 + $420 + $910 + $180 + $0 = $2,690. The policy cap is $2,200 per affected package. The amount above the cap is $2,690 − $2,200 = $490. That arithmetic does not mean the insurer owes $2,200; it means the supported repair estimate exceeds the stated cap by $490, subject to the unresolved coverage and liability review. The earlier $2,700 was a rough rounding, and the “$500” excess was not exact.

16 September 2026, 11:02 — Hiro Kaur:
Confirmed the arithmetic. Also confirmed that neither the two stands nor the other cabinets belong in this repair calculation. The purchase invoice total is not the repair amount. The estimate includes no tax and no travel charge. Please keep the reserve separate from the claimant’s requested amount.

16 September 2026, 15:49 — Saltmarsh Freight reserve screen:
Gross estimate submitted: $2,690
Applicable stated cap: $2,200
Current reserve: $2,200
Payment authority: pending
Liability status: review incomplete
A reserve is an accounting entry, not a promise to pay. The screen help text says this in small type, presumably to ensure it is read by exactly nobody.

17 September 2026, 08:31 — Northwind Software service ticket follow-up:
The repair shop has confirmed the cabinet is still in service pending parts. We have not cancelled the training event. The event can use five cabinets and a loaner for the sixth. We are seeking the repair amount, not lost business income. No overtime, expedited freight, or replacement unit is included in our current estimate.

17 September 2026, 10:08 — Internal status note, Claims Review Queue:
Customer has incurred a business interruption loss because the event was rescheduled. Recommend adding $6,400 for lost use. The ticket says the cabinet is unavailable and the training event is affected.

17 September 2026, 10:26 — Uma Petrov:
The ticket says the event was not cancelled and a loaner is available. It does not state that the event was rescheduled, nor does Northwind request lost income. The status note has supplied both a new event and a dollar figure. Please remove the proposed $6,400 from the claim summary unless supporting documentation arrives. None has.

17 September 2026, 14:14 — Esi Sorensen:
Our training event went ahead on its scheduled date. The loaner was used for the one station that would otherwise have used C-4. There was no cancellation and no claim for lost use. Thank you for correcting the entry.

18 September 2026, 09:11 — Saltmarsh Freight legal reviewer:
The documents support a recorded impact while the consignment was in carrier transit and physical deformation to one panel and bracket at delivery. Contractual responsibility remains subject to the signed carriage terms and final review. No evidence in this file links the event to the equipment vendor or to a pre-shipment defect. The file does not support a conclusion that all pieces were damaged.

18 September 2026, 13:20 — Internal opinion draft, author hidden by export:
Proposed decision: deny because the consignee failed to report within five days. Delivery 5 September; notice 6 September; report was actually one day later. The five-day clause is not met. Close the claim.

18 September 2026, 13:55 — Uma Petrov:
The proposed conclusion contradicts its own dates. Delivery was 5 September and notice was 6 September, so the report was made the next calendar day, within five days. Whether that satisfies every contractual notice requirement is a separate review, but it cannot accurately be described as later than five days. I have marked the draft as factually incorrect.

19 September 2026, 08:48 — Saltmarsh Freight case manager:
The notice date is recorded as 6 September, and the delivery date as 5 September. We have no evidence of an earlier delivery or later notification. The five-day statement in the draft will not be used. The remaining issue is the contract’s scope and application of the per-package repair cap, not timeliness on the dates presently documented.

19 September 2026, 15:02 — Northwind Software attachment index:
A. Bill of lading 7751, showing Northwind Software as shipper and Saltmarsh Freight as carrier.
B. Delivery receipt dated 5 September 2026, with “corner crush, contents not inspected.”
C. Five photographs taken at receipt.
D. Joint inspection summary dated 8 September.
E. Technician report dated 13 September.
F. Repair estimate with cost lines and no tax.
G. Purchase invoice for $47,860, covering multiple goods and services.
H. Training calendar showing scheduled event on 17 September and completion as planned using a loaner.
I. Email from Foxglove Supply stating it did not arrange the shipment and had received no defect complaint.

19 September 2026, 16:40 — Hiro Kaur:
I have compared the attachment index with the file. The invoice amount is unrelated to the computed repair total except as purchase-value context. The training calendar and service note do not support interruption costs. The receipt notation and photos support the reported crate condition. The inspection and technician report support a repairable defect to one package’s contents. The claim remains subject to coverage and liability; no payment has been issued.

20 September 2026, 09:16 — Internal quality audit comment:
Audit prompt: Did the previous summary use the evidence, or repeat a pre-existing verdict? Finding: the 7 September “total loss” draft preceded inspection and was contradicted by the inspection. The 14 September “decline by $500” draft used approximate arithmetic and did not distinguish the cap from a guaranteed payment. The 17 September interruption note invented a loss contradicted by the customer’s account. The 18 September late-notice draft misstated its own dates. These are not four independent confirmations; they are four reasons to check the primary documents before repeating a confident sentence.

20 September 2026, 10:01 — Uma Petrov:
Agreed. The current file should separate: (1) what was physically observed; (2) what amount is documented; (3) what the cap says; and (4) whether the carrier ultimately owes anything under the whole contract. At present, the evidence supports a repair estimate of $2,690 before tax for one affected package, with a stated $2,200 maximum for that type of repair. The estimate is not a payment authorization. The exact outcome of the liability review is not stated in the documents available to this ticket.

20 September 2026, 16:32 — Saltmarsh Freight portal export:
Case stage: coverage review
Requested claimant amount: $2,690 before tax, per estimate
Potential cap: $2,200
Amount paid to date: $0
Claim closed: no
Liability accepted: no
Liability denied: no

21 September 2026, 08:07 — Esi Sorensen:
We are ready to proceed with the repair if the surveyor confirms the carrier’s inspection is complete. Please retain the current file status accurately. We have not withdrawn the claim, and we have not received payment. We are not asking anyone to call the equipment a total loss. It is a working cabinet with a damaged panel and bracket. A less theatrical description would be welcome, though we are not optimistic.

21 September 2026, 10:45 — Final internal handoff, Uma Petrov:
For the next reviewer: the claimant and carrier identities are established by the bill of lading, not by the equipment vendor’s name in the product database. The physical findings are limited to the crate corner and one cabinet’s panel and bracket. The two stands and the inspected cabinets are not documented as damaged; the sixth cabinet’s exterior showed no visible deformation and it was later confirmed functional by the technician’s follow-up. The claimant’s documented repair estimate is $2,690 before tax. The quoted cap is $2,200 per affected package for this category, so the estimate is $490 above the cap. The claim remains unresolved; a cap calculation alone is not a final award. No lost-use amount has been claimed or supported. Notice on 6 September followed delivery on 5 September by one day. These statements should survive contact with the source documents.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE RECEIVING NOTE — TYPED TRANSCRIPTION
Found folded behind the delivery receipt during the 21 September scan. The handwriting is compact, the punctuation is aspirational, and the spelling has been retained where it does not obscure meaning.

“Sat 5 Sept. truck came about 3:40. Dalia showed me the corner before we signed. split/pressed in on bottom right. I wrote corner crush, contents not checked. no wet marks. straps still on. crate did not fall off truck in front of me. could have happened before the dock; I did not watch whole trip. took phone pictures. told Esi same day. did not count cabinets while driver waited because we would have needed to cut all the wrap. kept crate and blocks by receiving cage.

“9/8 inspection: stands okay. cabinets not all opened at start. when opened, C-4 side panel has dent/crease and bracket bent. C-4 powered on when technician checked later. Other open units looked fine. I am not saying the crate was perfect. It was not. I am also not saying every machine was ruined. It was not that either. A damaged corner is not a magic wand that damages everything inside. Please stop asking whether I ‘confirm total loss’ as if the question itself were evidence.

“9/17 event happened. used loaner for one station. no cancellation, no lost revenue calculation. Did not ask carrier for event costs. Repair part and bracket only. End.”

Margin note in different hand, attribution uncertain: “Whole shipment condemned; customer confirmed total loss; expedite $48,000.” Beneath it, in Esi’s handwriting: “No. This is not what I said. Five cabinets fine/under test then. C-4 runs. Parts repair requested. The line above should not be copied into claim facts.”

The note has no separate signature. The scan metadata records it as received on 21 September; that is not necessarily the date it was written. The margin note’s author cannot be identified from the copy. It is included because it was physically attached to the receipt, not because it is reliable. The main note matches the delivery notation and later inspection in material respects. Where a handwritten estimate of time differs from the signed delivery record, the signed record controls the file’s delivery date. The note does not state a repair cost and should not be used to calculate one.

The workbook was assembled from portal exports and manually transcribed documents. It is not a substitute for those documents. Several rows repeat verdict language because the audit team wanted the problematic statements visible; repetition does not make them accurate. The “bad draft” rows are intentionally retained and marked as such. The live claim record shows no payment, no accepted liability, and no final denial. A reviewer should not infer that the claimant received the cap merely because the reserve equals the cap. A reserve describes money held for accounting purposes. It does not describe money transferred.

The workbook’s first draft used the vendor invoice grand total as the claim amount. Esi Sorensen objected because the invoice includes six cabinets, two stands, accessory parts, installation, and an extended service plan. The later estimate isolates the damaged panel and bracket and the labor needed to install them. This is why the estimate totals $2,690 rather than $47,860. The two numbers answer different questions. Subtracting one from the other would not identify covered damage, and dividing either by the nine manifest pieces would not establish a per-piece loss.

The policy extract refers to “reasonable repair or replacement cost” for specified removable external fittings and panels, with a maximum of $2,200 per affected package, excluding tax. The quoted extract does not say that every claim with an estimate above $2,200 should be denied in full. It states a maximum for the described repair category. The extract also does not, by itself, establish that the carrier is liable, that all other policy conditions are met, or that a payment is authorized. Those questions remain for the review. The spreadsheet’s cap calculation is therefore a scope comparison, not an outcome notice.

For clarity, the arithmetic is recorded without rounding: panel $1,180 plus bracket $420 equals $1,600; labor 6.5 hours times $140 equals $910; $1,600 plus $910 equals $2,510; adding $180 diagnostic and handling gives $2,690; adding the listed $0 travel leaves $2,690. Compare $2,690 with the $2,200 cap: the estimate is $490 higher. The old draft’s $500 difference came from comparing a rounded $2,700 estimate with $2,200. It is a near miss, not the exact difference. Nothing in the estimate supplies a tax figure, and the cap extract says tax is excluded. No tax calculation can be made from the information in this file.

The delivery-date issue is similarly straightforward once the source dates are used. The signed receipt says 5 September 2026. The ticket was opened and the carrier notified on 6 September 2026. The difference is one calendar day. The proposed five-day breach statement is inconsistent with those dates. This does not prove that every legal or contractual notice requirement has been satisfied; it only makes the draft’s assertion that the report was later than five days factually wrong. There is no evidence in this compilation of a different delivery date, a different notification date, or a separate notice deadline shorter than one day.

The first review draft’s whole-shipment conclusion also fails against the records. The delivery receipt establishes a damaged crate corner, with contents not inspected at delivery. The joint inspection later documents two intact stands, an intact accessory case, four visually undamaged opened cabinets, one cabinet with a creased removable panel, and one cabinet initially still wrapped but subsequently reported functional without documented damage. The technician confirms C-4 operates and identifies a repairable panel and bracket issue. Esi repeatedly says the request concerns those parts, not the whole shipment. There is no source for a total-loss finding, and no source for a $48,000 claimed amount. The customer’s own claim amount is the technician’s repair estimate of $2,690 before tax.

The insertion concerning lost use does not survive comparison with the customer’s statement. The training event was held as scheduled. A loaner served the station associated with C-4. Northwind says it is not seeking business-interruption costs, and no supporting $6,400 calculation appears anywhere in the file. The event-related verdict is therefore not a fact about this claim. No amount for cancellation, lost revenue, expedited freight, or replacement equipment is in the current request.

The party identities are recorded in multiple primary sources. Northwind Software is the shipper, owner, and claimant. Saltmarsh Freight is the carrier on the bill of lading and the company operating the delivery. Foxglove Supply sold the equipment but did not arrange this shipment. The automated routing system selected Foxglove because it recognized the word “cabinet”; both Northwind’s claims liaison and Foxglove’s reply corrected that route. The issue is not a product defect alleged against the seller. The reported occurrence is a transit impact, and the carrier file is the active freight claim file.

An acknowledgment, inspection appointment, reserve, and portal progress banner each have limited meanings. The acknowledgment shows that the carrier received notice. The inspection records observed condition. The reserve records an accounting estimate. The banner records a system status. None alone constitutes acceptance of liability or a payment decision. The portal explicitly shows that liability is neither accepted nor denied and that the claim remains in coverage review. The amount paid is zero. Those status fields should be preserved even if a later decision changes them.

A copied cell comment says to choose total loss and not inspect the arithmetic. It has no authority over the facts. The cell is retained because it was found during the audit and because it neatly illustrates the workbook’s tendency to mistake decisive-sounding text for a decision. The same applies to the internal draft opinions: their existence is evidence that someone wrote them, not evidence that their conclusions are correct. When their claims conflict with the signed receipt, inspection, technician report, or claimant’s explicit statement, the source records control.

The file contains no final coverage letter. It contains no final liability determination. It contains no payment confirmation. It contains an estimate, a stated cap, and a pending review. A final reviewer may later accept, partially accept, or deny some part of the request after applying the full contract and any other relevant conditions. That future possibility does not change what this file presently supports. In particular, the estimate being over the cap by $490 does not prove that $490 is payable, and it does not prove the entire claim should be declined. The appropriate description remains that the supported repair estimate is $2,690 before tax, the quoted cap is $2,200 for the affected package and repair category, and the final claim outcome is unresolved.

[{"state":"Larkspur Dental — consolidated transport review for Copperleaf Supply
Prepared by: Callum Moreau, Network Operations
Distribution: Regional logistics management, accounts payable, customer service
Reporting period: 4–18 September 2026

Purpose and scope
This review consolidates the status update issued to management, the relevant messages exchanged by dispatch and the consignee, and the supporting carrier invoice. It concerns shipment LD-44720, a palletized order of dental chair components and sterilization supplies moving from Copperleaf Supply’s North Quay depot to Larkspur Dental’s receiving centre. The review is intended to distinguish what was planned, what was actually tendered and delivered, what the customer requested, and what the carrier billed. Several preliminary labels copied into the internal dashboard are reproduced below for audit purposes; those labels are not independent evidence. Dates and amounts in the body refer to the records identified in the appendices.

Shipment particulars
Customer account: Larkspur Dental, receiving centre 3
Supplier: Copperleaf Supply, North Quay depot
Consignee contact: Esi Okafor, receiving coordinator
Supplier contact: Kwame Haddad, dispatch supervisor
Operations reviewer: Callum Moreau
Shipment reference: LD-44720
Carrier reference: Gannet Freight GF-99108
Purchase order: PO-LD-80614
Goods: 12 cartons, 2,160 kg gross, one non-stackable pallet and one stackable pallet
Service booked: scheduled road freight, delivery appointment requested for 11 September
Booked pickup: 8 September, 08:00–12:00
Booked delivery: 11 September, 09:00–12:00
Recorded pickup: 8 September, 10:42
Recorded delivery: 11 September, 10:18
Customer’s original delivery note: “Please keep the 11 September slot if possible; our technicians are booked for the afternoon.”

Executive status update to the manager, 18 September
The shipment was collected within the booked pickup window and delivered within the booked delivery appointment. The receiver signed for all 12 cartons, subject to a note that the external wrap on the rear pallet was scuffed. The receiver’s signed note does not state that any carton was missing or that goods were damaged. The receiving coordinator later confirmed that the contents were intact after inspection. No delivery appointment change was requested by the customer, and the carrier record shows no failed attempt.

The internal dashboard displayed “late delivery — customer confirmed” on 12 September. That entry was copied from a preliminary clerk note, not from the proof of delivery or a customer message. The time stamps in the carrier record show delivery at 10:18 on 11 September against an appointment window ending at 12:00 on 11 September. In the booking record the customer requested a delivery appointment, but did not ask for compensation or a refund. The coordinator’s later request concerned a carrier accessorial fee posted to the supplier invoice, not the goods or the service charge paid by the customer.

Finance also found a preliminary comment reading “duplicate liftgate charge verified; approve credit.” The comment was entered before the line-level review was completed. The invoice includes two liftgate-related descriptions, but one is the contracted liftgate service and the other is a separately documented, customer-authorized redelivery-to-dock handling service. The first delivery was completed at the appointed dock; the second service was never performed. The invoice nevertheless contains only one actual liftgate charge, and the second description is a no-charge informational entry. Finance’s comment therefore does not accurately describe the billed amount or the evidence. See the invoice section and the supporting authorization records below.

A final dashboard annotation reads “refund requested by consignee.” It is correct only in the broad sense that the consignee asked the supplier to reverse a specific carrier fee that had been passed through on a draft statement. The consignee expressly did not request a refund of the freight service, the goods, or the customer’s payment. The distinction matters when classifying the request. The complete wording appears in the email thread.

Status chronology
7 September, 14:06 — Copperleaf Supply transmitted the shipping notice and packing list. The notice listed 12 cartons and a total gross weight of 2,160 kg. It identified one pallet as non-stackable because of the instrument trays and one as stackable because it contained sealed supply cartons.
8 September, 08:00 — Beginning of the booked collection window.
8 September, 10:42 — Gannet Freight driver checked in at North Quay. Dispatch recorded both pallet identifiers and the seal number. The driver’s scan marked the shipment collected at 10:51.
9 September, 16:20 — Line-haul scan at West Fen cross-dock. The pallet count remained two. No exception code was recorded.
10 September, 05:55 — Arrival scan at the destination hub. The shipment was assigned to a vehicle with a tail lift, as requested on the booking form.
10 September, 15:03 — Carrier appointment system confirmed 11 September, 09:00–12:00. This was a confirmation of the existing appointment, not a rescheduling.
11 September, 10:18 — Delivery scan at Larkspur Dental receiving centre 3. The driver’s electronic proof of delivery recorded 12 cartons received and included the receiver’s note, “outer wrap scuffed at rear corner; contents to be checked.”
11 September, 10:34 — Esi Okafor emailed dispatch: “Thank you. We have the full count. I will check the trays after the morning intake.”
11 September, 13:46 — Esi sent a follow-up: “I have now opened the cartons. The contents are intact; only the stretch wrap was marked. Please retain the delivery photo with the file.”
12 September, 09:12 — A dashboard clerk entered “late delivery — customer confirmed,” without linking a source message. The same entry was copied into the weekly exception spreadsheet.
13 September, 11:07 — Copperleaf accounts payable received a draft carrier invoice showing a disputed handling fee. The dashboard comment “duplicate liftgate charge verified; approve credit” was added at 11:24, before the invoice attachments were reviewed.
14 September, 08:32 — Esi asked Copperleaf to remove the particular handling fee from the draft pass-through statement, explaining that the fee did not apply because the driver had delivered to the appointed dock on the original attempt.
14 September, 10:16 — Kwame replied that he would check whether the separate authorized service had been performed and whether the fee appeared on the carrier invoice.
15 September, 16:40 — Carrier invoice and proof-of-delivery attachments were received. The invoice shows one charged liftgate service, a no-charge reference line for the unperformed separate service, and no second charged liftgate fee.
16 September, 12:05 — Esi confirmed by email that her request was limited to reversing the stated handling fee on the draft statement. She did not request repayment for the delivered freight or goods.
18 September, 09:30 — Callum reviewed the booking, event scans, signed delivery record, customer messages, authorization, and invoice line items, and prepared this report.

Manager’s working questions and dashboard labels
The weekly dashboard used the following phrases: “late delivery — customer confirmed,” “duplicate liftgate charge verified,” and “refund requested by consignee.” These are quoted here because they were used in operational summaries. They should not be treated as findings merely because they appear in a system. The first is inconsistent with the appointment and delivery time and has no cited customer confirmation. The second is inconsistent with the itemized invoice and the performance record. The third requires careful scope: the consignee did ask for a reversal of one specified fee, while explicitly declining to seek a refund of the freight or goods. The audit questions at the end of this document concern the stated propositions, not whether the dashboard used those words.

Booking and service record
Copperleaf created booking GF-99108 on 7 September at 13:18. The order was entered as two pallets, 12 cartons, 2,160 kg. The service selection was “scheduled road freight; dock delivery; tail lift required.” The booking notes state: “Receiver has a staffed intake dock. Use booked dock on first attempt. No inside placement requested. Appointment requested, not guaranteed until carrier confirms.” A separate optional service, “alternate indoor drop / redelivery to receiving room,” was shown on the carrier portal but was not selected at booking.

At 13:42 on 7 September, Esi Okafor acknowledged the booking details. Her message says: “The 11 September morning slot works. Please call on arrival. We can receive at the loading dock; no room-of-choice handling is required. If there is a failed first attempt, contact me before arranging any alternate drop.” The phrase “if there is a failed first attempt” describes a contingency, not a request to perform a second service. The carrier’s booking record accordingly contains no authorization for an alternate drop at that time.

On 8 September, after pickup, Gannet’s dispatch system generated a standard option notice listing a possible paid “alternate indoor drop” service. The notice was sent to Copperleaf, not to Larkspur. It said that the service would be chargeable only if separately approved and actually completed. Copperleaf did not approve it. On 9 September, Kwame forwarded the notice to Esi for information. Esi replied: “No alternate drop is needed. Please use the dock in the existing appointment. If circumstances change, ask before adding a fee.” This is an explicit refusal of the optional service at that stage, not a cancellation of the booked dock delivery.

The destination driver’s route sheet instructed him to use the receiving dock. The vehicle had a tail lift because the pallet weight and site access profile required one. At 10:11 on 11 September, the driver called the number on the booking. At 10:18 he recorded arrival and completed the unload to the dock. The carrier’s route sheet records no waiting-time charge, no redirection, and no second visit. The proof-of-delivery photograph shows both pallets beside the receiving dock. The image timestamp is 10:21. A separate carrier service code, AID, is defined in the carrier’s tariff as alternate indoor drop; the service record for shipment GF-99108 has no performed AID event.

Customer communications: email thread
Subject: LD-44720 appointment and statement query

From: Esi Okafor, Larkspur Dental
To: Kwame Haddad, Copperleaf Supply
Date: 7 September 2026, 13:42
“We can receive the two pallets at the loading dock on 11 September, between 09:00 and 12:00. Please ask the driver to call on arrival. The instrument trays must remain upright. We do not need a room-of-choice or inside-placement service. If the booked dock cannot be used, please call me before arranging anything else.”

From: Kwame Haddad, Copperleaf Supply
To: Esi Okafor
Date: 7 September 2026, 14:02
“Noted. The carrier booking records a dock delivery in the requested window, with tail lift. It does not include inside placement. We will send the collection and delivery updates when the carrier scans them.”

From: Gannet Freight system notice, forwarded by Kwame
To: Esi Okafor
Date: 8 September 2026, 15:31
“Optional accessorial available: alternate indoor drop to a nominated receiving room. Additional charge applies only after written approval and successful completion. This notice is not a change to an existing booking.”

From: Kwame Haddad
To: Esi Okafor
Date: 9 September 2026, 08:14
“Forwarding for visibility. No change has been made to your booked dock delivery. Please tell us if you want us to request the optional service.”

From: Esi Okafor
To: Kwame Haddad
Date: 9 September 2026, 08:29
“Please do not add the optional service. The dock is suitable and our staff will take the pallets from there. If the carrier cannot make the booked delivery, call before proposing another arrangement.”

From: Kwame Haddad
To: Esi Okafor
Date: 11 September 2026, 10:34
“The carrier has recorded delivery at 10:18. The proof of delivery shows both pallet IDs and 12 cartons. The driver noted scuffed outer wrap. Can you confirm whether the contents need a damage report?”

From: Esi Okafor
To: Kwame Haddad
Date: 11 September 2026, 13:46
“I have checked all 12 cartons and opened the instrument-tray carton. Everything inside is intact and usable. The stretch wrap has a scuff at one corner; no goods are damaged or missing. Please keep the photo with the delivery file.”

From: Esi Okafor
To: Kwame Haddad
Date: 14 September 2026, 08:32
“On the draft statement, please reverse the £42.00 ‘alternate indoor drop’ handling fee. We accepted delivery at the booked dock and did not ask for the extra drop. This request is only about that fee. We are not asking you to refund the goods or the booked freight charge.”

From: Kwame Haddad
To: Esi Okafor
Date: 14 September 2026, 10:16
“Thank you. I will check the underlying Gannet invoice and the service scan before deciding whether the £42.00 should be removed. I will not treat the dashboard comment as proof by itself.”

From: Esi Okafor
To: Kwame Haddad
Date: 16 September 2026, 12:05
“To clarify the wording on the draft: I am requesting reversal of the £42.00 line only. The delivery was completed and the items are usable; I am not requesting a refund of the freight or a return of the order.”

Quoted reply in the same thread, included by the mail client
From: Copperleaf shared mailbox
Date: 12 September 2026, 09:12
“Exception note: customer confirmed late arrival; recommend goodwill refund.”

From: Kwame Haddad
Date: 12 September 2026, 09:40
“I cannot find a message confirming lateness or asking for a refund. The scan currently shows delivery at 10:18 against the 09:00–12:00 appointment. I will leave the exception open until the source is checked.”

From: Esi Okafor
Date: 12 September 2026, 10:03
“I did not tell anyone that it arrived late. It arrived in the booked window. My first note was only that I needed to inspect the wrap and contents.”

Forwarded internal mail, attached to the customer thread
From: Wanjiru Kowalski, service desk clerk
To: Copperleaf shared mailbox
Date: 12 September 2026, 09:12
“Copied from yesterday’s queue screen: ‘late delivery — customer confirmed’. I have not spoken to the consignee. The note may refer to a different reference; the queue view displayed several shipments together. Please verify the scan and the original message before using it.”

From: Service desk team lead
To: Wanjiru Kowalski
Date: 12 September 2026, 09:25
“Do not convert a queue phrase into a customer statement unless the underlying contact is attached. Keep the source field blank for now. The phrase is a provisional classification, not an evidence record.”

The shared mailbox’s auto-generated digest later shortened the quoted exchange to “customer confirmed late arrival.” That digest omitted Wanjiru’s qualification and Kwame’s response. The digest was copied into the dashboard, which explains how the phrase circulated; it does not make the phrase accurate. The original messages, carrier event timestamps, and appointment record are preserved in the case file.

Delivery evidence and handling notes
Proof of delivery, signed electronically by Esi Okafor at 10:23 on 11 September, identifies shipment LD-44720, two pallets, and 12 cartons. The signature screen includes a condition field. Esi entered: “Outer wrap scuffed at rear corner; count complete; contents to be checked.” The screen’s checkbox for “visible product damage” was left unselected. The driver entered “delivered to dock; receiver present” and selected the carrier’s standard tail-lift service. The driver did not select “alternate indoor drop,” “redelivery,” “rebooked slot,” or “failed attempt.”

At 13:46 the same day, Esi’s email documented the inspection result. She said all cartons were present, the instrument trays were intact, and only the stretch wrap had a scuff. Copperleaf’s customer-service form created at 14:05 records a packaging observation, not a product-damage claim. Its disposition says “monitor only; no claim opened.” A photograph attached to the record shows intact carton corners beneath the marked stretch wrap. The image does not establish that every internal component was independently tested, but Esi’s written inspection does establish that she checked the contents and found them intact and usable.

A separate shipment, LD-44702, appears in a nearby section of the hub’s daily exception export. That shipment was delivered after its appointment and had a consignee note asking for a review. The dashboard clerk’s queue view displayed both references on the same screen. The preliminary “late delivery — customer confirmed” phrase may therefore have been copied across from the adjacent record. The actual records for LD-44702 are not part of this shipment’s performance assessment. Its presence explains a plausible source of confusion, but does not alter the LD-44720 timestamps.

The carrier’s event export uses local time throughout. The pickup and delivery scans are not converted from a different time zone. The 11 September appointment confirmation is stored as 09:00–12:00 local time. The proof-of-delivery screen records 10:18 as the completion scan and 10:23 as the receiver signature time. Both fall inside the same appointment window. The 10:18 scan is the relevant carrier delivery event; even using the later signature time, the delivery remained before noon.

Invoice review: Gannet Freight invoice GF-INV-73019
Invoice date: 15 September 2026
Supplier account: Copperleaf Supply
Shipment reference: LD-44720
Currency: GBP
Invoice terms: 30 days from invoice date

Line 1 — Scheduled road freight, two pallets, 2,160 kg: £286.00
Line 2 — Tail-lift service at booked receiving dock: £36.00
Line 3 — Fuel adjustment, 8.0% of scheduled road freight (£286.00 × 0.08): £22.88
Line 4 — Appointment booking: £0.00, included in booked service
Line 5 — Alternate indoor drop reference, no performed service event: £0.00
Line 6 — Waiting time: £0.00, no waiting-time event
Line 7 — Redelivery: £0.00, no second attempt
Net charges: £344.88
Tax: £68.98
Invoice total: £413.86

The invoice’s line 5 is a reference-only line generated when an optional service was quoted. Its amount is zero, and its description says “not performed / no event scan.” The fee disputed in Copperleaf’s draft customer statement was £42.00, not a charge on this Gannet invoice. Copperleaf’s draft had provisionally passed through a manual placeholder amount against “alternate indoor drop.” The placeholder came from an earlier estimate for a different service option and was not matched to a performed service. It was not part of Gannet’s invoice total. The customer’s request to reverse it applies to that placeholder on the draft statement.

The invoice’s arithmetic checks: £286.00 + £36.00 + £22.88 + £0.00 + £0.00 + £0.00 + £0.00 = £344.88 net. Tax is stated as £68.98; the carrier invoice uses its own tax rounding and tax-category summary. Net plus tax equals £344.88 + £68.98 = £413.86. The invoice does not show a second £36.00 tail-lift charge and does not show a £42.00 alternate indoor drop charge. The line descriptions must be read with their amounts and event references; the appearance of two liftgate-related or handling-related words in a summary does not establish two billed services.

The finance reviewer’s preliminary note, entered 13 September before the invoice was attached, reads: “Duplicate liftgate charge verified; approve credit for £42.00.” This is a planted conclusion in the record, not a calculation or invoice finding. The underlying invoice has a £36.00 charge for the single tail-lift service actually used at the booked dock, while the alternate indoor drop reference is £0.00 and marked not performed. The £42.00 was a manual placeholder on Copperleaf’s draft statement. The customer did ask for that placeholder to be reversed, but the statement “duplicate liftgate charge verified” is not supported by the carrier invoice. Later finance comments correctly distinguish the two matters: “Remove the unsupported £42.00 draft pass-through; do not describe it as a duplicate carrier liftgate charge.”

Invoice workflow notes
12 September, 15:08 — Copperleaf statement preparation created a draft customer ledger entry: “Alternate indoor drop estimate, pending confirmation: £42.00.” The entry was marked “unmatched,” not “carrier-billed.”
13 September, 11:24 — Preliminary dashboard note: “Duplicate liftgate charge verified; approve credit.” No invoice image or event scan was attached at the time.
15 September, 16:40 — Gannet invoice received. Accounts payable matched the billed tail-lift item to the booked service and dock delivery scan. The invoice’s alternate indoor drop reference line was £0.00 with no performance event.
16 September, 09:15 — Accounts payable reviewer: “The £42.00 is not on the Gannet invoice. It is a Copperleaf draft estimate. Reverse the draft pass-through at customer level; retain the single £36.00 contracted tail-lift line on the carrier invoice.”
16 September, 10:02 — Operations reviewer: “Confirmed. Do not classify the carrier bill as a duplicate. The customer asked for the placeholder to be removed, which is consistent with the absence of an alternate-drop event.”
17 September, 14:20 — Customer ledger corrected: the £42.00 placeholder was removed from the draft; no credit was issued against the Gannet invoice. The contracted freight and tail-lift charges remained payable by Copperleaf to Gannet under the carrier agreement.

A note in a spreadsheet says “£36 + £42 = £78 accessorial exposure.” This is an aggregation of the real £36 tail-lift service with the unsupported £42 placeholder. It is not evidence of two actual billed accessorial services. The £36 is in the carrier’s invoice and corresponds to the delivered dock service. The £42 was on Copperleaf’s draft only and was removed before final customer billing. The invoice’s final total remains £413.86. No additional £42 is to be added to it.

Customer account and service interpretation
The goods were ordered under PO-LD-80614. The customer paid no separate freight charge at the point of delivery; freight was arranged by Copperleaf under its carrier account. The draft statement was a proposed pass-through, not a settled customer payment. Esi’s phrase “please reverse the £42.00” refers to taking that unsubstantiated line off the proposed statement. Her subsequent clarification explicitly excludes a refund of the booked freight and a refund of the goods. There is no return authorization, goods credit request, or complaint seeking repayment for the order in the file.

The words “refund” and “credit” appear in copied internal notes and in the customer’s description of the requested reversal. The relevant object of a request must therefore be retained: the customer seeks removal/reversal of a specific draft accessorial fee, not repayment of the freight or the merchandise. The dashboard phrase “refund requested by consignee” is broad and could be mistaken for a request to refund the shipment. Read in context, the consignee’s request is limited to the £42.00 draft line. This report records the distinction so the service desk can code the issue as a disputed proposed fee rather than a product return or freight refund.

Operational assessment
Collection was completed during the booked window. Delivery was completed during the confirmed appointment. The two-pallet and 12-carton counts agree across packing list, pickup scan, proof of delivery, and receiver confirmation. The outer wrap observation was followed by a customer inspection that found contents intact. No claim for physical damage or missing goods was opened. The optional indoor service was not selected, was later expressly declined, and has no performance scan. The driver delivered to the booked dock with the contracted tail-lift service.

The customer did not request a different appointment or ask for a late-delivery remedy. The source behind the “late delivery” phrase was not a direct customer communication; it was a queue label later qualified by its author as potentially referring to another shipment. The consignee directly denied having reported late arrival, and the carrier time records independently show delivery before the appointment window closed. The phrase is therefore not a reliable statement of what happened.

The carrier invoice supports one tail-lift charge, for the booked dock delivery. It does not support a duplicate charge or a charge for alternate indoor placement. The customer’s objection to the £42.00 draft placeholder is supported by the absence of a corresponding carrier charge and service event. That finding does not mean the customer requested a refund of freight or goods. It means the proposed fee should not be passed through as though it were an incurred carrier charge.

Records checked
1. Booking confirmation GF-99108, created 7 September.
2. Copperleaf packing list for PO-LD-80614.
3. Gannet pickup and hub scan export, 8–11 September.
4. Carrier appointment confirmation, 10 September.
5. Driver route sheet and proof-of-delivery record, 11 September.
6. Receiver emails from Esi Okafor, 11, 12, 14, and 16 September.
7. Forwarded internal service-desk messages, 12 September.
8. Gannet Freight invoice GF-INV-73019 and its line-item detail.
9. Copperleaf draft statement history and customer ledger correction.
10. Optional-service quote notice and service-event export.

Records not treated as dispositive
The dashboard’s “late delivery — customer confirmed” label is not treated as a customer statement because no source contact was attached and the clerk who copied it said the queue might have displayed a different shipment. The preliminary finance label “duplicate liftgate charge verified” is not treated as an invoice finding because it predates the invoice and is contradicted by the itemized charges. The shortened mail digest is not treated as a complete transcript because it omits the qualification and the direct customer correction. A spreadsheet total that adds the £36 carrier service to the £42 draft placeholder is not treated as a billed total, because the two amounts belong to different records and only one is in the carrier invoice.

Conclusion for the case file
For shipment LD-44720, the delivery record supports on-time performance, intact goods after inspection, and completion of the booked dock service. The preliminary note alleging lateness is not supported. The preliminary note alleging a duplicate carrier liftgate charge is not supported. The consignee did ask to reverse the £42.00 placeholder on the draft statement and expressly limited the request to that line; she did not ask for a refund of the freight or goods. The carrier invoice has one £36.00 tail-lift charge, no £42.00 indoor-drop charge, and a final total of £413.86.

Audit propositions
For classification, determine whether each statement is supported by the records above. Do not treat a dashboard label or preliminary note as proof when the underlying evidence conflicts with it.

[{"state":"# Saltmarsh shop floor / Slack export, typed up from the shift channel

Export note: messages below are from the fictional Saltmarsh Rentals small manufacturing shop. The shop builds short-run pump brackets and hose couplers, repairs returned fixtures, and packs orders for local distributors. Times are local. Some entries were copied from paper board notes; spelling and shorthand left as found. The channel has been noisy this week because the laser cutter was moved, two people were out, and the schedule board was rewritten twice. Read the underlying records rather than relying on anyone’s verdict.

## Monday, 07:12 — #floor

Mateo Kaur: Morning. Cutter 2 is still showing the old home point after the move. Don’t run the tall bracket program till Viktor checks the fence. Green bin is for verified pieces, grey bin is rework, blue tub is the customer-return stuff. Labels on the tubs are half peeled, so read the traveler too.

Greta Moreau: I put a fresh tape line down but the tape line is not a machine datum. Please stop calling it “zero.” The hard stop is 4 mm to the left of the old chalk mark. I measured twice with the same steel rule and once with the digital gauge. Gauge battery warning was on, so use the steel rule for now.

Viktor Rahman: Rechecked. Fence is square enough for setup, not released for production. Need one dry run with scrap, then compare the first two holes. Do not infer release from the green light; green light only means door interlock is closed.

Beatriz Delgado: There’s a pallet of Quill Supply stock at receiving. Packing slip says 24 pieces, count says 23. One was loose under the stretch wrap, found it, total is 24 now. No shortage. Tag says alloy 6061, PO says 6061-T6; ask before cutting because the tag does not state temper.

Uma Fischer: Customer returns from yesterday: four small couplers in the blue tub. Two look scuffed, one has a dent, one looks fine. The return slip only says “fit problem.” Don’t put them into good stock based on how they look. Need lot numbers before deciding anything.

Oren Haddad: I am not changing the schedule until the material question is closed. If the truck comes before lunch, put the pallet by rack C, not next to the saw. Forklift battery is low and I don’t want people shuffling the pallet twice.

Mateo Kaur: Understood. Also, ignore any old note that says cutter 2 released. It was copied from Friday’s board and is not today’s check.

## Monday, 08:06 — #quality

Greta Moreau: First dry run with scrap only. Program BR-17 loaded, but it was the file for the short bracket. Fixture sketch says tall bracket. I stopped before cut. No customer piece made.

Viktor Rahman: That is correct. Old filename was “BR17-final-final”; current revision on traveler is BR-17C. We have two files with similar names. Deleted nothing; moved old file to archive so audit can see it.

Beatriz Delgado: Paper traveler on the bench has BR-17C and batch 441, 12 pieces planned. Board had batch 414 from old job. I crossed out 414 on board and wrote 441. Photo sent to channel. Don’t read my first message as a new batch number; it was a correction.

Uma Fischer: The returned coupler with blue paint mark is lot H-208. Paint mark is customer’s mark, not a shop disposition. I found one more return slip in the envelope, same lot H-208, “thread binds after two turns.” It is not the same physical piece as the dented one; slip count and tub count both say four total.

Oren Haddad: I’m holding shipment cartons until the first article is signed. Not because I think there is a defect; because the process gate says hold. Please don’t turn a hold into a rejection in the log.

## Monday, 09:20 — #floor

Viktor Rahman: Scrap dry run passed travel check. First hole center measured 18.02 mm from left edge; drawing tolerance is 18.0 plus/minus 0.2. Second hole is 42.01 from edge; nominal 42.0, same tolerance. Those are scrap measurements, not first article approval.

Greta Moreau: We used the steel rule for the fence and gauge for hole position. The digital gauge had warning earlier but stayed on, then was replaced with a fresh cell at 08:55. Zero checked against the 20 mm block. Not claiming calibration certificate; only daily check.

Mateo Kaur: I see a green check in the cutter screen. That check means the maintenance checklist has all boxes clicked. It does not mean quality signed the part. I have left the run disabled pending the first article.

Beatriz Delgado: Another note on the board says “OK to ship.” That was my note from last week about the coupler order, not the bracket batch. It was stuck over the new board by mistake. Removed it; photo in thread.

Uma Fischer: Customer service asked whether we can promise noon pickup. I said no promise yet. Truck can arrive at noon but paperwork and inspection still need to happen. There is no confirmed pickup time in the email.

## Monday, 10:04 — #quality

Greta Moreau: First article cut from the correct alloy after temper confirmed as T6 by the certificate in the receiving folder. Piece ID 441-FA. Hole centers 18.03 and 42.02. Edge-to-hole distances inside drawing limits. Thickness 6.03 mm, drawing 6.0 +/- 0.1. Burr on lower right is visible with fingertip, and the drawing calls for deburr all edges. I am not signing until burr removed and rechecked.

Viktor Rahman: Deburred at 10:17. Greta rechecked with cotton swab and loupe. No snag after second pass. The rework note is about this first article only; it doesn’t mean the whole batch had burrs.

Mateo Kaur: First article approved 10:24, signed by Greta. Run released for batch 441, quantity 12. Keep pieces in green bin only after individual visual check. We have not approved batch 414; that number is obsolete board text.

Oren Haddad: I posted “all twelve good” in the order chat too early. Correction: that was a plan based on the traveler quantity, not a count of finished good parts. Sorry. At 10:30 there were only two cut, one signed first article plus one in process.

Beatriz Delgado: Copying correction into dispatch: no cartons closed, no shipping label printed. A draft label exists in the printer queue from Friday. Please don’t treat a queued draft as a shipped parcel.

## Monday, 11:00 — #floor

Mateo Kaur: Cut count is now 8. Visual check 1 through 8 complete. IDs 1-7 in green; ID 8 has a sharp corner and is in grey rework. That is one rework out of eight, not a scrap count. It can be fixed with hand file per work instruction WI-09.

Greta Moreau: I checked the sharp corner on 8. Material is not cracked. File pass and deburr needed. Recheck after. Don’t put it back in green until I mark it.

Viktor Rahman: We have three bins that look similar. Green tape means approved, grey tape means waiting for recheck, blue tape means customer return. A green label on the outside of a pallet is not enough if parts inside have no ID cards.

Uma Fischer: I counted 8 cut pieces at 10:58, not 9. The ninth line in my sheet is the first-article reference, not a separate production piece. My formula was including the FA row. I corrected the sheet; do not use the old screenshot.

Oren Haddad: Dispatch asked me for quantity. Answer is seven released, one pending rework, four still to cut. If you say “eight complete,” people will hear eight released, which is not true.

## Monday, 12:15 — #order-441

Beatriz Delgado: Customer asked whether all twelve brackets pass. Reply draft says “yes, all twelve passed.” That is not supported yet. We have seven released and one pending rework; four not cut. I deleted the draft, no email sent.

Mateo Kaur: Good catch. The mail client shows a green “sent” icon on drafts sometimes if it syncs the folder; actual sent folder has no copy. The customer has not received an answer from us today.

Greta Moreau: ID 8 rework done, corner softened and cotton test passes. I inspected it. Released at 12:23. So eight released now; four still not cut.

Viktor Rahman: Cut machine paused because the air line pressure dipped. No parts were cut during pause. Maintenance restored pressure at 12:41. First cut after restart is to be checked before continuing.

Oren Haddad: Please don’t count the test coupon as bracket 9. It is a rectangular scrap, marked SCRAP, and not part of the order.

## Monday, 13:02 — #quality

Greta Moreau: Restart check piece is a scrap coupon. Hole position is fine but coupon is not same outline and cannot replace a bracket first article. Batch 441 drawing rev C remains current. First article from before pause was approved; restart coupon is not an additional first article unless procedure calls for it.

Viktor Rahman: WI-17 says after an air-pressure alarm, cut one scrap travel check, inspect for movement, then resume if the clamp witness marks stay aligned. Witness marks stayed aligned. I logged the alarm and check. No requirement to scrap already approved pieces.

Mateo Kaur: Run resumed 13:14. Pieces 9 and 10 cut. Piece 9 passed visual and dimensions spot check. Piece 10 has a shallow tool mark, within cosmetic allowance? Need compare to photo standard, not guess.

Greta Moreau: Photo standard says marks are acceptable only if fingernail does not catch and no coating planned. This batch is bare alloy; fingernail does not catch. Mark is acceptable. ID 10 released. That is now ten released, two to cut.

Uma Fischer: Board says 11 done. It counted the scrap restart coupon as one. I changed the board to ten released, one scrap coupon, two remaining. There were twelve ordered. Count the named bracket IDs, not the rows.

## Monday, 14:30 — #floor

Beatriz Delgado: The customer’s pickup window is 16:00-17:00, but dispatch cutoff for same-day paperwork is 15:30. If last inspection is after 15:30, parcel waits until tomorrow. We have no guarantee the carrier will accept it late. This is a window, not an appointment.

Oren Haddad: Pieces 11 and 12 are cut. 11 passes. 12 has a small burr at the inside slot. Grey bin, pending deburr. Don’t count it released yet.

Greta Moreau: 12 deburred and checked 14:48. All edges smooth by cotton and visual. Released. Current released count 12. Separate scrap coupon does not change ordered quantity. Final tally: twelve bracket IDs, all released, one scrap coupon, one rework operation on ID 8, one deburr on 12.

Mateo Kaur: I’ve signed the traveler. There is no separate inspection for packing, but dispatch must match IDs to traveler. No order quantity discrepancy.

Viktor Rahman: I saw a note in the tool cabinet: “batch short one, ship 11.” That is from a different job last month. It has no date or batch ID. Ignore it for 441.

## Monday, 15:06 — #dispatch
