10. Foxglove Rentals repair slip: three plates received; two named in authorization email, one inspection only; X2 specifically needs manager review before straightening. The handwritten “all approved” note is unsigned and contradicted by the email restrictions.

## Appendix C — notes on shop conventions copied from controlled sheets

WI-09: Grey-marked parts are not released until the named operation is complete and the inspector signs recheck. A part can move from grey to green after successful recheck. Scrap coupons are not order pieces even if their measurements resemble the workpiece.

WI-17: A new batch requires a first-article check. After an air-pressure alarm, use a scrap travel check and verify clamp witness marks before resuming. The rule does not say all previously approved parts become invalid automatically. Any conclusion about a given part still depends on its own traveler and recorded checks.

WI-04: For the H-208 type of coupler, the final gauge sampling plan on the card calls for five pieces. A five-piece pass is evidence about those sampled pieces and the documented process check; it does not convert the record into a 100% inspection.

Packing rule: “packed” means protected and labeled in the dispatch area; “collected” requires carrier scan; “delivered” requires a receiving event or customer confirmation. The board sometimes uses “ship” loosely, but the register should use the defined stages.

Accounts note: An invoice can be marked paid only after a payment is matched in the ledger or a recognized payment record is entered. Customer receipt of goods is not payment. A vendor invoice and a customer invoice may sit in the same folder; read issuer, recipient, and transaction direction.

Return rule: A customer claim is recorded as a claim, the shop inspection as an observation, and cause as a separate engineering conclusion. Approval to replace is a remedy decision and does not by itself prove fault timing or origin.

Order rule: A request for quote, an estimate, an email asking whether a date is possible, and a conditional preference do not replace a signed purchase order or change order. A handwritten schedule note does not create customer authorization.

## Appendix D — later correction thread, Monday following week

Mateo Kaur: Reviewing the prior week export for handover. One person copied the “all four defective” line into a new tracking row. Please stop that copy. The signed case card still says two gauge failures, two passes, cause open.

Greta Moreau: The row now says “two of four fail repeat gauge; one visibly dented; cause undetermined.” That is accurate as of the last test. We have not received a new test result.

Viktor Rahman: Customer replacement shipment has now been collected Monday at 09:12, two units, H-211, labels checked. Customer acknowledgement is not yet in. So the items are shipped, not yet documented delivered.

Beatriz Delgado: Correct. Customer requested Tuesday delivery, but tracking estimate is Tuesday. An estimate is not proof of delivery. I’ll update after a receiving scan or their reply.

Uma Fischer: New inventory count: H-211 replacements were two finished couplers; issue two from shelf, balance now zero in that bin. Original H-208 return items remain four, segregated. Don’t add replacement units to the original return count.

Oren Haddad: I see an automated dashboard verdict “case closed: 4 of 4 replaced.” Wrong. It counts four return lines rather than two authorized replacement lines. Case remains open for delivery confirmation and root-cause disposition.

Mateo Kaur: Dashboard rule has been corrected to count replacement IDs R-62-1 and R-62-2. It now displays two shipped, pending receipt, investigation open. Please do not rely on yesterday’s cached view.

Greta Moreau: No fresh finding on cause. The original five sampled pieces passed at production; that doesn’t rule out all possible later variation, and two current failures don’t alone prove when they began. Keep the conclusion at undetermined.

Viktor Rahman: Confirmed carrier scan has two IDs, not four. One carton. Weight is 0.9 kg gross. This corroborates two replacement items, but weight itself isn’t the primary count.

Beatriz Delgado: Customer message received 10:05: “box is on the way, thanks.” That is not receipt. No delivery scan yet.

Oren Haddad: Updated row says pending. I also removed my old “four replacements sent” note from the live view, leaving it in archive with the correction record.

## Appendix E — end-of-export audit reminders

The export contains several confident statements that were later corrected. “All twelve good” appeared before twelve parts had been produced. “Shipped” appeared before a carrier scan. “All four defective” appeared before the return inspection and was contradicted by item-level measurements. “All 16 passed” appeared while one production part was still uncut. “Paid” appeared once based only on a delivery receipt, then became true later after a matched bank payment. “Four replacements sent” was a count-copying error; two replacements were approved, packed, and later collected.

The proper reading depends on the question’s time and definition. If asking whether batch 441 ultimately had all ordered pieces released, the traveler supports twelve out of twelve. If asking whether the early Monday board proved that, it did not. If asking whether all four H-208 returns failed, repeated gauge results contradict that claim: only B and C failed; A and D passed. If asking whether root cause was known, the notes consistently leave it open. If asking whether the customer’s payment was ultimately received, the matched ledger entry supports yes, but the earlier delivery confirmation alone did not.

The message authors are not always careful with stage labels. “Done,” “OK,” “shipped,” “bad,” and “paid” occur in casual notes and may refer to plans, intermediate steps, or copied text. Controlled traveler fields, item-level inspection marks, carrier scans, bank matches, and signed customer authorizations provide the decisive evidence where available. Preserve superseded entries for traceability, but do not treat them as current fact merely because they remain visible in the export.

Nothing in this export authorizes changing a customer order, waiving a required first article, claiming a root cause, counting scrap as production, or treating a request as an approval. When evidence supports a narrow conclusion, state that conclusion narrowly. When a draft verdict conflicts with the underlying records, the conflict should be documented rather than resolved by repeating the draft. When later evidence changes a status, the status should be time-qualified: for example, packed Monday, collected Tuesday; unpaid on the morning snapshot, paid after the matched transaction; two replacements packed Friday, collected Monday, delivery still pending at the last message.

The shop’s shorthand can also collapse roles. Quill Supply is a supplier in the material and vendor invoice records; Granite Foods is the buyer for the bracket order; Saltmarsh Rentals is the shop making and invoicing the brackets; Foxglove Rentals is the customer for a separate plate-repair job. A name appearing next to a lot, invoice, work order, or message does not by itself establish who owes whom or who made a request. The field headers and transaction direction matter.

Finally, counts should be tied to their population. Twelve is the 441 order quantity, not the return count. Thirty is the H-208 production lot, not the number gauge-tested. Four is the number of couplers returned, not the number that failed or the number of replacements authorized. Sixteen is the 447 order quantity, not the number of pieces in a single carton. Two is the approved replacement quantity, not the number of original failures inferred from a customer’s first broad complaint. A near-matching number elsewhere in the thread is not a substitute for checking the IDs and records.

message.content:
[{"state":"Product review and community test dossier: Emberwake Realms, patch 4.8.2

Typed up from the review channel, test-room notes, and the attached session ledger. Typos in the original shorthand are left in where they do not make a sentence unreadable. The review was posted by Xiu O'Neill, who plays under the handle KettleComet. Xiu has played Emberwake Realms for about six months and usually tests co-op quests with a small group. The game is an online action role-playing game. This dossier covers the review’s claims about refund eligibility, the guild-voice setting, and the weekly event reward. The tester’s verdicts are included as claims to check, not as replacements for the underlying records.

Review channel post, Monday:

“I came into patch 4.8.2 wanting to like it. The new marsh map is pretty, the lantern animation is good, and the little bell sound when a party member finds a chest is weirdly satisfying. I’m not saying the whole thing is broken. I am saying the store and some of the settings are a mess if you actually read the screens instead of guessing from the icons.

“I bought the Warden’s Wake cosmetic bundle. The store card said it included a cloak, a shoulder lantern, and a dye voucher. In my account I see the cloak and lantern. The voucher isn’t there. Support asked me to relog twice, so I did. Still no voucher. I haven’t asked for a refund yet; I asked whether they could add the missing item. I’m mentioning this because the first staff reply called it a ‘refund demand,’ which it isn’t.

“The voice setting is also confusing. I set guild voice to off, or thought I did. I could still hear the guild during the opening lobby, but not once the expedition loaded. Maybe that lobby uses another channel. I don’t know. Don’t turn that into ‘voice was on the entire time.’ My friend Bao Sorensen says the sound was coming from a video in the background, but the lobby transcript has a guild member talking. I checked the setting again after the session, and it showed off.

“Last thing: the weekly Lantern Run. The post in the event panel said a player needed 12 route marks to claim the badge. I got 11. The badge page said ‘complete,’ which I took to mean the run itself was complete, not that I got the reward. The tester note says I qualified for the badge. That’s not right if the rule is twelve and the ledger really says eleven. I could have missed a mark, sure, but the server record is what I’m asking you to read.”

Review metadata: account KettleComet; purchase date 6 September; review date 22 September; bundle Warden’s Wake; patch 4.8.2; game region North Lantern; party size usually three; device type not used to determine any of the questions below.

Reviewer’s item list, copied into the post:
- Warden’s Wake cloak: present in wardrobe.
- Warden’s Wake shoulder lantern: present in wardrobe.
- Warden’s Wake dye voucher: absent in inventory at time of post.
- Purchase confirmation: present, 1 bundle, 1,200 brass.
- Refund request sent: no.
- Support contact asking for missing voucher: yes.

Internal review worksheet, initial pass:
“Refund: likely requested; player unhappy about missing voucher and store item not delivered. Keep under review. Voice: probably enabled, since player heard guild speech in lobby. Event: badge earned, panel says complete. Overall sentiment: mostly positive, with a few small concerns.”

The worksheet was entered by a volunteer reviewer who did not open the account ledger or the audio-channel trace. A second volunteer added: “These summaries are only shortcuts. Verify the original evidence before using an outcome. ‘Complete’ in the event panel can refer to a run and does not automatically mean a reward threshold was met.”

Patch-specific customer support policy excerpt, current as of 1 September:
“Refund requests must be explicit. A report of a missing item, a request to restore an item, or a question about delivery is not by itself a refund request. A purchase becomes refund-eligible only when both conditions are met: (a) the player explicitly asks to reverse the purchase or return the purchase amount, and (b) the request is received no later than 14 calendar days after the purchase. The purchase date is day zero. Count the following calendar day as day one. A support agent may offer a fix instead, but an offer does not alter what the player requested. If a player first asks for a replacement and later expressly asks for a refund, use the date of the express refund request. Do not infer a refund request from dissatisfaction, a missing entitlement, or a staff member’s summary.”

Account purchase and contact ledger:
6 September, 09:14 — Purchase posted: Warden’s Wake cosmetic bundle, 1,200 brass.
7 September, 18:20 — Player opens ticket: “The dye voucher did not show up after relog. Can you add the missing voucher or tell me where it is?”
8 September, 11:02 — Support response: “We can re-sync the entitlement. We cannot treat this message as a refund request unless you ask to return the purchase.”
9 September, 21:16 — Player replies: “Please do the re-sync. I’m not asking to return the bundle at this point.”
15 September, 08:40 — Support marks voucher synchronization complete.
16 September, 12:07 — Player confirms cloak and lantern show; voucher still absent.
20 September, 17:55 — Player posts review.
22 September, 10:03 — The review worksheet is completed.
There is no later message from the player requesting a refund in the provided ledger.

A moderator note attached to the initial worksheet reads: “Player says ‘still absent’ after repeated support contact. That is obviously a refund demand under normal usage. Mark yes; don’t overcomplicate it.” The note’s writer did not cite a sentence asking for the purchase to be returned. The policy excerpt above is the rule for this review exercise.

Guild audio settings: help page excerpt, revision 4.8:
“Guild Voice has a per-session toggle. When disabled before entering a session, the client should not receive guild voice audio in the expedition instance. The social lobby has a separate preview channel, used to play recent guild announcements and voice snippets. The lobby preview can be heard even when expedition Guild Voice is disabled. A lobby preview does not prove that the expedition channel was enabled. Conversely, an enabled icon in the settings menu alone does not establish that audio was actually delivered; consult the channel trace when available. The mute button is not the same as the Guild Voice toggle. The mute button silences a selected speaker locally; the toggle controls whether the client joins the guild voice channel. Party voice and guild voice are distinct.”

Session settings trace for KettleComet:
Session ID NL-88403; 19 September; client version 4.8.2.
18:42:10 — User opens audio settings in social lobby.
18:42:18 — Guild Voice toggle set to OFF.
18:42:19 — Client confirms setting saved.
18:46:00 — Social lobby preview channel plays guild announcement snippet, speaker label “TernSeven.”
18:47:31 — Expedition instance begins.
18:47:33 — Guild Voice subscription state: DISABLED.
18:47:33–19:19:08 — Guild voice packets delivered to client: 0.
18:47:33–19:19:08 — Party voice packets delivered: 428.
19:19:12 — Expedition ends.
19:20:04 — User opens settings; Guild Voice toggle displays OFF.
19:20:15 — User leaves lobby.

The session trace is the server-side record for this session. It distinguishes the preview channel from the expedition channel. A community helper looking only at the review post might see the words “heard the guild” and conclude that the toggle was enabled. Another helper might notice the setting was off at the end and conclude it was off throughout. Neither shortcut is as strong as the sequence in the trace: the toggle was saved off before the expedition, the lobby preview occurred before the expedition, and the expedition subscription was disabled with no guild packets delivered. The party voice count does not change the guild voice state, because the two channels have separate labels and separate packet totals.

Volunteer tester’s audio verdict, attached to the worksheet:
“Guild Voice was enabled for the run because KettleComet heard a guild speaker. This is a confirmed settings failure.”

Audio audit comment by moderator Rosa Petrov:
“Don’t repeat the verdict just because it is written down. The statement may be right or wrong; inspect the channel rows. The lobby sample is not the expedition feed. Also, ‘voice’ without a channel name is too broad to answer a question about Guild Voice during the expedition.”

Event page, weekly Lantern Run, rules shown for 15–21 September:
“Players earn route marks by completing marked branches. A player must have at least 12 route marks recorded before the weekly reset to claim the Lantern Keeper badge. ‘At least 12’ includes 12 and any higher number. The event completion banner means the player finished one run; it does not certify the badge threshold. Marks from an abandoned run do not count. Marks earned after the weekly reset apply to the next week. The account page can take several minutes to refresh, but the server ledger is authoritative.”

The event has three map branches and several optional lantern caches. A run completion may happen with fewer than twelve marks. Players can also collect marks across more than one run during the same event week. The number of runs is not itself the badge condition. A player can complete the run banner and fail the badge threshold, or reach the threshold and claim the badge after several runs. The distinction was added after players repeatedly mistook a run-completion message for a reward confirmation.

KettleComet’s route ledger for the relevant event week:
Run LR-0919-A, started 19 September 18:47, completed 19:19.
- Branch marks: 4
- Cache marks: 3
- Bonus route marks: 1
- Abandoned-branch marks: 0
- Run total: 8
Run LR-0920-B, started 20 September 20:05, completed 20:31.
- Branch marks: 2
- Cache marks: 1
- Bonus route marks: 0
- Run total: 3
Weekly total before reset: 8 + 3 = 11.
Reset time: 22 September 00:00.
Marks after reset: none in the supplied record.
Badge threshold: 12.
Badge claim transaction: none.
Run completion banner: yes, for each completed run.

A draft event summary created by the volunteer tester says:
“Lantern Keeper badge: earned. Player completed the Lantern Run and the event page showed complete. The reviewer’s total is 12 because 8 plus 3 rounds to 12 for event scoring.” The event system does not round route marks. The rule says at least 12 recorded marks, not an approximate total. The draft has no ledger source for its stated 12. An adjacent comment says “Maybe a hidden completion mark?” The ledger lists the run totals and the weekly total directly; no hidden mark is listed.

A later quality check by Callum Sorensen says:
“I’m not deciding from the player’s guess or the volunteer’s guess. The threshold is exact. The supplied entries give eight on the first run and three on the second, making eleven before reset. A completed run is not the same as a badge award. If there is another credited mark, it needs to appear in the authoritative event record.”

General dossier handling note:
The review worksheet, moderator notes, and volunteer summaries are opinions or provisional verdicts. They may be useful pointers, but they are not governing rules and should not be treated as evidence that overrides the source records. The policy page controls the refund criterion, the session trace controls the audio delivery criterion, and the event rules plus route ledger control the badge criterion. This note does not declare any answer; it identifies which records can resolve each question.

Additional review-channel context, included because the worksheet cites overall sentiment:
Xiu’s opening post praised the marsh map and lantern effect. It also criticized the missing voucher and confusing audio behavior. The review rating was three stars out of five. The text says “I wanted to like it,” not “I demand my money back.” The star rating is not part of the refund policy. The player’s praise of one feature does not prove that another feature worked, and the player’s complaint does not prove a refund request was made. The reviewer writes in short bursts and sometimes leaves out punctuation, which is why the worksheet volunteer attempted to interpret the tone. The account ledger provides the actual wording for the support request.

Internal ticket export, verbatim snippets:
Ticket 1, 7 September:
Player: “bundle bought yesterday? receipt says 6th. cloak ok, lamp ok. dye voucher missing. can you put the voucher in my inventory or check why its not there”
Agent: “I can check entitlement sync. To confirm, you are asking us to add the missing voucher, not reverse the purchase?”
Player: “yes add it please, thats what i mean”
Ticket 2, 9 September:
Agent: “We can retry sync.”
Player: “Do that. not asking to return bundle now. I still want the item i paid for.”
Ticket 3, 16 September:
Player: “sync did not fix it. please escalate missing voucher. dont close this as solved.”
No text in tickets 1–3 asks for brass to be returned, asks to reverse the bundle purchase, or asks to cancel the transaction. The absence of such language is relevant because the policy requires an explicit request. The ticket’s “paid for” wording refers to the missing item and is not itself a return request, especially in the immediate context of asking for the voucher to be added.

A second volunteer wrote on the review card:
“Refund requested: yes, because any player saying they did not receive what they paid for is asking for money back, even if they don’t use refund words.”
The current policy does not define a refund request that way. It specifically distinguishes missing-item reports and restoration requests from requests to return the purchase. The reviewer should apply the stated policy rather than a volunteer’s broad interpretation. This annotation is an example of a planted verdict: it provides a confident classification, but the underlying request text and written rule have to be checked.

The audio topic also generated two different summary notes:
Volunteer note A: “Guild audio was on, because KettleComet says they heard guild talk.”
Volunteer note B: “Guild audio was off, because the settings screen showed OFF after the expedition.”
The two notes reach the same eventual yes/no possibility by different shortcuts only if the question is phrased vaguely. The criterion here is specifically whether Guild Voice audio was delivered during the expedition. To answer that, use the trace’s expedition subscription and packet rows. A social-lobby preview is not the expedition feed, and the post-expedition screen is not by itself a full history of the session. The trace supplies both timing and channel identity.

The event topic generated a similar pair:
Volunteer note A: “Badge earned, the page says complete.”
Volunteer note B: “Badge not earned, the tester’s ledger calculation says 11.”
The second note happens to agree with the raw arithmetic, but the reason must still be checked against the rule and authoritative entries. The first note treats a run banner as a badge confirmation, although the rules explicitly say it is not. A correct review should distinguish an outcome supported by evidence from an outcome repeated from a planted summary.

Review publication note:
The community team does not ask reviewers to decide whether Xiu is generally trustworthy, whether the game is fun, or whether the volunteers meant well. The questions below concern only whether particular claims are supported by the provided records. Do not convert uncertainty about one subject into an answer about another. The purchase ledger, audio trace, and event ledger are separate evidence sets, even though the same account appears in each. The score, patch version, party size, and review tone do not alter the written threshold or channel trace.

Appendix: how event marks are recorded:
Each successful branch mark is written as an integer to the event ledger when the branch gate closes. Optional cache marks are written separately. A bonus mark is only granted when the full route condition is met; the field is zero if it is not. The weekly total is the sum of credited entries for the account during the active event window. The interface may show a run-completion banner after a completed route, irrespective of the mark total. The badge service reads the weekly total and creates a claim transaction only if the threshold is reached. A missing claim transaction does not, by itself, prove a player was below the threshold if the record is incomplete; in this dossier, however, the route ledger is supplied as the weekly account record and includes both completed runs and the total before reset. No third run or separate mark grant appears in the supplied record.

Appendix: channel terms used in the log:
“Guild Voice” is the group channel attached to guild membership. “Party Voice” is the voice channel for the current party. “Lobby Preview” is an announcement playback feature in the social lobby, not a live expedition subscription. “Packets delivered” counts audio payloads received by the client in the named channel during the stated interval. A zero count in the Guild Voice row means no guild voice packets were delivered in that expedition interval. It does not say the player heard no sound of any kind, because party voice and lobby preview are separate. The question should not be broadened to all audio or to whether the player heard a voice at any point.

Appendix: customer-service terms used in the policy:
“Explicitly asks” means the player’s words state a request to reverse the purchase or return its purchase amount. “Can you add the missing item?” asks for restoration of the entitlement. “I’m unhappy” expresses a view but does not state a return request. The date window uses calendar days, not business days, and purchase day is day zero. The time between the purchase and the first ticket is within the stated period, but timing alone cannot satisfy the separate explicit-request condition. A policy outcome requires both conditions, not either condition alone. A volunteer cannot waive either requirement by labeling a complaint as a refund demand.

Appendix: source reliability note:
The server-side traces and the current policy excerpt are the records selected for this exercise. The review post is reliable evidence of what the reviewer wrote, but its phrase “heard the guild” does not identify the channel. The worksheet is reliable evidence of what the volunteer concluded, but not necessarily of the underlying event. The event banner is reliable evidence that a run completed, but its meaning is defined narrowly by the event page. The ledger gives the individual marks and the weekly total. Where an annotation conflicts with the rule or raw record, use the rule and record. This note describes the evidence hierarchy and is not itself an answer to any criterion.

More review comments, copied from the thread:
Bao Sorensen: “I was in the party. I remember hearing somebody in the lobby before we queued. In the map i mostly heard party chat. I did not check Xiu’s settings.”
Xiu O'Neill: “yeah, lobby was the bit i meant at first. once the map loaded it was quiet from guild. still confusing becuase the same word voice is on both screens.”
Moderator: “Please keep the report to what the log can establish. Other players’ memory can add context but not replace the session trace.”
A volunteer then wrote: “Player corrected themselves, so the original report is unreliable; mark the setting as unknown.” The server trace resolves whether expedition guild audio was delivered regardless of how the player initially described it. The correction does not turn the server record into an unknown. Another volunteer wrote: “Mark enabled because the player first said they heard guild.” That repeats the initial ambiguity without accounting for the player’s clarification or the separate lobby channel.

More event comments:
Xiu O'Neill: “I see 11 in the ledger, but the event screen had the word complete. If the threshold is really 12, then i missed it. I thought maybe completing the second run gave one extra.”
Moderator: “The rules say a completed run is not an extra mark unless an entry records a mark. Check the weekly total.”
Volunteer tester: “The badge is definitely earned. I tested a similar event last month and it awarded completion credit.”
Quality reviewer: “A different event is not evidence for this event. The current rule and this week’s ledger are the relevant sources.”
There is no record of an extra completion mark in the listed ledger. The volunteer’s claim that a similar event behaved differently is not an entry for KettleComet’s account during this week.

Review author’s handwritten-style note, transcribed by community staff:
“bundle missing dye. asked em to add it. not trying to send whole thing back. i know ppl keep calling it a refund but thats not my wording. guild sound only in waiting bit? likely preview. route total says 11, i did two runs. badge needs 12. somebody wrote 12 on the sticky but where from. dont use the sticky if the log says different.”
The transcription is retained as context, but the original ledger and policy remain available. The note uses clipped phrasing and contains a question mark after “waiting bit,” so it should not be used alone to establish the precise audio session behavior. It does, however, make clear that Xiu disputes the worksheet’s description of the purchase request and doubts the planted event total.

Additional quality-control checklist filled by Rosa Petrov:
1. Identify the criterion’s exact object. “Refund request” is not the same as “missing item report.” “Guild Voice during expedition” is not the same as “any voice heard.” “Badge threshold met” is not the same as “run completed.”
2. Identify which source controls the answer. Read the policy for refund conditions, the server trace for channel delivery, and the event rule with the full weekly ledger for marks.
3. Treat quoted opinions as claims to test. A reviewer, moderator, volunteer, player, or prior worksheet can be mistaken. Their confidence is not a substitute for the evidence.
4. Preserve exact wording and units. Calendar days are calendar days. Route marks are integer credits. The written minimum is at least twelve, not “about twelve.”
5. Do not infer a positive answer from an adjacent fact. A purchase is not automatically refundable because an item is missing; a voice is not automatically guild voice because it is heard in the lobby; a complete route is not automatically a badge.
Rosa’s checklist is procedural guidance. The source records above provide the actual facts to apply.

A final worksheet fragment, found under the event tab:
“Auto-summary: threshold met. Reason: player says the event was complete. Confidence high.”
The automated summary does not show its arithmetic and uses the run banner as its reason. The event documentation explicitly distinguishes the banner from the reward threshold. Another fragment under audio:
“Auto-summary: channel active. Reason: voice snippet heard.”
This also fails to name the channel or interval. Another fragment under purchase:
“Auto-summary: refund request. Reason: missing entitlement complaint.”
The policy expressly says a missing-item report is not, by itself, a refund request. These summaries are included so an auditor can compare them with the records; they are not authoritative fields.

The dossier ends with the source records rather than a final outcome, because the purpose of the review exercise is to apply the checklist to evidence rather than copy an earlier verdict. The account ledger records the player’s exact support requests. The session trace distinguishes the lobby preview from the expedition channel. The event ledger gives the marks and the written requirement.
