[{"state":"FORMAL SERVICE REVIEW PACKET — HARBORLIGHT HOTEL AND DINING ROOM
Reporting period: 4–10 September
Prepared for: Operations Review Committee
Purpose: Reconcile guest communications, restaurant records, and internal assessments for three service cases. The committee is to rely on the underlying records and the quoted communications, not on any preliminary label entered by staff. All amounts are in local dollars. Dates and times are shown as recorded by the hotel. The hotel’s standard practice is to record a refund request only when a sender explicitly asks for money back; a complaint, request for an explanation, or request for a replacement is not by itself a refund request. A food concern is recorded as a guest-reported issue only when the guest’s own communication describes it. Staff assessments are retained for audit purposes but are not substitutes for the source material.

CONTENTS
A. Case A — room folio reconciliation and guest correspondence
B. Case B — restaurant meal concern, support ticket, and kitchen record
C. Case C — voicemail transcript and dining service review
D. General handling notes and appendices

A. CASE A — ROOM FOLIO RECONCILIATION AND GUEST CORRESPONDENCE

A1. Folio extract
Guest reference: HL-4107
Room: 218
Stay: 4 September, 15:20 check-in; 6 September, 09:10 check-out
Reservation name in the hotel system: Maren Vale
Booking channel: direct telephone reservation
Room rate: 184.00 per night
Number of nights billed: 2
Room subtotal: 368.00
Local occupancy tax: 36.80
Restaurant charge posted to room: 42.00
Parking charge posted to room: 18.00
Total folio: 464.80
Card payment captured at check-out: 464.80
Balance after payment: 0.00

The guest signed the folio at the desk. The printed folio included the room subtotal, occupancy tax, restaurant charge, and parking charge as separate lines. The restaurant charge corresponds to a dinner ticket dated 5 September and the parking charge corresponds to the vehicle registration entered at arrival. The payment terminal record shows one capture for 464.80. No additional payment capture appears under the guest reference or the card-token suffix recorded on the folio. The folio export contains a note from the night supervisor, entered at 22:14 on 5 September: “Guest queried the total; explain final folio at departure.” The note does not say that the guest asked for a refund.

A2. Guest message received 6 September, 13:05
From: Maren Vale
To: Guest Services
Subject: Question about checkout statement

“Hello. I have now looked at the statement. I see two nights, tax, dinner, and parking listed separately. Could you explain why the dinner was placed on the room account rather than paid at the dining room? I signed the folio, but I would like to understand the procedure. Please send me an itemized copy showing the dinner ticket time and the parking entry. I am not asking you to return any money; I want the entries explained and documented. Thank you.”

A3. Staff case note entered 6 September, 13:22
Author: Desk Associate L. Fen
Status selected: REFUND REQUEST — GUEST DISPUTES CHARGE
Comment: “Guest disputes dinner posting and wants money back. Send to accounts.”

A4. Accounts review, 7 September
The accounts clerk compared the charge posting time with the restaurant point-of-sale ticket. The 42.00 dinner ticket was closed at 20:46 on 5 September, signed with the room number, and posted to the folio at 21:03. The guest’s message asks for an explanation and an itemized copy. It expressly says that the guest is not asking for money to be returned. The associate’s status label is therefore not supported by the guest’s words. The clerk left the status in the system pending committee review rather than overwriting the original audit entry. The clerk’s factual conclusion reads: “No explicit request for repayment located in source message.”

A5. Follow-up from Guest Services, 7 September, 09:10
“Dear Ms Vale, thank you for contacting us. We have attached the itemized folio and verified that the dinner charge is the restaurant ticket you signed on 5 September. The parking line matches the vehicle registered at arrival. We have not made any adjustment to the folio. Please let us know if you need another copy.”

A6. Additional review notes
The guest did not use the words “refund,” “return the payment,” “credit my card,” or any equivalent request in the message. The guest did not state that the dinner was not consumed. The guest asked for an explanation and documentation. The internal status was a preliminary staff interpretation, not a quotation from the guest. The signed folio and charge details are included to provide context; they do not change what the message asks for. The case is closed as an information request for operational tracking, while the staff status remains visible in the audit history.

A7. Desk training reference copied into the case file
The hotel uses the following distinction when coding guest messages. “Refund request” means that the sender explicitly asks the hotel to return money, reverse a payment, issue a credit, or otherwise repay a specified charge. “Charge question” means that the sender asks for an explanation, a copy, or a reconciliation without asking for repayment. An employee may initially select a code based on an assumption, but the code must be checked against the sender’s actual message. The reference is included here because the preliminary code and the source message differ. It is not an instruction to infer that every charge question is a refund request.

B. CASE B — RESTAURANT MEAL CONCERN, SUPPORT TICKET, AND KITCHEN RECORD

B1. Support ticket header
Ticket: DIN-8821
Opened: 8 September, 19:34
Location: Harborlight Dining Room
Table: 12
Reservation: two guests, 19:00
Ticket category chosen by first recipient: “No dietary or meal issue”
First recipient’s comment: “Guest was happy; no problem reported.”
Status: awaiting quality review

B2. Message from guest, 8 September, 19:31
From: Elian Shore
Channel: dining-room contact form

“Good evening. I am writing about tonight’s dinner at table 12. I told the server before ordering that I cannot eat sesame. The menu description for the green bowl did not mention sesame, but the bowl arrived with sesame dressing. I pointed it out before tasting it, and the server took it away. I then ordered the plain rice and grilled vegetables. The replacement plate had the same dressing on the side, so I asked for another plate. The second replacement was prepared without sesame and I ate that one. I was not taken ill and I am not saying that I ate the first bowl. Please record that the first two servings contained sesame despite my request. I am also reporting that the replacement took a long time and that the server did not tell me the dressing was included. I do not need a medical response; I want the kitchen and service team to know what happened.”

B3. Restaurant ticket record
Table 12, 8 September:
19:06 — two menus delivered.
19:12 — guest asks server about sesame in green bowl.
19:18 — order entered: green bowl, no sesame; rice and grilled vegetables.
19:31 — first bowl delivered with standard sesame dressing; returned before tasting.
19:39 — replacement order entered; note says “dressing separate.”
19:48 — replacement plate delivered; side dressing appears on tray. Server records “guest says sesame issue.”
19:51 — second replacement requested.
20:08 — plain rice and grilled vegetables delivered, no dressing; guest eats.
20:16 — table check presented.
20:22 — payment complete.

The kitchen’s standard green-bowl preparation includes sesame dressing unless the order ticket carries the allergy flag. The initial order carried a plain-text note but the allergy flag was not selected. The replacement ticket carried the note “dressing separate,” which did not prevent a dressing cup from being sent. The second replacement ticket carried the allergy flag and a no-sesame instruction. The kitchen review found no record that the guest ate either serving containing dressing. The review did find two servings sent with sesame dressing after the guest had said sesame must be avoided.

B4. Server’s incident statement, 9 September, 08:15
“I remember the guest asking about sesame. I told the kitchen and entered ‘no sesame’ in the notes. I should also have selected the allergy marker. I brought the first bowl and the guest immediately said it had dressing. I removed it. The next plate had a small dressing cup on the side; I did not see it until the guest pointed it out. The last plate had no sesame dressing. The guest seemed calm, thanked me, and ate the last plate. I did not hear a request for compensation.”

B5. Kitchen supervisor review, 9 September, 10:40
The supervisor examined the order screen, kitchen printer slips, and the server statement. The initial ticket’s omission of the allergy marker contributed to the first incorrect plate. The “dressing separate” note on the replacement did not make the plate sesame-free and was not an adequate substitute for the allergy flag. The second replacement was correctly prepared. The guest’s account and the restaurant records agree that two servings containing sesame dressing were sent to the table and that the guest identified both before eating them. The records do not support a conclusion that the guest consumed sesame or suffered an illness.

B6. Preliminary quality-control entry, 9 September, 11:02
Author: Review Clerk M. Dorr
Summary field: “No issue reported. Guest was satisfied after replacement; close without action.”
Reason entered: “No medical event and final plate eaten.”

B7. Quality manager’s correction note, 9 September, 11:20
“The preliminary summary is not consistent with the guest’s report or the service records. Whether the guest became ill is not the only criterion for a reported food concern. The guest explicitly reports that two servings contained sesame dressing after the guest had disclosed an inability to eat sesame. The guest also reports a delay and a failure to communicate that dressing was included. The fact that the last plate was eaten does not erase the earlier events. Keep the preliminary summary in the audit trail and code the report from the source evidence.”

B8. Service recovery correspondence, 9 September, 12:04
From: Dining Room Manager
To: Elian Shore

“Dear Mr Shore, thank you for documenting your experience. We are sorry that the first bowl and the first replacement both arrived with sesame dressing after you had explained your restriction. We have reviewed the order notes and will remind the team to use the allergy marker as well as written notes. We have also discussed clear communication about sauces and replacement timing. Our records show that the final plate was prepared without sesame dressing. We appreciate that you brought the issue to our attention.”

B9. Internal handling guide excerpt
A reported meal issue may concern an ingredient, preparation, temperature, timing, service communication, or another feature of the meal. It is not limited to illness or injury. A staff comment such as “no issue” is an assessment to be checked against the guest’s report and the transaction record. For this packet, count a category only when the guest’s own message supports it. Do not infer that a guest ate an item when the guest says it was removed before tasting. Do not infer that a resolved problem never occurred. When a message reports multiple distinct problems, preserve each supported category rather than selecting only the most serious one.

B10. Follow-up call log
9 September, 14:30 — Manager called the guest. The guest confirmed that the report was intended to cover the two plates containing sesame dressing, the replacement delay, and the lack of clear information about the dressing. The guest again said the first plate was not tasted and that the final plate was eaten. The guest did not claim illness. The manager offered to answer any questions about the kitchen review. The guest said the written acknowledgement was sufficient. No additional issue was raised during this call.

B11. Payment and service record
The guest paid the printed amount for the meal. The payment record contains no reversal or additional charge. The restaurant’s ordinary procedure allows managers to consider a goodwill adjustment, but no adjustment was promised in the contact form or the call. This payment information does not negate the reported meal concerns. The report is about the meal and service; the guest did not ask for repayment in the source form. The ticket’s “no issue” category was selected before a quality reviewer compared the source message with the restaurant records.

B12. Detailed chronology for quality review
18:42 — host records both guests as arrived.
18:55 — guests seated at table 12.
19:02 — server presents menus and identifies the evening’s specials.
19:06 — water is served.
19:12 — guest asks whether the green bowl contains sesame. The server consults the printed menu, which does not list the dressing ingredients, and then asks the kitchen verbally.
19:16 — kitchen response is relayed: standard bowl has sesame dressing, but it can be omitted.
19:18 — order is entered with a written “no sesame” note. The server does not activate the allergy marker.
19:31 — first bowl reaches table with dressing already mixed through the greens. Guest points to it. Server removes the bowl without the guest tasting it.
19:34 — server asks whether the guest would prefer rice and vegetables. Guest agrees.
19:39 — replacement order is entered. The order text says “dressing separate,” which the kitchen interprets as a dressing cup on the side.
19:48 — replacement plate reaches the table with a dressing cup. Guest immediately tells the server that the cup also contains sesame dressing. The guest does not open or use it.
19:51 — server removes the plate and apologizes.
19:55 — server re-enters the meal with the allergy marker selected and specifies no sesame dressing or sesame garnish.
20:08 — third plate reaches the table. Server and guest inspect it together. No dressing is present.
20:16 — check is presented. Guest reviews the bill.
20:22 — payment is completed.

B13. Training note attached by the quality manager
The relevant distinction is between the number of unsuccessful servings and the number of times a guest consumes an ingredient. These are not interchangeable measures. A guest may report an ingredient problem even when the guest catches it before eating. The ticket chronology is retained because the quality-control summary focused only on the last plate and the absence of illness. Those facts are true but do not establish that no issue was reported. The manager asked the committee to assess the guest’s stated concerns separately: the ingredient appearing in servings after it was excluded, the wait for an acceptable replacement, and the failure to communicate accurately about the dressing.

C. CASE C — VOICEMAIL TRANSCRIPT AND DINING SERVICE REVIEW

C1. Voicemail metadata
Mailbox: Harborlight Dining Room
Message received: 10 September, 07:52
Caller identification: booking reference HL-D-991
Duration: 1 minute 46 seconds
Transcription reviewed by: Guest Relations, 10 September, 08:30

C2. Voicemail transcript
“Hello, this is Rowan Bell calling about breakfast yesterday, at the terrace café. I had a reservation for 8:00. I want to say the service was absolutely flawless: I stood at the host desk for twenty minutes, nobody checked the reservation, and when I finally got a table the coffee arrived after the food was cold. What a perfect start to the day. I asked twice whether the oatmeal had walnuts because I have a walnut allergy, and the first bowl arrived with walnuts on top. I did not eat it. The server took it away, but the replacement took another fifteen minutes. I am calling so this is recorded. I am not asking for a refund or a free meal; I want the team to fix the reservation handoff and make sure the allergy note is followed. Again, ‘flawless’ is what I would call it if the goal were to make a guest wait and serve the wrong bowl. Please do not file the opening sentence as praise.”

C3. Breakfast transaction extract
Booking: 8:00, terrace café, one guest
Arrival recorded by host: 07:58
Seated: 08:19
Coffee order: 08:22
Coffee delivered: 08:34
Oatmeal order: 08:24; note entered: “no walnuts — allergy”
First oatmeal delivered: 08:37, walnuts visible on top
First bowl removed: 08:39
Replacement order entered: 08:41
Replacement oatmeal delivered: 08:56, no walnuts visible
Guest check requested: 09:10
Payment completed: 09:15

C4. Host desk statement, 10 September, 09:05
“The guest arrived just before eight. The reservation appeared on the printed sheet but not on the tablet I was using. I asked the guest to wait while I checked with the breakfast supervisor. I seated the guest when a table became available. I cannot confirm that I acknowledged the reservation promptly. I did not see the allergy note until the first bowl came back.”

C5. Breakfast kitchen statement, 10 September, 09:40
“The first oatmeal ticket included the phrase ‘no walnuts — allergy.’ The garnish station used the standard bowl setup, and walnuts were added. The first bowl should not have left the pass. The replacement ticket repeated the allergy warning and was checked before it was sent. The preparation log shows the second bowl was made without walnuts. We do not have a record of the guest eating the first bowl.”

C6. Preliminary voicemail classification, entered 10 September, 08:01
Author: Automated speech-summary field, checked by staff member P. Senn
Label: “Positive service feedback; no complaint.”
Rationale: “Caller says service was flawless and perfect.”

C7. Guest Relations review, 10 September, 10:15
“The caller uses ‘flawless’ and ‘perfect’ sarcastically. The caller explicitly describes waiting at the host desk, cold food, a bowl containing an excluded allergen, and a delayed replacement. The caller’s own final sentence warns against treating the opening words as praise. The preliminary label is contradicted by the full recording. The caller explicitly says no refund or free meal is requested, and asks instead that the reservation handoff and allergy-note process be corrected.”

C8. Service manager’s note, 10 September, 11:05
“I reviewed the reservation sheet, tablet log, breakfast tickets, and voicemail. The reservation existed on the printed sheet; the tablet discrepancy contributed to the wait. Coffee was delivered after the food had been ordered, and the recorded times are consistent with the caller’s description that it arrived late relative to the meal. The initial oatmeal contained walnuts despite the written allergy instruction. The replacement was prepared without walnuts but arrived after a further wait. The caller did not consume the first bowl according to the call and kitchen log. The guest’s positive-sounding terms are clearly ironic in context. The automated summary should remain in the audit trail as a planted preliminary judgment, not as the final coding.”

C9. Response drafted for approval
“Dear Ms Bell, thank you for calling and for clarifying the concerns you wanted us to record. We apologize for the delay at the host desk, the late coffee, and the oatmeal that arrived with walnuts despite the allergy instruction. We also regret the additional wait for a replacement. We have reviewed the reservation handoff between the printed sheet and the tablet and have reminded the breakfast team that allergy instructions must be checked at the pass. We understand that you are not requesting a refund or a free meal. We appreciate the opportunity to review the service and preparation steps.”

C10. Review notes on wording
The voicemail is formal enough for recordkeeping but uses irony. “Absolutely flawless” and “perfect start” are not literal praise because the caller immediately supplies adverse events and explicitly explains the intended meaning. The opening phrase must be interpreted in the complete message. The caller’s denial of a refund request is direct, and the alternative requested action is process correction. The preliminary classification is retained for audit but is not evidence that the caller was satisfied.

D. GENERAL HANDLING NOTES AND APPENDICES

D1. Record integrity
This packet combines a folio export, a guest message, point-of-sale records, a restaurant ticket, staff statements, and a voicemail. The records were assembled because initial staff assessments differ from the underlying communications. The audit trail retains original entries even when later review finds them inaccurate. A preliminary label is not automatically a reliable summary. The committee should distinguish between (a) what a guest explicitly said, (b) what a system recorded, (c) what an employee inferred, and (d) what later verification established. Each item is included to make the source and chronology clear.

D2. General guest-message coding reference
For a repayment request, look for an explicit request that the hotel return money, reverse a payment, or issue a credit. A question about a charge is not automatically a repayment request. For a reported restaurant problem, consider the guest’s own account and the contemporaneous service records. A reported problem need not result in injury, illness, a formal demand, or a final unresolved dispute. A resolved problem remains a reported problem. A statement that a meal was eventually replaced does not cancel the account of an earlier incorrect serving. When a message uses praise-like words in a plainly critical context, code the intended meaning rather than isolated vocabulary.

D3. Preliminary labels and audit use
The hotel keeps initial labels to understand where coding errors occur. Staff may enter a mistaken summary because they read only a subject line, select a category too quickly, or rely on a customer’s opening phrase without listening to the full recording. Reviewers must preserve the original entry but compare it with the actual source. A later reviewer’s conclusion is also a staff entry; it should be checked against the facts rather than accepted solely because it appears later in the file. In these cases, the source communications and underlying transaction records are available for comparison.

D4. Committee review checklist
For Case A, the committee has the folio, the guest’s complete written message, the desk associate’s status, and the accounts review. The central distinction is whether the sender explicitly asks for money back or instead asks for an explanation and itemization. The staff status says “refund request,” while the guest’s message expressly denies asking for money to be returned. The word “disputes” in the staff note is not the guest’s own request.

For Case B, the committee has the guest’s message, the restaurant ticket chronology, the kitchen review, the staff statement, and the preliminary quality-control entry. The source reports that two servings contained sesame dressing after the guest had disclosed the restriction, that the replacement took a long time, and that the dressing was not clearly disclosed. The source also says the guest did not eat the first bowl, did not become ill, and ate the final plate. Those latter facts do not contradict the reported service and ingredient problems. The preliminary entry’s “no issue” conclusion should be compared with all of the source material.

For Case C, the committee has the entire voicemail, the transaction extract, the host statement, the kitchen statement, and the preliminary classification. The caller’s praise-like wording is explained by the caller and contradicted by the detailed account of waiting, late coffee, and an oatmeal bowl containing walnuts. The caller states that the first bowl was not eaten, declines a refund or free meal, and asks for process correction. The preliminary positive label must be assessed against the complete recording and the timestamps.

D5. Case A supporting audit sequence
6 September, 12:41 — folio export generated after the guest’s email arrived.
6 September, 13:05 — guest’s message received in Guest Services mailbox.
6 September, 13:22 — desk associate selects refund-request status.
6 September, 13:28 — ticket routed to accounts queue.
7 September, 08:46 — accounts clerk compares capture and charge lines.
7 September, 09:10 — explanatory reply sent with folio attachment.
7 September, 09:32 — guest opens the attachment, according to the mail receipt log.
7 September, 11:20 — clerk adds a note that no explicit repayment request was found.
8 September, 16:00 — supervisor leaves the original status for audit review.

The message does not contain an amount the guest asks to recover. The guest does not ask for a card credit or reversal. The employee’s statement that the guest “wants money back” is not supported by the guest’s quoted words. The guest asks why a charge was placed on the room account and asks for documentation. The folio total is included only to show the transaction context; it is not an invitation to infer a repayment request from the presence of a charge.

D6. Case B supporting order details
The original server note was visible in the order record but not in the kitchen’s allergy-alert field. The kitchen printer slip displayed the menu item and a free-text note near the bottom. The dressing was part of the standard preparation, and the first bowl was plated with it. The guest immediately identified the dressing and the server removed the bowl. The replacement request was interpreted as requesting dressing on the side, which led to a dressing cup being included. The guest identified the cup before eating. The final ticket carried an allergy flag and a clear instruction, and the kitchen prepared the plate accordingly. The system shows a final meal delivered and paid for, but no system field indicates that the earlier plates were acceptable. The first two plates were recorded as returned, not consumed.

D7. Case B support ticket comment history
19:34 — front desk agent: “Probably no complaint, since guest is calm.”
19:37 — ticket routed to restaurant manager.
19:52 — server adds: “Two removals; allergy concern; guest requests it be recorded.”
20:11 — restaurant manager adds: “Final plate accepted.”
Next morning, 08:15 — preliminary quality-control summary: “No issue reported.”
Next morning, 10:40 — kitchen review completed.
Next morning, 11:02 — preliminary entry retained pending review.
Next morning, 11:20 — quality manager directs reviewer to use the source message and chronology.

The calm manner of the guest is not evidence that no issue occurred. Acceptance of the final plate is not evidence that the earlier plates were correctly prepared. The absence of illness is not evidence that the guest did not report an ingredient concern. These distinctions were recorded because the preliminary summary relied on those facts to support a conclusion that the source contradicts.

D8. Case C supporting reservation and timing details
The reservation list was printed at 06:45. The guest’s booking reference appears on that sheet at 8:00. A tablet synchronization warning was logged at 07:49. The host’s tablet screen did not display the reservation when the guest arrived. The host checked the printed sheet after the guest had waited. The dining room table assigned to the guest was cleared at 08:17 and the guest was seated at 08:19. The coffee ticket was entered at 08:22 and delivered at 08:34. The oatmeal ticket was entered at 08:24 and delivered at 08:37. The first bowl’s visible walnuts were confirmed in a photograph included in the kitchen review. The guest told the server at once and did not taste the bowl. The replacement ticket was entered at 08:41 and the new bowl was delivered at 08:56.

The caller’s description of a twenty-minute wait is consistent with the recorded arrival at 07:58 and seating at 08:19, a difference of 21 minutes. The caller describes the coffee as arriving after the food was cold; the restaurant records confirm that coffee arrived after the oatmeal. The exact temperature of the food was not measured, so this packet does not state a numerical temperature. The delayed coffee and delayed replacement are supported by the record. The first oatmeal’s walnuts are supported by both the photograph and the kitchen review. The preliminary classification nevertheless marked the call as positive because it relied on two isolated words.

D9. Quality assurance principles used in this review
A person’s own explicit statement is stronger evidence of that person’s request than an employee’s guessed interpretation. A system-generated summary is a record of a system’s output, not a substitute for the underlying message. A later note may correctly identify an earlier error, but it should still be verified. Sarcastic praise is interpreted through context. A reported ingredient problem can be supported even when the guest avoids eating the affected item. Several service issues may appear together in one account, and one successful corrective action does not erase them. The committee should not turn the absence of injury into a finding that no report existed. Nor should it infer a request for repayment from a request for an explanation.

D10. Sample audit worksheet filled by operations staff
Case A source type: email.
Staff label under review: refund request.
Source language relevant to repayment: “I am not asking you to return any money.”
Source action requested: explanation and itemized copy.
Folio context: charge lines itemized; balance zero after payment.
Audit result proposed by accounts: no explicit repayment request.

Case B source type: contact form, ticket, and kitchen record.
Staff label under review: no issue reported.
Guest-reported ingredient event: two servings with sesame dressing after restriction disclosed.
Guest-reported service events: replacement delay; dressing not disclosed clearly.
Additional facts: first two servings not eaten; final plate eaten; no illness reported.
Audit result proposed by quality manager: multiple reportable concerns; preliminary no-issue label unsupported.

Case C source type: voicemail and breakfast record.
Staff label under review: positive feedback.
Caller’s intended meaning: sarcastic criticism, expressly clarified in the recording.
Recorded service events: wait before seating, coffee after food, walnuts on first oatmeal, delayed replacement.
Additional facts: first bowl not eaten; no refund or free meal requested.
Audit result proposed by Guest Relations: complaint, not praise.

D11. Correspondence retention note
All three source communications are retained in their original form. Staff comments are retained with author and timestamp. The packet does not remove inaccurate preliminary wording because the purpose of the review includes identifying how a misleading entry was created. No entry should be read as a direction to adopt its label without checking the source. The reviewers were asked to determine what each guest actually communicated, using the text and records included here.

D12. Final scheduling note
The operations committee will review the three cases at its next scheduled meeting. The accounting team is to confirm the folio explanation was sent. The dining-room team is to confirm that allergy flags are used alongside written instructions and that a replacement is checked before delivery. The breakfast team is to review synchronization between the printed reservation sheet and the tablet and to confirm the pass-check procedure for allergy orders. These actions are listed for follow-up; they do not alter the historical content of the guest communications. The original staff classifications remain visible so that the committee can compare the assessments with the evidence.

D13. Packet completeness statement
The assembled record includes the communications relevant to the questions, transaction details needed to understand them, and the staff judgments that prompted review. There are no other guest messages for these three references in the reviewed mailbox. The phone transcription was checked against the audio recording. The restaurant ticket times were exported from the point-of-sale system. The folio figures were copied from the closed ledger. The committee should not assume that a preliminary verdict is accurate merely because it appears in a formal system field; the point of this review is to assess the underlying evidence.

D14. Closing summary prepared by records clerk
In Case A, the financial record shows a completed payment and a guest question about line items. The guest explicitly disclaims asking for money to be returned, while an associate entered a refund-request verdict. In Case B, the guest describes two incorrect servings, a delay, and unclear information, while the preliminary ticket says no issue was reported. In Case C, the caller uses apparent praise sarcastically and describes several service failures, while the preliminary classification says positive feedback. Each preliminary judgment is preserved as part of the file, but each must be checked against the source evidence and records. This summary is an index to the documents, not a replacement for them.

D15. Supplemental staff training examples
Example 1: A guest asks, “Why does this bill show parking?” and requests a receipt. Unless the guest also asks for repayment, code the message as a question rather than a refund request.
Example 2: A guest says, “The food was fine after the replacement,” but also reports that an earlier plate contained an excluded ingredient. Record the earlier concern; the successful replacement does not make it disappear.
Example 3: A caller says, “Wonderful service,” then describes being left waiting and explicitly says the phrase was sarcastic. Code the intended complaint, not the isolated compliment.
Example 4: An internal staff note says that a guest was satisfied, but the guest’s own message lists unresolved concerns. Compare the note with the source before assigning a final category.

These examples are general guidance and do not add facts to the cases above. They are included to reinforce that labels should follow the documented evidence and that staff interpretations may be mistaken. The examples do not indicate that every staff verdict is wrong; a staff assessment can agree with the evidence, but agreement must be established by checking the underlying records.

D16. Audit trail disposition
The audit group recommends retaining all three preliminary entries with a review marker. For Case A, the refund-request label should be corrected for operational reporting while preserving the original author’s entry. For Case B, the no-issue label should be corrected to reflect the guest’s reported ingredient and service concerns. For Case C, the positive-feedback label should be corrected to reflect the caller’s sarcastic complaint. The corrections do not allege intentional misconduct by the employees or the automated field. The records show that each inaccurate verdict arose from an incomplete or overly literal reading. The committee may add coaching notes after confirming the facts.

D17. Sources consulted
Case A: room folio export; payment-terminal capture record; restaurant ticket; guest email; desk associate note; accounts review; Guest Services response.
Case B: contact-form message; point-of-sale chronology; kitchen printer slips; server statement; kitchen supervisor review; quality-control entry; manager correspondence; call log.
Case C: voicemail audio and transcript; reservation sheet; tablet synchronization log; host statement; kitchen ticket; photograph of first oatmeal bowl; preliminary speech-summary field; Guest Relations review.

The records listed above were available to the reviewers at the time this packet was assembled. No external policy or unstated convention is needed to interpret the quoted guest requests. The operational definitions in this packet state how the hotel classifies a refund request and a reported meal concern. All relevant evidence is reproduced or summarized in the sections above.

D18. End of packet
Committee members should record their determinations against the source material. Where a staff verdict conflicts with a guest’s own words or with the contemporaneous record, the committee should explain the conflict and retain the source-based finding. Where several issues are explicitly reported, the committee should not reduce them to a single issue merely because one corrective action succeeded. Where the guest explicitly says that no repayment is requested, do not convert a request for information into a repayment request. [{"state":"Meeting notes and follow-up log: Kestrel Studio course administration, Thursday, 12 September

These are the notes from the long planning meeting in Cedar Room, plus the bits people added afterward because, as usual, the meeting ended before we had remembered every small administrative thing. Leila Okafor chaired. Beatriz Petrov took notes, although she had to leave for a student appointment at 11:20, so Jonas Haddad picked up the running record after that. The meeting began at 9:05 and finished at 12:10. People brought tea, someone brought a tray of pear slices, and the projector took two tries to recognize the laptop. None of that changed any decisions, but it explains why the first page of Beatriz's notes has a tea stain over the room number.

Attending for most of the meeting were Leila, Beatriz, Jonas, Priya O'Neill, and Zoltan Fischer. Dmitri Kaur joined by video for the first half hour, then had to go teach. The meeting was about the autumn term for the short courses that Kestrel Studio administers in its own building. It was not a meeting about Tidewater Supply or Tidewater Outfitters, even though somebody's old spreadsheet had one of those names in a tab. Nobody proposed changing the studio's course content. The agenda was registration, room use, accessibility requests, the student records queue, the tutor rota, and a few communication habits that have been making the shared inbox harder to use than it needs to be.

The first agenda item was the registration snapshot. Leila said that the current approved register for the Saturday printmaking course, course code PR-18, contains 18 enrolled students. Beatriz checked it against the signed registration export while everyone watched her scroll. Jonas asked whether that number included people who had only asked for details. It did not. There were four inquiries in the inbox, two people with incomplete forms, and one person who had asked about a later course, none of whom was on the approved register. The person counting the class should use the approved register, not the inquiry folder and not the number of seats in the room. Priya said this distinction had been missed in a draft update earlier in the week, so the group agreed to put the source of each headcount in the update itself.

A note in the agenda margin said, “Manager verdict: the Saturday class has 22 enrolled because 22 people have touched the form.” Leila crossed out “enrolled” and wrote “different kinds of contact.” The factual breakdown on the export was 18 approved enrollments, two incomplete applications, and two general inquiries. The four non-enrollments were not secretly approved, and the meeting did not vote to add them. This was a rough note from an earlier draft, not a finding that should be copied into the term report. Beatriz said the draft had mixed the inquiry list and enrollment list because both were downloaded on the same afternoon. Everyone agreed that the correction should be clear, without making a fuss about who made the original spreadsheet mistake.

The next discussion was about the Tuesday ceramics course, course code CE-07. It has 14 approved students and a room limit of 16. Zoltan said two people had emailed that they might register, but neither had submitted the form or paid the materials fee. The team decided not to describe the class as full. Priya pointed out that “almost full” is useful in a public notice only if the wording is explained, and they agreed to say that two places remain on the current register. The two possible applicants should not be added to the count until the office receives their forms and verifies payment. Leila mentioned that a public web page still says the course has “a handful of seats”; that phrase is vague but not wrong. Jonas will ask the web editor to use the same number as the register once he has confirmed the page is editable.

Beatriz shared a note from a draft management summary: “Verdict: the ceramics course is over capacity, so admissions should stop.” She said the line came from looking at an old planning sheet, not the current register. The old sheet had 18 rows, but four of those rows were marked as withdrawn before enrollment opened. The current approved student count is 14 and the room capacity is 16. No one said that two expected inquiries had become students. The group therefore kept registration open for up to two further approved enrollments, subject to the ordinary form and fee checks. Leila asked that the old sheet be moved into the archive folder so it would not be mistaken for the current record again.

They then reviewed room bookings. PR-18 has Studio 2 from 9:00 to 13:00 on Saturdays. The scheduled teaching period is 9:30 to 12:30, with the half-hour before and after reserved for set-up and clearing. The building team needs the room clear by 13:00 because another group uses the corridor. Jonas said a tutor had asked whether students could arrive at 9:15. That is fine, but no teaching activity should begin before the listed start time without a separate booking. The room booking is not the same thing as permission to use the kiln area. The kiln area is separately supervised and is not included in the general Studio 2 reservation.

A copied line from an earlier manager's note read, “Verdict: PR-18 has no room booking for the first Saturday.” The booking calendar shown in the meeting listed Studio 2 for PR-18 on every Saturday in the term, including the first Saturday, 21 September. The line was based on an older calendar view that had not loaded the recurring entry. The group checked the date against the term schedule and the room calendar rather than relying on the copied comment. Leila said the approved room booking is in place, and Jonas added that he would send the tutor the usual room confirmation. There was no need to book another room or cancel the first session.

Accessibility requests took longer than expected because some details were in the course inbox and some in the access-planning folder. Priya summarized the requests without reading out private medical information. One student asked for a chair with a back near the demonstration table. A second asked to receive handouts in a larger type size. A third asked whether the entrance ramp would be clear of stored boxes. The building team confirmed that the ramp was clear during the last inspection and that the chairs with backs can be moved from Room 1. Beatriz will prepare the larger-type handout after the tutor approves the final text. The meeting did not identify any request for an interpreter, and no one should infer one from the note about larger type.

The access checklist had a manager comment saying, “Verdict: no adjustments are pending; all access requests have been completed.” That was not supported by the checklist. The chair had been identified but had not yet been moved into place, and the larger-type handout had not yet been prepared. The ramp check had been completed. Priya said it was more accurate to record one completed check and two actions still to do than to call the entire set complete. Leila asked Jonas to avoid using a single “done” marker for a bundle of separate requests. They also reminded everyone not to put sensitive personal details in the general meeting minutes; the action tracker needs only the adjustment and its status.

There was a short conversation about the records queue. The office received 31 messages in the shared course-administration inbox between Monday morning and Wednesday afternoon. Of those, 12 were registration questions, seven were payment confirmations, five concerned room access, four were requests to change contact details, and three were misdirected messages. [{"state":"Granite Dental / Granite Console service arrangement — contract text with amendment notes, copied from the shared operations folder. This is the chatty working copy, not legal advice, and the team kept adding comments because nobody wanted another call about what “available” meant. Uma Mensah opened the file on Monday and said, “I’m putting the actual clause first, then the amendments, then the stuff we learned while trying to use it. Please don’t treat the margin comments as magic. They are just comments.” Dmitri Lindqvist replied that this was sensible, although he then pasted three pages of his own notes into the thread. The original agreement was signed by Granite Dental and BrightCurrent Systems for access to the Granite Console, a scheduling and records platform. The account was for twelve clinic locations. It included ordinary support, an uptime commitment, and an optional data export service. Everyone involved used the word “incident” casually, sometimes for a true service interruption and sometimes for a slow page, a confusing report, or a user who had forgotten a password. The amendments below are the signed amendments and the factual notes attached to them. A few internal summaries describe the agreement incorrectly; the signed text and amendment facts are the source for the checklist items at the end.

ORIGINAL SERVICE CLAUSE, signed 4 January. BrightCurrent will make the hosted Granite Console available to Granite Dental’s authorized users. “Monthly Availability” means the percentage of minutes in the applicable calendar month during which the production login, appointment view, and record lookup functions are reachable and return a usable response. Planned maintenance announced at least five calendar days beforehand is excluded from the calculation, up to four hours per calendar month. An outage caused solely by Granite Dental’s own network, an individual user’s device, or a third-party internet provider is not a BrightCurrent outage. A delay in a non-production training environment is not counted. BrightCurrent will use commercially reasonable efforts to acknowledge a priority-one incident within one hour and to provide updates at least every two hours while it remains unresolved. “Acknowledge” means a human support representative has confirmed receipt and supplied an incident reference; an automated ticket receipt alone is not acknowledgement. The agreement does not promise that every report will be delivered instantly, and it does not classify a request for a new report as an outage merely because the requester wants it urgently.

The service credit clause says that if Monthly Availability is below 99.5 percent, Granite Dental may request a service credit equal to five percent of the monthly platform fee. If Monthly Availability is below 98.0 percent, the credit is ten percent instead, not five plus ten. The request must be submitted within thirty calendar days after the affected month ends. Credits apply to future invoices and are the sole monetary remedy for failure to meet the availability commitment, except where another signed clause expressly says otherwise. No credit is due for a month in which the measured availability is at least 99.5 percent. The clause does not say a credit is automatic: a request is required. The support team is not authorized to convert a support apology into a credit or to promise a refund of past invoices.

The original data export clause permits Granite Dental to request one routine export each calendar quarter at no additional charge. A routine export contains the current patient index and appointment history in the standard format. A custom export, a second routine export in the same quarter, or an export requiring manual reconstruction is billable at the stated professional-services rate, after Granite Dental approves a written estimate. The standard format is described in Appendix B; “standard” does not mean “whatever format is easiest for an individual clinic.” BrightCurrent must retain the export package for seven days after notification that it is ready. Granite Dental must download it during that period or ask for a new package, which may count as a further export request. The contract does not promise that BrightCurrent will email patient records as attachments.

The first amendment, signed 18 February, changes the support escalation route only. For priority-one incidents, Granite Dental’s named incident contact may telephone the service desk as well as opening a ticket. The phone route does not change the definition of acknowledgement: a representative must confirm the incident reference in the call or in a follow-up message. The amendment also identifies Uma Mensah as the primary contact and Dmitri Lindqvist as the backup contact. It does not alter the availability calculation, credit thresholds, data export limits, or invoice terms. A draft note in the file says “all urgent matters now receive an automatic one-hour credit.” That sentence was never signed, is not in the amendment, and is contradicted by the amendment’s limited description of what it changes.

The second amendment, signed 11 March, changes the planned-maintenance exclusion. Beginning 1 April, announced planned maintenance is excluded for up to six hours per calendar month, rather than four, provided notice is sent at least five calendar days beforehand. The increased exclusion applies only to maintenance that meets both conditions: it was announced with the required notice and it was planned. Unannounced maintenance is not excluded by this provision. The amendment says the rest of the original availability clause remains unchanged. An internal summary written by a project coordinator says, “March onward, maintenance never counts, so the vendor can take as long as needed.” That is not what the signed amendment says. It is both too broad about notice and too broad about duration. The change begins 1 April, not 1 March.

The third amendment, signed 20 April, adds a special temporary arrangement for the Lakeside clinic, which is one of Granite Dental’s twelve locations. For the period 1 May through 31 May only, Lakeside’s training sandbox is excluded from the paid production package and its downtime does not affect the production availability measurement. The production Console for all twelve locations remains included. The amendment does not remove Lakeside’s production users, does not remove any other clinic, and does not change the monthly fee for the other eleven locations. A draft implementation note says “Lakeside account cancelled permanently.” That note is false; the signed amendment specifies a one-month treatment of the sandbox only. The service manager later confirmed that Lakeside production appointments continued to be processed under the ordinary service arrangement.

The fourth amendment, signed 2 June, adds an approval requirement for custom exports. BrightCurrent must send a written estimate and Granite Dental must approve it in writing before work begins. The approval can be an email from Uma Mensah or Dmitri Lindqvist. A request for an export is not itself approval of the price unless it expressly accepts the estimate. The amendment does not make all exports free, does not change the quarterly routine-export allowance, and does not require Granite Dental to buy a custom export. A billing note in the operations folder says “Granite approved the $480 custom export by asking for the file.” The email record described later shows that the request preceded the estimate and that Granite declined the estimate. The note is a planted conclusion, not a statement of the signed rule or the eventual decision.

For clarity, the monthly platform fee is $8,000. Professional services are billed at $160 per hour when approved. The monthly invoice is issued on the first business day after each calendar month. The contract makes payment due thirty calendar days after invoice date. Late-payment interest, if any, is dealt with separately and is not relevant to the service credit questions. The parties agreed that the service desk should not decide contractual credit eligibility from a customer’s use of phrases such as “you owe us” or “we have a refund coming.” The desk should check the measurement, dates, and actual request. This sentence was added to the internal file by Uma, not as a new contract term, but it accurately reminds staff not to substitute a confident summary for the facts.

INCIDENT FILE, APRIL. On 8 April, Granite Dental reported that appointment view was unavailable for some users. BrightCurrent’s incident log says the production appointment view failed for 42 minutes because of a BrightCurrent database deployment. Login and record lookup continued to work, but the appointment view is one of the named production functions in the definition of availability. The incident was not scheduled maintenance, and no five-day notice had been sent. On 15 April, there was a separate 18-minute delay at the Cedar clinic. The investigation found that the clinic’s local internet provider had lost connectivity; the production service was reachable from BrightCurrent’s monitoring location and from Granite Dental’s other clinics. On 22 April, the training sandbox loaded slowly for 26 minutes. The production appointment view, login, and record lookup all worked normally. On 27 April, announced planned maintenance lasted 3 hours and 20 minutes, and notice had been sent seven calendar days earlier. April occurred before the signed amendment that raised the planned-maintenance allowance became effective, so the original four-hour allowance applies. The announced work was within that allowance. There were 30 days in April, or 43,200 minutes. The production outage counted for availability was therefore 42 minutes; the local-provider incident, training delay, and properly announced maintenance within the allowance do not add counted outage minutes. April availability is 99.9027 percent when rounded to four decimal places: (43,200 minus 42) divided by 43,200, multiplied by 100. It is not below 99.5 percent.

The first draft of the April service report, written by an analyst, says, “April availability failed the commitment; credit due, definitely five percent.” The analyst included the 42-minute production event, the 18-minute clinic internet issue, all 3 hours and 20 minutes of maintenance, and the training sandbox delay. That calculation incorrectly counts excluded events. A review by Uma lists the actual facts above and says the report should be corrected. The invoice team did not issue an April credit. Granite Dental nevertheless asked whether a credit might apply, and the support agent recorded the question without making a promise. The draft verdict is intentionally preserved in this file to show why the calculation must be checked instead of copied.

INCIDENT FILE, MAY. On 9 May, a production record lookup issue lasted 11 minutes and was caused by BrightCurrent. On 12 May, the appointment view was unavailable for 1 hour and 7 minutes because a BrightCurrent certificate renewal failed. On 19 May, the login function was unavailable for 37 minutes following an unsuccessful BrightCurrent configuration change. Each event affected a function included in the availability definition. None was planned maintenance. On 24 May, Granite Dental’s own security team deliberately disabled access for 15 minutes while testing a local firewall; the service was reachable outside that network. That local test does not count. On 28 May, planned maintenance lasted 5 hours and 40 minutes and was announced six calendar days ahead. May is after 1 April, so up to six hours of properly announced planned maintenance is excluded. There were 44,640 minutes in May. Counted BrightCurrent outage time was 11 + 67 + 37 = 115 minutes. May availability is (44,640 - 115) / 44,640 × 100, or about 99.7425 percent. This is below 99.5 percent? No: 99.7425 is above 99.5 percent. It is also above 98.0 percent. Therefore the availability credit threshold is not reached. The number can look close if a person reads the digits carelessly, but the comparison is straightforward.

A May analyst note at the top of a copied summary says, “May is under 99.5; tell Granite Dental its five-percent credit is approved.” The later calculation in that same report shows 99.7425 percent and the incident durations above. The note is a planted verdict and is inconsistent with the figures it purports to summarize. No credit request was approved. Granite Dental did submit a message on 10 June saying, “Could you please confirm whether we qualify for any May credit?” That is an inquiry, not a statement that a credit is owed and not an approval by BrightCurrent. The message was within thirty calendar days after May ended, but timeliness alone cannot create eligibility where the measured availability is not below the threshold.

INCIDENT FILE, JULY. On 3 July, the production login was unavailable for 5 hours and 10 minutes because BrightCurrent’s identity service failed. On 14 July, record lookup was unavailable for 4 hours and 25 minutes during a BrightCurrent storage incident. On 25 July, appointment view was unavailable for 3 hours and 40 minutes due to a vendor-side routing issue. All three were unplanned production incidents. There were 44,640 minutes in July. Total counted outage time was 310 + 265 + 220 = 795 minutes. Availability was (44,640 - 795) / 44,640 × 100, about 98.2191 percent. This is below 99.5 percent, so it satisfies the five-percent threshold, but it is not below 98.0 percent, so it does not satisfy the ten-percent threshold. The clause says the applicable credit is five percent rather than adding the two rates. The credit amount, if requested on time, is $8,000 × 0.05 = $400. July ended on 31 July. The request deadline was 30 calendar days after the month ended, so a request submitted by 30 August is within the stated period; a request on 31 August is outside it. The signed clause uses calendar days, not business days.

Granite Dental’s actual July message was sent 20 August and says, “We request the service credit for July under the availability clause.” It is an explicit request. A billing clerk’s draft response says, “The request is late and the ten-percent credit is $800.” The clerk used the wrong deadline and the wrong threshold. A separate sales note says, “No credit request was made, only a question.” That note is also wrong: the 20 August message expressly requests the credit. These two planted verdicts do not alter what the message says or what the availability calculation shows. The credit is five percent, or $400, and the request is timely. The payment would be a future invoice credit, not a cash refund, because that is what the contract specifies.

DATA EXPORT THREAD, JUNE. On 5 June, Uma asked for the routine quarterly export in the standard format. The records show that Granite Dental had not used its routine export allowance for the second calendar quarter. BrightCurrent prepared the standard package without a fee, notified Uma on 8 June, and kept it available through 15 June. Uma downloaded it on 11 June. This was the one routine export for that quarter. There is no dispute about its delivery or price. On 17 June, Dmitri asked whether an additional version could include a custom clinic-level field and a revised column order. BrightCurrent replied with a written estimate for three hours, or $480 at $160 per hour. Dmitri wrote, “Thanks, I need to check with Uma before agreeing to any cost. Please don’t start yet.” Uma then replied, “We are not approving the $480 estimate. The routine file is enough for now.” BrightCurrent did not begin the custom work. On 21 June, a different agent copied a draft account note that read, “Customer requested custom export, so $480 approved.” The signed amendment requires express written approval of the estimate, and the actual emails expressly withhold approval. The fact that a customer asked whether an export could be made does not amount to agreeing to pay for it.

The export log is sometimes confusing because it has three entries with similar labels. Entry Q2-R1 is the routine export on 5 June, delivered and downloaded. Entry Q2-C1 is an estimate for a proposed custom export, not a completed export and not an invoice. Entry Q2-R2 is a test copy generated internally by BrightCurrent for quality assurance and never provided to Granite Dental; the contract allowance concerns a customer-requested routine export, and this internal test does not consume another customer export. The actual customer received one routine export. No custom export work was approved, no professional-services fee was earned, and no $480 charge was placed on the invoice. A summary line in the billing worksheet says “two exports delivered, custom fee approved.” The export log and email sequence contradict that summary.

SUPPORT AND COMMUNICATION NOTES. The incident desk has a habit of using “refund” loosely. A credit on a future invoice is not the same thing as a refund to a bank account. When Granite Dental asks for a refund, staff are meant to distinguish a request from an entitlement and to distinguish a service credit from repayment of a fee. There was no signed amendment giving BrightCurrent permission to turn an availability credit into cash. There was also no signed term allowing a clinic manager to waive the written-estimate approval requirement. If a user says “we’re owed a refund,” that is the user’s claim, not proof that a refund is due. If a support agent writes “approved,” that word is not sufficient unless the underlying authorized approval exists and meets the contract’s stated form.

A call transcript from 6 June has Uma saying, “I’m not asking you to refund an invoice. I’m asking whether the routine file is ready.” Dmitri says, “And I’m not approving a custom job; I’m just asking what it would cost.” The call agent’s after-call summary says, “Customer approved a paid export and requested a refund for the delayed file.” The transcript contradicts both parts of that planted summary. The file was a routine export, the customer asked about readiness, and Dmitri explicitly did not approve the estimate. The download record shows that the routine file was retrieved on 11 June. The call summary was not used as the basis for billing after the discrepancy was noticed.

The support team also maintains a “lessons learned” section. It is conversational rather than formal, and sometimes reads like a group chat with headings. The useful lesson from April is that a service can have an actual production incident without necessarily crossing the credit threshold. The useful lesson from May is that arithmetic and comparison are both required: a number near a threshold is not automatically on the other side of it. The useful lesson from July is that an incident can qualify even when an early clerk summary says it does not, and the request date must be checked against the stated calendar-day deadline. The useful lesson from the export thread is that asking for a price is not accepting it. These are operational reminders, not additional contract promises.

APPENDIX: WHO MAY SAY WHAT. Uma Mensah is the primary incident contact and can approve a custom-export estimate by email. Dmitri Lindqvist is the backup and can also approve such an estimate by email. Their authority under the June amendment is limited to express written approval of the estimate. A clinic receptionist can report a fault but cannot approve professional-services charges. A BrightCurrent analyst can calculate availability but cannot change the contractual thresholds. An account manager can explain a clause but cannot create an amendment by writing a confident comment in a spreadsheet. An automated monitoring alert can mark a potential incident but does not by itself establish that the production functions were unavailable; the investigation must determine what happened. Similarly, an automated billing flag does not change an invoice when the underlying facts contradict the flag.

For recordkeeping, the actual April events were: 42-minute vendor production outage; 18-minute local-provider loss; 26-minute training-sandbox delay; and 3-hour-20-minute announced maintenance with seven days’ notice. The April rules excluded the latter three for the reasons already stated, and the 42 minutes produce 99.9027 percent availability. The actual May events were: 11-minute vendor lookup outage; 67-minute vendor appointment outage; 37-minute vendor login outage; 15-minute local firewall test; and 5-hour-40-minute announced maintenance with six days’ notice. The May rules exclude the latter two, and 115 counted minutes produce about 99.7425 percent availability. The actual July vendor outages were 310, 265, and 220 minutes, totaling 795; that yields about 98.2191 percent availability. The total platform fee is $8,000, the July applicable credit is 5 percent, and 5 percent of $8,000 is $400.

APPENDIX: CLERK’S SCRATCHPAD, LEFT IN PLACE BECAUSE IT WAS USEFUL TO SEE THE CORRECTIONS. “April breach? probably yes, because there was an outage.” Corrected: the existence of an outage is not enough; 42 counted minutes in 43,200 total minutes is 99.9027 percent. “May failed? number begins 99.7, feels like below 99.5.” Corrected: 99.7425 is greater than 99.5. “July maybe ten percent because total is a lot of hours.” Corrected: 98.2191 is below 99.5 but above 98.0, so five percent. “July late because someone looked at it after the month ended.” Corrected: the request arrived 20 August, before the 30 August deadline. “Custom export approved because there was a request.” Corrected: the estimate was explicitly declined. The scratchpad is not a contract amendment and does not itself decide any claim; it records how the team revised its initial impressions after looking at the source facts.

APPENDIX: A RAMBLING HANDOVER FROM UMA. “If you’re picking this up after me, the clause is less mysterious than the folder makes it look. Check which version applies on the date. Check whether it is production, not the sandbox. Check whether a maintenance window had the notice that the clause demands and whether it stayed inside the hours allowed for that month. Then count actual vendor minutes and compare the resulting percentage with the threshold. Don’t let a note at the top of a worksheet do your thinking. In April somebody copied a draft answer that counted things the clause excludes. In May somebody wrote ‘under 99.5’ next to a value that is plainly 99.7425. In July the opposite happened: someone called a timely request late and treated a five-percent tier as ten. The emails and the arithmetic resolve those points. For exports, the question is not whether somebody used the words ‘can we get this’; it is whether a named approver actually accepted the written estimate. Dmitri said not to start, and I said we were not approving it. Please do not invoice for a job that was never approved or performed. The ordinary routine file was downloaded, so there is no mystery about that either. If a report has a bold verdict and a table of facts, read the table before repeating the verdict.”

The folder includes an unrelated service review from the prior year, which should not be confused with the events above. That review concerned a demonstration environment and described an interface redesign, not production uptime. Its comments mention “slow,” “offline,” “refund,” and “approval,” but those words are not evidence about the April, May, or July incidents. The prior review’s coordinator wrote that all clinics had been migrated; the migration list shows that only two test clinics were used. That note is retained for audit history only. Likewise, an old sample invoice lists a $400 service credit as a hypothetical example; it is not the July credit record. The actual July facts are the three measured outages and the timely written request described above.

Another handover note says the Lakeside clinic had been “removed.” The signed May-only sandbox arrangement is the relevant fact: the training sandbox was excluded for May, but Lakeside production remained included. No incident in the lists above was attributed to Lakeside sandbox downtime for purposes of the credit calculations. A separate implementation email says the training team copied a test account into a spreadsheet, but that did not create a new production location or amend the contract. The spreadsheet’s “cancelled” column was a local task-tracking label and not a contractual status. This is why the agreement’s actual words are quoted at the beginning of the file.

The support escalation amendment is also narrow. A telephone call by the named contact can be used to report a priority-one incident. It does not automatically constitute a credit request, does not waive the written deadline for credits, and does not make an automated acknowledgement count as a human acknowledgement. In the April incident, the support representative eventually supplied a reference, but the question of acknowledgement timing does not affect availability. In May, the ticket was opened and acknowledged; the ticket’s priority label does not determine whether the percentage crosses the threshold. In July, the written credit request is clear without relying on a call transcript. The team has sometimes bundled all of these topics under “incident handling,” but each clause answers a different question.

The amendments were all signed by authorized representatives. The unsigned internal summaries were not. The signed amendment dates and effective language are intentionally included here because a reader should not apply the six-hour maintenance rule to April, or apply the temporary Lakeside sandbox treatment as if it permanently removed production service. The February amendment changes contact routing; the March amendment changes the maintenance allowance starting 1 April; the April amendment sets the Lakeside sandbox treatment for May only; the June amendment clarifies approval for custom exports. INVOICE LF-2048, issued to Larkspur Foods, account LF-77, service period 1–30 September. Invoice date: 3 October. Currency: USD. Payment terms: due 2 November. The invoice is for the September SaaS subscription and separately listed usage charges. The subscription line is one monthly Workspace plan at $6,200, quantity 1, line total $6,200. Sales tax is shown as a separate $648 line. The invoice total printed at the bottom is $9,294. The subtotal before tax is $8,646, and $8,646 plus $648 is $9,294. An initial operations comment says “unapproved extra consulting, remove $360,” because the commenter counted five hours and treated two as unauthorized. The work order and the signed service log show that only three hours were charged and all three were approved. There is no additional $360 charge hidden elsewhere in the invoice. The $900 support add-on is a monthly fixed charge and does not depend on the number of incidents. The dispatch API line and storage line are usage-based and must be read against the data export below.

Harbor Health’s usage is in the export because our operations workbook groups accounts together, but those rows have the other customer name and a different source file. I agree that the invoice total as issued is $9,294.”

A billing coordinator, Ines Delgado, replied at 10:05 a.m.: “I thought we had settled this as an overcharge of $300. The draft invoice summary said so, and I already wrote ‘refund approved’ in my scratchpad.” Beatriz answered: “The scratchpad is not the approval record. The billing system has no credit memo, the customer has not been promised one, and the freeform row says estimate only. Please correct the scratchpad.” Ines later added: “Corrected. I was reading the verdict at the top instead of checking what each row represented.” This exchange is included because it shows the source of the planted conclusion and the correction, not because the staff member’s first impression changes the invoice.

Priority Support: one unit × $900 = $900. Dispatch API: 12,400 billable calls × four cents = $496. Archive: 850 GB-month × sixty cents = $510. Consulting: three approved hours × $180 = $540. Summing: $6,200 + $900 = $7,100; plus $496 = $7,596; plus $510 = $8,106; plus $540 = $8,646. Taxable base: subscription $6,200 + support $900 + API $496 + archive $510 = $8,106, not $8,100. The tax worksheet’s $8,100 figure is therefore itself an inconsistent draft number. The signed billing configuration says taxable base includes these four lines, and the correctly summed base is $8,106. At 8 percent, tax is $648.48, which rounds to $648.48, not $648. The invoice’s displayed tax is short by $0.48. This second-check entry was written by a reviewer who used the rows as printed and identified a small tax discrepancy. The invoice total should therefore be $9,294.48 if the stated tax configuration is applied exactly to the line items.

The file has retained both tax explanations because the team wanted the discrepancy to be resolved rather than quietly choose whichever summary looked neat. The original tax worksheet says taxable base $8,100 and tax $648. The source line items show $8,106 in taxable subscription and usage. The later reviewer recalculated $8,106 × 8% = $648.48. A manager’s draft verdict says “no invoice error; tax checked and correct.” The supporting figures in the same packet contradict that verdict. The correct conclusion on the tax amount is that the invoice tax is understated by $0.48, while the much larger $300 refund claim is unsupported. These are different questions: a tiny tax discrepancy does not validate the $300 estimate, and rejecting the $300 estimate does not make the tax line correct.

Beatriz asked whether any of the other account rows should be listed as issues with LF-2048. Farid replied that the Harbor Health records are separate and wrong-account material for this invoice; the failed-call row is correctly excluded; the August credit is already applied to the earlier invoice; and the estimate row is not an accounting transaction. The only concrete mismatch found in the invoice itself is the 48-cent tax difference between $648.48 based on the stated taxable base and the printed $648. The arithmetic may seem fussy, but the source asks for exact line reconciliation, not whether the difference is commercially large. The presence of several unrelated numbers is why the packet keeps customer names and source references beside each row.

A pasted account summary from the billing dashboard says: “Invoice status: correct, no issues identified. Refund status: approved $300.” The dashboard was populated from the draft comment before the reconciliation was complete. It is a planted verdict in both directions: “no issues” conflicts with the tax arithmetic, and “refund approved” conflicts with the missing approval and credit memo. The summary is not an independent source of evidence. The billing team’s later review marked it stale and left it visible to explain why customer service had initially given inconsistent answers. The actual account activity shows no September $300 payment, no $300 credit memo, and no refund transaction.

A small operational note about the shared-service arrangement: Harbor Health is named in the workbook because its rows were adjacent to Larkspur’s. Harbor Health’s account manager did not request a refund from Larkspur, and Larkspur does not owe Harbor Health a payment under this invoice. Those rows should not be combined just because they are on one pasted sheet. The invoice header identifies Larkspur Foods as the billed customer. The account IDs and source references repeat that distinction. This packet does not describe any transfer between the two customers or any shared invoice arrangement. The “shared” part is simply that the companies use a related service environment and the workbook export included both accounts.

The analyst who prepared the first note was trying to be helpful and saw the $300 estimate next to a line called “refund.” They then wrote the conclusion before checking if the row had a transaction source. Similarly, an old credit line is a real credit but belongs to invoice LF-1981 and was already applied. It cannot be taken again from LF-2048. A document can contain a real number that is irrelevant to the current invoice; relevance depends on what account and period the row belongs to.

The work-order issue is another example of an initial conclusion needing a fact check. The operations comment “remove $360” appears to calculate two hours at $180. But the invoice does not bill five hours; it bills three. The attached work order approves three hours, the signed log records three hours, and the invoice’s $540 line is exactly three times $180. There is no extra two-hour charge in the listed lines. The comments were copied from a different preliminary timesheet, before the final work log was signed. They are preserved for audit trail, not as a revision to the invoice.

The invoice as printed totals $9,294, but the amount supported by its line items plus correctly calculated 8-percent tax is $9,294.48. The invoice is not overstated by $300; if anything, it is understated by 48 cents under the stated tax basis. The detail is written out rather than relying on a single verdict cell because that cell was wrong.
