[{"state":"Product review submitted by Sven Rahman concerning a refrigerated shipment from Meridian Software

Shipment reference: MR-4816
Delivery date: 14 September
Review date: 18 September

The cartons arrived at the stated delivery address shortly before noon. The outer packaging was clean and dry, and the driver waited while I checked the temperature indicator. The indicator remained within the range printed on the shipping label. The contents were packed in separate insulated compartments, and the seals on all six compartments were intact. I counted the units against the packing slip before signing for the delivery. The count matched exactly: six cartons, with twelve sealed trays in each carton.

I am writing this review because the carrier’s public service summary gives the impression that every part of this delivery was handled well. Some parts were. The driver was courteous, and the booking confirmation arrived promptly. However, the shipment was scheduled to arrive on 12 September, and it did not arrive until 14 September. The dispatch notice sent on the morning of 12 September said the vehicle had been reassigned. A later message said the delivery would be made the following day, but it was not. The tracking page eventually showed a revised delivery date of 14 September. No one contacted me directly to explain the second delay.

The delay disrupted our receiving schedule. Staff had been assigned to inspect and store the shipment on the original date, and we had to arrange for someone to return two days later. The goods themselves were still acceptable when they arrived, so I am not reporting spoilage or damage. I have seen other reviews describe warm or broken shipments, but neither happened in my case. The temperature reading and intact packaging are useful evidence, not a general endorsement of the whole service.

There was also a question about the delivery charge. The booking summary showed a delivery charge of 48 credits, and the final receipt also showed 48 credits. I checked the two figures because one earlier online comment mentioned an unexpected extra fee. That comment does not describe my transaction. I was not charged more than the amount displayed when I booked, and I have no dispute about the charge.

A staff member who reviewed the case left this note: “Customer confirms the shipment was timely and is fully satisfied; close without further action.” That summary is inaccurate. I did receive the goods, and I am satisfied with their condition, but I did not say that the shipment was timely. The scheduled date and the actual date are both recorded above, and the messages in the tracking history confirm the delay. The note appears to have confused acceptance of the goods with satisfaction about the delivery schedule.

I am not asking for money back. I have not requested a refund of the delivery charge or the value of the goods. My purpose is to record the late arrival and the lack of a clear update. Please use the dates and the receipt details in this review rather than the staff summary when classifying the issue. I would consider the service improved if the carrier notified recipients promptly when a revised delivery date changed again. The driver’s conduct and the condition of the goods deserve credit, but they do not make the delivery punctual.

For completeness, the review form asked whether the parcel was delivered to the correct address. It was. The address on the label matched the receiving location, and the driver handed the cartons to me. There is no missing-parcel claim here. The issue is confined to the delay and the communication about it.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"A late-delivery complaint means the sender says the shipment arrived after its scheduled delivery date. From: Ines Okafor, Larkspur Foods receiving office
To: Carrier support desk
Subject: Delivery condition and account note

Tuesday, 09:12 — Ines to support:
I am writing about shipment LF-2097, delivered to our east receiving bay yesterday afternoon. The driver arrived at the address shown on the label. We received all four insulated boxes listed on the manifest, and our receiving clerk signed for them after counting the boxes. The delivery itself was not late: the booking confirmation gave Monday as the delivery date, and the tracking page records completion on Monday at 15:40.

On opening the boxes, we found that two inner containers had cracked lids. The contents of those two containers had leaked into their liners. The other containers were intact. We photographed the damaged lids and the wet liners before moving the goods, and I have attached the photographs to this message. The outer boxes did not appear crushed, but that does not change the condition of the inner containers. We have placed the affected items aside for inspection.

I am not reporting a short count, a wrong address, or a delay. The manifest count and our physical count agree. Our concern is the damaged condition of the two containers. Please tell us what information you need to assess the damage claim.

Tuesday, 10:03 — Support desk reply:
Thank you. Our preliminary case note reads: “Customer reports missing cartons and requests a refund for the late delivery.” I have opened a review using that summary. Please confirm whether it reflects your report, and whether the full delivery charge is disputed.

Tuesday, 10:27 — Ines to support:
That summary does not reflect my report. No carton is missing, and the shipment was not late. I did not ask for a refund, and I am not disputing the delivery charge. I am reporting two damaged inner containers. The photos show the cracked lids and leakage. Please correct the case description before it is passed to the claims team.

Tuesday, 11:02 — Support desk reply:
I appreciate the clarification. The intake form has separate boxes for missing items, damage, and delay. I will ensure the claims team receives the damage information and the attached photographs. The earlier note was copied from an unrelated case template and should not be treated as a statement by you. It is useful that you have specified which parts of it are incorrect.

Wednesday, 08:41 — Ines to support:
Thank you for confirming. For clarity, the four boxes were all physically present when delivered. Only two inner containers were damaged. We have not yet decided whether to dispose of the affected contents; our quality staff are inspecting them. Please do not describe the entire shipment as unusable. The remaining containers appear intact, although we will finish checking them before recording the final condition.

Wednesday, 09:15 — Support desk reply:
The case record now identifies two damaged inner containers, no missing cartons, and no reported delay. The claims team may contact you about the photographs and inspection result. The amount paid for delivery remains unchanged in the account record. We have not issued or promised any credit.

Wednesday, 09:44 — Ines to support:
That is an accurate account of what I reported. My request is for the damage to be reviewed under the carrier’s claims process. I am not asking you to refund the delivery charge, and I have not asked for a replacement shipment. I will send the inspection result when it is complete. Please retain the photographs with this case so that the claims reviewer can compare them with the packing record.

The correspondence above is the full exchange relevant to this shipment. The first support summary was a mistaken staff note, not a description of the sender’s complaint. I mention those details because a preliminary quality-control entry describes this order as a missed delivery, which is not what happened.

The package contained three labeled trays. I checked the labels against the order document before opening the packaging. All three trays were present, and each label corresponded to the correct component type. The first and second trays were in good condition. The third tray had a split plastic cover, and several small components had come loose inside the tray. The shipping carton had no obvious puncture, although one corner was slightly compressed. I took photographs before separating the loose pieces for inspection.

The quality-control entry says: “No physical damage confirmed; customer is dissatisfied because delivery was delayed.” That entry is not supported by the facts above. The delivery was on the promised date, and the damaged cover was visible as soon as the tray was unpacked. I cannot yet say that any component is defective. The loose pieces have not been electrically tested, so I am reporting packaging damage and loose components, not a confirmed failure of the components themselves.

I have not found a discrepancy in the order quantity. The packing list states three trays, and I received three trays. I have also compared the shipping charge on the checkout confirmation with the final receipt. Both show 27 credits. I am not complaining about the price, and I am not asking for a refund. The review form’s billing and delivery-delay categories do not fit this report.

Our receiving clerk kept the damaged tray and its packaging in the inspection area. The other two trays are being stored normally. I will provide the results of the component test if the inspection shows anything beyond the broken cover and loose pieces. Until then, please do not use a future possibility as though it were already established. The observable issue is limited to the condition in which the third tray arrived.

The service was otherwise straightforward. The tracking notices were easy to follow, and the courier handed the package to the correct person. Those positive points do not erase the damage. Similarly, the fact that the carton was mostly intact does not prove that the tray inside was undamaged. A reviewer should distinguish the condition of the outer carton from the condition of its contents.

I am submitting this review so the carrier can record the damaged tray and tell us whether photographs are sufficient for its review. - candidate-description style for this batch: descriptions phrased from the sender's point of view ('I want my money back')
- names you may use (never reuse a name across sources): Greta Kaur, Quentin Sorensen, Viktor Fischer, Leila Tanaka, Bao Sorensen, Wanjiru Sorensen; companies: Meridian Rentals, Quill Foods, Harbor Supply, Saltmarsh Outfitters

[{"state":"Meridian Rentals Recruiting Operations Review
Prepared for the fictional hiring team
Reporting period: 6–30 June

Purpose and reading guide
This document collects the recruiting team’s working notes, application records, interview schedules, and a few internal quality checks for the open Facilities Coordinator role. It is longer than the decisions it supports, because the team has recently discovered that short summaries tend to acquire confidence faster than they acquire accuracy. The records below are fictional and self-contained. A reviewer should distinguish dated events from opinions, and should use the underlying entries rather than treating a label in a margin as proof. Several comments are dry, because the team’s preferred alternative—earnest enthusiasm about calendar invitations—has not improved hiring outcomes.

The role
The Facilities Coordinator supports four Meridian Rentals sites. The posting asks for two years of facilities or office-operations experience, comfort maintaining inventory records, clear written communication, and availability for occasional early shifts. A degree is not required. The recruiting team accepts applications through the careers form or by email when an applicant cannot use the form. The team does not treat an incomplete application as a completed submission. It does, however, record received materials even when the applicant has not provided every requested item.

Recruiting team thread, 6 June, 9:05 a.m.
Greta Kaur: The Facilities Coordinator listing is live. Please use the same checklist for every applicant, and please do not decide that a person has “applied” because someone pasted their name into a spreadsheet. We have been through this.
Quentin Sorensen: I have added columns for application received, résumé received, interview scheduled, interview completed, and offer issued. There is also a notes column, which I will try not to let become a second, less reliable database.
Viktor Fischer: The application form accepts a résumé without a cover letter. The cover letter is optional. I checked. No, I did not check by submitting an application for myself.
Leila Tanaka: The public posting says the same thing. I will handle applicants who email documents directly and record what actually arrived.
Bao Sorensen: I can help schedule screens. I will not mark an invitation as an interview. An invitation is a promise to meet, not evidence that anyone met.
Wanjiru Sorensen: Agreed. Also, please stop describing every calendar event as “completed” just because it has a green check mark. The calendar has no hiring authority.

Application tracker excerpt, exported 7 June
Applicant: Greta Kaur. Application received: 6 June, 4:18 p.m. Résumé: received. Cover letter: not received; optional. Screen: scheduled for 10 June. Screen completed: pending.
Applicant: Quentin Sorensen. Application received: 6 June, 4:41 p.m. Résumé: received. Cover letter: received. Screen: not requested; employee referral record only, not an application for this role.
Applicant: Viktor Fischer. Application received: 7 June, 8:02 a.m. Résumé: received. Cover letter: received. Screen: scheduled for 11 June.
Applicant: Leila Tanaka. Application received: 7 June, 8:36 a.m. Résumé: received by email. Cover letter: not received; optional. Screen: not scheduled.
Applicant: Bao Sorensen. Application received: blank. Résumé: blank. Cover letter: blank. Screen: blank. An internal note says “Bao asked about the role in the kitchen; maybe applicant?” The note is a question, not a submission.
Applicant: Wanjiru Sorensen. Application received: 7 June, 9:10 a.m. Résumé: received. Cover letter: received. Screen: scheduled for 12 June.

Quality-control note, 7 June, entered by an automated worksheet
“Six people are in the tracker, so six applications have been received.”
Correction from Leila: The tracker includes a referral-only record and a person mentioned in a question. Four application receipts are evidenced in this excerpt. The worksheet’s verdict is not supported by its own rows. This is the sort of arithmetic one can do without opening a calculator, which makes the mistake especially economical.

Email thread, subject: Facilities Coordinator application, 8 June
From: Greta Kaur
To: Meridian Rentals Recruiting
I am applying for the Facilities Coordinator role. My résumé is attached. I have worked in office operations for three years and have maintained supply and maintenance records. I do not have a cover letter ready, but the listing says one is optional. Please confirm you have received the résumé.

From: Recruiting inbox
To: Greta Kaur
We received your application and résumé on 6 June. A cover letter is optional, so nothing is missing on that account. We have tentatively scheduled a screen for 10 June. We will send the video link separately.

Quoted reply from Greta
Thanks. To be clear, I am asking you to confirm receipt, not asking to withdraw or change the application. I will attend the screen if the invitation arrives.

Internal margin note, author not identified
“Applicant has not submitted a complete application because there is no cover letter; mark application missing.”
Leila’s follow-up: This note contradicts the posting and the receipt record. The cover letter is optional. Greta’s application and résumé were received. The team should not convert an optional document into a required one by writing it in the margin.

Screening schedule, 10 June
9:00–9:25 Greta Kaur — invitation sent 7 June at 11:20 a.m.; attendee present; call notes saved at 9:28 a.m.; screen completed.
9:30–9:55 Viktor Fischer — invitation sent 7 June at 11:25 a.m.; applicant requested a different time on 9 June; original meeting canceled; no call notes.
10:00–10:25 Leila Tanaka — no invitation; no screen.
Calendar digest auto-caption: “All three candidates screened today.”
Quentin’s correction: The digest counts rows from a planning sheet, not completed conversations. Only Greta’s screen is evidenced in this block. Viktor’s meeting was canceled, and Leila had no meeting. A scheduled or canceled slot is a poor substitute for an interview, though it does make the calendar look busy.

Interview notes, Greta Kaur, 10 June
Greta described tracking routine repairs at a small office and keeping a record of replacement supplies. She gave an example of noticing repeated requests for the same item and adding a reorder reminder. When asked about early shifts, she said she could cover them with advance notice. Her written follow-up was clear and addressed the questions asked. The interviewer recorded “meets listed experience requirement” and “inventory records: relevant example.” No offer decision was made during the screen.

Interview notes, Viktor Fischer, 11 June
Viktor attended the rescheduled screen. He described two years of facilities support and gave a specific example of logging repairs by site and date. His notes were concise. The interview panel wrote “meets experience threshold; proceed to reference check.” The reference check was requested but had not been completed by the date of the tracker export.

Hiring summary draft, 12 June
“Greta Kaur is the only applicant who completed an interview. Viktor’s interview was canceled, and Wanjiru did not attend. Close the other files.”
Review comment by Bao: This is wrong. The 10 June Viktor slot was canceled, but the rescheduled interview happened on 11 June and has notes. Wanjiru’s 12 June screen also has attendance and notes. The summary appears to have copied the old calendar state and omitted later records. An outdated summary does not become current merely by using a decisive verb.

Interview notes, Wanjiru Sorensen, 12 June
Wanjiru attended the scheduled screen. She described coordinating building access and logging supply requests. She has more than two years of related operations experience. She answered the written scenario in a clear sequence and confirmed that occasional early shifts were acceptable. The panel recorded “meets listed requirements” and “advance to references.” The notes do not say that an offer was made.

Candidate status table, 13 June
Greta Kaur: application received; résumé received; screen completed; references not requested; offer not issued.
Viktor Fischer: application received; résumé received; screen completed 11 June; references requested; result pending; offer not issued.
Leila Tanaka: application received by email; résumé received; screen not scheduled; offer not issued.
Wanjiru Sorensen: application received; résumé received; screen completed; references to be requested; offer not issued.
Bao Sorensen: no application receipt located; no résumé located; no screen; no offer.
Quentin Sorensen: referral-only mention; no application receipt for this vacancy; no screen; no offer.

Margin verdict entered 13 June by a reviewer
“Only one person has completed a screen, because only one candidate has a green check in the first calendar export.”
Quality-control response: The later interview notes and status table show three completed screens: Greta, Viktor, and Wanjiru. The old export is incomplete. The reviewer’s statement is contradicted by the records that follow it. Green checks remain decorative.

Email thread, subject: Materials received?, 14 June
From: Leila Tanaka
To: Recruiting operations
I received a résumé by email from an applicant on 7 June, and the message explicitly says it is an application for the posted role. The careers-form record did not import automatically, so the tracker initially showed no row. I entered the received date and attached the message to the file. I have not scheduled a screen yet.

From: Quentin Sorensen
To: Leila Tanaka
Thanks. Please preserve the original received date rather than the date you created the tracker row. The message arrived on the seventh; data entry happened on the fourteenth. Those are different events, despite the spreadsheet’s best efforts to make them look interchangeable.

Quoted automated import warning
“Application missing: no online form record.”
Leila: This warning is about the form import, not whether an application arrived. The applicant emailed a résumé and stated that it was an application. The record now includes that evidence.

Scheduling thread, 15 June
Bao Sorensen: I sent Viktor a new invitation for 11 June after he requested a different time. The calendar entry is marked completed, and I have the interviewer’s notes.
Viktor Fischer: Confirming I attended the rescheduled call on the eleventh. Thank you for moving it.
Greta Kaur: I attended on the tenth, as scheduled.
Wanjiru Sorensen: I attended on the twelfth. I can forward the written exercise if the panel needs another copy.
System digest: “Three interviews held.”
Quentin: For once the digest is right, though it arrived at the conclusion by an unusually scenic route.

Application materials inventory, 16 June
Greta Kaur — application form and résumé received; cover letter absent and optional; work history includes three years in office operations.
Viktor Fischer — application form, résumé, and cover letter received; work history describes two years of facilities support.
Leila Tanaka — email application and résumé received; cover letter absent and optional; experience is described in the résumé, but no screen has been scheduled.
Wanjiru Sorensen — application form, résumé, and cover letter received; related operations work exceeds two years.
Bao Sorensen — no application documents found; kitchen conversation note is not an application.
Quentin Sorensen — referral entry only; not an applicant record for this vacancy.

A reviewer’s checklist, marked “final” on 16 June
[ ] Application received
[ ] Résumé on file
[ ] Interview completed
[ ] Offer issued

Beside the checklist: “Four records look active; maybe that means four offers.”
Viktor’s correction: “Active” is not an offer status. The table explicitly lists no offer for anyone. Please do not infer an offer from a row being visible. Visibility is not a compensation package.

Reference-check log, 17–20 June
17 June, 10:15 a.m. — request sent for Viktor Fischer. Status: awaiting response.
18 June, 3:40 p.m. — request sent for Wanjiru Sorensen. Status: awaiting response.
19 June, 1:05 p.m. — Viktor’s reference replied. Status: received; review pending.
20 June, 9:30 a.m. — Wanjiru’s reference replied. Status: received; review pending.
Greta Kaur: reference not requested as of 20 June.
Leila Tanaka: screen not scheduled as of 20 June.

Draft decision matrix, 20 June
The role requires two years of relevant work. The matrix records Greta, Viktor, and Wanjiru as meeting the experience threshold, based on their application or interview materials. Leila’s résumé is on file, but the matrix does not yet assess her against the threshold. No offer has been approved or sent. Reference responses for Viktor and Wanjiru are received but not yet reviewed.

Planted note in a copied summary cell
“Offer sent to Greta; she is the only completed candidate.”
Panel chair’s comment: No offer has been sent to Greta. The status table says offer not issued, and the decision matrix says no offer has been approved or sent. Greta completed a screen; that is not the same event as an offer. The phrase “completed candidate” is also not a status in the process.

Recruiting stand-up transcript, 21 June
Greta Kaur: I wanted to check whether the process has a timeline. I am still interested in the role, but I have not received an offer.
Bao Sorensen: Correct. There is no offer in the system. We are reviewing references and application materials.
Quentin Sorensen: The tracker has a field for “offer issued,” and it is blank for every applicant. That is not a hidden yes. A blank field is the team’s chosen way of saying no offer is recorded.
Leila Tanaka: Please also keep my application in the received-materials list. I emailed it, and the message is attached. I understand a screen is not scheduled yet.
Wanjiru Sorensen: I submitted my application and attended the interview. I have not been told that a decision is final.
Viktor Fischer: Same. My reference response was received, but I have not been told the result.
Greta: Appreciated. I will continue to wait with the confidence usually reserved for printer maintenance.

Applicant communications log, 22 June
Greta Kaur — message received asking about timeline; no request to withdraw; no offer received.
Viktor Fischer — confirmation of continued interest; no withdrawal; no offer received.
Leila Tanaka — acknowledgement of receipt requested; no withdrawal; no offer received.
Wanjiru Sorensen — confirmation that reference details are available; no withdrawal; no offer received.
Internal note: “Candidates have all accepted.”
Correction: The messages say that some candidates remain interested and that references are available. None says an offer was made or accepted. Acceptance requires something to accept; the file contains no offer.

Hiring panel review, 24 June
The panel reviewed the three completed screens and the two reference responses received. Greta’s interview notes meet the posted experience and communication criteria. Viktor’s interview notes meet the posted experience and recordkeeping criteria; the reference review remains pending. Wanjiru’s notes meet the posted experience and communication criteria; the reference review remains pending. Leila’s application materials are retained for consideration, but she has not been screened. The panel did not select a finalist and did not authorize an offer.

Draft minutes, 24 June, copied from a previous meeting template
“Decision: Greta selected. Offer authorized. Other files closed.”
Handwritten review on the same page: This is template text, not the decision from today’s meeting. The signed minutes state that no finalist was selected and no offer was authorized. The draft line conflicts with the signed record. The template seems to have hired someone by typographical persistence.

Signed panel minutes, 24 June
Present: Greta Kaur, Quentin Sorensen, Viktor Fischer, Leila Tanaka, Bao Sorensen, and Wanjiru Sorensen.
Agenda item: Facilities Coordinator shortlist.
The panel reviewed candidate materials and screening records. The panel decided to complete reference review before choosing a finalist. No offer was approved. No candidate file was closed. The panel agreed to reconvene on 28 June.

Process audit, 25 June
Audit question: Does the file support that Greta has received an offer?
Evidence reviewed: offer field blank; status table says offer not issued; panel minutes say no offer approved; Greta’s message says she has not received an offer; recruiting stand-up confirms none exists.
Audit conclusion: No. A copied summary cell says an offer was sent, but that cell conflicts with each dated source record. The summary cell is not evidence of a sent offer.

Audit question: Does the file support that three candidates completed screens?
Evidence reviewed: individual attendance notes for Greta on 10 June, Viktor on 11 June, and Wanjiru on 12 June; later status table records all three as completed.
Audit conclusion: Yes. The initial calendar digest and a reviewer’s note say otherwise, but both are contradicted by the later attendance records and notes.

Audit question: Does the file support that Leila submitted an application?
Evidence reviewed: email received 7 June stating it was an application, attached résumé, and the recruiter’s receipt entry dated 14 June preserving the original arrival date.
Audit conclusion: Yes. The automated warning refers only to the absent online-form record, not the application received by email.

Audit question: Does the file support that Bao applied?
Evidence reviewed: tracker contains a question about whether a kitchen conversation might mean Bao was an applicant; no application or résumé is located; no receipt record exists.
Audit conclusion: No application is evidenced. The question is not a submission.

Reference review notes, 26 June
Viktor Fischer’s reference response confirms that he maintained facilities logs and coordinated routine repair requests. The reviewer has not entered a final recommendation. Wanjiru Sorensen’s reference response confirms operations experience and reliable attendance. The reviewer has not entered a final recommendation. The team has not asked Greta for references yet. These are partial process facts, not a decision.

Slack thread, 27 June, #facilities-hiring
Quentin Sorensen: Does anyone have the final panel decision? The tracker still says none.
Leila Tanaka: The panel is reconvening tomorrow. No one has been selected so far.
Greta Kaur: Thanks for the update. I am still interested; I have not accepted anything, since no offer exists.
Viktor Fischer: Likewise, no offer received on my end.
Wanjiru Sorensen: I have not received one either.
Bao Sorensen: A copied dashboard tile says “Greta—offer accepted.” Is that a real status?
Quentin: No. The tile was cloned from a sample record during setup. It has no applicant ID, no date, and no corresponding offer document. We removed it. In a process that involves actual people, sample data should ideally stop pretending to be a decision.

Dashboard snapshot, 27 June, before correction
Applicants received: 4
Screens completed: 3
References received: 2
Offers authorized: 0
Offers sent: 0
Offers accepted: 0
Sample tile: Greta Kaur — accepted

Dashboard snapshot, 27 June, after correction
Applicants received: 4
Screens completed: 3
References received: 2
Offers authorized: 0
Offers sent: 0
Offers accepted: 0
Sample tile removed; no offer event found.

The number four under applicants received refers to Greta, Viktor, Leila, and Wanjiru. Bao’s informal question and Quentin’s referral record are not application receipts for this role. The number three under screens refers to Greta, Viktor, and Wanjiru. Leila has not had a screen. The two reference responses belong to Viktor and Wanjiru. These counts do not imply a selection or an offer.

Candidate-file checklist, 27 June
Greta Kaur
Application receipt: yes, 6 June.
Résumé: yes.
Cover letter: no; optional.
Screen: completed 10 June.
Reference: not requested.
Offer: none.

Viktor Fischer
Application receipt: yes, 7 June.
Résumé: yes.
Cover letter: yes.
Screen: completed 11 June after rescheduling.
Reference: received, review pending.
Offer: none.

Leila Tanaka
Application receipt: yes, email received 7 June; entered in tracker 14 June.
Résumé: yes.
Cover letter: no; optional.
Screen: not scheduled.
Offer: none.

Wanjiru Sorensen
Application receipt: yes, 7 June.
Résumé: yes.
Cover letter: yes.
Screen: completed 12 June.
Reference: received, review pending.
Offer: none.

Other names in operational notes
Bao Sorensen: no application receipt or résumé located; a question in a kitchen conversation note only.
Quentin Sorensen: referral-only record; not an application for this vacancy.

A second copied verdict, found in the meeting packet
“Four interviews completed; the four active candidates have all advanced.”
Reviewer response: This sentence combines two incorrect claims. Four applications are recorded, but only three screens were completed. The records do not say all four advanced; Leila has not been screened, and the panel has not chosen a finalist. The number of active application files should not be silently substituted for the number of completed interviews.

Recruiting operations handbook excerpt, current as of 28 June
1. A received application is an application form submitted through the careers system, or an email that clearly states the sender is applying and includes application materials. A person’s name in a discussion does not count.
2. A résumé received by email is recorded using the email arrival date even if a staff member enters it into the tracker later.
3. A cover letter is optional for the Facilities Coordinator role. Its absence is not a missing required item.
4. A screen is completed only when the applicant and interviewer attend and notes or an attendance record are saved. A scheduled, invited, rescheduled, or canceled event is not a completed screen.
5. An offer is issued only when an authorized offer document is sent to the applicant. A draft, copied template, sample dashboard tile, or informal expression of interest is not an offer.
6. An offer is accepted only after an offer has been issued and the applicant accepts it.
7. When a summary conflicts with a dated source record, reviewers must inspect the source record. The summary is not automatically preferred because it is shorter or more confident.

Interpretation examples from the handbook
A calendar invitation on its own proves that a meeting was planned, not that it happened. If a later attendance record and interview notes show the meeting took place after rescheduling, those later records support completion. An email containing a résumé and a clear statement that the sender is applying can establish receipt even if an online form is absent. The absence of a cover letter cannot defeat an application when the posting calls the letter optional. A dashboard label showing “accepted” without an offer document or event is not an acceptance. A copied draft must be checked against signed minutes and the actual status fields. None of these rules requires a reviewer to guess what a blank field might mean.

Decision meeting, 28 June, 10:00 a.m.
Quentin Sorensen: We are here to finish the review, not to reuse the template’s decision text.
Leila Tanaka: The application count is four. The completed-screen count is three. The files support those figures.
Viktor Fischer: My reference response is in, but I understand it is still under review.
Wanjiru Sorensen: Mine too.
Greta Kaur: I remain interested and have not received an offer.
Bao Sorensen: The dashboard sample tile has been removed. There is no offer document for Greta or anyone else.
Panel chair: We will review the reference responses and discuss whether to schedule a screen for Leila. No final selection is made at this meeting. No offer is authorized.
Minutes clerk: Recorded. No offer authorized or sent; no candidate selected.

Follow-up email, 28 June, 11:42 a.m.
From: Recruiting operations
To: Facilities hiring panel
The signed meeting record is attached. It states that no candidate was selected and no offer was authorized or sent. The copied line in the prior draft was removed. Please use the signed record for any status report.

Reply from a reviewer
“I still think Greta has an offer because that is what the draft said.”
Reply from Quentin Sorensen
The draft was corrected before it was signed. Greta’s own message says she has not received an offer; the offer field is blank; the panel did not authorize one; and no offer document exists. The facts are not improved by repeating the obsolete sentence. We have a perfectly good word for this: obsolete.

Status report, 29 June
Application receipts evidenced: four.
Completed screens evidenced: three.
Reference responses received: two, pending review.
Finalist selected: no.
Offer authorized: no.
Offer sent: no.
Offer accepted: no.

Quality-assurance sample, 29 June
Question posed to reviewers: When a note says “offer sent,” what should be checked before reporting that an offer was sent?
Answer recorded: Confirm that an authorized offer document exists and was sent to the applicant; compare the claim with the offer field, dated correspondence, and signed panel record. A note alone is not enough when the underlying evidence contradicts it.
Second question: When a candidate is described as “the only completed screen,” what should be checked?
Answer recorded: Inspect attendance and interview notes for each candidate, including rescheduled meetings and later records. Do not rely solely on an early calendar export.
Third question: When an online-form alert says “missing,” what should be checked?
Answer recorded: Determine whether application materials arrived through another accepted channel. In this file, Leila emailed an application and résumé, so the alert does not establish that no application was received.

Appendix A: dated event ledger
6 June, 4:18 p.m. — Greta Kaur’s application and résumé received through the careers form.
6 June, 4:41 p.m. — Quentin Sorensen entered in a referral-only record; no application for the vacancy.
7 June, 8:02 a.m. — Viktor Fischer’s application, résumé, and cover letter received.
7 June, 8:36 a.m. — Leila Tanaka emailed an application and résumé.
7 June, 9:10 a.m. — Wanjiru Sorensen’s application and materials received.
7 June, 11:20 a.m. — Greta’s screen invitation sent.
7 June, 11:25 a.m. — Viktor’s original screen invitation sent.
9 June — Viktor requested a different time; original meeting canceled.
10 June — Greta attended screen; notes saved.
11 June — Viktor attended rescheduled screen; notes saved.
12 June — Wanjiru attended screen; notes saved.
14 June — Leila’s email application entered into tracker with original arrival date preserved.
17 June — Viktor reference request sent.
18 June — Wanjiru reference request sent.
19 June — Viktor reference response received.
20 June — Wanjiru reference response received.
24 June — Signed panel minutes say no finalist selected and no offer authorized.
27 June — Sample dashboard tile removed; no offer event found.
28 June — Panel reconvened; no selection and no offer authorized or sent.

Appendix B: common misreadings and corrections
Misreading: “There are six names in the tracker, therefore six applications.”
Correction: The tracker includes a referral-only entry and a speculative question about Bao. Four application receipts are evidenced.

Misreading: “Greta lacks a cover letter, therefore her application is incomplete.”
Correction: The role’s posting says a cover letter is optional. Greta’s application and résumé were received.

Misreading: “Viktor’s meeting was canceled, therefore he never completed a screen.”
Correction: The original slot was canceled, then a rescheduled meeting took place on 11 June with attendance and notes.

Misreading: “Leila has no online form record, therefore she did not apply.”
Correction: Her email states that she is applying and includes a résumé. The handbook accepts that route, and the original arrival date is recorded.

Misreading: “The draft says Greta was selected, therefore she was selected.”
Correction: The draft was template text. Signed minutes state no selection, and the later meeting also records no selection.

Misreading: “A dashboard tile says an offer was accepted, therefore the candidate accepted.”
Correction: The tile was sample data with no applicant ID, date, offer document, or corresponding event. It was removed. No offer was authorized, sent, or accepted.

Misreading: “Three completed screens means three offers.”
Correction: Screens and offers are different process events. The offer fields are blank and panel minutes authorize no offer.

Misreading: “A person’s interest in a role means an offer has been accepted.”
Correction: Candidates expressed interest, but the records show no offer to accept.

Appendix C: reviewer correspondence
From: Wanjiru Sorensen
To: Recruiting operations
Subject: Reference follow-up
I sent the reference details requested by the team. Please let me know if another detail is needed. I understand that this is not a selection notice, and I have not received an offer.

From: Recruiting operations
To: Wanjiru Sorensen
Thank you. We received the reference response on 20 June and are still reviewing it. No final selection has been made.

From: Viktor Fischer
To: Recruiting operations
Subject: Check-in
I am checking whether the reference was received. I am still interested in the role. I have not received an offer and do not want the tracker to imply otherwise.

From: Recruiting operations
To: Viktor Fischer
We received the reference on 19 June. It remains under review. The panel has not selected a finalist or authorized an offer.

From: Greta Kaur
To: Recruiting operations
Subject: Status
I remain interested in the Facilities Coordinator role. I have not received an offer. I would appreciate an update when the panel has reached a decision.

From: Recruiting operations
To: Greta Kaur
Thank you for checking in. The panel has not made a final selection and no offer has been issued.

Appendix D: records-management note
The tracker is an index, not an independent source of truth. It links to application messages, interview notes, reference correspondence, and signed minutes. Entries added later should preserve the date of the event they describe. A copied dashboard tile or draft statement should not override the linked records. Staff should correct an inaccurate label when discovered and keep the correction history visible. The purpose is not to produce a spreadsheet that looks serene; it is to describe what happened.

Appendix E: hiring-team debrief, 30 June
Greta Kaur: The process had a few moments where the tracker seemed to be interviewing itself. The signed record was clearer.
Quentin Sorensen: The initial count of six applications came from counting names, including a referral and a question. We should distinguish people mentioned from applicants received.
Viktor Fischer: The canceled first slot was correctly replaced by the completed rescheduled interview, but the early summary did not refresh.
Leila Tanaka: The online import warning was understandable as a technical warning, but it was copied into a human status without checking email intake.
Bao Sorensen: The sample tile should never have appeared in a live dashboard. It has been removed, and the audit did not find an offer event.
Wanjiru Sorensen: I recommend that summaries include a date and link to the record they summarize.
Panel chair: Agreed. For the next hiring round, the team will use source-linked status fields and remove sample records before opening the dashboard. The present record remains: four applications received, three screens completed, no finalist selected, and no offer authorized, sent, or accepted.

Appendix F: final fact check
Application receipt for Greta: supported by the 6 June careers-form receipt and attached résumé.
Application receipt for Viktor: supported by the 7 June careers-form receipt and attached materials.
Application receipt for Leila: supported by the 7 June email stating that she is applying and including her résumé.
Application receipt for Wanjiru: supported by the 7 June careers-form receipt and attached materials.
Application receipt for Bao: not supported; only a question appears, with no submitted materials.
Application receipt for Quentin: not supported for this role; the entry is explicitly referral-only.
Completed screen for Greta: supported by 10 June attendance and notes.
Completed screen for Viktor: supported by 11 June rescheduled attendance and notes.
Completed screen for Wanjiru: supported by 12 June attendance and notes.

[{"state":"Subject: Lantern Quay weekend, one last pass through the moving parts

Hi everyone,

I’m pulling the planning thread back together because the little details are now bigger than the big details, as usual. The autumn makers’ weekend is at Lantern Quay on 18 and 19 October, with doors at ten, public close at six, and load-out allowed until eight. Leila Petrov is coordinating the event for Kestrel Labs, which is hosting the weekend as a community open house. Hiro Alvarez is handling the venue contact and supplier paperwork. The event itself is not a Kestrel product launch, despite what the first draft of the poster said; it is a small public market with demonstrations, food, and a short evening music set. Please use “Lantern Quay Makers’ Weekend” in the vendor emails, not “Kestrel Expo.”

For the record, the room booking is confirmed for both days. The north hall is for tables and demonstrations, the glass room is the quiet room, and the covered courtyard is where the food stalls go if the weather behaves. If it does not, the venue can move the food stalls into the side corridor, but only if the fire officer approves the layout on the Friday walkthrough. Nobody should tell a food vendor that the indoor move is guaranteed. The venue has four folding screens and six spare tables; the plan does not assume more furniture than that. We have asked whether the courtyard lights can stay on through load-out, and Hiro is waiting for a response.

A quick note about the ticket page: general entry is free, and the booking form is only for estimating attendance. The page asks for an email address so we can send a practical arrival note, not because tickets are limited. The page’s old footer still says “all purchases final,” which is leftover language from a different Kestrel event and does not describe any payment for this weekend. We removed the paid-ticket button last month. There is no admission fee to refund. Vendor stall fees are separate and are covered by the vendor terms, which are attached in the shared planning folder.

Quoted reply from Hiro, Tuesday, 9:14 a.m.:
> I have the venue’s updated map. One thing: the green rectangle marked “storage” is not available to us. It belongs to the building’s maintenance team. We can use the little alcove by the north entrance for empty boxes, but it must stay clear enough for the door to open all the way. The venue manager said the accessible route needs to remain open, even during setup. I’ve told the table team, but please repeat that instruction because the old map is still in two people’s inboxes.

Quoted reply from Leila, Tuesday, 9:26 a.m.:
> Thanks. I will replace the old map in the drive and send the current one to the stallholders. I also asked the venue about the coat rack, because the note from last year says “rack supplied,” but that was for the upstairs room. This year we have the north hall, so I do not want to assume anything. We can bring two portable racks if they say no. The venue is checking whether its own rack is in the closet.

Hiro again, quoted from Wednesday:
> Confirmed: no venue coat rack in our room. We can bring two. The side entrance can be used by vendors between 7:30 and 9:30 in the morning, but visitors should use the main doors. The side entrance is not a separate public entrance, and we should not put a sign there that makes it sound like it is. Security will be stationed near the main doors from 9:45.

The food plan is a mix of things, not a formal sit-down service. Foxglove Outfitters is loaning the outdoor banner frames, although the company is not a food vendor and is not paying for the event. There will be a soup stall, a tea table, and a small bakery stall. The bakery has confirmed that its items will be individually labelled. The soup vendor is checking whether the serving station can fit on one table. The tea table has asked for access to an electrical outlet, but no high-power appliance is planned. We should not promise free food to visitors: the vendors set their own prices. The event team will provide water for volunteers.

The volunteer roster is still being adjusted. Leila has the morning check-in, Hiro has venue access and the first walkthrough, and the table team has two people assigned to each entrance. There are six volunteers who can help with setup, not six volunteers per room. Two people are scheduled for the quiet room at a time, and they can also cover the nearby information desk when the room is empty. We have asked everyone to wear the blue lanyard, but plain clothes are fine. Nobody needs a branded uniform. The first-aid kit is in the host office, and the venue has its own emergency equipment; we are not responsible for moving that equipment.

Quoted reply from Leila, Thursday afternoon:
> The flyer proof has the right dates now. It still says the market closes at seven, though. Public hours are ten to six. Load-out is later, but that is not public opening time. Could someone please stop changing the closing time in the shared graphic? I think the first version had seven because the music slot was pencilled in until 6:45. We shortened that slot. It ends at 6:30, with the sound off by 6:35, and visitors are still asked to leave by six. The extra half hour is for performers to pack quietly.

Hiro’s reply:
> I’ll fix the graphic and put “music for booked guests” nowhere, because it is not a ticketed guest event. The set is in the courtyard if the weather allows, and otherwise we cancel the set rather than move speakers inside. The hall must remain quiet enough for the vendors to pack and the venue has asked us to keep amplified sound outside. That does mean we need a weather decision by noon on Saturday, not at the last minute.

SMS exchange, copied into the thread because it clarifies the stallholder question:

Leila, 4:02 p.m.: Hi, I saw your note saying the vendor fee was paid twice. I checked the ledger and only one payment is recorded. Could you send the transaction reference for the other one?

Hiro, 4:05 p.m.: I think that note may be from the earlier test invoice. I’ll look.

Leila, 4:08 p.m.: Found the test invoice. It was voided before anyone paid it. The actual stall fee is one payment, recorded on 2 September.

Hiro, 4:10 p.m.: Okay, that explains the duplicate-looking entry. The spreadsheet has the voided invoice in the same tab as the live payments.

Leila, 4:12 p.m.: I’ll label it VOID so it doesn’t keep appearing in the total. Also, just to be clear, the stallholder is asking us to refund the fee because their assistant can no longer attend. They are not asking for a refund of the event admission price; admission is free. Their email says they want the vendor fee back, and the terms say a cancellation made more than fourteen days before the event can be refunded. Their cancellation came in on 20 September, so it is more than fourteen days before 18 October. I am checking the paperwork, not promising an immediate transfer.

Hiro, 4:15 p.m.: The ledger note currently says “no refund requested—vendor only asked about a replacement assistant.” That is not what the email says. I made that note after reading the first sentence and missed the next paragraph. Please correct it. The email explicitly asks for the stall fee back. We should use the signed terms and send a proper confirmation once finance has processed it.

Leila, 4:21 p.m.: Right, I have corrected the note. I’ll forward the request to finance with the cancellation message attached. We should not describe the request as an admission refund because the admission page is free. The request is a vendor-fee refund. I’ll also tell the vendor that the request is being reviewed under the fourteen-day clause, rather than claiming it has already been paid.

For clarity, the vendor terms have three relevant points. A stallholder may cancel in writing. A request received more than fourteen calendar days before the event is eligible for a refund of the stall fee; a request received later is not eligible unless the event itself is cancelled by the organizer. The terms do not say that the refund is automatic on the day the email arrives. Finance checks the account and returns the payment to its original method. A replacement worker does not change the terms, and a stallholder can ask for a refund even if they mention a possible replacement in the same message. It is the actual request that matters, not the first summary somebody writes in a spreadsheet.

The vendor’s email, pasted below by Leila:
> Hello Leila and Hiro,
> We have a staffing problem for the October weekend. Our assistant cannot come, and we cannot run the stall with the people left on our rota. We have looked at a replacement but do not have anyone confirmed. Please cancel our stall and refund the fee we paid. If a replacement becomes available we will let you know, but please do not hold the stall open on that possibility. We are writing now so you have the request in time. Thank you for understanding.

Hiro’s margin note from the first read:
> No refund request; they are only asking whether a replacement is possible.

That margin note is wrong, as the quoted email itself makes plain. It was a rushed summary, not an instruction and not a decision. The request says to cancel the stall and refund the paid fee. The subsequent mention of a possible replacement is expressly uncertain and does not withdraw the request. Leila has attached the original message to the finance ticket. We should keep the summary corrected so a later person does not rely on the mistaken margin note.

A separate table request came in from another stallholder who asks only whether they can send a substitute worker if they personally get sick. They did not cancel their stall, and they did not ask for a refund. That message should not be mixed up with the cancellation above. They are still listed as attending. Their contact card says “backup person: to be named,” which means no substitute has been confirmed yet. If they later ask to cancel, we will assess that later message under the terms.

The display table checklist is below, because apparently the checklist in the checklist folder was missing its checklist. We have reserved six tables for maker displays, two for food, one for the information desk, and one for the quiet room. The six display tables are not six extra tables beyond the venue’s stated supply; four are venue tables and two are the ones Leila is bringing from the office. The table labels should show the stall name and any accessibility or power needs. We are not printing prices because vendors may change them. The venue requested a narrow aisle beside the north wall. Please do not move the tables to make a photo backdrop unless Hiro confirms that the aisle remains clear.

The power plan is intentionally modest. The tea table has one kettle, subject to the venue’s check. The bakery uses no plug-in equipment. The information desk has a phone charger. The music performers bring their own battery equipment, and they have agreed not to use the indoor sockets. We are not running extension cables over any public walking route. If a vendor asks for more power, record the request and pass it to Hiro; do not answer “sure” on the spot. The venue may say no, and a request is not the same thing as approval.

A note about signs: the main entrance sign says “Welcome—free entry.” The side entrance sign says “Vendor setup only.” The courtyard sign points toward the public market but can be turned around if the outdoor area is closed. The sign team has two copies of the old map, and Leila has asked them to recycle those rather than put them up. The old map puts the quiet room beside the kitchen, which is wrong. The quiet room is in the glass room on the east side. Nobody should be sent to the kitchen to find it.

We have a small accessibility review on Friday. Those are venue requirements, not optional decoration. We have ordered large-print schedules, but if they have not arrived by Friday, we can print them locally. The schedule is one page, and it will show the two days separately so nobody mistakes Saturday’s music note for Sunday’s. The quiet room is available both days. It is not a staffed childcare room and should not be described as one.

We do not have permission to use the loading bay as all-day parking. Hiro will meet the driver. Leila will check the stall list against the signed confirmations. The list currently shows seven makers, three food vendors, two performers, and one community information table. That is thirteen entries if the two performers are counted separately. The public program has fourteen lines because it also includes the welcome note. Those two counts are different things and should not be compared as if one is a missing vendor.

The event budget is a planning estimate, not a commitment to spend every line. The estimate includes printing, table cloths, water, and the venue room charge. The borrowed banner frames have no rental cost. The bakery has not asked us to subsidize ingredients, and the soup vendor is responsible for its own stock. Any leftover water can go to volunteers. We have no cash box because vendors collect their own payments. If someone asks the information desk to break a large bill, the answer is that we do not handle vendor cash.

There was a question about whether Kestrel Labs can announce the names of all stallholders in advance. The signed form lets us publish the stall name and a short description. It does not let us publish private mobile numbers, home addresses, or dietary notes. The public copy of the schedule should use the vendor’s public contact address, if the vendor supplied one, or no contact information at all. A draft with personal phone numbers was briefly in the shared folder, but Leila removed it. If you downloaded it earlier, please delete it and use the new file.

The check-in desk should have the printed stall list, the venue map, the emergency contact sheet, the volunteer rota, and a few blank incident forms. The emergency contact sheet stays with the team; it is not a public handout. The stall list has a note column for arrivals, not a column for whether people have paid. Payment status stays in the finance copy. The public desk should not have bank details. If a vendor asks about their payment, refer them to Leila rather than opening the finance spreadsheet at the desk.

The rain plan has been asked about at least five times. If light rain starts, the courtyard can remain open under the covered section. If wind makes the banner frames unsafe, the frames come down. If the venue closes the courtyard, the food stalls may use the side corridor only after the fire officer has approved the arrangement. If approval does not arrive, food service pauses; we do not squeeze stalls into the north hall. The indoor market can continue in the north hall because that room is separate. The music set is cancelled if it cannot safely happen outdoors. We will post a simple notice at the entrance and on the event page.

Sunday is meant to be a little quieter. The makers can keep their tables open, the food vendors can decide whether to return, and the music set is scheduled for Saturday only. There is no Sunday performance. The venue will still provide the booked rooms on Sunday. We are not promising that every Saturday vendor will return on Sunday; the confirmations list indicates who has booked both days. The schedule should use the words “participating vendors” rather than “all vendors” in the Sunday blurb.

The social post draft says, “Everything is sorted, every stall is confirmed, and there will be music both days.” That is overconfident. We can say that the workshop seats are limited if the workshop booking page is still active, but that is a separate activity in the side room and does not restrict general entry.

The workshop is a short paper-lantern activity, scheduled twice on Saturday. It has ten seats per session because the room is small. Registration is free. We have asked the venue whether scissors can be supplied, but the host can bring blunt-tip scissors if they are not. We will not use craft knives. Any photographs taken during the activity should avoid showing registration forms with personal details.

The photo plan is simple. Leila can take a few wide shots of the market after opening. Anyone who does not want to be photographed can use the small blue sticker at check-in, and the photo volunteer will avoid them. The sticker is optional and does not affect entry. We should not photograph the quiet room. The vendors may take pictures of their own stalls, but they should ask before including a visitor prominently. We have one lost-property box at the information desk. It should be checked at the end of each day and handed to the venue office after Sunday load-out. Cash, keys, and devices should be recorded separately and passed directly to venue staff. We do not promise to hold items for a particular length of time; the venue’s lost-property process applies after handover. If someone reports a missing item, note the description and approximate time without writing unnecessary personal information in the public log.

The end-of-day routine is: stop public entry at six, make the announcement, allow visitors to leave, check the rooms, and then begin vendor packing. This is the event team’s combined planning note for the Tidewater Dental autumn open studio at Bracken Hall. Tomasz Novak is coordinating the booking, Yara Bergstrom is keeping the vendor list, and Ines O’Neill has the building contact. These names are only for the planning team; the public page should use the event address, not anyone’s personal number. The open studio is planned for 7 November, with public hours from 11 a.m. to 4 p.m. The team can arrive from 8 a.m. and must have the hall cleared by 6 p.m. The event is a casual afternoon of demonstrations, local makers, and refreshments. It is not a dental appointment day, despite the host company name, and there will be no patient records or clinical treatment at the event.

A small orientation note before the terms: the signed booking is for Bracken Hall and its attached gallery. The gallery is available for displays and the hall is where the public tables go. The kitchen is staff-only. The side patio is available if the weather permits, but the building manager can close it for safety. The lift serves the entrance level and the gallery. The rear delivery door is not a public entrance. None of those conditions changes the event’s public hours. The team should describe the venue simply as “Bracken Hall,” not as the neighboring civic theatre, whose name appeared on an early mock-up.

The booking form has a section called Event Basics. It lists the host as Tidewater Dental, the event title as “Autumn Open Studio,” the date as 7 November, the rooms as hall and gallery, and the expected attendance as “around 90.” That attendance number is an estimate, not a cap. The free online RSVP page helps us plan tea and chairs, but people without an RSVP may still attend. There is no admission charge. The “purchase price” field in the form is blank because no tickets are sold. The event team should not describe an RSVP as a paid booking.

The attached terms are the current signed version, dated 12 August. Earlier versions are in the folder for comparison and should not be treated as current. The terms say the host may cancel the room booking in writing. If the host cancels more than twenty-one calendar days before the event, the room fee is refundable after the building office receives the cancellation notice. If the host cancels twenty-one days or fewer before the event, the room fee is not refundable, unless the building itself cancels access. The exception applies only when the building cancels access; bad weather, a low RSVP count, or a change in the host’s plans does not by itself trigger that exception. If the building cancels access, the office returns the room fee regardless of when it notifies the host.

The terms also make clear that a request for a refund is not the same thing as a refund having been paid. The host must send a written cancellation, the office must verify the booking, and finance then returns any eligible amount to the original payment method. A phone call asking about options does not cancel the booking. A message saying “we might cancel if the speaker cannot attend” is conditional and is not a cancellation. A later written instruction can replace an earlier tentative message, and the office uses the latest clear instruction from the authorized host contact. The fee receipt records one room-fee payment; it does not include a ticket payment because tickets are free.

There is a note in the booking desk’s first review that reads, “Refund not due: host cancelled after the twenty-one-day cutoff.” That note has been circulated in a few internal replies, so it is worth preserving the context rather than treating it as a ruling. The note writer copied the date from a draft calendar that said 20 November. The signed booking and the current calendar both say 7 November. The cancellation email, if one is received, must be compared with the actual event date and the exact terms. Do not let the old review note decide a question that depends on the signed dates and the actual message.

For the planning calendar, the event date is Friday, 7 November. The date printed on the signed cancellation message in the file is 10 October. October has 31 days; from 10 October to 7 November is 28 calendar days. That is more than 21 calendar days. The building office’s later receipt stamp is 10 October as well. The message says, “We are cancelling our room booking for the Autumn Open Studio. Please return the room fee under the cancellation clause.” It is not framed as a possibility or a question. It is a written cancellation from the authorized host contact. In the sample training file, the building has not cancelled access, so the ordinary host-cancellation rule applies. The earlier desk note’s claim that the cancellation came after the cutoff is contradicted by the date in the signed message and the event booking.

> Hello, this is our written cancellation of the Bracken Hall booking for the Autumn Open Studio on 7 November. Please cancel the booking and return the room fee according to the signed terms. We are making this decision now, not asking for a hold or a provisional option. Please confirm receipt when convenient.

The office copy includes the confirmation stamp and the original event booking. The booking desk note is retained because the office wants the discrepancy visible for training, not because the note has authority over the message. The note was written before someone checked the signed calendar. It does not amend the terms, change the event date, or turn a clear cancellation into a tentative inquiry.

The terms have other ordinary logistics points. The host provides its own tablecloths, signs, extension-free display equipment, and refreshments. Bracken Hall supplies the tables and chairs listed on the floor plan. Nothing may be taped to painted walls. The host must keep exits, the lift lobby, and the rear delivery route clear. No open flame is allowed. Battery candles are acceptable if they are stable and kept away from fabric. The building may ask the host to move an item that blocks a route. This is not a reason to assume the room booking has been cancelled; it is an ordinary safety condition.

The page’s previous draft said “reserve your paid seat,” which came from a template and was removed. The page now says there is no admission charge. The welcome pair can point to the lift, the gallery, and the accessible route. A first-aid kit is held at the building desk. Any incident should be reported to building staff and recorded in the event log without unnecessary personal details.

The host’s logo can appear modestly on the welcome sign, subject to the usual building approval.

The insurance form lists the event as a public community open studio, with makers’ displays, demonstrations, and refreshments. The terms distinguish those situations deliberately, even if a short email summary leaves out the distinction.

Eligibility is not proof that finance has completed payment; the office still confirms the original transaction and processes the return.

A separate message from the host on 3 October asked, “If our demonstrator becomes unavailable, could we cancel without losing the room fee?” The office answered by quoting the terms and asking the host to send a clear written decision if it chose to cancel. It is also the latest clear instruction in the record. The earlier hypothetical does not undo or replace the later direct message.

The relevant sample cancellation arrived 28 days before the booked event, so it clears the stated cutoff.

Controlled copy for internal and applicant-facing use. Department: People Operations. Effective date: 1 April. This page describes ordinary application handling for the junior records coordinator and associated administrative vacancies. Where an individual vacancy notice gives a specific instruction, that notice governs the affected item; otherwise, this page applies.

Section A — Receipt and acknowledgment. An application is considered received when the portal displays a successful submission receipt or when Applicant Services logs a complete paper application. An automated acknowledgment confirms receipt only. It is not an offer, an interview invitation, or a confirmation that the applicant meets every qualification. Staff must not describe an acknowledgment as a hiring decision. A receipt should be retained with the applicant file.

Section B — Required application materials. Unless a vacancy notice says otherwise, the application consists of a completed application form and a résumé or employment history. A cover letter is optional. A transcript is required only for vacancies whose notices expressly require one. Staff should record which materials were received and should not mark an optional document as missing when it was not submitted. If a required item is absent, the applicant may be contacted for clarification before the file is marked incomplete.

Section C — Interview invitations. An interview is scheduled only after the applicant receives an invitation specifying a date and time. Applicants may confirm, request an alternate time, or decline. A confirmation preserves the scheduled appointment. A request to change the time is not a withdrawal from consideration. A decline of one proposed time is not necessarily a decline of the vacancy; staff should seek clarification if the wording is unclear. A withdrawal must be expressed by the applicant or an authorized representative and documented in the communication record.

Section D — Application withdrawal. A candidate’s application is treated as withdrawn only when the candidate clearly asks to withdraw, asks that the application be closed, or otherwise gives an unambiguous instruction that they no longer wish to be considered. A clerk’s menu selection, a reviewer’s proposed disposition, or an unverified summary is not a candidate instruction. If the file contains both a candidate communication and a staff summary, staff must check the original communication. The original communication controls unless a later candidate message changes it.

Section E — Contact details and availability. Applicants may give a preferred callback period. The preference is used for outreach planning and does not restrict the candidate’s availability unless the candidate expressly says that other times are impossible. If an applicant says that a listed time works, that statement is evidence of availability for that time. It should not be replaced by assumptions based on a staff note.

Section F — Corrections and audit trail. Corrections must preserve the original entry, identify the person making the correction, and state the reason. A draft comment may be retained for audit purposes, but it does not supersede the recording, email, or portal submission on which the file is based. When two staff fields disagree, the disagreement should be resolved by checking the source record. Pending correction does not authorize staff to represent an unsupported conclusion as the applicant’s own statement.

Section G — Equal administration. Applicants are assessed using the same published criteria. Internal comments may guide follow-up but do not add qualifications or remove requirements. No application may be rejected solely because an optional item was not provided. A staff member who identifies a discrepancy should refer it to the recruitment coordinator rather than silently changing the source evidence.

Section H — Sample case attached to the policy page. Applicant: Greta Castillo. Vacancy: records support assistant. Portal receipt: successful submission, 3 June, 08:16. Submitted documents listed in the portal: completed form and résumé. Cover letter field: blank. Vacancy notice excerpt: “A cover letter is welcome but not required. No transcript is required.”

Reviewer’s preliminary note, 3 June, 09:02: “Incomplete: no cover letter; do not advance.” The note was entered before the reviewer opened the vacancy notice. A second line in the reviewer’s draft says, “The applicant failed to include the required letter.” The draft remains visible in the file pending quality review. It is a staff assessment, not a quotation from Greta Castillo and not an amendment to the vacancy notice.

Document verification log, 3 June, 09:19:
Application form: received.
Résumé: received.
Cover letter: not received.
Transcript: not required by notice.
Submission receipt: successful.

Quality reviewer’s factual check, 4 June, 10:30: The published notice identifies the cover letter as welcome but optional. The file contains the two standard required materials. No other missing item is listed. The reviewer has not yet removed the preliminary note, because the correction must preserve the audit trail. The file remains in the ordinary screening queue; this policy page does not dictate the eventual hiring outcome.
