[{"state":"FOXGLOVE FOODS FIELD SERVICE POLICY PAGE AND DISPUTE FILE

Revision 8.4 — Service recovery, callouts, and repair disputes
Owner: Customer Operations
Applies to: Foxglove Foods' kitchens, cold rooms, wash stations, and company-owned repair equipment
Status: Active

A note from the operations desk

This page has been rewritten because the previous version caused confusion, and because several people apparently believe a loud complaint is itself proof of what happened. It is not. Read the event record, distinguish an actual request from a possible future request, and do not let a supervisor's confident summary substitute for the underlying facts. The rules below are intended for dispatchers, site managers, field technicians, and the person who has to approve a credit after everyone else has gone home.

1. What counts as a service visit

A service visit is a technician's attendance at a listed Foxglove Foods site for inspection, diagnosis, maintenance, or repair. A phone call, a remote review of photographs, and an unaccepted appointment offer are not attendance. A visit may include several tasks if the same technician remains on site and the tasks are recorded under one work order. A return visit on a later date is a separate attendance even if it concerns the same machine and the same unresolved symptom.

The work-order record should identify the location, equipment tag, reported symptom, arrival and departure times, work performed, parts used, and the name of the person who accepted the technician's findings. If a person refuses to sign, the technician records that fact and may attach a photograph or dispatch timestamp. A missing signature does not erase the visit. A dispatch entry alone, however, does not prove that the technician arrived.

When more than one item is mentioned, record each item separately. A leak from a washdown hose is not automatically a refrigeration defect; a door that will not latch is not automatically a compressor problem; and a general complaint that the kitchen is unreliable should not be turned into a diagnosis without inspection. Sites must give the technician reasonable access. If access is blocked, document the obstacle and do not report the attempted visit as completed repair work.

2. Request, complaint, and remedy are different things

A customer can report a fault without asking for money back. A request to inspect, repair, explain, reschedule, or send a senior technician is not a refund request unless the customer actually asks that a payment, callout charge, or other specified amount be returned. The words “this is unacceptable” and “I expect you to fix it” are complaints and repair demands, not, by themselves, requests for a refund. Conversely, an explicit request such as “please return the $180 callout fee to my card” remains a refund request even if the customer also wants the equipment repaired.

Do not infer a request solely from a supervisor's note, an agent's dropdown selection, a customer's threat about what they may do later, or the fact that a credit could be appropriate under another section. A customer who says “if nobody fixes this by Friday, I will ask for my money back” has described a possible later step; the customer has not yet made that request. If the customer then sends a separate message asking for the money, record the later request and its date. Do not backdate it to the original complaint.

A refund is a return of money previously paid. A waived future charge is not a refund. A replacement part provided without charge is not a refund. A credit against an unpaid invoice is an adjustment, not money returned, unless the customer specifically asks for a refund and the company approves one. These distinctions matter because the file may include several kinds of remedy at once. The person reading it must not collapse them into a single label just to make the report look tidy.

3. Callout fees and inspection fees

The standard callout fee for the listed kitchen equipment is $180 per completed visit. The fee covers attendance and diagnosis, not replacement parts or follow-up labor. If the work order identifies a covered warranty fault, the fee is waived. If inspection establishes that no covered fault exists, or that the reported condition resulted from misuse identified in the signed maintenance schedule, the standard fee may be charged. The fee cannot be charged merely because a technician wrote “customer caused” in a short summary; the inspection record must identify what was observed and how it fits the schedule.

For a return visit caused by a documented failure of the same repair within seven calendar days, no second callout fee is charged. The seven-day period begins the day after the first visit. A different fault, a new item, or a later recurrence after the period is not automatically included. A supervisor can waive a fee as a courtesy, but a courtesy waiver must not be described as a refund of a fee already collected if no payment was made.

4. Repair-quality review

A repair-quality review asks whether the work recorded on a specific visit was performed with reasonable care and whether the condition reported after that work is connected to it. A review should compare the before-and-after readings, technician notes, photographs, parts removed, and any follow-up diagnosis. It should also consider whether the equipment was operated outside the posted temperature range or left without the required cleaning. A later failure is not automatically proof of bad work. Equally, a technician's use of the phrase “customer damage” is not proof of customer damage.

If the company determines that its technician caused damage, the company arranges a correction or pays the approved repair cost. If the evidence does not establish who caused the condition, record “cause undetermined”; do not convert uncertainty into a finding against either side. A manager may state a preliminary opinion, but the final disposition must follow the inspection material. The complaint file should preserve disagreement between a manager and the factual record rather than silently editing one into the other.

5. Customer remedies

The customer may request repair, a replacement part, a credit, or a refund. Each request is evaluated separately. An eligible warranty repair does not automatically create a right to a refund. A callout fee paid for a visit that should have been waived may be returned if the customer requests it, or may be returned proactively under the approval matrix. A refund request may be recorded as received even if it is denied. The status “requested” describes what the customer asked for; it does not mean the company agreed.

A customer can ask for a refund in ordinary language. Staff should not demand a particular phrase or a form number if the requested return of money is unmistakable. “Put the $180 back on my card” is clear. “I want compensation” may need clarification because it could mean a refund, a credit, or another remedy. When clarification is needed, record the exact wording and the follow-up question. Do not pretend the customer asked for less merely because the request is inconvenient, and do not claim a request exists because a manager expects one.

6. Escalation and file integrity

Escalate threats of injury, active food-safety risks, electrical hazards, and repeated failures affecting a production line. Escalation is not a finding that the company is liable. Preserve original messages and timestamped records. A later summary may be appended but must not overwrite a source document. Where a summary conflicts with a message or inspection entry, mark the conflict and use the underlying evidence to decide what happened.

Do not coach customers to use particular words. Do not tell dispatch to suppress a refund request because the technician believes the repair was correct. Do not ask a customer to withdraw a request as a condition of receiving a safety inspection. Staff who make a mistake should correct the record with an attributable note. A second person should be able to see both the original entry and the correction.

7. File attached to this policy page: West Kitchen case

Site: Foxglove Foods, West Kitchen, equipment bay 3
Equipment: Chill cabinet FC-17 and rinse station RS-2
Work-order references: WF-77104, WF-77139, WF-77202
Customer contact: Dalia Moreau, site manager
Dispatch contact: Ansel Reed, evening coordinator
Service provider: Northbank Mechanical, a Foxglove Foods contractor

The case file is included as a worked example because the same dispute was copied into the regional dashboard several times, and the dashboard's summary is not reliable. The service desk has received complaints about the length of this section. That is not a reason to omit the dates or the messages.

7.1 Initial report, Monday 6 May

At 07:42 Dalia reported that FC-17 was displaying 8.9 degrees and that the cabinet door appeared not to seal. She wrote: “The cabinet is warm again. Please send someone to inspect it and tell us whether it can safely hold prepared stock. I am not asking for money back at this stage. I need a working cabinet before lunch, and I need a straight answer.” The report was logged as an urgent inspection request. It did not request a refund.

The dispatch system offered a 10:00 to 12:00 arrival window. At 08:03 Dalia replied, “Fine, send the technician. Please do not send the person who left the floor wet last time.” That was a request about staffing, not a request for money. Ansel recorded the note and assigned technician Ivo Pell. The earlier work order concerned RS-2, not FC-17.

At 10:26 Ivo arrived. The entry record shows the technician signed in at the service entrance. At 10:34 Dalia showed him the display and the door. The temperature probe reading was 8.7 degrees at the cabinet's rear shelf and 4.1 degrees at the front. Ivo noted a damaged door gasket and a loose internal fan connector. He photographed both. The cabinet was taken out of food service while the connector was reseated and the gasket adjusted. At 11:18 the readings were 3.8 and 3.9 degrees. Ivo wrote that a replacement gasket should be ordered because the existing one was torn near the lower hinge.

Dalia signed the visit record but wrote beside her signature, “This is a temporary fix. Please arrange the new seal.” She did not ask for a refund. The technician's invoice for the visit was $180, but the charge remained pending while the warranty status was checked. A supervisor later described this as a “no-charge repair.” That phrase refers to the pending fee; no money had yet been returned.

7.2 Internal note entered Monday afternoon

Regional supervisor Len Marr added: “Customer is satisfied, no refund requested, issue appears to be operator damage.” The first two parts of that sentence were not supported by the attached exchange. The last part was also premature. The file contained a torn gasket photograph but no observation showing when or how it was torn. This note was not a customer statement and did not replace the signed work record.

At 14:11 Dalia emailed dispatch: “The cabinet is holding at 4 degrees for now, but it is not fixed. Please order the gasket you said was needed. Also, I want the $180 callout fee returned to the card we used last month. I paid that fee for the failed visit on 29 April, and I do not accept being charged again for the same continuing problem.” This is an explicit request to return a previously paid callout fee. It concerns the 29 April visit, not the 6 May visit. The 29 April receipt in the attached ledger shows a $180 card payment. Dalia's reference to “the same continuing problem” is her description of the fault; it does not establish that the earlier repair caused the torn gasket.

At 14:32 Ansel replied: “I have recorded your refund request for the 29 April fee. We have not decided it yet. The new gasket is on order, and the current 6 May fee is still on hold.” Dalia answered: “Good. Please keep the request open. I am angry that I had to ask twice, but I have not asked you to cancel the repair.” The request remained open. A later dashboard line saying “customer only asked for repair” is contradicted by these messages.

7.3 Earlier visit, 29 April

The 29 April work order shows that technician Nera Vos attended RS-2 from 15:07 to 15:49. The complaint was that the rinse station hose sprayed toward the floor when the valve was turned fully open. Nera tightened a clamp and ran the station for six minutes. A photograph taken at 15:40 shows the floor dry and the hose directed into the basin. Dalia's note on the receipt reads, “Paid $180 by card; please send the report.” It does not say that the FC-17 gasket was inspected. The work order's asset field says RS-2. This is why Dalia's later claim that the same ongoing issue involved FC-17 cannot be accepted as a factual finding about the 29 April visit without further evidence; her refund request is still a request regardless of whether the rationale is right.

A dispatch export lists a 28 April appointment offer for FC-17, but the offer was declined because the kitchen was closed. No technician attended on that date. The export also lists a 30 April remote call lasting four minutes. Remote calls do not count as completed visits under section 1. These entries appeared next to the 29 April invoice and caused one analyst to call it “the second cabinet visit.” That characterization is wrong. The fee was paid for the rinse-station attendance.

7.4 Parts and return visit, Thursday 9 May

The replacement gasket arrived on 8 May. Ivo attended on 9 May from 09:12 to 10:05 and fitted it. He recorded that the door now closed evenly and that the cabinet held 3.7 degrees for twenty minutes. Dalia said the temperature had been acceptable overnight but asked for a longer monitoring period. She again asked that the 29 April $180 be returned. The record confirms that Ansel had already logged that request on 6 May; this repetition did not create an unrelated second refund amount.

At 10:18 Ivo reported that the loose fan connector was secure and that the replacement gasket was seated. His report does not establish the cause of the original tear. The installation was completed without a new callout charge under the warranty review. Dalia did not request a refund of the 9 May visit because she was not charged for it. A courtesy credit of $30 for spoiled ingredients was discussed, but Dalia said, “Do not substitute a food credit for the fee I asked you to return. Decide the fee separately.”

7.5 The rinse-station follow-up, Friday 10 May

Dalia reported that RS-2's hose had begun to spray again. The entry says she asked for a no-charge inspection under the seven-day return-visit rule. The first completed RS-2 visit was 29 April, so the 10 May report came more than seven calendar days later. The rule does not automatically waive a new visit outside that period. Dalia was told a separate inspection fee could apply. She replied, “I am not asking you to refund anything for the hose today; just tell me whether you will inspect it.” That statement is about the hose and does not withdraw her earlier request concerning the $180 fee.

A technician attended RS-2 on 13 May. The work record notes a split hose sleeve, a different part from the clamp tightened on 29 April. The sleeve was replaced. The invoice was $72 for the part and no additional callout fee was charged after a supervisor approved a courtesy waiver. No refund was paid as part of that visit. The courtesy decision should not be used as evidence that the 29 April payment had been returned.

7.6 Ledger extract

29 April: card payment, $180.00, description “RS-2 callout and diagnosis,” settled.
6 May: proposed callout, $180.00, status “held pending warranty review,” not settled.
9 May: gasket part and covered labor, $0.00 charged to site.
13 May: replacement hose sleeve, $72.00; callout line $0.00 after waiver.
15 May: refund transaction, none recorded.

The ledger is an accounting record. It shows that the 29 April amount was paid and had not been refunded by 15 May. It does not prove that the fee was incorrectly charged, and it does not erase Dalia's explicit request to have it returned. Any final approval or denial must be recorded separately.

7.7 Conflicting review comments

On 11 May Len Marr wrote: “Refund denied; customer never asked for one and the $180 was for a different asset anyway.” The first clause is contradicted by Dalia's 14:11 email, Ansel's acknowledgment, and her 9 May repetition. The second clause appears to refer to the 29 April payment being for RS-2 rather than FC-17; that asset distinction may matter to the merits of the dispute, but it does not change what Dalia asked for. The note is a supervisor's verdict, not primary evidence of the customer's wording.

On 12 May quality reviewer Sella Brant wrote: “The customer requested a refund for the paid 29 April callout. This is not an approval. The asset record shows RS-2, while the later cabinet complaint concerns FC-17, so the claim that the earlier callout was for the same cabinet fault is not established.” This review agrees that a request was made and carefully distinguishes the request from its justification. The review is consistent with the messages and asset fields.

7.8 Closeout guidance

A final response should say whether the $180 request is approved, denied, or still being reviewed, and why. It should not say “no refund was requested.” If denied, the reason should address the fact that the charge was for RS-2 while the later fault concerned FC-17, rather than pretending the customer asked for nothing. If approved, the payment reference and return date should be recorded. The 6 May fee was held and the 13 May callout was waived; neither entry is a return of the 29 April payment.

The case is not an example of a customer receiving every requested remedy. It is an example of a record in which a request was made, the supervisor's contrary verdict was wrong, and the merits of the request remained a separate question. Anyone reporting the event as “no refund requested” should revisit the original email before submitting the monthly service-quality figures.

8. Dashboard fields and examples

The dashboard has separate fields for fault reported, service performed, customer remedy requested, company decision, and amount actually returned. Populate each from the appropriate evidence. Do not copy one field into another. A “repair requested” entry does not imply that no refund was requested; a “refund requested” entry does not imply approval; an “approved” decision does not imply a completed payment until the transaction appears in the ledger. If the dashboard offers only one primary remedy, use the remedy most directly stated by the customer and add a note for the rest.

Examples from training files, all fictional:

Example A: “The motor is rattling. Send a technician.” Record a repair request. Do not record a refund request.

Example B: “Return the $180 you charged last week, and send someone to fix the motor.” Record both a refund request and a repair request. The second request does not cancel the first.

Example C: “If you fail to fix it, I will ask for the fee back.” Record a complaint and a conditional future intention, not a current refund request. If the person later says “I am asking now for the fee back,” record the later request.

Example D: A manager writes “no refund request,” but the customer's message says “put the fee back on my card.” Record the customer's actual request and flag the manager's summary as inconsistent.

Example E: A manager writes “refund requested,” but the customer's only message says “please send a technician.” Do not manufacture a request from the manager's label. This is why the original customer text must remain accessible.

Example F: A customer says “I want something done about this,” and no further context identifies whether that means a repair, a credit, or returned payment. Ask what remedy the customer means. Do not label the unresolved phrase as a definite refund request.

9. Records retention and service language

Keep the call recording, texts, invoices, visit sheets, and report attachments for the period required by the site contract. If a document is unavailable, note that it is unavailable; do not reconstruct a quotation from memory and present it as verbatim. When a customer corrects a mistaken summary, retain both the summary and correction. Angry wording does not make a message less evidential, and polite wording does not make an unsupported assertion true.

The company may disagree firmly with a customer. Staff should not describe a customer as “satisfied” merely because the customer permitted work to continue, signed an attendance sheet, or stopped replying. A signature acknowledges attendance unless the form expressly says otherwise. Likewise, a customer who says “thank you for coming” has not necessarily accepted the diagnosis, withdrawn a complaint, or waived a remedy.

10. Service manager checklist

Before closing a disputed case, answer these questions in order: What did the customer report? What did the technician observe? Which asset and visit does each charge refer to? Did the customer actually ask for money to be returned? Was a decision made? Was money actually returned? Are there statements in the file that conflict with the source messages? If the answer to the last question is yes, identify the conflict instead of hiding it behind a single status label.

This checklist is not an extra hurdle for customers. It is a safeguard against lazy file handling. It does not authorize staff to postpone a safety response while they debate accounting. It does not require the company to approve every request. It requires the record to describe what happened accurately before the company decides what it will do.

11. Anger, urgency, and professional response

A site manager may be angry because food is at risk, a production schedule has been disrupted, or a previous repair did not solve the problem. Staff should acknowledge the practical effect without conceding facts that have not been established. “I understand the cabinet outage has disrupted service” is appropriate. “You are right that our technician damaged it” is not appropriate unless the review supports that finding. The reverse is also true: staff must not deny a supported fact simply because the customer is angry.

Do not retaliate by delaying dispatch, charging an extra fee without reference to the schedule, or marking a customer as difficult in place of recording the reported fault. Keep the tone direct. Customers do not need a lecture about internal queues when they have asked whether their fee will be returned. They do need an honest answer about whether the request is pending, granted, or declined.

12. Current disposition at publication

As of 16 May, the $180 payment from 29 April remains in the ledger, the request for its return is open, and no refund transaction is recorded. The company has not made a final approval or denial in this attached file. The customer received a repair to FC-17, a new hose sleeve for RS-2, and a waived later callout. Those service outcomes do not mean the customer failed to request a refund, and they do not prove the requested refund was granted.

The policy page owner has asked that analysts stop using the phrase “refund requested: no” for this case. That instruction is not an invitation to mark every angry complaint as a refund request. 4. Covered attendance

For listed equipment during the active agreement term, one diagnostic attendance for a covered mechanical failure is included per reported incident. An attendance is the engineer's on-site visit, not a remote call or parts delivery. A fee quoted but not settled is not a payment. If a fee has already been settled and the company later determines that the attendance should have been covered, the account team may return the amount to the original payment method or issue an agreed account credit. The customer's explicit request for a returned payment should be recorded even before the coverage determination is complete.

5. Excluded damage

A customer may be charged for repair of damage caused by impact, unauthorized alteration, operation contrary to the safety instructions, or failure to secure a listed component after written notice. The company must identify the evidence supporting the exclusion. A code or preselected field in an electronic report is not, by itself, evidence. A preliminary observation that the cause is undetermined cannot be converted into a customer-caused finding by copying a manager's note. Where the physical cause cannot be attributed on available evidence, the record remains undetermined pending further inspection.

6. Estimates and approved work

An estimate is not an invoice, an admission of fault, or a payment obligation unless accepted in writing by the customer and then invoiced under the agreement. An internal estimate created before acceptance must not be represented as a charge already paid. Work required to make covered equipment safe may proceed while an unrelated estimate is reviewed, if the customer authorizes the work. A customer may dispute an estimate while requesting a repair.

7. Service fee review

The account team reviews an attendance fee against the agreement and the work-order record. The existence of an earlier payment does not prove that a later visit is covered, and a later pending line does not erase an earlier settled payment. If a customer asks for money back, record the request separately from the decision on eligibility. The staff member who first entered a claim may not mark the request resolved merely because the technical review has not finished.

8. Corrections and summaries

An automated or manual closeout summary is a convenience, not a substitute for the original correspondence, invoice, or engineer's report. If a summary says that a customer accepted a charge, verify that a written acceptance exists. If it says no refund was requested, check the customer's messages. Preserve conflicting records. A correction should identify the author and date and should not delete the earlier summary.

9. Safety and access

A tagged-out gate must not be operated until the engineer clears it. The customer may request an inspection, repair, replacement, refund, or other remedy in the same exchange. Requesting one does not waive another. A customer may refuse an estimate without refusing safe corrective work under the agreement.

Please send the corrected total and tell us whether the draft should be voided."}]},"appendix_a_call_recap":{"heading":"Call recap, written in a chatty style by Dalia because the structured fields alone did not capture why the scope kept getting confused","text":"At 07:42 Ines called from the Pier Annex kitchen. The immediate practical issue was the walk-in display occasionally blanking and an alarm having sounded. She did not report that every product was spoiled, did not ask for a replacement refrigerator, and did not tell dispatch to skip authorization. She wanted someone that day because the neighboring cold room was already busy. That is a scheduling and service priority, not a blank cheque. Dalia initially saw the phrase ‘whatever it takes’ in the intake transcription. On the follow-up, Ines clarified that she wanted a prompt diagnosis and a list of options, and specifically did not want any board ordered before she received an estimate. The clarification was made before the technician began billable diagnosis, entered by the service coordinator, and repeated in the work-order note. The call was not a later customer attempt to avoid a charge; it is an early scope definition.\n\nThere are several ways to misread the approval because the ticket screen shows the initial two-hour diagnosis cap beside the later approval. If somebody adds the numbers without reading the label, the total ceiling can look like three hours. That arithmetic is correct as a number of hours potentially covered: the source records give 1.25 hours of billable diagnosis and one additional hour of approved repair, for 2.25 labor hours authorized in the completed work. The diagnostic cap was ‘up to two hours’ but the technician stopped diagnosis at 1.25 and called before the repair. The customer did not authorize the remaining 0.75 repair hour merely by saying she wanted the unit stable. The manager summary's phrase ‘total work only three hours if we ignore the little bits’ is not a substitute for the approval details. It also confuses actual work, approved work, and billed work, which are separate measures.\n\nCallum's contemporaneous entry is frank: he exceeded the new one-hour repair allowance by 0.75 hours while monitoring and finishing. It would be inaccurate to erase the work from the service history. It would also be inaccurate to bill that 0.75 as authorized when there is no extension. The point of the authorization rule is not to decide whether the technician's judgment was reasonable in the moment; it is to decide what the customer had agreed to. If the team later obtains a documented customer agreement, that would be a later record. The exported packet contains no such record, and the 13:54 message says not to order a board and asks for an estimate if one is still needed. It does not say ‘I accept all work performed’ or ‘add the extra time to my invoice.’\n\nThe draft total can also mislead because it is internally arithmetical. Its line amounts do add to $868 before tax: $150 diagnosis, $210 repair, $60 second technician, $36 closeout, $46 capacitor, $8 clip, $310 board, $68 visit, less $20 credit. A sum that adds correctly is not necessarily a supported invoice. Two labor lines describe time that the policy excludes or the attendance log refutes. Two parts are not used at all. Only one parts line is supported. The presence of a number on a draft invoice does not turn it into an approval record. The billing queue's green status is an automated workflow state, not a customer signature.\n\nThe corrected amount is not obtained by simply deleting every questionable amount without checking the agreement. The service visit fee remains chargeable because one visit occurred. The $8 retaining clip remains chargeable because it was used and the recorded service agreement permits consumables below $10. The $20 recovery credit reduces the invoice once. The capacitor was not installed; a return request is not a completed return, but that warehouse distinction does not make it a customer charge. The board was only quoted. The closeout is explicitly no-charge. Rosa's canceled calendar placeholder cannot establish another person's attendance. Once these are resolved, the supported before-tax amount is $270 labor plus $8 plus $68 minus $20, which is $326. It is possible to debate the appropriate operational response to the unapproved 0.75 hours, but not to count it as approved based on this packet.\n\nThe contact record requires similar care. An older site card contains the name Iris, and one copied appointment was made under Rosa's dispatch calendar. Neither is the decision maker for this job. The ticket identifies Ines as the caller and her approval is recorded by Rosa. Do not infer that another Harbor Foods employee authorized the work simply because the organization name matches. Nor does the phrase ‘customer asked for quick fix’ identify a scope. The recorded approval is specific: one extra hour, drain/fan cleaning and testing, maximum $120, no control board. The written and verbal records agree on those limits.\n\nFor the record, a no-charge diagnostic check appears near the start of the technician log. It lasted 0.75 clock hours. The billable diagnosis entry is separate, lasting 1.25 hours. The first is excluded by the stated billing policy; the second is billed in the draft and supported. The no-charge closeout lasted 0.30 clock hours, and that is not chargeable either. The van return and photograph entry is 0.25 clock hours and explicitly not billable. The calculated $326 is not based on rounding the visible clock time to a whole three hours. It follows the recorded billable units and the extra authorization limit.\n\nOne copied comment says ‘customer accepted the board because it is on the invoice.’ This reverses the direction of evidence. A line item is an assertion by the drafter, not a reply from the customer. The actual customer message says not to order the board today. The parts record says quoted only, not ordered, not installed. The technician agrees. The board line is contradicted three ways by the source records. Likewise, a draft description saying ‘second technician support’ does not prove that a second technician attended. The attendance record has a canceled calendar event and no work entry; dispatch confirms nobody else came.\n\nThere is no indication in this packet that Harbor Foods paid the draft, that a final invoice was sent, or that the corrected invoice has been accepted. The status is closed pending invoice review, and the final billing email says it will not release or mark the item paid. If asked whether the customer has been charged already, evidence does not support that. If asked whether the draft has a substantial unsupported overstatement, the records support yes. These are different questions. The language in the draft and the preliminary manager comment should not cause a reader to collapse them into a single conclusion.\n\nThe purpose of retaining this long recap is not to make every decision mysterious. It is to preserve which details are source facts and which are interpretations. The service work helped the unit, and the temperature later held. That favorable operational outcome can coexist with an invoice draft that is incorrect and with some work that occurred outside the written limit. The customer can appreciate the repair without having approved every hour. The service company can charge valid portions without charging unsupported parts. The technician can have performed useful additional monitoring without that time automatically becoming approved labor. There is no contradiction in those statements once the categories are kept separate.\n\nA final minor point: the amount of tax shown in the draft is calculated as a stated $69.44, but it was generated on the unsupported draft subtotal. The current review question is about the before-tax charge. Do not try to reverse-engineer a tax rate from that total or add tax to the corrected figure unless a later invoice process supplies the applicable tax rule. No tax rule is included in this case packet, and it is unnecessary for checking the supported pre-tax service amount. The relevant calculations are explicit in the structured record: 2.25 authorized hours times $120 is $270; add the one used clip at $8 and one visit at $68, then deduct the $20 credit, for $326. The draft's own pre-tax lines total $868, so its pre-tax overstatement is $542."},"appendix_b_activity_digest":{"heading":"Long-form activity digest from the field service portal; entries below are narrative context, while numbered source records above control billing decisions","day":"2026-04-11","entries":[{"time":"07:42","author":"intake queue","text":"Ticket opened from Harbor Foods Pier Annex. In particular, the copied billing preview is not a contemporaneous field entry."},"appendix_c_reconciliation_commentary":{"heading":"Billing reviewer scratchpad, preserved after correction","paragraphs":["Start from the question being asked, not from the invoice total or the status color. This is a draft, not a receipt. The core billing rule requires recorded work and recorded approval. We have a valid site visit, billable diagnosis, limited repair approval, one used low-cost clip, and a credit. Each item can be traced to a source entry.","The diagnostic time is 1.25 hours, not 2 hours. The policy says up to two hours may be used for diagnosis without another call; it does not require billing the entire two hours. Since the record shows 1.25, the supported diagnostic labor is 1.25 times $120, or $150. The rest of the initial visit was expressly no charge.","The later authorization was a further one hour, not a further three hours. Its written maximum is $120, and the call note describes cleaning and testing the drain and fan. The repair entry runs 1.75 hours. Therefore only one of those 1.75 hours is within the new approval. At $120 per hour, one hour is $120 and the unapproved 0.75 hour would be $90 if it were ever separately approved. The source packet shows no such later approval.","Total supported labor is 1.25 plus 1.00, or 2.25 hours. At $120 per hour, that equals $270. The draft's 1.25 diagnosis plus 1.75 repair already totals 3.00 hours and $360, $90 above the approved labor. It also adds 0.50 hour for a nonexistent second technician and 0.30 hour that policy marks no charge. Draft labor is $456; supported labor is $270; difference is $186. That difference can also be seen as $90 unapproved repair, $60 unsupported second tech, and $36 no-charge closeout, totaling $186.","The parts comparison is not a question of whether each part appears somewhere in the work order. The clip was used and its $8 amount fits the specific consumable rule. The capacitor was never installed, and the fact that a return is merely requested is not an argument for billing it: the ledger states it was not consumed. The control board was quoted only and expressly declined. Therefore supported parts are $8, while the draft has $364 of parts ($46 + $8 + $310), a $356 unsupported parts excess.","The fee and credit must not be lost among the disputed lines. One visit occurred, so the $68 visit fee is allowed. The $20 recovery credit appears once and reduces the supported amount by $20. Do not subtract the credit a second time because a summary mentions that it is a recovery credit; the actual invoice record contains one line.","The full supported pre-tax calculation is $270 + $8 + $68 - $20 = $326. The draft pre-tax calculation is $150 + $210 + $60 + $36 + $46 + $8 + $310 + $68 - $20 = $868. The difference is $868 - $326 = $542. One can verify the difference from the labor discrepancy of $186 plus the parts discrepancy of $356, also $542. This cross-check is useful because it catches accidental omission of the clip or double subtraction of the credit.","Rosa's early note is the planted conclusion most likely to be repeated: ‘within cap’ and ‘customer accepted the board because it is on the invoice.’ Both claims are contradicted by the cited facts. Her later correction is explicit, and Dalia's status update follows the sources. This does not mean every person-written verdict in the packet should automatically be rejected. It means the factual fields must be checked, and a verdict that conflicts with them does not control.","The fact that the customer said the unit is steadier is relevant to the service outcome. It is not evidence of a price agreement. The fact that Callum did extra work is relevant to the work history. It is not proof of approval. The fact that a board appears on the draft is evidence about what the draft contains. It is not evidence the board was ordered. The canceled calendar tile is evidence a placeholder existed. It is not evidence a second technician attended.","One might be tempted to use the three-hour number appearing in a copied summary. The arithmetic behind actual authorized labor does not produce three hours: it produces 2.25 authorized hours. Actual billable work entries sum to 3.00 hours, but 0.75 of those hours exceed the written limit. The distinction between actual and authorized is the decisive reconciliation, and it is why the question cannot be answered by spotting a single number in the ticket overview.","Do not infer that the original two-hour diagnosis allowance and one-hour repair expansion combine into a blanket three-hour allowance for any activity. Their scopes are stated separately. Here the technician used only 1.25 diagnostic hours, leaving unused diagnostic capacity that does not automatically transfer to repair. The one-hour added approval was expressly for drain/fan cleaning and testing. The source records do not say unused diagnosis time could be reassigned to monitoring or finishing. The policy's authorization rule requires a recorded approval before work beyond the allowance proceeds.","Do not bill the $310 board because the customer asked for an estimate. Asking to receive a price before deciding is the opposite of approving installation. The message says not to order it today. The board record says it was never ordered or installed. This is a clean factual conflict with the preliminary summary, not a subtle inference about a vague customer tone.","Do not bill the $46 capacitor just because it was on the van and a return had been requested. The rule says a merely requested return may remain billable only if installed or consumed. The record says neither. The actual status is not ‘accepted return’ but that does not rescue the charge; the decisive fact is unused inventory. These two statuses are often conflated in a rushed review.","No claim of food loss appears in the ticket. The concern about temperature is real and explains urgency, but it does not authorize additional labor or prove a product loss. The initial intake phrase ‘food safety risk’ is a priority category and not a customer statement that inventory was spoiled. This is irrelevant to the arithmetic except as context, but retaining it prevents later readers from turning a priority label into an extra approval.","The service was not a failure simply because the invoice draft is wrong. The unit was reported as stable after cleaning and connector work. Similarly, a successful repair does not cure a billing defect. Operational status and invoice validity should be tracked separately. At export, the job is closed pending invoice review, while the draft is held. There is no payment confirmation, and the email expressly says it will not mark the invoice paid.","The desk should preserve both the initial and corrected summaries. Replacing the old statement without a trail would make it hard to explain why the invoice was held. The preliminary note says its author had not opened the audit. The subsequent source check corrected it. That sequence is plausible and useful; it is not a reason to privilege the first conclusion because it came earlier or was written by a manager.","This reconciliation uses only amounts and rules in the packet. It does not need outside tax rates, parts catalogs, or assumptions about Harbor Foods' procurement practice. If someone later supplies a signed extension or a revised agreement, the result can be recalculated. - state length: about 7782 words each (a long thread, a multi-section document, a log dump or a report with appendices); every state within ±30% of that

- domain: clinic and appointment administration
- genres to spread across the sources: status update to a manager, handwritten-style note typed up, FAQ excerpt
- tone: terse with typos
- instruction style for this batch: plain questions ('Did the customer ask for a refund?')
- candidate-description style for this batch: descriptions that avoid the words used in the text (paraphrased)
- names you may use (never reuse a name across sources): Yara Fischer, Amara Kaur, Quentin O'Neill, Priya O'Neill, Nadia O'Neill, Aiden Mensah; companies: Kestrel Dental, Copperleaf Health, Foxglove Software, Harbor Logistics
- focus traps: planted_verdict. Every question in this batch uses this trap (others may occur naturally).

[{"state":"Kestrel Dental | admin packet for Monday review. Typed up from desk notes, status updates, and the appointment FAQ. Terse, spelling not checked. Names and examples in this packet are fictional. Keep patient details inside the clinic. This packet is for checking the appointment desk workflow, not for making clinical decisions. No diagnosis is included. The examples below use ordinary scheduling language and should not be read as advice about treatment. When a note says “done,” it means the administrative action was recorded, not that any care was provided. When a note says “pending,” it means the desk has not yet confirmed completion. Staff should check the day’s appointment screen before calling anyone, since a copied list can be behind. A desk entry is not proof that a patient received a reminder. A reminder sent by text is not proof that the patient read it. The final booking record is the source used for current appointment status. If an entry is unclear, ask the desk lead rather than guessing. No urgent clinical issue is discussed here. For a clinical concern, use the normal nurse line and do not rely on this admin packet.

STATUS UPDATE TO MANAGER — Monday, 08:10. From: Yara Fischer, front desk. To: desk manager. Subject: morning list and older open items. Hi, I checked the screen against the paper diary before opening. Three changes from Friday were entered, and one old paper note still needs a scan. The printer jammed again but it is working now. There are two people waiting for a call back about their preferred times. I have not changed their bookings. Please see the short summary first, then the dated entries. Sorry, some spelling is bad. The status column is from the live screen at 08:05 unless another time is written beside it. The hand-written sheets are in the blue folder. The FAQ excerpt is copied at the end so the casual cover person can find the standard steps.

The first current item is Amara Kaur. The appointment screen says her cleaning visit is booked for 14 May at 09:20. A text reminder was sent on 12 May. No cancellation is recorded, and the slot still appears under her name. The paper diary also has 14 May, 09:20. A margin note says “maybe move?” but the call log has no request from Amara to move it. The note was made by a staff member while looking at a different day, so it is not a patient request. The desk has not offered the slot to anyone else. Manager’s draft line in the prior summary says “Amara cancelled; release the room.” That line is wrong. The live booking remains active, and there is no record of Amara cancelling. Do not release the room based on the draft. If she calls later and asks to change it, update the booking then. Current desk result: leave the appointment as booked.

Quentin O’Neill is booked for a review on 16 May at 15:40. A voicemail from Quentin on Friday asked whether a morning time might be available in June. He did not ask to cancel the May review. Yara called back and left a message offering two June choices, but neither has been accepted. The May slot is still confirmed on the screen. An older note from the previous shift says “Q wants out of May,” but that was a staff shorthand for “asked about June”; it is not an accurate cancellation entry. A manager’s draft says “Quentin cancelled the May visit.” The call log does not support that conclusion. Keep the 16 May booking until Quentin actually requests a change and staff record it. The June choices are suggestions only. No appointment has been moved. Do not tell another caller that the 15:40 slot is open.

Priya O’Neill has a new patient appointment booked for 20 May at 11:00. The registration form is complete except for one optional contact preference. The appointment is not waiting on that preference. A message from Priya says she will bring the missing detail at check-in. There is no note saying she wants to postpone, and there is no request for a refund or credit. The account summary shows a deposit marked received. A draft manager comment in the old spreadsheet says “no deposit, likely no-show.” The payment record directly below it says “deposit received, 7 May,” and the appointment screen remains confirmed. The comment was copied from a blank template and was not checked. Do not treat it as a verified payment status or a patient intention. The current record supports that a deposit is on file and a booking is active.

Nadia O’Neill called the desk on Friday about the time of her appointment. She asked whether 13:30 could be changed to 14:00, because the earlier time conflicted with a bus connection. The desk offered 14:00, and Nadia said that worked. The live screen now shows 14:00. The handwritten sheet still shows 13:30 because it was not rewritten after the call. A margin stamp says “patient declined.” That stamp was applied in error: the call recording summary says she accepted the offered 14:00 time. The manager’s first draft repeats “Nadia declined the new slot.” The later dated call note and current booking screen both show the opposite. Current action: keep 14:00. Do not call her to re-offer a time she already accepted unless she contacts us again.

Aiden Mensah’s visit is not yet confirmed. The clinic sent two proposed times by text, and the message has no reply. The screen labels the request “awaiting response,” not “booked.” The paper list has a tick beside Aiden’s name, but Yara says that tick means the reminder was sent, not that a time was accepted. The manager’s draft says “Aiden confirmed Tuesday.” There is no confirmation from Aiden in the call log, text thread, or booking screen. The correct desk action is to leave the request pending and follow the ordinary contact procedure. Do not mark it as confirmed based on the tick. If Aiden chooses one of the offered times, the desk can then create the booking.

Older open item, 06 May: a caller asked whether a missed appointment fee could be removed. The caller was not asking the clinic to return money already paid; the fee had not yet been charged. The desk explained that the request would be reviewed. The note says the caller wanted the fee waived. The account shows no payment against that fee. A separate refund form belongs to another file and should not be attached. The manager’s draft says “refund issued.” That does not match the ledger or the call note. No refund is recorded. This packet does not decide whether the fee should be waived; it records only what was asked and what the account shows. The open review should stay open until an authorized person makes the fee decision.

Desk handover, 08:22: I called the supplier about the label rolls, not about any patient booking. They will drop them off after lunch. The appointment reminder queue is current through Sunday evening. Two texts bounced, one because a number was missing a digit and one because the phone was switched off. The failed messages are not evidence of cancellation. The desk should try the approved alternate contact method where one is already on file. Do not add a new contact number from a casual note without confirming it with the patient. The call-back list has a yellow tab for pending and a green tab for completed. A green tab means a staff member returned a call; it does not mean the patient agreed to a change. Each call should be logged with date, time, staff initials, what the patient asked for, and what the desk actually changed.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed from the blue folder — 09 May, probably 16:40. “Amara? 14th still there. She asked nothing today. check screen. old line says cancel but not her words. Dont erase booking just from this sheet.” The handwriting is untidy and one word is overwritten. Yara checked the call log and found no contact from Amara that day. The note’s question mark refers to the staff member checking the name, not uncertainty about the booking. The second line says “maybe room change?” but there is no room change on the live screen. A clerk’s pencil note on the back reads “cancelled??” The double question marks were a reminder to check, not a decision. The manager’s draft summary, written before checking the screen, states “Amara cancelled.” The screen, paper diary, and call log all show that the appointment remains active and that no cancellation request is recorded. Use the checked records, not the unchecked summary.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed from the same folder — 10 May, time unclear. “Quentin rang. June morning better if poss. May 16 still ok he said. We will call with options. not a cancel.” Under that, a different hand wrote “May cancelled?” The desk lead has marked that line as a question from the cover shift, not a confirmed change. The call summary says Quentin asked for an additional option in June and explicitly said to keep the May review for now. The manager’s draft says the patient had cancelled the May slot. That is not what the dated call note records. The screen still displays the 16 May appointment. If a later call changes the plan, the next staff member must enter the new request and the time of the call. Do not infer cancellation from a question mark or from discussion of a possible future appointment.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed from a loose slip — 11 May. “Nadia wants 2pm not 1.30. offered it. said yes. I changed live screen but paper diary needs pen.” There is a small arrow from 13:30 to 14:00. The other side says “declined?” in red ink, apparently copied from an old template. The call log records acceptance of 14:00. The manager draft says Nadia declined the revised time, but this draft was made before the call log was attached. The live screen is current and shows 14:00. The appointment remains booked. If the paper diary is corrected, write the date and initials beside the correction; do not cover the original entry so the audit trail remains visible.

HANDWRITTEN-STYLE NOTE, typed from a pocket pad — 12 May. “Aiden text sent, no answer. dont tick as booked. tick only reminder. asked desk if Tue was possible? no reply yet.” A checkmark appears next to the line, and a second staff member wrote “confirmed?” The mark is explained by Yara as confirmation that the message went out, not confirmation of a visit. The booking screen has no appointment time assigned. The manager draft says “confirmed Tuesday,” but that statement was copied from the checkmark without checking what the mark meant. The text thread has no incoming reply. Keep the record as awaiting response.

Daily desk sequence, in brief: At opening, compare the live appointment screen with the paper diary. Use the patient name and date of birth to avoid mixing records. If a patient asks about a possible time, record it as a question until the patient accepts an offered slot. If they accept, update the live screen and make a dated paper correction. If the patient asks to cancel, record the request and follow the clinic’s cancellation process. If a staff member merely wonders whether an appointment was cancelled, do not enter a cancellation. A note that says “call them” is an instruction to staff, not evidence that the patient made a request. A forwarded message can contain another person’s words; record who made the request, not just the words themselves. If one staff member quotes a manager, do not treat that quote as the underlying patient’s decision. Confirm by checking the patient-originated call, message, or signed form.

The desk received several unrelated calls this week. One caller asked for directions from the bus stop. Another asked whether the waiting room had step-free access. A third asked what time the clinic closes on Thursday. Those inquiries are not requests to book or cancel. A caller asking “could I come later?” has not necessarily changed a booking; staff must offer an available time and confirm that the caller accepts it. A caller asking “what if I need to cancel?” has not cancelled. A patient saying “I can’t do that time” may be asking to reschedule, but the desk should clarify the intended action and record it accurately. No staff member should mark a slot open merely because the patient expressed difficulty getting there. When an appointment is changed, the record should show the old time, the new time, who asked, and when the change was made.

FAQ EXCERPT — For cover staff. Q: What counts as a confirmed appointment? A: A specific date and time shown in the live booking screen after the patient has accepted it, or a previously confirmed time that has not been changed. A proposed option, an unanswered text, a reminder tick, or a paper note without an accepted time is not a confirmed new booking. Q: Can I use a manager’s summary instead of the call log? A: Use it as a pointer only. If it conflicts with the dated patient contact or live booking record, check the source record and ask the desk lead. A summary can be mistaken or stale. Q: If a note says “cancel?” should I release the slot? A: No. A question mark is not a patient request. Confirm what the patient said and follow the cancellation process. Q: If someone asks to move to a different time, when is the old time removed? A: After the patient accepts an alternative and the change is entered, or after a clear cancellation request is processed. Do not assume that asking about an alternative means the patient has given up the original slot.

FAQ EXCERPT — More desk questions. Q: Does a reminder mean the patient confirmed? A: No. It means the clinic sent a reminder. A delivery receipt can show that a message reached a device, but it does not establish that the patient accepted a change or even read the content. Q: If a patient says “that should work,” can I finalize the time? A: Clarify if needed and record the answer in the normal way. Do not turn an uncertain phrase into a completed booking without checking the context. Q: Can the handwritten diary be used to override the screen? A: It can point out a possible error, but compare it with the dated call or message and ask a lead if records differ. Keep the correction traceable. Q: Should a draft report decide which record is correct? A: No. A report is not a substitute for the source record. It may contain copied text, an earlier view, or a staff interpretation. Q: Does an unreturned call count as an accepted offer? A: No. Leave the offer pending. Q: If a patient asks whether a fee can be reviewed, has money been returned? A: No. A question or review request is not a completed payment reversal. Check the ledger for any actual transaction.

At 09:05, Yara reviewed the live screen again. Amara remained booked for 14 May at 09:20. Quentin remained booked for 16 May at 15:40. Priya remained booked for 20 May at 11:00. Nadia remained booked for 14:00 on the date shown in her record. Aiden remained pending, with no slot assigned. This is the direct status check after the earlier draft notes were found. The staff did not change any of these records during the check. The review was administrative only. If the appointment screen is refreshed and a new patient contact is added, that later record may change the status; nothing in this packet describes such a later contact.

Front desk call log excerpt, for cross-checking the summary. 08 May, 10:14: Amara Kaur: no incoming call; outgoing reminder delivered. 09 May, 16:40: Yara checked Amara’s booking, no change made. 10 May, 12:02: Quentin O’Neill called; asked about June morning availability; requested that May 16 remain. 10 May, 12:19: callback placed, no answer; message left with June options. 11 May, 09:31: Nadia O’Neill called; asked for 14:00 instead of 13:30; accepted 14:00 when offered; screen updated. 12 May, 15:06: Aiden Mensah reminder sent; no reply received as of 15:30. 12 May, 16:10: Priya O’Neill confirmed that she would bring the optional contact preference at check-in; no booking change requested. These entries were entered by the staff member who handled each contact. They are not copied from the draft summary.

Draft summary history. Version A, saved at 07:42: “Amara cancelled. Quentin cancelled May. Nadia declined change. Aiden confirmed Tuesday. Priya missing deposit.” Version B, saved at 08:02 after Yara’s screen check: “Several statements above not supported. Check each against live screen and call records.” Version A was prepared from old margin marks and a blank template. The author had not opened the call log or account ledger. Version A is retained to show why the discrepancy was reviewed; it must not be used as the current appointment status. Version B is not itself the source of truth either; its comments point to the relevant records. The actual evidence is in the live booking screen, the patient-originated call notes, and the ledger entries described above. No update is needed to the appointments except the already recorded Nadia time change.

The paper diary has two columns: “message sent” and “patient accepted.” The mark for Aiden appears only in the first column. The mark was put there by the cover clerk after sending the reminder. There is no mark in the acceptance column. A faint line crosses the page near Tuesday, but it is a printer artifact and not a booking entry. The manager’s phrase “confirmed Tuesday” appears on a separate draft sheet, not in the diary. No patient message says “Tuesday works.” No staff member heard Aiden accept Tuesday by phone. The correct interpretation of the record is pending response. If a response arrives later, log it with its exact time and update the live screen.

For Amara, the live screen and paper diary match. The reminder text was sent, and its delivery status reads delivered. Delivery is not a cancellation. The entry “maybe move?” was written by a staff member who was checking room capacity. It did not come from Amara. The draft statement that she cancelled was not based on a patient contact. The call log contains no cancellation request. The booking is active. If an authorized staff member needs to move the room for operational reasons, follow the internal room-assignment process without changing the patient’s attendance status. Do not call that a patient cancellation.

For Quentin, the call note distinguishes between asking about June and changing the May appointment. He asked for possible morning times in June and said the existing May review could stay.
