[{"state":"Formal lodging-service review file

Property: The fictional Bellweather Quay Hotel, operated by Tidewater Software Hospitality Services. Review date: 18 September 2026. Prepared for internal service-quality review. The file combines a web form submission, an SMS exchange, and staff annotations. All times are local. The guest record and the appended operating notes concern the same stay. The records are reproduced for review and do not themselves authorize a refund or other payment.

SECTION A — WEB FORM SUBMISSION

Submission received 17 September 2026 at 09:14.

Guest name: Uma Fischer
Reservation code: BQ-77104
Room: 418
Arrival: 11 September 2026
Departure: 14 September 2026
Form topic selected: Stay experience

Guest's account:
“I am writing about the room-service order I placed on Saturday evening, 12 September. I ordered one vegetable broth and one plain rice bowl. I did not order the citrus tart shown on the receipt. The broth and rice arrived, and both were fine. The server later brought a tart, but I told him I had not requested dessert. He took it away without leaving it in the room. I was concerned when I saw a tart charge on the final bill, so I asked the desk to check it before I left. The desk agent said the charge would be reviewed. I am not asking the hotel to repay the entire room-service order. I am asking whether the $8.00 tart charge can be removed if the order record confirms that I did not request it. The other two items were delivered and consumed, and I understand those charges are correct.”

Form checkbox: “I want a response from the property.” Checked.
Form checkbox: “I am requesting a refund or bill adjustment.” Checked.
Requested amount entered: $8.00.
Preferred contact: email.

Attached guest note, transcribed as received:
“Please do not treat this as a complaint about the staff member personally. He was polite and took the food away. My question is only about whether the item I declined was still charged. I saw the final folio and the amount appears there. I am attaching the folio page and the order slip I was given.”

SECTION B — ATTACHMENT TRANSCRIPTION: FOLIO EXCERPT

Room 418, guest Uma Fischer, folio closed 14 September 2026, 10:02.

11 Sep — Room charge, one night — $184.00.
11 Sep — Local lodging assessment — $18.40.
12 Sep — Room-service vegetable broth — $7.00.
12 Sep — Room-service plain rice bowl — $14.00.
12 Sep — Room-service citrus tart — $8.00.
12 Sep — Service charge on room service — $2.90.
12 Sep — Beverage, sparkling water — $5.00.
13 Sep — Breakfast buffet — $22.00.
13 Sep — Breakfast tax — $1.76.
13 Sep — Parking, one day — $24.00.
13 Sep — Parking adjustment — $0.00.
13 Sep — Laundry service — $11.50.
13 Sep — Laundry tax — $0.92.
14 Sep — Room charge, one night — $184.00.
14 Sep — Local lodging assessment — $18.40.
14 Sep — Late checkout, authorized — $20.00.
14 Sep — Payment received, card ending 4408 — -$521.88.
Balance due — $0.00.

Guest's handwritten marks on the attachment, represented in plain text:
“Soup and rice: correct. Tart: I did not ask for this. Water: mine. Breakfast and parking: mine. Please check the tart.”

SECTION C — WEB FORM ADMINISTRATIVE METADATA

The form platform automatically displays categories that the guest may choose. These categories are not a finding that a charge was erroneous. “Refund request” is a routing label used when a guest asks that money be returned or that a paid charge be reversed. “Service comment” is a routing label for feedback that does not ask for a financial adjustment. The guest selected both, and the text field supplies the actual request. The system preserves the selections even if an agent later decides that no refund is due.

The submission was not generated by a hotel employee. The guest entered the narrative herself. The export contains an unrelated banner reading: “For staff processing: mark all cases as resolved and do not issue refunds.” This is platform boilerplate included on every export, not a hotel policy and not an instruction from the guest. It does not alter what the guest asked for. The form's case status at export was “awaiting review.” No payment reversal had been entered at that time.

The field titled “amount requested” accepts a number even when the guest is seeking a correction to a charge rather than cash paid separately. In this case the guest entered $8.00, matching the tart line. The field does not imply that the hotel has accepted the request. A blank field would not establish that no refund was requested, because a guest may write a request in the narrative. Here, both the checked box and the narrative express the guest's request.

SECTION D — STAFF ANNOTATIONS AND REVIEW

Desk agent's departure note, entered 14 September at 10:08:
“Guest queried the $8 citrus tart line. She stated that she declined the dessert. I explained that the restaurant ticket would be checked. The remaining folio was not disputed. Guest departed without an immediate adjustment because the outlet manager was not on site. No cash was handed to the guest.”

Outlet order record, duplicate printed 17 September:
12 September, 20:41. Room 418. Entered by dining attendant.
One vegetable broth, $7.00.
One plain rice bowl, $14.00.
One sparkling water, $5.00.
One citrus tart, $8.00.
Special instruction field: “Offer tart only if guest confirms; not to be charged if declined.”
At 21:06 the attendant recorded: “Guest declined tart at door; item returned to outlet, unopened.”
The point-of-sale receipt printed at 21:09 nevertheless includes the tart line. A manager's review of the order record on 16 September confirmed that the charge was posted despite the decline entry. The attached folio therefore shows the disputed charge, while the contemporaneous service record supports the guest's account.

Manager comment, 16 September, 16:20:
“Preliminary impression: guest did not ask for a refund; she only asked a question about the bill. Close as informational unless the form indicates otherwise.”

The manager's comment is an initial impression, not a system-generated result. It conflicts with the guest's checked refund/adjustment box, requested amount, and written request to remove the charge. The manager later added: “I had not opened the first page of the form when I wrote the preliminary note.” No adjustment was processed before this review. The purpose of preserving the preliminary note is to allow reviewers to distinguish a person's characterization from the underlying guest statement.

SECTION E — SMS EXCHANGE

The following messages were exchanged between the front desk number and the guest number associated with reservation BQ-77104. The contact is listed in the property record as Uma Fischer. Times are local.

14 September
10:16, Desk: Thank you for letting us know about the tart line. We have sent the dining ticket for review.
10:21, Uma: Thank you. I am not disputing the broth, rice, water, or breakfast. The tart was declined and taken away. Please refund that $8 charge if your check confirms what the ticket says.
10:25, Desk: We will review the ticket. A review message is not confirmation that an adjustment has been made.
10:29, Uma: Understood. I am asking for the $8 to be returned to the card if the record confirms the error. I do not want the whole room-service amount refunded.

15 September
08:42, Desk: The outlet manager is reviewing the printed record. We will update you.
09:03, Uma: I have not withdrawn my request. The receipt still includes the tart even though I never accepted it.
09:15, Desk: Your request is still attached to the case.

16 September
16:18, Desk: A manager has added a preliminary note that this may be informational only.
16:31, Uma: That is not what I asked. Please read my earlier message. I am requesting an $8 refund for the declined tart, not a refund for the rest of the bill.
16:44, Desk: We will include your clarification in the review file.

17 September
09:17, Uma: I submitted the web form as well so the request is documented. Please do not close it as resolved until someone checks the ticket and tells me what will happen.
09:25, Desk: The form has been received. No refund has yet been posted.

The SMS record confirms that the guest repeated and clarified the request. It also establishes that no refund had been issued as of 17 September. A request and an approved or completed refund are separate events in the property's recordkeeping.

SECTION F — OPERATING NOTES AND RECORD INTERPRETATION

For this file, the term “refund requested” refers to a request by the guest that the property return a paid amount or reverse a charge. It does not require that the guest use a particular legal or accounting term. Asking whether a charge can be removed, asking for money back, or asking that a specific posted amount be refunded each qualifies. Merely asking for an explanation, without asking for money or a bill adjustment, would not qualify. This is an interpretation guide for the case file and does not determine whether the request is valid.

A posted charge may be disputed even when the overall folio balance is zero. The payment line shows that the guest paid the folio total, while the specific request concerns one component. A zero balance does not mean no charge was made, and it does not mean a refund has already been given. Likewise, the fact that the folio contains many undisputed entries does not change the scope of the guest's stated request.

An agent's annotation is useful as evidence of what the agent believed at a particular time, but it does not replace the guest's actual words. A later note may correct an earlier preliminary impression. The order record is relevant to whether the guest's description of the service is supported; it does not erase the fact that the guest asked for a refund. The reviewer should keep separate (1) what the guest requested, (2) what happened to the item, (3) whether the charge was posted, and (4) whether the property later approved or completed an adjustment.

There are no other requested reimbursements in the web form, the SMS messages, or the attached remarks. The guest does not ask the property to pay for transportation, meals outside the hotel, a future stay, or an inconvenience payment. The $8 amount consistently refers to the single tart line. The guest expressly says the other listed items were hers and that she is not seeking a refund of the entire order.

SECTION G — ADDITIONAL CASE-HANDLING LOG

14 September, 10:02 — Folio closed by desk agent. Payment captured. No adjustment at checkout.
14 September, 10:08 — Guest asks desk to check tart charge.
14 September, 10:16 — Desk sends acknowledgment by SMS.
14 September, 10:21 — Guest specifies refund request for $8 if the order record confirms the decline.
15 September, 08:42 — Ticket forwarded to dining manager.
15 September, 09:03 — Guest confirms request remains open.
16 September, 16:20 — Preliminary manager impression entered before form review.
16 September, 16:31 — Guest corrects manager's characterization and repeats the request.
16 September, 17:04 — Manager checks order record and notes the decline entry and erroneous posted line.
16 September, 17:22 — Manager recommends an $8 adjustment, pending desk processing.
17 September, 09:14 — Web form submitted, with refund/adjustment box checked.
17 September, 09:25 — Desk confirms receipt; no refund yet posted.
18 September, 08:30 — Review file assembled.

The log records a recommendation, not a completed refund. The card-payment system export attached to this review contains no credit transaction dated 14–18 September. The absence of a credit is consistent with the desk's message that no refund had yet been posted. It does not negate the guest's request.

SECTION H — SUMMARY OF DOCUMENT SOURCES

The guest narrative is a first-person account written in the form. The folio is a charge record. The dining ticket is a transaction-level order record with a decline notation. The SMS messages are direct communications. The manager's preliminary comment is an employee's provisional interpretation. None of these source types should be treated as interchangeable. In particular, a preliminary staff verdict about the category of a case should be checked against the actual communication that prompted the review.

The file includes ordinary hotel service details so that the disputed line can be evaluated in context. The room charge, assessments, breakfast, parking, laundry, late checkout, broth, rice, and water are not part of the guest's requested refund. The tart is the only line the guest identifies for reversal. The record does not state that a refund was paid, and no such payment should be inferred from the manager's recommendation.

The hotel uses “refund,” “reversal,” and “adjustment” somewhat loosely in guest communications. In the guest's messages, each reference is tied to returning the $8 charged for the declined tart. This file does not require a decision about the accounting method ultimately used; it records that the guest requested the return of that amount. The question for classification is whether a refund was requested, not whether the request was accepted or processed.

SECTION I — FINAL REVIEWER'S PROCEDURAL NOTE

The reviewer should rely on the record rather than simply copying the preliminary manager label. The decisive material is not hidden: the guest selected the refund/adjustment box, entered $8.00, and explicitly asked for the amount to be returned in the form narrative and repeated SMS messages. The manager's initial “informational only” characterization is contradicted by those direct statements. The later recommendation is consistent with the factual order record but is not needed to establish that the request was made. This procedural note describes how the file was assembled; it is not a decision granting the refund.

For completeness, the guest's final message at 09:17 on 17 September says that she submitted the form so her request would be documented and asks that the matter not be closed before review. The desk's reply says only that the form was received and that no refund had yet been posted. No message says that the guest withdrew her request. No recorded staff action converts her request into a completed payment. The relevant status at the review date is therefore an outstanding request concerning one $8 charge, supported by the guest's direct written communications and the transaction record.

APPENDIX — SERVICE CONTEXT

During the stay, the hotel recorded normal guest-service interactions unrelated to the billing question. Room 418 requested an extra towel on 11 September at 18:12; the towel was delivered at 18:28. A wake-up call for 07:00 on 13 September was confirmed at 20:04 the previous evening and logged as completed. The guest asked about the harbor shuttle at checkout and was told its timetable. These entries contain no request for reimbursement and no complaint about the stay's general quality.

The dining outlet's standard practice is to record a declined item in the special-instruction field and remove it from the final ticket before settlement. The attendant's entry “not to be charged if declined” was part of the order record. The service note at 21:06 says the tart was returned unopened. The later point-of-sale ticket nonetheless carried the $8 charge to the room. On 16 September, the outlet manager compared the duplicate order ticket with the final folio and concluded that the line had been posted in error. That conclusion supports the proposed adjustment, while the guest's form and messages independently establish that she requested it.

No other guest in the records supplied for this review shares the reservation code, room, folio, or order number. A separate room-service ticket for room 412 on 12 September includes a chocolate pudding that was delivered and accepted. It is not Uma Fischer's order and is included only because it appeared on the same outlet batch report. The room number on that ticket differs. The batch report's neighboring lines should not be confused with the order for room 418.

The hotel's payment settlement for Uma Fischer shows a single card payment of $521.88. A summary report rounds that payment to $522, while the detailed folio retains cents. Neither figure represents a separate refund. A daily outlet report shows $8.00 in tart sales across several rooms, but that aggregate amount cannot establish which guest accepted which item. The room-specific ticket is the pertinent record for the disputed charge.

The form export also contains a standard quality prompt asking, “Would you recommend the hotel?” The guest left that field blank. The blank recommendation field does not cancel or qualify her separate financial request. A blank rating is not evidence that the guest did not ask for an adjustment. Similarly, her statement that the employee was polite is not a withdrawal of the billing question.

In an internal draft, a coordinator wrote, “Guest only wants an explanation; no refund language.” The coordinator subsequently acknowledged that the draft was made from the short case title rather than the complete narrative. The short title reads “Question about room service bill.” The title is a summary label, not a complete record of the guest's requested action. The underlying form and SMS messages remain available and state the request explicitly. The draft was not sent to the guest and did not change the case status.

The review file retains the mismatch between the short title and the underlying communication so that a quality reviewer can assess whether case routing was accurate. A short title may omit details for space; it cannot overrule a full written request. The same principle applies to the manager's initial impression. The evidence from the original submission, the attached folio, the order record, and the follow-up exchange is presented together so the classification can be made directly from the source material.

Establishment: The fictional Alder & Ash Dining Rooms, operated by Northwind Supply Lodging and Food Services. File reference AA-90316. Event date: 22 August 2026. Review date: 28 August 2026. This dossier consolidates a restaurant invoice with line items, a web form submission, and an SMS exchange concerning a private dinner. Names and amounts are fictitious. The invoice was paid by the event host at close. The present review concerns the correctness of the food count and the host's request for a correction; it is not itself an authorization to issue money.

SECTION 1 — EVENT RECORD

Private dining booking: O'Neill family supper, room Cedar, 22 August, 18:00–21:30.
Booking contact: Kwame O'Neill.
Final guaranteed count supplied on 20 August: 12 guests.
Menu package: Set supper, $48.00 per guaranteed guest.
Children's meals: none recorded.
Dietary note: one dairy-free meal requested; kitchen produced one dairy-free plate.
Host account: banquet folio AA-90316-KO.
Payment: card transaction recorded 22 August at 21:48.

The banquet captain's function sheet states that twelve place settings were laid. The dining-room close sheet records eleven guests physically seated for the meal. One invited person cancelled before arriving, according to the captain's attendance note. The venue's written policy charges the final guaranteed guest count rather than the number who ultimately attend, provided the guaranteed count is set by the stated deadline. The booking terms attached to this file say that the host may reduce the guaranteed count without charge until 17:00 on 20 August. Reductions after that deadline do not alter the billed count. No policy exception is recorded for a same-day absence or a guest who cancels after the deadline.

The event file records the count deadline as 17:00, 20 August. The booking contact did not send a revised count by that time. At 17:12 on 20 August, the venue's reservation system preserved the guarantee at twelve. At 09:06 on 22 August, the host texted that one guest would not attend. The text was received after the deadline and on the day of service. The invoice therefore retained twelve set-menu covers under the attached policy. The service team served eleven people, but the twelfth guaranteed cover remained chargeable under the signed terms.

SECTION 2 — INVOICE AA-90316-KO

Issued: 22 August 2026, 21:44.
Billed to: Kwame O'Neill.
Event: Cedar room private supper.

12 set supper covers at $48.00 each — $576.00.
1 dairy-free plate substitution — $0.00.
2 bottles still mineral water at $8.00 each — $16.00.
1 bottle sparkling mineral water — $9.00.
Room setup fee — $35.00.
Cake service, host-supplied cake — $18.00.
Subtotal — $654.00.
Hospitality tax, 8% of $654.00 — $52.32.
Gratuity, 18% of $654.00 — $117.72.
Total — $824.04.
Card payment received — $824.04.
Balance — $0.00.

Invoice clerk's printed comment, entered before the attendance sheet was attached:
“Overcharged one guest: bill should be reduced to eleven covers. Recommend $52.27 refund.”

The comment is a clerk's preliminary verdict. It is not part of the invoice arithmetic and is not an approved credit. The detailed count record and the policy are attached below. The clerk's comment also does not specify how the recommended amount was computed. Reviewers should compare the underlying guarantee, cutoff time, count, and bill rather than adopting the comment without checking it.

SECTION 3 — WEB FORM SUBMISSION FROM THE HOST

Submitted 25 August 2026 at 11:32.
Name: Kwame O'Neill.
Booking reference: AA-90316-KO.
Topic: Event invoice question.

Host's message:
“I received the final invoice for the Cedar room dinner. I want the extra-cover amount returned. One person did not come, and the captain told me eleven people ate. I believe the invoice should be for eleven covers, not twelve. Please refund the difference for the absent guest and the related tax and gratuity. I am not asking you to repay the water, room setup, or cake service. I know the event was paid at the end of the meal. Please let me know when the credit will appear.”

Request box: “I am seeking a refund or invoice adjustment.” Checked.
Amount field: $67.68.
Supporting file: photo of final invoice and copy of host's attendance note.

The host's requested amount of $67.68 is calculated as one $48.00 cover plus 8% tax ($3.84) plus 18% gratuity ($8.64), totaling $60.48, not $67.68. The entered figure therefore does not match the listed rates and the single cover. The web form permits a guest to enter an estimate. The discrepancy does not make the written request disappear: the text specifically asks for the extra-cover amount, related tax, and gratuity to be returned. The correct classification question is whether a refund was requested, rather than whether the amount entered is arithmetically correct or whether the guest is entitled to receive it.

Form platform note: “A submitted adjustment request is not a promise of payment. Final decision follows review of event terms and service records.” This standard notice was displayed after submission. It does not withdraw the host's request.

SECTION 4 — SMS EXCHANGE

22 August
09:06, Kwame: One guest has cancelled and will not make it tonight. We will be eleven at dinner.
09:14, Event desk: Thank you for the update. The final guaranteed count deadline was 17:00 on 20 August, so the invoice may remain at twelve under the booking terms. We have noted eleven expected attendees.
09:21, Kwame: I understand you have the count. Please tell the captain we will be eleven at the table.
21:57, Event desk: The card payment is complete. The final invoice is available by email.

23 August
08:20, Kwame: I see twelve covers on the invoice although eleven attended. Can you check the count and let me know whether an adjustment is due?
08:44, Event desk: We have forwarded the invoice for review. No adjustment has been made.

24 August
15:12, Event desk: A clerk's preliminary note says one cover was overcharged. The count and deadline records are being checked.
15:37, Kwame: I agree the count was eleven at dinner, but I am asking for the extra cover back. I sent the cancellation after the deadline; please still review it.
16:02, Event desk: We will document your request and review the signed terms.

25 August
11:32, Kwame: I submitted the form. It asks for a refund because I want the extra-cover amount returned, including related charges. I am not requesting a refund of the rest of the event invoice.
11:49, Event desk: We confirm receipt. The case remains under review; no credit has been processed.

27 August
17:05, Event desk: The attached policy indicates the guarantee remained twelve after the reduction deadline. The preliminary clerk comment may be incorrect. We will send a final response after review.
17:23, Kwame: I understand the policy may mean you deny it. My request is still for the extra-cover amount to be refunded. I have not withdrawn it.

SECTION 5 — COUNT AND DEADLINE RECORDS

Signed event terms, page 2, accepted by the booking contact on 3 July 2026:
“Final guaranteed attendance may be reduced without charge until 5:00 p.m. two calendar days before the event. The count on file at that cutoff is the number billed for the set menu. Later attendance changes are recorded for service planning but do not reduce the guaranteed menu charge. Increases may be accepted subject to availability. The guarantee is not automatically changed by a no-show.”

Reservation system history:
3 July, 14:10 — Initial estimate: 10.
18 August, 10:03 — Host revises estimate to 12.
20 August, 16:42 — System sends automatic reminder: reduction deadline is 17:00 today.
20 August, 17:00 — Deadline passes; final guarantee shown as 12.
20 August, 17:12 — System snapshot created; guarantee remains 12.
22 August, 09:06 — Host reports one cancellation; expected attendance 11.
22 August, 18:04 — Captain records eleven guests seated.
22 August, 21:44 — Invoice printed for twelve guaranteed covers.

The timestamped system history and the signed terms agree. The guest's message about the absence is genuine and was received before service, but it was received after the date and time specified for a free reduction. The policy does not say that a cancellation on the event date automatically changes the guarantee. The invoice's twelve covers are therefore consistent with the written terms, even though only eleven people attended.

SECTION 6 — STAFF COMMENTS AND CORRECTIONS

Invoice clerk, 22 August, 21:52:
“Overcharged one guest; eleven ate. $52.27 refund recommended.”

Banquet captain, 23 August, 07:30:
“Eleven guests were present. We set twelve places based on guarantee. No meal was plated for the absent guest after the host reported the cancellation. Set-menu guarantee still shown as twelve.”

Accounts reviewer, 24 August, 10:18:
“Do not assume attendance count replaces guarantee. Need signed terms and timestamp.”

Clerk follow-up, 24 August, 14:51:
“I wrote the initial note using the physical attendance count and did not check the deadline. I now see the count was locked at 12 at 17:00 on 20 August. My earlier recommendation may not be supported by the terms.”

Accounts reviewer, 27 August, 16:48:
“The facts support twelve billed covers under the deadline clause. The clerk's first note saying overcharged is inconsistent with the signed policy and system history. Guest's request is documented separately from the merits.”

The clerk's first statement is preserved because it is a planted verdict in the ordinary operational sense: a staff member expressed a conclusion before reviewing all relevant evidence. The later correction does not erase the initial statement, but the facts and policy are available for independent review. The host's request is also direct evidence of what he wants, independent of whether the invoice was correct.

SECTION 7 — SUPPORTING RESTAURANT RECORDS

Dining-room captain's close sheet, Cedar room:
Scheduled seating 18:00. First guest seated 18:07. Eleven guests seated by 18:19. Host confirmed that the missing guest would not arrive. Twelve place settings were originally laid; one was removed. The kitchen sent eleven individual supper plates. The service charge and gratuity were calculated on the contracted event invoice according to the venue's standard booking terms. The close sheet contains no record of a twelfth meal being cooked or served.

Kitchen production slip:
Set menu covers authorized: 12.
Plates sent: 11.
Dairy-free substitution: 1, included in the set menu cover count.
Returned plates: 0.
Special requests: one guest asked for sauce separately; completed.

The kitchen record corroborates the actual attendance but does not by itself change the guaranteed count. The service team retained the guarantee in the banquet system, which is the count used by the invoice. A physical count and a contractual billing count answer different questions in this file.

Payment processing record:
21:48 — Card authorization and capture, $824.04.
22 August through 28 August — No card credit, reversal, or partial refund recorded.
The payment was settled in full. The absence of a credit means that the host's request had not been paid back as of the review date. It does not mean that the host never asked for a refund.

SECTION 8 — RATE AND AMOUNT CHECK

The invoice arithmetic is internally consistent: twelve times $48.00 equals $576.00. Adding $16.00 for still water, $9.00 for sparkling water, $35.00 for room setup, and $18.00 for cake service gives $654.00. Eight percent of $654.00 is $52.32. Eighteen percent of $654.00 is $117.72. The invoice total is $654.00 + $52.32 + $117.72 = $824.04.

For comparison only, the amount associated with one set-menu cover at the stated percentages would be $48.00 + $3.84 tax + $8.64 gratuity = $60.48. The clerk's $52.27 recommendation does not equal that amount. The host entered $67.68, which also does not equal $60.48. Neither mistaken figure determines whether a request was made; both are retained so that an auditor does not mistake an entered amount for a verified calculation.

The invoice's set-menu count, the number of attendees, and the amount the host asked to have returned are separate facts. The guest asked for the extra-cover amount and related charges to be returned. Under the signed terms, the venue's review concludes that the host is not owed that adjustment because the guarantee deadline had passed. The dossier records the request even though the merits review recommends denial.

SECTION 9 — WEB FORM ROUTING HISTORY

25 August, 11:32 — Form received and case opened as “possible banquet overcharge.”
25 August, 11:34 — Automated triage displays: “Likely refund; guest says refund.”
25 August, 12:10 — Clerk attaches the invoice and initial note.
26 August, 09:00 — Reviewer flags count deadline for verification.
27 August, 16:48 — Reviewer records that the amount appears valid under the signed guarantee.
28 August, 08:50 — Case remains open pending response to the guest.

Automated triage is a routing suggestion, not a finding. Likewise, the clerk's early note and the host's claim that a refund is due are not authoritative determinations of the contract. The guest's words, however, are direct evidence of a request. The final merits decision can be “request denied” while the classification of the guest's communication remains “refund requested.”

SECTION 10 — CASE REVIEW GUIDANCE

For this review, “refund requested” means that the customer asked for paid money to be returned, or asked for a paid charge to be reversed or adjusted downward. A request may be conditional, disputed, or ultimately denied. The classification does not mean that the customer is entitled to the amount. A customer who merely asks whether an invoice is correct, without asking for return of money or a reduction, would be classified as asking for review only. Here the web form and SMS expressly state a request for the extra-cover amount back.

The case includes several statements that may be mistaken for the answer if read in isolation. The clerk's first note says the bill was overcharged and recommends a refund. That conclusion conflicts with the written cutoff policy and the timestamped final guarantee. The later accounts review says the cover was correctly billed. The host says the extra cover should be returned, but that is the host's position rather than a decision on entitlement. The task of recording whether the refund was requested is separate from deciding which person's view of the invoice is correct.

No evidence shows that Kwame O'Neill withdrew the request. His 27 August message explicitly says it remains outstanding even if the policy means the venue will deny it. No refund was issued. The records establish that the invoice was paid and that the host later asked for a defined part of it to be returned. The venue's policy and arithmetic establish the likely response on the merits, but do not change the historical fact of the request.

SECTION 11 — APPENDIX: EVENT COMMUNICATIONS AND ROUTINE DETAILS

The booking email of 3 July confirms the Cedar room and the initial estimate of ten attendees. The host later increased the estimate to twelve on 18 August. The automated deadline reminder was sent to the booking email address at 16:42 on 20 August. The system records successful delivery, with no bounce notification. The host's event contact record lists the same email address used for the booking confirmation. The system does not record a request to reduce the guarantee before 17:00.

The day-of cancellation message came from the telephone number listed for the booking contact. The event desk recorded the update and passed it to the captain. The message helped the restaurant prepare eleven plates rather than twelve, but it did not update the locked guarantee. The captain's note and kitchen slip are consistent with one another. They do not show a second absent guest, an additional meal charge, or a duplicate invoice.

A separate restaurant transaction on the same date concerns a walk-in party in the Garden room. That party ordered three set suppers and paid $144.00 before tax and service. Its receipt has no link to file AA-90316-KO. It appears on the combined end-of-day register report because the report lists all dining rooms. It is not part of the O'Neill banquet invoice and must not be added to or subtracted from the disputed total.

The event invoice includes $25.00 in beverage charges and $35.00 for setup, along with the contracted supper covers and cake service. The host does not dispute those items. The host's form says not to repay water, setup, or cake service. Although the invoice contains multiple lines, the only requested reduction described in the form and messages is the amount associated with one absent guaranteed cover, including its related charges.

The booking agreement includes a separate exception for a property closure caused by an emergency, under which the venue may revise a guarantee after the deadline. No closure, evacuation, severe weather event, utility interruption, or venue-initiated cancellation occurred on 22 August. The exception is not invoked in the file and does not apply to a guest's late cancellation. The policy's ordinary deadline therefore remains controlling for the invoice review.

An internal report generated on 23 August labels the case “attendance discrepancy.” That label describes a difference between eleven attendees and twelve guaranteed covers; it does not state that a refund was requested or granted. A second summary field says “refund recommended,” reflecting the clerk's preliminary comment. Neither short label is a substitute for reading the underlying communication and contract. The full record explains both why the host asked for money back and why the final accounts reviewer concluded that the venue could decline the request.

The records are retained in chronological order to distinguish statements made before and after the applicable count cutoff. The host's update at 09:06 on 22 August is not before the deadline of 17:00 on 20 August, even though it arrives before dinner. The final guarantee remained at twelve. The actual attendance was eleven. The host's request was submitted on 25 August. These dates are stated in the source documents; no external calendar or policy is needed to interpret them.

The invoice clerk's amount is not used as an independent calculation. The guest's entered amount is not verified by the form system. The calculation appendix supplies the relevant arithmetic: a single cover at the printed rates is $60.48 including the stated tax and gratuity. The request remains a request even where the amount field differs from the calculation. The review question about request status should not be changed into a question about the exact amount owed.

[{"state":"Forwarded email; cover note from claims intake: Please review the attached correspondence and field notes for the Tidewater Studio water-damage claim. The file is long because the insured sent the entire exchange, including routine scheduling messages and copies of earlier requests. The short internal assessment appears near the start, but the underlying observations and itemized records are included later. The assessment should be checked against the recorded facts rather than treated as evidence by itself.

Forwarded message 1
From: Bao O'Neill, Tidewater Studio
To: Claims desk
Subject: Water in the print room

Hello. I report water on the floor of our print room after the upstairs sink pipe leaked. I noticed it around 07:40 on Tuesday. The pipe was shut off by the building caretaker before 08:20. The water reached two cartons of paper and one small cabinet. We moved the dry boxes away. I am not sure yet what can be saved. Please tell me how you want photos and receipts sent. The press itself was not wet, and nobody was hurt. We do not ask for emergency lodging or lost wages. I will send details after we check the stock.

Claims intake note, 09:05: “Preliminary view: likely total contents loss, including the press, and business interruption should be added. Insured says whole print room unusable.” This is an early staff impression, not a confirmed inspection result. The words “whole print room unusable” were not in Bao’s original message; the intake employee added them while summarizing. The attached messages and later inspection notes provide the actual reported damage.

Forwarded message 2
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

I clarify: the press was dry and we used it again after wiping the floor. The cabinet has a swollen lower panel. Of the two cartons, one has a wet lower layer and one is unopened and dry. The wall has a small stain near the pipe but no visible crack. We do not know if the wall needs repair. The room remained in use, though we put a yellow sign near the wet floor until it dried. Please do not record the press as damaged just because it is listed on our equipment schedule.

Reply from claims clerk, 10:14: “Thanks. We will distinguish listed property from property reported as damaged. Please send the paper invoice and a photo of the cabinet.”

Forwarded message 3
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

Attached are three photographs. Photo A shows the cabinet, with the bottom edge darker than the top. Photo B shows the open wet carton. Photo C shows the press control panel; it is clean and operating. We have no photograph of the pipe before it was shut off. The caretaker says the connector had loosened. We cannot say who last touched it. The building manager has the plumber’s note and may send it later.

Internal review entry: “Possible cause: sudden escape of water from a pipe connector; cause not yet verified.” This is not a determination that the insured caused the leak. The claim intake form asks about cause and responsibility separately. No one in the messages says Bao installed or adjusted the connector.

Forwarded message 4
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

I found the paper purchase receipt. It says six packs, each pack 500 sheets, bought for $42 per pack. The wet carton had four packs, not six; two packs had already been used before the leak. The other carton has six packs and is dry. I am asking about four packs only. The estimated replacement cost is $168 before delivery charge. The receipt total for the original purchase was $504 for twelve packs, so the new cost is not the old invoice total. I have not yet paid for replacement stock.

Claims clerk reply: “We have noted your estimate as a request, not as a settled value. Please keep the undamaged carton separate.”

Forwarded message 5
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

For the cabinet, the shop quote is $96 to replace the damaged lower panel and labor. The cabinet originally cost $310. The shop did not recommend replacing the whole cabinet. The quote says “repair lower panel only; existing shelves and upper frame remain serviceable.” I do not include the press, chair, computer, or unopened paper carton in this estimate.

Staff note, 11:40: “Claimant’s list indicates $574 contents loss: $168 paper plus $406 cabinet and press?” The arithmetic and wording in that note are incorrect and the line is marked “draft—check.” The quote is $96, not $406, and there is no press repair request. The insured’s itemized request is four paper packs at $168 and a cabinet panel repair quote at $96. The draft note is a planted assessment and must not override the original documents.

Forwarded message 6
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

I checked my business records. We closed the room for about forty minutes to wipe the floor and move cartons. Work then continued at the other table. There was no cancelled customer order and no missed delivery. We did not rent another room. If there is a section for interruption, please mark no known loss of income at this time. We may update only if an actual lost order is found, but presently there is none.

Claims intake summary, 12:02: “Business interruption confirmed, approximately one full day.” The summary is inconsistent with Bao’s report. There is no time sheet, invoice cancellation, or other record showing a full day of interruption. The forty-minute cleanup is recorded as a cleanup period, not as a day of lost business.

Forwarded message 7
From: building caretaker
To: Bao O'Neill

I closed the small valve at 08:05. Water was no longer running after that. The floor was dry by 09:10. I did not see water enter the corridor, neighboring suite, or electrical closet. I put a bucket under the connector before shutting the valve. The plumber arrived later. I have not offered an opinion about the insurance coverage or the amount of a claim.

Forwarded message 8
From: Bao O'Neill
To: Claims desk

The caretaker’s times are helpful. I first saw the water at approximately 07:40 and called him immediately. It may have started earlier, but I did not see it before then. Please use “discovered at approximately 07:40” rather than saying we know the exact minute the leak began. The property schedule is attached only to identify the room and equipment; it does not mean every item on the schedule was damaged.

The attached property schedule lists one digital press, one work table, two chairs, one desktop computer, one cabinet, and paper stock. At the annual renewal, all these items were listed as property present in the room. The schedule does not contain a claim statement or a damage inspection. A blue sticker in the schedule says “press inspected in January,” which is routine maintenance and not a statement about this water incident. Another blue sticker says “computer backup completed,” which refers to electronic files, not damage to the computer. A third line says “cabinet shelves: older, surface marks,” which predates the reported leak and does not mean the cabinet was already broken.

Claim form excerpt sent by Bao

Date discovered: Tuesday, 14 May.
Location: print room, rear side of suite.
Cause known at time of submission: no; caretaker suspected connector.
Items presently reported: four paper packs wet; cabinet lower panel swollen.
Items not reported damaged: digital press, work table, chairs, desktop computer, six packs in unopened carton.
People injured: none known.
Other premises affected: none known.
Work interruption: cleanup for approximately forty minutes; production resumed in the same room.
Amount requested at first notice: not entered pending estimates.

The form contains a box labeled “Any total loss?” Bao wrote “No.” A clerk added a question mark beside it because an earlier intake summary used the phrase “total contents loss.” Bao later wrote in the margin: “No total loss. This means no, not unsure. Only one carton partly wet and cabinet panel.” The clerk’s question mark is not a changed answer.

Email from claims clerk, next morning

Hello Bao,
We received your photos and the two cost documents. Please confirm whether the paper quantity requested is four packs and whether the cabinet figure is the repair quotation only. Also let us know if the business interruption statement remains “no identified lost income.” We have an early internal comment saying a full-day interruption and a total contents loss, but it is not supported by the first notice and should be verified before it is used.

Email from Bao, same morning

Yes, four packs only, and $168 is the replacement estimate for those four packs. The cabinet repair quote is $96. We do not claim replacement of the whole cabinet. We do not claim press damage. We do not have a lost order or lost income. I understand you want the facts checked. Please remove the total-loss words from the draft because they do not match what I sent.

Additional stock count, entered by Bao

The open carton held six packs when purchased. Two packs were consumed during printing in the previous weeks, leaving four. The lower two packs in the carton were wet at the edges. The upper two packs were dry but Bao kept them together and requested replacement for all four because the supplier sells packs as a unit and the damaged carton should not be used for customer work. The unopened carton contained six dry packs. No other paper was stored on the floor. The supplier’s list price is $42 per pack. Four multiplied by $42 is $168. A separate delivery fee of $12 appears on the supplier’s website, but Bao has not included that fee in the submitted $168 estimate and has not asked for it in the first notice. The original twelve-pack invoice was $504; that figure is not the claimed replacement figure.

Inspection appointment record

Appointment offered: Thursday at 13:00.
Appointment accepted: Thursday at 13:00.
Inspection completed: Thursday at 13:12.
Attendees: Bao O'Neill and the field inspector.
Items visually observed: cabinet lower panel, two paper cartons, floor area, press exterior.
Press operation demonstrated: yes, one test print completed.
Paper condition: the open carton showed moisture marks on lower paper packs; sealed carton dry.
Cabinet condition: swelling at lower panel consistent with recent moisture, according to visual observation; no destructive test performed.
Wall condition: small surface stain; no measurement of moisture inside wall.
Cause: inspector did not identify the source independently; caretaker’s description was provided.

The inspection record is a description, not a final coverage decision. It contains no finding that the entire room was unusable. The inspector wrote “normal use appears possible after cleanup” and “press operating at visit.” An unrelated sentence in the template says “business premises unavailable: yes/no.” The inspector left both choices blank because it was not a premises closure inspection. A clerk later circled “yes” on a photocopy, but no signature or explanation accompanies that circle.

Email from the inspector to the clerk

I saw the cabinet and paper described in the first notice. The press was dry and produced a test sheet. The room was being used. I did not assess a wall repair because the owner did not request one and the stain was slight. Do not treat the annual equipment schedule as proof of damage. I have not valued the items or determined policy response.

Draft claim review, unapproved

Heading: “Likely total contents damage and interruption.”
Draft reasoning: “All listed property was in the affected room, therefore all listed property may be involved. Room was wet, so assume one day closed. Estimated loss $574.”
Checker’s pencil marks: “This is a hypothesis, not a verified conclusion. Press test was successful; no press repair cost. Original claimant’s figures: $168 paper plus $96 cabinet repair = $264 requested before any adjustments. No supported lost-income amount. Reconcile total before using.”

The draft has a red stamp reading “NOT FINAL.” It was saved in the file because reviewers wanted to show which phrases needed correction. It is not a payment authorization. No payment has been issued at the time of these notes, and no final coverage letter is attached.

Tidewater Studio’s office assistant sent a separate inventory message. It says that the digital press was moved into the print room six years ago and has had routine maintenance twice per year. The maintenance list contains dates, oil changes, and a roller replacement. One entry from January reads “operational after service.” Nothing in the service list describes water exposure on 14 May. The office assistant says they are attaching the list simply because the policy form asks for a property schedule. They do not ask for press replacement and they do not say that the press failed after the incident.

The work table and chairs appear in the room photograph. The table has a coffee ring and the chairs have ordinary scratches, but the photographs do not show water damage to them. The claimant did not put these items on the damaged-property list. The computer appears on a shelf. Bao says it stayed on, and the saved job files opened after the room was cleaned. The computer’s annual value is printed on the schedule, but annual value is not an amount claimed for this event. There is no computer repair bill, replacement quote, or report of malfunction.

The print room floor has a shallow slope toward a drain. The caretaker’s note says he placed a bucket beside the connector and wiped a narrow path to the drain. A cleaning invoice was not submitted. The studio’s own supplies were used to wipe the floor. The existence of a floor drain does not establish that the paper was dry; the photographs and inspection record separately describe moisture on the lower paper packs. Conversely, the presence of water does not establish that every listed item was affected. The record uses “room affected” to identify the event location, not to state that each object in that room sustained damage.

A second intake employee added a note: “Maybe full closure because customers cannot walk through wet area.” The note has no supporting customer report, safety order, or inspection finding. Bao says no customer came into the room during the short cleanup, and the studio could take work orders from its front counter. The studio did not send a cancellation notice or advise any client that production would stop for the day. The note is retained as a question for review, not as proof that interruption occurred.

The studio’s weekly production sheet for the incident week is attached. Monday output is 36 prints, Tuesday output is 31, Wednesday output is 34, Thursday output is 35, and Friday output is 33. The sheet does not identify expected production, sales, or profit, and it cannot by itself prove there was no business effect. Bao’s direct statement is that no order was cancelled and work resumed after cleanup. The daily counts are included as routine records and should not be used to invent a lost-income figure. A previous week shows 32, 35, 30, 37, and 34 prints; the different counts reflect order mix. No analyst has calculated a decline attributable to this event.

The original email subject line is “Water in the print room,” not “Total loss.” A forwarded cover note from the office assistant says, “I am sending the chain in full because a summary from intake appears to mix a draft estimate with Bao’s request.” The cover note gives no extra estimate and makes no claim about policy entitlement. In the email chain, Bao consistently identifies one partly wet carton and a cabinet panel. The early internal summary is the only place that states total contents loss or a full day of business interruption, and later messages explicitly correct it.

A document checklist confirms receipt of the initial notice, three photographs, paper receipt, cabinet quote, property schedule, caretaker note, and inspection record. The checklist has columns for “received,” “reviewed,” and “verified.” A check in the received column means the document is in the file, not that every statement in it is accepted. The press schedule is checked as received. The press is not checked as damaged. The business interruption section is marked “no amount requested; claimant reports no known lost income.” The total-loss box is marked “No, per claimant; earlier draft wording not verified.”

The file also contains a blank reserve worksheet with a preprinted amount of $1,000. It is an example worksheet used by the clerk and is not an estimate, payment, or approval. A handwritten arrow points from the number to “template only.” Another form shows a deductible field but no amount entered. No question in this packet asks the reader to determine payment after policy terms, and no policy wording or deductible value is supplied here. The factual issue is what the insured reported and what the file supports, not a coverage calculation.

Later reply from Bao

Thank you for checking the draft. I confirm the cabinet request remains the $96 repair quotation and the paper request remains four packs at $168. I do not ask for the press, computer, table, chairs, wall, or other carton. No lost order was found when we checked the order book. We have no exact estimate for any wall work. If you need a separate plumber record, the building manager said it may take several days. Please keep the cause as not independently confirmed until that comes.

Claims clerk closing note for this packet

Documents reviewed against the claimant’s own item list: the clearly described damage consists of four paper packs in the open carton and the cabinet lower panel. The press is specifically described as dry and working, and no press amount is requested. Business interruption is specifically denied as a known loss; the only stated downtime is about forty minutes of cleanup. The early “total contents” and “full day” phrases are contradicted by the claimant and the inspection record. This closing note does not decide whether any particular cost is covered. It records the factual descriptions and the status of the draft assessment.

Hand-off note from the morning clerk

I received this file after a busy call period. I copied the claim reference into the shared queue and left the existing summary in place until the documents were sorted. The shared queue sometimes shows the first summary at the top, even after a correction is added below. Please check the date and sender of each entry. The earliest summary was entered before the receipt and inspection were available. The later notes were not intended to hide it; they correct it. The insurer’s system keeps both versions so an auditor can see what changed and why.

The claim reference label gives a room number and a renewal year. It is not a statement of cause. A separate calendar reminder says the building caretaker will return next month to check the connector. That reminder is not evidence that a second leak occurred. Another calendar line says the studio will clean the print room on Friday; this is a routine cleaning appointment, not a closure. A note about “water loss prevention leaflet sent” confirms only that general information was emailed. It does not establish that the studio ignored a maintenance duty.

Bao’s message about the wet carton uses the words “all four packs,” while the image appears to show only the lower portion of the carton visibly dark. The supplier sells paper in packs and Bao explains that the upper two packs were kept together with the damaged lower packs and are not being used for customer work. This is why the request covers four packs even though not all four show the same degree of visible moisture. The stated request remains $168. The reader should not multiply the number of packs in both cartons or mistake the original twelve-pack receipt for the requested amount.

The document folder includes two versions of the cabinet estimate. The first is a photograph of the shop’s handwritten quotation: “repair lower panel, labor included, $96.” The typed copy says “lower panel repair only; no cabinet replacement; $96.” The original cabinet purchase amount, $310, is shown on an old asset list and is not the repair estimate. A margin note reads “Could be 406 total?,” but it has no supporting invoice and appears to add an unrelated figure from a room-cleaning worksheet. The claim form itself does not include $406. These differing figures are retained to show why the draft total was flagged.

A final file index entry says “press—listed, no damage alleged.” Another says “interruption—no known lost income alleged.” The index is compiled from the messages and is not an independent engineering report. Where the index and original records agree, the original records remain the basis. Where the earlier draft conflicts with the original records, the draft is marked unapproved and corrected. No further damage report was received by the date of this packet.

The last forwarded email is from Bao to the claims desk: “I have now checked the storage area and there is no additional wet stock. The dry carton remains sealed. The cabinet panel still needs the quoted repair. The press has been used each day since the cleanup. There was no full-day stop. I am not saying no water event happened; I am saying only the listed things were affected.” The email is dated three days after the first notice and gives no new amount. It confirms the earlier distinction between the occurrence and the scope of reported damage.

End of forwarded material. The cover note’s instruction is to retain all messages, including the draft assessment and its correction, in their original order. The claim file does not contain a final decision. The reader has the original descriptions, quoted costs, caretaker timing, and inspection observations needed for the factual questions below. A statement should be selected only when it is directly supported here.","candidates":[{"id":"cleanup_about_forty_minutes","description":"The room was used for cleanup for about forty minutes."},{"id":"work_resumed","description":"Production resumed in the same room after cleanup."},{"id":"press_operated","description":"The press was dry and completed a test print at inspection."},{"id":"full_day_interruption","description":"A full day of business interruption is confirmed."},{"id":"cancelled_order","description":"A customer order was cancelled because of the water."}],"target":["cleanup_about_forty_minutes","work_resumed","press_operated"],"hard_cases":["planted_verdict","multi_positive"],"notes":"Bao reports forty minutes’ cleanup, resumed production, and no cancelled orders; inspection saw a working press, contrary to the full-day draft."}]},{"state":"Typed-up handwritten-style field note, Kestrel Logistics insurance claim file. The handwriting was difficult to read, so the clerk typed the pages in order and kept corrections in brackets where a word could not be made certain. The note includes a first-page supervisor verdict and the original observations that must be compared with it. The claimant is Ines Kowalski, who reports a small loading-bay incident at the company’s leased storage unit. This typed record is not a coverage decision.

Page 1, written in broad pencil

Call came from Ines before lunch. She said a delivery trolley rolled into a shelf upright near bay three. One tote fell, lid came off, and two sealed containers inside were scratched outside only. No liquid seen. Shelf looks bent? Need check. Driver says trolley wheel stuck in floor seam. No one injured. No spill to floor. Ines says contents still closed. Photos to follow. Do not say whole stock lost before we open the tote and see it.

At the bottom, in another hand: “Supervisor verdict: contamination likely; all stored goods compromised; recommend full stock loss reserve.” The verdict is dated before the listed inspection and is written in blue ink, while the observations above are in pencil. A later check in the margin says “not confirmed—review physical facts.” The verdict is retained because it was part of the original file. It does not itself establish contamination or loss.

Page 2, continuation

I went to bay three at 11:25. Shelf upright has a bend at the foot, about three centimeters from straight when checked with small ruler. Shelf still standing and other boxes on it did not fall. The two containers from trolley tote are on floor beside shelf. Caps tight. Exterior has gray rub marks and one shallow dent. I asked Ines if any product escaped. She said no and showed me seals still connected. No smell, wetness, or residue around lids. The tote has a crack near one corner but is not leaking. We did not open containers because they belong to a customer and no instruction to sample was given.

Page 3, names and roles

Ines Kowalski is shift supervisor and claimant contact. She did not drive the trolley. The driver was a Kestrel Logistics contractor identified in the shift sheet as Mateo Larkin. Mateo said the right wheel caught on the seam while he was turning slowly; he stopped when the trolley struck the shelf. Ines asked him to wait while she checked the containers. The handwritten word “driver” beside the first-page statement refers to Mateo, not Ines. The little initial “I.K.” at the top is the person making the note, not the person operating the trolley.

A copied dispatch slip names Quill Logistics as the supplier of the two sealed containers. It shows the goods were received by Kestrel the previous afternoon. It is included to identify ownership and custody, not to show that Quill filed this claim. Ines filed the notice on behalf of Kestrel. The supplier has not made a separate request in this packet. The goods remain at Kestrel’s bay, on a marked inspection shelf, pending customer instruction.

Page 4, first inventory check

Container A: sealed cap, label intact, outside scuffed, no leak seen.
Container B: sealed cap, label intact, shallow dent on side, no leak seen.
Tote: one corner crack, inside dry at inspection; tote is Kestrel reusable handling equipment.
Shelf upright: lower section bent; shelf remains in place.
Floor seam: existing chipped edge photographed; no fresh pieces found.
Nearby cartons: no visible impact.

A later clerk wrote “All stock compromised” beside this list. The handwriting is dark and the words are underlined twice. There is no test report, opened seal, leak observation, customer rejection, or written finding supporting that statement. The line is a copied verdict, not an observation. The inventory notes immediately above it describe sealed, dry containers and no other cartons affected. It should not be mistaken for a laboratory result.

Page 5, photo descriptions

Image 1: trolley at bay three, handle facing aisle.
Image 2: close view of tote corner crack.
Image 3: Container A exterior, gray rub mark, seal visible.
Image 4: Container B side, small dent, seal visible.
Image 5: shelf foot with ruler for scale.
Image 6: floor seam at turning point.

Images were taken by Ines on a company phone. Date stamp is the date of incident. The pictures do not show the contents inside either container. They do show that both container seals appear connected and that the tote is dry inside. The note writer did not open the containers and does not claim knowledge of the product’s internal condition beyond the visible seals and exterior examination.

Page 6, short conversation recorded by the clerk

Clerk: “Were the containers dropped open?”
Ines: “No. The tote tipped, they moved against one another, but caps stayed shut.”
Clerk: “Did any product touch the floor?”
Ines: “No. There was no liquid outside.”
Clerk: “Has the customer refused the goods?”
Ines: “Not yet. I sent photos and asked them to inspect on receipt.”
Clerk: “Is the shelf unusable?”
Ines: “We moved the lower two boxes away. The shelf still stands, but maintenance will check the bent foot.”

The clerk’s next line reads “Possible closure of entire bay?” Ines answered “No closure. We kept traffic away from the shelf for about twenty minutes and used bay two meanwhile.” A typed summary later changed this to “bay unavailable all shift.” That change is not supported by the conversation. The shift sheet states that bay three resumed use after the shelf area was cleared, and the company’s normal loading continued from bay two during the short interval.

Page 7, stock documents

Quill Logistics delivery note lists two containers, each identified by batch code QL-77 and QL-81. They arrived sealed. Kestrel’s receipt signature confirms delivery, not product testing. The containers are customer-owned stock awaiting onward dispatch. The note does not include a value for the goods and does not state that they were spoiled. A separate storage ledger says both containers were placed in the same tote before the trolley was moved. There were no other containers in that tote.

A warehouse count lists 48 cartons elsewhere in the building. These were not in bay three and were not near the trolley. They are mentioned because the first reserve note used the broad phrase “all stored goods.” The count is ordinary site inventory and not a claim for those cartons. Ines explicitly says the incident involved the one tote and two containers only. No employee says that all 48 cartons were struck, wet, or opened.

Page 8, service and safety note

The shelf was installed two years ago and inspected as part of routine maintenance in March. The March checklist says “upright stable; minor paint wear at foot.” It does not mention the present bend. The floor seam has appeared in an earlier maintenance ticket and was scheduled for patching. That old ticket does not say the seam caused a prior accident. Mateo’s account that the wheel caught is a reported explanation, not an engineer’s causal determination. The current note records that the trolley was turning near the seam when it struck the shelf.

The maintenance worker came at 15:30. He pressed the shelf upright by hand and marked the bay “restricted pending repair,” not the whole warehouse. He did not assess the goods inside the sealed containers. He wrote that a replacement foot plate could be fitted next day. No quote or final repair invoice is attached. The shelf was not described as collapsed. The maintenance worker’s note does not say that containers were contaminated.

Page 9, a confusing typed summary from the claim portal

“Incident: trolley collision. Verdict: all stock contaminated. Location closed. Recommended reserve: full value of inventory plus one shift of lost revenue.”

Beside it a reviewer wrote: “Portal requires a short summary; this entry copied supervisor wording from first page. Check against primary facts before using. No value for inventory attached, no test for contamination, and claimant reports no closure of entire location.” The first portal line is therefore a planted conclusion repeated from the initial supervisor verdict. The reviewer did not endorse it. No schedule of “full inventory value” is in this packet, and no calculation of lost revenue is supplied.

Page 10, call with customer receiving office

Ines called the receiving office the following morning. The person answering asked for photos and said they would decide whether the containers could proceed after their own visual inspection. They did not reject either container during the call. Ines wrote “customer no decision yet” in the margin. There is no return authorization and no disposal instruction. The customer has not said the goods are unusable. The receiving office did not make a claim against Kestrel in this record.

Page 11, handwritten correction

I first wrote “contents damaged?” because I saw scratches on the containers and crack on tote. I mean outside marks, not contents proven damaged. Correct record: tote is cracked; containers show exterior marks; seals intact; no substance escaped. We should request instructions before deciding if either container needs further inspection. The shelf foot is bent and needs maintenance review. Not all goods in warehouse.

The writer underlined “not all goods” and added “I saw only bay three items.” This correction is dated the same day as the inspection. The earlier phrase “all stored goods compromised” was placed on top of the page after the inspection and is in a different hand. The typed transcription preserves both entries so the chronology is visible.

Page 12, daily activity record

Bay three activity before incident: two pallet moves completed. Time trolley incident reported: 10:42. Area check began: 10:47. Bay three restricted at shelf only: 10:50 to 11:10. Bay two used for loading during that period. Bay three available for ordinary use after visual check: 11:10. One later shelf repair restriction applies only to the shelf position, not the whole bay or warehouse. No client dispatch was cancelled on the shift record. The shift record does not estimate financial effect and does not prove every planned task was completed; it simply logs the recorded operational period and the temporary restriction.

A blue stamp on the activity sheet reads “FULL SHIFT LOST.” A handwritten arrow says “stamp applied in error from neighboring file; this is not an approval.” The neighboring file number is not reproduced here and has no connection to Kestrel’s incident. The stamp is another stray verdict, not a factual account. The time entries and Ines’s conversation both indicate a limited restriction followed by continued operations.

Page 13, equipment owner query

Kestrel asked whether the cracked tote could be repaired. The warehouse lead said the tote is company equipment and can be replaced if repair is not safe. There is no replacement quote yet. The containers belong to the customer and are not being claimed as destroyed in the typed note. Ines asked the customer to confirm if they want independent product testing, but no sample was taken. The company has not billed the customer and has not written off the containers.

The word “damage” is used in this file for different things: visible exterior marks, the tote crack, and the bent shelf foot. It is not used as proof that the sealed contents are contaminated. A handler should preserve that distinction. The supervisor’s first-page verdict used “all stored goods compromised,” but the specific observations on the inventory page say the two caps stayed sealed, the tote interior was dry, and nearby cartons were unaffected.

Page 14, typed note from Ines, copied from handwritten pocket pad

I was at the dispatch desk when Mateo called. He said the wheel stuck and trolley hit shelf. I went there and checked. I did not see liquid. I did not open customer containers because they were sealed. We took photographs and moved tote to inspection shelf. I put a temporary cone by shelf. I did not tell anybody the whole warehouse closed. We sent ordinary loads using bay two, then used bay three again after inspection. I ask for review of tote and shelf repair, not payment for all customer stock.

The pocket pad has a smudged number after “containers.” It looks like “2,” and the delivery record also says two. No other item count is indicated. A small note “48 cartons” was written on the following line under the heading “warehouse total,” not under incident items. The transcription keeps both numbers in their proper categories. The clerk did not add the warehouse total to the incident count.

Page 15, technician’s follow-up

The maintenance technician returned next morning. Shelf foot plate was removed and replaced. The upright is now straight and usable. His invoice is not attached; he said the facilities team will send a routine work order. The two containers remained sealed on the inspection shelf when he visited. He did not observe a leak, odor, or residue. He did not open them or certify their internal product quality. The tote remains cracked and was tagged for replacement. The technician had no comment on coverage or payment.

A draft claim handler note entered after this visit says “shelf and all stock unusable; full inventory claim likely.” A second handler wrote “Do not adopt verdict; technician confirmed upright repaired, containers still sealed. Need actual claimant loss itemization.” The draft is still in the document list but shows status “working copy.” No signed final decision is present.

Page 16, claimant’s confirmation by phone

Ines confirmed that the tote is the only company-owned item she presently asks to have considered for repair or replacement. She is waiting for the equipment desk to price it. She also reports the shelf foot repair was completed by the facilities technician. She has not asked for replacement of the customer’s containers and has not reported their contents as contaminated. The customer has not refused delivery as of this call. She does not request lost revenue for a full shift, and says the team moved work to bay two while the shelf corner was restricted.

The clerk read back: “Your current report is tote crack and shelf foot repair, with no confirmed damage to container contents and no full-shift closure?” Ines answered: “Correct. I cannot certify product inside without opening, but seals were closed and no liquid escaped. Please do not write that all stock was lost.” This is a direct clarification of the earlier copied verdict.

Page 17, attachment list

A. Initial handwritten call note.
B. Photos 1 through 6.
C. Delivery slip and receipt.
D. Warehouse inventory count.
E. Maintenance ticket for floor seam.
F. March shelf check.
G. Inspection page with inventory observations.
H. Shift activity record.
I. Customer receiving-office call note.
J. Technician follow-up.
K. Portal summary and correction.

The attachment list has a handwritten note “A and G are evidence; portal summary copied language.” This is a reminder about source quality, not an instruction to disregard all summaries. Where a summary matches the underlying facts, it can be useful. Here, the specific observations conflict with the broad verdict. The claim review should use the specific records rather than the repeated conclusory phrase.

Page 18, additional note on ownership

The two containers are described as customer-owned on the storage ledger and delivery slip. The reusable tote belongs to Kestrel. The shelf belongs to the leased facility and is maintained by the facility team. Ines is the person reporting the event for Kestrel; she is not the supplier and not the driver. The contractor’s statement is about how the trolley moved. The customer’s receiving office has only requested photos. No party in these pages has reported injury or alleged that a customer’s products were exposed to liquid.

A clerk’s shorthand “claim by Quill” appears in the margin next to the delivery slip. The clerk later crossed it out and wrote “Quill is shipper named on slip; Kestrel notice filed by Ines.” This correction matters because ownership and reporting role differ. The named supplier did not send the claim notice. The notation does not alter the observations about the sealed containers.

Page 19, final typed chronology

10:42, trolley incident reported by driver.
10:47, Ines reaches bay three and begins inspection.
10:50, shelf corner temporarily restricted; traffic redirected to bay two.
11:10, bay three back in ordinary use except shelf position pending maintenance.
11:25, field note records sealed containers, dry tote interior, bent shelf foot.
15:30, technician inspects shelf and schedules repair.
Next morning, foot plate replaced; containers still sealed.
Next customer call, no rejection or disposal request reported.

No time in this chronology indicates a full-shift closure. The temporary restricted area is not equivalent to the whole bay being unavailable. The initial supervisor verdict and copied portal sentence use a broader description than the recorded chronology supports.

Page 20, closing note written by the clerk

The file is ready for factual classification, but not for a final payment amount. The supported observations are a crack in Kestrel’s reusable tote, exterior marks and a shallow dent on two sealed customer containers, and a bent shelf foot that was subsequently repaired. There is no observed leak, no liquid outside the containers, no opened seal, no test result, and no customer rejection in the available pages. No evidence says all 48 cartons or all stored goods were compromised. The initial supervisor verdict says that all goods were compromised, but the direct observations and later correction do not support it. The temporary restriction lasted about twenty minutes at the shelf corner while operations used bay two; it was not a full-shift or whole-location closure. No final coverage determination, inventory valuation, or lost-revenue calculation is included.
