[{"state":"Harbor Health Appointment Administration Review Packet

Prepared for: clinic operations review
Reporting period: 4–18 September
Compiled from appointment-desk records, patient correspondence, staff notes, and public feedback

This packet was assembled after repeated complaints about the appointment desk. Several entries contain angry language, duplicated notes, staff opinions, and customer summaries. The entries are retained as received because the operations team asked for a review of what was actually said and recorded. A staff member’s conclusion is not itself a substitute for the underlying correspondence or appointment record.

SECTION 1 — FORWARDED EMAIL WITH COVER NOTE

Cover note from Dalia Rahman, appointment-desk supervisor:
Please review the forwarded message below. I have already marked the patient as having requested a cancellation, but I am furious that this keeps happening and I do not want another argument about what the email means. The record should make the request clear.

Forwarded message
From: Leila Okafor
To: Harbor Health appointment desk
Sent: 9 September, 10:14 a.m.
Subject: Thursday visit

I am writing because your reminder says I have an appointment on Thursday at 2:30. I am not asking you to cancel it. I still intend to come in, and I have arranged time away from work. Please confirm that the appointment is still in the system and tell me whether I should arrive fifteen minutes early. Last time I waited nearly an hour without anyone explaining what was going on. I am angry about that, but I do not want this Thursday’s appointment removed. If the doctor has to change the time, contact me before changing anything; do not treat this message as permission to cancel.

Desk record, 9 September, 10:29 a.m.:
Appointment remains active for Thursday at 2:30 p.m. Patient asked for confirmation and arrival guidance. No cancellation entered.

Dalia Rahman’s follow-up note, 9 September, 11:02 a.m.:
I saw “cancel” in the message and classified it as a cancellation request. This is probably another patient who changed her mind and is now blaming us for the record. The desk should not have to decode every irritated email. I have put “patient requested cancellation” in my review notes even though the appointment record is still active.

SECTION 2 — FAQ EXCERPT AND FRONT-DESK HANDLING NOTES

Harbor Health appointment FAQ, current version posted at reception:

Q: How do I change or cancel an appointment?
A: Call the appointment desk or reply to your appointment reminder and clearly say that you want to cancel or reschedule. Asking us to confirm an appointment does not cancel it. Saying that you are unhappy with a previous visit does not, by itself, cancel a future appointment. If you write that you still plan to attend, staff should leave the appointment active unless you later send a clear request to change it.

Q: What if I cannot attend?
A: Tell the desk as soon as possible. If you are unsure whether you can attend, explain that uncertainty and ask us to contact you. An expression of frustration, a question about whether an appointment is still booked, or a hypothetical statement about what you might do later is not a cancellation request.

Q: When will the desk confirm a change?
A: Staff should record the patient’s actual request, check the appointment system, and tell the patient what action was taken. A staff member’s assumption or shorthand description is not enough to alter an appointment.

Reception handout, internal copy:
“Do not infer a cancellation from a complaint. Do not erase a booked visit unless the patient asks us to do so. If a message contains both anger and a direct request, follow the direct request and document it accurately.”

Training log excerpt, 10 September:

09:05 — New staff member asked whether “I’m sick of waiting; is Thursday still booked?” should be treated as a cancellation. Trainer answered no: the patient is asking for confirmation.

09:19 — Another staff member asked whether “I might cancel if this happens again” should be recorded as cancellation. Trainer answered no: that is conditional and refers to a possible later decision.

09:37 — Supervisor reminded the team that patients may use angry language without asking to end an appointment. Read the entire message before selecting a record category.

09:51 — Desk clerk asked whether a patient can cancel by saying “please remove my Thursday appointment.” Trainer answered yes, because that is a direct request.

10:04 — The team reviewed a record in which the note said “patient cancelled,” while the message said “I am not cancelling; please confirm.” The trainer said the message controls the interpretation and the record note must be corrected.

10:22 — A clerk complained that the instructions were too obvious and said the team should simply follow the supervisor’s label. The trainer disagreed. Staff labels can be mistaken, including labels written by supervisors.

Appointment-desk operations memo:
The desk has received complaints about missed confirmations, calls put on hold, and inaccurate shorthand in appointment notes. Managers are expected to inspect the original patient communication when a note is disputed. The review should distinguish among a request to cancel, a request to reschedule, a request for confirmation, a complaint about service, and a hypothetical statement about a future choice. The desk must not convert an angry tone into a request the patient did not make.

The appointment system retains the original message and the time each action was entered. A staff member can add a comment, but a comment does not change the appointment’s status. Only an actual cancellation or rescheduling action entered in the scheduling system changes the status. When the patient’s words and a staff member’s summary differ, the reviewer should record both and state which one is supported by the original communication.

SECTION 3 — APPOINTMENT RECORD EXTRACTS

Record A — Leila Okafor
Appointment: Thursday, 12 September, 2:30 p.m.
Status as of 9 September, 10:29 a.m.: Active
Patient message: “I am not asking you to cancel it. I still intend to come in… Please confirm that the appointment is still in the system.”
Desk action: Confirmation requested; appointment left active.
Supervisor review label: “Patient requested cancellation.”
Audit comment: Label conflicts with the message; no cancellation action exists.

Record B — Jonas Mensah
Appointment: Monday, 16 September, 9:00 a.m.
Patient message, 11 September, 3:41 p.m.: “Please cancel my Monday appointment. I cannot attend and do not want another time booked. Confirm once you have removed it.”
Desk action, 11 September, 3:47 p.m.: Appointment cancelled; no replacement visit booked.
Staff note: “Patient wants to cancel.”
Manager’s review label: “No cancellation request was made; patient only asked a question.”
Audit comment: The message is a direct cancellation request, and the system action matches it.

Record C — Amara Bergstrom
Appointment: Wednesday, 18 September, 11:15 a.m.
Patient message, 13 September, 8:06 a.m.: “I am angry that nobody called me back. I am still coming on Wednesday. Please tell me whether the entrance is open before 8:30.”
Desk action: Appointment remains active; entrance question referred to reception.
Clerk’s note: “Patient upset; may cancel.”
Audit comment: The patient states an intention to attend and asks about the entrance. The clerk’s possibility is not a cancellation request.

Record D — Aiden Fischer
Appointment: Friday, 20 September, 4:00 p.m.
Patient message, 14 September, 1:52 p.m.: “I might cancel if I have another bad experience, but for now please leave the appointment alone and confirm the time.”
Desk action: Appointment remains active; confirmation sent.
Team lead’s label: “Cancellation received.”
Audit comment: The patient describes a possible future action, then explicitly asks the desk to leave the current booking alone.

Record E — Dalia Castillo
Appointment: Tuesday, 17 September, 10:30 a.m.
Patient message, 12 September, 2:17 p.m.: “I need to move Tuesday’s visit to a later date. Please do not cancel the whole referral; call me with available dates.”
Desk action: Appointment moved to 24 September at 10:30 a.m.; referral remains open.
Clerk’s note: “Patient cancelled care.”
Audit comment: The patient asked to reschedule the visit and specifically said not to cancel the referral.

Record F — Leila Okafor, separate older visit
Appointment: 22 August, 1:00 p.m.
Patient message, 20 August: “Cancel the visit on Thursday, please. I have found another clinic.”
Desk action: Appointment cancelled on 20 August.
Staff note: “Cancellation confirmed.”
Audit comment: The request and action agree.

The records above are selected examples from the review period. They are not all from the same patient or the same appointment. Similar names, repeated appointment days, and emotionally worded complaints led to several inaccurate draft summaries. Staff were reminded not to use a prior visit or a different patient’s action to interpret a current message.

SECTION 4 — PUBLIC PRODUCT REVIEW OF THE PATIENT PORTAL

Review title: “The portal is a mess, and the appointment desk needs to read”
Reviewer: Jonas Mensah
Posted: 15 September

I have used Harbor Health’s portal for two appointments now, and I am furious that I have to spend my own time correcting the desk’s notes. The portal itself shows the right time when it works, but the messages people type into the notes seem to become more important than what we actually say. I do not want to cancel my next visit. I want the desk to stop pretending that a complaint means I am leaving.

For the record, I did cancel the Monday appointment on 16 September. I sent a clear message saying, “Please cancel my Monday appointment. I cannot attend and do not want another time booked.” The portal showed it as cancelled a few minutes later. That part was done correctly. The problem was the manager’s review note claiming that I had only asked a question. I did not merely ask whether it was cancelled; I asked for it to be cancelled.

My other complaint is about a different visit. On 18 September I am still coming in. I asked whether the entrance is open before 8:30 because I may arrive early. Someone wrote that I might cancel, which is ridiculous. I said I was still coming. Why does every irritated sentence get turned into a cancellation in one record, while an actual cancellation request gets dismissed in another?

I am not praising the service. The desk took too long to answer, and the portal’s status notes are confusing. The staff should read the whole message before making a claim about what a patient asked for. If the clinic wants fewer angry reviews, it could stop putting words into people’s mouths and correct the wrong labels instead of defending them.

Reviewer follow-up, 16 September:
To avoid another misunderstanding: I am not asking the clinic to restore the Monday appointment. I asked to cancel it and it was cancelled. I am asking the clinic to correct the manager’s account of my request. My next visit is a separate booking, and I have not asked to cancel it.

Internal product-team response draft:
“Reviewer is dissatisfied with appointment handling. The review confirms a cancellation request for the Monday booking and confirms no cancellation request for the later booking. The manager’s note on the Monday booking appears inconsistent with the original message. The clerk’s note on the later booking is also not supported by the patient’s words.”

SECTION 5 — CORRESPONDENCE AND REVIEWER COMMENTS

Email from front-desk clerk to supervisor, 16 September, 9:12 a.m.:
I am frustrated by this review. Patients send long messages and then expect us to know which sentence matters. I marked the Monday booking as “question only” because the manager’s review label said that. I now see the original wording asked us to cancel. I did not change the appointment status myself; the cancellation action was already in the audit history. Please tell the manager the note needs correction.

Reply from Dalia Rahman, 16 September, 9:40 a.m.:
I have read the original message. I was wrong to call it a question-only message. The patient directly requested cancellation, and the system cancelled the booking. I am annoyed that this took a public review before anyone checked the record, but the wording is plain. I have asked records staff to correct my review label.

Email from reception to appointment team, 16 September, 10:06 a.m.:
Please do not copy an old cancellation label into a new appointment. The 22 August visit and the 12 September confirmation message are different events. The fact that Leila cancelled an older visit does not mean she cancelled the September visit. In the September message she explicitly said she was not asking us to cancel and asked for confirmation. The active booking should stay active.

Team reply, 16 September, 10:18 a.m.:
Understood. I have removed “patient requested cancellation” from the September review note. The appointment remains active. I have also added a note that the patient was angry about the prior wait but still intended to attend.

Manager’s daily summary, 16 September:
Several draft classifications were based on the first phrase noticed rather than the complete message. “Cancel” appears in messages that deny cancellation, describe a different visit, or discuss a possible future action. The word alone does not establish a request. Conversely, a direct request can be present even when a manager’s label says it is absent. Reviewers should rely on the original message and the relevant appointment record, not on an unsupported conclusion.

SECTION 6 — FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS FROM PATIENTS

Question: If I say I am angry, will you cancel my appointment?
Answer: No. Anger is not a cancellation instruction. Tell us directly if you want the appointment cancelled or moved. If you say that you still plan to come, we will not treat the message as a cancellation request.

Question: If I ask whether my visit is still booked, does that cancel it?
Answer: No. A request for confirmation is not a request to cancel. The desk should confirm the status and leave the booking as it is unless you clearly ask for a change.

Question: If I say “I might cancel if this happens again,” have I cancelled?
Answer: No. That describes a possible future decision, not a cancellation now. The desk should not cancel the current booking based on a hypothetical statement.

Question: Can a staff note overrule the message I sent?
Answer: No. Staff notes can summarize a request, but they can be wrong. If the summary conflicts with the original message, the original message should be checked and the summary corrected.

Question: What if I really do want to cancel?
Answer: Say that clearly, identify the appointment, and ask the desk to cancel it. We will record the request and confirm the action. A request to reschedule is different from a request to cancel all care, and a request to cancel one visit does not automatically cancel other visits or a referral.

SECTION 7 — STAFF MEETING MINUTES

Meeting date: 17 September
Attendees: appointment-desk staff, reception representative, records coordinator

The meeting began with a complaint about the amount of time spent reviewing messages. One clerk said the patient’s wording should not matter if the supervisor already selected a category. The records coordinator replied that a category is a summary, not evidence. The group reviewed the examples in this packet and agreed to check the original communication whenever a patient disputes a label.

The supervisor acknowledged that her cover note about Leila Okafor was inaccurate. Leila wrote that she was not asking to cancel, said she still intended to come, and requested confirmation. The appointment remained active. The supervisor said she had reacted to the word “cancel” without reading the sentence around it. She apologized for putting the inaccurate conclusion into the review notes.

The team also discussed Jonas Mensah’s Monday booking. His message directly asked the desk to cancel the appointment and said he did not want another time booked. The system shows that the booking was cancelled. The manager’s draft label saying “no cancellation request” was inaccurate. The manager has acknowledged the mistake and asked for the review record to be corrected. Staff agreed that an angry complaint can still contain a clear, valid instruction.

A third example concerned the later appointment that Amara Bergstrom said she was still attending. A clerk wrote “may cancel,” but that was speculation. No request to cancel was made. The booking remained active. Staff agreed that speculation about what a patient might do is not the same as a patient request.

The appointment desk will keep the distinction among cancellation, rescheduling, confirmation, and complaint visible on the intake screen. The team will not use “patient cancelled care” for a request to move a single visit. The team will not use “cancellation received” for a hypothetical statement. The system should record what the patient asked, what the desk did, and whether the action was completed.

The meeting ended with a discussion of customer tone. Staff said some messages are insulting or unfair. The supervisor said staff may document abusive language under the conduct procedure, but they still must record the appointment request accurately. A patient’s anger does not make a false summary true, and a patient’s polite wording does not make a clear request disappear.

SECTION 8 — APPENDIX: AUDIT TRAIL EXCERPTS

Audit trail for Leila Okafor, 12 September appointment:

9 September, 10:14 — Patient message received. Text includes: “I am not asking you to cancel it. I still intend to come in.”
9 September, 10:29 — Desk records confirmation request. Status active.
9 September, 11:02 — Supervisor review note added: “Patient requested cancellation.” No status change.
16 September, 10:18 — Review note corrected to state that no cancellation request was made and appointment remains active.

Audit trail for Jonas Mensah, 16 September appointment:

11 September, 3:41 — Patient message received. Text includes: “Please cancel my Monday appointment. I cannot attend and do not want another time booked.”
11 September, 3:47 — Booking status changed to cancelled.
16 September, 9:12 — Clerk asks supervisor to review manager’s “question only” label.
16 September, 9:40 — Supervisor acknowledges that the message directly requested cancellation; correction requested.

Audit trail for Amara Bergstrom, 18 September appointment:

13 September, 8:06 — Patient message received. Text includes: “I am still coming on Wednesday.”
13 September, 8:20 — Clerk note says “Patient upset; may cancel.”
13 September, 8:23 — Booking status active; no cancellation action.

Audit trail for Aiden Fischer, 20 September appointment:

14 September, 1:52 — Patient message received. Text includes: “I might cancel if I have another bad experience, but for now please leave the appointment alone.”
14 September, 2:10 — Confirmation sent; booking remains active.
14 September, 2:16 — Team lead classification added: “Cancellation received.”

Audit trail for Dalia Castillo, rescheduled appointment:

12 September, 2:17 — Patient message received. Text includes: “I need to move Tuesday’s visit to a later date. Please do not cancel the whole referral.”
12 September, 2:36 — Appointment moved to 24 September; referral remains open.
12 September, 2:42 — Clerk note says “Patient cancelled care.”

The audit trail stores actions and comments separately. A comment can be wrong even when the status is right, and a status can remain unchanged even when a comment suggests a change. For that reason the review team must not infer the patient’s request solely from a staff label or from a status field. The original message supplies the patient’s words; the action history supplies what the clinic did. Both are needed to understand the record.

SECTION 9 — OPERATIONS REVIEW CONCLUSION

The review found that several staff conclusions were not supported by the messages they summarized. In the September confirmation message, Leila Okafor explicitly denied asking for cancellation and said she intended to attend. The supervisor’s cancellation label was wrong. In the Monday appointment record, Jonas Mensah explicitly asked for cancellation, and the system completed that action. The manager’s claim that he had only asked a question was wrong. In the later visit records, patients either said they still intended to attend, asked for confirmation, or described a possible future decision; those statements were not current cancellation requests.

The review also found examples where staff conclusions matched the evidence. One patient directly asked for a visit to be cancelled, and the record shows it was cancelled. Another patient asked to move a visit while keeping the referral open, and the appointment was rescheduled. These examples are included so that the review does not teach staff simply to reject every staff conclusion. The correct practice is to compare the conclusion against the words and actions in the relevant record.

The clinic’s response to this packet is to correct inaccurate labels, retain the original messages, and remind staff to distinguish actual requests from complaints, questions, denials, and hypotheticals. Patients may be angry, and staff may be angry in return, but neither person’s tone changes what the text says. The appointment desk should not claim a cancellation was requested when the patient says not to cancel; it should not deny a cancellation request when the patient clearly asks for one; and it should not expand a request to reschedule one visit into a cancellation of all care.

[{"state":"Larkspur Court Property Management — angry incident postmortem, resident submission, and SMS record

Case file LC-4421. Prepared for the building operations review after a week of arguments about a leaking ceiling, access notices, and an disputed ledger entry. This file combines the original web form, the maintenance record, a postmortem, and the resident’s SMS exchange. The writer is angry throughout; the tone does not change the recorded facts. The review team is instructed to check dates, amounts, and actions in the source records rather than accept anyone’s summary as established fact.

WEB FORM SUBMISSION — received October 14, 2026, 09:18

Submitted by: Dalia Fischer
Unit: 4C, Larkspur Court
Lease account: LC-4C-88
Subject selected: Repair / water intrusion

Resident’s message:

“I am furious that this has been handled so badly. The ceiling stain over the hallway has been there since I first reported it. I am not saying the whole apartment is flooded; the water was in the hallway ceiling and there was a damp patch by the closet after the storm. I sent the first report on October 2. The stain got wider on October 6. I put a bowl down on October 8 when I saw two drops, and I told the evening desk. I am tired of being told to wait while people write cheerful little notes saying everything is fixed.

“I am asking for a rent credit for the period the hallway was affected. I am also asking for someone to inspect the ceiling and closet, and to confirm in writing what work was done. I am not asking you to reimburse me for a hotel. I stayed here. I am not asking you to replace my furniture; nothing was damaged. I did move a shoe rack away from the wall. Please stop confusing the shoe rack with a claim for damaged property.

“I want the ledger checked too. My rent is $1,480 a month. The amount I paid for October was $1,480 on October 1, as shown by the bank receipt attached. The portal still showed a $35 service charge on October 12. I dispute that charge because my lease addendum says a service charge is not due when a maintenance request remains open beyond the response period. I am not claiming that I paid $1,515. I did not. I paid $1,480, and the extra $35 is still on the screen as a charge, not as money I paid.

“I have been told that a technician came on October 7. That is wrong. The entry log shows a scheduled visit on October 7, but no one entered my unit that day. The work-order system says the visit was postponed by the contractor. A person came on October 9, looked at the hallway ceiling, and said the source might be a roof seam. He did not open the ceiling, did not inspect the closet, and did not tell me the matter was closed. I want this file read rather than skimmed. If someone has already decided I am exaggerating, they should at least read the dates.”

Resident attachments indexed by the portal:
1. Bank receipt: October rent transfer, $1,480, dated October 1.
2. Screenshot: account page dated October 12, showing rent line paid and service charge $35 outstanding.
3. Photograph: hallway ceiling stain, taken October 6.
4. Photograph: small bowl under the ceiling, taken October 8.
5. Photograph: closet wall, taken October 8; no visible damaged belongings.
6. Lease addendum excerpt, attached as a page image.

Lease addendum excerpt transcribed by the clerk:
“Where a maintenance request affecting the premises remains open after the stated response period, the resident may request review of a service charge. A request for review does not itself constitute payment of that charge, nor does it automatically determine the outcome of the review. Any rent credit must be separately approved and recorded.”

PORTAL ROUTING DETAILS

The online form offered categories: plumbing, heating, access, rent account, and other. Dalia selected “Repair / water intrusion.” The form asked whether there was active water at the moment of submission. She selected “No active flow now.” It asked whether she wanted a rent credit, and she selected “Yes.” It asked whether she had incurred hotel costs, and she selected “No.” It asked whether personal property was damaged, and she selected “No.” The form generated case LC-4421 and displayed a confirmation that the submission had been received. It did not say that a credit had been approved.

The portal’s automated confirmation read: “Your request has been sent to the property team. This message is not a decision on eligibility, an approval of a credit, or confirmation that repairs are complete.” The confirmation was delivered at 09:19. Dalia replied in the portal at 09:24: “I know that is not an approval. Please have a person read it.”

MAINTENANCE AND ACCOUNT RECORDS

October 2, 08:41 — Resident submitted initial leak report, describing a ceiling stain in the hallway. Status: received.
October 2, 09:05 — Desk clerk acknowledged report. No technician dispatched yet.
October 3, 14:10 — Work order assigned to North Quay Repairs for inspection. Planned appointment: October 7, 10:00–12:00.
October 6, 17:32 — Resident uploaded wider-stain photograph. Status remained open.
October 7, 09:11 — Contractor notified office that its technician was unavailable. Appointment changed to October 9. No entry attempted. No key used. No resident contact recorded at the unit.
October 8, 20:16 — Resident called evening desk about two drops and placed a bowl under the ceiling. Desk note: “No active stream observed during call; advised resident to keep area clear and send photos.”
October 9, 11:07 — Technician checked hallway ceiling from inside unit. Technician note: “Stain visible. No active dripping at inspection. Possible roof seam or flashing; requires exterior check. No ceiling opening. Closet not inspected; resident was not present when technician arrived and access was limited to reported hallway location.”
October 9, 11:38 — Work order updated to “follow-up needed,” not “completed.”
October 10, 13:20 — Roof inspection request sent to building vendor. Status: awaiting scheduling.
October 12, 16:02 — Ledger screenshot generated. October rent $1,480 marked paid. Service charge $35 marked outstanding and under review. No $35 payment posted.
October 14, 09:18 — Case LC-4421 received.
October 14, 10:06 — Case assigned to property manager for review.

Account transaction extract:
September rent: $1,480, paid September 1.
October rent: $1,480, paid October 1.
Service charge: $35, posted October 11, unpaid at time of extract.
Credit issued: none shown.
Hotel reimbursement: none shown.
Property-damage reimbursement: none shown.

INTERNAL INCIDENT POSTMORTEM — draft circulated October 15

Incident summary by operations coordinator:
“Resident reports a continuing ceiling leak, but the technician attended October 7 and resolved the issue. The resident has no basis for a rent credit because the issue was fixed on the first visit. The resident also appears to have paid $1,515 for October, including the service charge, and is now seeking the same amount back. The request for reimbursement of hotel costs and damaged belongings should be denied. The account is therefore complete except for sending a standard closure message.”

This draft was entered as an initial opinion, not as an approved determination. Several statements in it are inconsistent with the underlying records. The visit log says the October 7 appointment was postponed and no entry took place. The October 9 technician note says follow-up was needed. The ledger and bank receipt show $1,480 paid, while the $35 service charge remained outstanding. The form expressly records no hotel expense and no damaged property. The request for a rent credit is present in the form and in the resident’s message, but no credit is shown as approved or paid.

Review comments attached to the draft:

Property manager, October 15, 10:40: “Do not send the closure template yet. We have a follow-up request outstanding. Check whether the roof inspection has been scheduled. The first draft is plainly too confident about October 7.”

Maintenance supervisor, October 15, 11:12: “The contractor did not enter on the seventh. October 9 was an observation, not a repair. There is no record of a ceiling repair or a completed roof inspection. Keep the work order open.”

Accounts clerk, October 15, 11:30: “The $1,515 sentence is wrong. Rent received is $1,480. The $35 is a pending charge, not a payment. Do not describe it as a refund due or as money collected.”

Resident liaison, October 15, 12:02: “The resident asks for a credit and an inspection. She does not claim hotel costs or damaged property. Her complaint is angry, but the selections and narrative agree on those points.”

The postmortem draft was not sent to the resident. The file shows no final credit decision as of October 16. The property manager requested a roof inspection and asked accounts to hold the disputed $35 charge for review. A hold is not a waiver, collection, payment, or credit. The maintenance work order remains open pending exterior inspection.

FOLLOW-UP WORK PLAN

The plan lists separate tasks so that a status note cannot be mistaken for a completed repair. Task one: contact the roof vendor and obtain an appointment window. Task two: notify Dalia before access is needed. Task three: inspect the roof seam and flashing above unit 4C. Task four: inspect the hallway ceiling from inside the unit if the resident permits access. Task five: inspect the closet wall, which was not examined on October 9. Task six: document whether there is active moisture or only an old stain. Task seven: report findings to the property manager. Task eight: decide the rent-credit request under the lease and applicable building procedure. Task nine: separately decide the $35 service-charge dispute. Task ten: send the resident a factual status update, not a closure message.

The work plan cautions staff not to use “resolved” merely because no dripping was seen during one visit. It also cautions staff not to promise a credit before the review. The two questions are separate: whether the maintenance issue has been repaired, and whether a rent credit should be granted. The current records establish that the request was made, but do not establish that a credit was approved.

SMS EXCHANGE — October 15

09:02 Dalia: I saw the draft note in the portal. It says you fixed it on the seventh. Nobody came in on the seventh. Your own contractor moved it. That is not a tiny wording problem.

09:08 Property desk: We are checking the visit log. The October 9 note says the stain was seen and a roof check was recommended. The follow-up is still open.

09:11 Dalia: Then stop calling it complete. I want the inspection and I want the credit request reviewed. I am not asking for a hotel bill. I did not stay anywhere else.

09:15 Property desk: Understood. The account shows October rent paid at $1,480. It shows a $35 service charge outstanding, not paid. Accounts will review the charge separately.

09:19 Dalia: Good. The draft said I paid $1,515, which is nonsense. I paid the rent. I did not pay that extra charge.

09:24 Property desk: We have corrected the internal note. No credit has been issued yet. The roof inspection is being scheduled.

09:27 Dalia: Please make sure the next person reads the actual file before sending me another congratulatory message saying the leak is magically fixed.

09:32 Property desk: We will send a factual update after the vendor confirms an appointment.

CASE REVIEW — October 16

Reviewer’s findings:

The incident began with a report on October 2 and remained open in the maintenance system through October 16. The record supports that a stain was present and that the resident reported two drops on October 8. It does not support saying the repair was completed on October 7. The scheduled appointment was postponed, and the only recorded visit was October 9. The technician observed the stain and recommended an exterior inspection. The follow-up work order remained open.

The resident did request a rent credit. The form’s “Yes” selection and the written request both establish that. This is not evidence that a credit was granted. No rent credit appears in the account extract, and the resident was told on October 15 that none had yet been issued.

The rent payment was $1,480. The separate $35 service charge was outstanding and under review. The draft’s statement that the resident paid $1,515 is contradicted by the bank receipt and ledger. The resident did not ask for hotel reimbursement and explicitly selected “No” for hotel costs. The resident did not report damaged personal property and explicitly selected “No” for damage. The shoe rack was moved but was not claimed as damaged.

The initial postmortem wording is therefore unreliable on the visit date, repair status, amount paid, and requested reimbursements. Its presence in the file does not turn those claims into facts. The later review comments identify the discrepancies and direct staff to check source records. The resident’s anger does not change the classification of the requests. The correct record should distinguish requested remedies from approved remedies, unpaid charges from paid amounts, and an observation from a completed repair.

APPENDIX A — MESSAGE AND STATUS AUDIT

The audit was added because several staff members were relying on the first postmortem summary rather than the underlying timestamps. The audit compares each claim in the summary with the record that would ordinarily support it. It does not make a legal conclusion about habitability, eligibility, damages, or the validity of a charge. It records only what this case file says.

Claim in draft: “Technician attended October 7.”
Source check: Contractor notification at 09:11 on October 7 says unavailable and rescheduled to October 9. The unit entry log contains no October 7 entry. Resident states no one entered. Result: unsupported and contradicted by the schedule-change record.

Claim in draft: “Resolved on first visit.”
Source check: There was no October 7 visit. The October 9 note says no active dripping was seen at that moment, identifies a possible roof seam or flashing issue, and requests an exterior check. The work order was set to follow-up needed. Result: not resolved in the recorded system.

Claim in draft: “Resident paid $1,515.”
Source check: Bank receipt records $1,480 on October 1. Ledger marks $1,480 rent paid and $35 service charge outstanding. Result: the amount $1,515 is not a recorded payment.

Claim in draft: “Resident seeks hotel costs.”
Source check: Form answer is No; narrative says she stayed in the unit and is not asking for hotel reimbursement. Result: not requested.

Claim in draft: “Resident seeks damaged-property reimbursement.”
Source check: Form answer is No; narrative says nothing was damaged and the shoe rack was moved. Result: not requested.

Claim in draft: “Resident requests a rent credit.”
Source check: Form answer is Yes; narrative asks for a rent credit for the affected period. Result: requested. No approval is recorded.

The audit also notes that an outstanding account line should not be rewritten as a payment merely because it is visible in the portal. A balance shown on a screen is not equivalent to a transaction receipt. Likewise, a resident’s request for review does not itself erase the charge. Accounts has placed the charge under review, but the file contains no final disposition as of October 16. Staff should avoid both overstatement and understatement: the resident has not paid the $35, but she has disputed it; the property has not issued a credit, but she has requested one.

APPENDIX B — MAINTENANCE EVENT DETAIL

The maintenance team reconstructed the event sequence from the work-order platform, vendor email, desk log, and photographs. The reconstruction is included because “the visit” was used ambiguously in the initial draft. A scheduled window is not proof of attendance. A technician’s observation is not proof that a repair was completed. A recommendation for an exterior check is not itself an exterior check.

October 2: The portal generated a leak report for the hallway ceiling. The desk acknowledged receipt. The record does not show an emergency dispatch on that date. The initial photo was not attached until October 6, but the report itself was received October 2.

October 3: The work order was assigned to North Quay Repairs. The appointment window was set for October 7, 10:00–12:00. The assignment record shows a planned visit, not an actual visit.

October 6: The resident added a photo of the stain and wrote that it had widened. The upload time is 17:32. No repair is recorded that day.

October 7: The vendor notified the office that its technician was unavailable. The appointment was moved to October 9. No entry was attempted. The event log has no key checkout, no access notice acknowledgment, and no technician report for the unit on October 7.

October 8: The resident called the evening desk after observing two drops. The desk advised her to keep the area clear and provide photographs. The call record does not indicate a continuous stream or an emergency evacuation. It does confirm that the resident reported drops and placed a bowl under the area.

October 9: A technician entered for a limited look at the hallway ceiling. The note says no active dripping was visible at that time. It says the stain was visible and that the source might be a roof seam or flashing. It expressly says no ceiling opening was made and the closet was not inspected. The technician requested an exterior check. The work-order status was changed to follow-up needed.

October 10: A request was sent to the roof vendor. It had not yet been scheduled by the time of the October 16 review. No exterior inspection report is present in the case file.

The sequence contains no recorded repair of the ceiling, roof, flashing, or closet wall. It also contains no recorded decision that the condition is harmless or that the resident’s report was false. The absence of active dripping during the short October 9 inspection is one observation at one time. It does not cancel the earlier report of drops or establish that the suspected source was corrected.

APPENDIX C — ACCOUNT RECONCILIATION

The accounts clerk reviewed the transaction ledger rather than relying on the summary sentence in the postmortem. The rent due for October, as displayed in the account record, is $1,480. The bank receipt shows a transfer of $1,480 on October 1. The ledger marks the October rent line paid. The service-charge line is $35 and is dated October 11. The status is outstanding and under review. There is no receipt, bank transfer, card transaction, or ledger posting showing payment of the $35.

The arithmetic that produced the draft’s $1,515 appears to be $1,480 plus $35. That sum is $1,515, but it is not the amount paid. It combines a paid rent amount with an unpaid service charge. The sum of separate lines does not establish that both lines were paid. The account record must be described by status as well as value.

The resident’s October 14 submission disputes the service charge under an addendum and asks for review. The addendum says a resident may request review when a maintenance request remains open after the stated response period. It also says a request for review is not payment and does not automatically decide the result. The case file does not include a final decision on whether the fee will be retained, removed, or adjusted. Therefore the record should say “$35 outstanding, under review,” not “$35 paid,” “$35 refunded,” or “$35 waived.”

No rent credit transaction is recorded. The resident’s request for a credit is distinct from a credit actually issued. The property manager’s October 15 comment tells staff to review the request after checking the repair status; it does not approve a credit. The October 15 SMS expressly says no credit has been issued yet. No later transaction appears through October 16.

APPENDIX D — STAFF HANDOFF NOTES

Outgoing desk clerk, October 15, 13:10: “The resident is upset and the case has become noisy. Please do not let the tone substitute for checking the records. The first summary says the unit was visited on the seventh, but the vendor changed that appointment. I have asked maintenance to confirm the follow-up.”

[{"state":"Customer chat transcript and internal FAQ extract — Granite Freight / Northwind Outfitters, case GF-88417

Administrative record: This document consolidates a customer-service conversation and the applicable excerpt from the carrier’s service FAQ. It is retained for ticket triage, audit, and routing purposes. The customer is Leila Castillo, logistics coordinator for Northwind Outfitters. The shipment reference is GF-88417, a carton of display fixtures moving from the Northwind consolidation site to its Alder Quay retail location. The conversation took place over the carrier’s support channel on 18 September. The shipment was booked on 11 September for a scheduled delivery on 16 September. The record contains statements made by the customer, statements made by support personnel, copied system fields, and a later supervisor’s disposition. These sources should not be treated as equivalent: the system’s measured scan data and the FAQ’s stated rule establish the relevant facts; a person’s summary or recommendation is not a substitute for those facts.

Chat transcript, 08:42. Leila Castillo: “Good morning. I am opening a service ticket for GF-88417. The carton arrived yesterday, 17 September, rather than on the appointment date of 16 September. The receiving desk signed at 15:26. The outer carton was intact. I am asking whether the service credit applies, not asking for a refund of the merchandise.”

08:44. Intake agent: “I have noted a late-arrival concern and a possible package condition concern. The first scan was at Alder Quay on the 17th. Was the shipment tendered on time?”

08:46. Leila: “Yes. The origin handoff is recorded as 12 September at 09:10. The booking confirmation says the appointment was for the 16th, and the dispatch record shows the carton departed the regional depot on the 15th. There is no damage claim. Please do not convert ‘possible condition concern’ into a damage report; that was your phrase.”

08:48. Intake agent: “Understood. I will separate the two categories. I can see a note from a previous shift reading, ‘No carrier delay; customer selected a later slot.’ I will leave that note in place until the appointment history is checked.”

FAQ EXTRACT — SERVICE CREDITS FOR APPOINTMENT COMMITMENTS

Purpose and scope. This section applies to shipments expressly booked under an appointment commitment. It does not apply to ordinary estimated-arrival services, customer-selected delivery windows that were changed after booking, or shipments delayed solely because the receiving party was unavailable. The booked service field and the event record for the specific shipment govern. The account’s overall service plan, another shipment’s status, and a general estimate displayed on the customer portal do not replace those records.

Commitment standard. For an appointment commitment, the named delivery date is the final date for the carrier’s delivery performance. A delivery scan after that date is a late arrival unless an applicable exclusion below is established. A shipment scanned before the appointment date is not late merely because a customer reports inconvenience. A shipment scanned on the appointment date is treated as timely even when the scan occurs after the receiving desk’s preferred internal hour, unless a separate time-of-day commitment was purchased and recorded.

Eligibility. A customer may request the published service credit when the shipment was tendered within the required origin window, the carrier’s event record shows delivery after the committed date, and no exclusion applies. A service credit is not a refund of the goods, an award for inconvenience, or a replacement shipment. The amount, if payable, is calculated under the separate tariff table and is outside the scope of this excerpt. This section determines only whether the timing condition is met.

Exclusions. No credit is payable for a late event caused solely by an address correction requested by the shipper after dispatch; a documented hold requested by the consignee; a verified closure or refusal at the destination; or a customer-approved appointment change entered before the original commitment expired. The exception must be supported by a timestamped record tied to the shipment reference. A generic account note, agent recollection, or later summary without an associated event is not sufficient evidence of an exclusion.

Evidence hierarchy. The confirmed booking receipt establishes the service class and promised date. The carrier’s event scans and electronic proof of delivery establish handling and delivery dates. A signed customer receiving record may corroborate delivery timing. A free-text disposition or proposed outcome is an administrative opinion and does not override those records. Where records conflict, staff must identify the conflict and seek clarification rather than assume that the free-text disposition is accurate.

Processing sequence. First, verify that the reference in the inquiry matches the reference on the booking and event record. Second, verify the service class and committed date. Third, compare the delivery event with that date. Fourth, test each stated exclusion against a recorded event. Fifth, route an eligible request for tariff calculation. The sequence is mandatory because a conclusion based only on the customer’s wording or on a copied summary may confuse a service credit with a product refund, or may assign the events of one shipment to another.

Examples. A carton booked for an appointment on 4 May and delivered on 4 May is timely under this timing test, even if the recipient expected it before noon and no such time commitment was purchased. A carton booked for 4 May and delivered on 5 May is late, subject to the exclusions. If the consignee recorded a hold on 3 May and the carrier’s event history links that hold to the later delivery, the hold exclusion applies. If a later note merely asserts that the consignee requested a hold but no linked event exists, staff must not treat the assertion as established. If a shipper changed an address after dispatch and the carrier records the resulting delay, the address-correction exclusion applies; a routine pre-dispatch address confirmation does not qualify.

Clarifications. A customer saying “I did not ask to reschedule” is relevant but should be checked against the event record. A support agent saying “the customer selected a later slot” is likewise not proof unless the appointment history contains that change. A booking can have both a general estimated range and a specific appointment date; when the specific appointment commitment is confirmed, the specific date governs this rule. A late delivery does not automatically mean that the shipment was lost or damaged. It may establish only the timing element of a service-credit request.

Internal handling notes. Do not close an inquiry as denied merely because an automated dashboard labels the delivery “within window.” The dashboard may display an estimated range associated with the account rather than the shipment’s booked commitment. Do not grant an exception simply because a customer’s account has a good or poor historical performance score. Do not copy a supervisor’s suggested disposition into the factual chronology. The reviewing employee should preserve the original notes, record the facts used, and distinguish a verified exception from a disputed assertion.

FAQ revision record. The current text was approved by the carrier’s service governance desk on 2 August. An earlier draft referred to “delivery on or before the service window.” That wording was removed because it did not distinguish a specific appointment date from a general estimate. The current rule uses the confirmed booking field. Agents should not rely on an obsolete printed quick guide where it conflicts with this extract. The revision does not change the tariff amount, the definition of a damaged shipment, the process for merchandise claims, or any requirement to retain the original proof of delivery.

From: Nadia O'Neill, distribution controls, Granite Analytics
To: Kwame Fischer, freight claims review, Harbor Freight
Subject: GF-77106 / quantity discrepancy and disposition check

To: Granite Analytics distribution controls

The driver presented paperwork for 48 units. We signed for 42 received, with a notation that six were not present at the bay. We did not refuse the consignment, and our bay was open. The manifest establishes that 48 were tendered at origin, whereas the signed dock record and contemporaneous ledger establish 42 accepted at destination. The invoice charges the quantity 48. GF-77160 / HF-20481: 36 ordered, 36 manifested, 35 accepted, 36 billed; this record is under a different purchase order and destination. The account dashboard displays both as completed movements. Their quantities are not evidence concerning GF-77106. The records are reproduced because a bulk download placed them in the same export and a prior automated check appears to have compared neighboring rows.

Operations memo, 22 October, 12:00. The reviewer must record separate figures for ordered, manifested, accepted, and billed quantities. For this file, the purchase order states 48 requested, the dispatch manifest states 48 loaded, the proof of delivery acceptance field states 42, the receiving ledger records 42, and the invoice bills 48. The handwritten shortage notation identifies a variance of six units between billed and accepted amounts. This arithmetic is a count comparison, not an inference that the order itself was only for 42. The order remains 48. The manifest remains 48. The receipt remains 42. The invoice remains 48. Similarly, a signature on a proof of delivery can acknowledge an arrival while recording a shortage. Document owner: Ines Fischer, finance operations. Incident date: August 14. Review participants: Priya Delgado, AP lead; Leila Alvarez, procurement analyst; billing operations and receiving. Tone in the meeting was angry and blunt. The report records what the documents establish, not what anyone hoped they would establish. A handwritten-style note typed up by the AP lead is included in Appendix C. An early manager verdict is reproduced because it was circulated before the supporting records were checked.

1. Executive summary

Foxglove Analytics sent Saltmarsh Foods invoice FA-2086 for a cold-room temperature monitor, installation, and a one-year monitoring subscription. The invoice total was $4,680. Saltmarsh’s purchase order SF-6019 authorized one monitor at $3,600 and installation at $600, for a total of $4,200 before any applicable tax. It did not authorize a subscription. The receiving record confirms delivery of one monitor and completion of installation. It explicitly says no monitoring service was activated, requested, or demonstrated at handoff. The invoice was placed on hold because its line items did not match the purchase order. The dispute is not about the monitor or installation: those ordered items were received and accepted. It is about the additional $480 subscription line, which lacks approval and evidence of performance.

An early internal verdict stated that Saltmarsh had accepted the subscription and should pay the entire invoice. That verdict came from a hurried reading of a portal status reading “accepted for processing.” The status meant the invoice file had passed format validation into the AP queue; it did not mean that Saltmarsh had accepted every billed service. The underlying records contradict the verdict. After review, Foxglove’s billing team agreed to remove the $480 line and issue a corrected invoice. The corrected payable amount for the authorized goods and installation is $4,200. The original invoice has not been paid in full, and the extra subscription charge is not an agreed payable item.

2. What happened

On August 7, Foxglove delivered one temperature monitor to Saltmarsh Foods’ North Pier cold room. The delivery was accompanied by installation. The receiving employee signed for one unit and wrote “installation complete; monitor powers on.” The same receiving record has a separate subscription field, marked “not activated.” A note below says the supplier offered to discuss a monitoring plan later, after the customer reviewed its internal requirements. No subscription account credentials were issued, no monitoring dashboard was enabled, and no recurring service start date was recorded.

On August 9, Foxglove emailed invoice FA-2086 to the Saltmarsh AP mailbox. The invoice contained three lines: one monitor, $3,600; installation, $600; and one-year temperature monitoring subscription, $480. The invoice total was $4,680. The email subject line said “equipment and service invoice.” It did not include an approved change order or a separate service agreement. Saltmarsh’s system recognized the vendor and invoice number and placed the file in the processing queue. That system event was later misread as customer acceptance.

On August 10, Priya Delgado compared the invoice with purchase order SF-6019. The PO listed the monitor and installation only. She placed the invoice on hold, selected “line item not on order,” and asked Foxglove to provide approval for the subscription or remove it. Her comment was direct: “We did not order monitoring. Do not treat our receipt of the hardware as approval for a recurring service.” The hold remained active through August 14.

On August 11, an automated vendor portal sent Foxglove a notice that the invoice file was “accepted for processing.” This is a system routing status, not a determination that the goods and services match the purchase order. The notice also said “payment pending review.” The two phrases appeared next to one another. A later internal manager copied only the first phrase into a summary and called it acceptance. That summary was not a customer statement and was not based on the receiving record.

On August 12, Leila Alvarez checked the procurement archive. She found no service addendum, no revised PO, no subscription election, and no email from an authorized Saltmarsh buyer approving a $480 monitoring service. She found a vendor brochure describing a “one-year plan” at a similar price, but a brochure is not an order. The brochure was not signed and does not name Saltmarsh. Leila attached it to the investigation only to explain why the invoice line may have appeared; she did not regard it as authorization.

On August 13, Foxglove’s billing desk replied that its account page showed “plan selected.” The screenshot was reviewed in the postmortem. It showed an unsubmitted selection in a quotation tool, created while the sales representative was preparing options. The page had no customer signature, no acceptance timestamp, and no activation record. The words “plan selected” were a draft tool label. The screenshot cannot show that Saltmarsh purchased the plan.

On August 14, AP lead Priya called the billing desk. She was angry because the automated reminder described the entire $4,680 as overdue even though the invoice was on hold and the main $4,200 matched the order. She asked Foxglove to issue a corrected invoice for the authorized equipment and installation, and to remove the subscription charge. Foxglove initially said the matter would be escalated. Later the same afternoon, its billing reviewer confirmed that the subscription had been added in error and approved a $480 credit. The corrected invoice is to show $4,200 due, subject to the normal payment process. The credit had not yet appeared in the portal at the time this report was drafted, so the original portal balance still displayed $4,680. The balance display is not evidence that Saltmarsh accepted the subscription.

4. Documents examined

Purchase order SF-6019: issued August 2 by Saltmarsh procurement. One temperature monitor, quantity one, unit amount $3,600; installation, quantity one, amount $600. Total authorized before tax: $4,200. The PO does not mention a monitoring subscription, recurring service, renewal, dashboard access, or annual plan. The purchase order includes a standard instruction that additions require written approval from an authorized buyer. No such approval is in the file.

Receiving record RF-1153: dated August 7. One monitor received and serial number recorded. Installation status marked complete. The receiving employee’s note says the unit powered on. The service activation box is marked “not activated.” The form says, “Vendor offered follow-up plan discussion; customer will consider separately.” Signature confirms physical receipt and installation, not acceptance of a separate subscription.

Invoice FA-2086: dated August 9. Goods line $3,600, installation line $600, monitoring subscription line $480, total $4,680. The invoice does not list a subscription start date or a service account number. It has no attached customer approval.

Portal event history: “File received,” “format validated,” “accepted for processing,” and “payment pending review.” In this system, “accepted for processing” indicates that the file is readable and has entered the work queue. It does not indicate purchase approval. The invoice continued to carry a hold flag after the portal event.

Quotation tool history: a draft quote prepared by a Foxglove sales user. An option labelled “one-year monitoring plan” was clicked during preparation. The quote was not sent for customer signature. The page has no customer account acceptance, date of activation, or order reference. The vendor’s screenshot labels the selection “plan selected,” but the event history identifies it as an internal draft action.

AP hold log: entered by Priya Delgado on August 10. Reason “unapproved line item.” Comment requests evidence or correction and expressly states that monitoring was not ordered. No later AP action releases the hold before the billing reviewer’s decision.

Billing correction log: entered August 14 by the Foxglove reviewer. It says “subscription line unsupported; remove $480 and reissue invoice at $4,200.” Credit posting pending at report time. This is the vendor’s correction of the billing record, not an assertion that the original line was valid.

5. Financial reconciliation

The purchase order has two authorized amounts: $3,600 for the monitor and $600 for installation. Adding those authorized amounts gives $4,200. The invoice includes those same two lines plus $480 for a subscription. Adding all three invoice lines gives $4,680. The $480 difference is exactly the unapproved subscription line. There is no other quantity, price, tax, freight, or currency discrepancy identified in the records reviewed. No payment was made against FA-2086 before the hold. The vendor’s corrected-document request removes the $480 and leaves the authorized $4,200 invoice amount for normal processing. The figure $4,680 remains visible in the original portal screen only because the revised document had not yet posted.

The postmortem does not conclude that the hardware was rejected. Saltmarsh received the monitor and accepted the installation recorded on RF-1153. Nor does it conclude that the whole invoice was accepted. The line-specific evidence matters: acceptance of the delivered goods does not supply approval for an additional service that was neither activated nor ordered. The two accepted purchase-order lines can proceed through normal AP after the revised document arrives; the disputed subscription line cannot.

6. Impact and response

The incident delayed processing and generated an inaccurate overdue reminder. It also required AP and procurement staff to spend time locating the original order, checking the receiving form, and explaining the portal’s routing terminology. Priya was understandably angry that the reminder characterized the full balance as overdue while the invoice was held for a mismatch. Foxglove’s billing desk initially repeated the portal’s status without checking the documents. Once the reviewer examined the signed PO and receiving record, the correction was approved.

No funds were transferred for the disputed invoice during the incident. There was no late fee posted to Saltmarsh’s ledger. A standard payment-terms paragraph appeared on the invoice, but the file contains no separate late-fee transaction. The correction requested is limited to the unsupported $480 subscription. Saltmarsh did not request a refund because it had not paid the invoice. It requested a corrected invoice and removal of the extra line.

7. Root cause

Foxglove’s invoice generation process imported an optional subscription choice from a draft quotation into the final invoice without a customer acceptance event. The AP portal then used the generic phrase “accepted for processing,” which was misunderstood by the vendor manager as substantive customer acceptance. Those are separate process failures. The supporting documents were available, but the initial summary was written before the reviewer compared them. The account page’s loose label “plan selected” added confusion because it did not distinguish a draft selection by the sales user from a purchase selection by the customer.

Saltmarsh’s AP hold process worked as intended: it identified the mismatch, recorded a clear reason, and kept the invoice from being paid while evidence was requested. The receiving record also captured the scope correctly. The failure was not a failure by Saltmarsh to communicate its decision. Priya’s note explicitly rejected the subscription, and the PO never included it.

8. Corrective actions

Foxglove billing will require a customer approval reference before an optional recurring service can be placed on an invoice. The quotation tool label will be changed from “plan selected” to “draft option,” until the customer signs or submits an order. The invoice-generation job will compare service lines with accepted order data before issuing an invoice. The portal status will be clarified so that file-format acceptance cannot be mistaken for purchasing approval. A separate status will identify an invoice as held for review.

Saltmarsh AP will continue to distinguish receipt of goods from authorization of additional services. The team will attach the PO and receiving record to future disputes and will not release a held invoice solely because a vendor portal shows a processing status. These steps do not shift the responsibility for the incorrect invoice to Saltmarsh; they are safeguards for the AP team’s normal review.

The billing reviewer will send the corrected invoice and credit record to Saltmarsh. The original FA-2086 will remain in the file as the superseded document. The revised statement should show $4,200 as the amount for the ordered monitor and installation, with no monitoring subscription line. AP will then process it under ordinary terms. Any reminder generated from the unrevised $4,680 record should be disregarded and withdrawn.

APPENDIX B — Status terminology supplied by portal administrator

“File received” means the portal has received the uploaded file. “Format validated” means the file passed basic readability and required-field checks. “Accepted for processing” means that the file has been added to the AP work queue. It does not mean the buyer approved the invoice or accepted every billed line. “Payment pending review” means no payment decision has been made. “On hold” means an AP user has stopped the invoice for investigation. In this case, the file was format-validated and routed but remained on hold. The status history contains no event representing customer approval of the subscription.
