Category selected: Workplace scheduling and attendance
Urgency selected: Normal
Subject entered by employee: “Request to correct attendance record and discuss temporary schedule”

Message entered by Tomasz:

Hello People Operations. I am writing about my attendance entry for 12 June and also my schedule for the next few weeks. I arrived at North Annex at 07:52 for an 08:00 shift. The east entrance badge reader did not accept my card twice, so I used the reception desk telephone. Bao Kaur opened the side door at 08:04. The paper sign-in sheet at reception has my handwriting and 08:04 written next to my name. I worked the full shift until 16:30. The time system says I was absent for the day, not late, and the weekly report also shows one full absence. Please correct the record to show the time I actually entered and the hours I worked. I am not asking for the four minutes to be erased; I want the record to match the sign-in sheet and the hours worked.

I also request a temporary change to my starting time from 08:00 to 08:30 on Tuesdays and Thursdays, beginning 18 June and ending 11 July. The shuttle service I use has changed its published arrival time, and on those two days it now reaches the North Annex at about 08:20. I can stay until 17:00 on those days to complete my scheduled hours. On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday I can continue with the normal 08:00 start. I am asking for a four-week temporary schedule arrangement, not a permanent change. I understand my supervisor must check coverage and that this request may need approval.

The schedule request is not a request for paid leave, unpaid leave, or an absence from work. I plan to work the hours described above. I do not ask the company to excuse a day I did not work. I have not asked anyone to change my job title or remove my regular duties. I can still perform the stockroom coordinator duties and can cover the receiving desk as planned. I can provide the shuttle timetable if needed.

Please tell me what records you need for the attendance correction and who decides the temporary schedule. I have already spoken to my shift supervisor, Yara Castillo. She said she would check the department coverage sheet and send a note to People Operations. I am not submitting a medical document or claiming an illness. This is a transport timing issue and a request to adjust two start times for four weeks.

Form fields, as copied from the portal:

Employee name: Tomasz Bergstrom
Employee number: SO-2716
Work location: North Annex
Manager: Yara Castillo
Dates involved in attendance correction: 12 June
Schedule dates requested: Tuesdays and Thursdays, 18 June through 11 July
Requested change: Start at 08:30 instead of 08:00; stay until 17:00
Employee comment on paid leave: “No leave requested.”
Employee comment on job duties: “No change requested.”
Attachments listed: shuttle_schedule_june.pdf; reception_signin_12_june.jpg

PORTAL AUTO-SUMMARY, GENERATED AT SUBMISSION

The portal summary is a convenience display and is not a determination under company policy. It compresses selected form fields and may omit context. The text displayed to the queue reviewer was: “Employee reports absence on 12 June and requests a temporary schedule adjustment.” The word “absence” came from the attendance category selected by the employee in a drop-down list; it did not come from the employee’s written explanation. The employee selected “attendance record issue” and then chose “absence/late entry” from a required subcategory menu because no option named “badge access and incorrect system entry” was available. The summary is not a substitute for the form message or attached records.

AUTOMATED ROUTING AND FIRST REVIEW

At 09:13 the system routed the ticket to the Attendance Correction queue. At 09:14 the system added a second routing label, Temporary Schedule Request. The ticket was not routed to Leave Administration. A reviewer opened the form at 09:26. The portal displayed the first paragraph and then a panel with the supervisor’s preliminary comment. The attachment thumbnails were below the fold and were not opened during the first review.

Internal comment, Yara Castillo, shift supervisor, 14 June, 09:20:

I spoke with Tomasz yesterday and understand there may be a door-access issue on 12 June. The reception sheet should be checked. The time record showing a full absence does not match what Tomasz told me. I have not approved any alteration yet because I need to verify the paper sheet and badge log. For the proposed June/July schedule, I need to compare the request with receiving coverage. I have not told Tomasz the request is denied. I also have not said the schedule is approved. My note is preliminary, not a final decision.

Internal comment, first queue reviewer, 14 June, 09:35:

Initial recommendation: no action. The employee has an absence in the system and is requesting a schedule exception, so it looks like a leave matter rather than a record error. The schedule request should be rejected as not a policy request. I did not see the attachments when writing this note. This is only a recommendation for the queue, not a People Operations decision and not a finding that the employee failed to work.

A second reviewer marked the first recommendation “needs evidence check” at 10:02. The first recommendation remained visible in the audit history and continued to appear in the top summary panel until the ticket was reopened. It was not deleted. The top panel’s “No action recommended” wording was written by the first reviewer and was not generated from a verified policy assessment.

ATTACHMENT A — RECEPTION SIGN-IN EXTRACT

North Annex reception paper sign-in sheet, date 12 June. The extract below was typed by People Operations from the photographed page. All entries are retained in the order they appear. Handwriting was compared against Tomasz’s earlier visitor forms by the receptionist; the receptionist marked the entry as legible and attributable to Tomasz. This transcription is for review and does not itself determine payroll treatment.

07:41 — Leila Delgado, vendor delivery, appointment with receiving
07:46 — Xiu Moreau, staff, badge replacement appointment
07:52 — Tomasz Bergstrom, staff, east reader did not accept card; waiting for door
07:58 — Yara Castillo, staff, supervisor
08:04 — Tomasz Bergstrom, staff, entered with Bao Kaur through side door; handwritten initials TB
08:07 — Bao Kaur, staff, reception return from loading bay
08:11 — delivery visitor, appointment with receiving

The sheet has a printed note at the bottom: “Visitors and staff using reception assistance should record the time at the desk. This sheet supports access review; the electronic time record remains a separate record.” There is no entry showing Tomasz leaving and returning later that day. A scan of the whole page is attached. The cropped thumbnail in the portal did not display the 08:04 line, but the full scan does.

ATTACHMENT B — BADGE ACCESS EXTRACT

Access desk extract, 12 June, local time:

07:51:42 — Tomasz Bergstrom badge presented, east entrance, denied, reader offline
07:52:16 — Tomasz Bergstrom badge presented, east entrance, denied, reader offline
08:03:51 — Bao Kaur badge presented, side entrance, granted
08:04:09 — Tomasz Bergstrom badge presented, side entrance, granted
08:04:11 — door contact, side entrance, open
08:04:39 — door contact, side entrance, closed

The access desk states that the reader outage affected three employees that morning. The log records access through a door, not hours worked. The log does not prove by itself how long someone worked. The combination of the badge log, reception sheet, supervisor’s note, and later stockroom records is reviewed below. The employee’s claim is not accepted merely because it appears in the form; each source is checked against the others.

ATTACHMENT C — SHIFT AND WORK RECORD EXTRACT

The published shift roster for Tomasz on 12 June shows 08:00–16:30. The stockroom task board has the following entries:

08:12 — receiving count opened under Tomasz’s staff login
08:19 — pallet discrepancy note saved under Tomasz’s staff login
09:05 — receiving count completed, supervisor review pending
11:36 — transfer request sent from stockroom terminal under Tomasz’s login
14:48 — inventory adjustment entered under Tomasz’s login
16:22 — end-of-day handover note filed under Tomasz’s login

The terminal logs are not conclusive proof that an employee personally performed each action; staff accounts can be used at shared terminals. Yara Castillo confirms that she saw Tomasz working in the stockroom shortly after 08:10 and again during the afternoon. Bao Kaur confirms that she opened the side door and saw Tomasz enter at approximately 08:04. The roster and records together support that he worked the shift. There is no indication in the available records that he was absent for the full day. The hours system’s full-day absence appears to have resulted from a missing clock-in after the badge reader failure.

ATTENDANCE CORRECTION POLICY — EXTRACT PROVIDED WITH TICKET

Section 4.1: An employee who believes a time entry does not match attendance should report the discrepancy to the supervisor or People Operations as soon as practical. A discrepancy report is not itself a request for leave.

Section 4.2: A supervisor may ask for supporting information, including access records, reception records, schedules, or work records. A record correction should reflect verified information. A late arrival should not be converted into a full-day absence if available evidence supports work later that day. The policy does not require a supervisor to erase minutes actually missed, and it does not permit an employee to claim hours unsupported by evidence.

Section 4.3: If the available evidence shows an employee entered after the scheduled start, the time record should distinguish the late arrival from a full-day absence. Payroll adjustments, if needed, are handled under the separate payroll process. A reviewer should not infer a leave request only from a drop-down label when the employee’s written explanation says otherwise.

Section 4.4: A preliminary queue recommendation is not a final action. The supervisor and People Operations must check the underlying records before closing an attendance discrepancy.

The excerpt is the applicable section supplied to the reviewer. It contains no rule stating that a badge-reader failure automatically makes all time paid, no rule requiring an attendance discrepancy to be denied, and no rule that every employee with an absence code is on leave. The policy asks for a review of supporting information.

ATTACHMENT D — SCHEDULE COVERAGE MATERIALS

Tomasz’s normal roster for the four weeks in question is 08:00–16:30 Monday to Friday. His proposed temporary hours on Tuesdays and Thursdays are 08:30–17:00, keeping the same total scheduled shift length. The requested dates are 18, 20, 25, and 27 June, and 2, 4, 9, and 11 July. The request does not include weekends or any date outside that range.

The department coverage sheet lists two staff members assigned to the receiving desk at 08:00 on Tuesday and Thursday, and three assigned from 08:30 onward. The sheet also lists a supervisor on site from 07:45 each day. On two Tuesdays, deliveries are forecast between 08:00 and 08:30; on the other requested mornings, no delivery appointment is listed before 08:30. The delivery forecast is not a guarantee that a delivery will arrive. The receiving desk can be staffed by the other listed employees during the requested 30-minute interval, subject to the manager’s normal approval.

Yara’s coverage note, 14 June, 10:10:

I checked the current sheet. I believe the proposed four-week change may be workable because two other people are assigned at the desk before 08:30, but on the 25th and 9th there is a delivery forecast. I have not decided whether those days need a different arrangement. Tomasz says he can stay until 17:00, which appears to preserve the shift length. We need to check whether this creates an overtime issue or a handover issue. My note does not approve or deny the request. I want People Operations to confirm which approval route applies.

Coverage policy, internal scheduling guide, section 2.3:

A temporary shift-time adjustment may be considered by the supervisor when it preserves scheduled hours and can be covered. The supervisor should review actual coverage, customer or receiving commitments, and any handover requirement. A request is not approved merely because an employee says coverage is possible. A request is also not automatically denied merely because one forecast delivery appears on a calendar. The supervisor may propose a limited adjustment if a specific date presents a genuine coverage problem. People Operations can advise on process but does not replace the supervisor’s operational review.

Section 2.4:

When the requested change is for a stated short period and the employee remains at work for the planned hours, classify it as a temporary schedule request, not as leave, unless the employee also requests time away from work. Do not classify an ordinary schedule request as medical accommodation without evidence that it is being made as one. Employees need not disclose private information that is not relevant to the request.

Section 2.5:

If the employee asks for a change that would reduce hours, the supervisor should clarify whether the employee is requesting paid leave, unpaid leave, or a reduced-hours arrangement. If the employee specifically says no leave is requested and offers replacement work time, the reviewer should record that statement and evaluate the proposed schedule separately. Do not treat a proposed later start as a full-day absence without further evidence.

ATTACHMENT E — SHUTTLE TIMETABLE AND EMPLOYEE FOLLOW-UP

Tomasz attached the current shuttle timetable. It lists arrival at North Annex at 08:20 on Tuesdays and Thursdays, effective 17 June. The previous timetable listed arrival at 07:45. The timetable is not a company-issued transport guarantee, and the company does not promise to change schedules to match public or private transport. It is provided as context for the request, not as an independent approval.

Follow-up message from Tomasz, 14 June, 10:31:

Thank you for checking. To be clear, I am not asking to take a half hour of leave on those days. I propose to begin at 08:30 and finish at 17:00. I can attend the usual handover at 16:45 before I finish, or we can agree another handover method. If a particular date cannot be covered, please tell me which date and I can discuss another option. Follow-up message from Yara Castillo, 14 June, 11:02:

Confirmed, these are separate issues. The record correction can be checked against the sign-in page and the access log. The schedule remains pending my coverage review. I have not told Tomasz to stay home, and I have not marked any of the requested dates as leave.

First reviewer mark: No.

09:13 — assigned to Attendance Correction queue

09:26 — reviewer opens ticket

Date: 12 June
Scheduled: 08:00–16:30

The schedule request should not be merged with the attendance correction. The fact that both topics appear in one form does not make them the same request. POLICY CROSS-REFERENCE — GENERAL PEOPLE OPERATIONS GUIDE

Section 1.1, Accurate records:

Employees and managers should report and correct a record that is known to be materially inaccurate. A time system entry is evidence of what was entered into that system; it is not conclusive where the system has a known outage or missing event. Supporting information may include a written sign-in sheet, access log, witness account, roster, or work activity. Reviewers must distinguish an unrecorded clock event from a verified absence.

Section 1.2, Requests versus labels:

A request is determined from the employee’s stated purpose and proposed action, read in context. A portal category, routing label, subject field, or generated summary can help locate a request but does not override clear written words. If a category conflicts with the written request, reviewers should record the conflict and use the written explanation as primary evidence, subject to clarification where needed.

Section 1.3, Preliminary comments:

Manager and reviewer comments may be provisional. A preliminary note must not be represented as final approval, final denial, or confirmed policy conclusion unless the author says it is final and the appropriate decision process has been completed. Comments that expressly say evidence has not been checked should not be used as a finding about that evidence.

Section 2.1, Temporary schedule changes:

A temporary schedule proposal is an employee request for a schedule decision. It is not an approved schedule until the authorized supervisor confirms it. It is not a leave request where the employee proposes to work the planned hours and does not request time away. Reviewers should identify the requested dates, hours, duration, stated reason, and operational questions, then refer the proposal to the supervisor for a decision.

Section 2.2, Clear decision records:

The record should say whether a proposal is approved, declined, or still under review. “May be workable,” “needs checking,” and “recommendation” are not equivalent to approval. A reviewer should avoid turning a forecast, draft, or automated status into a completed decision.

Section 2.6, No assumption from unrelated evidence:

A record correction concerning a past date and a request for a future schedule change are separately assessed. Evidence supporting one does not automatically decide the other. A badge record on one day does not establish the schedule coverage for a later month. A schedule proposal does not determine whether a past-day absence code is accurate.

Section 3.1, Employee communication:

When a request is unclear, ask a focused question rather than assuming the employee intended a different request. Where an employee has already stated that no leave is requested and has described replacement work hours, preserve that statement in the case notes. Do not ask for irrelevant personal or medical details when the stated request is a transport-related schedule discussion.

Section 3.2, Operational coverage:

The supervisor should use the current staffing plan and actual operational needs. An anticipated delivery may be relevant, but a forecast alone is not proof that a change cannot work. The supervisor can discuss alternatives, such as a different start on a specific date or a different handover arrangement. Any decision should identify the dates and reasons rather than using a broad label without explanation.

Section 4.5, Corrections and audit trail:

Do not erase the old entry from the audit trail. Make a dated correction that explains the evidence and records the original code, the verified information, and any pending payroll action. If a queue reviewer made a recommendation before seeing relevant records, preserve it as a recommendation but do not treat it as a verified determination.

The guide does not say the employee always gets the schedule requested. It does not say the employee must be absent because the system displays an absence code. It does not say that a preliminary “no action” entry becomes final simply by being placed in a top panel. These distinctions are included because the ticket contains a preliminary recommendation that conflicts with the documentary evidence and the employee’s written statements.

REVIEW MEETING NOTES, 17 JUNE

Participants: Tomasz Bergstrom, Yara Castillo, People Operations specialist
Purpose: clarify outstanding matters and verify that the written request has been read correctly

People Operations: “For the 12 June record, are you asking us to change the entry to show 08:00 even though the reception and access logs show 08:04?”

Tomasz: “No. Please use what the records support. I arrived at reception at about 07:52, got in at 08:04, and started the work shortly after. I am not asking you to show I entered earlier than I did. I am asking you not to call the whole day absent.”

Yara: “I saw Tomasz in the stockroom around 08:10. I can confirm he worked that shift. I do not know whether the system should deduct any minutes, so payroll should handle that part.”

People Operations: “For the June and July schedule, the proposal is two later starts per week, with later finishes, and no leave?”

Tomasz: “Yes. No leave. If you cannot cover one of the delivery days, I am open to a discussion for that day. The request is temporary, and I can do my regular tasks.”

Yara: “I have the coverage sheet. I am still checking the two delivery dates and the handover. I have not approved all eight dates yet.”

Meeting note status: clarification only; not approval of schedule and not a payroll decision.

The meeting was held to check meaning, not to change the original request. It confirms that the employee does not ask to have the actual late entry erased. It also confirms that the future request remains pending and that the supervisor has not approved every date. A later clarification should be considered together with the original form, rather than replacing the parts that remain consistent.

RECEIVING COVERAGE DETAIL

The coverage sheet for Tuesday, 25 June, lists Leila Delgado at 08:00, Xiu Moreau at 08:00, and Yara Castillo as supervisor at 07:45. The delivery forecast shows one standard pallet scheduled between 08:00 and 08:30. A note from the receiving lead says the pallet can be checked by either of the two desk employees, but asks that the handover note be available before 08:30. The sheet does not specify that Tomasz personally must be present for that pallet.

The coverage sheet for Tuesday, 2 July, lists the same two desk employees at 08:00. The forecast shows no scheduled delivery before 08:30. The sheet includes a maintenance task at 08:15, assigned to the facilities team, not to Tomasz.

The coverage sheet for Thursday, 20 June, lists Bao Kaur and Xiu Moreau at 08:00, with Yara on site. There is a delivery forecast at 08:10. The receiving lead’s note says that one staff member can process a standard delivery while the other handles the desk. This is a plan, not proof that an unscheduled event cannot happen.

The sheet for Thursday, 27 June, lists Bao Kaur and Leila Delgado at 08:00. It shows no delivery appointment before 08:30. The sheet for Thursday, 4 July, lists Bao and Leila at 08:00 and a routine stock count. The count is assigned to the group, not to Tomasz alone.

The sheet for Tuesday, 9 July, lists Xiu Moreau and Leila Delgado at 08:00. A delivery forecast is present, and the receiving lead has not yet confirmed who will sign for it. The sheet for Thursday, 11 July, lists Bao Kaur and Xiu Moreau at 08:00 and no early delivery appointment. No entry on the sheet says that the proposed schedule has already been approved or denied.

The coverage detail supports asking the supervisor to assess the specific delivery mornings. It does not support saying that every requested morning is uncovered. It also does not support saying that each date is definitely covered without the manager’s final review. The operational material is included so that the question about request type is not confused with the separate question of approval.

EMAIL FROM PEOPLE OPERATIONS TO SUPERVISOR, 17 JUNE, 15:08

Subject: SO-HR-4187 — separate record correction and schedule review

Yara,

The available records support that Tomasz entered the building at approximately 08:04 on 12 June and worked that shift. Please arrange the attendance-record correction through the normal process so that the full-day absence is not retained as though no work occurred. Keep the 08:04 evidence and the original entry in the audit trail. Payroll can determine any treatment of the short late arrival; People Operations is not deciding that calculation in this note.

For the temporary schedule proposal, please review the listed dates, coverage, and handover. Tomasz has requested 08:30–17:00 on Tuesdays and Thursdays from 18 June through 11 July and says no leave is requested. This note does not approve the proposal. Please communicate which dates you can cover or what alternative you propose. Do not classify the request as leave unless Tomasz changes the request and asks for time away.

Regards,
People Operations specialist

The email is an instruction to complete a review and correction process. It does not say that the schedule is approved, and the phrase “please arrange” applies to the attendance correction, not to granting the future schedule. The email keeps the two issues distinct.

SUPERVISOR’S FINAL COVERAGE RESPONSE, 18 JUNE, 08:40

I reviewed the proposed dates. The coverage sheet confirms at least two other employees at the receiving desk before 08:30 on each of the requested mornings. For 25 June and 9 July, I asked the receiving lead to confirm who will handle the forecast delivery. The receiving lead confirmed that either Leila or Xiu can sign for the standard delivery and that Tomasz’s later handover note is workable. I approve the temporary 08:30–17:00 schedule on all eight requested dates, 18 June through 11 July, with the same scheduled hours and regular duties. This is my schedule decision. It is not leave, and it does not change Tomasz’s normal schedule outside the listed dates. If an unexpected coverage problem occurs, we will speak with Tomasz and document any specific adjustment.

This later response is the authorized supervisor’s completed decision. It supersedes the earlier statement that the request was pending. The initial queue reviewer’s recommendation to reject the request was made before reviewing the coverage materials and was not the supervisor’s decision. The supervisor’s final note records approval for all eight dates after checking the forecast delivery coverage.

FINAL ATTENDANCE CORRECTION ENTRY, 18 JUNE, 09:05

Original system entry: full-day absence, no clock events.
Verified records: reception sheet and access log support entry at approximately 08:04; supervisor confirms Tomasz worked the shift; stockroom activity is consistent with work during the day.
Corrected attendance description: entered after scheduled 08:00 start; worked shift, with arrival and hours supported by records.
Payroll review: referred separately; no pay calculation made in this entry.
Audit: original code retained; correction recorded with date and sources.

The correction does not claim an 08:00 arrival, does not erase the four-minute difference, and does not describe a full-day absence. The entry is based on the source records and the policy excerpt. The correction was made after the initial recommendation was flagged as unverified.

PORTAL STATUS HISTORY AFTER REVIEW

18 June, 09:05 — attendance row corrected, payroll review remains separate
18 June, 09:11 — temporary schedule request marked approved by Yara Castillo
18 June, 09:12 — ticket closed after two matters documented

The final status is later than the initial closure and does not make the first reviewer’s recommendation correct. The final status also does not mean that every proposal in the first submission was approved by People Operations: the attendance correction and schedule approval were recorded by their respective processes. The supervisor approved the schedule after considering coverage, and the attendance record was corrected after evidence was checked.

REFERENCE NOTES FOR FUTURE REVIEWERS

This packet is long because it preserves the web form, source records, preliminary opinions, policy excerpts, and the later completed actions in one place. The length is not a reason to treat the first visible summary as the whole case. The correct reading requires distinguishing the employee’s written statement from a drop-down label, a provisional recommendation from a finding, and a past record correction from a future schedule proposal.

For the past date, the employee’s own text states that he arrived after the scheduled start, asks for a record correction, and explicitly says he is not asking for the four minutes to be erased. The paper sheet and badge log agree on entry at about 08:04. The supervisor saw him working, and the work records provide further support. The full-day absence code is contradicted by those sources. The relevant policy says not to treat an unrecorded clock event as conclusive proof of absence and to distinguish a late arrival from a full-day absence when evidence supports work.

For the future dates, the employee describes a specific temporary schedule: later starts and later finishes on Tuesdays and Thursdays for four weeks. He says he will work the planned hours and does not request leave. The applicable guide says such a request is a temporary schedule proposal, not leave, where the employee remains at work for the planned hours. The proposal was initially pending because coverage required review. The supervisor later approved all eight dates after checking coverage. The initial reviewer’s contrary recommendation was not the final decision and was written before the attachments were opened.

For the labels in the portal, “absence/late entry” was a required subcategory and the portal summary used the word “absence.” Neither label overrides Tomasz’s written explanation. Similarly, “no action recommended” was the first reviewer’s unverified opinion, not a verified result. The support packet preserves that opinion as part of the audit trail so later reviewers can see it and compare it with the facts. The opinion is not made true merely by appearing first or in a highlighted panel.

A careful review should not infer that the employee sought leave from an absence code, should not infer that he entered at 08:00 when the evidence says 08:04, and should not infer that the schedule request was automatically approved before Yara’s final note. The correct outcome follows the documented records and the applicable policy, not the wording of a provisional verdict. This reminder is included because the ticket has several summary fields and preliminary comments that do not align with the underlying facts at the time they were written.

H. First queue reviewer recommendation and worksheet
I. People Operations clarification and review notes
J. Meeting notes of 17 June
K. Supervisor final coverage response of 18 June

- instruction length: long (30-80 words, with a sentence of context or a definition)
- domain: banking and card disputes
- genres to spread across the sources: policy page, forwarded email with a one-line cover note, customer chat transcript
- tone: non-native English
- instruction style for this batch: operational routing questions ('Should this go to the billing queue?')
- candidate-description style for this batch: full sentences with a definition

- multilabel: at least one question in the batch has 3-5 correct candidates

A request to repair, replace, credit a future invoice, or explain a charge is not by itself a refund request. Read the whole message, including its sender and any quoted text. A carrier's demand that the customer pay is not the customer's request for a refund. Q: Does the word refund decide the issue? A: No. The word may appear in a denial, a quotation, or a request for a different remedy. The original sender and the requested action matter. Q: Does a clerk's summary settle what was asked? A: No. Check the message and the referenced transaction. A summary is a routing aid, not the underlying evidence. If the customer expressly asks for a return of money, classify that as a refund request even if a clerk labels it an adjustment. If no such request appears, do not infer one merely from a complaint, a disputed invoice, or a credit memo. Q: What if the customer says it wants money back only if a future event occurs? A: Record the condition, but do not report an actual present refund request unless the customer also asks for the refund now. Q: What if the customer accepts repair instead? A: The final accepted remedy controls only for a question about the current request; preserve earlier messages where the question asks what was requested at an earlier date. Q: What if the accounts table has a negative line? A: Read the description and transaction status. A proposed credit is not proof that a customer requested cash back. [{"state":"SMS exchange, copied into Greta Novak’s booking file, with Greta’s permission. The trip is for a Copperleaf Software planning retreat, and the booking was made through a fictional travel desk called Juniper Lane Travel. The desk’s ordinary rule, included here because Greta asked about it, is that a traveler can request a refund only if the booking is refundable; a nonrefundable fare can instead be changed for a fee. Greta’s itinerary is for the fictional city of Bellwether Bay, leaving on October 18 and returning October 21. The thread is a little messy because Greta and the desk agent, Ivo, texted while both were moving between meetings. Messages are shown in order, with local times.

09:02 Greta: Hi, can you check the Bellwether booking? I have the confirmation open but I’m not sure which fare I picked. I was comparing two tabs while booking, one that said flexible and one that said saver. The confirmation says saver, I think. I’m asking because our retreat dates changed once already and I don’t want to assume I can get the money back if the new dates don’t work.

09:04 Ivo: I can look. Your booking reference is JL-5831, right? I see the outbound flight on the eighteenth and the return on the twenty-first. The confirmation attached to that reference lists the Saver fare. That fare is nonrefundable, but it can be changed if seats are available, subject to the change fee shown on the receipt. I’m not saying you should change it; just explaining the fare conditions.

09:06 Greta: Yes, JL-5831. I found the receipt too. It says $418 total for the ticket, and there’s another line for a seat selection. I don’t need the seat money back particularly, I just wondered about the ticket. Our office coordinator said “you can always cancel,” which sounded different from what you just said.

09:08 Ivo: “Cancel” and “get a refund” are not the same thing under this fare. You may cancel the reservation, but the ticket price isn’t refundable. The receipt’s seat-selection amount is listed separately as $24. The receipt says that seat selection is also nonrefundable. I can send the fare conditions again if useful.

09:10 Greta: Please. Also, there is a note on our shared travel sheet that says, “Refund approved; customer asked for refund.” I didn’t write that, so I’m trying to work out what it refers to. Could be someone copied the wrong row. I have not asked your desk for a refund so far; this text is me checking what the policy says.

09:12 Ivo: I see that note in the file. It was added yesterday by a person in our office, not by the airline. I can’t treat it as approval. My booking screen says no refund request has been submitted for JL-5831. To be clear, that note doesn’t change the fare conditions or create a refund request on your behalf.

09:14 Greta: Good, thanks. I’m going to ask a couple of very literal questions because the travel sheet is getting passed around. Did I ask for a refund in this exchange? I’m not asking you to submit anything, and I’m not asking whether I’m allowed to request one. Just whether I actually asked for one.

09:16 Ivo: In the messages so far, no. You asked about the fare and about whether money could be returned. Asking about a policy isn’t the same as requesting that I process a refund. You haven’t told me to cancel the booking or asked me to submit a refund request.

09:18 Greta: That matches what I thought. The sheet also has a comment, “Traveler explicitly requested full refund at 09:10.” That is not what I said. I asked about the note, and I said I hadn’t asked your desk for a refund. Please leave the booking active while I sort out whether the new retreat dates are final.

09:21 Ivo: Understood. Booking remains active. I’ll mark that the 09:10 comment is inconsistent with the messages, and I won’t cancel or file anything. Just so the file doesn’t get more confusing, the question about getting money back doesn’t count as a request to refund the ticket.

09:27 Greta: Thanks. I should say the retreat dates might move again, but that is only a possibility. If the dates change, I may ask whether a change is possible. I haven’t decided to change it, and I’m not asking for a refund now.

09:29 Ivo: Noted. Your ticket remains as booked. I’ll put the fare conditions and your clarification in the message history. The only request I have from you at this point is to keep the reservation active and clarify what the existing note means.

09:33 Greta: One more thing: a colleague saw the words “refund approved” in the travel sheet and told our manager the airline had already agreed to pay us. That would be lovely, but it isn’t true. Can you confirm there’s no approval from the airline in the actual booking record?

09:36 Ivo: Correct. There is no refund approval from the airline in the booking record. The words on the sheet are a staff comment, not an airline decision. It doesn’t match the fare terms or the booking screen. The record still shows a nonrefundable Saver ticket and no request submitted.

09:40 Greta: Great. I’ll let the coordinator know. I’m trying not to turn an inquiry into an instruction accidentally. For the record, I’m not telling you to cancel, I’m not asking you to return the ticket cost, and I’m not authorizing a change. I just wanted the file checked.

09:42 Ivo: Understood. I haven’t made any change. The reservation is active and unchanged.

10:03 Greta: I looked again at the shared sheet. There’s another line with a different reference, JL-5837, and a note saying that traveler requested a refund. That’s not mine. My reference ends 31. Please don’t merge the two rows just because they’re in the same retreat folder.

10:05 Ivo: Thanks, I’ll keep them separate. JL-5837 belongs to a different booking. For JL-5831, the messages and record show no refund request. I’ll avoid copying the note across.

10:11 Greta: This is probably overkill, but my manager will ask what we know. I said I might need to change dates if the retreat changes, and I asked whether the fare allows money back. Neither statement means I actually requested money back. If the dates stay as they are, I’m happy to travel as booked.

10:14 Ivo: That’s a fair summary. I’ve recorded it as an inquiry about the fare conditions, not a refund request. Your reservation is unchanged. If later you decide to submit a request, you can tell us explicitly, though this fare’s terms say the ticket is not refundable.

10:20 Greta: Thanks, I’m done for now. Please don’t interpret “I’m done” as canceling the trip; I mean done texting about it.

10:22 Ivo: Understood. No cancellation or refund request has been entered.

10:31 Greta: I found the original confirmation email. It has the words “refundability: no” and “changes: permitted with fee.” So your reading is consistent. There is still no reason to do anything with the reservation.

10:34 Ivo: Yes, that matches the record. The travel sheet’s approval line is the only item that conflicts with the booking details and this conversation. I’ll leave a note that it is not supported by the source record.

10:40 Greta: My colleague says maybe the sentence “I wondered about the ticket” counts as asking for a refund because I was asking about money. I think that’s stretching it. I didn’t ask you to pay anything back; I asked what the fare does.

10:43 Ivo: I agree with your distinction. You asked for information about the refund rule, not for the desk to process a refund. A request for information is not a request to return the ticket price.

10:51 Greta: Perfect. I’ve copied this conversation to our coordinator so nobody mistakes the note for a real approval. I’ll follow up only if I decide I need a change, which I haven’t.

10:54 Ivo: Received. No further action taken.

11:06 Greta: For completeness, if I later send “please request a refund,” that would be different from what I’ve said here. I’m not sending that message now. This is just an example of wording I could use if I ever did want to ask.

11:09 Ivo: Correct. No such request has been received in this thread. The example wording is hypothetical and does not change the current booking.

11:15 Greta: Okay. I’m going to stop rereading this now. Thanks for being patient with all the caveats.

11:17 Ivo: Happy to help. I’m leaving the ticket as it is.

File annotations appended by Juniper Lane Travel: The analyst who reviewed the shared sheet wrote, “Refund approved, traveler asked at 09:10.” That assessment is not reliable. At 09:10 Greta said she had not asked the desk for a refund so far and asked what a note meant. The booking record contains no submitted refund request and no airline approval. The note appears to have been copied from another row, although the exact origin is unknown. A separate booking reference, JL-5837, appears in the same folder, but no details for that traveler are included here. The source messages establish only that Greta inquired about fare conditions, asked that the booking remain active, and explicitly distinguished an inquiry from an instruction. The traveler did not request a refund in the exchange. The booking’s nonrefundable condition is not needed to infer whether she asked; it is included to explain why she was asking questions. Do not interpret questions about eligibility as requests to process anything. Do not interpret a possible future date change as an actual change. Do not interpret the words “refund approved” in the staff note as an airline decision. The booking record and the messages are the evidence for the questions below.","questions":[{"type":"binary","instruction":"The customer asked for a refund.","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"The shared-sheet verdict claims a request, but Greta asks about policy and explicitly says she has not requested a refund."},{"type":"binary","instruction":"The airline approved a refund.","target":false,"hard_cases":["planted_verdict"],"notes":"The planted “refund approved” note is contradicted by Ivo’s booking-record check: no airline approval exists."}]},{"state":"Forwarded email, cover note: Uma Iyer forwarded this thread to the Northwind Health travel coordinator with the note, “Could you check what actually happened? The summary in the file may be off.” The following is the full thread as exported from the fictional booking desk’s mail system. It concerns a work trip booked through Lantern Route Travel for the fictional city of Mossbridge. The travel desk’s quoted policy says that a traveler who asks the desk to cancel a ticket has made a cancellation request; an inquiry about possible options is not a request to cancel. A booking can also be canceled by an administrator, but that does not mean the traveler asked for it. The policy is included to clarify the distinction and is not a rule about whether a request is approved.

From: Uma Iyer <uma@northwind.example>
To: Lantern Route Travel Desk <help@lantern.example>
Date: Monday, May 6, 08:12
Subject: Mossbridge itinerary question

Hi there, I’m checking the trip for the Northwind Health workshop. I have the itinerary in front of me, but our workshop organizer is still deciding whether the sessions will start on the morning of May 20 or the afternoon. Could you tell me what the options are if we need to move the outbound flight? I am not asking you to change or cancel anything at this point. I just want to know whether there are seats later in the day and what the fee might be. The reservation code is LR-2049, and it is currently booked for May 19 through May 22. Please keep it as it is while I find out the final meeting schedule.

From: Dalen, Lantern Route Travel Desk <help@lantern.example>
To: Uma Iyer <uma@northwind.example>
Date: Monday, May 6, 08:31

[{"state":"A very polite customer review and account correspondence packet for Saltmarsh Health

Document control
Prepared with thanks for the careful attention of the accounts team. This packet gathers a customer’s product review, the invoice record attached to it, and the relevant policy-page extract. The material is provided so that colleagues can understand the customer’s comments and the status of the associated payment without needing to consult another file. Please treat every statement below as part of this packet, including the review, the accounting entries, the policy text, and the courteous internal comments. The customer’s product is the Willow Bay desk lamp, supplied by Saltmarsh Health’s small workplace-goods division. The customer is Uma Rahman, who ordered two lamps and one replacement shade for an office reception room. All amounts in the invoice register are in dollars. The entries are copied as recorded; no additional tax calculation or external rule is needed to read them.

Product review, received Tuesday
Dear Saltmarsh Health team, thank you very much for sending the lamps so promptly. They look handsome on the reception counter, and I am grateful for the care taken in wrapping them. The shades are an especially pleasant colour, and the instructions were mercifully clear. I am pleased to say that both lamps work properly. The order arrived in good condition, the box was not crushed, and nothing was missing. I am not writing to ask for a refund, and I do not wish to return either lamp. I would simply like to let future purchasers know that the finish is a little more matte than the photograph suggests. That is a small observation rather than a complaint. I hope it is useful, and please accept my thanks for your help.

Review page moderation card
Item reviewed: Willow Bay desk lamp.
Customer name: Uma Rahman.
Date posted: Tuesday, 14 May.
Rating selected by customer: four stars out of five.
Review text received: the complete text is reproduced above.
Order reference: SH-4418.
Customer selected the page topic “appearance and finish.”
Customer did not select “billing problem,” “return,” or “refund request.”
Moderation status: published.

Internal review handling note
A reviewer has left the following conclusion in the moderation system: “Customer is dissatisfied with the lamps and wants the purchase price refunded.” This conclusion is not a quotation from Uma Rahman and is not supported by the review text. The reviewer appears to have treated the phrase about the finish as evidence of a billing complaint. The customer’s own wording is available above in full. No refund request was entered into the service queue. The note remains visible because the moderation form preserves comments even when the reviewer’s conclusion is mistaken. To avoid confusion, the account record below should be used for payment facts, while the review itself should be used for the customer’s stated request.

Order and invoice register
Order reference SH-4418 was created on 2 May. Two Willow Bay desk lamps were listed at $48 each, and one replacement shade was listed at $12. The invoice total was $108. Payment of $108 was received on 3 May and allocated to invoice SH-4418 on the same day. The ledger currently shows a zero balance due. There is no credit memo and no refund transaction. A note entered by a clerk says, “Refund still owed because customer disliked colour.” The note is an unsupported conclusion; it does not alter the allocation or the transaction entries. The transaction history shows the customer paid the invoiced amount, and the company has not issued any money back. This section is included to distinguish a customer’s product comments from the separate question of what the ledger records.

Invoice detail copied from the billing screen
Invoice: SH-4418.
Customer: Uma Rahman.
Order date: 2 May.
Invoice date: 2 May.
Item one: Willow Bay desk lamp, quantity two, unit price $48, extended amount $96.
Item two: replacement shade, quantity one, unit price $12, extended amount $12.
Invoice total: $108.
Payment recorded: $108 on 3 May.
Open amount: $0.
Credits applied: $0.
Refunds issued: $0.
The billing screen includes a free-text staff remark: “Balance is overdue; kindly pursue payment.” The remark is inconsistent with the amount fields shown immediately above it. The invoice was paid in full, and the screen’s open amount is zero. The remark is retained here as an example of a conclusion that should not be treated as a transaction.

Customer service correspondence
On 14 May, Uma wrote: “Thank you for the lovely service. The lamps are working well. The shade is a little darker than the listing photo, but that is not a serious issue. I am not requesting any money back. I wanted to share the observation politely.” A service agent replied: “Thank you very much for letting us know. We are grateful for your thoughtful review and are pleased that the lamps are working well.” The agent did not offer a refund and did not say that one had been requested. A later supervisor entry read: “Please mark refund requested; this is standard whenever someone mentions a colour difference.” That supervisor instruction is a description of a mistaken local practice, not a statement by the customer. The customer’s direct message above remains clear.

Policy page extract: reviews and billing enquiries
We are pleased to provide the following guidance in a courteous and transparent manner. A product review is a customer’s description of their experience with a product. A mention of appearance, packaging, delivery, or general satisfaction does not by itself count as a request to return goods or receive money. A refund request exists when the customer clearly asks the company to send money back, reverse a payment, or otherwise reimburse the purchase. A question about whether a refund might be possible is an enquiry, not necessarily a request to issue one. Staff should preserve the customer’s wording and should not convert a neutral observation into a request.

For invoice status, staff should consult the posted payment and credit entries. A written label such as “unpaid,” “overdue,” or “refund due” does not replace the actual amounts and allocations. If the payment allocated equals the invoice total and the open amount is zero, the invoice is settled unless a later transaction changes that status. If a credit or refund is issued, it must appear as a transaction. A reviewer’s interpretation is not itself a ledger event. We ask colleagues to be especially careful when transferring notes between the review page and accounts payable, since those systems have separate purposes and may contain comments entered by people who have not checked the underlying record.

The policy is intended to be read with its examples. A customer who says “The blue finish is darker than expected” has supplied feedback but has not necessarily asked for money. A customer who says “Please return the $40 I paid” has made a clear request for reimbursement. A clerk who writes “refund due” has not established that the customer asked for one or that the company issued one. The exact text and the transaction record should be respected. We appreciate the care taken by staff in using these distinctions.

Review workflow appendix
When an online review is received, the moderation form records the product, date, rating, and topics chosen by the customer. The topics are supplied by the customer, not inferred automatically from keywords. A reviewer can add a comment, but a comment does not amend what the customer selected. If a review includes a product observation and no explicit request for money, the customer-service queue may respond with thanks or ask a follow-up question. It should not automatically create a refund case. If the customer later sends a clear request, the new message should be recorded separately with its own date and wording.

In this case, the review page records “appearance and finish.” There is no billing topic selected. The review says both lamps work properly, states that the order arrived in good condition, and expressly says the writer is not asking for a refund or return. A moderation comment alleging dissatisfaction and a refund request has no evidentiary force against those direct statements. This appendix repeats the relevant facts because the review packet is sometimes exported without the ledger page. We are grateful to anyone who takes the time to compare the customer’s own text with the internal summaries.

Accounts payable reconciliation appendix
The invoice register is generated from item quantities and prices. Two lamps at $48 each produce $96, and the shade at $12 makes the invoice total $108. The payment record is $108, dated 3 May, and its allocation points to SH-4418. The open amount is therefore displayed as $0. A staff remark saying that the balance is overdue does not correspond to the posted transaction data. The refund field is also $0, so no reimbursement has been recorded. These statements are copied directly from the screen and are not a recommendation about what the company ought to do.

The reconciliation process asks the clerk to compare invoice total, payment received, amount allocated, and remaining balance. A note in the comment field may be helpful when it accurately explains a transaction, but it should not be used to infer a transaction that is absent. Here, the only payment entry equals the invoice total; no credit or refund appears. The supervisor’s message about marking every colour observation as a refund request is not a policy rule and is contradicted by the policy page above. It is also contradicted by Uma’s explicit wording. The correct handling is to retain the review as product feedback and leave the account settled.

Additional customer review context
Uma has previously reviewed office supplies from other sellers, but those unrelated reviews are not part of this order. The packet contains no statement that she reported a defective switch, missing component, late delivery, or damaged package. The only product observation in her review concerns the shade’s appearance in comparison with the listing photograph. She says the difference is not serious and that both lamps work properly. Her courteous opening and closing do not obscure the substance of the message. A reader should not infer an unstated billing request from her use of polite language or from the fact that the company has a refund policy.

A staff member suggested that the customer’s four-star rating might itself imply a wish for compensation. The rating is a rating, not a request. Another staff member suggested that the phrase “little more matte” could be coded as “not as described” and therefore trigger an automatic payment return. The policy page does not say that; it says staff should preserve the distinction between feedback and an explicit request for reimbursement. Both suggestions are recorded here solely to explain why inaccurate internal conclusions may appear alongside the source material.

Polite response template supplied with the packet
Dear Uma, thank you very much for taking the time to share your kind review. We are glad that the lamps are working well and appreciate your helpful observation about the finish. We have noted your comments for our product team. We understand from your message that you are not requesting a refund or a return, and no such request has been entered. If you would like to discuss anything further, please let us know and we will be pleased to assist. With thanks, Saltmarsh Health customer care.

The template was drafted after the review and reflects the customer’s actual statement. It was not sent as a substitute for the original message. A separate draft in the account system says: “We are sorry the lamps failed; your refund has been approved.” That draft was created by a staff member who had not read the full review. It was never sent, no refund was approved, and the product record does not show a failure. The existence of a draft should not be mistaken for an action or for the customer’s request.

Cross-system notes
The product page displays the review as written. The service queue displays the customer’s message and the agent’s courteous acknowledgement. The accounts ledger displays invoice SH-4418, its payment, and its zero balance. The moderation system displays the reviewer’s erroneous verdict. These systems do not all have equal relevance to every question. For whether the customer asked for money back, her review and service message are directly relevant. For whether the invoice remains unpaid, the ledger entries are relevant. A conclusion in a free-text note is not a replacement for the underlying evidence. We ask readers to make decisions from the stated facts with care and kindness.

Closing note
Thank you for reviewing this packet. Uma’s review is positive overall, includes one mild observation about the finish, and expressly declines a refund or return. The invoice was paid in full and shows no outstanding amount or refund transaction. The internal verdicts stating that she requested money or that a balance remains due are contradicted by the source text and posted figures. We are pleased to explain our handling of customer messages. A customer may ask whether a payment has been received, whether it has been assigned to the correct invoice, or what balance remains. These are account-status questions and should be answered using the ledger. They do not, by themselves, ask the company to send money back. Where the customer expressly says that no refund is wanted, staff should record that statement accurately.

Internal annotations and staff conclusions are not customer instructions. If a note says “refund requested” but the customer’s own words say otherwise, the customer’s words control whether a request was made. If a note says that a payment is unmatched but the allocation fields show a full match, the transaction fields should be checked before deciding the balance. We kindly ask staff to avoid turning a simple question into an assumed demand. A reimbursement is not complete unless the relevant credit or refund transaction is recorded.

Customer: “Could you please tell me whether the $80 payment reached invoice A?” Agent: “Yes, it is allocated, and the balance is zero.” This exchange is an enquiry about allocation, not a request for reimbursement. Supplier: Larkspur Outfitters.

Larkspur Outfitters aims to respond graciously to every account enquiry. Staff may thank a customer for checking a payment, explain a balance, and offer a statement copy. A message should not be classified as a refund request merely because it contains words such as “payment,” “invoice,” or “balance.” The act requested matters. The supervisor’s note says “overpaid by $24,” but the arithmetic and account fields show equal amounts. A conclusion written in a comment field is not evidence of a transaction, an unpaid amount, or a customer’s intention. We appreciate your care in reading each source in its proper context.

Internal review log
10:20, accounts agent: Payment allocation checked; invoice settled.
10:26, queue assistant: Customer must want cash back because she asked about payment. Suggested classification: refund request.
10:31, accounts agent: Reviewed complete SMS; customer says no refund is sought. Classification returned to account-status enquiry.

The log is included as an administrative history, not as a replacement for the original words. The payment is settled whether or not a comment was once added to the queue.

Dear Esi, with many thanks for checking with us, we confirm that your payment has been received and applied to invoice LO-7821. The account is fully settled, and we have not issued or scheduled a refund. We understand that you were seeking confirmation only, and we are grateful for the opportunity to clarify this. Please accept our thanks for your courteous note.

Policy examples and clarifications
If a customer writes, “Has my transfer been matched to the bill?”, staff should check the allocation. If the customer writes, “I paid twice; please return one payment,” that is a request for repayment, subject to verification. If an employee writes “customer wants money back” without a customer statement supporting it, the employee’s words remain an internal assertion. Where the records show that one payment equals the invoice, that fact should be reported as it stands. We are pleased to remind colleagues that courtesy and accuracy are mutually supportive.

[{"state":"Foxglove Labs claims intake transcript and attached review packet

File reference: FL-8041. The packet was assembled for the insurer's claim review meeting. It includes the complete customer chat, intake fields, a short policy summary supplied by the insurer, and internal handling notes. Times are local office time. Names in the file are fictional. The claim concerns water in a rented workroom used by Foxglove Labs. No one disputes that water was present; the question is how it entered and what property was affected.

CHAT TRANSCRIPT, Monday 8 April

09:02 Intake bot: Welcome. Please describe what happened and when you first noticed it. If you have pictures, please send them after the chat. Do not send bank passwords or payment card details.

09:04 Esi Novak: I came in at 07:40 today. There was water under the back wall, near the shelves. I thought first the roof, because rain was hard in night. But the ceiling paper is dry and the wall is wet from bottom upward. I closed the little storage door and called building manager.

09:06 Intake bot: Was there a storm, a leak, a pipe problem, or another event? Please say what you observed, not only what you suspect.

09:09 Esi Novak: Rain started around 22:00 yesterday, heavy until after midnight. At around 08:00 today I saw a thin muddy line coming from below the rear wall. The room is below street level, maybe 40 centimetres. The drain outside was full of leaves. I did not see a pipe break. The sink and radiator are dry. Water was not falling from ceiling.

09:12 Intake bot: Any injury, electrical issue, or evacuation?

09:13 Esi Novak: No injury. I switched the power strip off before touching it. We moved the boxes to the front room. Nobody was staying overnight.

09:15 Intake bot: What property may be affected?

09:17 Esi Novak: Two Foxglove testing laptops, one portable monitor, paper samples, and some packing cartons. The laptops were on the bottom shelf but not under water. Their cases have moisture at the ports. The paper samples are wet at the lower corner. I cannot tell yet if equipment works. We do not claim the whole office, only these things and drying service if needed.

09:19 Intake bot: Please provide approximate values and ownership. Estimates are acceptable; receipts can follow.

09:23 Esi Novak: Laptop A bought used for $1,180, Laptop B $960, monitor $240. They belong to Foxglove, not me. Samples maybe $380 to remake. Cartons maybe $45. We have not had a repair person inspect. A neighbor told me this happened in the block last year, but I don't know if that matters.

09:25 Intake bot: Did anyone advise you to discard property or begin repairs?
